synopsis: EMB145 flight crew reports getting well off track flying the DIXXY 6 departure from ROA. The crew set the depicted course of 252 degrees to fly the back course LOC departure.
summary: The crew flying a pilot NAV departure on the DIXXY SIX procedure deviated 5 miles left of course due to suspected reverse sensing on the EHSI while tracking the LOC. ATC vectored them right to DILNN after the deviation was detected at 4,000 feet.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: MD83 Captain questions MEL 78-1 which was applied to his aircraft by locking out the right thrust reverser and tying down the reverse lever. He believes a performance decrement should have been taken due to no RTO function.
summary: The flight crew operated an MD8x with a tied-down right thrust reverser under MEL 78-1, potentially taking off overweight due to conflicting manual guidance on performance penalties. Maintenance Control confirmed the lever should not have been tied down and agreed to correct the MEL documentation to clarify auto-spoiler and weight reduction requirements.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew experiences stuck flaps during approach when the flap lever is first selected from 25 to 30 then quickly retracted to 25 then 15 as a wind gust threatens to overspeed the flaps when the flaps cannot be extended, bug speeds are adjusted and a flaps 15 landing ensues. Flaps retract normally after landing.
summary: During an ILS 09 approach to MIA at 1,400 feet, the crew experienced a 30-knot airspeed increase when extending flaps to 30 degrees. They retracted flaps to 15 degrees, inhibited the low flap warning, and completed a normal landing with flaps stuck at 15 degrees until retraction after clearing the runway.

synopsis: CRJ200 First Officer reports a runaway rudder trim climbing to FL220. The aircraft rolls 25 degrees to the right before control is regained and the trim is centered. The flight continues to destination landing uneventfully. Maintenance attempts to blame the autopilot and defers it. The crew realizes that the autopilot has no inputs to the rudder trim and refuses the aircraft. Later Maintenance discovers frayed rudder trim wiring which caused the anomaly.
summary: The crew encountered a runaway rudder trim to full right deflection at altitude, causing a 25-30 degree bank, but regained control and landed safely. Maintenance Control incorrectly deferred the autopilot based on the report, but the crew refused the aircraft until a frayed wire in the rudder trim panel was replaced.

synopsis: A Captain and First Officer report about the loss of effective braking on landing in their CRJ-200 aircraft. The left and right inboard main tires were found blown and the outboard main tires had deep bald spots. No EICAS messages or fault indications were displayed in the flight deck, only a rising temperature for the left outboard brake.
summary: The First Officer and Captain experienced a complete loss of braking and three blown tires immediately after touchdown due to locked brakes. They used full reverse thrust to stop, diverted to a holding area for safety, and were towed to the gate after passengers were bussed to the terminal.

synopsis: ERJ170 Captain reports rejecting a takeoff at 80 KTS when IDG 2 OIL LOW EICAS immediately followed by GEN 2 OFF BUS EICAS Messages appear.
summary: The Captain rejected takeoff at 80 KTS after IDG 2 OIL LOW and GEN 2 OFF BUS EICAS messages appeared. The aircraft returned to the gate for a swap, departing 2.5 hours late, with no maintenance cause identified despite recent servicing.

synopsis: DHC100 flight crew detects strange elevator response during takeoff and initial climb. The crew elects to return to the departure airport where maintenance discovers the autopilot elevator servo is partially jammed. Tail winds during the elevator check prior to takeoff apparently masked the condition.
summary: The First Officer reported elevator heaviness and a 3-5 second response delay during takeoff and landing flare, causing pitch oscillations. The crew returned to the airport for a firm landing; the flight was canceled after maintenance found a partially jammed autopilot elevator servo.

synopsis: A DHC-8-200 Captain rejected the first takeoff of the day because the Autofeather System did not arm even after it checked satisfactorily during the pre takeoff runup. The flight was canceled.
summary: The Captain and First Officer aborted takeoff on a first flight of the day when the Autofeather System failed to arm during the roll. The flight was canceled after maintenance could not reset the system, forcing the crew to return to the gate and deplane passengers.

synopsis: MD11 Captain reports requesting Runway 7L at LAX for landing and being assigned Runway 6R. The Runway 7L ILS is placed in the FMC in the secondary flight plan. Twenty NM west of LAX, the approach is changed to ILS Runway 7R but the First Officer is unable to activate the secondary plan in a timely manner and the flight is vectored around for another attempt. With more time the First Officer is successful.
summary: During the approach phase, the Captain and First Officer accepted a late runway change from 06R to 07L but initially failed to load the new ILS into the FMS. The crew requested vectors for a re-entry, which provided sufficient time to complete the programming, resulting in an uneventful landing despite the time pressure.

synopsis: B757-200 First Officer reports a right generator failure at 110 KTS during takeoff with the right AC bus remaining unpowered and isolated. Once safely airborne, the right generator is restored using the QRH to reset the generator, which restores power to the right AC bus. The crew elects not to cycle the bus tie switch to resume normal bus tie operation, but does elect to divert to an airport near the destination with a longer runway.
summary: During takeoff at 110 KTS, the right generator failed, unpowering the right AC bus. The crew continued the flight, restored power via the QRH, and landed at an alternate airport with longer runways to mitigate risks if the generator failed again during landing.

synopsis: An unidentified air carrier aircraft suffered the failure of the Left IDG. They disconnected the drive, started the APU and continued to their destination.
summary: During climb, the left IDG failed, causing loss of the left generator. The pilot not flying executed checklists, disconnected the drive, and started the APU; with sufficient fuel at the ETP, the flight continued uneventfully to the West Coast.

synopsis: B757 First Officer reports a right engine high stage light after V1. The right-hand bleed valve is turned off in compliance with the QRH, but some bleed pressure remains and the crew elects to return to the departure airport.
summary: The pilot experienced a right engine high stage bleed light during takeoff on a Boeing 757, which persisted after turning the switch off. The aircraft returned for an overweight landing, and maintenance revealed the right engine had been replaced the previous night without a required high-power run.

synopsis: EMB145 Captain experiences a PTRIM MAIN INOP EICAS message climbing out of 10,000 FT. The QRH is consulted and the Main Pitch Trim cutout button is pressed. The QRH also states to continue the flight, but the Captain elects to return to the departure airport.
summary: The flight crew experienced a PTRIM MAIN INOP EICAS warning while climbing through 10,000 feet after departing for ZZZ1. Following procedures to cut out the main pitch trim, the pilot elected to return to ZZZ due to weather between the departure and destination airports.

synopsis: A CRJ-200 flight crew, faced with an unresponsive right engine thrust lever, shut the engine down, declared an emergency, and diverted to an airport with longer runways and better facilities for CFR, maintenance, and passenger handling.
summary: During initial descent, the First Officer reported the right engine became unresponsive at 92% N1, prompting a diversion to ZZZ for a single-engine landing. The crew executed the Jammed Thrust Lever checklist, shut down the engine, and landed safely on the 10,000-foot runway.

synopsis: Preoccupied with abnormal procedures generated by a bleed air duct temperature warning, the Flight Crew of a CRJ-200 failed to broadcast the alert to the Flight Attendants as they passed through 10,000 FT MSL as required by their company SOP.
summary: The flight crew managed a 14th stage bleed air duct warning and declared an emergency, landing with the left engine at idle. Due to task saturation during the abnormal event, they omitted the cabin signal for descent through 10,000 feet, a step the crew suggests reinstating in the checklist.

synopsis: Fatigued from a long duty day, lengthened by operational delays and being dispatched with a right thrust reverser deferred inoperative, a CRJ-200 Captain inadvertently shut down the left engine instead of reversing 'only' the left engine he intended. Both pilots reported significant fatigue which affected their performance.
summary: A fatigued flight crew on a multi-leg pairing mistakenly shut down the left engine at 90 KTS during landing instead of deploying the thrust reverser. The pilot attributed this error to exhaustion caused by excessive duty hours and insufficient rest, though the aircraft was safely stopped using normal braking.

synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew enroute to ZGGG describes ATC delays due to weather and traffic, resulting in a declaration of minimum fuel. This information is difficult to convey to the Controller, but eventually results in a clearance direct.
summary: The flight crew reported minimum fuel to Guangzhou Control while orbiting 500 miles from ZGGG due to ATC-imposed delays and speed restrictions. The controller subsequently cleared the aircraft direct to BSE at normal speed, allowing an uneventful arrival despite the fuel concern.

synopsis: A B737-700 Captain provided a detailed description of the debilitating effects of flight pairing reassignments and delays encountered on flight crew's ability to perform effectively. Also provided examples of ATC disfunctionalitly he believes may be exacaerbated by similar fatigue inducing scheduling practices.
summary: Flight crews experienced scheduling delays, maintenance issues, and lost communications with a slow-responding Center Controller while descending to 2,000 feet. The crew eventually re-established contact, landed safely despite inaccurate ATIS, and attributed the chain of events to fatigue, poor coordination, and inadequate maintenance communication.

aircraft: Airbus Industrie Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: A Line Technician reports that an Airbus aircraft returned to gate after he had replaced hi-speed fan blower for popping the vent blower extract fan circuit breaker. The vent blower fan had been on MEL deferral.
summary: A mechanic troubleshooting an Airbus avionics cooling fan circuit breaker at the gate replaced the blower and assumed both fans worked based on flow bar indications. The error occurred because the mechanic did not wait for the low-speed warning or reverse the MEL procedure, leading to a gate turnback.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic describes his efforts to accomplish an Engineering Order and Fleet Campaign Directive (FCD) to untie, reroute and use filler material for a Right Recirculation Fan Wiring bundle. A Line Inspector also notes the confusion involving the use of Guideline tape in the FCD to secure the wire bundles.
summary: An AMT and Inspector on a B757-200 used guideline tape to secure a recirc fan wire bundle because provided filler material was insufficient, violating a later Engineering Order revision. The outcome was a rejected repair, teaching the reporter to stop work if required materials are unavailable rather than deviating from directives.

synopsis: A Mechanic reports he jacked the fuselage nose of a company CRJ aircraft in their hangar to level the airplane after noticing the aircraft in a slightly nose down attitude. Than he realized the tail stand was still installed.
summary: A mechanic performing a gear door task on a jacked CRJ-700/900 noticed tail dents after briefly leveling the aircraft with the tail stand installed. Although the mechanic suspected causing the damage, dirt on the dents suggested they were pre-existing, leading to a deferral and a recommendation for improved jacking procedures.

synopsis: When the engine failed to start, the pilot of a BE-36 exited to turn the prop through and failed to turn off the magnetos. The engine started and the uncontrolled airplane taxied into another aircraft.
summary: The pilot reported that while pre-flighting a Bonanza, the engine unexpectedly fired during a slow prop turn, causing the aircraft to taxi into a Beech Sierra 200. The pilot could not shut down the engine, and authorities were notified.

synopsis: Two training flights, a C172 and a PA28 suffered an NMAC while maneuvering on the course reversal for the same practice GPS at a non-towered airport. The C172 was utilizing the correct CTAF frequency, but the PA28 was utilizing an incorrect frequency for a different airport.
summary: A pilot and student on a practice GPS 21 approach at EYE encountered another aircraft on the same approach while monitoring CTAF. The other pilot, tuned to a nearby frequency, dove to avoid a collision, leading the reporter to suggest radar advisories from IND Approach could have prevented the incident.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: A general aviation pilot reports inadvertently entering a TFR and landing at the nearest airport when a call is heard on guard frequency. An iPad with Foreflight application was used for planning and enroute navigation, but TFR did not appear.
summary: The pilot inadvertently violated a TFR while flying VFR under clouds on a regular route because Foreflight did not display the restriction. After hearing a garbled violation call on guard frequency, the pilot diverted and landed safely at the nearest airport.

synopsis: A C210 pilot was unable to obtain a green landing gear safe light after repeated cycles. Upon landing the right main gear slowly collapsed resulting in a runway excursion and minor damage to the aircraft.
summary: The pilot landed an aircraft with a faulty right gear indicator light after visual confirmation from the tower. Despite the gear appearing down, the right gear collapsed on touchdown, causing the airplane to veer off the runway with minor damage to the elevator and tire.

synopsis: Required to extend his downwind pattern leg due to preceding traffic, the pilot of a J3 Cub failed to employ carburetor heat at his usual point abeam the numbers. The engine subsequently failed to respond to the throttle on short final and the pilot diverted to a gravel area short of the runway. Some damage was incurred due to contact with power lines.
summary: The pilot of a training aircraft experienced a total power loss on final approach while following a Cessna 150, likely due to carburetor ice from idle power. The pilot executed an off-field landing in a gravel lot, sustaining minor propeller and wing tip damage from power lines but avoiding injuries.

synopsis: A C152 on a maintenance test flight suffered fluctuating RPMs, declared an emergency and landed safely.
summary: A pilot conducting a maintenance test flight experienced engine RPM fluctuations that worsened from 50 to 250 RPM during the approach phase. After declaring an emergency and receiving clearance to spiral south, the pilot landed safely with power and carb heat applied, attributing the issue to previous spark plug carbon buildup.

synopsis: The pilot of a Stearman believed the lack of recent landing experience and the obstruction of vision due to a front seat passenger contributed to his loss of control, runway excursion and collision with a landing light after touch down.
summary: The pilot of a Stearman with a front-seat passenger veered off the runway onto grass during rollout, damaging the wing on a light. The pilot attributed the incident to minimal recent practice, delayed control inputs, and indecision about executing a go-around.

synopsis: An FBO Mechanic reports a left Main Landing Gear (MLG) tire and wheel assembly had separated from a SportStar Evektor aircraft on takeoff, two days after he had completed a 100-hour Inspection.
summary: A mechanic performing a 100-hour inspection on a SportStar Evektor installed an incorrect cotter pin due to rushing, causing the left wheel to detach during a touch-and-go. The incident resulted in minor aircraft damage but no injuries, prompting the mechanic to acknowledge the error and commit to double-checking work.

synopsis: A BE35 pilot descended to 1,500 FT before crossing the initial approach fix 2,500 FT constraint because he was using the autopilot Vertical Speed mode while managing the landing gear and monitoring LOC capture, but with glideslope capture not armed.
summary: The pilot descended below the assigned 2,500 FT while intercepting the ILS 33 approach, mistakenly believing the autopilot had captured the glide slope after engaging NAV. The pilot manually recovered after an altitude alert at 1,500 FT, attributing the error to confusing localizer capture with glide slope engagement.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A corporate jet which departed GEU Northwest bound took last second evasive action during a near miss with ATC reported but unseen TCAS traffic at about 3,000 FT.
summary: The crew of a departing aircraft from GEU received a TCAS RA while being vectored toward VFR traffic by Luke AFB Departure. The pilot executed an abrupt descent to avoid the conflict, which occurred because ATC was unaware of the uncontacted VFR aircraft.

synopsis: Tower Controller described the handling of an emergency aircraft and the current equipment and Tower space restrictions that hampered the operation.
summary: The Local Controller reported that during a high-traffic west flow, an aircraft with a rough-running engine was diverted to Runway 17R due to coordination difficulties caused by Tower Cab congestion and limited ETVS positions. The controller noted that while coordination was eventually achieved, the cramped environment and equipment limitations posed a safety risk during time-critical emergencies.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described the handling of an emergency aircraft noting a number of less than clear and missed communications by the aircraft in question.
summary: An air traffic controller missed a Cessna 152's engine failure call during high workload while coordinating a Boeing 737 departure. The controller later vectored the pilot to a Class C airport after the pilot initially confused it with another airport due to poor audio comprehension.

synopsis: BOS Tower Controller described an unauthorized airport movement area entry event by an airport vehicle. The reporter noted airport vehicles do not have a clear understanding of the ATC clearances required.
summary: An air traffic controller reported a Massport vehicle entering the movement area at BOS without ATC authorization during MVFR conditions. The controller attributed this unsafe event to a systemic lack of understanding by vehicle operators regarding movement area clearances and recommended mandatory training.

synopsis: Enroute Controller providing OJT described a confused communications event with military aircraft participating in refueling activities. The reporter noted that increased standardized of phraseology during these instances is necessary.
summary: An air traffic controller coordinated a K135 tanker and F15s during refueling, where the tanker initially claimed to advise MARSA but later admitted it had not. The incident highlighted a lack of standard phraseology for tankers to confirm MARSA responsibility, prompting a recommendation for updated procedures.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: Enroute Controller described a very busy session on combined positions when a Supervisor directed the positions be split without observing the sector and/or exploring other alternatives, i.e. first providing a D-Side.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller reported that a Supervisor split a busy low-altitude sector without assessing actual workload, causing excessive stress and a performance discussion for missed land-line calls. The Controller attributed the issue to the Supervisor relying on the Traffic Situation Display rather than observing conditions or assigning a D-Side controller.

synopsis: A B737-700 flight crew allowed themselves to be pushed back and depart without following SOP while the airport was being struck by thunderstorms, which were causing the ramp to be closed to ground personnel for their own safety.
summary: The Captain and First Officer pushed back and started engines without completing checklists or ground monitoring due to a sudden ramp closure during thunderstorms. The crew later realized this violated FOM procedures and exposed ground personnel to lightning hazards, prompting a safety review of ramp closure adherence.

synopsis: OAK ATC noticed an Air Carrier on a visual approach to OAK Runway 29 lined up and descending to the HWD Runway 28R PAPI and after a verbal alert the Captain focused on the OAK PAPI.
summary: The First Officer, flying an approach to Oakland Airport, visually misidentified nearby Hayward Airport and descended too low before correcting to land safely on Runway 29. The reporter attributed the incident to visual misidentification, a lack of briefing regarding Hayward's location, and insufficient cross-checking of flight instruments.

synopsis: After suffering the loss of their number one hydraulic system the flight crew of an EMB-145 declared an emergency, landed safely and was towed to the gate.
summary: The crew received a hydraulic #1 system failure warning after lowering the gear, prompting an emergency declaration and fire truck response. The aircraft stopped on the runway and was subsequently towed to the gate.

synopsis: After sensing smoke emanating from the vicinity of the First Officer's station as they descended toward their destination, a Dash 8 flight crew declared an emergency, landed and evacuated the aircraft after clearing the runway.
summary: The Captain and First Officer detected smoke from an unknown source during approach, declared an emergency, and performed an evacuation via the forward door after landing. Maintenance later identified engine bleed air and the air cycle machine as possible causes, though the specific source remains undetermined.

synopsis: A Line Avionics Technician reports he was unable to find the correct DC Voltage values in their Troubleshooting Guidelines that matched the newer 60-0-60 Angle of Attack (AOA) vanes used in their MD-80 aircraft. He noticed the lack of specifications in AMM 27-81-00 while troubleshooting a repeated Auto-Slat fault.
summary: Two mechanics troubleshooting an out-of-service MD-82 for an auto-slat fault found the installed 60-0-60 Angle of Attack vane was not covered by the Maintenance Manual troubleshooting guide. Consequently, they could not determine the required DC voltage values to complete the repair.

synopsis: Confused by the Tower's changes in landing runway assignments and experiencing difficulty in maintaining visual awareness of the two parallel runways as distinct from long, more clearly defined parallel taxiways, the pilot of a Cessna 400 landed on Runway 28L at FCM instead of 28R as cleared.
summary: The pilot landed on the wrong parallel runway (28L instead of 28R) after a last-minute clearance change and visual confusion caused by the runway's dark color. The controller identified the pilot deviation during the rollout, prompting the pilot to attribute the error to infrequent airport visits and lost visual reference.

synopsis: A Learjet flight crew encountered multiple flight path control and system anomalies, some of which may have been self inflicted, immediately after takeoff. All were resolved with the assistance of ATC who provided a large block altitude in which they were able to return the aircraft to normal operations.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced a pressurization failure and loss of pitch trim shortly after takeoff due to a bleed air leak. The Captain manually controlled the aircraft, reset emergency switches, and restored normal operations, allowing the flight to continue to its destination with shaken but uninjured passengers.

synopsis: An SR22 pilot and his passengers suffered an NMAC with a UAV while entering the pattern at RMN, located between two closely spaced MOAs.
summary: A pilot and passengers reported an oblong UAV passing within 100 feet of the left wing during the final approach to Runway 15 at RMN. The object did not trigger a TCAS threat, prompting the pilot to request that such vehicles either appear on cockpit displays or remain within Military Operations Areas.

synopsis: Unanticipated IMC, no available ILS and fatigue combined to cause a breakdown in CRM on the flight deck, an eventual poorly managed go around for a B757-200 flight crew.
summary: Fatigued crew attempted a visual approach in low clouds despite the First Officer's objections, leading to a go-around at 1,500 feet after the First Officer inadvertently disconnected the autopilot. Contributing factors included poor sleep, a fogged windshield, and lack of vertical guidance, resulting in a subsequent localizer approach to the opposite runway.

synopsis: A G450 engine auto shutdown after takeoff for unknown reasons but a Blue CAS message L ENG MAINT 150 was displayed during preflight which the QRH stated was a dispatchable item.
summary: The crew departed with an active Blue CAS L ENG Maint 150 message. Shortly after takeoff at 5,000 to 6,000 feet, a thump and left yaw indicated left engine failure, prompting an emergency return to the departure airport without attempting a restart.

synopsis: ANC Controller providing OJT described an unsafe event when traffic utilizing the water lanes was not positively separated.
summary: An ATC trainee cleared a Taylorcraft to land on the west water lane while a Cessna, whose position was unverified, entered the same lane. The Taylorcraft stopped safely, but the incident occurred because the controller assumed the Cessna was still starting engines and would not cross the water lane without clearance.

synopsis: A B737-700 diverted to land after it became likely they had suffered tire damage on their takeoff. Upon landing it was clear the likelihood was confirmed.
summary: The crew diverted and declared an emergency after Minneapolis Center reported possible tire debris, leading to a landing with a destroyed right inside main gear tire. Maintenance changed the tires on the runway before the aircraft was towed, and passengers were rebooked on another flight.

synopsis: When the flaps refused to extend to the selected landing position as they were configuring for landing, the flight crew of a B737-700 initiated a go around and, in violation of the associated abnormal checklist, inadvertently operated the flap handle in response to the go around commands proper for an aircraft with properly responding flaps. They reconfigured the handle to conform to the position of the flaps and made an uneventful landing.
summary: The crew experienced a flap indicator discrepancy on final approach, triggering a "TOO LOW FLAPS" warning and a go-around. They initially violated the QRH by changing the flap handle position but corrected the error, completed the checklist, and landed safely after maintenance fixed the issue.

synopsis: Rushed by pre-takeoff duties during a short taxi the First Officer of an A321 inadvertently used brakes to correct for drift on the takeoff roll which triggered a low speed RTO due to autobrake initation.
summary: The pilot flying inadvertently applied brakes during takeoff roll due to distraction and poor foot placement, causing a rejected takeoff that accelerated from 60 to 75 knots. Maintenance found no hot brakes or tire damage, and the aircraft completed a subsequent uneventful flight.

synopsis: DCA ATIS reported the LDA-R approach active but because no LOC/GS signal was received an air carrier crew tuned the LOC, re-briefed the approach and continued to land after a low altitude alert prior to 4 DME.
summary: The pilot and First Officer flew an LDA-DME 19 approach but inadvertently descended below 1,000 feet prior to 4 DME due to using FLCH instead of FPA after being left high. This triggered a low altitude alert from Tower, though the landing remained normal.

synopsis: An A321 First Officer reported encountering wake vortex from preceding aircraft on arrival to LAS that was a factor in missing a crossing restriction.
summary: The flight crew encountered severe wake turbulence from a preceding aircraft while descending on the GRNPA ONE arrival into LAS. To avoid the turbulence, they switched to a 1,000 FPM V/S descent, which caused them to miss the LUXOR 12,000 FT crossing restriction.

synopsis: An A319 Captain expressed her concerns for the safety impact of her company's flight crew scheduling patterns which force pilots to work on alternating body clock cycles within a single given sequence of flights.
summary: A pilot reported fatigue, irritability, and operational errors during a flight from XA15 to XE59 caused by the company's schedule requiring frequent shifts between day and night rest cycles. The pilot stated that flipping between early morning and late night start times within a single trip disrupts sleep regulation and compromises safety.

synopsis: A CE560XL flight crew discovered evidence of frozen water inside the tailcone of their aircraft after a short flight that encountered little or no precipitation. It appeared that a service bulletin concerning the installation of drain holes in that area had not yet been complied with.
summary: The pilot reported frost accumulation under the tail cone after a flight through clouds, suspecting internal ice formation due to missing drain holes. The aircraft skin remained cold and collected moisture post-landing, but flight controls were unaffected and the plane was written up for record.

synopsis: After landing on Runway 25L, a B737 exited on the G2 high speed where ATC cleared them to hold short 25R on Taxiway F8 but the Captain missed the clearance, did not turn right on F and incurred Runway 25R.
summary: The First Officer landed at PHX and transferred controls to the Captain while exiting the runway, during which Tower issued taxi instructions. The Captain misidentified Taxiway F's location, causing the aircraft to overshoot the Runway 25R hold short line by 5-6 feet before stopping.

synopsis: A SR22 ALT 2 alerted a generator two failure after takeoff so the pilot returned to the departure airport after completing the ALT 2 Steady ON checklist.
summary: A pilot flying a Cirrus SR22 solo on a VFR training flight experienced an Alternator 2 failure five minutes after departure. Although the pilot did not declare an emergency, ATC initiated an alert and dispatched a fire truck, which met the aircraft upon landing for a debrief.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A Corporate pilot reported a near miss with an F16 at 2,200 FT after departing MGM with no alert from ATC or TCAS warning.
summary: A civilian pilot reported a near mid-air collision with an F-16 at 2,200 feet while climbing from MGM Runway 28. The military aircraft crossed the nose in a steep turn without ATC warning or TCAS alerts, which the pilot attributed to incompatible military speed and altitude operations.

synopsis: A C208B pilot identified a potential fuel control failure and, fearing an engine failure, declared an emergency about fifteen miles from his destination. A normal approach and landing were accomplished.
summary: The pilot in Class Bravo airspace declared an emergency due to potential fuel control failure and task saturation, mistakenly squawking 1340 instead of 7700. The aircraft landed safely without engine failure and was shut down after clearing the runway.

synopsis: A LR45 GEAR warning annunciated after takeoff with each power reduction during climb and while troubleshooting that anomaly the L ESS BUS VOLTS caution alerted with an amber 22 VDC, so an emergency was declared and the flight diverted to a nearby airport.
summary: The flight crew experienced intermittent gear warnings and electrical failures during climb, leading to a diversion after mistakenly pulling the L ESS BUS breaker, which caused autopilot and pressurization loss. They landed safely, and while no cause was identified, a suspect contactor was replaced and Data Acquisition Units were swapped.

synopsis: EMB120 First Officer reported exposure to Jet-A fumes during pre-flight that resulted in mild symptoms that lasted hours.
summary: A pilot experienced Jet-A fumes during pre-flight power-up after starting the APU and turning on PACs. Although the issue was isolated and the aircraft deemed airworthy, the pilot reported mild symptoms persisting hours after the exposure.

synopsis: An Avionics Technician reports about the installation of a First Officer's forward windshield on a post merger B757-200 aircraft. Difficulties using the merged Air Carrier's Work Card Package that had only one sign-off for Step-4 of the Service Bulletin (SB) 757-30-0019 window heat wiring harnesses, were also noted.
summary: Two mechanics working on a B757-200 windshield replacement improperly torqued a nut on terminal block TB5038 because the work card lacked partial sign-off options for multi-technician steps. The reporter attributed the issue to the improper torque and the need for better training on the paperwork.

synopsis: JAX Controller described an event where a displayed flight plan status was in fact IFR contrary to all VFR data block indications.
summary: An air traffic controller accepted an Orion IFR flight from Sealord airspace, but the NAS system incorrectly displayed it as VFR, disabling MSAW protection. The controller identified that Sealord failed to update the flight plan after the aircraft reverted to IFR, causing a dangerous data discrepancy and delayed arrival strip printing.

synopsis: SFO Controller voiced concern regarding the very different same company pilot techniques during takeoff's, the reporter noting performance within the same airline should be more consistent.
summary: An air traffic controller cancelled an A320's takeoff clearance due to excessive delay in starting the roll while traffic was on final. The controller attributed the unsafe aborted departure to inconsistent flying techniques compared to a subsequent identical aircraft, creating hazards for intersecting runways.

synopsis: A long time Enroute Controller experience a loss of separation event, the reporter noted that fatigue was indeed a factor in the event.
summary: An air traffic controller lost separation between a B717 and an MD88 converging on a STAR arrival intersection despite issuing speed and altitude adjustments. The controller attributed the error to fatigue caused by a schedule change that reduced sleep time, noting that management refused to adjust shifts despite the long commute.

synopsis: TRACON Manager reported a recent discovery regarding the incorrect clearance depictions on facility video maps. The reporter listed a number of actions being taken to correct the deficiency.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller and Flight Line Manager discovered that STARS video maps incorrectly displayed 3 NM obstruction rings instead of the required 5 NM rings beyond 40 NM from the ASR-9 antenna. The facility issued a mandatory briefing and SOP change to use corrected overlay maps while permanent video map and MVA chart corrections are processed.

synopsis: An International Relief Pilot addressed his inability to get required sleep in the crew rest facility of his fleet due to noises associated with cockpit door, a nearby lavatory and the release and reattachment of the cockpit security door.
summary: A relief pilot on a mainland-Japan-mainland sequence reported interrupted rest in the crew rest area due to noise from the security barrier, cockpit door, and lavatory. The pilot attributed the resulting fatigue to the barrier's poor design and the rest area's proximity to these noise sources.

synopsis: First Officer reports departing on an ETOPS flight using Release 1 with amended takeoff weights, to discover enroute that the amended weights were for Release 2. Fortunately the route had not changed.
summary: The flight crew departed with an outdated dispatch release (Release 1) while the aircraft was loaded per Release 2, resulting in a 1,900-pound weight discrepancy. The error occurred because the Captain likely signed Release 2, but both crew copies remained Release 1, potentially exacerbated by fatigue during the post-midnight departure.

synopsis: SF340 flight crew reports rejecting a takeoff for a tail pipe hot warning at 100 KTS. The warning ceases before any crew action and Maintenance Control is contacted for advise. Maintenance advises to attempt another takeoff, which is successful. Upon landing the crew is advised that an Airworthiness Directive is involved and maintenance action is required.
summary: The crew rejected takeoff at 100 KTS due to a brief tail pipe hot warning, stopping with 1,000 feet remaining. Maintenance Control initially cleared the flight as a false positive, but later cited an airworthiness directive requiring inspection before further operation.

synopsis: A319 First Officer reported an NMAC with a C130 in the vicinity of IWA.
summary: During an IFR arrival into Phoenix, a pilot executed an immediate climb to avoid a C-130 that passed 400–500 feet below. The near-miss occurred due to wildfire smoke reducing visibility and the VFR aircraft lacking Mode C, which ATC claimed did not require reporting.

synopsis: A First Officer noted that after a DFW BONHAM 5 Arrival with a short approach to Runway 35C he understood why FOQA data was identifying an unusual number of unstabilized approaches.
summary: The First Officer and Captain flew a DFW arrival on the BONHAM 5, receiving a late short approach clearance that required rapid descent and configuration. The pilot attributed the unstabilized approach to the 220 KTS speed restriction at STONZ, expectation bias, and delayed ATC communication regarding the short approach.

synopsis: EMB145 First Officer reports errors made entering a flight plan composed of fixes designated by two letters and four numbers for each fix. Some of the numbers become transposed or entered in error resulting in a track deviation.
summary: A first officer incorrectly entered waypoint KG1464 instead of KG1494 into the FMS during preflight, a mistake undetected by the captain. The aircraft deviated slightly in cruise until ATC identified the error and issued a clearance to a subsequent point.

synopsis: A CRJ200 crew was given unexpected delays on a BOS arrival and declared minimum fuel because their dispatch fuel did not include an alternate or additional fuel.
summary: The flight crew declared minimum fuel during descent into BOS after holding and delay vectors reduced their fuel below the planned bingo amount. They received priority handling and landed with 2,150 LBS, concluding that additional fuel should have been carried for this no-alternate flight into busy airspace.

synopsis: BE1900 Captain describes an unsafe gear indication during approach resulting in a go around. Manual pumping does not result in a safe gear indication but the lack of a landing gear warning horn with the thrust retarded is a positive indication and a near normal landing ensues. The aircraft had a history of unsafe gear indications.
summary: The flight crew of a BE1900 experienced a right main gear extension failure on approach, indicated by missing green lights and a persistent red in-transit light. After executing a missed approach, emergency checklists, and a visual flyby, they landed safely with the gear confirmed down, though the in-transit light remained illuminated.

synopsis: BE1900 Captain describes an unsafe gear indication during approach resulting in a go around. Manual pumping results in a safe gear indication and a normal landing ensues. The aircraft had a history of unsafe gear indications.
summary: During final approach, the right landing gear indicator failed to illuminate and the gear motor tripped a circuit breaker, prompting a go-around and emergency declaration. The crew successfully extended the gear using the manual extension checklist, landed safely, and noted this was a repeat of a failure reported two days prior.

synopsis: A B737-800 crew identified a fuel leak after takeoff so they declared an emergency, completed the QRH, shut the engine down and returned to the departure airport where maintenance identified a crack somewhere in right wing fuel plumbing prior to the engine.
summary: The crew experienced a right fuel leak causing an imbalance and right engine shutdown shortly after takeoff. They declared an emergency, returned for a single-engine landing slightly over maximum weight, and maintenance later found a cracked refueling coupler on the right wing.

synopsis: A MD-82 Captain executed a go-around at 500 FT after Tower alerted WINDSHEAR ALERT and during the climb experienced a zero VSI with 18 degrees nose up, followed by a 3,000 FT plus FPM climb with nose down.
summary: The crew encountered a wind shear alert during ILS approach to Runway 30L, triggering a go-around where the autopilot caused an uncommanded climb to 4,400 FT. The pilot manually disconnected the autopilot to stop the climb, held for weather clearance, and completed a successful landing 40 minutes later.

synopsis: A DC-10-30's number one engine failed to relight after it was shut down on post C-Check maintenance test flight, so an emergency was declared followed by a normal landing.
summary: During a post C-Check test flight on an MD-10-30, the number one engine failed to relight during normal shutdown/restart procedures. Despite emergency checklists, altitude changes, and declaring an emergency 70 miles from the destination, all restart attempts failed, though the aircraft landed uneventfully.

synopsis: An A310 flight crew departing SJU contacted Departure immediately after departure as directed by the narrative page of their commercially (2) provided ACONY RNAV SID procedure. Departure sent them back to the Tower to receive clearance to change frequencies.
summary: The flight crew departed SJU and switched to Departure Control immediately after takeoff, following the RNAV SID's bold instruction to contact Departure. The Tower Controller reprimanded them for changing frequencies without clearance, stating they should wait for explicit instructions in the future.

synopsis: A DC10 crew noticed a very slight vibration after landing and were notified by Maintenance that the number 6 tire was blown which caused damaged to the left inboard flap.
summary: The flight crew reported slight landing gear vibrations during takeoff and landing with no EICAS warnings. Post-flight maintenance revealed a blown number 6 tire with tread separation and damage to the left inboard flap section.

synopsis: A C172 Instructor with a student on a weekend training event took taking evasive action from an aircraft after an apparent skydiving drop 15 miles from F90.
summary: A pilot conducting a dual VFR cross-country flight to French Valley Airport encountered a descending aircraft at 5,500 feet while east of skydiving activity. The pilot executed a right turn to avoid the traffic, noting a potential information gap between SCT and MIV controllers regarding the skydiving aircraft.

synopsis: An Instructor pilot and his Student were momentarily blinded by a green laser while in level flight at 4,500 MSL.
summary: A student and instructor flying level at 4,500 feet were blinded for 3-4 seconds by a green laser from a residential community near St. Augustine. The laser illuminated and tracked the aircraft, temporarily obscuring night vision and requiring several minutes to fully acclimate.

synopsis: BE400 First Officer describes a rejected takeoff for a trim induced takeoff warning horn. After returning to the ramp and shutting down an engine for troubleshooting the warning is found to activate even though the trim is correctly set. After running the trim up and down several times the warning ceases to activate inappropriately and the flight departs.
summary: The crew of a Beech Jet rejected takeoff at 65 KIAS after a trim misconfiguration horn sounded twice despite initial attempts to silence it. They resolved the issue by cycling the trim on the ramp, confirming the system was functional, and successfully completed the flight.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A high performance corporate jet Captain refused to turn to heading 270 after takeoff from LAX because the previous flight's early turn resulted in an Airport Authority letter. This departure LAX Controllers need separation and were unhappy.
summary: During departure from LAX, the pilot flying refused an ATC instruction to turn heading 270 degrees early, citing airport restrictions, while the monitoring pilot failed to intervene. The incident highlighted a conflict between the crew and Tower, leading the reporter to conclude that controllers' instructions must be followed immediately for safety.

synopsis: HCF Controller voiced concern regarding the Kaneohe SID and associated required coordination. The reporter noted the Mugge SID was safer with regard to clearing parachute activity areas.
summary: An Orion P3 departing Kaneohe on the Kaneohe 1 Departure turned to heading 320 without clearance to stay over water, requiring ATC coordination to re-route it to heading 260. The controller attributed the incident to the departure procedure's design, which forces aircraft over land and lacks depiction of parachute jumping areas on charts or radar scopes.

synopsis: SAV Controller voiced concern regarding the recently interpreted FAA separation requirements reference R3005 (UAS activity), noting the procedure unduly restricts SAV aircraft activity.
summary: SAV Approach controllers could not conduct IFR approaches to Runway 10 because the US Army denied access to the Pembrooke call-up area due to UAS activity in R3005. The FAA's requirement for a three-mile buffer caused delays and forced crosswind operations, which the reporter attributes to a misapplication of separation standards for non-dangerous activities.

synopsis: A B737-700 Captain, concerned that his First Officer was visually continuing a low minima approach in heavy rains based on inaccurate assessment of the visible runway environment, directed a go-around at low altitude. A second successful approach was flown by the Captain assisted by a HUD system accessible to him in the left seat.
summary: The Captain initiated a go-around below 100 feet during a heavy rain approach to Runway 30L due to poor visibility and perceived VASI drift while the First Officer was flying. The Captain subsequently flew the second approach using the HUD and flaps 40, resulting in a safe landing despite reduced braking performance.

synopsis: A B737 took evasive action from a glider at about 10,000' while descending for a daylight visual approach to TUS Runway 11L. Suggest transponder equipped gliders near airports.
summary: The flight crew encountered a glider without a transponder while on a visual approach to Runway 11L near 11,000 feet MSL. The pilot manually maneuvered right to maintain separation, reporting a minimum distance of less than 1,000 feet and one mile to Approach.

synopsis: A B737-300 rejected their takeoff upon receipt of a takeoff warning horn determined to be the result of the Captain's trim indication being in the green band, but not the First Officer's. By electing the most conservative of the two displays a subsequent takeoff was uneventful.
summary: The crew aborted takeoff due to a Takeoff Warning Horn caused by a discrepancy between the Captain's and First Officer's stabilizer trim pointers. After adjusting the trim to match the lower reading, the aircraft was successfully reconfigured and departed without further incident.

synopsis: A B737 crew descended below 5,000 FT prior to CALLS intersection on a TUS Runway 11L night visual approach and received a momentary 'Caution Terrain' alert while climbing.
summary: The crew descended below the 5500' minimum vector altitude while on a visual approach to TUS Runway 11L, triggering a terrain caution. The First Officer had incorrectly set 5000' based on the approach chart, causing the aircraft to reach that altitude outside the CALLS DME fix before the crew climbed to comply with ATC.

synopsis: B757 Captain reports receiving a revised weight and balance after takeoff indicating a 2500 pound fuel increase and 13 additional passengers.
summary: The flight crew experienced a ten-minute departure delay and received updated weights 36 minutes after takeoff, showing increased fuel and zero fuel weight. The pilot reported this discrepancy could have represented an 80,000-pound error.

synopsis: A B757 EICAS alerted TE FLAP ASYM after flaps 1 was selected so the crew declared an emergency, completed all the checklists and landed at the filed destination.
summary: The First Officer flying a 173,000-lb aircraft experienced a trailing edge flap asymmetry at 230 KTS while extending flaps to 1. After ATC vectored the crew into a holding pattern for checklists and maintenance consultation, the Captain declared an emergency, took control, and landed safely.

synopsis: A320 First Officer reports noticing right hand roll spoilers 2, 3, and 4 are extended during approach with noticeable aircraft yawing and a continuous noise. There were no ECAM messages and the Beta target was well displaced out to the right but remained green. Captain elects to continue the approach to landing where all spoilers extend normally on touch down and retract normally when disarmed.
summary: The Captain, acting as pilot flying on approach, experienced right yaw and noise due to right spoilers 2, 3, and 4 failing to retract without an ECAM memo. A normal landing was achieved, and the spoilers retracted normally after touchdown.

synopsis: A319 flight crew reports a Captain's Pitot Fault followed 30 seconds later by an Eng 2 Reverser Fault. There are no ECAM actions listed but the Flight Manual indicates landing ASAP is required. The crew elects to err on the side of caution and divert. After touch down a Landing Gear System Disagree is displayed.
summary: The flight crew diverted and declared an emergency during cruise after receiving Anti-Ice Capt Pitot and Engine 2 Reverser Fault ECAMs, acting on FOM "LAND ASAP" guidance despite no ECAM prompt. A Landing Gear System Disagree occurred on landing, and the same faults recurred on the subsequent flight.

synopsis: Air Carrier with ZNY was denied a weather deviation resulting in an emergency declaration to avoid build ups.
summary: A pilot flying at FL340 in New York Center airspace requested a weather deviation, which ATC denied and replaced with a conflicting clearance. The pilot declared an emergency to maintain the original route after the controller accused them of seeking a more direct path and dismissed the weather hazard.

synopsis: A CRJ200 on a night visual to TUS Runway 11L received an EGPWS Terrain Warning at about 5,200 FT 2 miles prior to CALLS and executed the escape maneuver just as ATC called to notify them about that location's 5,900 FT MVA.
summary: The flight crew received a visual approach clearance to TUS Runway 11L at night and triggered a terrain warning at 5,200 feet due to unknown Minimum Vectoring Altitude of 5,900 feet. The pilot climbed to 6,500 feet after the controller alerted them to the low altitude, attributing the event to insufficient approach plate review and lack of terrain awareness.

synopsis: A B757-200 flight crew, suspecting water in the Electronics Compartment due to heavy rains during the aircraft's layover, returned to its departure airport when multiple unrelated EICAS Warnings, Cautions Status and Advisories messages were displayed shortly after takeoff.
summary: The crew encountered unrelated EICAS warnings and suspected water in the electronic compartment, prompting a return to the airport. Maintenance confirmed water in the compartment, likely from cargo pallets, after the aircraft landed at 205,100 lbs.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic describes his efforts to multi-task a #2 engine dry-motor operation while taxiing their ERJ-170 aircraft and communicating with Ground Control. He felt pressure from lack of time to accomplish all the scheduled maintenance work.
summary: The pilot of an ERJ-170 taxiing to a hangar accidentally shut down the #1 engine instead of stopping the #2 engine dry-motor operation. This error occurred while the pilot was distracted by a radio clearance readback and exceeded starter duty limits due to time pressure.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic reports he did not pull and collar Circuit Breakers that were called out in their MD-11 Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) Chapter 71-10-00-2 for replacement of the # 1 Engine Integrated Drive Generator (IDG). He had been working multiple gates and the Out of Service (OTS) MD-11 aircraft.
summary: A mechanic opened the MD-11's #1 engine cowl for an IDG replacement but failed to pull and collar required circuit breakers due to working multiple gates and a hectic turnover to hangar crew. The reporter attributed the error to manpower shortages and suggested assigning dedicated staff to Out of Service aircraft.

synopsis: G-IV Captain reports exceeding altitude and speed restrictions departing Runway 24 at TEB on the RUUDY4 departure. Autothrust was thought to be engaged to maintain 200 KTS but was fixed at takeoff thrust.
summary: During departure from Teterboro Runway 24, a Gulfstream IV crew failed to notice disengaged autothrottles while task-saturated, causing the aircraft to exceed 250 KTS. The flying Captain reduced power to idle to recover airspeed, and the crew attributed the event to a false sense of comfort regarding automation.

synopsis: C208 First Officer reports HSI/DG's 'sticking' during departure from ORD resulting in in a track deviation of 40 degrees initially.
summary: The pilot flying a Caravan departing ORD unintentionally deviated 40–60 degrees from assigned headings for 10 minutes due to a stuck Captain's DG that was not slaved to the compass. No traffic conflicts occurred, and the crew manually reset the instruments to resume normal operation.

synopsis: Experimental aircraft pilot experiences fuel exhaustion while attempting to return to base during a Phase 1 test flight. An emergency landing in a farmers field ensues without damage to the aircraft.
summary: The pilot of an experimental aircraft conducting Phase I flight testing experienced an engine stoppage due to fuel starvation two miles short of the intended landing field. The incident resulted from unverified fuel flow and quantity indications caused by a focus on cooling system modifications, leading to an uneventful field landing with no damage.

synopsis: C182 pilot at 9,500 FT, using flight following with Luke Approach, is issued a 030 degree heading to avoid a 'high altitude traffic pattern.' Since there is no indication of military airspace on available charts or GPS the reporter declines the request.
summary: A VFR Part 91 pilot flying near PHX was vectored by Luke Approach into Alert Area A231 without traffic advisories or a stated reason. The pilot refused the turn, citing uncharted special use airspace, and later spoke with a supervisor who claimed authority to vector VFR flights under AIM Chapter 5.

synopsis: A Quality Control Supervisor describes how a shredded washer, found during a Turn-Around Check by a Mechanic on a Eurocopter AS350-B3 helicopter, led to the discovery of three untorqued and unsecured bolts that connect the short shaft and flex-coupling between the main rotor transmission and engine. Maintenance practices at their Contract Maintenance facility were also noted.
summary: During a post-inspection turnaround, a QC manager discovered untorqued and unsafetied flex-coupling bolts on an aircraft engine after a 600-hour inspection. The manager admitted failing to personally verify the work signed off by mechanics and an inspection authority, accepting responsibility for the safety oversight.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A corporate jet crew reported being switched from a DCA Runway 1 Mount Vernon Visual to a Runway 33 visual. Then, ATC issued them a go around because an air carrier departing Runway 1 interfered with them.
summary: Pilots on a visual approach to Runway 33 at DCA executed a go-around at 500 feet AGL after ATC cleared a departing airliner from Runway 01, creating a spacing conflict. The crew later reported that an FAA Safety Inspector contacted them regarding a possible pilot deviation during the missed approach.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: ZNY controllers described the complications of handling a lifeguard aircraft with regards to interfacility coordination and procedures. The aircraft eventually received direct routing.
summary: A Sector 26 controller attempted to hand off a Lifeguard flight at FL230 to Sector 39 against traffic flow without prior coordination or APREQ. The Sector 39 controller refused the handoff due to safety concerns and LOA violations, forcing a reroute to Sector 92 for descent to FL170.

synopsis: ZBW Controller described a confused routing event, suggesting a URET/HOST software patch that would alert controllers when preferential routings were being applied.
summary: A ZBW Center Controller cleared Air Carrier X direct to BAF VORTAC after departure from KBOS, causing the URET/HOST computer to automatically apply an unintended preferential route. The aircraft deviated from its filed flight plan but was handed off without traffic conflicts, prompting a recommendation for a system patch to alert controllers of such routing changes.

synopsis: ZMA Controller providing OJT during a very busy and complex traffic period, complicated by multiple weather deviations, experienced a loss of separation event. Both controller and pilot reports provide excellent perspectives.
summary: A Radar Controller and trainee in Aluto Sector managed heavy weather deviations when a C550 and Air Carrier Y lost vertical separation due to conflicting descent and climb instructions. The controller issued a descent clearance to the climbing B712, triggering a Resolution Advisory and requiring a climb-descent transition to recover separation.

synopsis: CRQ Controller described a potential conflict event involving inbound aircraft from SCT and aircraft within Class D airspace, noting SCT frequently violates the existing LOA with regard to communications transfer requirements of inbound aircraft.
summary: SOCAL Approach transferred a light twin and a PA28 to CRQ Tower inside the required 7-mile limit, violating the Letter of Agreement. This caused traffic conflicts with departing C172 and PA28 aircraft and a PC12 on visual approach before Tower established contact.

synopsis: ZMP Controller described a loss of separation when an IFR aircraft departed non-towered airport without a release, conflicting with an IFR inbound.
summary: Aircraft X departed JMR in IFR conditions while in clouds, conflicting with inbound Aircraft Y on GPS 35. The controller issued heading and climb clearances to separate them, resulting in a 2.5-mile lateral separation with altitude difference, though Aircraft Y detected Aircraft X on TCAS.

synopsis: B737-700 First Officer reports descending below MVA during a night visual approach to Runway 11L at TUS after a last minute runway change from Runway 29R. The reporter was attempting to descend to the FAF altitude prior to reaching CALLS. The crew, ATC, and the EGPWS all became concerned at the same time and corrective action was taken.
summary: The flight crew experienced a terrain caution while descending for a visual approach to Runway 11L after a runway change. The incident occurred because the crew failed to verbally brief step-down altitudes when cleared direct to the FAF, preventing a safe VNAV path.

synopsis: While in cruise at FL370 an MD-11 Flight Crew declared an emergency and diverted to their nearest suitable airport after responding to Engine number two fire warnings (later determined to have been false).
summary: The pilot flying received Level 3 Engine #2 fire warnings at FL 37,000 during cruise. After completing memory items and declaring an emergency, the crew descended for an uneventful landing where no fire was found, and the aircraft was secured.

synopsis: An A320 First Officer's airspeed indication failed with numerous ECAM and aural alerts so the Captain rejected the takeoff and returned to the gate. The Aircraft previously had an ADRU 2 deferral.
summary: The First Officer lost airspeed indications at 100 KTS during takeoff roll, triggering ECAM warnings and autothrottle disengagement. The Captain aborted at 125 KTS due to the failure, which was linked to a deferred ADRU 2 defect, resulting in high brake temperatures and a return to the gate.

synopsis: An air carrier Relief Pilot reports that his aircraft had no suitable flight crew rest location and so he was unable to rest, resulting in fatigue and some ensuing communications and procedural errors.
summary: A relief pilot on the outbound leg could not rest due to excessive noise in the designated bunk area and lack of alternative seats, leading to fatigue that caused missed Class II requirements and confusion with ATC instructions. The pilot attributed this safety degradation to the inadequate rest facility, noting that a better-equipped aircraft on the return leg allowed for successful rest.

synopsis: A Citation 560XL flight crew was rerouted via the SSCOT1 RNAV STAR for their arrival into X51 (Homestead General Aviation) but discovered the arrival was in neither their FMS database or their EFB for use into their destination and so advised ATC. Miami Center believed that to be incorrect but provided fix by fix clearances allowing the flight to continue to X51.
summary: Pilots en route to X51 reported that Miami Center and subsequent frequencies assigned the non-existent SSCOT1 arrival, which is unavailable in the FMS and EFB for that airport. The controller insisted their system showed the arrival existed, forcing a reassignment to fixes due to a data mismatch between ATC computers and aircraft navigation systems.

aircraft: Regional Jet CL65; Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Regional Jet First Officer describes forgetting to extend the landing gear when requested by the Captain, then both pilots missing the gear handle in the up position on the landing checklist. The GPWS sounds to alert the crew and the Captain extends the gear. Fatigue is cited as a factor in the incident.
summary: Fatigued Captain and First Officer on the final leg of a five-day trip failed to lower landing gear due to impaired mental focus and non-sterile cockpit conversation. The gear horn sounded below 1,500 feet AGL, prompting the Captain to manually extend the gear for a stable landing.

synopsis: A Dispatcher reported a B767-300ER had declared an emergency and returned to its departure airport when they shut down the left engine due to low oil pressure and landed modestly overweight.
summary: The flight crew declared an emergency and returned to the departure airport after shutting down engine #1 due to low oil pressure. Despite burning fuel to avoid an overweight landing, the aircraft arrived 20,000 kilos over the maximum landing weight.

synopsis: An A320 Flight Crew performed an emergency descent after noting the cabin altitude approaching 10,000 feet. When level, they performed appropriate ECAMs and checklists, switched to an alternate system and continued to their destination.
summary: The flight crew lost auto cabin pressurization at FL280, triggering an emergency descent to 10,000 feet and later 8,000 feet MSL. They regained control by selecting Pressurization System 2 and completed a normal approach and landing.

synopsis: CRJ Captain reported encountering wake vortex following an A320 on takeoff from CLT, resulting in a brief stick shaker.
summary: The pilot reported encountering wake turbulence from a preceding A320 immediately after rotation on Runway 18C, causing a brief stick shaker activation due to angle of attack changes. The aircraft climbed out uneventfully with airspeed around 170 KIAS, and the pilot attributed the event to warm, calm conditions retaining vortices over the runway.

synopsis: A B737-400 pressurization control malfunctioned causing the Cabin Altitude Alert to sound so an emergency was declared and the flight diverted. The autothrottles and transponders were also malfunctioning.
summary: The crew experienced transponder, autothrottle, and pressurization failures on departure after maintenance could not duplicate the issues. The Captain manually controlled cabin pressure and executed an emergency descent to 13,000 feet, resulting in no injuries or mask deployment.

synopsis: B747 Captain reports tripped circuit breakers associated with high lift devices during taxi out and returns for maintenance. A Wing Overheat Light had been experienced earlier and was thought to be related and Maintenance discovered a faulty PDU on the right wing. Arrival airport noise curfew and crew duty day began to be issues and the crew ended up departing without entering the tripped circuit breakers in the logbook.
summary: The crew encountered multiple maintenance issues, including fire detection faults, FMS lockups, wing overheat lights, and popped circuit breakers, during preflight and taxi. Due to runway quiet hour constraints and fatigue from ground transportation, the crew departed with a deferred PDU issue but failed to fully document the popped circuit breakers in the logbook.

synopsis: While preparing for departure on a ferry flight, a B737 Captain smells smoke and sees a Maintenance man pulling a flaming ground power cord from the aircraft receptacle. The aircraft is shut down and the crew evacuates through the main cabin door.
summary: The flight crew and a maintenance technician were on the ground during pre-departure when a flaming external power cord caused smoke in the cockpit. The maintenance technician disconnected the power while the crew evacuated the aircraft, preventing severe damage and injuries.

synopsis: Although they had programmed the the FMS to meet their ATC directed crossing restriction at NEWES, the Flight Crew of a B737-700 failed to note they were more than a thousand feet above the required descent gradient until the the CDU advised them they were not going to make the restriction. Herculean flight crew efforts failed to overcome the deficit.
summary: Pilots flying a jet at FL330 received an "unable next altitude" CDU message while descending to cross NEWES at FL240, resulting in a 700–1,000 foot altitude deviation. The reporter attributed the incident to unknown FMS path deviation causes and recommended better software and more diligent monitoring.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: A MD80's left engine turbine section failed during climb so an emergency was declared, the checklists completed and the flight returned to the departure airport.
summary: During climb out, the crew experienced a loud pop and severe left yaw caused by a #1 engine failure with severe aft turbine damage. The Captain declared an emergency, returned to the departure airport, and executed an overweight single-engine landing on Runway 27 with no injuries or visible external damage.

synopsis: A B757 EICAS alerted R HYD QTY, the RSVR light illuminated and the quantity indicating 0.09 so the QRH procedure was completed, an emergency declared followed by a normal landing after which all quantity indications returned to normal.
summary: During descent through FL220, the crew observed right hydraulic quantity and reservoir warnings with an 'RF' status indication. They followed the QRH, declared an emergency, and landed the aircraft without incident.

synopsis: A Cargo flight crew described fatigue induced communication and procedural errors during flight after their inability to sleep during the previous daylight rest cycle.
summary: A fatigued Captain and First Officer lost radio contact due to unmonitored speakers and missed a flap 35 configuration on final approach, triggering a GPWS warning. They corrected the flap setting and landed safely, though the Captain admitted fatigue caused the errors and a go-around should have been executed.

synopsis: An Air Carrier Maintenance representative reports he was contacted by two company line maintenance stations regarding their inability to configure the right recirculation fan wiring on two B757-200 ETOPS aircraft as called-out in their Fleet Campaign Directive (FCD) 21-25-XXX. Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2009-12-03 involved.
summary: Maintenance teams at ZZZ1 and ZZZ2 could not configure right recirc fan wiring on two B757-200 ETOPS aircraft due to a missing stud on the connector bracket. Work was reassigned pending Project Engineer review after inspections confirmed no wiring damage and proper clamping.

synopsis: A Line Inspector reports he has found numerous B767-300 aircraft with damaged Recirculation Fan Filter Box support rods behind the aft bulkhead nylon curtain in the forward cargo compartment. Damaged rods were noted while he was accomplishing Galley Spill Inspections.
summary: A mechanic discovered damaged Recirc Fan Filter box support rods on B767-300 Aircraft Z and A during a galley spill inspection, exceeding Maintenance Manual limits. Engineering denied a repair authorization, leaving two aircraft out of service due to damage caused by cargo containers pressing against the rods.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic reports a new, expanded Inspection Required Checklist for maintenance work accomplished that was implemented after their merger, was poorly communicated by Management and contributed to his missing an inspection item on a B747-400 brake change.
summary: A mechanic replaced a Main Landing Gear brake on a B747-400 alone under time pressure and was later cited for failing to flag the torque arm for inspection. The reporter attributed the error to inadequate training on new inspection lists and poor communication regarding expanded requirements following a company merger.

synopsis: A pilot reported loosing control of a Maule Amphibian on takeoff after he lifted off to soon in a crosswind causing a wing to stall and forward parts of the floats to contact the runway.
summary: The pilot lost control of a Maule Amphibian during takeoff in strong crosswinds, lifting off too soon and stalling the left wing. The aircraft turned into the wind and contacted the ground with its floats, an incident the pilot attributed to the crosswind and premature lift-off.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: A Student pilot misjudged his Liberty XL2 height during landing and after a bounce he added power to arrest the descent so that the crosswind correction plus the P factor rotated his aircraft causing it land off the runway's edge.
summary: During a touch-and-go crosswind approach, the pilot landed hard on the left gear, causing a left yaw that turned the aircraft off the runway despite a go-around attempt. The pilot leveled the wings and stopped safely on the grass with no damage, attributing the incident to insufficient power on approach.

synopsis: A DC3 crew departed on a training flight but declared an emergency and returned to land after a hot burning smell was detected followed by rapidly rising oil temperature. The approach and landing were normal.
summary: The flight crew of a repainted aircraft departing Runway 21 detected a burning odor 90 seconds after liftoff and returned to the field. Upon observing rapidly climbing right engine oil temperature while entering downwind, they declared an emergency to secure runway access and landed normally.

synopsis: A-139 flight crew experienced inflight failure of tail rotor deicing system. Post flight inspection revealed electrical arcing in tail rotor assembly.
summary: During a multi-leg training flight, the pilot experienced recurring Tail Rotor Degraded caution lights while using the Ice Protection System. Post-flight maintenance identified electrical arcing to the tail rotor assembly as the cause.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: A pilot departing DVT on a right downwind departure reported a near miss with an arriving aircraft at 2,400 FT with no ATC alert until after the encounter.
summary: A departing aircraft experienced a close call with a descending low-wing airplane at Deer Valley Airport after Tower issued takeoff clearance. The reporter attributed the incident to a lack of timely traffic advisories from the controller and suggested installing primary radar to improve separation at the busy airport.

synopsis: Tower Controller described a loss of separation event when traffic inbound to the pattern entered an opposite direction downwind.
summary: Local Control reported a Meridian pilot deviated from a cleared Visual Approach for Runway 2R, turning left for Runway 20R and losing vertical separation with a Cirrus. The controller issued a traffic alert and re-routed the Meridian to Runway 2L, attributing the incident to pilot error and a potential failure by Approach to ensure level-off before frequency transfer.

synopsis: GEG Controller voiced concern regarding the published 4,000 altitude restriction on the Spokane Two Departure, noting ATC is expecting aircraft to climb to 12,000, the reporter recommending modifications to the SID chart.
summary: A pilot flying an Airbus on the Spokane Two Departure questioned Ground Control regarding the significance of a 4,000-foot altitude restriction. The reporter attributes this recurring confusion to unclear chart wording and recommends a NOTAM and chart revision to clarify that the altitude is extraneous.

synopsis: SJC Controller described a conflict between a VFR point out from NCT and an IFR Air Carrier departure from Runway 30R, the VFR traffic apparently not complying with airport crossing instructions.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller at SJC reported a C172 unexpectedly turned toward a departing B737's corridor after the controller issued a "no factor" clearance based on delayed radar data. The C172's unanticipated course change created a potential conflict, though no collision occurred, prompting the controller to note the need for increased vigilance regarding non-radar-controlled VFR traffic.

synopsis: While climbing through about 17,000 FT, a B737-700's Cabin Altitude Warning horn sounded so an emergency was declared and the flight returned to the departure airport.
summary: During climb after departure, the crew experienced transponder failure, FMC mode loss, and a cabin altitude warning reaching 12,500 feet. The pilot flying descended while the other pilot coordinated a return to the departure airport, where the cabin was successfully controlled in manual mode.

synopsis: An EMB 145 flight crew declared an emergency and descended below 10,000 MSL in response to a slow but steady increase in cabin altitude, ultimately reaching 12,100 FT at which point the O2 masks were manually deployed for the passengers. Upon leveling at 10,000 MSL the flight diverted to a nearby airport.
summary: The flight crew experienced a pressurization failure during climb, causing cabin altitude to exceed 10,000 feet. They declared an emergency, descended to 10,000 feet, deployed passenger oxygen masks, and diverted to a safe airport for a normal landing.

synopsis: A MD83 L OIL PRESSURE LOW alerted during climb so an emergency was declared and the flight returned to the departure airport where a go around was executed on the first approach because of an excessive aileron requirement and the overweight condition.
summary: The crew experienced a left engine oil pressure failure during climbout, declared an emergency, and shut down the engine. They executed a go-around on the first approach due to near maximum landing weight and excessive aileron input, then landed successfully on the second attempt.

synopsis: A CE680 Captain reported difficulty maintaining 2,000 FT on the RUUDY 4 departure from TEB due to the altitude alerter being set to 1,500 FT while attempting to engage the autopilot.
summary: During departure from Teterboro, the Pilot Flying managed an altitude excursion between 1,700 and 2,700 feet and delayed flap retraction because the Pilot Not Flying was unresponsive. The reporter attributed these errors to the Pilot Not Flying's absence from the flight deck, suspecting they were not present during the initial climb.

synopsis: C172 pilot approaching Runway 19 at TEB reports a NMAC with another C172 west bound at 2,000 FT. The Tower point out came after the west bound C172 had already passed over the reporter.
summary: A pilot flying a Cessna 172 on a visual approach to Runway 19 at Teterboro descended to 1,900 MSL and encountered an uncoordinated Cessna 172 at the same altitude. The pilot executed an immediate dive to pass 200 feet below the other aircraft, which appeared unaware of the conflict, and subsequently landed normally.

synopsis: A Diamond DA20 pilot reported engine failure due to fuel exhaustion despite what he calculated should have been sufficient fuel on board. A safe landing ensued at a nearby airport.
summary: The pilot of a Diamond DA20-C1 experienced an engine stoppage at 8,500 feet during descent due to fuel exhaustion caused by inaccurate fuel quantity estimates from an unknown 20-gallon tank capacity. The pilot diverted to a closer airport, landed safely with no injuries, and suspected faulty fuel gauges or a stuck sump contributed to the incident.

synopsis: P180 Captain reported losing cabin pressure and then finding he had never turned the bleeds on.
summary: The crew experienced a cabin pressure light during climb through 12,000 feet, prompting an emergency descent to 10,000 feet. The issue resolved after the pilot realized the bleed air switches were inadvertently left off since takeoff, allowing the flight to continue normally.

synopsis: CE550 Captain reports inadvertently flying the TEB 8 procedure for Runway 19 while departing from Runway 24. This results in both track and altitude deviations, and a conflict with an aircraft arriving Runway 22 at EWR.
summary: The SIC and PIC departed Teterboro Runway 24 but inadvertently flew the Runway 19 departure procedure due to a chart layout error. ATC intervened to correct the climb profile after the crew exceeded the 1,500-foot restriction, creating a potential conflict with inbound Newark traffic.

synopsis: Tower Controller described a potential collision between a departure and a Flight Check aircraft conducting opposite direction operations, the reporter offering a number of preventive recommendations.
