This action has a positive effect and a normal landing ensues at the diversion airport.
summary: During climb through FL180, pilots received a HYD G RSVR OVHT ECAM and secured the PTU and ENG 1 pump, causing severe airframe vibration. They diverted, declared an emergency, and restored the pumps to stop the flutter, resulting in a safe overweight landing with no recurrence of the issue.

synopsis: A MD-11 cargo compartment Fire Suppression System alerted and activated at cruise so after visually verifying foaming action, an emergency was declared and the flight diverted to a nearby foreign airport.
summary: Flight crew at FL340 diverted after the Fire Suppression System automatically discharged foam into cargo positions 7L and 7R due to a detected heat source. The crew declared an emergency and landed safely, citing uncertainty about remaining agent capacity as a key factor in the diversion decision.

synopsis: B757-200 flight crew reports a R AUX PITOT light after pushback and contacts Dispatch for an MEL. A failure to communicate ensues when the Dispatcher assumes that the crew is aware that the flight cannot be dispatched with this failure. Eventually the crew comprehends and returns to the gate for an aircraft swap.
summary: The flight crew mistakenly recorded a Dispatcher's employee number as the Maintenance Control number while taxiing after an R AUX PITOT light illuminated. Upon realizing the error and receiving a message prohibiting departure due to visible moisture, they returned to the gate, transferred cargo to another aircraft, and departed two hours late.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports a Captain had found an outflow valve in the crew forward closet on an ERJ-145 aircraft. Maintenance had missed a step in the MEL Manual when putting the Air Conditioning Pack System back into service after troubleshooting and repairs.
summary: Two mechanics repaired Pack-1 and Pack-2 systems on an ERJ-145 during a hangar service check, signing off the work after successful operational checks. The aircraft's outflow valve was later found in the crew closet because a step in the MEL manual was missed during the return-to-service process.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) was informed that a white arc on the face of an Airspeed Indicator (A/I) he had installed at the First Officer's (F/O) position, was not correct for a Beechcraft 1900-D aircraft. Their Parts Department had previously assured Technician their computer system automatically pulls up correct interchangeable part numbers.
summary: A mechanic installed an interchangeable airspeed indicator on a Beechcraft 1900-D to fix a pitot static leak, relying on computer-generated part data. The installed part was later found to have an incorrect white arc, prompting a recommendation to verify alternate part numbers manually.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic reports he continues to be harassed by Maintenance Management for discovery of obvious defects and moisture ingress at the L-3 (Left) and R-3 (Right) cockpit side windows on their B757-200 aircraft.
summary: A pilot reported moisture ingress on the L-3 cockpit window of a B757-200 while unlocking the door for a contractor. The pilot states management harasses them for documenting this defect, which poses an electrical arcing risk, despite the carrier's awareness of the fleet-wide issue.

synopsis: A Lead Mechanic reports a deferred Autopilot System had been cleared after a Mode Control Panel (MCP) had been replaced on a B757-200 aircraft. However, after departure, the flight crew notified Maintenance Control the Left, Center and Right autopilots would not engaged. All three Flight Control Computers (FCCs) Circuit Breakers (C/Bs) were still collared.
summary: After maintenance cleared an Autopilot MEL on a B757-200, the flight crew found three FCC Servo circuit breakers still collared during en route flight, preventing Autopilot engagement. Maintenance Control authorized resetting the breakers, restoring the system without further action, though the reporter recommended improved MEL clearance verification procedures.

synopsis: A pilot under going CFI training in a C172RG with his instructor, noticed signs of an electrical system failure and so together they split tasks to successfully extend the gear, complete the checklists and land.
summary: During a CFI training flight, the pilot and instructor experienced pulsing radio displays and failed gear extension, prompting an emergency return to the departure airport. After the tower visually confirmed the gear was down, the instructor landed safely, attributing the successful outcome to effective crew resource management.

synopsis: As a PA-32 became airborne, the pilot noticed the front baggage door open and immediately pulled power and landed. At the FBO discovered that he had not properly closed and locked the door.
summary: The pilot aborted takeoff immediately after rotation due to an unsecured front baggage door caused by improper locking. The aircraft landed safely on the remaining runway, was re-secured on the ramp, and continued to its destination with no damage.

synopsis: Two C206 pilots conducting training discovered that the NoCal Approach frequency was switched on their Garmin G530, but they did not discover the switch until after a near miss.
summary: During a VFR training flight, two pilots inadvertently switched their Garmin G530 radio to an incorrect frequency while adjusting volume, causing them to miss a traffic advisory from NorCal Approach. This resulted in a 300-foot vertical separation with another aircraft before ATC identified the frequency error and issued the missed alert.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A corporate jet pilot reported that all FRG ATC functions were being handled by one person at a very busy time of the day, which caused extensive clearance and departure delays.
summary: The pilot reported that a single overworked controller at FRG managed Tower, Ground, and Clearance frequencies during a busy mixed-traffic day. This staffing shortage caused significant delays, late visual approach clearances, and a taxiway blockage due to frequency congestion.

synopsis: An SR22 experienced a severe electrical system malfunction which caused the loss of all communications, but the pilot was able to declare an emergency inbound.
summary: A pilot flying a Cirrus SR22 VFR experienced progressive electrical failure 55 minutes into flight, resulting in a no-flap landing and an inability to communicate with ATC. Unable to taxi normally due to construction, the pilot crossed temporary runway markers to exit, later noting that poor communication and recent maintenance may have contributed to the incident.

synopsis: C172 pilot reports a botched landing in early morning darkness with variable gusty winds. Multiple bounces occur resulting in damage to the nose strut and a flat main gear tire.
summary: The pilot of a G1000-equipped aircraft experienced a hard landing with a "pogo-stick" bounce during a gusty RNAV (GPS) approach, causing a damaged strut and flat tire. The pilot subsequently leveled the aircraft, performed a second successful landing, and had the aircraft towed off the runway by FBO personnel.

synopsis: A C172 lost all electrical during night flight and after circling the destination airport from 2,500 FT down to 1,500 FT the pilot landed without ATC clearance.
summary: A pilot lost communications and all electrical systems while entering Class B airspace at 1,500 feet. After circling without tower signals, the pilot executed a no-flap landing, noting the tower did not observe the aircraft until short final.

synopsis: A PA-28R nose landing gear indicated unsafe when lowered and remained so after troubleshooting but locked in place seconds before landing which permitted a normal landing.
summary: During a landing phase for a WINGS seminar, the pilot and co-pilot experienced a nose gear indication failure showing only two green lights. After exhausting troubleshooting and two low flybys, the pilot held the emergency gear lever on final approach, resulting in all three green lights and a safe landing.

synopsis: HS125 Captain reports misunderstanding the RUUDY 4 crossing restriction of 1,500 FT at WENTZ, thinking it is at or above, and continues to 2,000 FT. ATC informs the reporter of his error.
summary: The flight crew departed TEB on the RUUDY 4 SID and climbed to 2,000 feet MSL instead of the required 1,500 feet due to the pilot misinterpreting the departure instructions. ATC cleared the aircraft to remain at 2,000 feet, and the crew attributed the error to reading the chart incorrectly rather than following the printed text.

aircraft: Citationjet (C525/C526) - CJ I / II / III / IV
synopsis: A CE-525 pilot shut the same engine down on two consecutive flight and diverted after low oil pressure warnings from oil loss. Eventually, all accessories were replaced and the ferry flight completed.
summary: A single-pilot Cessna 525 experienced two separate in-flight low oil pressure events at FL300 and FL330, causing emergency descents and engine shutdowns. Mechanics replaced a starter generator seal and other components to fix the leak, after which a test flight confirmed no further issues.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: An IFR pilot descending through 2,000 FT into LNS had a near miss with a departing aircraft but was never alerted about its presence until he saw it pass within 300 FT.
summary: A pilot on an IFR arrival to LNS reported a near-midair conflict with a climbing Cessna while descending to the base leg for Runway 26. The pilot stated that despite LNS having radar, the tower failed to alert them to the traffic or vector the Cessna away from the arrival path.

synopsis: A BD-700's Honeywell Primus 2000 FMS missed the TEB JAIKE 13,000 FT constraint as the aircraft slowed to 250 KTS and was apparently descending and slowing so as to comply with ILENE, the next 13,000 FT constraint.
summary: Pilots on a JAIKE 3 RNAV arrival into TEB failed to cross JAIKE at 13,000 feet due to incorrect FMS VNAV calculations. They manually increased descent rate to meet the restriction after the controller intervened, noting that closer FMS monitoring would have prevented the deviation.

synopsis: An RA390 crew descending into a high altitude airport on a night VFR approach executed the EGPWS escape maneuver following a 'PULL UP' alert after 8,000 FT was set in the altitude alert instead of 9,000 FT.
summary: A fatigued Part 135 crew conducting proving runs received an EGPWS 'Pull UP' alert during a night visual approach after mis-setting the altitude bug to 8,000 feet instead of 9,000 feet. The pilot flying executed a go-around, attributing the incident to fatigue, poor night visual perception, and accepting a visual approach at an unfamiliar airport.

synopsis: C150 pilot reports a near collision after landing on a grass strip, with a high wing tail wheel aircraft taking off in the opposite direction. The reporter clears the runway to the left while the departing aircraft continues to takeoff.
summary: A Cessna 150 pilot taxiing on Runway 13 at GA2 encountered a high-wing, tailwheel aircraft taking off from Runway 31 heading directly toward them. The pilot exited the runway to avoid a collision, maintaining a 20-foot separation, attributing the conflict to the other aircraft's restricted forward vision.

synopsis: CL300 Captain reports a loss of cabin pressurization at FL410 and the resulting emergency descent and diversion to a suitable airport.
summary: The crew experienced a depressurization at FL410 while enroute 60 miles west of ZZZ. They conducted an emergency descent to 13,000 feet, squawked 7700, and diverted to ZZZ without further incident.

synopsis: F11 Controller described a go around event when traffic on final executed the procedure during heavy precipitation, the reporter indicating that efforts to land too many aircraft, given the weather, contributed to the event.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller managed two Boeing 737s on final approach to MCO Runway 35R during heavy precipitation. Separation was lost when the second aircraft descended to 1,600 feet while the first was climbing to 3,000 feet after a go-around, prompting the controller to advise stopping arrivals in extreme weather.

synopsis: Enroute Controller described a conflict event between IFR traffic that was handed off, but still in another controllers area, and unknown/unreported VFR traffic apparently participating in fire fighting activities. The reporter listed a RADAR coverage problem that may have contributed to the event.
summary: An air traffic controller failed to issue a traffic advisory for a Bonanza and an IFR firefighting aircraft, resulting in a reported 300-foot vertical near miss. The controller attributed the oversight to focusing on other traffic and delayed Conflict Alert activation due to known non-radar coverage below 11,000 feet.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described a conflict event when an adjacent Controller, receiving OJT, turned an aircraft into occupied airspace. The Controller expressed concern regarding the OJTI's minimal experience.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller working departures and arrivals reported a conflict between a BE1900 and a C750 at 3,000 feet caused by a newly certified CPC training a D Controller. The trainee incorrectly believed the C750 was climbing to 5,000 feet, allowing it to turn into the BE1900's path before the CA/CA alert triggered a climb.

synopsis: B737 flight crew, given a line up and wait clearance at a runway/taxiway intersection, misinterpreted the Local Controller's distance remaining advisory as clearance for takeoff and initiated takeoff. Controller issued a go-around to traffic approaching a crossing runway.
summary: A new Captain and First Officer initiated an unauthorized takeoff from Runway 12R Intersection D due to task saturation and misinterpreting Tower's distance remaining call as a takeoff clearance. They continued the takeoff after hearing another aircraft go around, attributing the error to high workload, unfamiliar taxi instructions, and a lack of explicit clearance verification.

aircraft: Bell Helicopter Textron Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: BHT-430 pilot inadvertantly entered IMC on a VFR approach and declared an emergency due to the fact that the helicopter was restricted to VFR flight because of an autopilot malfunction. While on an ILS approach coordinated by ATC, pilot broke out into VMC and landed VFR.
summary: A pilot flying a VFR-restricted aircraft with a deferred autopilot entered inadvertent IMC during cruise and declared an emergency. Approach provided vectors to an ILS approach, which the pilot flew using the inoperative autopilot before breaking out and landing safely.

synopsis: A BE-400XP passenger informed the crew about an extremely hot cabin sidewall and after verifying the report the Captain diverted to a nearby airport for a precautionary landing.
summary: During intermediate cruise, the Captain diverted to Kind after passengers reported overheated cabin walls caused by uncontrolled temperature despite manual full-cold settings. The aircraft landed uneventfully after the temperature normalized during descent and power reduction.

synopsis: An MD-83 flight crew accelerated toward normal climb speed in violation of the recently revised restriction of 250 KTS until advised for all departures on the O'HARE SIX SID from ORD.
summary: The flight crew departed ORD on runway 32L and exceeded the 250 KTS speed limit while climbing through 13,000 FT due to missing a revised chart restriction. After ATC advised the limit, the crew reduced speed, attributing the error to an unclear chart update that many other aircraft also missed.

synopsis: An SR20 Instructor took evasive action to miss another aircraft by 150 FT while flying at 2,500 FT near BTL Class D Airspace.
summary: A flight instructor and student experienced a near-miss while maneuvering into Battle Creek Class D airspace during autopilot training. The instructor dove to avoid converging traffic by 150 feet, attributing the incident to distraction, poor visual scan, and TCAS failure to alert.

synopsis: Both of a LR45's AHRS failed climbing out of FL310 but were recovered after the AHRS 1 and 2 AHRS circuit breakers were reset.
summary: During climb out of FL310, both pilots lost heading and navigation displays due to simultaneous AHRS failures. Resetting the AHRS circuit breakers restored all systems, though the autopilot remained in ROLL mode during the incident.

synopsis: Military aircraft inbound to NPA with slant ALPHA equipment was cleared direct to a newly developed GPS fix and then questioned by ATC reference the less than accurate track being flown.
summary: A T-39 pilot reported that while returning to Navy Pensacola, the aircraft missed the JERYS GPS fix by five miles due to TACAN-only navigation limitations. The pilot requested reverting to the TRADR TACAN fix if Houston ATC and the military cannot resolve the incompatibility between the new GPS procedure and Slant Alpha equipment.

synopsis: A C-150 engine began running rough after rotation permitting a 100 FT/minute, so the pilot turned downwind at 400 FT to land on the active runway while the Instructor advised ATC about the flight's difficulty.
summary: The pilot flying and an instructor experienced rough engine operation and poor climb performance shortly after takeoff. They returned for a safe landing on the active runway and taxied to maintenance.

synopsis: R44 helicopter flight crew experiences engine failure on liftoff and completes a forced landing.
summary: The pilot experienced a loss of main rotor RPM and power during initial climbout after takeoff, resulting in a forced landing.

synopsis: A C-208B autopilot malfunctioned on a coupled ILS so the pilot disconnected it, executed a go around and returned to land. ATC inquired about the event and was told maintenance action would follow.
summary: The pilot experienced an autopilot malfunction during an ILS approach to runway 26R, causing erratic turns and altitude oscillations. The crew executed a missed approach, successfully completed a second attempt, and reported the fault for scheduled maintenance.

synopsis: A Challenger LSA HKS 700e engine quit in flight forcing an off field landing which resulted in minor landing gear damage. The aircraft was airborne 2.5 hours with takeoff fuel for 4.5 hours, so a fuel filter fitting leak is suspected.
summary: The pilot experienced an engine failure at 2,800 feet MSL during cruise, forcing a precautionary landing that damaged the landing gear. Inspection revealed an empty fuel tank and dry filter, leading the pilot to suspect an en route fuel leak despite preflight checks showing no leaks.

synopsis: A TRACON Controller providing OJT had a probable loss of separation involving several Air Carrier aircraft and a flight of military fighters.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller training a student managed a busy final approach involving F-15s, an A320, and a Dash 8 when a military emergency caused confusion and high-speed feeds. The controller diverted aircraft to resolve the situation, noting that unclear military communications and excessive feeder speeds contributed to the chaotic environment.

synopsis: A CRW Controller is concerned about the long standing Approach Lighting System (ALS) outage, claiming users are negatively impacted by this equipment limitation.
summary: A pilot reported that the Runway 23 Approach Lighting System (ALS) has been out of service for over three years, causing access denials and raised minimums during fog. The reporter attributed this to low maintenance priority and warned of potential fatalities if the equipment is not repaired.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: Conflict developed between two air carriers conducting parallel approach procedures. The Automated Terminal Proximity Alerts (ATPA) tool introduced a measure of confusion contributing to the event.
summary: An air traffic controller misinterpreted an ATPA display while managing a turboprop on a 330-degree heading, mistakenly believing it was on final. The controller corrected the error after a CA alert, though the turboprop pilot had already responded to a TCAS alert caused by a B737 maintaining visual separation.

synopsis: A B737 First Officer reported becoming ill from WD40 chemical fumes after Maintenance treated his sticking seat track. He later found that WD40 use is not allowed in the cockpit.
summary: Maintenance heavily sprayed WD40 on the First Officer's seat tracks during a positioning leg, causing strong fumes that made both pilots nauseated during descent and subsequent ferry flights. The crew reported the smell and symptoms disappeared when the cockpit door was opened for ventilation, and Maintenance later admitted the spray was unauthorized.

synopsis: An A300 began rolling after pushback because the Mechanic did not ask the flight crew to set the parking brake before disconnecting the tug and towbar.
summary: During pushback and engine start, the aircraft rolled forward unexpectedly after the tug moved it, causing the Captain to apply brakes. The crew attributed the incident to a miscommunication where the mechanic failed to explicitly instruct them to set brakes, compounded by cockpit distraction.

synopsis: An A320 Captain refused an aircraft when a section of the inlet cowl acoustical material was found loose after the same section was temporarily repaired prior to the previous flight.
summary: The crew discovered a disintegrating acoustic repair patch on the right engine cowl that posed a foreign object damage risk. Despite Maintenance Control stating missing lining was within tolerance, the Captain refused to fly the aircraft because loose patch pieces could enter the engine.

synopsis: B747 First Officer describes a turbulence encounter with wave action, that results in the aircraft climbing 800 FT above FL350 while exceeding Mmo. The event occurred several hundred miles east of Japan over the Pacific Ocean.
summary: While cruising at FL350, the aircraft encountered moderate turbulence with extreme wave action, causing an 800-foot deviation above the assigned level and a momentary Mmo exceedance. The Captain disconnected the autopilot to avoid structural limits and successfully returned to altitude within 60 seconds.

synopsis: A B757 arrived after an ETOPS flight having used seven quarts of oil in the left engine. Maintenance talked the crew into a return flight where the aircraft was taken out of service because of the continued high oil usage.
summary: The crew departed for an ETOPS flight with a left engine showing a spiking oil consumption trend, relying on Maintenance Control's interpretation that the rate remained airworthy. Upon arrival, the engine required six quarts of oil, confirming an unsafe trend that grounded the aircraft and highlighted concerns over ambiguous guidance and economic pressure.

synopsis: An A321 Flight Attendant reported a dirty socks odor and experienced symptoms during takeoff and climb to 10,000 FT. The aircraft was removed from service at its destination.
summary: A C Flight Attendant on an A321 reported a musty odor and burning eyes during takeoff and climb to 10,000 feet, which subsided after the pilot turned off a PED. The aircraft was written up and grounded for maintenance troubleshooting, causing the outbound flight to be canceled.

synopsis: An EMB-145 Captain reported deviating below altitude assignment on arrival to JFK when they were distracted by a wake vortex encounter.
summary: The pilot not flying reported a potential 150 to 200-foot altitude deviation near DMYHL on the JFK VOR 13L approach, likely caused by wake turbulence from a preceding aircraft that was not visually acquired until 1 NM before the fix.

synopsis: A Flight Attendant reported fatigue because of multiple legs following an all night flight and as a result he felt unable to drive home safely.
summary: The pilot reported an aborted takeoff requiring a return to the gate, which extended their duty day by nearly two hours. This fatigue led to a near-car crash on the way home, prompting the pilot to criticize the carrier's scheduling of multiple legs after all-night trips.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic performing multiple tasks on two aircraft with another Mechanic was informed they had installed a replacement Passenger Seat Row that was effective for the B737 aircraft, but not at the row they had installed it.
summary: Two mechanics performed overnight maintenance on Aircraft Y, installing a seat row intended for a different location due to an incorrect MEL and fatigue. The mismatched serial number was discovered after departure, revealing that workload and time constraints caused multiple personnel to overlook the error before the aircraft flew.

synopsis: An Aircraft Inspector reported that during a C-Check, a Mechanic noticed a Firex Bottle sense line was not connected in the Forward Cargo Compartment right-hand aft sidewall. Inspector had signed-off for the Firex Bottle's Safety and Security on the A320 aircraft approximately two years earlier.
summary: During a C-Check, a mechanic found the Cargo Compartment Firex Bottle sense line was not connected as specified in Task Card Page five, Item J. The mechanic verified the safety and security of the components.

synopsis: A G-IV electric pitch trim failed while climbing into RVSM airspace which caused an altitude overshoot at FL283 so RVSM was canceled and the flight continued at FL280.
summary: During climb, the aircraft porpoised and lost electric pitch trim twice, causing autopilot disconnections and an altitude deviation to 28,300 feet. The crew hand-flew to correct the deviation, reset the trim, and descended to FL280 after declaring the aircraft no longer RVSM equipped.

synopsis: Bell-206 pilot monitoring transmissions related to a medical mission, missed an ATC advisory regarding range activity in a Restricted Area through which the pilot had previously been cleared.
summary: A pilot on an ambulance flight received clearance to transit a restricted area but was later told they flew near active ranges because the agency needed time to shut them down. The incident highlighted that special use airspace clearances may not immediately deactivate ground activities, requiring pilots to anticipate delays in range shutdowns.

synopsis: When their right engine lost power and illuminated multiple system anomaly annunciations the flight crew of an SA227 shut the engine down per checklists, declared and emergency and proceded to their destination due to superior runways and CFR facilities.
summary: During a single-pilot training leg in an SA227 Metroliner at 10,000 feet, the right engine lost power and triggered multiple warnings. The crew secured and feathered the engine, declared an emergency, and landed safely on an ILS approach with no visible external damage found post-flight.

synopsis: A Tower Controller observed a Trainee's lack of knowledge regarding light signals.
summary: A trainee Ground Controller incorrectly flashed red and green light gun signals to a NORDO C172 while issuing a taxi clearance. The supervisor intervened after noticing the error, noting the trainee was unaware the signals meant "exercise extreme caution" and required further instruction on light gun operation.

synopsis: A SJU Controller observed a departure vs. a weather balloon conflict. He now questions the procedures for releasing the balloons.
summary: An air traffic controller cleared a Caravan for takeoff from Runway 10 seconds after a weather balloon was released, placing it near the runway. The pilot executed a sharp left turn to avoid the balloon and resumed course without incident, prompting the controller to recommend immediate balloon release upon approval.

synopsis: JFK Controller described a confused take off event when an Air Carrier initiated a take off without being cleared, confused by another another Air Carrier's clearance departing an intersecting runway.
summary: An A320 on Runway 4L mistakenly read back a B757's takeoff clearance due to similar call signs and began its roll before stopping. The controller clarified the error, issued the correct clearance, and both aircraft departed safely with no loss of separation.

synopsis: A Tower Controller described a runway excursion that occurred when traffic made a touch and go exiting the runway and hitting a light.
summary: While the Local Controller and reporter discussed changing runways due to wind, a PA32 VFR aircraft slid off Runway XX during a go-around after being instructed to enter downwind for Runway YY. The aircraft damaged a runway light, and the reporter noted no Low Level Wind Shear was reported.

synopsis: ERAM anamalies provided the distraction that resulted in an airspace incursion for a ZMP Controller.
summary: An air traffic controller managing a B737 at FL370 and a Citation Jet climbing to FL450 failed to timely point out the B737 to Sector 42 due to distraction from an ERAM software bug. The controller completed the handoff late after the B737 crossed the sector boundary, attributing the error to the system malfunction.

synopsis: A single MDW Runway 22L PAPI light, second from the left, does not illuminate as brightly as the other three array lights making glide path accuracy difficult to determine.
summary: A pilot on a visual approach to Runway 22L at MDW reported that the second PAPI light from the left was dim and indistinguishable, hindering glide path determination. The reporter attributed this to a malfunctioning light and requested repairs to ensure proper guidance on the runway lacking electronic glide slope information.

synopsis: An EMB-145 flight crew, unable to raise their landing gear following receipt of an air/ground switch failure warning, returned uneventfully to their departure airport for maintenance attention.
summary: Pilots reported an EICAS 'LG AIR/GND FAIL' message immediately after takeoff, preventing landing gear retraction. They returned to the departure airport for a safe landing below maximum structural weight and notified Maintenance and Operations.

synopsis: An A319 Captain was unwilling to carry an improperly vetted and labeled cooler, allegedly containing cancer medications for a fellow employee's son, that had been inadvertently left behind when the employee left on the previous days flight. An eventual confrontation with a customer service supervisor ended abruptly when the Supervisor refused to discuss the Captain's concerns further, grabbed the cooler and exited the aircraft.
summary: The Captain reported that an unmarked cooler containing medicine was placed in the cockpit by a gate agent and Customer Service Manager without proper screening or tags. This security breach caused a 45-minute departure delay and was resolved when the manager removed the cooler after the Captain questioned its compliance with TSA and FAA requirements.

synopsis: IWA Air Carrier IFR arrival experienced a conflict event with traffic apparently engaged in fire fighting activities, the reporter suggesting this type of activity be briefed to crews flying in the area.
summary: During descent on the JCOBS 2 arrival, the crew received a TA alert for a C-130 at 11,500 FT that ATC had not advised due to a missing Mode C transponder. The First Officer stopped the descent, passing the aircraft at 400 FT, while the pilot noted that wildfire activity and lack of ATIS warnings reduced situational awareness.

synopsis: ATL Air Carrier arrival reported a 'below Class B speed infraction' when failing to correctly identify his/her position relative to the airspace.
summary: The First Officer reported that during the CANUK arrival into Atlanta, the aircraft briefly descended below the 8,000-foot Class B shelf while maintaining 250 KIAS, violating the 200 KIAS speed limit. The incident was caused by high workload and fatigue on the fifth leg of a 12-hour duty day, which impaired situational awareness regarding the aircraft's position relative to airspace shelves.

synopsis: CRJ-200 had a 'HYD 2 LO PRESS' caution message climbing through FL250. The crew complied with QRH procedures and diverted to the nearest suitable airport, landing with the number two hydraulic system failed due to loss of fluid.
summary: During climb through FL250 in a CRJ-200, the crew encountered a HYD 2 LO PRESS caution and subsequent pressure loss causing a noticeable attitude shift. Following QRH procedures, they declared an emergency, landed safely on the longest runway, and were escorted to the gate.

synopsis: When the Captain's side window shattered at about 10,500 MSL on the climbout the flight crew of an E-145 opted to return to their departure airport for maintenance.
summary: The Pilot Not Flying reported that the Captain's side windshield shattered at 10,500 feet during climb, causing an emergency return and overweight landing by the First Officer. No bird strike was found during post-flight inspection, and passengers remained calm throughout the event.

synopsis: Bell-407 pilot initially missed sighting the destination hospital while utilizing GPS and night vision goggles in a well-lit city environment. Pilot may have also inadvertantly infringed on nearby Class D airspace.
summary: A pilot flying a medical helicopter under night vision goggles overflew the destination hospital by one mile and likely entered Class D airspace due to inadvertent radio pin switch failure and poor crew coordination. The pilot returned to the hospital without establishing contact with ATC, noting that better communication and an advisory call would have prevented the airspace incursion.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Air Carrier experiencing equipment difficulties requested ATC to keep approach/landing area sterile most likely prompting ATC to initiate emergency handling
summary: The crew received a radar vector to Runway XX at 4,000 feet MSL when a lost CA RA input triggered CONFIG warnings and sirens. The Captain extended landing gear early to silence the alerts, requested a sterile approach, and later contacted Tower by phone.

synopsis: Air Carrier experienced a number of equipment failures and notified ATC of a request to keep the area sterile, the event handled as an emergency with all participants handling the event as required.
summary: During the ILS approach to Runway XX from 3,800 feet, the crew received gear unsafe warnings, lost the Captain's flight director, and heard a siren. Extending the landing gear cleared all warnings, allowing for an uneventful landing after the Captain requested the sterile area remain clear.

synopsis: Wide Body Aircraft Captain is informed by ATC aircraft is reentering Class B after having been out of it. Reporter comments on the difficulty of monitoring Class B in the flight deck with current instruments.
summary: A pilot vectored for a visual approach to Runway 27 at MEM was advised by ATC they had briefly exited and re-entered Class B airspace during descent from 4,000 to 3,000 feet. The reporter attributes this to the lack of practical real-time tools for pilots to detect their position relative to Class B airspace boundaries.

synopsis: A Lead Mechanic was informed he had not provided enough information in the logbook and maintenance computer to explain the cause of an 'Eng Grd/Flt Idle Cont' Circuit Breaker (C/B) to open (pop) on a DC-10 aircraft and justify deferring # 3 Engine's Main Engine Control (MEC) GRD/Flt Idle solenoid. All three engines had defaulted to the Flight Idle mode on landing.
summary: A mechanic troubleshooting a popped Engine Ground/Flight Idle Control circuit breaker on a DC-10 identified a faulty #3 engine solenoid and deferred the engine per MEL. Although maintenance procedures were completed, the mechanic failed to document the incident details in the aircraft logbook due to multiple simultaneous events and departure pressure.

synopsis: A Lancair pilot departing on a IFR flight plan experienced an NMAC with a Cessna single flying a practice approach to a different runway.
summary: The pilot of a Lancair Evolution climbing to 2,000 MSL after takeoff narrowly avoided a Cessna drifting across the runway end during a practice approach. The reporter attributed the conflict to the controller's failure to warn of the Cessna and unfamiliarity with the Lancair's high climb performance.

synopsis: A C172 pilot extended his downwind to allow the aircraft ahead to simulate an engine out gliding approach. Turning base well beyond the point at which the other aircraft turned base, the reporter lost sight of the traffic but continued the approach to landing. Upon rolling out the reporter was informed by the pilot of the other aircraft that he had to go around due to the close proximity of the reporter's aircraft on final.
summary: The pilot reported a potential conflict with another aircraft during a touch-and-go at a non-towered airport. While the pilot believed they maintained separation, the other pilot claimed the reporter came too close on final, forcing a go-around, though the reporter disputed this based on visual observations and distance.

synopsis: A C-150 pilot opted to declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable airport, a military field, following a significant loss of power due to a swallowed valve in the number two cylinder.
summary: The pilot experienced significant engine power loss at 5,500 feet due to a stuck open #2 cylinder exhaust valve. After declaring an emergency and coordinating with FSS, the pilot successfully landed at a nearby military airport.

synopsis: A Mechanic reports that a full Landing Gear swing was not accomplished, as required per Gulfstream's Computerized Maintenance Program (CMP), on a G-V aircraft after replacement of the Nose Gear Door Actuator. Maintenance Manager said the cycling of Nose Gear Doors was good enough.
summary: A mechanic replaced the nose gear actuator door but did not perform the required landing gear swing, as the Maintenance Manager deemed cycling the doors sufficient. Consequently, the aircraft was released without completing Step-E (5) of the Gulfstream CMP Card.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: S46 Controller described a very busy traffic period when supervisors were apparently unaware of the building traffic and taking no action to assist, the reporter noting a continued lack of attentive supervision in the control room.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller reported excessive workload while managing combined arrival positions for Seattle, Boeing, and Paine airports under new procedures. The controller attributed the situation to a Supervisor's failure to proactively split positions or provide assistance despite rising traffic volume.

synopsis: B737-300 flight crew experiences a LE Flap Transit light when the flaps are set after engine start. The flaps are cycled at the direction of maintenance and the light disappears, only to reappear at rotation causing a momentary stick shaker. The light disappears again prior to flap retraction and does not reappear again although the crew elects to make a precautionary emergency landing at destination using flaps 15 and Vref15 + 5 as the approach speed.
summary: The flight crew experienced a #2 LE Slat failure and momentary stall warning immediately after rotation on takeoff with flaps 1. They declared an emergency, followed the QRH for a flaps 15 landing with maximum autobrake, and landed safely with emergency crews standing by.

synopsis: While taxiing for takeoff at ORD an A320 Captain had to brake abruptly to avoid a collision with an employee shuttle bus crossing the taxiway ahead of them.
summary: The flight crew at ORD stopped the aircraft abruptly while taxiing on taxiway A to avoid a collision with an employee shuttle bus that surged onto the taxiway. The bus stopped one-third across the taxiway, and no cabin crew were injured during the emergency stop.

aircraft: Citationjet (C525/C526) - CJ I / II / III / IV
synopsis: A CE525 departed on the TEB RUUDY 4 following an extensive ATC reroute during taxi and subseqent FMS reprogramming but forgot to level off at 1,500 FT and were told by ATC at 2,000 FT to descend.
summary: The flight crew departed Runway 24 TEB on the RUUDY 4 and crossed WENTZ at 2,000 feet instead of 1,500 due to an incorrect altitude setting. This error resulted from a rushed departure brief, FMS programming distractions, and pressure to depart on time during late-night IMC conditions.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An Air Carrier crew executed an IMC go around after failing to remain VMC on the DCA River Visual and, because no missed approach procedure was specified, were extremely task saturated keeping up with the aircraft and ATC's instructions.
summary: A fatigued crew executing a River Visual 19 approach at DCA initiated a missed approach due to cloud layers, resulting in a flap overspeed to 240 knots caused by task saturation, conflicting RNAV availability information, and autopilot disengagement. The crew subsequently landed safely after ATC provided vectoring and altitude clearances.

synopsis: Two pilots report about a Flap Handle positioning problem that arose during approach on their DC-10 aircraft. After slat extension, the Flap Handle could only be moved while rotating the Dial-a-Flap thumb wheel.
summary: During an ILS approach to Runway 36L, the crew encountered a binding flap handle that required rotating the Dial-a-Flap thumb wheel to extend flaps. Despite high speed and workload, they completed checklists and executed a manual landing, later logging the flight control binding for maintenance.

synopsis: Following the failure of the left main gear safe light to illuminate upon gear extension, a B757-200 flight crew performed a go around, declared an emergency and landed safely despite their inability to resolve the anomaly using checklist procedures.
summary: During an ILS approach to Runway 15, the crew noted a missing left main gear indication light and executed a go-around. After tower visual confirmation that the gear was down, they declared an emergency and landed safely with fire services standing by.

synopsis: An Air Carrier Engine Shop Mechanic questions an in-house blend repair on a PW-2000 Engine 7th Stage Compressor blade that was found damaged, bent on the knife edge of the blade. Per their Air Carrier Engine Inspection paperwork, the blade could only be repaired by an Outside Vendor (OSV).
summary: A mechanic reported that an inspector performed an unauthorized blend repair on a damaged 7th stage blade, violating Pratt & Whitney Manual 72-53-42 which requires Outside Vendor repair. The blade remains slightly bent, and the reporter noted the repair lacked authority under the Engine Inspection paperwork.

synopsis: CL604 corporate Captain reported a wake vortex encounter when crossing the path of a B747 at FL230.
summary: The pilot reported striking B747 wake turbulence during a climb after ATC cleared them to 1,000 feet below the heavy aircraft. The encounter caused a sharp jolt and minor pitch and roll deviations, but no passengers were on board as it was a positioning flight.

synopsis: A Cessna Turbo 210 pilot suffered a track deviation when he misprogrammed his IFR route into the aircraft's GPS based navigation system. ATC advised of the deviations and the reporter corrected the error.
summary: The pilot omitted the Cutbank waypoint when programming the aircraft GPS for an IFR flight from Great Falls to Springbank, causing a deviation toward Lethbridge. An air traffic controller queried the position, revealing the error and prompting the pilot to correct the route.

synopsis: A C-170 pilot became concerned that his fuel system was malfunctioning and so landed at the nearest suitable airport which turned out to be towered but he confused it with a similarly named nearby CTAF airport.
summary: A pilot delivering an aircraft for maintenance diverted to a towered airport due to a suspected fuel gauge failure, but contacted the wrong frequency because two airports shared the same name. The pilot landed safely, refueled, and departed after realizing the error, attributing the incident to confusion over airport names and a focus on avoiding fuel exhaustion.

synopsis: ZFW Controller described a loss of separation event when attempts to provide weather deviations resulted in a conflict.
summary: An air traffic controller lost separation between two aircraft during a severe weather deviation while managing a climb and turn. The controller attributed the incident to prioritizing the climb before the turn, using an insufficient 40-degree turn for a 40-knot overtake, and fatigue from an extended shift.

synopsis: CID Controller reported LAHSO markings on Runway 31 create confusion as LAHSO is not permitted on Runway 31.
summary: An SR20 crossed unnecessary LAHSO hold lines on Runway 31 while back-taxiing near a departing aircraft on Runway 9. The controller reported that these markings on a non-LAHSO runway created confusion and concern, though the SR20 slowed and turned before reaching the intersection.

aircraft: Regional Jet CL65; Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: ZID Controller witnessed an unsafe condition when adjacent sectors were combined for training and handoffs were not completed as required, the reporter stating the combined sectors should have been split long before the event.
summary: A Radar Controller at IND/HI intervened to separate traffic after an over-tasked trainee failed to maintain separation during a combined sector training session. The incident resulted from the trainee's inability to handle live traffic volume and the supervisor's refusal to split the sector, creating an unsafe environment.

synopsis: En route Controller provided emergency handling to an aircraft experiencing equipment difficulties.
summary: An air traffic controller treated Aircraft X as an emergency after the pilot reported a maintenance issue while at 35,000 feet entering Center airspace. The controller cleared the aircraft to descend to 34,500 feet and turn right direct ZZnZZw.

synopsis: Controller witnessed a loss of runway separation event, indicating the Local Controller froze up, failing to acknowledge the developing situation.
summary: A Ground Controller reported a runway incursion where a B767 reached the departure end of Runway 27 while a B737 was landing on the same runway. The incident occurred because the newly qualified Local Controller froze, failed to communicate the conflict, and had a history of struggling with traffic management.

synopsis: ZAU Controller described a TCAS RA event involving a military tanker operation break up maneuver. The reporter suggested increased training for facility personnel covering these types of procedures.
summary: An air traffic controller cleared a military tanker to climb to 39,000 feet while another tanker in the refueling track responded to a resolution advisory. The incident highlighted a need for definitive training on managing uncommon military operations to prevent confusion in active airspace.

synopsis: NCT Controller described a possible MVA infraction involving a SQL departure routed via V334. The reporter noted recent MVA increases and limited airspace make this routing difficult to handle and suggests formalized SIDs to ease workload.
summary: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft Y, an SR22/G, left instead of right, causing a temporary loss of communication before the pilot corrected the turn. The controller also noted Aircraft X entered a 4,100 FT MVA while climbing to 4,000 FT, prompting a recommendation for new departure procedures to mitigate risks in this complex airspace.

synopsis: A320 Captain reports returning to the departure airport after an ELAC1 fault, which had occurred several times previously to this aircraft.
summary: During climb through 13,000 feet, the crew felt a vertical jolt followed by an ELAC 1 fault. They coordinated with Dispatch and Maintenance Control to return for an overweight landing, which was completed uneventfully after performing required checklists.

synopsis: An A320 flight crew rejected their takeoff due to the loss of FMC generated V speeds on their ASIs.
summary: The flight crew aborted takeoff at 70 knots when FMC V speeds disappeared from the Airspeed Indicators. The aircraft returned to the gate for maintenance to resolve the display failure.

synopsis: Another A320 Captain experiences the loss of both FMGC's during approach when the 'no star' function is used to clean up the approach after being vectored off an arrival.
summary: A pilot reported simultaneous dual FMS failures on an Airbus during approach at CLE and SEA after selecting 'No Star' and attempting to clear waypoints. The failures caused navigation and pressurization data loss, which the pilot suspects stems from a systemic software or database issue triggered by this specific procedure.

synopsis: Air Carrier taxiing for departure at TPA questioned ATC's lack of runway information contained in the taxi clearance. ATC responded that the runway information was contained on the ATIS and not required in the taxi clearance.
summary: The pilot reported that Tampa Ground issued incomplete taxi instructions omitting the runway, leading to a heated exchange when the controller insisted the active runway was implied by the ATIS. The pilot concluded that the controller failed to use standard phraseology by not explicitly clearing the aircraft to Runway 18R.

synopsis: An SF340 developed a number 2 engine vibration after takeoff so the engine was shutdown, an emergency declared, and the flight returned to the departure airport.
summary: The flight crew experienced severe vibrations on climbout, isolated to engine #2, and executed an emergency return to the departure airport. A post-landing inspection revealed a loose propeller blade on the affected engine.

synopsis: An EMB-145 flight crew failed to conduct the checklist for an EICAS ice system message when it disappeared on its own prior to takeoff. After takeoff additional EICAS and ICE protections messages illuminated and fuel burn became excessive to the point they decided to land short of their destination for fuel.
summary: The flight crew incorrectly executed the QRH for a transient anti-ice message during taxi, leading to continued flight with active ice protection advisories and unexpected fuel burn. They diverted for fuel, declared an emergency due to poor deceleration, and landed safely after gear extension cleared the messages.

synopsis: A B737-800 First Officer immediately shut down the right engine when he noted the forward cargo door was being opened by ground crew prior to setting the parking brake and shutting down the engines.
summary: During final taxi with both engines running, the First Officer observed the forward cargo door light illuminate and immediately shut down the right engine. A subsequent ramp inspection confirmed no injuries occurred.

synopsis: When faced with a pilot induced need to choose between track perfection versus avoiding an approach to a stall while flying the CLARE RNAV SID off Runway 17R at DFW, the Captain chose the latter and limited bank angle to avoid a flaps up approach to a stall. The First Officer and Relief Pilot worried over, and continually reminded the Captain, of the resultant track deviation.
summary: The Captain of a Boeing 767-300 deviated 1.5 NM from the Clare RNAV SID at DFW while manually limiting bank angles to maintain airspeed during a turn over TREXX. The deviation occurred because the Captain selected HDG Select mode to avoid stall buffet, a decision attributed to rusty airmanship after a month-long absence.

synopsis: A DC-10 flight crew took appropriate QRH actions when they received a fire warning on the number two engine as they taxied into position for takeoff. The warning was ultimately determined to have been false.
summary: The crew received a #2 engine fire indication while taxiing to hold Runway 25R, despite an MEL locking out detection loop B. After discharging a fire bottle and a negative CFR heat scan, a second warning occurred and persisted at the gate.

synopsis: A B757-200 Captain reported he missed a speed restriction on arrival into LAX when he was distracted by a wake turbulence encounter.
summary: The flight crew descended via the RIIVR arrival to Runway 25L in VNAV PATH while encountering wake turbulence. Distraction from minimizing wake effects caused slow deceleration, resulting in crossing GRAMM Intersection faster than the 280 KIAS restriction.

synopsis: Captain reports a BLEED-1 LEAK EICAS message appeared in their ERJ-190 aircraft while climbing through the mid 20s, followed by a BLEED-2 LEAK EICAS message ten minutes later. Flight crew diverted. Maintenance discovered leaks on both Bleed-1 and 2 Precoolers. Captain questions if a design or manufacturing defect exists in precoolers.
summary: Pilots experienced simultaneous Bleed 1 and 2 leaks during climb, causing cabin altitude to rise at 500 FPM to 10,300 feet. They descended to 10,000 feet and diverted after maintenance confirmed failures in both bleed precoolers, suggesting a potential design defect.

synopsis: An E-145 First Officer discusses the debilitating effects of abusive flight time and duty time schedules, bad weather, equipment problem, lack of food and other factors which combine to decrease the capability of flight crews to safely transport their passengers.
summary: Pilots reported fatigue and missed radio calls during a four-day trip involving severe weather, maintenance delays, and lack of crew meals. They refused an aircraft with inoperative windshear systems and ultimately called in fatigued due to cumulative sleep deprivation and operational stress.

synopsis: An E-145 Flight Crew rejected their takeoff and returned to the gate following the failure of the right engine as power was advanced at the start of their takeoff roll.
summary: The Captain experienced a right engine failure with an ENG 2 OUT EICAS message while advancing throttles for takeoff, despite all indications being normal. The crew aborted the takeoff, completed the checklist, and returned to the gate.

synopsis: A CRJ-200 Captain reported encountering significant wake turbulence following a B757 into ATL.
summary: A CRJ-200 pilot encountered moderate wake turbulence from an unannounced B757 at 7,500 feet on downwind to ATL, causing a 45-degree roll that struck a flight attendant's shoulder. The pilot recovered smoothly without injury or damage, attributing the event to ATC silence due to frequency congestion.

synopsis: Following multiple revised taxi clearances at IAH the flight crew of a B767-300 found themselves on NR which is restricted for use by aircraft with wingspans greater than 125 FT.
summary: The flight crew taxied an aircraft with a wingspan exceeding 125 feet onto Taxiway NR, which has a restriction for such aircraft, due to unclear markings and multiple routing changes. Ground Control stopped the aircraft, and airport operations provided wingwalkers to safely move the aircraft to the correct route.

synopsis: A ground crew headset, previously noted as 'giving them trouble' may have contributed to a breakdown in communication between the flight and ground crews when an engine start at a remote location at night ran amok due to uncommanded movement of the aircraft.
summary: The flight crew attempted an engine start using a ground air cart while parked remotely. Ground personnel warned of aircraft movement via a faulty headset, but the crew only stopped the engine after seeing smoke from the right wing, leading to an evacuation.

synopsis: A commuter jet flight crew experienced the failure of the flaps to extend to a normal landing setting. They opted to land on their destination airport's 8,000 FT runway as their AOM indicated they would need only 6,000 FT of runway to come to a stop based on the setting at which the flaps had failed. After coming to a stop using maximum effort braking they had 2,000 FT of runway remaining.
summary: The flight crew experienced a 'Flaps Fail' message during visual approach configuration at AVL, resulting in a landing with flaps stuck at 17. They elected not to declare an emergency, landing at the 2,000 FT marker with maximum braking that triggered white Brake Temperature Monitoring System indicators.

synopsis: ERJ-170 flight crew ingested a bird and suffered engine failure shortly after liftoff. They ran the QRH, secured the engine, and returned to departure airport.
summary: The First Officer and Captain experienced an Engine #2 failure due to a bird strike shortly after takeoff gear retraction. They declared an emergency, returned to the departure airport, and landed safely with no fire or significant damage reported.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew heard and read back clearance from Center Controller to 'climb to 280.' During subsequent climb, Controller advised flight crew that the clearance was for 'heading 280.'
summary: During climb, the crew misinterpreted a heading 280 clearance as a climb to FL280, ascending to 18,200 feet before ATC ordered a descent to 17,000 feet. The pilots attributed the incident to a misunderstanding of the controller's instruction despite their belief that they correctly read back the clearance.

synopsis: A large Flight Attendant discovered his assigned jump seat harness was jammed and unusable for someone of his stature. When other duties prevented him from attempting to fix the jam he was compelled to sit in another seat contrary to SOP. He ultimately left the aircraft with the seat belt still jammed after completion of his flights.
summary: A flight attendant found a jammed shoulder harness at jump seat 1 left inboard during preflight, preventing safe restraint due to their stature. They utilized the outboard seat for takeoff and landing, later verifying the defect with a local representative.

synopsis: A Q400 flight attendant was injured during climb after a service cart fell over on her ankle in smooth air because the brake apparently failed to hold the already unstable cart.
summary: A cabin crew member was injured during the climb phase above 10,000 feet when a service cart flipped onto their ankle despite the brake being set. The reporter attributes the incident to unstable carts and recommends prohibiting service until the aircraft levels out or replacing the equipment.

synopsis: A Lead Mechanic was asked if he would 'look at' Engine Fire Bottle Squibs that had been installed approximately one week earlier on an ATR aircraft and to sign-off for the RII Inspection requirement that had not accomplished at the time of installation.
summary: Lead Mechanic X refused to sign off a Required Inspection Item (RII) for an ATR aircraft's fire bottle squib replacement performed previously at another station. The mechanic cited unfamiliarity with the ATR procedure and concerns that backdating the inspection violated regulations, leading to a remote verification by Lead Mechanic Z instead.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic reports that his lack of experience with understanding two deferrals for an A300 aircraft contributed to his changing only the Engine Nacelle Cooling Valve on the outboard Reverser half of #1 engine, even though both Cooling valves were locked 'Open'.
summary: A vendor mechanic working alone on an A300 replaced only one of two locked-open Nacelle Cooling Valves due to confusion over MELs and diagrams. The aircraft flew ten flights over six days before a vendor mechanic discovered the second valve was locked closed, with no safety event occurring.

aircraft: Airbus Industrie Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Line Mechanic explains a logbook sign-off and the troubleshooting procedures he used to address a 'DFDR OFF' light that would not illuminate and a Windshear Alert Warning that would not test properly on an Airbus aircraft, at departure time. A pilot also reports he wrote-up both discrepancies on the same logbook sheet instead of two separate Log sheets.
summary: A mechanic troubleshooting an Airbus pre-departure DFDR and windshear alert failure found debris in an engine oil pressure switch connector causing false engine running indications. Although the mechanic cleaned the connector and verified system functionality, time pressure led to an incomplete logbook sign-off regarding the multiple reported discrepancies.

synopsis: General Aviation aircraft experiencing landing gear difficulties questioned ATC's 'emergency' declaration that resulted in inquiries from the local FAA FSDO.
summary: The pilot experienced an unsafe nose gear indication during approach but landed safely after the gear held. The pilot reported that Air Traffic Control incorrectly classified the incident as an emergency without a pilot declaration, raising concerns about FAA policy and pilot-in-command authority.

synopsis: SD3 First Officer reports loosing 400 feet from FL190 while passing between thunderstorms in IMC with with some moderate down drafts. The engines were operating near their limits, delaying the return to assigned altitude.
summary: Pilots flying a cargo aircraft at FL190 encountered a moderate downdraft while deviating for weather between thunderstorm cells near Houston. The event caused a 400-foot altitude loss and high turbine temperatures, but the crew returned to FL190 and completed the flight to Shreveport without further incident.

synopsis: LR60 Captain reported and uncontrolled 800 FT climb from FL290 because of updraft.
summary: Pilots flying at FL290 encountered an unexpected updraft causing an uncontrollable vertical ascent of 700 to 800 feet. After regaining control and returning to the assigned altitude, they confirmed all passengers were safe and continued to the destination without further incident.

synopsis: PA-28 pilot experienced high cylinder head temperature followed by engine vibration in cruise flight. He declared an emergency and made a successful engine out landing at a nearby airfield.
summary: The pilot of a Piper Arrow III with two passengers declared an emergency during climb at 8,500 feet after cylinder #3 overheated and failed, causing severe vibration. The engine subsequently seized on final approach, but the pilot executed a power-off landing at an alternate airport using a forward slip to dissipate energy.

synopsis: P28R pilot lost #3 cylinder, shut down the engine, and diverted dead stick to an appropriate nearby airport.
summary: The pilot of a Piper Arrow III with two passengers declared an emergency during climb at 8,500 feet after cylinder #3 overheated and failed, causing severe vibration. The engine subsequently seized on final approach, but the pilot executed a power-off landing at ZZZ airport using a forward slip to dissipate energy.

synopsis: A Cessna 350 pilot departing from a non-towered airport suffered an NMAC with a high wing single taking off opposite direction from the same runway. After the event, both pilots declared themselves to have been utilizing appropriate CTAF procedures, declaring their position and intentions prior to their takeoffs.
summary: The pilot and a pilot-passenger experienced a near mid-air collision with an opposing aircraft during takeoff from Runway 34 at Yolo County. The reporter attributed the event to the other pilot failing to transmit on CTAF, combined with his own distraction from conversation and failure to maintain a sterile cockpit.

synopsis: Insufficient training in the recently highly modified BE-40 and rushed cockpit preflight and checklist procedures during a short taxi for takeoff resulted in the flight crew failing to reset both generators after performing a 'silent' checklist conducted solo by the First Officer. As a result, shortly after takeoff they suffered the loss of both FMS's and their associated NAV displays in IMC as battery power was drained.
summary: The flight crew of a modified aircraft experienced a total electrical failure shortly after takeoff from Zurich due to unreset generators following a checklist item. They executed an emergency landing using alternate gear extension, but subsequent tire fuse plugs blew while waiting on the taxiway, requiring the aircraft to be towed.

synopsis: Following the temporary loss of electrical power and subsequent difficulty utilizing the emergency landing gear extension procedure of his PA24-180, the pilot was unable to prevent the aircraft from exiting the runway during the landing. He rolled onto a taxiway and no damage resulted.
summary: The pilot experienced total electrical failure shortly after takeoff at a towered airport, requiring emergency gear extension and multiple fly-bys before landing. While manually holding the gear down to prevent retraction, the pilot could not operate the hand brake or flaps, resulting in an excursion onto the grass before taxiing to the ramp.

synopsis: PA-24 pilot reported engine failure at 8,500 FT in cruise. Pilot declared an emergency, was unable to make it to an airport, and landed in an open field with no damage or injuries.
summary: The pilot experienced a hard engine failure at 8,500 feet due to a loss of fuel pressure despite switching tanks and troubleshooting. After declaring an emergency and descending, the pilot successfully executed an off-airport landing in a field to avoid obstacles, resulting in no injuries or aircraft damage.

synopsis: A Mechanic requests his Supervisor initiate a maintenance follow-up to inspect the Nose Wheel Handle Steering, Upper Torque Shaft coupling attach rivets for damage on a company B757-200 aircraft. He had initially applied a Torque Test on the Torque Limiter without disconnecting the nose gear Upper Torsion Link first.
summary: A mechanic suspected Nose Wheel Tiller Shaft damage after failing to raise the Upper Torsion Link during an AMM 32-51-00-735 steering test, causing the torque wrench to jump and cam rollers to remain stationary. The team subsequently scheduled an inspection of the shaft between the Load Limiter and Tiller Handle per IPC 32-51-01-05.

synopsis: King air Captain experiences an explosive loss of cabin pressure climbing through 16,000 FT and initiates an emergency descent. ATC is notified and the flight diverts to a suitable airport.
summary: During a normal climb between 16,000 and 18,000 feet, the pilot experienced an explosive loss of cabin pressure. The pilot initiated an emergency descent to 10,000 feet, diverted to ZZZ for maintenance, and continued unpressurized in VMC.

synopsis: ZLC Controller described a probable MIA infraction involving an EKO VFR departure requesting IFR. The reporter acknowledged that a more thorough scan of the MIA minimums on his part may have prevented the event.
summary: An air traffic controller issued a climb to 12,000 feet to an aircraft departing VFR from EKO Airport, inadvertently placing it below a 12,600-foot MIA polygon. The controller later corrected the clearance to 13,000 feet after an MSAW alert, attributing the error to a failure to thoroughly scan MIA polygons due to high workload.

synopsis: Tower CIC described a go-around event resulting from the Local Controller's questionable spacing judgment between an arrival and departing aircraft.
summary: The CIC and Local Controller managed a near-loss of separation between two E145s on Runway 24L when a departure was launched between closely spaced arrivals. The incident resulted from poor spacing decisions, delayed go-around instructions, and controller inexperience, causing confusion and an AMASS alarm.

synopsis: LAX Controller described an airspace infraction when an aircraft departing on the FIXIT1 RNAV departure was not issued the required heading. The reporter noted that the RNAV SID sets controllers up for errors.
summary: An LC1 controller failed to issue a required 250-degree heading to an Air Carrier X aircraft on a FIXIT1 RNAV departure. The aircraft subsequently turned 219 degrees into DR1 airspace instead of DR2, prompting the controller to call for the procedure's suspension due to systemic safety flaws.

synopsis: ZOB Controller reported clearing an aircraft 'Direct Charleston' expecting him to navigate to HVQ, but the aircraft set up course for CHS. Both VORs are Charleston, and both were on the filed route, so reporter recommends changing the name of one of the VORs.
summary: An air traffic controller issued a direct clearance to Charleston VOR for a weather-deviating flight, but the pilot proceeded to CHS instead of the intended HVQ. The controller attributed the error to the identical names of both VORs and recommended renaming or phonetically spelling them to prevent confusion.

synopsis: MDW Controller described a mandatory ASDE Alert go around, the reporter noting the alarm activated when the subject traffic was still on base and the departure was rolling.
summary: Local Control issued takeoff clearances to Aircraft X, which delayed its roll, while Aircraft Y was on a tight base leg. An ASDE alert triggered a go-around for Aircraft Y, though the system later determined the alert occurred while Y was on base rather than final.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: ZMP Controller described a possible airspace incursion with an adjacent sector when a flight of military aircraft participating in a refueling exercise requested a break-up. The reporter listed complexity, volume, and unfamiliarity as causal factors.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller in Sector 10 managed complex traffic including an unplanned aerial refueling breakup and MSP departures while using ERAM. The controller attributed distractions to delayed flight plan data, unpassed strips, and new crossing restrictions, though separation was maintained.

synopsis: A B737-700 flight crew, cleared for a visual approach from a long left base to MAF Runway 16R, determined they were too high and requested a 270 degree turn to lose altitude and establish a stabilized approach. While doing so they allowed their altitude to get too low and the Tower advised of a low altitude alert. They corrected their rate of descent and contintued to an uneventful landing.
summary: During a visual approach to Runway 16R at MAF, the crew misjudged pattern altitude at 4,000 feet MSL while turning to final, prompting a Tower altitude alert. The Captain leveled off near radio towers, climbed to 4,500 feet, and subsequently corrected the glidepath for a normal landing without ground proximity warnings.

synopsis: A B737-500 flight crew was unable to locate Taxiway F at DTW. After seeking assistance from Ground Control they located a painted ramp marking for F which was not consistent with the location depicted on their commercially produced airport page.
summary: The flight crew at DTW became confused while taxiing to Runway 3R because Taxiway F was located differently than depicted on their charts. They stopped to request clarification from Ground Control, performed a 180-degree turn, and eventually found the taxiway near the de-ice ramp without traffic conflicts.

synopsis: When confronted with multiple system anomalies--including an FMS position error and the failure of the pressurization system--shortly after takeoff, the flight crew of a B737-300 declared an emergency, initiated an emergency descent from FL230, and returned to their departure airport.
summary: The flight crew experienced multiple system failures, including IRS, TCAS, and GPWS, followed by a cabin altitude warning at FL230. They declared an emergency, descended to 7,000 feet, and returned to LAX for an overweight landing after systems eventually recovered.

synopsis: Dash 8 Captain reported receiving a low oil pressure light on Number 2 engine during takeoff roll. Takeoff was rejected, and the problem was solved when oil was added.
summary: The flight crew rejected takeoff just prior to rotation when the Number 2 engine oil pressure warning light illuminated due to low oil quantity. The aircraft stopped with over 3,000 feet of runway remaining, was returned to the gate for oil replenishment, and subsequently passed an engine run-up with normal indications.

synopsis: A B737-800 Captain reported a sparking/smoking coffee maker in the aft galley prior to leaving the gate. The Flight Attendant shut off the device and pulled the associated CB. After inspection by CFR and the removal of the unit the flight departed.
summary: During the before-start checklist, a Flight Attendant reported fire, sparks, and smoke from an aft galley coffee maker and isolated power. A mechanic removed the unit with burnt wiring, and the aircraft departed after the Fire Chief determined no active fire existed.

synopsis: First Officer reports that pilots do not have any place or resource to go to get unbiased information about Airworthiness concerns of their aircraft. An outer pane of a Captain's forward windshield was found cracked on their BBD-700 aircraft, Speed Tape was applied. An Engineer, the Director of Maintenance (DOM), Director of Operations and Designated Airworthiness Representative (DAR) OK'd the aircraft to be flown to Home Base without any technical data.
summary: The pilot reported a cracked outer windshield pane on a Bombardier aircraft, which was taped and flown at 250 KTS and 26,000 FT to Home Base. Maintenance and the DAR stated no ferry permit was required as the outer pane is non-structural, though the pilot expressed concern about the lack of available technical data and potential misinformation.

aircraft: Cessna Single Piston Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An instructor pilot aboard a C-162 Skycatcher lost track of his position relative to HPN--their departure airport--while giving basic flight training to a Student Pilot. As a result a possible NMAC with an inbound jet arrival occurred.
summary: A flight instructor and student in a Cessna 162 drifted east of course near the Hudson River while monitoring Tower frequency, causing a close call with an arriving jet at HPN. The instructor attributed the incident to losing track of their position and forgetting that traffic was arriving on Runway 16.

synopsis: When the autopilot failed to capture a crossing restriction altitude on a TEB SID the flight crew was forced to manually attempt to return to the charted alititude. ATC assisted by clearing them to a higher altitude.
summary: The pilot flying on a TEB8 departure from TEB disengaged the autopilot after it failed to capture an imminent altitude restriction. ATC subsequently assigned a higher altitude of 3,000 MSL, prompting the pilot to plan reduced climb rates and closer monitoring for future departures.

synopsis: Local Controller described a conflict event where an Air Carrier on final requested a 360 for altitude loss and eventually conflicted with following traffic on downwind, the reporter acknowledging a loss of situational awareness.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller managing Air Carrier X on final for Runway XXR and Aircraft Y on a visual approach for Runway XXL failed to issue traffic advisories due to distraction by departures. Consequently, Air Carrier X overshot the final approach and passed slightly ahead of Aircraft Y, requiring the controller to establish visual separation for wake turbulence.

synopsis: HCF Controller described a below MVA event when traffic issued a VOR A approach into MKK executed an incorrect turn on a Missed Approach Procedure.
summary: An ATC controller reported that Aircraft X deviated from the VOR A missed approach by turning right instead of left, entering a 7,000 FT MVA while requesting a visual approach. Although the pilot was cleared for a visual at 2,800 FT MSL and no separation loss occurred with overflying ACR Y, the controller noted the pilot failed to follow the published missed approach procedure.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described a loss of separation event and TCAS RA. Contributing factors listed include the handling of an emergency aircraft needing an immediate return to the airport, along with the lack of an open assist controller position.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller issued a descent clearance to Air Carrier X that was not received due to communication confusion during an emergency, causing a loss of separation with Air Carrier Y. The pilots executed a TCAS climb resolution advisory, resulting in a 400-foot vertical miss before landing safely.

synopsis: M98 Controller failed to note the type aircraft involved when establishing the final approach sequence, resulting in an overtake situation. The reporter listing a recent procedural change as contributing factor.
summary: An air traffic controller created an unintentional overtake between a slow piston Air Carrier Y and a faster SW4 turboprop while sequencing arrivals into MSP in 40-knot southerly winds. The controller attributed the error to recent procedure changes mixing turboprops at lower altitudes with piston aircraft, removing the altitude cue previously used to distinguish them.

synopsis: ZMP Controller described an uncertain hand off event indicating that ERAM anomalies were at the root of the problem.
summary: The controller suspected an ERAM issue when Air Carrier X checked on the frequency and coordinated with OMA Approach regarding radar contact. OMA reported a system glitch but believed it did not affect the handoff, prompting a request to fix ERAM.

synopsis: B737-300 flight crew experienced electrical malfunction that included multiple flashing lights and electrical smoke. Crew declared an emergency and diverted to a suitable airport.
summary: During night cruise at FL370, pilots experienced multiple false system warnings and electrical fumes after resetting a Zone 5 circuit breaker on Maintenance's advice. The crew subsequently declared an emergency, diverted to a nearby airport, and landed uneventfully, criticizing the maintenance guidance and communication delays.

synopsis: A B737-700 flight crew failed to properly program ATC descent clearances into their FMS and Altitude Alert window and, thus, stopped their descent from FL400 at FL370 vice FL360.
summary: The flight crew at FL400 failed to descend to FL360 after entering FL370 in the FMS and selecting VNAV, despite FL360 being set in the MCP. Confusion regarding the altitude restriction prompted ABQ Center to issue a "descend via" clearance, allowing the aircraft to proceed uneventfully to PHX.

synopsis: After receiving a crossing clearance 50W of BDF at FL240, the flight crew of a B737-700 failed to monitor autoflight performance and crossed at FL280.
summary: The flight crew descended into MDW on the MOTIF 4 arrival but arrived 4,000 feet high at the BFD crossing restriction. The pilot attributed the error to VNAV switching to Speed mode, which went unnoticed during the descent.

synopsis: A B717 flight crew, below 1,000 FT AGL flying a visual approach backed up by the ILS, suffered an NMAC with what the Tower casually identified as '...must be the mosquito sprayer.' The PF flying followed the RA commands and, when clear of traffic, regained the glide slope and continued to an uneventful landing.
summary: The flight crew received a TCAS RA during a night visual approach to Runway 6 at RSW, causing them to climb and pass 200 feet above a mosquito sprayer. Approach and Tower provided no traffic advisories, and Tower appeared unconcerned when the crew reported the conflict.
