summary: The pilot reported a steering failure during taxi after shutting down engine #2, caused by the First Officer inadvertently turning hydraulic pumps OFF instead of ON. Once the pumps were corrected, steering was restored, allowing the aircraft to taxi uneventfully to the gate.

synopsis: DHC 8-200 Captain experiences Radar Altimeter failure at low altitude during a visual approach. This causes the yaw damper to trip off and the Flight Directors to fail, each with their own failure indications. The approach continues to a safe landing, but the aircraft is refused for the next leg.
summary: During a visual approach, the Captain experienced erratic radio altimeter readings, yaw damper failure, and flight director failure, yet landed safely. The crew subsequently declined the aircraft for a night IMC flight due to multiple MELs that would disable EGPWS, citing excessive risk.

synopsis: A Captain and Relief Pilot report at length about the inconsistency in responses from Company Maintenance personnel at two Stations when challenged about speed tape applied to the Outlet Guide Vanes (OGVs) on two CF6-80 engines, on two separate B767-300 aircraft.
summary: A pilot reported inconsistent maintenance interpretations regarding damaged speed tape on B-767-300 Outlet Guide Vanes during two separate flights. Maintenance personnel provided conflicting explanations on whether the repair was temporary or permanent, leading to one aircraft being grounded and the other released without clear documentation or wear limits.

synopsis: A B777 Flight Attendant reported a Manager initiated aircraft boarding for an international flight shortly after the flight attendants boarded, before the cabin preflight was complete and as aircraft cleaning was in progress.
summary: A cabin manager forced boarding before the purser completed mandatory safety checks, leaving hazards like vacuum cords and blocked emergency equipment on board. This management override of standard operating procedures prevented required preflight inspections and crew briefings, compromising flight safety.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic reports he deferred a #2 Engine Oil Impeller Bypass message on an EMB-145 aircraft after referencing maintenance actions that he and another Mechanic had performed. He was later notified the Fault Isolation Manual (FIM), which he did not use, would have been a better reference souce for the deferral.
summary: Two mechanics investigated an Engine 2 Oil Impeller Bypass message on a boarding aircraft and deferred it using MEL 79-35-01-1 after confirming no red indicator or debris. The reporter noted that while teamwork was effective, the Fault Isolation Manual was not used and cross-checking the other mechanic's work was missed.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic reports about an MD-11 aircraft that arrived with a Right Forward (R-1) Entry door escape slide that was previously blown, deferred, and laying on the aircraft's ballast pallet. Mechanic noted there should be two separate deferrals indicating whether a blown slide should be removed from the aircraft or remain onboard.
summary: A pilot discovered a blown escape slide on an MD-11 ballast pallet during cockpit checks, noting the MEL placard was unclear on disposal. The pilot removed and shipped the slide, attributing the issue to improper MEL application and ambiguous placard instructions regarding the deferred item.

synopsis: BE9L Captain reports departing on a two leg flight in an aircraft that had spent the night out in the rain, with both legs of the flight also in rain. During approach on the second leg the right engine shuts down. QRH procedures are complied with and the engine is successfully restarted and a normal two engine landing ensues. Maintenance discovers a substantial amount of water in the fuel system.
summary: The pilot reported a Number 2 engine flame-out at 14,000 feet during an IFR flight in rain, caused by water ingestion likely from unsumped fuel. The engine restarted after an emergency declaration, allowing a safe RNAV 23 landing, though the exact water entry point remains uncertain.

synopsis: When the Private rated student rotated the PA-46 Malibu prematurely the instructor pilot took control but was unable to prevent the aircraft from settling back onto the runway where they touched down with either the gear up or having collapsed.
summary: During takeoff, a student pilot rotated early and lost directional control, causing the aircraft to drift left. The instructor took control, but the plane landed with gear up, striking the ground with the propeller before stopping on the runway without injuries.

synopsis: N90 Controller voiced concern regarding a loss of 'wake remnant' separation determination made by the QA office, the reporter noted current Orders do not cover this anomaly and ATC equipment can not identify same.
summary: An air traffic controller at JFK reported a wake remnant separation event involving an A340 and an A319 on final approach. The controller stated they were held responsible for the event despite lacking FAA guidance, training, or display tools to identify or avoid wake remnants.

synopsis: A80 Controller described a PRM equipment failure noting failures of this equipment is becoming more common place and needs attention.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller working Precision Monitor V experienced erratic keystrokes and frozen data blocks on the scope during a high-complexity final approach with wind override. The controller shared resources with a colleague to maintain separation without loss, attributing the incident to recurring equipment failures requiring immediate replacement.

synopsis: ZTL Controller experienced a reported loss of separation, the reporter indicated computer detected error measurements within tenths of a mile are not discernible to controllers at the operational positions.
summary: An air traffic controller reported a proximity event between an A320 and a CRJ-200 inbound to the same airport, resulting in 4.79 miles and 700 feet of separation. The controller suspects a target jump near the VORTAC caused the automated report, noting that current FAA reporting standards may document such occurrences more frequently than in the past.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: ZMA Controller described possible airspace incursions due to weather deviations and the Supervisor/TMU failures to coordinate and provide re-routes prior to the incidents.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller reported that severe weather forced aircraft into active Warning Areas W174B and E because the Traffic Management Unit failed to reroute traffic or issue ground stops. The Controller deemed the operation unsafe and upset, attributing the issue to the Supervisor's inaction and lack of proactive traffic management.

synopsis: N90 Controller described a loss of separation event complicated by a flight check aircraft.
summary: An air traffic controller managing a combined Feeder and Final position reported a loss of separation between an E135 and an A319 at 5,000 feet. The controller attributed the event to high workload from a flight check and navigation issues, noting the A319 dangerously led a turn on the STAR, causing both aircraft to respond to a resolution advisory.

synopsis: MYF Controller described a NMAC involving a helicopter climbing eastbound and an air carrier arrival into SAN. The reporter listed coordination failures with SCT as contributing to the event.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller reported a near mid-air collision between a climbing helicopter and a rapidly descending A320 in Class E airspace, where the jet passed 200 feet above the helicopter. The controller attributed the incident to a lack of coordination and failed communication, noting the A320 likely received a Resolution Advisory.

synopsis: CRW Controller voiced concern regarding non-RADAR procedures utilized by an adjacent sector. The reporter noted LOA procedures are not being followed.
summary: An AZQ air traffic controller transferred a non-RADAR C560 inbound to BKW at 070 to the reporting controller despite instructions to keep the aircraft. The reporter attributes this recurring procedural violation to a lack of alignment between sectors and calls for a new Letter of Agreement.

synopsis: Air carrier flight crew experiences a R ENGINE FILTER BYPASS caution light just after rotation. QRH procedures are complied with and flight returns to departure airport. The filter is replaced by Maintenance and the engine is run up with the First Officer's help. It is learned after the fact that engine run ups are not permitted by Maintenance with passengers on board.
summary: After a right engine fuel filter bypass caused a return to the gate, a pilot assisted mechanics in starting the right engine with passengers onboard. The pilot noted that while there was no danger, the procedure was violated because mechanics should not start engines with passengers present.

synopsis: A long range air carrier flight had to return to their departure airport when a failed ADC and the need to utilize RVSM airspace proved incompatible.
summary: During departure at 1,500 AGL, the right Air Data Computer failed, causing altitude and airspeed flags on the First Officer's display. After resetting the circuit breaker failed and RVSM requirements necessitated two functional units, the crew diverted and landed uneventfully.

synopsis: An A320 Captain expressed his displeasure at being pushed by three flight managers to accept an aircraft which, on their previous leg, had received an ECAM warning for an overheat condition in the left air conditioning pack which had been previously deferred inoperative. As required by the MEL, the pack was selected off prior to and during the flight on which the overheat warning was received.
summary: The flight crew received an ECAM overheat alert on a deferred left pack and refused the aircraft for the next leg. Flight managers violated sterile cockpit rules by pressuring the crew to fly the inoperative aircraft, but the crew maintained the refusal after confirming the managers lacked authorization.

synopsis: B757-200 flight crew describes a rejected takeoff for a low engine oil pressure light at 120 KTS. It was the First Officer's takeoff, but he did not see the low oil pressure indication when the Captain called for the reject and assumed command. The low oil pressure light extinguished shortly after the reversers were deployed. The Flight Attendant in charge also provides her perspective.
summary: The Captain aborted the takeoff roll due to a left engine low oil pressure light, causing a heavy brake stop on the runway. The crew completed the checklist, taxied back to the gate, and deplaned passengers with no injuries reported.

synopsis: An A320 ECAM alerted AUTO BRKS and NORM BRKS when the gear was extended for landing but no corresponding NORM BRKS checklist was found so during the go around the crew cycled the ANTISKID switch as per the AUTO BRKS ECAM which switched to the alternate BSCU and removed the ECAM alerts. During this event the cockpit was illuminated by a green laser which appeared to have a lock on and which caused eye discomfort.
summary: Pilots on approach were blinded by a green laser while experiencing AUTO BRKS and NORM BRKS ECAMs caused by a BSCU computer failure. They executed a missed approach, reset the antiskid switch to clear the warnings, and landed safely after maintenance confirmed the fault.

aircraft: Boeing Company Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: A Captain reported accepting an aircraft that had been written up on the inbound flight for three dual FMC failures. The discrepancies are signed off by Maintenance as reset FMCs. The problem appears again over the North Pacific on the return flight.
summary: The crew experienced a dual FMC failure over the Pacific while approaching the US West Coast, caused by a previous improper reset in ZZZZ. The Captain restored navigation using the right FMC, preventing a potential deviation or tragedy, and reported that maintenance in ZZZZ must stop signing off faults to avoid delays.

synopsis: An A319 developed a dirty socks odor on the crew's third flight of the day in that aircraft so an emergency was declared and the flight diverted where four crew members were taken to a hospital with headaches and high blood pressure.
summary: The crew diverted an aircraft due to a strong "dirty socks" odor causing nausea and headaches, initiating QRH smoke procedures. The reporter attributed the incident to a potential fume event and criticized the Dispatcher's advice to continue to the destination and Operations' request to hold for a different gate.

synopsis: A B757-200 flight crew, cleared via the OLDEE STAR to LAX was confused by disruptions to the published procedure and descended prematurely prior to a crossing restriction. Fatigue and frequent ATC deviations from published terminal procedures were cited as contributing factors.
summary: The crew experienced an inadvertent altitude deviation below 16,000 feet while descending via the OLDEE ONE STAR at LAX due to multiple ATC route changes and high workload. The First Officer attributed the error to fatigue and failing to monitor the VNAV path while managing simultaneous tasks.

synopsis: Confusion reigned when the flight crew of a CRJ-200, cleared to 'descend via' the TRUPS RNAV STAR to DCA was given a questionable heading as they approached FRDMM, but were then re-cleared again to 'continue' the arrival. The next fix, STAND, had a crossing restriction of 210/6,000 and the crew was uncertain if they were required to comply with that restriction. When they were unable to get timely clarification and continued their descent, Approach advised they were 'not' cleared to descend below 8,000.
summary: The flight crew descended below the 8,000 FT restriction at FRDMM while on the TRUPS1 arrival due to conflicting ATC instructions regarding "continue on" versus "descend via." The crew subsequently returned to 8,000 FT after the controller clarified that the descent clearance was no longer valid.

synopsis: An E-145 flight crew, fatigued and undernourished due to a long workday and lack of meal opportunities, failed to reduce thrust per the after takeoff checklist and exceeded the five minute limit by nine minutes.
summary: The Captain and First Officer, both fatigued, failed to reduce engine thrust from takeoff mode for nine minutes after takeoff due to distraction by climb profiles. Maintenance confirmed no engine parameters were exceeded, and the aircraft continued on schedule.

synopsis: The Captain of an air ambulance helicopter flight, overflying a military installation, received a Tail Rotor Gearbox Chip Detector warning, declared an emergency and successfully requested and completed an emergency landing on the military ramp directly beneath them.
summary: A pilot flying a patient transport helicopter declared an emergency when the tail rotor gear box chip light illuminated over a military airport ramp. The pilot landed safely in a restricted area with assistance from security and maintenance crews, while the patient was transferred to an ambulance.

synopsis: B767-200 Captain was informed by maintenance that post flight inspection revealed the right main landing gear door was missing from aircraft, and adjacent hydraulic lines were damaged and leaking fluid. Pilot had no indication and was not aware that anything was amiss during flight and taxi.
summary: The pilot reported that a mechanic discovered a missing right main gear door and a hydraulic leak after landing. The flight proceeded without abnormal noises, vibrations, or EICAS warnings, and the aircraft was shut down for maintenance repairs.

synopsis: A MD-82 wheel well hydraulic component 'O' ring failed on takeoff allowing hydraulic fluid to enter the aircraft air conditioning system. The odor made the pilots light headed so an emergency was declared and the flight returned to the departure airport.
summary: The flight crew detected a chlorine-like odor at 110 KTS during takeoff, which changed to turpentine by 1,500 feet. They declared an emergency, completed the smoke/fire/fumes checklist, and returned for an overweight landing.

synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reports a depression in the C9 Alley way near Spot 2 at LAX, that traps a stationary aircraft preventing it from moving with maximum allowable congested area thrust.
summary: The flight crew at LAX could not taxi the aircraft after pushback due to a known depression in the asphalt at spot 2. Operations towed the aircraft 15 feet to clear the hole, allowing normal taxi with less than 35 percent thrust.

synopsis: An MD-82 Captain was unwilling to accept the Maintenance request that he fly his next leg in an aircraft displaying symptoms of a pneumatic system problem in order to troubleshoot the system using a no longer current procedure. After landing the aircraft was taken out of service.
summary: The flight crew reported high pneumatic duct pressure after takeoff and refused Maintenance Control's advice to troubleshoot using an obsolete anti-ice procedure during a revenue flight. The aircraft was subsequently taken out of service for repair, and the pilot recommended that maintenance avoid suggesting troubleshooting with unpublished procedures.

synopsis: B727-200 First Officer stated the aircraft lost oil quantity on number one engine during initial climb and turned back to departure airport. Crew declared an emergency, shut down affected engine and landed uneventfully.
summary: During initial climb at 6,000 MSL, the pilot observed decreasing oil quantity on Engine 1, prompting a turn-back. After oil pressure dropped below parameters on final approach, the engine was shut down per QRH, resulting in an emergency landing with one engine out.

synopsis: The Captain of an ERJ 145 expressed his belief that his aircraft hasn't the VNAV sophistication required to perform the complex RNAV STARs such as the FRDMM ONE to DCA. He believes flight crew workload required to comply with crossing restrictions without full functioning VNAV/autoflight/autothrottle capability is excessive under the best of conditions. Under adverse weather and or tailwind conditions he believes compliance will require complete disregard of other flight safety considerations and may well simply overwhelm the flight crew's and aircraft's capacities.
summary: The pilot flying reported that while descending on the FRDMM ONE RNAV STAR into DCA in icing conditions, the aircraft drifted nearly one mile off course despite LNAV engagement. The pilot attributed this deviation to excessive workload and limited automation on the arrival, recommending the procedure be discontinued or refused due to safety risks.

synopsis: A B757 Flight Attendant reported being upset after an aborted takeoff and a long stressful day when the overnight rest was shortened with no consideration for their emotional or physical wellbeing.
summary: Flight attendants experienced an aborted takeoff due to a left engine oil pressure warning light, followed by a return to the gate. The crew reported inadequate post-incident support, an illegal layover, and poor treatment by company schedulers, leading to a decision to refuse future flights under similar conditions.

synopsis: It appears that a required engine power assurance test was not completed prior to the aircraft operating to another station. Once detected, the power assurance check was completed.
summary: Two mechanics performed engine inspections on a road trip but failed to complete the required power assurance check before signing the logbook due to fatigue and lack of experience. The oversight was discovered later when Maintenance Control questioned the missing check, which was eventually performed after the aircraft arrived at its destination.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic questions whether cargo pit loading procedures include verification by cargo loaders that intrusion into the forward pit, aft equipment bay neoprene curtain area has not occurred on B767-300 aircraft. He continues to find damaged support rods for the recirculation filter box assemblies behind the neoprene curtains.
summary: A mechanic at ZZZ found damaged support rods on a B767-300 caused by bulging cargo containers extending beyond floor stops. Management refused to cannibalize parts from other aircraft, citing a known fleet-wide issue, and instead sought a maintenance deferral while acknowledging the need for a protective barrier.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: A Captain rejected the takeoff on MKC Runway 1 from about 70 KTS as a tractor entered the runway.
summary: The flight crew aborted takeoff at 70 knots after a maintenance tractor entered the runway while the controller was distracted by a phone call. The controller admitted losing track of the vehicle while managing both Ground and Tower frequencies, but the aircraft safely back-taxed and completed an uneventful departure.

synopsis: C150 instructor pilot experiences an airspeed indicator malfunction during takeoff resulting in a low airspeed, but interpreted as excessive drag. Once safely airborne the iPad is turned on and GPS ground speed is compared with indicated airspeed to confirm that the airspeed indicator is erroneous.
summary: A flight instructor and student experienced a partial pitot block during takeoff from Runway 31R, causing misleadingly low airspeed indications and a shallow climb. The pilot declared an emergency, cleared obstacles, and landed safely on Runway 31L, attributing the delayed recognition of the failure to confusing departure clearances.

synopsis: CL65 Captain, as pilot not flying, looked up after changing frequencies during departure and notes the aircraft in a nose high attitude and the First Officer looking out the side window. When questioned the First Officer indicated that he thought the autopilot was engaged.
summary: During initial climb, the First Officer released the controls while distracted by looking for a house, causing an untrimmed aircraft to pitch up to 18 degrees. The Captain intervened to lower the nose, attributing the incident to the First Officer's lack of flight deck discipline and failure to properly trim or engage the autopilot.

synopsis: A GLF5 flight crew was confused by the manner in which their digital avionics suite displayed the TETERBORO RNAV SID, not realizing that the commercially provided digital chart displays utilized two separate charts, one for departures of Runways 1, 6 and 19 and the other for departures from Runway 24. Their confusion was exacerbated when their departure runway was changed to Runway 24 and, although the map display was appropriate for their newly assigned runway the chart displayed remained the one for the other runways. Because the altitudes were different and because ATC was unwilling or unable to help clarify their confusion altitude deviations ensued.
summary: The flight crew departed Teterboro Runway 24 in a Primus Epic aircraft after the FMS displayed an incorrect TEB8 chart due to duplicate procedure names. Despite ATC refusing to verify altitudes, the crew manually limited climb to 1,500 feet, though turbulence and wind shear caused an unintended ascent to 1,800 feet before Departure confirmed the correct altitude.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: A pilot landing on BVO Runway 35 had a near miss with a glider landing on the adjacent grass.
summary: The pilot, approaching BVO for a fly-in, executed a go-around and switched to Runway 35 but failed to see a glider landing on the adjacent grass strip until flare. The pilot attributed the near-miss to inadequate visual scanning, shading from a cap, and poor judgment by the glider pilot for entering high-traffic airspace.

synopsis: CE510 Captain experiences an unsafe gear indication during approach and elects to divert to an airport where repairs can be made. An IFR clearance for the diversion is relayed by the Tower and causes some confusion.
summary: The pilot experienced a gear unsafe light during a VFR approach while retrieving an aircraft from a paint facility. Confusion over conflicting Tower instructions regarding VFR status and IFR clearance caused an altitude deviation, but the pilot declared an emergency and landed safely after executing the checklist.

synopsis: While planning a future flight, a commercially rated pilot noted 'LP' minima on the RNAV/GPS approaches at his destination, an approach type with which he was unfamiliar and for which, a computer search revealed, his aircraft's commercially provided GPS database was unable to utilize.
summary: A pilot reviewing RNAV (GPS) Runway 32 approach plates for DTS misidentified an LP minimum as a typo for LPV. The pilot noted that current navigation databases do not support LP approaches, creating a risk where general aviation pilots could unknowingly descend below minimums.

synopsis: RV6 pilot, who was set up for a short field landing at a small private grass strip, observed wires on final, flew underneath them and landed without incident.
summary: The pilot on final approach for a short field landing nearly struck wires across the runway threshold due to target fixation and a failure to see the supporting poles. The pilot safely landed below the wires but noted that red obstacle balls would have improved visibility and vertical clearance.

synopsis: A C-182 departed a CTAF runway after the pilot mistakenly touched a brake as he was intending to push rudder in order to correct a crosswind drift during landing roll out.
summary: The pilot landed a single-engine aircraft slightly left of centerline and inadvertently applied the right brake while correcting for a crosswind, causing the right main gear to lift. The aircraft subsequently veered off the right runway edge into grass, where it stopped undamaged.

synopsis: A CE-421C propeller governor failed on takeoff and feathered the propeller so when the engine also quit the pilot completed the engine shutdown checklist memory items and returned to land.
summary: The pilot and four passengers experienced a right engine failure and propeller feathering at 500 AGL during the left turn after takeoff on Runway 35. The pilot attempted one restart, reviewed memory items, and successfully landed on Runway 35 using single-engine procedures.

synopsis: CLE Controller described an airspace incursion when an aircraft initiated a descent issued to a same company aircraft with a similar sounding four digit flight number.
summary: An Inner Low controller issued a descent clearance to Air Carrier XXXY instead of the intended Air Carrier XXXX due to similar call signs and an incorrect frequency change. The error was identified when the Outer Controller confirmed XXXX remained on his frequency, resulting in no traffic conflicts after XXXY was pointed out to the departure position.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported that on a LAX RNAV Departure, following initial departure vectors, they were cleared to what they thought was SEBBY Intersection when the Controller meant the PEVEE Waypoint.
summary: Pilots on an LAX departure misinterpreted an ATC clearance for SEBBY Intersection instead of PEVEE due to similar-sounding names. The crew turned northeast toward SEBBY before a subsequent controller corrected the heading, resulting in no aircraft conflict.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An Air Carrier crew reported an EGPWS alert from an antenna on a right base to final about six miles from BHM Runway 6.
summary: Pilots on a visual approach to Runway 6 at BHM received an EGPWS caution while flying base over an antenna tower. Despite reporting adequate vertical and horizontal clearance from the obstacle, the crew suggests modifying downwind positioning to prevent future false warnings.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An MD-80 was given a crossing restriction north of CRG VOR, but the distracted crew with no VNAV started the descent late so ATC raised the altitude constraint which they complied with.
summary: The Pilot Flying and First Officer missed a descent restriction at FL320 due to the Pilot Flying forgetting to set a reminder while eating. ATC accepted the missed restriction and cleared the aircraft to expedite descent to FL260.

synopsis: Following maintenance work on a CRJ-700 that required a rig pin to be placed in the rudder system, a Maintenance Technician was given the job card to verify the aft equipment bay was clear of any foreign objects. After a general visual inspection of the area, the technician closed the compartment, unaware that the rig pin was installed.
summary: A mechanic performing a block check on a CRJ-700 closed the aft equipment bay without noticing a rig pin left in the rudder quadrant. The aircraft later returned to the gate with a jammed rudder, which the mechanic attributed to the block check form failing to link the panel close-out task to the specific maintenance performed.

synopsis: While performing a complex inspection with paperwork that was unfamiliar, two Maintenance Technicians did not properly perform the required tasks. This was not recognzied until working on the second aircraft, one week after the improperly inspected aircraft was released for service.
summary: Maintenance personnel discovered two invalid part number entries for Boeing 757 slats during an AD 91-22-51 paperwork review. The errors resulted from unclear footnotes and were resolved after contacting the Boeing Desk to re-inspect the slats.

synopsis: M20 pilot reports departing on an IFR flight plan in VMC with one battery completely discharged. This caused some loaded information in the right screen to be compromised then the left screen malfunctioned. Later in flight it caused all navigation and communication to malfunction.
summary: The pilot reported that after an annual inspection where the maintenance firm drained battery 2, compromised data on the right screen caused the left screen to malfunction. This subsequently led to a total failure of all navigation and communication systems during the flight.

synopsis: An EA50 autopilot would not engage on a TEB RUUDY 4 departure, so the distracted pilot did not level at the WENTZ 1,500 FT constraint but descended to it after realizing his error.
summary: The pilot, flying a TEB RUUDY 4 departure, overshot the 1,500 MSL crossing altitude at WENTZ by 400 feet due to autopilot engagement failure. The pilot descended back to the required altitude and resolved to hand-fly to allow time for troubleshooting future autopilot issues.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: After discovering a large discrepancy between the GPS and the Controller's location of a fix, the pilots of an experimental aircraft cancelled the RNAV approach and flew a visual approach. Pilots later determined that they had accidentally entered the fix as a user waypoint at their current location.
summary: Two experienced pilots flying an aircraft with Avidyne Entegra and Garmin GTN 650 navigators encountered a position discrepancy during an RNAV 26 approach due to an accidental user waypoint entry and a zoomed MFD display. This confusion caused them to cancel the instrument approach and successfully complete a visual approach to LNS.

aircraft: Regional Jet CL65; Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: L30 Controller described a below MVA entry event involving missed approach aircraft from Runway 25L, the reporter voicing concern regarding current procedures covering missed approaches at LAS.
summary: A controller conducting OJT at LAS approved a Tower request to vector a CRJ departure on runway heading while a B737 went around, causing the CRJ to descend below 85 MVA due to high terrain and controller distraction from combined sector traffic. The reporter attributes the incident to dangerous standard procedures and a lack of effective separation methods for parallel runway operations.

synopsis: En route Controller described a precautionary engine shut down event, where the flight crew elected to divert but not to declare an emergency.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller cleared a Dash 8 en route to divert after the pilot reported a precautionary single-engine shutdown. The controller issued approach clearances, omitted an altitude restriction, and facilitated a visual approach without declaring an emergency as the pilot requested no assistance.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reports a NMAC with parachutists while on the downwind segment of the ROKIT 1 arrival to Runway 4 at HOU. Evasive action is taken and the incident is reported to ATC.
summary: During the ROKIT arrival to Runway 4 at HOU, the First Officer spotted parachutists, prompting the pilot to disconnect the autopilot and turn right to avoid them. ATC was unaware of the jumping activity, which occurred extremely close to the aircraft.

synopsis: B777 Captain refuses an aircraft when it is learned that the brake temperature system is MELed and the destination airport temperature is expected to be 118 degrees. After refusal the system is repaired in 20 minutes.
summary: The flight crew refused a B777 with an inoperative brake temperature monitoring system, citing MEL data indicating a potential melt zone during the planned quick turnaround. Although the repair took only 20 minutes, the crew was charged with a delay after the Duty Manager initially suggested using cooling fans instead of fixing the aircraft.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: An air carrier at about 4,000 FT being vectored for TYS had a near miss with a VFR aircraft after being advised separation was adequate from that aircraft also communicating with ATC.
summary: The pilot flying reported a TCAS Resolution Advisory to climb during approach to TYS after ATC provided conflicting sequencing instructions and failed to maintain separation with a VFR government aircraft. The crew executed the climb to avoid the traffic, which was 300 feet below, while the controller appeared overwhelmed by high traffic volume.

synopsis: Air carrier First Officer is advised by ATC of VFR traffic ahead maintaining a 500 FT lower altitude. TCAS indicates a 200 FT separation and issues a climb RA, which is complied with.
summary: The crew on downwind at EWR received a TCAS RA to climb due to a survey aircraft reported at 4,500 FT but appearing only 200 FT below. The pilot executed a TCAS climb to 5,500 FT, suspecting the survey aircraft was not maintaining its assigned altitude or altimeter setting.

synopsis: A B777 First Officer reported after his walk around that the Number 8 brake wear indicator pins were at the maximum allowable wear but the Captain would not put the anomaly in the aircraft maintenance log for an inspection.
summary: During a B777 preflight walk-around, a pilot reported brake wear indicator pins on tire 8 were not protruding beyond flush, contrary to the manual. The Captain, a high-level manager, refused to log the discrepancy to avoid delay, creating cockpit tension despite the pilot's insistence on following procedures.

synopsis: A B737-800 pilot reports being instructed to maintain 180 KTS to the FAF for Runway 9 by ATC and advising unable. Upon landing ATC instructs the crew to turn off at H4 then H5 (no longer exist) then cancels the takeoff clearance of an aircraft departing on Runway 12. The B737 crew is admonished by ATC for not advising that they will be using the whole runway.
summary: A pilot landing on Runway 9 at MIA in IFR conditions stopped short of intersecting Runway 12 after Tower cleared another aircraft for takeoff without issuing land and hold short instructions. The pilot attributed this dangerous situation to Tower's noncompliance with regulations regarding runway occupancy and clearance procedures.

synopsis: Air Carrier pilot reports setting up for Runway 8L at MIA then being informed to expect Runway 9, which is selected from the arrival page of the FMC. ATC then offers a choice and the reporter requests Runway 8L but 8L is no longer an available option on the arrival page even after re-selecting the RNAV arrival, so back to Runway 9.
summary: The pilot of SSCOT1 arriving in Miami requested Runway 8L but could not configure the FMS for that approach due to a system limitation. Consequently, the crew accepted Runway 09, crossed the Runway 8L localizer during vectors, and joined the final approach for Runway 09 without incident.

synopsis: MD83 pilot reports being dispatched with the right pack inoperative and discovering airborne that the left pack has also failed. Flight returns to the departure airport for an overweight landing.
summary: The crew departed with placards on the Thrust Limit Indicator, autothrottle, and right pack, then lost pressurization after takeoff due to a left pack failure. They declared an emergency for an overweight landing and air return, noting the event would have been safer with a functioning autothrottle.

synopsis: A B737-800 crew declared an emergency and diverted to a nearby airport after a TE FLAP ASYMMETRY and TE FLAP DISAGREE alerted on final at an airport with a relatively short runway.
summary: Flight crew on a visual approach to Runway 19 experienced trailing flap asymmetry and a split at 1,300–1,500 feet AGL, with flaps stuck at 27 and 29 degrees. They initiated a go-around, declared an emergency, diverted to a nearby airport, and landed safely after completing checklists.

synopsis: Global 5000 First Officer accepts a clearance to descend to 2,800 FT during approach to VAPO. This triggers a GPWS warning and a call from ATC to climb up to 3,800 FT.
summary: The flight crew descended to 2,800 feet during a VOR approach at Pune, triggering an EGPWS 'Too Low Gear' warning due to a miscommunication where the controller intended 3,800 feet. The crew climbed back to 3,800 feet after the controller corrected the clearance, attributing the error to a language barrier and false confidence in the precise vector.

synopsis: A MD-88 APU developed an oil leak during pushback which filled the cabin with smoke so the aircraft was returned to the gate where the crew were assigned another aircraft and departed with an open maintenance item.
summary: The crew and maintenance staff operated an aircraft with an expired three-day maintenance exemption because a mechanic failed to enter the change order into the computer system. This oversight occurred after a last-minute aircraft change caused by an APU oil leak and smoke, leading to the flight departing with invalid maintenance status.

synopsis: A C210 pilot detected a burnt plastic odor and a small amount of white smoke, so he returned to his departure airport where he discovered a failed portable GPS receiver which was wired into the aircraft electrical system.
summary: The pilot reported burnt plastic and white smoke while climbing to 9,500 feet, with all engine instruments remaining normal. Suspecting the cause was a handheld GPS installed during the annual inspection, the pilot returned to the departure airport, landed safely, and found no further smoke after shutdown.

synopsis: Despite CTAF transmissions and visual contact with other aircraft in the pattern, a C-150 pilot just airborne from a non-towered airport suffered an NMAC with another aircraft executing a go-around that had been on final to the same runway, but was unobserved by the reporter.
summary: The pilot of a departing aircraft at an untowered airport failed to see another aircraft on final approach while taxiing for takeoff. The landing pilot executed a go-around, avoiding a collision, which the reporter attributed to not distinguishing between two separate CTAF announcements and an inadequate visual scan.

synopsis: A student pilot on his first solo landing, with his instructor observing on the ramp, applied too much rudder correction and brake which resulted in the aircraft departing the runway without damage or injury.
summary: A student pilot soloing a Cessna departed Runway 9 in 4-knot winds and exited the runway during landing due to excessive braking causing a slide. The aircraft was towed back to the apron by airport rescue after the pilot shut down the engine.

synopsis: A C414 right brake suddenly failed during the landing roll so the aircraft rolled off the runway.
summary: During landing rollout, the pilot experienced sudden starboard brake failure, causing the aircraft to roll off the runway.

synopsis: TRACON Controller voiced concern regarding the actions taken by the Tower CIC when emergency information was relayed to the Tower. The reporter questioned the CIC's capability.
summary: A pilot flying a Throp at 5,500 feet VFR reported low oil pressure and received expedited handling from Approach. The Local Controller failed to follow emergency procedures by sounding the siren but neglecting to contact the Fire Department, forcing response vehicles to request information on the Ground frequency.

synopsis: P31 Controller described a likely loss of separation event involving three ATC facility's. The report indicated that miss communications was the primary causal factor.
summary: A trainee controller at PNS experienced a potential conflict between a B350 and MD90 due to unclear coordination with ZJX regarding who held communications for the B350. The aircraft approached within two miles before the B350 finally climbed, an incident attributed to ambiguous handoff procedures rather than a lack of radar coverage.

synopsis: An A319/20 Captain reported the failure of the aircraft's FMGC and autoflight systems to comply with the altitude and airspeed restrictions while conducting the FRDMM RNAV STAR to DCA.
summary: Pilots descending via the FRDMM STAR into DCA reported the Airbus autopilot disregarding FMGC altitude and speed restrictions while in DES mode. The crew manually managed the profile, logged a malfunction, and had Maintenance reset the FMGCs, noting this issue occurs frequently on this aircraft type.

synopsis: An air carrier flight crew cleared via the FRDMM RNAV STAR to DCA failed to comply with the crossing altitude restrictions at BRVRY.
summary: The pilot reported that while descending via the FRDMM One RNAV STAR with autopilot engaged, the aircraft descended below FL240 at BRVRY to FL233 despite appearing on profile. The pilot disengaged the autopilot to correct the descent, recovered the aircraft, landed, and subsequently reported the system malfunction.

synopsis: Air carrier under N90 control experienced a TCAS RA with reported VFR traffic 500 FT below. The Controller indicated the TCAS RA response cause another conflict.
summary: While being vectored for approach into Newark at 6,000 feet, the crew received a TCAS Resolution Advisory when VFR traffic climbed within 400 feet. The crew executed a climb to 6,700 feet to resolve the conflict, though the controller disputed the proximity and the resulting climb.

synopsis: A CRJ200's GEAR DISAGREE alerted after takeoff, so the Gear Disagree Checklist was completed, an emergency declared and the flight returned to the departure airport.
summary: The crew experienced a Gear Disagree warning on takeoff due to landing gear failing to fully retract, forcing an emergency return. The pilot noted conflicting ATC altitude instructions and criticized the QRH for lacking a gear cycling step for this specific malfunction.

synopsis: When faced with a LE ASSYM EICAS warning shortly after takeoff the transatlantic bound flight crew of a B767-300ER found their tasks seriously compounded by: A. Having been dispatched with the autothrottles MEL'd inoperative, B. Multiple fuel dump system anomalies precluding their ability to dump fuel to minimize exposure to high landing speeds and resulting braking hazards, C. A narrow speed window between exceeding the flap limit speed at the high end due to their heavy weight and the stick shaker for their flap configuration at the low end, the proximity to which proved an issue when having to manually control thrust due to the deferred autothrottles.
summary: The crew of a 380,000-lb aircraft experienced LE asymmetry and autothrottle failure shortly after takeoff, leading to an emergency return and overweight landing. High workload and inoperative autothrottles caused multiple stick shaker activations and an inadvertent flap overspeed, though the aircraft landed safely with minor fuel dump system issues.

synopsis: A MD-82's left hydraulic system quantity began decreasing during climb and after accomplishing the QRH, with hydraulic quantity at zero, an emergency was declared.
summary: During climb at FL250, the First Officer noticed decreasing left hydraulic quantity. After the Captain executed the QRH procedure, the level dropped to zero, prompting an emergency declaration and an uneventful landing.

synopsis: After landing at MEM a First Officer took control of an aircraft and forcefully stopped it because Captain was not following taxi instructions and putting the aircraft into a conflict.
summary: The First Officer stopped the aircraft during taxi after the Captain attempted to pass right of a parked plane at a gate. The Captain attributed the error to fatigue, and both crew members agreed to file reports regarding the incident.

synopsis: Rain water which accumulated in a B757 E and E compartment flowed onto several computers at rotation causing the loss of several Captain's flight instruments, so the crew returned to the departure airport.
summary: During takeoff and climb, the Captain's airspeed and altimeter failed, triggering erroneous windshear and GPWS warnings and a Mach/SPD trim failure. The crew diverted back to the departure airport, landing safely after instruments stabilized at 3,000 feet.

synopsis: C172 instructor reports OJC taxiway markings and signage are inadequate and in need of refurbishment with reflective paint.
summary: A pilot reported that Johnson County Executive Airport's taxiway and runway markings are invisible at night due to a lack of reflectivity and low contrast. The reporter attributed this safety issue to non-standard hold bars and faded paint, recommending immediate repainting and signage upgrades.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: ICT Controller witnessed an unexpected go-around by an aircraft on an instrument approach into 1K1 reportedly due to men and equipment on the runway, no NOTAM was issued by the Airport Manager.
summary: The pilot executed an unplanned go-around during an instrument approach to 1K1 due to men and equipment on the runway. The Airport Manager stated construction was underway but admitted no NOTAM was issued.

synopsis: A90 Controller voiced concern regarding the lack Class C requirements demonstrated by some controllers at MHT.
summary: An H60 helicopter departed VFR from MHT while the reporter, an approach controller, noted the Tower failed to provide required Class C radar services. The reporter attributed this to Tower controllers' lack of understanding regarding Class C requirements, warning that such non-compliance could cause a mid-air collision.

synopsis: SEA Controller described a go-around conflict event during parallel runway operations. The reporter provided several actions that would would have prevented this incident.
summary: An air traffic controller reported a potential conflict at SEA between a departing Dash 8 and a B737 executing a go-around in foggy conditions. The controller attributed the situation to the Dash 8 being issued a 230 heading before the B737's landing was assured, noting that better coordination or a straight-out departure would have prevented the issue.

synopsis: Confusion between Approach Control and an air carrier flight crew may have resulted in a premature descent on a visual approach to Runway 04 at AMA.
summary: During a visual approach to Runway 04 at AMA with primary radar down, the crew descended below 5,300 feet while turning to final after the LOC became active. The pilot reported potential confusion with the Tower Controller regarding the definition of "established on final," fearing the controller expected the aircraft to be wings level and aligned before descending.

synopsis: After takeoff a MD-11 EICAS alerted LVL 1 AIL DEFLECT INOP followed by LVL 2 AIL DEFLECT DISAG so an emergency was declared and because of language difficulty the fuel dump and divert to a nearby airport were difficult.
summary: The flight crew experienced aileron control failures and a circuit breaker trip during climbout, causing an uncommanded roll and preventing autopilot use. They declared an emergency, diverted to dump 124,000 lbs of fuel, and hand-flew the aircraft to a safe landing.

synopsis: A MD-11's EICAS alerted RUD STBY UPR OFF and RUD STBY LWR OFF so fuel was dumped and the flight diverted to an enroute airport for repairs.
summary: The crew diverted an MD-11 after takeoff due to rudder standby alerts, dumping fuel at FL290 to reach 500,000 lbs. They landed uneventfully, replaced the Hydraulic System Controller, and resumed the flight without further issues.

synopsis: A B737-400 takeoff was rejected at about 50 KTS because the nose wheel steering was found to be inoperative.
summary: The First Officer rejected takeoff at 50 KTS due to unresponsive nose wheel steering via rudder pedals. The aircraft returned to the gate for MEL maintenance, which allowed subsequent operation without rudder pedal steering.

synopsis: CRJ-200 First Officer described wake vortex encounter on takeoff in ATL behind a B757.
summary: The pilot experienced wake turbulence from a preceding B757 shortly after takeoff, causing a 10-degree left roll and brief stick-shaker activation. The pilot lowered the angle of attack to recover, and the flight continued normally with no deviations in airspeed, altitude, or track.

synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported a 'partial upset' at FL330 when he encountered the wake of a B777 8 miles ahead.
summary: During cruise at FL330, the crew experienced a rapid 30-degree right roll, likely caused by wake turbulence from a B777 eight miles ahead. The pilots recovered using Control Wheel Steering, descended to FL290 per ATC instruction, and continued with no injuries or altitude loss.

synopsis: A MD82 crew discovered after the FMA annunciated HEADING that the compass headings were up 40 degrees different, so an emergency was declared and the flight returned to the departure airport where maintenance on the compass had previously been performed.
summary: Pilots experienced a gyro compass failure shortly after takeoff, causing heading discrepancies, Flight Director loss, and autopilot disengagement at 16,000 feet. They declared an emergency and returned to the departure airport for a safe landing due to the system malfunction.

synopsis: Pilot reports that Maintenance Control may have applied an incorrect MEL to their B737-800 aircraft after he noted that right duct pressure was only 5-PSI and left duct at 40-PSI, with engine bleeds off, APU bleed on and Isolation Valve closed.
summary: The Captain of a B737-800 observed a temporary right duct pressure drop during climb, which Maintenance Control attributed to a possible Precooler Condition Valve failure. The crew questioned whether the issue was properly addressed, noting the gauge was placarded but the MEL restrictions were not applied before the aircraft departed for another flight.

synopsis: A MD-82's left hydraulic system developed a leak and the quantity decreased to zero during climb out so an emergency was declared and the flight returned to the departure airport.
summary: During climbout to FL250, the First Officer observed decreasing left hydraulic quantity, which dropped to zero after the Captain executed the QRH. The crew declared an emergency, returned to the departure airport, and landed uneventfully.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports about the reluctance of their Maintenance Management to address the numerous incidents of electrical shocks mechanics were experiencing after connecting a portable ground power cart to their ERJ-170 aircraft, including aircraft with open fuel tanks.
summary: Maintenance personnel performing nightly hangar work on an aircraft reported receiving electrical shocks while connecting a dual ground power cart. The reporter attributes the hazard to poor hangar wiring and dry soil around the grounding rod, which prevents proper voltage return despite management's claim that electricians found no significant issues.

synopsis: The Maintenance Technician attempted to comply with the MEL for an avionics cooling fan fault, but discovered that the circuit breaker would not reset. He utilized the MEL and collared the circuit breaker thinking that is was only affecting that fan. By doing so, he did not comply with the approved MEL procedure.
summary: A DC-10 pilot encountered an air system fail alert and a non-resetting circuit breaker during pre-flight testing. The pilot collared the breaker without contacting Maintenance Control, later admitting this deviation from MEL procedures was an error despite confirming no safety of flight risk.

synopsis: A CE-501 squat switch failed at FL350 causing a rapid loss of pressurization, so an emergency was declared and the flight descended to 11,000 FT then continued to its planned destination.
summary: The flight crew executed an emergency descent after a rapid pressurization loss triggered the 10,000-foot horn, descending from FL240 to 11,000 feet following ARTCC clearance. Maintenance found no definitive fault, and the aircraft completed the flight with no injuries or damage.

synopsis: While taxiing for takeoff, ATC questioned a B757 crew about the transponder code and the crew then realized they had not gotten their PDC clearance and transponder code at the gate.
summary: Two pilots missed setting the transponder and obtaining a PDC during preflight due to fatigue, complacency, and distraction from new taxi procedures. Ground Control queried the code on taxi out, prompting a safe stop to correct the error before a normal departure without traffic delay.

synopsis: A solo C-172 student pilot lost all electrical power, squawked 7600, called his instructor on a cell phone and landed on a closed runway after failing to see ATC's red light signal.
summary: A solo pilot experienced a total electrical failure during steep turns, losing radio and navigation equipment. Unable to receive tower light signals, the pilot landed on a closed runway without clearance, resulting in no injuries or damage.

synopsis: The instructor and student pilot of a C-172 departing on an instrument training flight at dusk had a close encounter with a Cirrus that had landed a minute or more previously but had not cleared the runway.
summary: A pilot and student departing an IFR training flight encountered a Cirrus aircraft parked on the active runway during takeoff roll. The pilot continued the takeoff and passed over the stationary Cirrus at 100 feet AGL after the Cirrus pilot announced they were remaining on the runway.

synopsis: A CE-501 encountered severe turbulence for one minute at FL350 and advised ATC they were unable to maintain RVSM because of altitude variations up to 400 FT.
summary: The crew encountered severe turbulence and downdrafts while level at FL350 in IMC, causing altitude loss to 34,650 feet despite clear onboard weather radar. They advised ATC they could not maintain RVSM separation, received a block altitude of FL340-350, and deviated 30 degrees left to exit the weather.

synopsis: AS-350 pilot on a post maintenance test flight heard a clicking noise and onboard Mechanic detected vibration in cruise flight. Pilot returned to base and a depression in the blade and a deformation in the trim tab of the main rotor was discovered.
summary: The Captain and Mechanic conducted a maintenance test flight on an AS-350B2 to track and balance a new rotor system. After a second adjustment, inspection revealed a depression on a main rotor blade and a deformed trim tab, likely caused by a tool left inside the aircraft.

synopsis: A Varga Kachina pilot declared an emergency and started to divert to a nearby airport because of an engine malfunction, but after turning the fuel boost pump ON flew safely to his home airport.
summary: The pilot experienced an engine power loss at 4,000 feet in an experimental Varga Kachina during slow flight, likely caused by running the mixture too lean. After declaring an emergency and restoring partial power, the pilot landed safely at the home field, noting that activating the boost pump earlier might have prevented the issue.

synopsis: MBS Controller witnessed a traffic pattern conflict when the Local Controller issued a questionable clearance resulting in traffic on opposite base legs nose to nose.
summary: An Approach controller observed a potential conflict between an EA-50 and a Cessna on base leg to Runway 23 after Tower instructed the Cessna to go around and side step right. The Cessna cut in front of the EA-50, appearing very close on radar, while the controller remained silent due to supervisor presence.

synopsis: MKE Controller described a probable loss of separation event involving GRB's vectors of a Runway 3 ILS arrival. The reporter suggested these aircraft should be worked by MKE because of the airspace configurations.
summary: ATW and GRB controllers managed two aircraft near ATW, where a GRB arrival descended to 5,000 feet on a collision course with a PA-34. The ATW controller separated them by maneuvering the PA-34 and suspected GRB caused a loss of separation by violating descent restrictions.

synopsis: ZJX Controller described a conflict event when an aircraft climbed above cleared altitude, the reporters indicate a language barrier and equipment issues may have contributed to the event.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller and a Gulfstream G-IV pilot were involved in a near-miss near CAE VOR where the G-IV received a TCAS Resolution Advisory to climb. The controller attributed the conflict to a communication error regarding altitude clearance and potential radar issues, while the G-IV pilot reported the other aircraft lied about its altitude before passing 400 feet below.

synopsis: Tower Controller described a go around event resulting in a conflict between the go around aircraft and an aircraft cleared for take off, the reporter indicating the Local Controller has frequent separation issues.
summary: A Local Controller cleared a C172 for takeoff on Runway 14 while a PA46 was on short final, causing a separation loss. The Controller failed to calculate safe distances or cancel the clearance in time, forcing a go-around and immediate turns to avoid a collision due to poor situational awareness.

synopsis: TRACON Controller distracted by an emergency allowed an aircraft to stray onto the boundary of another facility's airspace without a point out.
summary: An ATC controller managing a combined sector declared an emergency for a departing aircraft with a flap failure. While focused on that emergency, the controller allowed a C402 on an ILS Runway 5 approach to make a late base turn, placing it on the boundary of N90 airspace.

synopsis: Air Carrier arrival into SDF voiced concern regarding the multiple runway changes issued during the descent into the airport listing the increased FMS workload needed to accommodate the changes.
summary: The flight crew on arrival at SDF experienced five runway changes during descent, causing high workload for FMC updates and verification. After hesitation from Approach Control regarding the arrival clearance, the crew intercepted the 35R localizer and landed visually, though the runway changed again after parking.

synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reports non standard terminology by the ATL Tower when issuing runway crossing instructions at 'the jet base'. The crew is confused and the Tower is not helpful.
summary: Pilots exiting runway 8L at intersection B11 received unclear instructions from a tower controller to cross runway 8R at an undefined "Jet Base." After clarification, the crew crossed at intersection B10 and reached the gate safely, attributing the confusion to the controller's poor use of non-standard phraseology.

synopsis: An ERJ-190 cabin altitude exceed 10,000 FT in cruise at FL300 so an emergency was declared, the aircraft descended and returned to the departure airport where it was discovered the same anomaly occurred the previous day.
summary: The flight crew experienced a slow cabin pressure climb to above 10,000 feet at FL300, triggering a Cabin Hi warning and an emergency descent to 10,000 feet. They returned to the departure airport safely, noting a similar unresolved pressurization incident occurred on the aircraft the previous day.

synopsis: An EMB-145 flight crew diverted in accorance with the QRH after receiving an EICAS Spoiler Fail message.
summary: The flight crew received an EICAS Spoiler Fail message 120 miles from destination and diverted per QRH after consulting Dispatch and Maintenance. They suspected a switch error but landed safely at the nearest suitable airport without further issues.

synopsis: A Captain reported for duty following a major storm which flooded the crew room and destroyed flight bags. He was issued a single bag for both pilots which they discovered had no airway charts after the aircraft's GPS malfunctioned.
summary: A reserve Captain and First Officer operated six flights without enroute charts after water damage to the crew room and a rushed inventory of an issued replacement bag. The crew mitigated the issue by obtaining printed FAA charts and operating VOR navigation below 18,000 feet following a GPS malfunction.

synopsis: A B737-800 aileron trim was not centered with hydraulic power ON so they returned to gate where Maintenance Control had Mechanics zero the trim and released the aircraft but charged the crew for the maintenance delay.
summary: Flight crew reported an aileron trim deviation during pre-flight hydraulic activation, requiring a return to the gate for maintenance. Although maintenance resolved the issue, management charged the crew with an avoidable delay, which the reporter claims is a false accusation pressuring them to bypass proper maintenance procedures.

synopsis: A B737-800 Captain on the DFW Cedar Creek Six Arrival reselected Runway 17L but did not know and failed to see that his action caused a FMC route discontinuity.
summary: The pilot flying a DFW arrival via Cedar Creek to runway 17L reselected the runway, causing a flight plan discontinuity after DIETZ. The aircraft failed to turn north, requiring the First Officer to manually correct the course due to the pilot's unawareness of the system behavior.

synopsis: A B767-300ER flight crew declared an emergency and made an expedited arrival to their destination due to electrical fumes, burning smells and, ultimately, an EICAS FWD ELEC EQUIP EXH message.
summary: The crew returned to the gate twice for fuel pressure issues before departing, then encountered electrical burning smells and fumes during descent. They declared an emergency, landed with a high-speed approach, and taxied for inspection after equipment cooling overheat warnings and an FWD ELEC EQUIP EXH message.

synopsis: An A330 returned to its departure airport after receiving a Green Hydraulic System Leak ECAM message. Maintenance later advised the system had been 'over serviced'
summary: The crew experienced a Green Hydraulic System leak during cruise, likely caused by over-servicing after a nose gear actuator replacement. They returned to the departure airport, declared an emergency, and landed safely with gravity-extended gear before being towed to the gate.

synopsis: After receiving abnormal gear light indications after takeoff the flight crew of an EMB-145 opted to divert to a nearby maintenance facility where, after performing a low pass for ATC observation purposes, the flaps failed to respond. An emergency was declared and they landed uneventfully.
summary: The flight crew diverted after an unusual right main gear indicator and a subsequent flap failure locking at 11 degrees during a go-around. They declared an emergency, received priority, and executed a successful reduced-flap landing with emergency services standing by.

synopsis: Air carrier arrival into SEA experienced confusion with regard to the published altitude restrictions on the STAR and ATC's expectations regarding altitudes after issuing vectors.
summary: A pilot descending into Seattle on the Olympia arrival was vectored direct to ARVAD without a new altitude restriction. The pilot queried ATC, who claimed the STAR's 12,000-foot restriction applied, but the crew eventually verified a clearance to cross ARVAD at 12,000 feet.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An MD-80 flight crew suffered multiple electrical system anomalies and diverted to the nearest suitable airport.
summary: The crew experienced rapid instrument cycling, radio noise, and electrical failures at FL300, causing AC voltage and frequency deviations. After unsuccessful initial APU starts, they declared an emergency, diverted, and landed safely once the APU started at FL200.

synopsis: When the flight crew identified a maintenance discrepancy on a B757 during the pre-flight inspection, a Maintenance Technician determined that the condition required a repair or replacement of the weather radar radome. Another Maintenance Technician determined that the damage did not exceed the maintenance manual limitations, and allowed the aircraft to be released for service.
summary: The flight crew and maintenance technicians inspected a punctured weather radar radome on a Boeing 757 before departure. A mechanic incorrectly signed off the discrepancy by taping the hole and claiming it did not penetrate, resulting in phantom radar returns during the flight.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An Air Carrier crew taxied beyond a red hold bar on LHBP Taxiway B2 prior the Runway 31L A2 hold line because they did not see it nor did the airport diagram depict it.
summary: The flight crew inadvertently crossed a red bar holding line on B2 Taxiway while taxiing to Runway 31L, as they only observed the standard hold short line. The pilot attributed the incident to missing the specific A2 holding point marking and noted that the red bar was not depicted on the commercial ground diagram.

synopsis: A B727-200 flight crew shut down their Number Two Engine due to vibration and returned to their departure airport. Maintenance discovered significant damage to the engine's stator vanes.
summary: During cruise, the crew felt vibration in the number two throttle lever and reduced it to idle, but the engine uncommanded accelerated to 92% N2. They declared an emergency, returned to the departure airport, shut down the engine, and landed safely; post-flight inspection revealed severe stator blade damage.

synopsis: Distracted after two tires blew out during taxi in after the subsequent landing, the flight crew of a CRJ-200 failed to write up an EICAS ANTI-SKID OUTBOARD message received and addressed on approach. A phone call to Maintenance Control resolved the error.
summary: The crew received an Anti-Skid Outboard caution on approach but landed normally. During taxi, two flat tires on the right main gear caused a stop, leading to passenger deplaning and a delayed maintenance report for the caution message.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A flight crew cleared on the RIC COLIN 5 then V16 entered the route from memory, but failed to enter the V16 segment and so when cleared direct MODEL realized the error because that fix was not in the FMC.
summary: The flight crew incorrectly programmed the FMS for the COLIN 5 departure by starting at the RIC VOR instead of MODEL due to confusion over V16's publication and ATC clearance delivery. This error caused an unintended left turn, which the crew corrected by manually entering MODEL and arming LNAV after realizing the flight plan discrepancy.

synopsis: EMB145 Captain notes Hydraulic System 2 at 50% during preflight, which is acceptable, and departs. Upon reaching cruise altitude the quantity is noted to be significantly lower, followed shortly by a HYD 2 LO QTY on the EICAS. The crew elects to divert to a suitable airport and is able to land before the system fails. Maintenance finds a significant leak at the engine driven hydraulic pump.
summary: The flight crew diverted during climb due to a dropping Hydraulic System 2 quantity caused by a leaking engine-driven pump. They managed the descent under 250 KIAS per QRH, landed normally, and confirmed the leak after maintenance troubleshooting.

synopsis: ATR42 Captain is informed by ATC during climb that a ground observer saw a tire fall from his aircraft after takeoff. A low approach is made at the destination airport and the Tower confirms that the left nose wheel is missing. After burning down to 1,500 LBS of fuel an uneventful approach and landing ensues with an evacuation on the runway.
summary: The crew continued flight after Departure Control reported a missing tire, confirmed by the Tower during a low approach. They declared an emergency, held to burn fuel, and landed safely with the left nose wheel missing, requiring an evacuation and tow.

synopsis: A B737-400 flight crew aborted their left engine start when its EGT warning light began flashing and the ground crew advised flame was coming out of the engine. This was the fourth similar event in the logbooks recent history.
summary: During left engine start on the deicing pad, flames were observed exiting the engine and EGT flashed, prompting the Captain to shut down Number One. The crew noted three recent similar aborted start write-ups for this engine in the aircraft history.

synopsis: A MD-83 pilot noted that the boost pump access covers within the area of the overwing heating pads may have excess sealant on the screw heads which could be ingested in an engine.
summary: A pilot reported that MD-80 boost pump cover screws lacked sealant or had excessive, unfaired blobs extending 1/2 inch into the airflow, contrary to a .015-inch limit. The pilot suspects these protrusions have been ingested by engines and questions why Maintenance Control considers the condition compliant.

synopsis: B757 flight crew experiences erratic engine indications in cruise with a Status Message, left engine speed card. With no QRH guidance available, the crew elects to divert to the nearest suitable airport.
summary: During cruise, the flight crew experienced erratic left engine, bleed, fuel, and hydraulic indications, including surging N3/N2 and fluctuating pressures. Consequently, they diverted to the nearest suitable airport and executed a precautionary landing due to these multiple system anomalies.

synopsis: Following two aborted departures due to fluctuating EPRs on the right engine the flight crew of a B757-200 refused the aircraft when asked to perform a max thrust run-up.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced right engine EPR fluctuations during two maximum power takeoff attempts on a lightly loaded aircraft. After maintenance placarded the EEC and replaced the EPR transmitter without resolving the issue, the crew declined a requested engine runup due to safety concerns and were reassigned.

synopsis: A Maintenance Technician inadvertently damaged a landing gear door panel while positioning docking equipment as a result of a breakdown in communication with his co-worker.
summary: A mechanic and spotter attempted to move wing dock sliders for aircraft inspection in poor lighting and high noise. Miscommunication caused the mechanic to extend the dock into the trunion door, and the operator subsequently pushed the extend button, damaging the aircraft.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic reports about the lack of proper documentation and deferral tracking of metallic type Speed Tape applied to the # 1 and # 2 Engine Outlet Guide Vanes (OGVs) on their B767-300 ETOPS aircraft.
summary: A mechanic discovered metallic tape on engine outlet guide vanes without required technical documentation during an ETOPS pre-departure check. Despite the mechanic's objections, a manager authorized the flight in violation of company procedures, citing conflicting maintenance manual revisions and a lack of applicable technical documents.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic reports their Boeing Fault Isolation Manual (FIM) Chapter 31-41-00-815, Figure 103, have Block item numbers -9 and -11 that reference a Block -10 that does not exists on the applicable FIM. The current FIM is for post Service Bulletin (SB) 767-32-0098.
summary: A mechanic reviewing the Fault Isolation Manual during an ETOPS pre-departure check found that Blocks -9 and -11 reference a non-existent Block -10. The report attributes this to missing or misnumbered blocks in the manual for aircraft with Service Bulletin 767-31-0098 and recommends contacting Boeing.

synopsis: A Line Mechanic reports about the lack of proper documentation and deferral tracking of metallic type Speed Tape applied to the # 2 Engine Outlet Guide Vanes (OGVs) on their B767-300 ETOPS aircraft.
summary: A mechanic found speed tape on the #2 engine cowling covering a scratch and requested a deferral using the incorrect ATA Chapter 54-99 instead of the correct ATA 71. The reporter attributed this error to an incomplete Deferral List lacking references for engine ATA chapters and recommended updating the manual.

synopsis: While taxiing to their hangar an instructor pilot and his student aboard a tail dragger LSA suffered a close encounter with an airport ground vehicle driven by a driver either unaware of the aircraft's presence or unwilling to abide by it's right of way on the airport.
summary: A pilot taxiing an American Legend Cub with a student reported that an airport vehicle cut between the aircraft and a fuel farm near the hangars. The pilot attributed the incident to the vehicle operator failing to yield right-of-way and cited limited forward visibility from the rear seat as a contributing factor.

synopsis: The flight crew of a DA-20 lost control of the aircraft upon brake activation following landing. They were only able to regain control after the aircraft's nose and left main gears exited the paved runway surface. Minor damage was noted by the reporters.
summary: The pilot flying and pilot monitoring experienced a sudden left slew immediately after normal touchdown due to uneven braking. The aircraft briefly departed the runway but was steered back on with minor damage after the pilot monitoring assisted with full right brake and rudder.

synopsis: C172 pilot reports attempting a go around due to a high approach and finds the engine will only produce partial power. With the airport behind and unreachable the pilot elects to land on a highway. Upon shut down fuel is discovered draining from the engine cowl. Maintenance inspection of the engine reveals an unapproved carburetor along with fuel line and wiring components that are not suitable for aircraft use. The aircraft had been recently purchased and a pre purchase inspection was accomplished.
summary: The pilot executed a go-around during approach when engine power faded due to a carburetor flood caused by an unapproved Marvel-Schebler carburetor with a stuck float. The pilot made a safe off-field landing on a highway, later discovering the carburetor was incorrectly installed with multiple maintenance discrepancies.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: An instructor pilot discovered the New York Sectional map depicted a lake about nine miles bearing about 225 degrees from MGJ, but the lake cannot be seen from air and presents a false visual navigation landmark.
summary: An instructor and student mistakenly entered Stewart (SWF) Class D airspace while attempting to land at Orange County (MGJ) due to a missing charted lake, relaxed vigilance, and similar runway layouts. The instructor allowed the student to continue the error before initiating a go-around and contacting the tower after landing.

synopsis: BE1900 Captain reports failure of the nose gear to extend during approach. An emergency is declared and manual gear extension procedures in the QRH are complied with. An uneventful landing ensues.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced a nose gear indicator failure during approach, prompting an emergency declaration and a visual approach. The Captain landed the aircraft gently, allowing the First Officer to manually secure the gear handle, after which maintenance secured the nose gear on the ground.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: An instructor with his student landing on GRD Runway 9 reported a near miss after another aircraft passed 30 FT overhead his aircraft which was in the landing flare.
summary: An instructor and student in a high-wing aircraft experienced a near-midair collision with a low-wing aircraft carrying three children while landing at GRD. The other pilot, distracted by passengers and assuming the runway was clear, landed 200 feet ahead with his gear passing 30 feet above the reporting aircraft.

synopsis: Experimental pilot reports a NMAC during descent, with another Vans aircraft that had departed one minute earlier with the same destination.
summary: Two experimental aircraft flying the same GPS track to DCU experienced a 100–200 ft vertical separation when the reporter descended under the Class C shelf. The reporter attributes the near-miss to autopilot tracking, lack of altitude communication, and the Class C shelf funneling traffic.

synopsis: A PA-24 pilot was unable to lower the landing gear and landed gear up after much troubleshooting. An exhaust manifold component broke off and blocked the nose landing gear which prevented the gear handle from extending.
summary: The pilot of a single-engine aircraft with two passengers experienced a landing gear malfunction during descent caused by a broken exhaust manifold fragment obstructing the nose wheel. After failed extension attempts, the crew performed a gear-up landing on a closed runway, resulting in bent propeller tips but no injuries or fire.

synopsis: A B737-300 flight crew initiated an emergency descent and diverted to a nearby airport when their cabin altitude exceeded 11,000 feet while in cruise at FL370.
summary: During cruise, the flight crew experienced a Cabin Altitude Warning horn with a cabin altitude of approximately 11,000 feet. They executed memory items, performed an emergency descent, completed the QRH, and diverted to the nearest suitable airport.

synopsis: Aged B737 lost pressurization.
summary: The flight crew reported a loss of cabin pressurization at FL370. The reporter attributed the incident to the need for newer aircraft.

synopsis: Air Carrier Captain preparing to depart Runway 10 at HDN notices a corporate jet landing Runway 28 and stops short of the runway but over the hold line. CTAF procedures had been used and an IFR release had just been received from Denver Center with no mention of in bound traffic.
summary: The crew departed from non-controlled Hayden Airport and crossed the hold short line for Runway 10 after receiving release from Denver Center without traffic advisories. They stopped to avoid a corporate jet landing on Runway 28, attributing the near miss to missed CTAF calls likely caused by checklist distractions.
