synopsis: An ERJ-190 Captain describes how that aircraft's FMS design makes complying with the BOS KRANN 3 and LGA HAARP crossing restrictions below 10,000 FT difficult. Both Arrivals' profiles require a deceleration to 250 knots followed by a crossing constraint in too short a distance.
summary: The E-190 crew descended below the 8,000 FT crossing restriction at ANSLY on the KRANN 3 arrival into Boston due to a strong tailwind and an FMS crossing altitude change. The pilot attributed the 7,640 FT deviation to programming an impossible descent path and delayed intervention, noting the aircraft's inability to simultaneously meet speed and altitude constraints.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Air Carrier on the ILS 28R at ORD experienced erratic glideslope indications that may have been caused by a parked aircraft awaiting taxi to another runway.
summary: The crew experienced glideslope displacement and a 200-foot altitude error on the ILS approach to ORD Runway 28R, likely caused by a heavy aircraft near the runway. They discontinued the instrument approach at WILLT, landed visually, and reported the anomaly, which ATC attributed to the nearby heavy aircraft.

synopsis: After takeoff a MD-80 Captain's airspeed indicated fifteen knots slow, the First Officer's Flight Direct, Fast Slow indicator, and autothrottles were inoperative. After selecting the Captain to CADC 2, as per the QRH procedure, most systems functioned, but an emergency was declared and the flight returned to the departure airport.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced airspeed discrepancies and autothrottle disengagement during takeoff due to a suspected CADC failure. They declared an emergency, returned to the departure airport, and performed a safe overweight landing with ARFF escort after switching to CADC 2 resolved the indications.

synopsis: A CRJ-900 depressurized automatically when, first the left bleed closed with the LEFT BLEED LEAK warning, then 30 seconds later, the right bleed automatically closed. The crew descended from 17,000 feet to 10,000 feet and continued to the filed destination.
summary: The flight crew managed a Left Bleed Leak warning enroute that triggered automatic depressurization and a Cabin ALT Warning. They executed an expedited descent to 10,000 feet, briefed passengers and cabin crew, and landed with priority handling to minimize ground delay.

synopsis: A BE50 departed normally but immediately after takeoff the pilot experienced the aircraft's aileron control inoperative, so he declared an emergency and returned to land where he discover the aileron yoke control disconnected.
summary: The pilot and two children experienced ineffective roll control during a Part 91 VFR takeoff due to a displaced positioning key from a prior dual-control installation attempt. The pilot declared an emergency, maintained control using rudder and differential power, and landed safely.

synopsis: A DA-40 student unconsciously applied left brake so the instructor rejected the takeoff but could not regain control and during the runway excursion the propeller and nose wheel pant were damaged along with a wing dent.
summary: During a student training takeoff on Runway 32, the aircraft veered left after the student reportedly removed hands and feet from the controls. The instructor attempted to correct but the plane struck a runway light and stopped in the grass with minor damage to the nose gear, propeller, and wing.

aircraft: Citationjet (C525/C526) - CJ I / II / III / IV
synopsis: A CE-525 crew noticed low oil pressure and performed a precautionary shutdown when the pressure did not return to the green band but no cause for the anomaly was discovered during post flight inspection.
summary: The pilot reported low oil pressure while VFR near the destination, leading to a precautionary engine shutdown per checklist. The aircraft landed single-engine with no physical signs of oil loss found during the post-flight walk-around.

synopsis: Two BE35 pilots report a runway incursion at AZO during taxi to Runway 17 via Taxiway D to hold short of Runway 23, which is not complied with for a variety of reasons.
summary: Pilots inadvertently crossed non-active Runway 23 during taxi to Runway 17 due to a lengthy clearance, non-standard markings, passenger distraction, and a last-minute PIC change. The controller did not monitor the taxi or intervene, allowing the aircraft to continue to the active runway after the error was reported.

synopsis: A B737 Captain declared an emergency then diverted to an enroute airport after loosing a large portion of the A Hydraulic system.
summary: The flight crew experienced a Hydraulic A system failure dropping to 12% while holding, leading to further fluid loss. They declared an emergency, diverted to a nearby airport, and landed normally with fire services inspecting the aircraft on the runway.

synopsis: Air Carrier on final for Runway 28L at SFO voiced concern regarding ATC handling with regard to staying behind an A320 on final for Runway 28R.
summary: The Captain of a Boeing 777 reported a threatened safety margin during a dusk visual approach to SFO Runway 28L behind an Airbus 320. ATC vectors and speed assignments created insufficient separation, triggering a TCAS RA and causing the crew to lose visual contact due to high altitude and closure rates.

synopsis: A B737-800 crew executed a go-around in IMC conditions after ORD Tower reported a LOW ALTITUDE ALERT and subsequent full range Runway 28R glideslope fluctuation.
summary: The crew on an ILS 28R approach in IMC executed a go-around due to unreliable glideslope indications and a low altitude alert. Subsequent reports indicated preceding aircraft experienced similar issues, possibly caused by an aircraft in the protected area, prompting a request to better protect ILS zones.

synopsis: A MD-80 Captain detected an inoperative elevator trim but because the aircraft was in a circling approach VMC with the airport in sight, no emergency was declared and flight landed as soon as possible in trim.
summary: During a circle-to-land approach in VMC, the crew discovered the horizontal stabilizer trim was jammed aft and could not move forward. They elected to land immediately rather than declare an emergency or attempt a go-around, citing the aircraft's correct trim setting and the urgency of the situation.

synopsis: During preflight, a DC10 APU auto shutdown and shortly thereafter Maintenance personnel entered the flight station declaring the APU was on fire, so both fire bottles where discharged.
summary: During pre-flight cargo loading, the APU auto-shut down, prompting maintenance personnel to direct the Captain to pull the fire handle and discharge the agent. The Captain complied immediately with the instructions for the reported APU fire.

synopsis: An aircraft on ATL Taxiway A7 stopped rapidly as a van drove under its nose. ATL Ground Control, Airport Police were notified.
summary: While taxiing at Atlanta, a utility truck drove under the aircraft after the crew received clearance to cross Runway 26R. The driver fled the scene, prompting the crew to notify airport police, the safety director, and the ramp manager regarding this reckless safety violation.

synopsis: Air Carrier landing BWI experienced glideslope oscillations while on the ILS Runway 10 approach. The reporter noted this anomaly had been experienced on a number of other occasions.
summary: A pilot reported consistent glide slope oscillations on the ILS Runway 10 approach at BWI, noticeable beyond 20 miles and causing flight director commands. The reporter suspects interference or installation issues, deeming the only CAT II/III approach at the airport unusable for CAT I operations.

synopsis: The pilot of an airtaxi twin experienced an NMAC with a float plane in the airspace interface between Merrill Field and Lake Hood near ANC.
summary: A pilot flying VFR near Merrill Field encountered a single-engine seaplane while switching from Approach to MRI Tower. The near miss occurred because the other aircraft likely lacked an operating transponder, preventing TCAS alerts and ATC advisories despite the pilot's use of recognition lights.

synopsis: ZME Controller described in detail an alleged unsafe operation that involved the Automated Information Transfer (AIT) procedure.
summary: A B737 climbing from BNA was stopped at FL230 by R62 due to a CRJ2 descending in T37 airspace for weather, creating a conflict. The reporter attributed the unsafe situation to T37's failure to coordinate with ZME and T41, and T41's lack of proactive communication regarding the traffic.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described a go around event when traffic vectored for a visual approach lost separation with preceding traffic.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller vectored a heavy A300 for a visual approach to Runway 17R during a south flow operation but failed to maintain wake turbulence separation. The pilot executed a go-around due to an unstabilized approach, prompting the controller to vector the aircraft for an ILS approach.

synopsis: A80 Controller described a loss of separation event claiming the local point out procedures are less than positive with regard to controller actions and responsibilities.
summary: An air traffic controller in Sector P failed to point out LJ60 to Departure Sector N, causing LJ60 to climb into the controller's F900 traffic. The controller issued a turn and descent to FL80 to avoid a close proximity, attributing the incident to misleading procedures and P Sector workload.

synopsis: DAL Controller described a runway incursion event on Runway 13R claiming the non-standard distance of the line form the runway is problematic and changes should be considered.
summary: A C177 pilot crossed the non-standard Runway 13R hold line while training a controller, prompting the instructor to intervene and order the aircraft back. The reporter attributes the deviation to the hold line's unusual 477-foot distance from the runway edge, which likely confused the pilot.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reports a strong nose wheel shimmy above 90 KTS during takeoff and continues. The vibration continues after gear retraction and eventually a burnt rubber odor is detected. Flight continues to destination where an emergency is declared and a normal landing ensues, with nose wheel shimmy again detected when it touches the runway.
summary: During takeoff and landing, the nose wheel shimmed and vibrated, causing a burnt rubber odor due to a suspected over-inflated tire melting against gear bay snubbers. The crew continued to destination, declared an emergency, and landed safely with fire rescue standing by for a post-landing nose gear inspection.

synopsis: B737-300 flight crew missed the fact that all of the aircraft altimeters had been set to 28.xx and leveled off 1,000 FT above assigned Flight Level.
summary: During the climb of a 737-300 at night, the crew discovered all altimeters were incorrectly set to 28.92 instead of 29.xx, causing a 1,000-foot altitude discrepancy with ATC. The error, attributed to poor lighting, small displays, and a likely maintenance oversight, was corrected after the crew identified the setting and climbed to the assigned FL300.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An air carrier Captain descending into MHT reported an airport Tower, possibly TEB, interfering with ATIS on 119.5 when the aircraft is further than 100 NM from MHT.
summary: The Pilot Monitoring on a flight to MHT spent over five minutes on the Number 1 radio to receive ATIS on 119.55 due to interference from a shared Tower frequency. The crew delayed obtaining the ATIS until within 100 miles of MHT, where the interference ceased.

synopsis: During a pushback using hand signals, a B737 Captain persisted in requiring a visual check of the nose bypass pin which had, in fact, been left in.
summary: The pilot and ground crew used hand signals for pushback after wireless headset failure. The crew initially failed to remove the nose gear bypass pin, but the pilot stopped the tug with a hold signal until the pin was removed and verified.

synopsis: An air carrier First Officer pleaded to be paid for flight time dropped due to cumulative fatigue as a result of extensive maintenance delays, minimum rest between scheduled flights and burdensome personal issues.
summary: A pilot reported being fatigued after a 5.5-hour maintenance delay in ZZZ and caring for a dying father, causing them to call in unfit to fly the following day. The pilot stated that excessive delays outside their control prevented sufficient rest, making it unsafe to operate the aircraft or drive home.

synopsis: The flight crew of a B777 declared an emergency and returned to their departure airport following receipt of numerous and inappropriate warning and caution lights late in the high speed regime of the takeoff roll.
summary: The First Officer reported numerous erroneous cockpit lights illuminating after liftoff during takeoff, while the Captain observed no abnormalities. The crew declared an emergency and landed safely; maintenance suspected an ELMS fault, as all lights extinguished upon touchdown.

synopsis: An air carrier First Officer reported company SOP to disarm emergency exit lights for some operations has resulted in passengers being boarded on subsequent flights with the lights disarmed in violation of pertinent FARs.
summary: Customer Service boarded passengers on a nearly full aircraft without arming the Passenger Emergency Exit Lights, violating SOP and CFR Part 25.811. This occurred because new 45-minute report times prevented proper arming before boarding began.

synopsis: A CRJ-700 returned to the airport after takeoff because the aircraft was not pressurizing and found that a relatively new employee had not properly closed the cargo door, but no door warning was activated.
summary: The flight crew experienced a pressurization failure during climb after takeoff, leveling at 6,000 feet MSL. Post-flight inspection revealed the cargo door was not flush despite the handle being locked, confirming a ground handling error caused by a new bag handler.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An Air Carrier aircraft departing TUL encountered severe turbulence and requested an emergency returned to the departure airport.
summary: The flight crew encountered severe turbulence and multiple EICAS warnings shortly after departing TUL while avoiding a storm cell, causing the aircraft to become nearly uncontrollable. They declared an emergency, returned to TUL, and landed safely despite high winds and extreme chop.

synopsis: BAE-125-850XP First Officer reported encountering wake vortex in trail of a Heavy on approach to IAD.
summary: During descent on the DELRO2 arrival into IAD, the crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding Heavy aircraft at 12 miles in trail, causing sudden rolls near 11,000 and 10,600 feet. The pilots disconnected the autopilot, requested a heading change and runway switch to 19C for separation, and reported no injuries to belted passengers.

synopsis: A B757-200 flight crew struggled to achieve a stabilized approach inbound to Runways 28L/R on the FMS BRIJJ visual with GS/PAPI/VASI OTS for both runways. Requests from ATC to keep their speed up to assist with a following aircraft with a medical emergency was a contributing factor.
summary: The Captain and First Officer flew a visual approach to SFO Runway 28R with inoperative glide slope and PAPIs. High speed and altitude caused by ATC, combined with sun glare and reliance on erroneous VNAV data, led to an unstable approach and EGPWS sink rate warnings before a stabilized landing.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An air carrier flight crew was issued the SBBR IRULI 1 Arrival to Runway 11, but no transition from the arrival to the Runway 11 was listed in either the FMS or EFB, so a radar vector was provided.
summary: During descent into SBBR, the flight crew could not load the IRULI1 arrival for Runway 11L in the FMC or EFBs, despite ATC confirming its existence. The crew requested and received radar vectors for the ILS 11L approach, resulting in an uneventful landing.

synopsis: After a lapse in resetting the altimeter passing the transition altitude the Captain opined that a change in company SOP regarding checklists was a contributing factor.
summary: During a climb to FL240 to avoid weather, the crew failed to reset altimeters to 29.92 until passing FL210. The pilot attributed this error to the recent removal of the altimeter setting item from the checklist, arguing that eliminating this error control increases the probability of such mistakes.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: A pilot was prepared for the HHR Runway 25 GPS approach, but because of GPS signal disruption was cleared for the LOC then overshot final as he transitioned NAV equipment and mental mapping to the non precision approach.
summary: A pilot flying an IFR flight to HHR in IMC experienced a GPS signal loss and avionics failure while transitioning from a requested GPS approach to a cleared Localizer approach. The pilot attributed the equipment failure to nearby military testing, which caused a course deviation and required traffic adjustments by ATC.

synopsis: A DA-40 landed with an apparent locked left wheel brake and the pilot was able to keep the aircraft on the runway with no major damage or injuries.
summary: During the landing phase of a night visual approach, the pilot reported the left main wheel locked up on touchdown, causing a tire blowout and runway excursion to Taxiway Charlie. The pilot safely stopped the aircraft with no injuries, though the specific cause of the wheel lockup remained undetermined after maintenance inspection.

synopsis: Confusion reigned between Approach Control and the instructor/student pilots of a C172 on vectors for the VOR Runway 16 IAP at DAB regarding the expectation to perform the published procedure turn.
summary: A pilot and student flying a VOR 16 approach at Daytona Beach International misunderstood an ATC clearance regarding a straight-in versus circle-to-land procedure. The pilot initiated a procedure turn after the controller denied a "straight-in" request, leading to a radio clarification and re-clearance to intercept the final approach course.

synopsis: A C208B pilot reported fatigue from long duty days, six days a week and momentarily climbing 200 FT about the 10,000 FT altitude assigned before an Approach Controller urgently demanded a descent.
summary: A fatigued pilot flying a C208B Caravan during climb reported a conflict with an Approach Controller who demanded an immediate descent due to perceived altitude discrepancies. The pilot attributed the confusion and loss of situational awareness to excessive fatigue from a demanding 6-day, 14-hour work schedule.

synopsis: A VFR C182 pilot in contact with Luke Approach was advised of traffic descending and as the near missed was recognized he took evasive action from a VFR light twin returning from the training area.
summary: A C182 instructor flying at 5,500 feet west of GBN VOR executed a right turn to avoid a descending light twin reported by Luke Approach at less than half a mile. The other pilot was not in contact with ATC, prompting the instructor to recommend that training traffic monitor Luke Approach for safety.

synopsis: Aural distraction during Departure Controller training contributed to the failure of the trainee to assign a higher altitude to a departing B737 off ELP. The departing aircraft was briefly below the MVA, although above all obstacles.
summary: A trainee controller assigned a B737 departing El Paso Runway 4 to maintain 8,000 feet, resulting in the aircraft being below the 9,000-foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude. The reporter attributed this error to distractions from a loud conversation in the TRACON and the lack of a westbound Standard Instrument Departure for Runway 4.

synopsis: ZMA Controller described a loss of separation event when assuming information not verified regarding departures off two adjacent airports, the reporter acknowledging assumptions were in part to blame for the incident.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller at Nassau/Abaco Low issued an IFR clearance to a C414 after assuming approval from Sector 21 due to poor audio and radar limitations below 14,000 feet. The controller admitted the error was acting on an unverified assumption, which resulted in a perceived airspace violation by the receiving sector.

synopsis: A B737 flight crew began pushback while tug was still under the aircraft's nose. Proper disconnect procedures were not followed through due to flight crew distraction of dealing with Operations.
summary: During pushback, the Captain released the parking brake and advanced the throttle while the tug was still present, causing the aircraft to move less than a foot before stopping. The incident occurred because the Captain failed to visually verify the tug's departure after clearing ground crew, while the First Officer was distracted obtaining a new release time.

synopsis: A B737-700 Number One Engine rolled back to 65% N1 while flying at FL400 over a tropical storm with ice forming on the windshield at -55C. After the igniters were selected to FLT and the engine anti-ice turned ON, the engine recovered in about 30 seconds.
summary: During cruise at FL400 in a tropical storm, the Number One Engine rolled back to 65% N1 due to sensor icing. The crew activated ignition and anti-ice, restoring normal operation within one minute, and Maintenance attributed the event to an iced sensor defaulting the engine.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An Air Carrier crew encountered severe turbulence between to thunderstorm cells at 16,000 feet climbing and because of aircraft lavatory and flight station disarray returned to the departure airport as a precaution.
summary: The crew of a flight departing IAH encountered severe turbulence while penetrating a thunderstorm cell between two intense cells at 10,000 feet. The event caused significant cabin and cockpit damage, including sprayed lavatory contents and scattered equipment, prompting an immediate return to IAH for inspection and re-crewing.

synopsis: B737 flight crew enroute to a foreign destination, decided to return to their departure airport due to an unruly aggressive passenger who had to be restrained and handcuffed.
summary: A disruptive First Class passenger became physical with cabin crew, prompting the flight crew to divert back to the departure airport. The pilots rejected Dispatch's fuel-focused alternatives to prioritize security, successfully returning with law enforcement meeting the aircraft at the gate.

synopsis: Wing walker reported a B737's pushback was abruptly stopped as a bus passed behind the aircraft, the tug driver had to stopped rapidly causing the tow bar shear pin to brake. No aircraft damage.
summary: A wing walker reported that a push tug driver braked suddenly to avoid a bus, breaking the shear pin while the walker was still near the wing. Maintenance inspected the aircraft and confirmed no damage occurred.

synopsis: A jetbridge rose damaging a B757's door hinges after the auto leveler failed in the ON position because of corrosion in a control mechanism.
summary: The auto leveler malfunctioned without alarming while in the ON position, causing the jetbridge to rise on its own. No alarm sounded during the uncommanded movement.

synopsis: After successfully marshalling and chocking the EMB into the gate, a ramp serviceman struck the aircraft with a towbar when the tug's brakes failed while attempting to attach the tow bar, which was totaled.
summary: The pilot chocked the aircraft and connected a push tug at the gate. When the tug brakes failed during a brake test, the pilot pushed the towbar into the aircraft, totaling the towbar head but causing no visible damage to the plane.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A flight crew departed MMTO (TLC) on the APAN1E SID but were cleared on the APAN3C which the crew did not see until ATC advised them of their error. The APAN3C was listed as one of six Runway 15 departures on a single page, not as a stand alone.
summary: The flight crew departed Runway 15 on the wrong APAN1E departure due to a misunderstood clearance and a heavy controller accent, while the correct APAN3C was hidden in a separate chart tab. ATC detected the deviation at FL220, vectored the aircraft to join APAN3C, and the crew corrected the FMS with no further incident.

synopsis: Air Carrier pilots experience a TCAS event at 9,000 FT descending into OGG that initially commands a maximum descent, then reverses and commands a maximum climb. Upon receiving a clear of conflict announcement the traffic is sighted at one to two O'clock and slightly above.
summary: A commercial crew descending to Kahului experienced conflicting TCAS RAs due to a VFR Cessna Caravan deviating from its assigned 8,500 feet to 9,300 feet. The pilot followed the commands to avoid a near midair collision, attributing the event to the Caravan's altitude deviation and lack of ATC separation in mixed airspace.

synopsis: Hawker 850XP First Officer experiences a master warning light during descent, with no other indications, that quickly extinguishes itself. At 13,000 FT an electrical burning smell is detected and an emergency is declared for an expedited landing at the destination airport.
summary: During descent, the flight crew detected a master warning light and a burning wire smell, prompting an emergency declaration and priority landing. The aircraft landed safely, and the Fire Department confirmed the odor, validating the crew's decision to declare an emergency.

synopsis: B757 flight crew experiences a L HYD QTY status message in cruise followed shortly by a L HYD ENG PUMP status message. The left engine pump is turned off in compliance with L HYD ENG PUMP QRH procedure. Soon after a L HYD SYS PRESS status message appears and the left electric pump is turned off. The crew elects to continue to destination. Prior to landing the PTU fails requiring alternate gear extension and electric flap extension using the alternate switches.
summary: The crew managed a left hydraulic quantity loss and pump failure by following QRH checklists, declaring an emergency, and landing uneventfully with alternate systems. Post-landing smoke from the left engine or strut required an engine shutdown, and the aircraft was towed to the gate due to lost nose wheel steering.

synopsis: A321 Captain reports being issued a go around on very short final due to the departing aircraft not being airborne. The reporter had determined that a go around would be necessary but elected to wait for the ATC instructions due to possible conflict with the departing traffic ahead and off parallel runways.
summary: The pilot reported that an inexperienced Tower Controller directed a go-around on short final due to spacing issues caused by a slow taxiing aircraft crossing the runway. The go-around was executed below 120 feet after the crossing aircraft delayed takeoff clearance, creating a potential conflict with the departing aircraft.

synopsis: TCAS TA and RA warnings were instrumental in separating the reporter's A320 and a military B737 which descended below its cleared altitude. Situational awareness was cited as a result of ATC and the B737 not communicating on the same frequency as civil operators.
summary: The pilot reported a TCAS RA encounter with a military B-737 at 33,000 feet while 25 NM from BAM VOR. The pilot manually descended and turned left after the other aircraft descended through clouds, noting a lack of ATC communication with the military flight as a contributing factor.

synopsis: An EMB-145 Captain believed ATC's failure to route them via their filed and cleared route resulted in the need to stop for fuel in order to remain legal to complete their planned flight.
summary: Pilots reported that ATC vectors over the ocean during departure created a longer route, causing a fuel emergency and diversion to an alternate airport. The crew attributed the incident to ATC deviating from the filed weather-clear route without prior notification, preventing adequate fuel planning.

synopsis: An ERJ Captain expressed concern that repeated dispatch of an aircraft with obvious periodic inflight vibrations, despite previous logbook writeups, presented a poor perception of his company's commitment to safety and encouraged flight crews to become complacent about deferred maintenance.
summary: The crew experienced non-synchronous vibration at 36,000 feet and Mach 0.76, which they resolved by descending or using engine anti-ice. The pilot reported that continuing operations with this known discrepancy degrades safety culture and discourages reporting.

synopsis: While landing in a crosswind the downwind tire of a PC-12 failed and the aircraft exited the runway to the left.
summary: The pilot landed a Pilatus on Runway XX in 18-knot crosswinds with 30 degrees of flaps. The left main tire blew out immediately after touchdown, causing the aircraft to depart the runway to the left, though the pilot reported no excessive side loads were imposed.

synopsis: An international relief pilot for an air carrier expressed misgivings about the implementation of a tablet type EFB by his airline, citing training, spares, battery issues and lack of 24/7 support.
summary: A relief pilot reported that the company's Electronic Flight Bag program is hazardous due to poor implementation, training, and approval processes. The pilot cited charging failures, app lockups, and inadequate support, noting that mission-critical equipment was approved after only mediocre video training.

synopsis: MD82 flight crew notices a pressurization outflow light illuminated at FL270. Inspection of the pressurization system panel reveals both packs at zero flow, cabin outflow valve fully closed, cabin rate indication climbing at 500 FPM, and cabin altitude around 6,500 FT. QRH procedures are unsuccessful and descent is initiated. At 14,000 FT packs return to normal operation but a diversion for fuel is deemed prudent.
summary: During cruise at FL270, the flight crew encountered a pressurization failure with both packs at zero flow and cabin altitude climbing. After declaring an emergency to descend below 10,000 FT, the packs recovered, but the crew diverted for fuel.

synopsis: A B737NG flight crew elected to divert to a nearby airport when the B Hydrualic System failed thus eliminating one of two sources for multiple flight controls. The crew declared an emergency in order to land on the longest available runway and into the prevailing wind.
summary: The flight crew diverted enroute after a System B flight control pressure loss left controls un-powered. They declared an emergency to secure Runway 35C, avoiding a crosswind on Runway 31R that was unsafe due to the inoperative yaw damper and spoilers.

synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reports diverting to a second alternate after their filed alternate and original destination are denied by ATC due to weather. During the non-precision approach the aircraft descends below MDA prior to arriving at the normal glide path. An emergency is declared during the diversion due to fuel and the aircraft lands with seven thousand pounds.
summary: The flight crew diverted to ZZZZ and accepted a VOR Runway 33 approach, where the aircraft pitched over at a higher-than-expected rate at the FAF. Due to fatigue, the pilot failed to monitor the vertical speed indicator, resulting in an unnoticed descent below the MDA before visual correction and landing.

synopsis: An alert B757 Captain questioned the loading of excessive amounts of Lithium Ion batteries in the cargo hold. After investigation the aircraft returned to the gate and the offending load removed.
summary: The Captain discovered a discrepancy regarding 2.5 kg of Lithium Ion Batteries in the forward cargo during preflight, which later manifested as 97 lbs on the Purser's manifest. The aircraft returned to the gate to unload the entire forward compartment, resulting in a two-hour delay due to the potential thermal runaway risk.

synopsis: G550 Captain reports a TCAS RA during arrival into TEB near SAX VOR.
summary: The flight crew, descending on radar vectors into TEB, received a TCAS climb resolution advisory while leveling at 5,000 FT. They climbed to 5,500 FT to clear the conflict, then descended to 3,000 FT after ATC issued a new clearance.

synopsis: A Captain and First Officer report noticing the Number 3 Engine EPR gauge on their MD-11 aircraft had a green 'REV' (reverser) indication during their walkaround but the indication turned to red right after takeoff. Pilots noted the MEL relief needs to explicitly state that an indication is unacceptable or the Maintenance Policy needs to reflect the FAA authorized relief.
summary: The Captain and First Officer flew an MD-11 with a deferred Engine 3 thrust reverser, encountering a false in-flight red REV indication caused by a dirty Cannon plug. Maintenance Control deemed the indication abnormal, leading to a landing at ZZZZ1 where mechanics cleaned the plug to rectify the issue.

synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reports being cleared for the TAMMY 4 arrival to MEM landing north. This clearance is misinterpreted to mean to use the north transition to land on Runway 18 L or R. In the end the Controller was in error but the misinterpretation by the reporter allowed it to go undetected until the course divergence at TAMMY.
summary: The flight crew and Memphis ARTCC controller experienced a clearance misunderstanding during the TAMMY 4 arrival due to ambiguous "landing north" phraseology conflicting with active south operations. Expectation bias caused the crew to initially load the wrong arrival, but the controller corrected the clearance to the south arrival after the crew queried the ROCAB restriction.

synopsis: B767 flight crew reports requesting that lithium metal battery dangerous goods be removed from the aircraft prior to departure. After a short delay the station reports that the dangerous goods have been remove. Over the North Atlantic the crew is informed that the wrong pallet was removed and the batteries are still on board. Flight continues to destination uneventfully.
summary: The flight crew discovered a hazardous material remained on board after the station mistakenly removed the wrong pallet despite confirming removal. The crew received updated documentation via ACARS and continued the flight without incident.

synopsis: B737-900 Captain reports receiving a EGPWS terrain warning departing Runway 28R at SFO with instructions to turn right to a 050 heading. Pitch was increased to silence the warning. Day VMC prevailed.
summary: A 737-900 crew departing SFO Runway 28R received a Tower clearance for heading 050 instead of the Quiet 4 departure. During the north turn in climb, a TERRAIN warning triggered, which ceased after the crew increased pitch.

synopsis: A319 Captain experiences the loss of the Green Hydraulic System as the gear is retracted after takeoff. The left main gear remains extended after the right main and nose gear retract. ECAM procedures are complied with for loss of the Green Hydraulic System and the gear handle is cycled to no avail. The gear is gravity extended and the flight diverts to a suitable airport.
summary: The crew experienced a Green hydraulic system failure with zero fluid quantity after gear retraction, causing the left main gear to remain down. Maintenance later identified a loose hydraulic line in the left gear as the cause, leading to a precautionary diversion and landing.

aircraft: Regional Jet CL65; Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: A CL-65 flight crew, cleared for a night time visual approach from a south downwind to Runway 6 at BHM, experienced an unstabilized approach when their ground track generated an EGPWS terrain warning for charted towers on the turn to base. Their recovery was, in turn, exacerbated by their failure to retract the previously extended spoilers which resulted in a momentary stick shaker.
summary: During a night approach to BHM Runway 6 with an Air Data Computer failure, the First Officer deployed flight spoilers while high, causing a stick shaker at 160 KIAS. The crew retracted the spoilers at 600 feet AGL and landed, attributing the event to ATC vectoring into obstacles, distraction from a caution, and lack of spoiler callouts.

synopsis: A Captain who had flown a B737-700 aircraft earlier in the day, was informed by an outbound Captain beginning their trip, that the Crew Oxygen (O2) on the same aircraft had a large drop in oxygen pressure when performing the Crew O2 Preflight Test. Maintenance found the Crew oxygen bottle valve handle was not opened all the way.
summary: Pilots reported a valid crew oxygen test at 1,800 PSI before departure, but a subsequent crew found an invalid test due to a maintenance error in ZZZ where the oxygen valve was not fully opened. The reporter noted that pilots cannot verify valve position on the B737, as the gauge displayed full pressure despite the fault.

synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew taxiing for departure at PHL passed an assigned turn and taxied under the arrival path for Runway 9L, no traffic conflicts occurred.
summary: The First Officer and Captain of a flight at PHL taxied past the turn onto Taxiway K, passing under the approach path of Runway 9L due to task saturation, weather delays, and a CRM communication breakdown. The crew corrected the error after contacting Ground Control, and the flight continued without incident.

synopsis: An E-145 flight crew suffered a blown main gear tire on takeoff. They remained in the pattern, performed two inspection flybys of the Tower, and landed uneventfully.
summary: The crew experienced a tire blowout and landing gear indication failure during takeoff, prompting an emergency return with gear left down. After visual confirmation and emergency extension attempts, they landed safely with the gear eventually indicating down and locked, allowing a slow taxi to the gate.

synopsis: A Gulfstream 200 flight crew declared an emergency and diverted due to right hydraulic system failure. Diverted again when their original diversion airport had inadequate runway length due to construction.
summary: The flight crew at FL390 declared an emergency after Right Hydraulic Low Level and Low Pressure EICAS messages indicated a mechanical failure causing fluid leakage. They diverted to a longer runway, landed using emergency brakes, and were unable to taxi due to lost nose wheel steering.

synopsis: Despite multiple, apparently erroneous, EICAS messages and malfunctioning communications radios the flight crew of a CL-300 elected to continue and complete their three hour IFR flight.
summary: The flight crew experienced erroneous EICAS messages and uncommanded NAV/COMM frequency flips during cruise, requiring multiple transmissions to maintain contact with Center. They continued to the destination for a visual approach, attributing the issue to not following updated Bombardier procedures to tune 121.5 on the reversionary panel.

synopsis: Miscommunications between ATC and the pilots as well as between the pilots resulted in confusion and a modestly unsettled but ultimately successful visual final approach for a B767-200 flight crew.
summary: During a visual approach to Runway 9 at KAVME, the crew misidentified the airport and captured a false glide slope after ATC issued a heading that did not intercept final. The First Officer corrected the descent and intercepted final following a low altitude warning, attributing the error to cockpit noise, miscommunication, and improper approach mode selection.

synopsis: The crew of a Boeing 757-200 received an EGPWS warning while maneuvering for a visual approach. The pilot flying climbed to a higher and safer altitude until closer to the airport, and continued to an uneventful landing.
summary: During a visual approach at 3,000 to 3,500 feet, the crew received an EGPWS warning 12 miles from the runway. They disconnected the autopilot, climbed to 3,500 feet, and continued the approach after reviewing terrain charts.

synopsis: A B777-200 flight crew declared an emergency and returned to their departure airport after suffering the loss of fluid and pressure to the right hydraulic system.
summary: The flight crew experienced right hydraulic quantity and pressure loss shortly after passing ZZZ, prompting an emergency declaration and fuel dump at FL320. They returned to the departure airport and executed a normal overweight landing at 519,000 LBS.

synopsis: A B757-200 flight crew elected to continue to their destination after the left hydraulic system failed as they climbed through 15,000 FT after takeoff. Problems extending both the flaps and landing gear at their destination forced a go around and completion of associated abnormal procedure checklists. After landing they were towed to the gate.
summary: The crew experienced a left hydraulic system failure with zero quantity during climb, leading to gear and flap disagreements on approach. They executed a go-around, performed alternate gear extension, and landed safely after ATC provided a center runway clearance.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: A pilot departed the FDK ramp with a clearance to Runway 23 via Taxiways B, A, but because of the absence of any signage taxied up H and was directed to D where he incurred Runway 23 before stopping at Runway 30.
summary: A pilot at FDK experienced a runway incursion while taxiing due to a lack of taxiway markings and misunderstanding Ground Control instructions. The pilot inadvertently crossed Runway 23 instead of Runway 30, was directed to backtrack, and subsequently took off safely after the confusion was resolved.

synopsis: Prior to leasing his PA34 to a flight school the owner attempted to test the inflight restart procedure to ensure its functionality. After shutting the left engine down the propeller failed to unfeather, the engine failed to restart and the electrical system failed, requiring the landing gear to be manually extended for the following safe landing.
summary: The pilot of a Seneca II attempted an in-flight engine restart for training evaluation, but the starter failed to turn the propeller and electrical systems degraded. The pilot declared an emergency, used the emergency gear extension procedure, and landed safely after total electrical failure.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A flight crew taxied out from the FBO Ramp and missed Taxiway A centerline at SMO, the taxiway signage and markings did not clearly indicate the taxiway boundary.
summary: The SIC, acting as pilot flying, deviated from the designated taxiway at SMO due to confusion over dashed double yellow boundary markings. The crew corrected the path after Tower instruction, resulting in no runway incursion or impact on other operations.

synopsis: A C210 pilot suffered the loss of all oil pressure shortly after takeoff on a long cross country. He landed safely at a nearby grass strip airport.
summary: A solo pilot flying a Cessna 210 experienced a loss of manifold pressure and zero oil pressure approximately 10 minutes after departure. The pilot safely landed without incident at a nearby grass strip.

synopsis: Fatigue and company pressure for on time operations were factors in a cluster of anomalous events for a CRJ-700 flight crew taxiing for takeoff with an inoperative APU.
summary: A fatigued Captain, pressured by on-time metrics, mismanaged a cross-bleed engine start during taxi, causing an ITT exceedance after confusing the START and STOP buttons. The incident resulted from fatigue, heat, and divided attention, but the engine was restarted safely without injury or equipment damage.

synopsis: JFK Controller described a questionable wake separation event involving a heavy followed by a large aircraft landing on the parallel Runway's 13.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller reported a potential 5 NM separation breach between a B767-300 and a B737-800 on a VOR approach to parallel Runways 13L and 13R. The incident highlights concerns that computer-measured point-to-point separation on curved approaches may not reflect actual flying miles, risking wake turbulence standards.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described a TCAS RA involving a VFR and IFR aircraft, the RA actions resulting in an IFR to IFR separation issue.
summary: An air traffic controller vectored a Gulfstream G550 IFR departure toward a DA40 VFR practice approach, causing a TCAS Resolution Advisory. The controller instructed the G550 to ignore the RA to avoid a C172, resulting in a 300-foot vertical separation with the DA40, which the pilot attributed to the controller's poor planning and unsafe instructions.

synopsis: Tower Controller described an unsafe event claiming the TRACON should release communications with inbound aircraft to the Tower earlier to avoid conflicts in/near the congested traffic pattern.
summary: A Local Control instructor and trainee managed a potential conflict between a helicopter, a Cessna 152, and an uncontacted Cessna 180 near the airport. The reporter attributes the risk to late handoffs from RADAR East and a safety culture that restricts Tower jurisdiction, preventing timely traffic exchange.

synopsis: A B737 experienced a Number 1 Engine failure due to low oil pressure. The crew declared an emergency and diverted.
summary: The crew experienced a Number 1 engine low oil pressure warning and loud bangs while cruising at FL390, causing an emergency descent to FL270. They shut down the engine, diverted to ZZZ, and executed a single-engine flaps 15 landing without further incident.

synopsis: During approach the Boeing 737-700 crew was vectored by ATC on a course that conflicted with a tethered balloon restricted area. The EGPWS activated and the crew took immediate evasive action.
summary: The flight crew received a GPWS obstacle warning while being vectored by Approach Control near a tethered balloon in restricted airspace. They executed a hard right turn to avoid the obstacle, and the controller attributed the delay to spacing conflicts with another aircraft at the same altitude.

synopsis: The Captain of a B737-700 took control and rejected the takeoff when the First Officer, the original pilot flying was unable to control the aircraft due to a failed seat latch which allowed his seat to slide full aft and he was unable to maintain directional control as a result.
summary: During takeoff roll at 90–100 KTS, the First Officer's seat slid back, causing loss of directional control and a loud thud. The Captain rejected the takeoff due to the sudden seat shift and confusion, resulting in an uneventful stop and subsequent seat replacement.

synopsis: A B737-300 flight crew declared an emergency and returned to their departure airport upon receipt of a cabin altitude warning as they climbed through FL290.
summary: The flight crew experienced an uncommanded cabin altitude warning during climb at FL290, forcing an emergency descent and return due to an undetected aft cargo door issue caused by a bungee cord. Maintenance later identified the door defect, which was associated with an existing MEL on the hold-open mechanism.

synopsis: During cruise flight the crew of an A300 lost the Number 1 Pressure Controller, followed by the loss of the Number 2 Pressure Controller, and descended to 10,000 on oxygen masks using the Manual Pressure Controller.
summary: The flight crew experienced dual Pressure Controller failures enroute at 34,000 feet. They utilized the Manual Pressure Controller, descended on oxygen to 10,000 feet under Center control, and completed an uneventful ILS approach.

synopsis: When climbing through 1,000 feet during a maintenance test flight, the right engine of a B717-200 developed a compressor stall. The crew leveled, reduced power on the malfunctioning engine, declared an emergency, and returned to land.
summary: During a maintenance flight's initial climb, the crew experienced a right engine compressor stall while turning right at 1,000 feet. They declared an emergency, followed QRH procedures with reduced power, and landed safely at the departure airport with no visible engine damage.

synopsis: A Flight Attendant on an A319 describes the in-cabin scenario after being notified by the Captain of a flap malfunction and subsequent emergency landing.
summary: Flight attendants prepared the cabin for an emergency landing after the Captain reported landing flap issues during approach and ordered a go-around. The crew briefed passengers on brace positions and exits, then remained seated until the aircraft stopped at the gate following the impact command.

synopsis: An engine failure at rotation, compounded by multiple and immediate calls from ATC, other aircraft and the flight attendants regarding a fire in the left engine and smoke in the cabin compounded the difficulties for the flight crew of a B757-200, yet a successful, albeit imperfect, synergistic chain of events followed to get all aboard safely back on the ground in short order.
summary: The crew experienced a left engine failure and fire report at rotation, causing task saturation that delayed gear retraction and checklists. They hand-flew an overweight landing after securing the engine and discharging a fire bottle, with no cabin fire or evacuation required.

synopsis: The flight crew of a CL601 believed ATC incorrectly accused them of crossing Runway 1 after landing on Runway 6 and being cleared to exit at B, hold short of Runway 1. The reporter believes that, if they did cross, it was inadvertent and poor lighting and markings at the area, a designated hot spot, were contributing factors.
summary: The flight crew stopped on Runway 1 instead of holding short after landing at Teterboro, despite reading back instructions correctly. The reporter attributed the deviation to a known hot spot with dim lighting and no specific illumination for the approaching runway.

synopsis: A private pilot and instructor experienced engine roughness and severe vibration. As they began to deviate to the nearest airport, the conditions worsened, so they performed a successful precautionary landing on a road.
summary: A student pilot and instructor flying a dual cross-country under Part 61 training experienced engine roughness and severe vibration while descending to 2,500 feet AGL. They declared an emergency and landed safely in an open road beside a canal with no injuries or damage.

synopsis: The pilot of an AW109 helicopter noticed string on the main rotor head during the post flight inspection.
summary: A helicopter pilot discovered hundreds of feet of string wrapped around the swashplate during a post-flight inspection after a passenger transport flight. The pilot reported no in-flight anomalies or control issues, but the aircraft was grounded for maintenance inspection, causing a passenger delay.

synopsis: When the flight crew of a G-IV sideslipped the jet to transfer fuel while at FL450 the right side (First Officer's) altimeter indicated 45,320 FT verses 45,000.
summary: During cruise, the First Officer applied rudder trim to slip the aircraft for fuel balancing, causing the Number 2 altimeter to falsely read FL450+320. This erroneous reading was transmitted by the transponder while the aircraft remained at FL450, as the autopilot relied on the accurate Number 1 altimeter.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: After loosing engine oil pressure, the pilot of a single engine high wing aircraft experienced loss of engine power and eventually engine failure, resulting in a landing short of the runway and collision with a post.
summary: During cruise, the pilot experienced zero oil pressure and engine failure, forcing a short landing to the right of the runway where the horizontal stabilizer struck a post. The pilot attributed the incident to a possibly loose oil filter adaptor, resulting in tail damage but no injuries.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described a conflict event during Flight Check operations noting that increased and detailed coordination between Flight Check and local ATC facilities is needed.
summary: A TRACON controller vectored a B757 away from a BE30 flight check aircraft at 3,000 MSL after the BE30 unexpectedly reversed course toward the B757's path. The controller attributed the conflict to poor coordination regarding the flight check's specific route requirements prior to arrival.

synopsis: TRACON developmental described an overtake event on final between a PAR and TACAN aircraft. The reporter listed coordination complexities and limited automation interface between the TRACON and the Navy base as causal factors.
summary: An air traffic controller training at a Navy airport lost communication with a BE20 while sequencing it behind a T34 on final approach. The incident resulted from manual coordination limitations between facilities and excessive strip management, which distracted the controller from effective scanning and separation.

synopsis: TRACON Controller experienced an MVA infraction when confused regarding a pilot's request for a clearance.
summary: A Tower controller and a BE90 pilot experienced a Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) violation when the pilot requested a direct route to an intersection while climbing to 10,000 feet. The controller issued a heading but later cleared the direct route without verbal coordination, causing the aircraft to penetrate the MVA by 0.25 to 0.5 miles.

synopsis: ZAB Controller indicated the possibility that several aircraft were directed through restricted airspace;listing airspace design, facility coordination and equipment updates as causal factors.
summary: An air traffic controller in Sector 90/80/47 incorrectly cleared a B737 through active White Sands Missile Range airspace R5103C due to a flawed MOS schedule display. The controller believed the airspace was inactive, but it remained hot, causing aircraft to enter a missile firing zone and prompting a military inquiry.

synopsis: After being dispatched with an inoperative APU a B737-NG flight crew was confronted with multiple system anomalies while attempting to start engines, resulting in returns to the gate for Maintenance and sweltering and unhappy passengers who were required to get off the airplane in order to add fuel burned while away from the gate because local rules would not allow fueling with them on board.
summary: The flight crew experienced repeated electrical and display failures on an NG aircraft with an inoperative APU due to a faulty Static Inverter and Standby Inverter. After returning to the gate for maintenance repairs and deplaning passengers, the crew successfully completed the flight to destination.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported wake vortex encounter in trail of a B777 on approach to SFO.
summary: During a visual approach to SFO Runway 28R, the crew observed a B777 turning hard left in front of them at 1,800 feet. The crew executed a 40-degree left bank and added power to recover, then continued the approach after the B777 cleared the path.

synopsis: A DHC-8-400 flight crew rejected their takeoff due to IAS warning messages. A high speed taxi test confirmed the fault. Maintenance was performed. Flight crew wanted another high speed test to confirm the repair. Their request was denied. Boarded passengers and attempted another takeoff. Same warnings returned. Rejected takeoff. Returned to gate and Maintenance advised they wanted another high speed test as well, but Maintenance Control turned down their request. Reporter was 'beyond upset.'
summary: The flight crew rejected takeoff twice due to a RED IAS and SSEC message indicating an internal fault in the ISI. Although Maintenance drained water from the line, the fault recurred on the second attempt, leading to another rejected takeoff and crew frustration over the lack of a high-speed taxi test.

synopsis: CRJ-200 First Officer reports an aircraft refusal for an inoperative windscreen wiper. The crew is chastised by a Chief Pilot and eventually the crew agrees to accept the aircraft with the First Officer's wiper on MEL.
summary: The Captain and First Officer initially refused to fly due to an inoperative windscreen wiper and forecast rain but yielded to pressure from the Chief Pilot and Maintenance. They proceeded with the flight, acknowledging the error of overriding their safety concerns regarding forward visibility during instrument approaches.

synopsis: An E145 flight crew opted to return to their departure airport following the failure of several autoflight related systems. While doing so they suffered a pack overload condition which emitted a burning smell but succombed to appropriate QRH measures.
summary: The crew returned to the departure airport after flight director and autopilot modes failed on the Captain's side and poor commercial radio communications hindered troubleshooting. During the return, a pack overload caused a burning smell that cleared after QRH procedures, resulting in an uneventful landing.

synopsis: EMB145 Captain is informed of electrical smoke and fumes emanating from a row of seats by a Flight Attendant. The recirculation fan is turned off as a precaution. After being informed of further smoke and smell incidents the Captain elects to declare an emergency and lands safely at the destination airport.
summary: Flight crew and cabin crew reported white smoke and an electrical smell near seat XA during the arrival phase. The crew declared an emergency to expedite landing, but emergency responders and maintenance found no fire or source upon arrival.

synopsis: The flight crew of an MD-82 received an intermittent 'Tail Compartment Temp High' warning during climb out, declared an emergency, and returned to the departure airport for maintenance action.
summary: The pilot reported a 'Tail Compartment Temp High' light cycling after takeoff at 7,000 FT, prompting an emergency return and uneventful landing. Maintenance found three air leaks in the tail compartment, noting that 42°C outside air temperature contributed to the situation.

synopsis: ATC leveled a B737-800 at 6,000 FT for traffic and once cleared for the ILS 24R the crew was rushed for the approach and landing preparation after become VMC at about 1,500 FT.
summary: The pilot flew an ILS 24R approach at LAX where ATC level-off at 6,000 feet caused a rushed descent requiring rapid acceleration and automation disengagement. The crew landed with 30 flaps instead of 40 to maintain stability, noting the ATC clearance created a situation where a 360-degree turn would have been safer.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reports departing Runway 14L from Taxiway U2 at ORD without verifying that U2 is an authorized intersection in the TPS [Takeoff Performance System] preplan. The result is a lift off point very close to the end of the runway.
summary: The First Officer and Captain departed from Runway 14L using Takeoff Performance Data for the full-length runway instead of the assigned U2 intersection (14LX). This error, caused by distraction during a complex taxi, resulted in a long takeoff roll with less than 1,000 feet of runway remaining.

synopsis: As they began the takeoff roll the flight attendants aboard an A319 began to notice numerous electrical lighting and galley power anomalies that went unattended by the cockpit crew. As quickly as the events started they ended and reset before the cockpit could be alerted.
summary: Cabin crew reported a total electrical failure and loss of communication with the flight deck during cruise after takeoff, causing inoperative systems and temperature control issues. Power and lighting eventually restored automatically, allowing contact with the cockpit and continuation of the flight with no further incident.

synopsis: The bolts holding a C-172RG mechanical crankcase fuel pump worked loose preventing pump operation and so the engine quit from fuel starvation. The pilot declared an emergency, made a 180 degree turn and landed safely on the runway he had just departed.
summary: During pattern practice, the pilot experienced an engine shutdown on downwind due to a fuel pump failure. After declaring an emergency and performing S-turns, the pilot landed at midfield on runway 02 and taxied to the ramp.

synopsis: G-V First Officer discovers extensive glider activity near MUGZY on the WILKES BARRE 4 STAR to TEB.
summary: An IFR crew on the WILKES BARRE 4 STAR arrival to TEB encountered two untracked gliders near MUGZY at 6,000 feet, unaware of local glider operations despite a VFR chart symbol. No evasive action was required, but the crew noted that ATC could not see the gliders and recommended chart updates to warn IFR traffic.

synopsis: After a C172 engine made an unusual sound during climbout, so the instructor declared an emergency and returned to the departure airport where he found a single magneto selected although the key appeared to point to the both position.
summary: A Cessna 172 pilot with a student declared an emergency and landed straight-in downwind after hearing unusual engine noises caused by the ignition key being misaligned on one magneto due to parallax. The aircraft landed safely, and the issue was confirmed as the engine running on a single magneto despite the key appearing to be in the 'both' position.

synopsis: C172 pilot reports confusing Runways 10L and 10R with Runways 28R and 28L, while arriving from the west. An inappropriate ground track is flown when instructed to make a right midfield downwind for 28R. With ATC assistance a successful landing ensues.
summary: The pilot confused runway headings while arriving from the west, leading to incorrect southeast flight despite ATC instructions for Runway 28L. After further confusion regarding downwind and base leg assignments, the pilot landed safely on Runway 28L without incident.

synopsis: After takeoff, a PA32R engine began surging then partially loosing power, so the pilot declared an emergency and returned to the departure airport with engine still developing power.
summary: The pilot experienced repeated engine surges and partial power loss while leveling off for a practice area, prompting an emergency declaration and immediate landing clearance from Tower. The aircraft landed safely without complete power loss, and the pilot is awaiting a mechanic's investigation into the cause.

synopsis: A C172 instructor landed safely off airport after the aircraft developed severe vibrations and lost power.
summary: During a Part 61 instructional flight with three souls on board, the aircraft experienced severe vibration and drastic power loss at 2,500 feet. The Pilot in Command declared an emergency and executed a precautionary road landing due to continued power loss and the risk of crashing into the city.

synopsis: A C421 pilot noted the Number 4 cylinder running significantly cooler than normal. Maintenance subsequently found two Number 4 cylinder hold down bolts sheared in addition to a small crankcase crack.
summary: The pilot of a Golden Eagle 421 experienced intermittent roughness and low EGT on cylinder 4 during descent, suspecting a spark plug failure. Maintenance later discovered two sheared cylinder studs and a case crack, though the pilot noted the initial symptoms made the specific mechanical failure undetectable in flight.

synopsis: An IFR C172 was unable to maintain 11,500 FT MSL due to mountain waves over Southern California mountains and after asking for ATC assistance to clear terrain were advised to call because of an IFR routing deviation.
summary: The pilot reported severe downdrafts during an IFR arrival caused a descent from 11,500 to below 10,500 feet MSL despite full power and Vx climb settings. ATC vectored the aircraft around terrain to clear the mountain after the crew deviated from IFR routing.

synopsis: C172 instructor pilot reports difficulties with his G1000 departing MRY on the MRY9 departure with a student at the controls, resulting in track deviations.
summary: A pilot and student experienced a G1000 GPS tracking failure during climbout from MRY to 6,000 feet, entering IMC before clearing clouds at 2,500 feet. The malfunction caused high workload and communication difficulties with ATC, though no traffic or airspace violations occurred.

synopsis: During a break briefing, the relieving Air Traffic Controller as well as the Trainer and Trainee were surprised to observe the tag for an IFR aircraft appear within a Restricted Area. The crew had not adequately established communication and the aircraft's transponder beacon had not been observed sooner for an unknown reason. The aircraft was provided a heading out of the Restricted Area and handed off to another sector.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller relieved a Trainee and Trainer to find Flight XXX, an IFR departure, inside a Restricted Area due to a missed briefing and a pilot misreading another aircraft's instructions. The controller immediately vectored the aircraft out of the restricted airspace without incident after the pilot failed to use his callsign or question the clearance.

synopsis: A B737-300 Windshear Warning alerted at about 800 FT on final to STL in clear, calm weather conditions so the crew continued for a normal landing.
summary: The Captain received a windshear warning at 800–900 feet on final approach in VFR conditions but continued the landing due to smooth conditions and a 4-knot surface wind report. The aircraft landed uneventfully, and Maintenance reported that such warnings occur regularly at STL.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A Captain described the complexity of complying with an ATC airspeed and altitude constraint change on the already complex MEM LTOWN 6 RNAV procedure.
summary: The flight crew descending into MEM on the LTOWN6 RNAV Arrival experienced confusion due to conflicting ATC speed and altitude clearances and a complex, two-frame chart layout. The pilot attributed the high workload and feeling of being behind to the chart's difficult presentation and frequent ATC restriction changes.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew experiences a sluggish takeoff from a 10,000 foot runway with an OAT of 29 C and a reduced thrust of an assumed temperature of 34 C. Once safely airborne it is found that the performance calculations were made using an actual OAT of -28 C. The crew believes this error caused the poor performance.
summary: The flight crew experienced sluggish acceleration during takeoff due to a TPS error caused by loading -28°C instead of the actual 29°C outside temperature. Despite the low thrust setting, the aircraft rotated safely with 2,000 feet of runway remaining.

synopsis: A B737NG Captain reported a minor flap 30 airspeed excedence which caused the flap load relief system to retract the flaps to 25.
summary: The Captain flying a visual approach into ZZZZ experienced a minor speed deviation that triggered the flap load relief system to retract flaps from 30 to 25 degrees.

synopsis: PA18 pilot experiences engine failure during approach to a small airstrip. The engine cannot be restarted before it is necessary to land in a bog short of the runway. The aircraft flips as it slows but no damage or injuries are reported.
summary: A pilot flying a PA-18 Super Cub experienced an engine failure at 800 feet AGL shortly after takeoff, likely due to fuel exhaustion despite adequate preflight fuel. The pilot executed a forced landing in a swamp bog, resulting in the aircraft nosing over and resting upside down with minimal damage.

synopsis: C210 pilot on an IFR flight plan with only partial electrical power and intermittent communications due to a faulty alternator, maintained VFR and navigated via handheld GPS and iPad to the destination airport.
summary: The pilot experienced an alternator failure and total electrical loss at 8,000 feet, forcing a cancellation of IFR and a VFR diversion around thunderstorms. After conserving battery power to regain brief radio contact and navigate, the pilot successfully extended the gear and performed a no-flaps landing at the destination.

synopsis: D01 Controller described a failure on the part of an Air Carrier departure to comply with assigned and anticipated altitude restrictions, the reporter listed the recent change to RNAV procedures as a possible causal factor.
summary: A B737 on the BRYCC SID climbed above its assigned FL100 without ATC clearance, likely due to confusion over new RNAV departure procedures. The aircraft was eventually contacted on a different frequency and handed off to Denver Center, avoiding separation issues despite the unauthorized climb.

synopsis: ZHU described a conflict event when an Air Carrier accepted a climb clearance intended for another aircraft, the Controller acknowledging his/her failure to issue a similar call sign warning.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller cleared Air Carrier X ABCD to FL390, but a blocked readback caused Air Carrier X ABED to mistakenly accept the clearance while climbing through 38,200 feet. The controller issued a descent to resolve the conflict with traffic at FL390, attributing the error to similar call signs and the lack of a specific warning.

synopsis: B737-500 First Officer reports an aircraft refusal when the logbook indicates a history of electrical issues that appear not to have been properly addressed by Maintenance. The inbound crew reported and wrote up flickering cabin lights.
summary: The flight crew refused to operate a revenue flight due to multiple unresolved electrical issues, including a previous cabin smoke incident and new lighting failures. Despite pressure from Maintenance and Dispatch to continue service under MELs, the crew removed the aircraft from service to ensure safety.

synopsis: ATC, Emergency Personnel and Company Personnel handled a B737 very well after the crew diverted following a specific bomb threat but airstairs to remove passengers and crew arrived twenty minutes after the aircraft parked at the remove spot.
summary: The pilot flying reported a bomb threat diversion where the Captain requested air stairs 20 minutes prior to landing. Despite emergency crews being present, a 45-minute delay in providing stairs and transport created an unacceptable safety risk due to poor coordination among airport and company personnel.

synopsis: B737NG flight crew experienced a left engine overheat shortly after takeoff. They shut down the engine per QRH and declared an emergency. A safe but modest overweight landing occurred due to an inadvertent miscalculation.
summary: During climbout, the number one engine overheated at 200–300 feet, prompting an emergency return. The Pilot Monitoring miscalculated landing weight due to the rushed QRH procedures, resulting in an overweight landing of 128,300 pounds instead of the calculated 125,300 pounds.

synopsis: A B737 Captain rejected the takeoff near 100 KTS after seeing the oil quantity rapidly decreasing.
summary: The Captain and First Officer rejected takeoff on Runway XX due to rapidly decreasing left engine oil quantity dropping to 23% before the 100-knot call. The aircraft stopped safely, and the crew determined it was airworthy to taxi back to the gate without assistance.

synopsis: When the B767-300 flight crew was confronted with a LEADING EDGE FLAP ASSYMETRY warning as they configured for landing at ZGSZ (Shenzhen, PRC) they encountered significant additional difficulties coordinating their needs with ATC due to their limited facility with the English language. Most prominent was ATC's failure to recognize their declaration of an emergency.
summary: The flight crew experienced a Leading Edge Slat Asymmetry while configuring for landing at ZGSZ and declared an emergency, but ATC failed to understand due to language barriers. Despite the confusion preventing emergency services from being dispatched, the crew landed safely with flaps 20 and taxied for inspection.

synopsis: A CRJ-700 Captain was advised by a Captain who had picked up his airplane a few days previously that maintenance action for an MEL item for an overhead passenger bin had failed to note that required emergency equipment was located in the bin when it was taped closed with 'multiple passes of high strength tape' and was, therefore, not accessible as required.
summary: The reporting pilot and crew dispatched an aircraft with a taped overhead bin containing required emergency equipment, violating MEL 25-23-01A. A subsequent captain identified the non-compliance, leading to a maintenance repair and MEL clearance before the next flight.

synopsis: A320 Captain reports his FMGC database depicts crossing EAGUL between FL230 and 18,000 FT, on the EAGUL 5 arrival to PHX. The chart, which is correct, indicates the lower limit should be FL180.
summary: A pilot descending via the Eagul5 Arrival into PHX identified a discrepancy where the A320 navigation database required crossing EAGUL at 18,000 FT (QNH) instead of the charted FL180 (QNE). Air Traffic Control confirmed FL180 was correct, warning that the database error could cause a clearance violation or accident if local altimeter settings were low.

synopsis: A DHC-8 flight crew rejected their takeoff due to low torque on the left engine.
summary: The pilot reported that the aircraft failed to meet takeoff power during the takeoff phase. The left engine was only able to produce 70% torque.

synopsis: B757 flight crew reports very stiff aileron controls during climbout. A Logbook review back more than nine days, reveals the aircraft has a history of aileron write ups. The crew elects to divert to a suitable airport.
summary: The pilot reported inaccurate, heavy aileron feel during takeoff and climbout, identifying it as a recurring issue. A precautionary landing was made to avoid crosswinds, but no maintenance met the crew, forcing an aircraft switch and departure.

synopsis: The flight crew of a MD-83 reported a flight attendant had stressed concerns about an MEL'd Observer O2 mask required for their use when, per security requirements, they occupy that seat while a flight crewmember is absent from the cockpit.
summary: The crew departed with an inoperative observer seat oxygen mask and did not brief the flight attendant at the gate. During a lavatory break, the flight attendant expressed discomfort with the MEL item, though oxygen remained available from the First Officer's mask.

synopsis: A B757-200 flight crew rejected their takeoff at low airspeed when EICAS alerted of low pressure and fluid in the left hydraulic system.
summary: The pilot aborted takeoff after EICAS indicated left hydraulic quantity and pressure loss with PTU activation. The crew lost all left hydraulic fluid, experienced steering difficulties, and was towed back to the gate after shutting down pumps and engines.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: A pilot reported a traffic position error when his Garmin 750 ADS-R displayed traffic at 1 o'clock, but it was acquired visually at 11 o'clock and corresponded with a Avidyne TAS-600 target.
summary: During a VMC cross-country flight at 2,200' MSL, the pilot observed a traffic discrepancy where the Avidyne TAS-600 correctly displayed traffic at 11 o'clock, while the Garmin GDL-88 incorrectly showed it at 1 o'clock. The reporter concluded the ADS-R uplink provided spurious data, creating a potential midair collision risk for aircraft without TAS or TCAS.

synopsis: Imprecise clearance phraseology and the failure to confirm understanding of the clearance resulted in the flight crew of a DA-90 descending to an altitude not intended by the Controller.
summary: Pilots descending from FL390 to FL330 via DENNY received a conflicting clearance from Washington Center to descend to FL350 with a 1500 FPM rate. The controller later clarified the misunderstanding, instructing the crew to maintain FL330 after they had already leveled at that altitude.

synopsis: D10 Controller described a loss of separation during dual ILS approaches. The reporter listed STARS equipment as contributing to the event.
summary: A DFW TRACON controller reported that a trainee at the Arrival 2 position caused an accordion effect, while STARS radar ghost targets obscured Air Carrier X's speed. This resulted in Air Carrier X landing less than 2.5 NM behind Air Carrier Y due to delayed speed adjustments and display limitations.

synopsis: Enroute Controller described an incorrect routing event expressing concern regarding the current 'state of ATC' with regard to controller performance and management oversight.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller reported that a B737 was cleared via the wrong VOR into military airspace due to multiple controllers failing to notice the routing error during handoffs. The controller corrected the clearance after the pilot read back the incorrect route, attributing the incident to a lack of attention to detail and poor coordination.

synopsis: A B757 First Officer's Flight Directer OFF flap appeared at about the same time as an electrical odor was detected in both the flight station and cabin so the flight diverted to a nearby airport for a normal landing.
summary: The crew at FL380 detected an OFF flag on the First Officer's Flight Director and a strong, unidentified odor throughout the aircraft. They executed the Smoke and Fumes Removal Checklist, diverted, and completed a normal landing and taxi to the gate.

synopsis: A Dispatcher reported that after a dispatch software program change he and another Dispatcher were able to assign an outbound flight and a delayed inbound flight the same code while both aircraft were at the same airport.
summary: A pilot and dispatcher assigned the same radio number, XXXT, to two different flights at the same airport due to Dispatch software failing to flag the duplicate. The pilot remained unaware of the conflict, and no operational problems were reported by the crew.

synopsis: Ground observer reports an aircraft rolling backwards slightly when the Captain releases the parking brake prior to pushback, without communicating with the pushback crew. A foot is narrowly missed.
summary: During pushback preparation, the flight crew released brakes before contacting the ramp crew, causing the aircraft to roll backward 6-8 inches. The plane nearly rolled onto the foot of the ramp service person.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports on his perspective of damage he previously found on an abradable shroud at the fan inlet case of a General Electric (GE) CFM-56 engine on a B737 NextGen aircraft that was different from the damage noted during engine removal. Damage had extended through the abradable shroud into the fan case parent material.
summary: A mechanic reported a discrepancy in documenting fan case damage on a B737 NextGen's Number 1 engine, where initial logs omitted parent metal damage later confirmed upon removal. The incident highlights the need for clearer photos and manual links to prevent misinterpreting abradable shroud wear as non-critical when parent metal is compromised.

synopsis: An A330 Captain reported losing electrical power on the ground and VHF 1 did not operate, so the crew had no means of contacting first responders or Dispatch unless their personal phones worked on foreign communications systems.
