summary: The pilot descended to 2,700 feet MSL on a visual approach to Runway 30 at ATW despite known traffic at 3,000 feet, triggering a TCAS 'CLIMB' RA. The pilot attributed the event to descending too early and declining a runway change, resulting in a stabilized but high-descent-rate landing.

synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported CFTT incident following loss of VNAV on approach in marginal weather conditions.
summary: The crew lost VNAV during an RNP approach in marginal weather while distracted by an iPad wind check, leading to a missed approach near trees. The First Officer attributed the incident to dispatcher pressure, inaccurate weather reporting, strong crosswinds, and equipment processing delays.

synopsis: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) describes the chain of events that led to a repetitive Weather Radar and FMS 'Configuration Module Fail' message on a DHC-8-400 aircraft.
summary: A mechanic and pilot attempted to repair a Weather Radar and FMS failure by installing an avionics coupler, but the radar unit was missing from a previous station. The operational test passed without removing the radome due to a communication breakdown and incomplete technical guidance, leaving the aircraft with an undetected missing component.

synopsis: An emergency landing was conducted following fuel exhaustion on approach to landing, resulting in damage to the aircraft. An inadequate amount of fuel was added even though an appropriate amount had been requested and purchased.
summary: During an instrument flight lesson, the pilot and student experienced an engine failure on short final due to receiving only one gallon of fuel instead of the requested ten. This FBO error caused an emergency landing that resulted in extensive damage to the left wing and horizontal stabilizer.

synopsis: ZOB Controller experienced an airspace incursion when failing to recognize that the automated handoff was initiated to the wrong sector, the reporter recommending auto handoff modifications.
summary: An air traffic controller managing Air Carrier X climbing to FL270 with an interim altitude request for FL290 failed to notice the aircraft auto-handed off to the wrong sector. The controller subsequently transferred the flight to the incorrect sector without a point-out because the interim altitude was removed from the data block.

synopsis: MEM Controller discussed an event with a local VFR C172 pilot who's aircraft was 'rocked violently' while holding near a departure runway, the reporter planning controller briefings to increase awareness.
summary: A VFR pilot holding short of Taxiway S at MEM reported violent aircraft rocking caused by departing traffic on Runway 36R while he waited for Clearance Delivery. The reporter requested a team briefing to educate controllers on managing this situation.

synopsis: ZMP Controller described an unsafe situation involving a balloon release up to FL600 with little or no coordination/contacts and no means of identifying the balloons for traffic information.
summary: Air traffic controllers reported that two unmanned WiFi balloons descended through their airspace without transponders, making them invisible on radar. The lack of accurate position data prevented controllers from issuing traffic advisories, prompting a recommendation to equip future balloons with Mode C/S transponders.

synopsis: B737-300 Captain reported confusion in attempting to comply with MEL and AOM with center fuel tank indicator inoperative.
summary: The flight crew departed with an inoperative center tank Fuel Quantity Indicator under MEL 28-7-04 but could not fully comply with both the MEL and AOM 16.12.4 due to conflicting pump low-pressure light requirements. The crew concluded the tank was essentially empty despite the procedural conflict preventing strict adherence to both documents.

synopsis: B737-700 Captain reported possible maintenance non-compliance with MEL application to inoperative yoke PTT switches.
summary: Pilots reported that after audio selector panel modifications, both yoke PTT switches failed to transmit on the interphone, though radio function remained normal. The crew determined the aircraft was unairworthy under MEL 23-16 and recommended checking if maintenance errors disabled interphone functions on other upgraded aircraft.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported he got an internal wind shear alert on takeoff roll that he chose to ignore because conditions did not seem conducive to windshear, but after takeoff he heard the Tower issue a similar alert to an inbound flight.
summary: The flight crew received a predictive windshear alert during takeoff roll between 90 and 100 KTS despite clear weather and no airspeed fluctuations. The crew continued the takeoff normally, later learning the Tower also received a conflicting windshear report for an arriving jet, suggesting a shared system anomaly rather than actual windshear.

synopsis: The pilots of a B747 observed an outflow valve fault during climb, but elected to continue the climb due to workload and considering the previous maintenance history. When they received a cabin altitude warning, they requested a lower altitude and attempted to remedy the issue per the flight manual. This was unsuccessful, so they dumped fuel and returned to the departure airport.
summary: During climb, pilots received an Outflow Valve L EICAS message and delayed the procedure, resulting in a Cabin Altitude warning above 10,000 FT. They descended to 8,000 FT, used manual outflow valve control, and returned to the departure airport after dumping 120,000 pounds of fuel.

synopsis: The pilots of a B757 observed engine oil pressure loss indications and the engine shut down on approach, so they declared an emergency and requested a longer landing runway.
summary: During approach at 6,000 feet, the right engine shut down with indicated oil pressure loss. The Captain flew while the First Officer ran checklists and requested a longer runway, resulting in a safe landing without further incident.

synopsis: HS-125-800XPC flight crew reported Collins FMS anomalies climbing out of EGE.
summary: During a VMC departure from EGE, a Hawker's autopilot incorrectly turned toward Snow VOR due to a GPS fix "leap frogging" on the MFD, delaying manual intervention. The crew eventually took control, received ATC vectors, and completed the flight without incident after reporting the Collins equipment anomaly.

synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported ATC advised left engine fire and sparks on taxi out. Flight crew shut down the engine and had ARFF check for hot spots before returning to gate.
summary: Tower reported a left engine fire and sparks during taxi out, prompting the crew to shut down the left engine and request ARFF inspection. Fire Marshal confirmed no hot spots, and maintenance later attributed the event to possible oil torching in the tailpipe, leading to a return to the gate and crew relief.

synopsis: The pilot of a Sonex experienced a partial nose gear collapse following a bounced landing.
summary: The pilot reported a bounced landing followed by a hard nose gear touchdown that caused partial collapse. An FAA representative on scene classified the event as an incident.

synopsis: The pilot of a C182 attempted to back taxi to the departure end of a runway that is not serviced by a taxiway when he misunderstood the intention of the ATC clearance.
summary: The pilot received a clearance to taxi to Runway XX via Alpha, which lacked a taxiway, prompting a back taxi on Runway YY. The Tower later stated the instructions did not authorize runway entry, though the pilot complied with an immediate departure request due to an aircraft on final approach.

synopsis: The pilot of a DA40 observed another aircraft pass very close to him, causing him to make an evasive turn. This aircraft had confirmed to ATC that he had the traffic in sight, but still passed at an unusually close distance.
summary: During climbout, a DA-40 pilot executed an evasive left turn when another aircraft passed within 200 feet horizontally from below and behind. Although the other pilot confirmed visual contact and dismissed the event, the reporter noted the close spacing created a potential midair collision risk.

synopsis: ZDC Controller described a technical airspace incursion when URET equipment failed to permit routing changes and in the process dropped the data block preventing a handoff.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller managed an A319 departing Denver when a system error deleted the flight plan after an RNAV SID amendment. The controller maintained radio contact and manually coordinated the handoff to Kansas City Center after automated transfers failed due to the missing data and receiving facility delays.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described a conflict event between an Air Carrier departure and a photo mission aircraft that was maintaining visual separation, the reporter detailing the event with the options available.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller managed a near-miss between a B737 on a slow-climbing SID X departure and a Cessna 206 photo mission at 4,500 feet. The B737 crew reported a TCAS RA and a one-mile separation, attributing the conflict to the Cessna's unpredictable path and the controller's reliance on visual separation.

synopsis: After experiencing uncontrolled compressor stalls of the left engine shortly after takeoff the flight crew of a B757-200 performed the appropriate checklists, shut down the engine, declared an emergency with ATC and returned to their departure airport where they were met by Maintenance.
summary: The pilot flying reported a left engine compressor stall with high EGT and smoke during climb after takeoff, causing an emergency return and single-engine landing. Mechanics later found disintegrated engine parts in the tailpipe, confirming the cause of the recurring stalls.

synopsis: Following receipt of an Avionics smoke ECAM warning an A320 flight crew performed the associated checklist procedures, declared an emergency and returned to their departure airport.
summary: The crew received an avionics smoke ECAM warning while climbing toward FL250. After declaring an emergency and returning to the departure airport, they landed safely and were inspected by CFR, who found no evidence of fire or smoke.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An Air Carrier pilot reported that the PTPN Runway is now 6,600 feet long but all current airport charts indicate it is 6,001 feet.
summary: The pilot reported a visual approach to Runway 27 at PTPN where the aircraft database and PAPI align with the original threshold, despite a 600-foot extension completed months ago. This discrepancy causes the 3-degree glide path to intersect the runway 1,600 feet from the new threshold, while charts remain outdated regarding the extension's usability.

synopsis: A B757 crew suffered pneumatic bleed valve problems on two successive flight segments culminating in a loss of pressurization and an emergency descent to 10,000 FT. Passenger masks did not deploy and they were able to complete the flight to destination.
summary: During climb and cruise, a broken PRSOV manual override shaft caused left duct pressure loss and cabin altitude warnings, forcing an immediate descent to 10,000 feet. The crew completed the checklist, confirmed passenger safety, and continued to the destination where maintenance replaced the broken shaft and regulator.

synopsis: After setting the parking brake upon gate arrival the flight crew of an A300 was surprised when the aircraft, with an engine still running pending connection of ground power, moved forward several feet. The aircraft was stopped using toe brakes which were functional.
summary: During parking, the aircraft moved 6 to 10 feet with the parking brake set and Engine 2 at idle after the Captain removed his headset. The pilots stopped the movement using toe brakes, and the nose wheel struck a chock without causing damage or injury.

synopsis: After evaluating the receipt of a FUEL 2 LO warning light aboard an EMB-190 with a history of erroneous warnings, the flight crew opted to divert to the nearest suitable airport despite the history.
summary: During climb after takeoff, the crew received an erroneous 'FUEL 2 LO LEVEL' ICAS message on an aircraft with a history of false warnings. They followed QRH procedures, declared an emergency, and diverted to the nearest airport while recommending a thorough electronics inspection.

synopsis: When cleared sequentially for two different but similar RNAV STARs into DEN the flight crew of an EMB-145 ended up confused miss-programmed and off course. ATC provided a simple clearance direct to the VOR with a hard altitude to resolve the dilemma.
summary: The flight crew encountered an FMS malfunction during the KOHOE 2 RNAV arrival that reverted the active procedure to WAHUU one. This caused a deviation requiring a manual heading change and a re-clearance from Approach to the DEN VOR at 13,000 feet.

synopsis: An EMB-145 flight crew experienced a close encounter with a light aircraft and complied with a TCAS RA while descending in contact with Approach Control.
summary: During descent from 5,000 to 4,000 feet, a general aviation aircraft turned into the commercial flight's path at 4,500 feet, triggering a TCAS climb resolution advisory. The crew climbed 300 feet until clear, then resumed descent, attributing the incident to the GA pilot's lack of situational awareness.

synopsis: CE-680 flight crew reported wake vortex encounter at FL200 from a preceding DC-10 that resulted in a violent 70-90 degree roll to the right. Their passenger suffered a slight injury as a result of the encounter.
summary: While descending on the KASPR4 arrival into MSP at FL200, the crew encountered severe wake turbulence from a preceding DC-10, causing a violent 70–90 degree roll and a 1,500-foot altitude loss. The pilot attributed the incident to ATC allowing insufficient separation and vertical spacing, resulting in an injured unbelted passenger and cabin damage.

synopsis: An MD-10 flight crew shut down the right engine in response to a high oil temperature warning. Maintenance determined a faulty temperature sensor was responsible.
summary: During descent, the crew received an erratic ENG 2 oil temperature warning reaching 225 degrees and shut down the engine per QRH. Maintenance suspects the probable cause was a faulty ENG 2 oil temperature sensor.

synopsis: An A321 APU developed an oil leak during boarding which contaminated the cabin air affecting the passengers and crew so the passengers were deplaned, the flight canceled and the aircraft removed from service.
summary: During boarding, a flight crew member reported strong fumes and breathing difficulties caused by an APU oil leak onto the packs. The Captain ordered deplaning, during which passengers and crew suffered headaches and an asthma attack, leading to the flight's cancellation.

synopsis: A Maintenance Controller describes how a high workload environment, new personnel, distraction and fatigue contributed to his applying an incorrect and more restrictive 'No-Icing' condition MEL on a DHC-8-400 aircraft for an engine intake bypass door stuck in the 'Open' position.
summary: A mechanic and maintenance controller incorrectly applied a restrictive "No-Icing" MEL for an engine intake adapter heater instead of the correct bypass door MEL due to fatigue, distraction, and high workload. This error unnecessarily restricted the aircraft's dispatch conditions.

synopsis: A breakdown in communication between a straight in Challenger and a base leg C150 at a non-towered airport resulted in a close encounter on final.
summary: A C150 on final for SNL Runway 17 encountered a Flight Check Challenger that flew underneath it after announcing the situation would not work. The C150 pilot executed a go-around and landed uneventfully, attributing the incident to the Challenger's maneuver while the C150 followed standard VFR traffic patterns.

synopsis: Widebody Captain reported wake vortex encounter in trail of a B777 on approach to MEM.
summary: The crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding B777 while on a visual approach to MEM 36L between 1,000 and 1,500 feet. This caused aircraft banking and windshear warnings, prompting a go-around before a normal landing was completed.

synopsis: A B737NG being vectored for an ILS, failed to level at 3,000 FT until established, as cleared. When a low altitude alert sounded the Approach Controller, no longer able to contact the flight, promptly called the Tower who advised they had done, so and directed a go-around as the flight was passing 1,400-1,600 FT MSL (400-600 FT AGL) and continuing their descent while still one mile outside the FAF/glideslope intercept altitude of 2,900 FT MSL. Difficulty in utilizing a company directed memory aid intended to insure proper autoflight configuration and a resulting improperly set altitude alert at field elevation +100 FT likely contributed.
summary: During an ILS approach in misty conditions, the crew executed a missed approach after receiving a low altitude alert because Level Change mode remained selected, causing the aircraft to descend to field elevation. The pilot attributed the oversight to fatigue from a 24-hour wakefulness period during a red-eye flight.

synopsis: Fatigue, as a result of erratic scheduling practices, may have contributed to an altitude deviation for a single pilot King Air ambulance Captain.
summary: The flight crew climbed to 17,000 FT instead of leveling at 16,000 FT due to an incorrectly set altitude alerter and fatigue from irregular shifts. ATC accepted the deviation, and the crew attributed the error to circadian rhythm disruption and unclear duty time definitions.

synopsis: Citabria instructor pilot reports a ground loop during the students forth landing with the tail hitting a runway light. A defective tailwheel locking mechanism is discovered on post flight.
summary: During a student training flight, the aircraft ground looped after touchdown due to a stuck tail wheel locking cam that prevented rudder steering. The tail struck a landing light, but no injuries or aircraft damage occurred, leading to the replacement of the faulty tail wheel assembly.

synopsis: Two Line Mechanics troubleshooting a chronic hydraulic leak and unfamiliar with B767-300 Aircraft Systems, cycle the Landing Gear handle with hydraulic pressure on using the Description/Operation (D/O) section of the Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) instead of the Adjustments/Tests procedures. Gear pins were not installed, nose gear collapsed.
summary: Three mechanics troubleshooting a hydraulic leak on a B767-300 collapsed the nose gear while performing a tail skid operational check using an incorrect manual. The gear collapsed violently when the landing gear handle was lowered, causing major fuselage damage and injuring one mechanic.

synopsis: BE36 pilot reports electrical failure at 8,000 FT on an IFR flight plan. The reporter diverts to a suitable airport using a hand held VHF. The gear is manually cranked down, but collapses upon landing.
summary: The pilot experienced a total electrical failure at 8,000 feet while on an IFR flight plan. Unable to verify gear extension due to no green lights, the manually cranked landing gear collapsed upon landing despite the aircraft being meticulously maintained.

synopsis: S56 Controller voiced concern regarding an unsafe condition when SLC departures were deviating for weather and entering MVA areas below the required altitude, the reporter questioning the actions of management decisions.
summary: An SLC arrival controller reported that a departure controller instructed a DC-10 to maintain its own terrain clearance while deviating southwest toward oncoming arrivals and high terrain below the MVA. The departure controller subsequently halted releases until facility managers coordinated a safe heading, citing a lack of leadership and unsafe instructions.

synopsis: ZMA Controller described an 'Extreme' turbulence encounter experienced by a foreign air carrier after being authorized to deviate, the Controller listing language barriers and lack of weather information as contributory.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller issued a right deviation clearance to Air Carrier X to avoid weather, but the pilot flew directly through it, encountering extreme turbulence and losing 500 feet. The controller attributed the incident to potential communication issues and distractions from a position relief briefing, though no aircraft damage or injuries occurred.

synopsis: Enroute Controller experienced an airspace infraction when uncertain of an adjacent facilities airspace/sector configuration, the reporter stated staffing was a contributing factor.
summary: An air traffic controller failed to coordinate a point-out for a Challenger 300 at FL450, causing an airspace violation into Center Y. The controller attributed the error to misdirected data blocks, unanswered coordination calls due to understaffing, and confusion over midnight sector configurations.

synopsis: Enroute Controller experiencing an emergency descent acknowledged failure to secure all required information from the aircraft, the reporter claiming lack of staffing as a primary causal factor.
summary: An under-staffed Approach controller managed a cabin pressure loss emergency while working two combined sectors alone. The controller nearly lost separation with another aircraft due to workload and lack of assistance, noting that delayed overtime approval and insufficient emergency training contributed to the unsafe situation.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described a loss of separation event when traffic on final for an ILS approach suddenly turned off the final in a descent and failed to respond to repeated radio calls.
summary: An air traffic controller vectored a PC12 for an ILS approach to Runway 29R when the aircraft turned left and descended to 1,700 feet due to an autopilot malfunction. The controller issued a blind warning, prompting the pilot to climb and avoid higher terrain and other traffic, though standard separation could not be maintained.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: Tower Controller described a primary RADAR unit failure and questioned the Class B operations that continued after the failure along with doubtful coordination with Maintenance.
summary: Air Traffic Controllers in Denver Tower experienced a frozen ASR-9 radar feed with untagged targets, forcing them to merge IFR traffic using a backup system. The reporter suspects the primary radar remained uncertified and unreported to Tech Ops for 20 hours due to management failure to switch feeds or initiate maintenance.

synopsis: Tower Controller witness an aircraft issued a go around turn crosswind and failing to climb impacted the ground.
summary: An air traffic controller instructed a Cessna to go around twice due to a runway incursion, but the pilot attempted to land again. The aircraft then made an early left crosswind turn, rapidly lost altitude, and impacted the ground.

synopsis: Tower Controller described a possible airspace infraction during an attempt to assist a pilot encountering weather challenges.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller guided a VFR pilot of Aircraft X who became disoriented in low clouds and descended to 200 feet near Runway XX final. The controller issued a low altitude alert and vectored the pilot to climb above the clouds, though the controller noted a possible omission in confirming radar identification.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described a conflict event between an IFR and VFR arrival when an air carrier initiated a wide base turn.
summary: An instructor and developmental controller managing an MD83, DHC8, and PA32 during a visual approach to Runway 17R allowed the PA32 to come close to the DHC8. The incident occurred because the team failed to anticipate the MD83's wide base leg and did not explicitly instruct the trainee to maintain the DHC8 1,000 feet above base traffic.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described a TCAS RA event between an IFR and VFR aircraft when distracted by other duties, the reporter stated an extra set of eyes would have been helpful.
summary: An air traffic controller working a combined position experienced a loss of separation between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y with 500 feet vertical separation, triggering a collision avoidance alarm. The controller issued traffic, but the outcome of the resolution advisory was unknown, prompting a request for additional staffing support.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An air carrier on a visual approach to BWI Runway 10 took evasive action to a TCAS RA from unknown traffic as they were about to turn base from the south.
summary: The Captain and PM on a right base at 4,000 feet received a visual approach clearance to follow traffic on a left base. A Traffic Alert and Resolution Advisory occurred because the other aircraft did not turn as expected, forcing a descent to avoid conflict before landing.

synopsis: B737-300 flight crew reported pressurization difficulties involving forward entry door seal. They returned to departure airport where they found the door very difficult to open.
summary: The flight crew and flight attendants experienced abnormal pressurization and loud noises from the forward entry door during climb on a -300 aircraft. The crew returned to the departure airport after the door seal failed to seat properly, requiring simultaneous inside and outside handle operation to open the door at the gate.

synopsis: Confusion ensued when ATC changed the B737-700's clearance from 'descend via the LDORA RNAV STAR to land north' to 'proceed direct LARKS (a fix on both assigned STARS), recleared to descend via the PEEKK RNAV STAR to land south.'
summary: Pilots flying a jet into Denver received a late arrival change from LDORA to PEEKK 2 while descending, causing FMC loading delays and a descent below the PEEKK 2 LARKS crossing restriction. The crew climbed to FL200 to comply with the restriction after ATC issued vectors, resulting in an altitude deviation that the Captain reported despite no ATC intervention.

synopsis: A B737 parked at the gate and having just under gone Hydraulic System Maintenance developed a heavy air conditioning mist and odor from hydraulic fluid ingested in the right pack so the Captain ordered an evacuation into the terminal.
summary: The crew evacuated the aircraft at the gate due to smoke and fumes caused by hydraulic fluid ingestion into the packs following maintenance over-servicing. All passengers and crew exited safely with no injuries, though pilots experienced eye and nose irritation before continuing the trip later in a different aircraft.

synopsis: B757 First Officer reports being dispatched with an unspecified bleed air MEL deferral which may have been a factor in the illumination of a LEFT ENGINE BLEED AIR OFF light during climb to FL380. With the right pack set to standby cold to maintain a reasonable cabin temperature the cabin altitude warning sounds and an emergency descent is initiated. Control of the outflow valve is regained manually and the flight continues to destination at 10,000 FT.
summary: During climb to FL380, a left engine bleed air light triggered a cascade of pressurization failures, causing cabin altitude to exceed 10,000 feet. The crew donned oxygen masks, initiated an emergency descent, and manually controlled the outflow valve to stabilize the cabin before continuing to the destination at 10,000 feet.

synopsis: MD11 flight crew experiences compressor stalls and high EGT on the number three engine at gear retraction. An emergency is declared and fuel is dumped before returning for landing at maximum landing weight.
summary: The First Officer flew a PW-engine aircraft that suffered a violent compressor stall and over-temperature on Engine 3 just after liftoff. After dumping fuel and returning for an ILS approach, a minor stall occurred on final, leading to Engine 3 shutdown post-landing with no visible damage.

synopsis: A321 Captain reports a TCAS RA descending through 7,000 FT on the PHLBO arrival to EWR. An RA climb is initiated to avoid a Cirrus climbing along the arrival route.
summary: A pilot and First Officer flying an RNAV arrival to EWR received a TCAS climb resolution advisory after NY Approach alerted them to a Cirrus aircraft not initially displayed on TCAS. The crew executed the climb to avoid the intruder, which was climbing in the same direction, and completed an uneventful landing.

synopsis: CE560 Captain experiences a dual heading system failure at FL310 with single failures occurring five minutes apart, and elects to divert. Heading information is regained before the divert can be initiated and the flight continues to destination.
summary: During cruise at 31,000 feet, the crew experienced sequential heading failures on both PFDs, initially correcting the left side via revisionary mode. After ATC provided initial headings and the crew selected an alternate airport, heading information was restored, allowing a visual approach to the destination.

synopsis: A CE-560XL flight crew inbound to BFI on the JAWBN RNAV STAR misread the intent of the crossing restriction at JAWBN. The reporter believes the format of the commercially produced chart restriction 'LANDING BOEING FLD/KING CO RWY 13...Cross at and MAINTAIN 11000' was a contributing factor.
summary: The flight crew en route to BFI misread a misleading arrival chart restriction at JAWBN, confusing runway assignments for Boeing Field and King County. The controller corrected the deviation by instructing a crossing of ALKIA at 12,000 feet, and the crew later recommended updating the chart to match the NOS version.

synopsis: B757 reports being filed to MPTO with SKCL as an alternate and being very uncomfortable with that choice of alternate due to the dangerous terrain, unfamiliarity with the airport, nighttime operations and airport not in the FMC database. A suitable alternate is agreed upon after being counseled by the Duty Manager.
summary: The B767 Captain rejected the Dispatcher's selection of SKCL as an alternate due to dangerous terrain, database absence, and weather, changing it to SKBQ. The Captain reported that fear of termination, following a colleague's dismissal for similar safety concerns, influenced his decision-making process.

synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reports a different interpretation of Tower instructions to fly heading 242 after takeoff with a PDC of the ROCKY7 departure.
summary: The Pilot Flying turned to heading 242 at 500 feet during the ROCKY7 SID departure from Indianapolis, deviating from the expected track to IFVJ. The First Officer attributed this to ambiguous Tower clearance phrasing and outdated DME-based procedures, though no immediate safety consequence occurred.

synopsis: A passenger agent was able to quickly remove his/her hands from danger when the Flight Attendant closed the passenger door from the inside as the reporter was reaching to do so from outside the aircraft.
summary: A ground crew member closing the passenger entry door from the outside nearly had their hands crushed when a flight attendant simultaneously closed it from inside. The crew member avoided injury by withdrawing their hands in time and immediately notified management.

synopsis: Ramp person reports a large hydraulic leak as he marshals the aircraft into parking. The fluid runs down the landing gear strut and onto the hot brakes causing a great deal of smoke. The fire bottle is manned but no flames erupt.
summary: During parking, a pilot reported a major hydraulic leak from the wing to the brakes, causing smoke from the main gear. Unable to contact operations due to a lack of supervisor leadership, the pilot called the Local Controller, citing insufficient resources to protect passengers and staff from potential explosion.

synopsis: An EMB-145 First Officer conducting the 10,000 FT APU shutdown Climb Checklist inadvertently selected the Baggage Smoke Warning test switch, which is similar in shape and location to the APU switch. The Captain then discharged the baggage fire bottle in response to the BAGGAGE SMOKE WARNING test.
summary: The non-flying pilot inadvertently deployed the baggage fire bottle while climbing through 10,000 feet by selecting the similarly shaped fire test button instead of the APU shutdown switch. This error triggered smoke warnings and an unnecessary memory item execution due to rushing under adrenaline.

synopsis: The flight crew of a B737-700 diverted to an enroute airport for maintenance attention following the loss of standby electrical power.
summary: During cruise, the flight crew encountered a standby power failure causing emergency cabin lighting and no PA. A popped circuit breaker on the standby power unit panel prompted a diversion for maintenance, after which the flight continued to its destination without issue.

synopsis: Distracted by runway changes due to winds the flight crew of a B737-400 failed to select the planned flap setting prior to initiating the takeoff roll. When the takeoff warning horn sounded the Captain elected to select five degrees during the continued roll. The flaps reached the desired setting prior to rotation.
summary: The Captain and First Officer missed the takeoff flap setting during taxi at an uncontrolled airport, triggering a takeoff warning horn. The Captain hesitated to abort but elected to continue the takeoff after flaps reached the correct position, resulting in a normal flight despite procedural errors.

synopsis: An MD-83 on departure responded to an apparently false TCAS RA.
summary: The flight crew received a false TCAS Resolution Advisory during climb after departing Runway 18L, showing a non-existent target at the same altitude. After complying with the descent and confirming no traffic with ATC, the crew resumed climb, deferred the TCAS at destination, and reported no injuries.

synopsis: A windshield pillar restricted the ability of a CE-402 pilot to spot threatening traffic during his IFR climb. A timely advisory from ATC provided the impetus to expand his traffic watch and take appropriate evasive action.
summary: A pilot climbing through 4,300 FT reported a close encounter with an unverified Bonanza at 4,500 FT after ATC provided a late traffic advisory. The pilot missed the traffic due to structural blockage but climbed over it by 100–200 FT, noting that TCAS or TIS-B would have prevented the situation.

synopsis: Q400 Captain experiences frequency interference (loud static) over 123.77 (PDX Tower) that is hard to talk over via the interphone.
summary: A pilot reported consistent frequency interference on 123.77 (PDX Tower) during final and departure phases at various altitudes, including below 1,000 FT AFE. The loud static, lasting over 15 seconds, hindered crew interphone communication but did not affect external transmissions, potentially stemming from sub-par Q400 radios.

synopsis: When cleared direct to HANAA waypoint the flight crew of a Dash 8 entered HANNA from their legs page, not realizing it had been misspelled in their filed route. The start of a 180 degree turn alerted them to the error and they were recleared direct to a local VOR.
summary: During climbout, the flight crew inadvertently programmed "HANNA" instead of "HANAA" into the FMS, causing an unintended 180-degree turn. After correcting the error and receiving a direct clearance to ALB from BOS Center, the crew continued the flight safely.

synopsis: A CRJ-200 flight crew experienced stab/autopilot/mach trim pitch axis anomalies while on descent to their destination. Windshear and weather ultimately precluded their emergency landing at their destination and they diverted to another area airport not yet so affected. The heavy workload thus encountered precluded a timely contact with Maintenance.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced stabilizer trim and autopilot trim failures during descent, leading to an emergency declaration and diversion due to windshear. The pilot attributed the outcome to high workload, potential checklist selection errors, and a delayed notification to maintenance.

synopsis: A B737-800 'B' Hydraulic System alerted LOW QUANTITY and PRESSURE descending through 8,000 FT on approach so an emergency was declared, the QRH completed and an uneventful landing followed.
summary: The flight crew experienced a complete loss of System B hydraulics while descending through 8,000 feet with flaps at 1 degree. They declared an emergency, completed the QRH checklist, and landed the aircraft uneventfully with no further incident.

synopsis: The flight crew of an MD-11 was confused by a clearance to proceed direct to an intermediate fix on and descend via the TAMMY RNAV STAR to MEM that did not include an altitude at which to cross the fix.
summary: The flight crew and Memphis Approach Controller were involved during the descent phase while en route to TAMMY. An ambiguous clearance to descend via the arrival caused the crew to incorrectly apply altitude restrictions early, a situation attributed to unclear ATC phrasing and crew expectation bias.

synopsis: When ramp personnel failed to obtain the requested air conditioning equipment the cabin temperature rose so high during passenger boarding the Flight Attendant reporter needed to exit the aircraft for relief. Ultimately a pilot arrived and started the APU to provide relief.
summary: The cabin crew reported excessive heat during boarding, causing nausea and requiring three trips to request air conditioning. The pilot eventually arrived and started the APU, stating that boarding should not have commenced at the high temperature.

synopsis: An Air Carrier Engineer describes his Logic/Analysis as to why he had the authority to issue an Engineering Authorization (E/A) for a Minor Repair he had approved to a Landing Gear Control cable feed-thru pressure seal on a DC-10 aircraft. The seal was subject to Airworthiness Directive (A/D) 2008-11-14 that referenced Service Bulletin (S/B) DC10-27A0237.
summary: An engineer approved minor damage to a landing gear seal on an aircraft subject to an Airworthiness Directive, but an Auditor and the Manufacturer later required replacement. The reporter concluded the conflict stemmed from a misunderstanding of Engineering's authority to approve minor repairs on AD-installed parts without FAA or Manufacturer approval.

synopsis: Sailplane pilot reports an NMAC with a DC10 15 miles east of ABQ at 12,800 FT. Evasive action is taken by the reporter to dive under the DC10.
summary: A glider pilot observed a DC-10 on a converging path at the same altitude during cruise. The pilot executed evasive action by diving 1,000 feet in 20 seconds using dive brakes, as the glider lacked a transponder or alert device.

synopsis: B757 Captain reported wake vortex encounter in trail of a B737-800 on departure from SEA that resulted in a course deviation.
summary: A Boeing 737-800 crew experienced a wake turbulence upset during the MOUNTAIN6 departure from SEA Runway 34C, causing a right bank. The First Officer subsequently led a turn at the NEZUG waypoint, mistakenly treating it as a flyby, which the Captain attributed to insufficient preflight briefing on the SID.

synopsis: An M-20 pilot at 3,000 FT encountered an updraft on approach which caused a pitch up, a 300 FT altitude gain and airspeed loss from which he recovered to complete a successful approach.
summary: The pilot experienced a transponder failure and severe turbulence while on an ILS 13 approach in IMC, causing an unintended altitude excursion to 3,300 feet. The pilot attributed the event to unpreparedness for downdrafts and updrafts, compounded by reflexive control inputs and power management errors.

synopsis: BE33 pilot reports failure of the nose landing gear to extend when the gear is selected down. All attempts at emergency extension are unsuccessful and a nose gear up landing ensues.
summary: The pilot departed with an unsecured passenger door, circled back, and discovered the nose gear failed to extend while main gear deployed. After burning fuel and declaring an emergency, the pilot landed at ZZZ on the main gear only.

synopsis: C172 pilot experiences a loss of GPS reception during a VMC RNAV 31 LPV approach to HIO and continues to a landing. Had the weather been IMC the missed approach procedure would have required an operational GPS.
summary: The pilot flying a new aircraft under VFR lost all GPS reception and terrain system alerts on final approach while using RNAV (GPS) 31 LPV guidance. The pilot landed visually, noting another pilot experienced the same failure, and expressed concern that the loss of GPS would have prevented executing a published missed approach in IMC.

synopsis: BE35 pilot is advised by ATC to have his compass checked after landing. It is found that the glareshield mounted Garmin 496 causes a 30 degree compass deviation.
summary: The pilot reported that Columbus Approach detected a 30-degree compass deviation while vectoring for ILS 24L. Investigation revealed a Garmin 496 GPS unit mounted on the glareshield caused the error, which resolved upon removal with no safety hazard.

aircraft: M-20 Series Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: A M20J engine failed in flight because the magnetos ceased to function after the controlling cam shaft lobe apparently broke.
summary: The pilot experienced a total engine power loss due to a broken crankshaft or camshaft lobe disabling the magnetos while descending toward an airport. With ATC assistance, the pilot successfully executed an emergency landing on Runway 32 with no injuries.

synopsis: A B737-800 crew diverted around a fast building, severe thunderstorm without clearance because ATC failed to answer their request in a timely manner but the Controller objected to their action because no emergency was declared.
summary: Enroute pilots in an aircraft at FL320 deviated 20 degrees north to avoid a severe thunderstorm after ATC initially stood by their requests. The controller later demanded an emergency declaration for the deviation, but company specialists confirmed no regulations were violated.

synopsis: A B737-700 crew and Dispatcher were confused about the proper preflight weight and balance fuel documentation procedure in accordance with the MEL when a single Center Tank fuel pump is inoperative.
summary: The flight crew departed with a MEL'd center fuel pump but failed to verify that 3,000 pounds of center tank fuel was included in the zero fuel weight on the load sheet. Although the flight proceeded safely using one pump, the crew later confirmed the load sheet was incorrect and noted the need for clearer MEL documentation.

synopsis: A pilot reported his aircraft's FMC TELLR 1 RNAV database depicted the CREDE waypoint crossing restriction at/above FL210 but the chart and ATC confirmed the restriction is actually at/above FL190.
summary: The flight crew identified a discrepancy between the charted and FMC database altitudes for the TELLR 1 STAR into DEN during the descent briefing. After ATC confirmed the charted CREDE crossing altitude of FL190 was correct, the crew updated the FMC and descended accordingly.

synopsis: In a fifteen minute period, an air carrier crew was issued three different RNAV arrivals from the West because of weather and was prepared to declare an emergency to avoid a thunderstorm just as ATC issued an acceptable vector.
summary: A pilot arriving at Denver in thunderstorms reported that three RNAV arrivals were assigned and rejected due to weather, causing a controller to initially deny a deviation request before clearing it. The pilot attributed the difficulty to complex, restrictive arrival procedures that became unmanageable when combined with severe weather.

synopsis: An A320 First Officer reported finding a partially full water bottle behind the rudder pedals. The bottle could have interfered with rudder movement and had apparently been in that location for a period of time.
summary: The First Officer discovered a 3/4 full water bottle beyond the rudder pedals prior to takeoff, noting it was not his and had likely rolled there previously. He expressed concern that such objects could lodge in the pedals during critical flight phases and suggested installing a floorboard barrier to prevent recurrence.

synopsis: B737-700 Captain reports the Standby Power Off light illuminated in cruise. QRH procedures are complied with and it is discovered that a circuit breaker is tripped on the P-6-5 Standby Power Control panel. The First Officer may have inadvertently tripped it retrieving his bag from the area but Maintenance directs a diversion for repairs.
summary: During cruise, the Standby Power Off light illuminated after the First Officer likely pulled the C5 Bat Bus Sect 2 circuit breaker while retrieving a bag. Dispatch directed a diversion for repairs, and Maintenance replaced the Standby Power system before the flight continued without incident.

synopsis: Regional jet Captain reports being cleared for the visual approach to Runway 28R at ORD and intercepting a false localizer before returning to heading select, then overshooting the real localizer because the approach mode had not been rearmed.
summary: During a visual approach to Runway 28R at Chicago O'Hare, the pilot reported the autopilot captured a false localizer, causing an unexpected left turn. The pilot disengaged automation, manually corrected the flight path to avoid an overshoot, and completed the landing safely.

synopsis: CRJ200 flight crew reports being asked to continue flying an aircraft with the autopilot deferred. This occurred over several days and the aircraft is eventually refused and ferried for maintenance.
summary: The Captain refused to dispatch the aircraft due to repeated autopilot pitch trim faults and FCC failures, citing MEL violations by Maintenance Control. During a subsequent ferry flight, the autopilot disengaged twice with severe pitch-down tendencies, requiring manual correction and QRH procedures before a safe landing.

synopsis: PA28 instrument flight instructor reports a NMAC with a light twin at 4,500 FT while training in the local training area. Evasive action is taken by the reporter to avoid collision but the other pilot apparently did not notice the conflict.
summary: A flight instructor flying a single-engine aircraft at 4,500 MSL during instrument training had to take control to avoid a converging light twin. The near-miss was attributed to high workload, similar aircraft paint colors reducing visibility against the coastal background, and the student's limited view.

synopsis: A C-172 pilot conducting under the hood instrument training with a safety observer took evasive action from a descending air carrier aircraft which was responding to a TCAS RA.
summary: During simulated instrument training in a Cessna at 10,500 feet, the pilot and safety pilot nearly collided with a B737 after ATC issued a late traffic advisory. The pilot attributed the near-miss to complacency during training, the safety pilot's failure to scan, and ATC's lack of earlier guidance, though both aircraft executed evasive maneuvers to avoid impact.

synopsis: EA50 pilot experiences an uncommanded nose gear retraction while stationary on the ramp after engine start.
summary: The pilot reported an uncommanded nose gear retraction while the aircraft was stationary on the ramp. After maintenance lifted the nose to extend the gear, the pilot flew with the gear down and breakers pulled to a factory facility as instructed by the Eclipse service center.

synopsis: SR20 pilot reports electing to go-around after touching down on a 3,000 FT runway with 1,000 FT remaining. The left wing contacts tree branches on the go-around. One hundred foot trees on both ends of the runway affected the approach and go-around.
summary: The pilot landed a small aircraft at a 3,000-foot airstrip with 100-foot trees and initiated a late go-around with 1,000 feet remaining. The left wing struck a tree branch while clearing obstacles, an outcome the pilot attributed to poor judgment and failing to recognize the stopping distance issue earlier.

synopsis: TRACON Controller experienced a loss of separation when attempting to establish visual separation between two successive departures, the second aircraft climbed faster than the first.
summary: An air traffic controller issued a visual separation clearance between a departing A320 and a GLF5, but the GLF5 lost sight of the A320 due to a higher climb rate. The controller admitted to incorrectly calling traffic before issuing a vector for separation, though separation was eventually established.

synopsis: TRACON Controller providing OJT described a loss of separation when instructing the Developmental to make a transmission in lieu of amending the instruction directly to the aircraft.
summary: The controller lost separation between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y during climb when a CPC-IT issued a climb to 7,000 FT before the controller could stop Aircraft Y at 6,000 FT. The controller attributed the incident to failing to issue the stop instruction directly instead of relying on the CPC-IT.

synopsis: B757 flight crew reports receiving a PDC from TPA for the BAYPO5 but does not note the transition. ATC questions the routing.
summary: The flight crew filed direct TAY but received a BAYPO5 departure with a DUNKN transition, which bypasses TAY. After takeoff, ATC queried their heading because the crew had manually inserted TAY into the FMC, causing a route discrepancy that was subsequently corrected without conflict.

synopsis: B767 Captain describes and evening departure from a large hub airport with three of his company's aircraft having similar sounding call signs and the miscommunications that ensue.
summary: Pilots of Flight XWA, Flight XA, and Flight WA reported confusion during departure due to three similar call signs on the same frequency. Rapid Ground Control instructions led to mistaken responses by the wrong aircraft, but errors were quickly recognized without causing clearance deviations.

aircraft: Boeing Company Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: A Boeing widebody crew report how their EGPWS entered an uncommanded Radar and Predictive Windshear System (PWS) test during takeoff with First Officer's ND selected to TERR while the Captain's was selected to RADAR using the EFIS drop down MENU.
summary: The Captain selected 'Radar' on his ND during the First Officer's takeoff roll, triggering an uncommanded system test and a 'windshear' EICAS message at 80 KTS. Despite the false warning, the crew continued the takeoff, which proceeded uneventfully through departure.

synopsis: CRJ-200 flight crew reported they got a stick shaker when they forgot the flight spoilers were still extended.
summary: During a visual approach to MGM Runway 10, the flight crew inadvertently left spoilers fully extended while descending and slowing, causing airspeed to deteriorate and triggering a stick shaker. The pilot not flying retracted the spoilers, allowing airspeed to recover and enabling a safe landing without altitude loss.

aircraft: Dash 8 Series Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Dash 8 First Officer reported EGPWS alert was triggered on night visual approach to SBY.
summary: During a night visual approach to Runway 14 at SBY, the Pilot Flying descended too low on a left base entry, triggering an EGPWS alert at 560 feet. The pilot corrected the descent to stabilize the approach, though the reporter noted the Pilot Monitoring should have remained inside to monitor instruments.

synopsis: Dash 8 Captain reported loss of Number 2 hydraulic system on approach. Flight crew ran the procedure, contacted appropriate departments, and landed safely.
summary: The flight crew experienced a Number 2 hydraulic system failure during approach, causing delayed gear extension and multiple caution lights. They declared an emergency, performed a missed approach, and landed safely with the gear pinned down by maintenance.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: MD-80 Captain reported he failed to properly position the fuel pump switches in a non-standard fuel load situation.
summary: The pilot inadvertently set center fuel pump switches to OFF instead of ON during the before takeoff checklist, causing a fuel imbalance during cruise. The crew reconfigured pumps to burn center fuel, landed normally, and attributed the error to failing to visually verify switch positions while rushed.

synopsis: CRJ-200 flight crew experienced a GPWS warning on a visual approach to an airport with rising terrain to the north. On advice of the First Officer who was familiar with the airport, the Captain altered the approach to the north runway.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced a GPWS terrain warning during a night visual approach due to the Captain's unfamiliarity with surrounding terrain and a miscommunication regarding the approach briefing. The crew executed a go-around and switched to a safer runway pattern after the warning.

synopsis: A B737-700 developed a strange, oil burning smell during climb which physiologically affected the flight attendants. The aircraft returned to the departure airport where the flight attendants were taken to the hospital and found to have elevated Carbon Monoxide blood levels.
summary: Cabin crew and pilots experienced carbon monoxide poisoning symptoms shortly after reaching 10,000 feet, forcing an emergency landing. While maintenance attributed the issue to an electric oven, the reporter suspects unburned chemicals from a new engine that was not run on the ground prior to flight.

aircraft: Citationjet (C525/C526) - CJ I / II / III / IV
synopsis: C525 Captain reported deviating from an arrival into OMA in part because his FMS cannot fly headings, only tracks.
summary: Pilots flying a MARWI1 arrival into Omaha on Runway 14L mistakenly followed their GNS-500 GPS direct to the airport instead of the required 320-degree heading after SWAAB. The deviation, caused by high workload and non-critical tasks, was corrected by ATC vectors with no further incident.

synopsis: An M20 pilot was on short final after announcing his position at several points, and observed a crop duster cross underneath him and land in the grass alongside of the runway in use.
summary: A pilot approaching Runway XX at 2,300 feet observed a crop duster crossing the flight path at 200 feet AGL. The pilot completed a touch-and-go landing instead of executing a go-around, later concluding that a go-around would have been safer.

synopsis: Two General Aviation aircraft approaching the airport did not establish visual contact until they experienced a near mid-air collision. They then took evasive action and one held outside the airport area until the other landed.
summary: The pilot mistakenly flew an opposite downwind on approach to Runway XX to avoid left traffic, failing to see an inbound aircraft on base until turning 180 degrees. The other aircraft broke off its approach, allowing the pilot to circle until the other aircraft landed.

synopsis: Tower Controller described a separation loss with two successive arrival aircraft, the first not clearing the runway prior to second crossing the runway threshold.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller issued landing clearance to a B757 following a B737 on a visual approach to Runway 21, allowing the B757 to cross the threshold before the B737's tail was fully clear. The controller admitted this violated AIM separation standards due to personal bias against issuing a go-around, acknowledging the decision was unsafe despite the aircraft eventually clearing the runway.

synopsis: Enroute Controller described a NMAC event between an IFR air carrier arrival and a VFR overflight, the reporter acknowledging he/she should have issued traffic in lieu of answering the landline.
summary: An air traffic controller reported a near mid-air collision between a descending B737 and a VFR Cessna 172 at 10,500 feet. The controller attributed the incident to their own failure to maintain traffic calls or stop the B737 after the C172 initiated a descent and the B737 responded to a TCAS resolution advisory.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described a loss of separation event during parallel visual approach procedures when anticipating arrivals would report the airport in sight as prior arrival had done.
summary: An air traffic controller vectored a B737-400 and an ERJ-190 for simultaneous parallel approaches while expecting the B737 to report approach lights in sight. The controller noted the B737 was searching and recommended using more positive separation instead of anticipating visual acquisition when applying the 30-degree intercept rule.

synopsis: TRACON Controller described an unsafe condition resulting from similar company flight numbers operating within the same airspace at the same time.
summary: A trainee controller confused a B737-800 arrival and B757-200 departure due to similar call signs, causing a wrong aircraft to answer a handoff and delaying vectoring. The incident increased frequency congestion but resulted in no loss or safety issues, prompting a recommendation to change the call signs.

synopsis: B737 First Officer reported they experienced several compressor stalls in right engine at FL370. Crew shut down the engine in accordance with procedure and diverted to nearest suitable airport.
summary: During cruise at FL370, the flight crew heard bangs near the #2 engine, observed an N1 drop to 70%, and identified compressor stalls. The Captain executed the Engine Failure Checklist, shut down the #2 engine, and performed an uneventful single-engine visual approach and landing at a diverted airport.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported a ramp employee walked in front of the operating Number 2 Engine. Captain promptly shut down the engine.
summary: During engine start after pushback, a ramp agent walked in front of a running engine to load a late bag, triggering cargo door warning lights. The pilot immediately shut down the engine and reported the unsafe action to operations.

synopsis: A fatigued Captain described the complexity and confusion around a PHX RNAV runway transition change after the initial descent began which resulted an altitude constraint overshoot after the constraining waypoint dropped from the FMS during programming.
summary: The fatigued pilot misinterpreted a NOTAM and struggled to update the FMC for a Runway 7R transition while descending, causing the aircraft to cross the SPINK waypoint 400 feet below the required altitude. The First Officer's monitoring prevented a more severe deviation, though the pilot attributed the error to fatigue, distraction, and improper route loading.

synopsis: A DHC-8-200 advisory panel alerted L AC GEN and L TRU so the checklist was completed which included selecting the L GEN OFF. Then, because of weather conditions, an emergency was declared and the flight diverted to a nearby airport.
summary: The crew at FL210 experienced multiple caution lights and flickering gauges, which stopped after turning off the left AC generator per checklist. Due to bad weather, they declared an emergency, diverted, and landed safely with no further incidents.

synopsis: A MD-83 engine failed at FL340 in cruise so an emergency was declared and the flight diverted to the nearest airport.
summary: The pilot reported a left engine failure at FL340 with no fire or vibration. An emergency was declared, and the aircraft diverted to the nearest airport.

synopsis: During climb after takeoff, a MD-83 Master Warning and TAIL COMP TEMP HIGH lights illuminated so an emergency was declared, the QRH completed and the flight returned to the departure airport.
summary: During climb through FL250, a TAIL COMP TEMP HIGH warning triggered an emergency return to the departure airport. Although the light extinguished within two minutes, post-landing infrared inspection by ARFF and maintenance resulted in the aircraft being taken out of service.

synopsis: An A300 landing gear would not retract after takeoff until the Landing Gear Position Detector System 2 was selected. Then with gear retraction, the #1 ADC, #1 Flight Director, the autothrottle system and both transponders failed so the flight returned to the departure airport.
summary: During takeoff, the crew experienced a gear retraction issue followed by multiple system failures including the transponder. ATC denied destination entry due to the inoperative transponder, forcing a return to the departure airport without incident.

synopsis: A First Officer and an International Captain, new to the B777, failed to see the destination glide slope out of service NOTAM and after the autoflight system did not capture a glide slope, the aircraft was high and unstabilized for the night landing.
summary: The crew missed a NOTAM regarding an inoperative glide slope, causing a late descent and unstable approach with high speed and tailwind at 500 feet. After the Pilot Monitoring called the approach unstable due to an incomplete checklist, the crew completed the checklist and executed a normal landing.

synopsis: When the flight crew of an A300 opted to make FMS crossing restrictions at DASAC, CLARK, and DIGLE on the LTOWN RNAV STAR to MEM hard altitudes vice at or above, as published, the autoflight initiated a descent and accelerated prior to crossing CLARK at 8,000/210 KTS.
summary: The pilot flying descended via the LTOWN RNAV STAR into Memphis and deviated 150 feet below the 8,000-foot CLARK constraint while accelerating to 230 knots. The reporter attributes the premature descent to the FMS prioritizing the hard-wired 6,000-foot DIGLE restriction, causing the aircraft to nose over faster than the auto-throttles could compensate.

synopsis: An A300 Captain noted a fuel quantity discrepancy while holding short for takeoff and discovered after returning to the ramp that the Right Inner Tank Quantity was indicating 15,000 lbs more than actually on board.
summary: Pilots discovered a 15,000 lb fuel imbalance while holding short of Runway XXR due to a Right Inner Tank quantity indication malfunction that caused incorrect refueling. The aircraft returned to the ramp to MEL the system, avoiding a takeoff with an unsafe wing-to-wing split that resulted from a recent change in fuel slip review procedures.

synopsis: A Maintenance Control Coordinator and another Controller report about a Forward Entry Door escape slide that was replaced on an ERJ-190 aircraft using the Manufacturer's Aircraft Illustrated Parts Catalog (AIPC). Escape slide installed was 'Not Effective' for the aircraft due to AIPC was found to have incorrect and misleading Part Number (P/N) information.
summary: Maintenance Control and a Supervisor installed an ineffective L1 door slide on an ERJ-190 due to a misleading Aircraft Illustrated Parts Catalog listing the wrong part number. The manufacturer later confirmed the catalog error, requiring the aircraft to be grounded for a correct part replacement.

synopsis: A C182 pilot in a CTAF landing pattern used the incorrect CTAF frequency for the proper position reports, but a Light Sport Aircraft pilot aborted his landing during a near miss after seeing the C182 ahead and below.
summary: A C182 pilot on short final at a CTAF airport inadvertently used the wrong frequency, preventing communication with a Light Sport aircraft in the same pattern. The other pilot saw the C182 below and delayed turning final, avoiding a conflict caused by the frequency error and the C182's high-wing obscuring the view.

synopsis: A Flight Instructor describes his efforts to reach out and physically pull the Left Main Landing Gear (MLG) forward into a 'Down and Locked' position, while his commercial Student flew their Cessna C-172RG aircraft. The Left MLG Pivot Axle had sheared preventing hydraulic extension of the gear. The left brake also failed to operate on landing.
summary: A commercial pilot and student experienced a left main gear failure due to a sheared pivot axle during practice at ZZZ. The pilot manually extended the gear by reaching out an open door, landed safely, but encountered left-side brake failure caused by the same defect.

synopsis: R22 instructor pilot took control of the helicopter and made a successful autorotation after the student pilot mistakenly shutoff the mixture control.
summary: A student pilot in a helicopter mistakenly pulled the mixture control full off during pre-landing checks due to confusion over a misplaced guard and fatigue. The instructor took controls and executed a safe autorotation from 100–150 feet, resulting in no aircraft damage.

synopsis: Near LUF, a PA-28 instructor pilot took evasive action from an aircraft which passed less than 300 feet overhead after Approach Control reported possible 4,500 feet traffic with which it was not communicating.
summary: A Cessna 172 pilot and student on a VFR flight at 4,500 feet received a traffic alert from Luke Approach regarding an eastbound aircraft. The pilot turned right, but the uncommunicating aircraft passed overhead less than 300 feet away at the same altitude.

synopsis: A pilot flying an Aviat A-1C-Husky aircraft hears a rattling noise and notices the piano hinge on the engine's right cowling migrating forward and cutting into the trailing edge of the composite propeller. Gaps had also developed at the aft hinge section as the hinge pin continued migrating forward, raising further concerns the cowling might start to tear from the aircraft.
summary: During initial climbout, a pilot flying a Husky with an MT composite propeller returned to the airport after a cowling hinge rod slid forward and struck the propeller blades. The rod chewed into the wooden layers of the blades, an incident the pilot attributed to missing 90-degree bends on the hinge pins.

synopsis: PDK Controller described a less than standard runway separation event when a second aircraft landed with the prior arrival still on the runway, the reporter listed non compliance with local SOP requirements as a causal factor.
summary: A Cab Coordinator at PDK Tower reported that Local 1 failed to send Cessna Y around despite a tight base leg, resulting in a landing with insufficient separation behind Cessna X on Runway 34. The reporter attributed the incident to Local 1's decision and Ground Controllers blocking runway exits contrary to SOPs.

synopsis: SCT Controller voiced concern regarding several radio frequencies that fail to operate as required, listing a TCAS RA event resulting from the subject communications problem.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller and a developmental trainee managed a near-midair collision between a B737 and a PC12 at SNA when the B737 mistakenly accepted a climb clearance to 070 intended for a BE20. The reporter attributes the error to similar call signs and poor radio frequency quality, noting that TCAS alerts prevented a collision.

synopsis: During the B737-700's second engine start at the gate, the Captain noticed the radar begin scanning and selected standby, but was puzzled whether it had been left ON from the previous flight or his preflight was incomplete.
summary: A pilot at ZZZ gate inadvertently activated the weather radar during the second engine start while a ramp agent stood 20–25 feet from the nose. The incident occurred because the pilot failed to verify the radar selector switch position, assuming it was in standby rather than radar mode.

synopsis: An air carrier Maintenance Personnel knew the B777 SLAT PRIMARY HYDRAULIC system had a recurring fault, but had mechanics sign it off as 'Primary System Test FSEU1 Carried Out, SATIS;' but when the Captain threatened to ground the aircraft at a foreign station, the flight was canceled.
summary: The pilot refused to fly an aircraft with a recurring SLAT PRIMARY HYDRAULIC system failure because maintenance could not defer the non-deferrable defect despite repeated in-flight occurrences. Consequently, the flight was cancelled, and the aircraft returned to a domestic airport after sitting on the ground for seven hours.

synopsis: A B737 crew at FL380 in level flight, experienced a loud engine report accompanied by a strong airframe vibration and surging power. They completed the ENGINE FAILURE QRH, declared an emergency and diverted to a nearby airport.
summary: The crew experienced an uncommanded N1 fluctuation and loud bang on Engine 2 during cruise at FL370, causing them to declare an emergency and divert. They shut down the engine, performed an overweight landing, and landed smoothly with no further complications.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An Air Carrier on approach to ORD 28L was issued a go-around because of an animal on the runway and on the second approach the Captain misidentified the airport, got low, and executed another go-around after a 'glideslope warning.'
summary: A fatigued crew misidentified the airport during a visual approach to ORD Runway 28R, descending below the glideslope and triggering low altitude warnings. The Captain executed a go-around at 1,000 feet AGL due to poor situational awareness and lack of First Officer assertion, eventually landing safely on Runway 27R.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: ZJX advised an air carrier pilot climbing through 9,500 FT about opposite direction, same altitude traffic and while climbing with traffic on TCAS and in sight, that aircraft passed 400 FT directly below.
summary: During climb, the crew received JAX Center traffic advisories for opposite direction traffic at 9,500 FT. After TCAS alerted "Traffic, Traffic," the pilot increased power and pitch, resulting in the other aircraft passing 400 FT below.

synopsis: A CRJ-900 had been weighed prior to the crew's first flight and incorrect numbers entered into the Basic Operating Index database which made the aircraft out of its normal trim limit for takeoff.
summary: Pilots experienced an out-of-balance condition and required excessive nose-down trim during takeoff due to incorrect Basic Operating Index data in the FMS. The incident was caused by erroneous weight data entered after a recent aircraft weighing, though the flight was completed safely.

synopsis: A CRJ-900 EICAS alerted SPOILERONS and FLT SPOILERS when the landing gear was lowered but because the crew could not find the proper checklist they landed prior to taking action and later found the proper checklists in the Emergency Landing Gear Checklist.
summary: During the base-to-final approach, the crew received spoiler cautions but could not locate the abnormal flight control checklist in the disorganized QRH. Relying on system indications and flight feel, they continued the landing uneventfully, later discovering the missing checklist was misplaced within the binder.

synopsis: BE35 pilot reports leveling off after a long descent to find the engine unresponsive. An emergency is declared before it is discovered that the mixture control had been left at a lean setting and power is quickly restored. Queries from a FSDO Inspector have left the reporter fearful of repercussions.
summary: A pilot declared an emergency during an IFR approach after experiencing power loss caused by an overly lean mixture setting. Although the issue was resolved by enriching the mixture, subsequent FAA inspection demands regarding documentation have made the pilot reluctant to declare future emergencies.

synopsis: PA28 pilot on flight following was notified by the Controller that he was in restricted airspace and given a heading, after being told by the previous Controller that the airspace was cold. The current Controller then learns the airspace is in fact cold and clears the reporter on course.
summary: A VFR pilot near KSFB entered active restricted airspace after Orlando Approach initially warned of hot zones then abruptly told the pilot to disregard. JAX Approach subsequently vectored the pilot out, provided a number for a potential pilot deviation report, but later instructed the pilot not to call after resolving the situation.

synopsis: C182 reports poor procedures and communications by skydiving pilots at ZZZ airport on a daily basis.
summary: A pilot reported that skydiving operations at ZZZ airport involved poor communication, runway incursions, and confrontational radio behavior by skydiving pilots. The reporter also alleged that these pilots manipulated ASOS cloud reports to conduct jumps through solid overcast ceilings at 14,000 MSL.

synopsis: SR22 pilot making an emergency descent out of icing conditions noted decreasing airspeed indications followed by an airspeed audible warning. Pilot turned on pitot heat which rectified the airspeed indication problem.
summary: The pilot experienced erroneous low airspeed and stall warnings during an emergency descent from icing conditions at -12°C. Activating pitot heat during the descent to 13,000 feet restored correct airspeed indications, allowing the flight to continue normally.

synopsis: Helicopter pilot reports hovering next to a power line tower while a worker was on the skid working on the line. A hoist used to hold the line failed and the line came down on the skid, causing the main rotor to contact a bond wire on the Tower.
summary: A pilot hovering near a power line tower reported that a failed hoist caused a line to strike the helicopter skid, pulling the aircraft down. This resulted in the main rotor blades contacting a bond wire above the structure while a worker was on the skid.

synopsis: ZDV Controller voiced concern regarding a controller/supervisor conversation that escalated into a significant distraction impacting communications with aircraft at the sector.
summary: An air traffic controller in Sector 14 reported that a debate with the Flight Line Manager regarding miles in trail requirements became a distraction. Although no separation loss occurred, the controller stated the FLM's disregard for safety guidelines impaired timely communication with aircraft.

synopsis: ZOA Controller described a loss of separation event when the R-Side failed to accept the suggestions of the D-Side and tried to climb above an aircraft, the reporter suggesting an altitude 'stop' would have prevented to event.
summary: An ATC trainee and instructor observed a B737-500 and MD-83 approaching a conflict while the trainee's R-Side issued a climb rate that failed to ensure separation. The trainee recommended stopping the B737-500 climb earlier to avoid the near-miss, citing poor controller judgment as the cause.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: ZAB Controller described a very complex and heavy traffic period involving PHX arrivals and departures. Aircraft on both routes requested weather deviations which resulted in conflicts, the reporter lists TMU, supervisory and maintenance failures as causal factors.
summary: An air traffic controller managing Phoenix arrivals and departures faced frequency failures during weather, causing communication loss and conflicting deviation requests. The controller manually descended arrivals below FL360 to separate them from departing traffic, resolving the safety issue but attributing the risk to management's failure to mitigate known equipment problems.

synopsis: NCT Controller described an unsafe event during side-by visual approach procedures at SFO when one aircraft failed to see parallel traffic, the reporter believes speed and a late hand off were causal factors.
summary: An A321 and B737 converged during visual approaches to SFO, triggering Resolution Advisories when the B737 failed to reduce speed or maintain proper separation. The reporter attributed the incident to delayed frequency transfer and insufficient altitude separation, resulting in both aircraft being re-sequenced for different runways.

synopsis: ZAU Controller experienced a loss of separation event listing parachute activity in the vicinity as work intensive and distracting from duties required of ORD arrivals.
summary: An air traffic controller lost standard separation between a CRJ7 and a PC-12 during ORD arrivals due to misjudging distance while managing parachute jump operations. The CRJ7 reported a resolution advisory, and the controller attributed the error to the distraction and workload caused by the jump aircraft conflicting with IFR traffic.

synopsis: Air Carrier initiated a descent but was questioned by ATC regarding a possible same company mix-up, i.e. the clearance was issued to a company flight.
summary: The crew mistakenly believed they heard their call sign while cruising at FL380 and initiated a descent to FL320. ATC subsequently instructed a climb to FL360 and noted the crew likely responded to another aircraft's call.

synopsis: B737 flight crew descending into AUS in IMC experiences a TCAS RA with VFR traffic not talking to Approach Control. A climb and a turn are initiated to avoid the intruder.
summary: The pilot reported two TCAS RA encounters while descending in IMC south of KALLA, involving untracked VFR traffic climbing rapidly into their path. The crew executed TCAS-directed climbs and turns to avoid the traffic, which passed within 400 feet, while ATC initially issued conflicting headings that were rejected.

synopsis: An Air Carrier pilot noted numerous hear-back/read-back errors when his air carrier assigns flight numbers ending in the same two numbers into airports and airspace concurrently.
summary: The pilot reported that similar flight numbers (ABC X24, Y24, Z22) from the same airline increased communication workload and risk of misheard clearances during taxi and enroute phases. Although aggressive readback prevented errors on this flight, the reporter identified the airline's flight number assignment as a safety issue requiring immediate correction.

synopsis: ATC deleted the ZOLAN 250 KTS restriction prior to MPASS on the ATL Runway 26L CADIT 7 MPASS transition and after doing so, an air carrier's FMS turned the aircraft precede direct ZOLAN.
summary: During departure from ATL Runway 26L, deleting a speed restriction at ZOLAN caused the FMC to turn the aircraft inside the MPASS waypoint. The crew attributed this deviation to FMC logic limitations and recommended delaying speed deletion until passing MPASS.

synopsis: A300 Captain on the CADIT 7 Departure from ATL is told to delete the speed restriction at ZELAN which is accomplished in the FMCG. This results in a turn direct ZELAN bypassing MPASS and an ATC admonishment.
summary: Pilots departing ATL on the CADIT 7 departure reported that deleting a speed restriction at ZELAN caused the FMC to fly inside the MPASS waypoint. The crew attributed this deviation to FMC logic limitations and noted that lowering the clean-up altitude to 1,500 feet may have contributed by accelerating slat retraction.

synopsis: Inbound to ATL and filed via the WARRR RNAV STAR the flight crew of a B717 misunderstood an ATC clearance to go direct to PAYTN (the initial waypoint of the PAYTN.WARRR arrival) as direct to CAYTN, a fix further along their enroute airway, J37, but which is not a part of any transition to the WARRR STAR.
summary: The non-flying pilot and ATC experienced a routing confusion where the crew was cleared direct CATLN but later instructed to go direct PAYTN due to similar fix names. The pilot attributed the error to failing to verbally question the clearance despite initial doubt, noting the fix names caused the misunderstanding.
