synopsis: Flight deck confusion and intermittent communications with ATC resulted in a B777 entering oceanic airspace without a clearance.
summary: The flight crew struggled to obtain an oceanic clearance due to poor HF communication and intermittent CPDLC/ADS while crossing the FIR boundary. Despite static and unusable frequencies, they eventually received and read back the clearance on HF 8864, maintaining the intended route throughout.

synopsis: A320 First Officer reports flap damage caused by Contract Maintenance when the flaps are extended at the gate with a fuel truck parked under the wing.
summary: Contract Maintenance personnel, unsupervised in the cockpit during flight planning, moved the flap lever without ensuring flight controls were safe. This action seriously damaged the aircraft and nearly injured refueling personnel while the fuel truck was connected.

synopsis: CRJ-200 Captain reports a thump passing through 10,000 FT on departure, followed by high ITT, N2 vibration and a burning oil smell. The crew elects to shut the engine down and return to the departure airport.
summary: The pilot reported a left engine ITT excursion, vibration, and burning oil smell at 10,000 feet during climb, likely caused by engine damage. The crew declared an emergency, shut down the engine, and landed safely after managing high workload from multiple simultaneous requests.

synopsis: While shooting the RNAV (GPS) Y Runway 30L approach to SJC the flight crew of a CE-560, equipped with only LNAV minima compliant avionics, failed to note the 1,480 MSL intermediate crossing restriction at FORUL for such aircraft. They had initiated a descent to the MDA (640 MSL) at the FAF and were issued a low altitude alert from the Tower prior to reaching FORUL.
summary: During an RNAV (GPS) Y Runway 30L approach, the flight crew descended below the 1,480-foot FORUL constraint due to distraction and a misbriefed altitude, triggering a TCAS alert and a Tower low altitude call. The pilots attributed the error to missing the intermediate step-down note and suggested improving the approach chart's profile depiction for LNAV-only operations.

synopsis: B777 Relief Pilot reports encountering severe turbulence while he is in the bunk. The area of severe turbulence was known prior to departure but the Dispatcher did not plan around it and the crew was discouraged from requesting a different route.
summary: A relief pilot reported that a Boeing 777/787 encountered severe turbulence causing a 100-foot altitude deviation and a temporary overspeed warning. The crew deviated over 100 NM from the flight plan, which the pilot claims discouraged requesting a safer alternate route due to cost concerns, resulting in a frightened cabin.

synopsis: MD83 flight crew experiences a left engine failure just as the power is pushed up for takeoff and rejects.
summary: The First Officer aborted takeoff at 20 knots after a loud bang and left yaw occurred when autothrottles engaged, caused by Foreign Object Damage that destroyed the left engine's aft turbine section. The crew safely exited the runway, shut down the affected engine, and taxied back to the gate.

synopsis: Captain reports he refused to accept a B757-200 aircraft as safe to fly overwater or high mountains with the Number 1 Engine Fan blade bent and N1 Overspeed already deferred, the Fan Case Attrition liner already on a Repetitive Inspection deferral for previous liner sections missing and an additional 5 to 6 feet of liner that had recently disappeared after the deferral.
summary: The Captain refused a B757-200 due to a missing engine attrition liner and conflicting maintenance deferrals, citing safety concerns for a night flight to mountainous terrain. The aircraft was grounded for an engine change after Rolls-Royce expressed concern over flight data recorder results, while the crew completed the trip on a replacement aircraft.

synopsis: An MD10 flight crew suffered the likely failure of the number one CADC. Performed associated checklists as landed uneventfully.
summary: During an IMC descent through 5,000 MSL, autothrottles and autopilot disconnected with conflicting airspeed indications, prompting an emergency declaration. The crew completed the QRH checklist and landed uneventfully, suspecting a CADC 1 failure as the cause.

synopsis: EMB-145 Captain experiences an Air/Gnd Fail message on the EICAS at takeoff as the gear is retracting. In an attempt to silence some of the many warnings the landing gear is extended to no avail then cannot be retracted. Flight returns to the departure airport for an overweight landing.
summary: The flight crew experienced a landing gear air/ground sensor failure and continuous aural warnings shortly after takeoff, preventing gear retraction. They returned to the departure airport, landed without thrust reversers, and stopped safely, though the captain noted they should have declared an emergency earlier.

synopsis: The Captain (SIC) of a Citation Sovereign took the initiative and braked the aircraft to a stop when the Captain (PIC) was unresponsive to his insistence that they were taxiing on the wrong taxiway per their ATC clearance.
summary: The First Officer stopped the aircraft on the ground at LAS after the Pilot-in-Command ignored taxi instructions and turned onto the wrong taxiway. The reporter attributed the deviation to the PIC's refusal to follow clearance and poor Crew Resource Management, requiring manual intervention to prevent a runway incursion.

synopsis: B757 First Officer reports a go-around during approach to MDPC due to a perceived loss of separation with the preceding aircraft. The flight is vectored around for a second VOR DME Runway 08 approach to a successful landing.
summary: The flight crew arriving at PUJ requested a go-around due to perceived separation issues with traffic below while in IMC conditions. This occurred after confusion regarding altitude clearances and an inappropriate visual approach clearance from PUJ Approach Control, leading to a radar vector back to the VOR/DME Runway 08 approach.

synopsis: A MD-83 takeoff roll was excessive and during climb with flaps and slats retracted a clean climb speed of 263 KTS was maintained to extinguish the ALPA SPD warning. Excessive takeoff weight suspected.
summary: The pilot departed from a shorter runway with a tailwind and packs off, noting a long takeoff roll and an unexpected high-speed alpha warning during climb. Suspecting an overweight condition, the crew reduced cruise altitude, requested an offload audit, and flew the arrival at higher speeds to ensure safety.

synopsis: A B777 on an RNAV arrival executed an uncommanded turn after the crew closed a route discontinuity miles down track near the ILS while the aircraft was close to the next and already active arrival waypoint.
summary: During an RNAV arrival, the crew closed an FMC discontinuity near a waypoint, causing an uncommanded right turn attributed to automation failure. The pilots corrected the deviation by disconnecting the autopilot, and ATC acknowledged the maneuver as the aircraft returned to the arrival path.

synopsis: A300 flight crew reported noticing smoke in the cockpit, prompting a divert to a nearby airport.
summary: The crew noticed smoke in the cockpit at FL360, declared an emergency, and diverted with ATC priority. Although no ECAM warnings appeared during descent, an avionics smoke warning triggered on rollout; fire services surrounded the aircraft, smoke dissipated, and the crew depowered the plane without egressing.

synopsis: B767-300 Flight Attendant reports a rushed departure to accommodate the flight crew's duty limits and approaching weather. The reporter did not have time to translate the required announcements nor do a full compliance check prior to takeoff.
summary: A cabin crew member reported that an early departure due to thunderstorms caused an unsecured galley and incomplete safety demonstration while taxiing from a remote gate. The flight deck's urgent departure commands prevented the crew from finishing the demo, translating announcements, or performing a full compliance check.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: A single engine aircraft pilot in an advanced avionics flight deck descended below the APF RNAV GPS 5 LPV DA and executed a go-around after ATC issued a low altitude alert.
summary: The pilot descended below the 446 FT LNAV/VNAV minimums to 295 FT on final approach to APF RNAV (GPS) 5 without visual contact. After receiving a low altitude alert, the pilot declared and executed a normal go-around.

synopsis: A B767 Captain reported that at FL360 in cruise both altimeter systems fluctuated independently in turbulence up to 200 FT after the aircraft was previously parked in heavy blowing rain for several hours. The aircraft remained stable during the repeated altimeter excursions.
summary: During cruise in RVSM airspace, the Captain and First Officer experienced rapid, independent altimeter fluctuations proportional to turbulence intensity, while the standby altimeter showed minor variations. The crew attributed the issue to possible water incursion into static ports following heavy rain, though they maintained precise altitude without ATC intervention.

synopsis: A Maintenance Controller reports he took a B757-200 ETOPS aircraft 'Out of Service' after being informed that a downlock spring had been removed instead of a broken uplock spring he had placed on an MEL. An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) also reports that a lack of an Illustration in MEL 32-32-01 contributed to his misidentifying the downlock spring as the uplock spring.
summary: A Maintenance Technician incorrectly removed a downlock spring instead of the uplock spring on a B757 to comply with MEL 32-32-01, causing the aircraft to depart with a missing part. The aircraft was later grounded after the error was discovered, attributed to the MEL lacking an illustration for spring identification.

synopsis: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) describes how a chain of events, starting with how the Airbus Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) is formatted, contributed to his inadvertently missing a required Main Landing Gear (MLG) Extension Check, after replacing the right MLG Proximity 'Squat' switch on an A320 aircraft.
summary: A mechanic replaced a right-hand #20GA Proximity Switch but missed the required jacking procedure due to a non-user-friendly Airbus AMM hyperlink format. Maintenance Control subsequently grounded the aircraft in ZZZ1 to perform the necessary clearance check.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An air carrier crew misunderstood ATC and flew the OGG RNAV Y Runway 2 but had been cleared for the RNAV Z which the crew did not have in either paper or electronic form. ATC said nothing until after the flight.
summary: Air traffic controllers and flight crew experienced a readback error during descent into Maui Airport regarding the RNAV approach. The crew flew the RNAV-Y approach after confirming it verbally, while ATC had intended the RNAV-Z, resulting in no incident due to lack of conflicting traffic.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A corporate crew on the SNA ELB 1 was issued an off route clearance after BOLDE to avoid a conflict with an air carrier, but the corporate crew remained on the ELB 1 track recreating the conflict. There may have been confusion between BALDI and BOLDE intersections, 45 miles apart on the ELB 1 SID.
summary: An air traffic controller issued a reroute via BOLDE Intersection to a climbing corporate jet to deconflict it from an air carrier. The pilot misidentified the fix as the similarly named BALDI Intersection, resulting in a 5.33-mile proximity at the same altitude before the next sector resolved the conflict.

synopsis: A B737-300 crew reported that having calculated an optimum cruise altitude of FL363, the aircraft would not climb above FL355 and with the 'A' alfa alert displayed speed increased to MACH .77 with a BUFFETT ALERT. The flight descended to FL340 where flight directors cycled OFF/ON which reset the system to normal operation.
summary: During a climb to FL360, the autopilot failed to correct excessive airspeed, triggering a buffet alert and an uncommanded descent of 400 feet. The crew manually disengaged automation, descended to FL340, and continued the flight after determining the autopilot was unresponsive to speed deviations.

synopsis: An A320 Captain refused an aircraft after the full rudder throw flight control check yielded only half the required movement on the ECAM Rudder Position Indicator. The MEL allowed dispatch after a visual check but no rudder position indicators are installed on the empennage.
summary: The flight crew discovered a rudder indication discrepancy during the pre-flight check and refused the aircraft after Maintenance Control admitted they could not visually verify full rudder travel due to a lack of markings. This refusal occurred because the Minimum Equipment List required a visual verification that the crew determined was impossible to perform safely.

synopsis: A B757 EICAS alerted TRAILING EDGE FLAP DISAGREE when flaps 25 was selected on approach so a go-around followed, as a result of winds a runway change was requested. After a second go-around was executed this time due to low visibility, a fuel emergency was declared followed by with a safe landing with 6,000 LBS remaining.
summary: The flight crew experienced a trailing edge flap disagree on ILS 13L approach, initiating a go-around and QRH checklist. After a second go-around due to fog on Runway 22L and low fuel concerns, they declared an emergency and landed safely on Runway 13L with flaps 20.

synopsis: A widebody cargo Captain explains that his Company provides insufficient and non FAR compliant enroute weather briefing data on extended Middle Eastern and Asian trips where access to computers products for additional weather information may be nonexistent.
summary: The pilot reported that the company provided inadequate weather packages for long international flights, often including irrelevant charts and omitting enroute data. This prevented the PIC from evaluating fuel reasonableness or weather hazards, forcing reliance on verbal briefings and creating an unsafe operating condition.

synopsis: An CRJ-700 landed on a runway after ATC reported poor braking but slid off the runway while turning 180 degrees and was then towed to the gate because of the ice conditions. No advanced warning was given about the conditions which affected a previous flight.
summary: The Captain landed an aircraft and lost directional control on an icy taxiway despite reported sanding, causing the aircraft to slide onto the grass. The pilot attributed the incident to inadequate surface treatment and a lack of accurate information regarding prior controllability issues at the airport.

synopsis: A319 Captain noted thunderstorm activity near destination airport, but elected to continue due to apparent air mass conditions that were not conducive to convective activity. A go-around was initiated at 2,000 FT due to windshear encounter.
summary: The crew encountered a windshear event with severe turbulence and a downdraft at 2,000 feet MSL while on final for a CAT 3 ILS approach in calm surface winds. They executed a go-around after realizing the saturated, cold air mass masked the intensity of nearby thunderstorms, concluding they should not have continued the approach.

synopsis: An A319 nose wheel turned beyond the steering limit and the tug struck the Number 1 Engine inlet when the Tug Driver lost control on an icy patch some distance beyond the gate during pushback.
summary: During pushback in dark, foggy conditions, a tug lost traction on hidden ice, jackknifed, and struck the Number 1 engine inlet. The reporter attributes the incident to the ground crew's premature engine start clearance due to poor ramp assessment and unclear communication regarding surface conditions.

synopsis: A ground crew pushing a B737-700 from the gate reported an APU fire, so the QRH was completed, an emergency declared and the aircraft towed back to the gate where no evidence of a fire was found. No fire warning sounded.
summary: During pushback, ground crew signaled an APU fire near the left horizontal stabilizer trim tab, though no cockpit or cabin indications were present. The APU was shut down, the aircraft was towed back for deplaning, and the flight was canceled while Maintenance investigated the false alarm.

synopsis: An ERJ-175 Captain reported that Scheduling change the actual flight time on this day with adverse weather at nearly all stations so as to keep the crew below 9 hours.
summary: Pilots reported that Scheduling reduced block times on multiple legs without Dispatcher consultation, despite adverse weather and delays. The crew suspected these adjustments were made to artificially maintain legal flight time limits, bringing them dangerously close to their 9-hour maximum.

synopsis: An ERJ-190 STAB LOCK FAULT amber annunciator alerted during climb, so after completing the QRH which included the command, LAND AT THE NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT, the crew declared an emergency and diverted to a nearby major airport.
summary: During climbout near FL220, the crew received a 'Stab Lock Fault' and amber pitch trim dashes, prompting a diversion to a major airport with better weather. Although the fault message cleared on descent, the crew landed safely on the longest runway; the fault returned on rollout, but the aircraft taxied to the gate without assistance.

synopsis: At 700 FT on an ILS final for EWR 4R, a DHC-8-400 localizer deviated left causing the autopilot to quickly follow but the First Officer disconnected the autopilot, returned to course and continued to a safe landing.
summary: The pilot flying an ILS 4R approach into EWR at 700 feet AGL disengaged the autopilot after it incorrectly turned left due to a suspected localizer reception anomaly. The aircraft was actually left of course while the instrument indicated right, requiring manual control to align with the runway for a stabilized landing.

synopsis: A319 flight crew observed ECAM FWD Cargo Door warning on climbout at 5,000 FT. Captain elected to perform an air return rather than continue climb to check for pressurization problem.
summary: The Captain and First Officer returned to the departure airport after an ECAM FWD Cargo Door warning at 5,000 feet during climbout. Maintenance later found a loose cannon plug on the door sensor caused by baggage loading, validating the decision to avoid pressurization risks.

synopsis: An A319 nosewheel steering failed during the landing roll but was recovered after following the QRH which allowed the crew to taxi to the gate. Following maintenance the aircraft taxied for takeoff only to have the steering fail again which required a tow.
summary: The PIC experienced nosewheel steering failure during landing rollout on Runway 25L and again during taxi on Runway 25R, causing two missed approaches and a gate return. Maintenance attributed the issue to a sensor requiring cleaning per Airbus procedures, though the pilot noted potential procedural disconnects between crews.

synopsis: Given a clearance to descend, EMB-145 flight crew entered the descent altitude and set 1,000 FPM descent rate in FMS. As the crew briefed the approach, ATC alerted them to the fact that the aircraft was climbing.
summary: Pilots climbing to 6,500 feet instead of descending to 5,000 feet after ATC clearance due to distraction during an unfamiliar visual approach briefing. The crew corrected the altitude error after ATC queried the climb, attributing the incident to failing to verify the aircraft was actually descending.

synopsis: Taxiing CRJ900 flight crew was alerted to frost on the starboard winglet by personnel in de-ice truck. First Officer had overlooked the winglet on walk-around.
summary: The pilot overlooked frost on the right winglet during preflight, though the wings were clear. An ice truck crew signaled the omission while taxiing, prompting a stop for re-deicing; the crew concluded the truckers withheld the information until the aircraft turned to reveal the missed spot.

synopsis: DHC8-300 flight crew experiences a loss of hydraulic fluid from the number two system as the gear is retracted after takeoff. Flight returns to the departure airport using the alternate gear extension method.
summary: The crew experienced a #2 hydraulic system leak and RUD FULL PRESS caution on climb-out, causing a return for an alternate gear extension landing. The First Officer initially flew while the Captain managed checklists and communications before transferring controls to execute the manual gear extension procedure.

synopsis: A B737NG flight crew failed to manually enter their aurally transmitted clearance into their FMS and a minor track deviation occurred prior to their discovering of the error.
summary: The pilot not flying entered incorrect fixes KU03O and PDT into the FMC due to an interruption by the De-ice Coordinator during the ground checklist. The error was detected enroute, causing the aircraft to deviate three miles off course before a direct clearance to JKNOX was issued.

synopsis: DHC8-200 Captain reports a CABIN PRESS warning light during cruise at 17,000 FT and initiates an emergency descent to 10,000 FT. The crew is able to continue to destination unpressurized.
summary: During cruise at 17,000 feet, the flight crew declared an emergency and descended to 10,000 feet after the cabin pressure warning light illuminated. Following checklists to depressurize the cabin, they amended their release and continued to the original destination with no further issues.

synopsis: Captain reported the Right Engine on an MD-88 aircraft overboosted while climbing through 3,000 FT. The Automatic Reserve Thrust (ARTs) had activated, ARTs light had illuminated, but the Right Engine would not respond to throttle movement. Emergency declared. Throttle linkage had separated at the Fuel Control Unit (FCU).
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced an uncontrolled right engine overboost on an MD-88 shortly after takeoff due to a disengaged Fuel Control Unit linkage caused by missing safety wiring. They shut down the engine, declared an emergency, and landed safely with no fire or damage.

synopsis: B757 Captain is informed of a passenger illness during descent for landing then notices that the left throttle has not been retarded by the auto throttles and cannot be retarded manually. An emergency is declared and ATC advised of the issue. With a minimum thrust setting of 1.25 EPR the engine is allowed to run through the approach and landing, and is shut down on the roll out.
summary: During descent, the crew managed a medical emergency and a binding left throttle that would not retard. They declared a double emergency, landed on one engine after shutting down the left engine on rollout, and the passenger recovered.

synopsis: A319 flight crew experiences an EGPWS terrain warning abeam BOG at 10,800 during an ILS to Runway 13R in VMC. Terrain was not a factor but the hill at 11,200 FT southwest of the localizer was thought to have been the trigger.
summary: The flight crew received conflicting arrival clearances and runway changes while approaching SKBO in VFR conditions. A terrain alert triggered near the BOG VOR after a heading change, which the pilot attributed to proximity to a spot elevation, but the crew arrested the descent and landed safely on Runway 13R.

synopsis: B737-800 pilot reports a low speed reject for a takeoff warning horn. All inputs to the takeoff warning system are checked and cycled and no anomalies are noted. The second takeoff attempt is successful.
summary: The flight crew aborted a takeoff at 30 KIAS due to an erroneous configuration warning despite correct flap, trim, and spoiler settings. After recycling controls and verifying spoiler stowage, the crew successfully completed a second takeoff with no further warnings.

synopsis: An aircraft taxiing for takeoff at IND lost control of the aircraft on Taxiway D2 because of NIL braking and steering without damage. A tug repositioned the aircraft on the taxiway after the taxiway was chemically deiced and plowed.
summary: The crew lost directional control and crossed the hold short line on Taxiway D2 due to black ice causing nil braking action at low speed. Maintenance treated the area and repositioned the aircraft, allowing the flight to continue after the incident.

synopsis: MD11 flight crew is informed by the Tower during landing roll that fluid was observed streaming from the left engine during approach and continues. The left engine is shut down with no change in the fluid flow. All engines are shut down and the aircraft is towed to the gate.
summary: The flight crew landed and taxied clear after Tower and another pilot reported a fluid stream from the Number 1 engine. Maintenance confirmed a fuel leak in the Number 1 engine pylon area, resulting in a 3,000-pound fuel loss and a tow to the ramp.

synopsis: MD11 flight crew experiences a 'Gen Drive 2 Fault' on the takeoff roll and rejects. The fault self clears and a high power run up is accomplished with no faults noted. The next takeoff attempt produces the same results and the generator is disconnected using MEL procedures and the third takeoff attempt is successful.
summary: The crew rejected takeoff twice at 60 KIAS due to a recurring Level 2 'Gen Drive 2 Fault' alert. After Maintenance directed an IDG disconnect per MEL 24-21-01 and an EGPWS reset, the aircraft successfully departed on the third attempt.

synopsis: CRJ900 Captain reports ACARS interference with with VHF ATC communication right after takeoff on numerous occasions with different aircraft. The problem is new to the fleet and may have begin with ACARS software changes required by FAR 117.
summary: Pilots reported that a new ACARS program update on CRJ 700 and 900 aircraft caused loud modem-like squeals below 10,000 feet, blocking ATC instructions and crew communication during busy departures. The noise, linked to new FAR 117 sign-in procedures, was distracting but did not result in operational errors.

synopsis: CRJ200 flight crew reports a rejected takeoff due to a jammed right rudder pedal caused by a water bottle blocking rudder pedal movement.
summary: The First Officer aborted takeoff at 70 knots after a water bottle obstructed the right rudder pedal, causing the aircraft to veer left. The crew removed the obstruction, performed RTO checks, and delayed departure for 15 minutes to cool brakes before continuing.

synopsis: The absence of the nose gear pin on first flight of the day preflight blossomed into mass confusion between Maintenance, Operations and the flight crew of the CRJ. After being cleared to fly the first flight of their sequence, they were first held, then released and then recalled prior to takeoff at the intermediate stop.
summary: The Captain departed with a missing nose gear pin after Operations advised it was unnecessary, but conflicting Maintenance Control instructions later forced a return to the gate and deplaning. The crew attributed the delay to unclear procedures regarding gear pin requirements for flight versus ground operations.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) describes how time, stress, confusion, weather conditions and lack of adequate communications contributed to an A319 aircraft thrust reverser on the Number One Engine not deploying upon landing.
summary: A mechanic on an A319 installed a vibration sensor and replaced a call horn but failed to complete the final task card step due to shift turnover, heavy rain, and communication breakdowns. The reporter cited time pressure, stress, and confusion as contributing factors to the incomplete maintenance before the aircraft was released.

synopsis: While a Maintenance Technician was starting an engine, a ground support vehicle drove through the restricted box in front of the aircraft.
summary: During engine start, a cabin cleaning van driver entered and stopped in the red restricted box before parking near the aircraft. The pilot reported the incident to Ramp Tower, attributing the violation to the driver's apparent lack of attention or disregard for safety protocols.

synopsis: The pilot of a Piper PA32 began a flight with a one thousand foot error in the altimeter setting which led to a low altitude warning. After climbing, and recognizing the altimeter setting error, the pilot's stress level made it difficult for him to perform an ILS approach. He elected to descend below the glideslope when he observed a break in the cloud layer, and landed safely.
summary: The pilot incorrectly set the altimeter to 30.61 instead of 29.61, causing a 1,000-foot low altitude error that triggered terrain and ATC alerts during departure. Subsequent mental degradation led to approach errors, but the pilot landed visually after deviating from ATC instructions to avoid IMC conditions.

synopsis: Helicopter pilot reports a NMAC with another helicopter while attempting to fly near LA78 beneath a low ceiling. TIS aboard the reporters helicopter was instrumental in avoiding the NMAC.
summary: A pilot flying a Mode S/TIS-equipped aircraft at 500 feet southbound along the Calcasieu River encountered a yellow helicopter that failed to respond to CTAF calls. The pilot descended 250 feet to avoid a collision when the helicopter passed 150 yards away and 150 feet above, then reversed course due to low ceilings.

synopsis: A Government UAV operated in US Domestic Airspace at FL270 and afterwords the controllers realized they were not provided with either the Certificate of Operation, Pilot Contact Information or Lost Link Procedures for that flight.
summary: An air traffic controller discovered that an Unmanned Aerial System mission checklist lacked critical pilot contact and lost link procedures for a flight operating at FL270/280. The controller attributed this inadequate coordination to training gaps, inconsistent scheduling, and password-protected Certificate of Authorization files that prevented access to essential mission data.

synopsis: B737-300 Captain is informed of smoke in the cabin by a Flight Attendant during initial climb after takeoff. The QRH is complied with, and emergency is declared and the flight returns to the departure airport. After maintenance action is performed the flight departs a second time and the scenario repeats in its entirety.
summary: The Captain and crew declared an emergency and returned to land after smoke and a lavatory fire alarm occurred at 5,000 feet. Maintenance found disconnected and unwrapped ducts, while the Captain criticized company procedures for distracting him from assisting passengers with special needs.

synopsis: While at the gate and awaiting push back clearance, this Boeing 737 First Officer reports that the gate agent, without prior notification, brought the jet bridge back onto the aircraft.
summary: A flight crew awaiting pushback clearance observed a ground agent attach the jetway to the aircraft with the beacon on, without notifying the crew. The agent claimed Operations instructed the action and disregarded safety warnings, creating a potential collision hazard during the pushback phase.

synopsis: Captain reports all three autopilots failed during climb on a B757 aircraft.
summary: The pilot reported that all three autopilots failed during the enroute phase of flight. No specific cause or outcome was described in the narrative.

synopsis: B747 First Officer, as part of a double augmented crew, elects to decline the duty period extension required (17 to 19 hours) for a late departing flight and the flight is canceled.
summary: The flight crew and Chief Pilot were involved in a pre-departure dispute regarding a 17-hour Flight Duty Period limit under FAR 117. The flight was cancelled after the First Officer refused to accept a 30-minute extension to 19 hours, citing scientific research supporting the standard limit.

synopsis: B757 First Officer reported he attempted a go-around because of an unstable approach due to either wake vortex or wind shear, and the go-around was sloppily executed.
summary: The pilot flying a Boeing 767 to EWR initiated a go-around due to excessive speed and altitude but delayed TOGA engagement by searching for switches based on B-737 muscle memory. This led to a brief autopilot-induced descent at 1,900 feet, which the pilot corrected with aggressive control inputs after realizing the gear remained down.

synopsis: B737NG flight crew arriving DEN report a track deviation due to multiple ATC adjustments during the arrival, transition changes and three runway changes. The HIMON transition to the RNAV Z 34L is not correctly entered in the FMC and when detected by ATC, the crew is offered a visual approach.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced an FMC programming error during a turbulent descent into Denver due to multiple runway changes and the First Officer's inexperience. The crew flew past the HIMOM waypoint instead of turning, but ATC cleared them for a visual approach, resulting in an uneventful landing with no traffic conflict.

synopsis: A ramp employee was startled by movement of the aircraft while closing the cargo door, causing him to fall from the belt loader.
summary: A ramp employee nearly fell from a belt loader while closing the rear pit when the crew released brakes without communication. The aircraft lurched backward due to wheel pressure against chocks, pushing the employee off balance.

synopsis: A B747-400 flight crew dumped fuel and returned to their departure airport after experiencing compressor stalls and eventual failure of the number one engine.
summary: During takeoff at 800–1,000 feet AGL, the crew experienced a Number 1 engine compressor stall and failure, causing autopilot disconnect. After initially turning left per engine-out procedures, they complied with ATC instructions to avoid arrival traffic, dumped fuel, and returned for an uneventful landing.

synopsis: EMB145 captain reports landing on Runway 10C at ORD contaminated with compacted snow with a reported braking action of fair. Full braking is applied on touch down and directional control becomes difficult with braking action nil. With the aircraft drifting toward the runway edge the brakes are released, directional control is regained and brakes reapplied with good results. De-ice fluid shed by departing aircraft was thought to have been a factor in this incident.
summary: The pilot reported a directional control issue during landing on ORD Runway 10C in fair braking action, caused by suspected anti-ice fluid contamination from preceding departures. The aircraft weather-vaned and skidded, triggering a rudder system failure, but the pilot regained control and exited the runway safely.

synopsis: A CRJ-700 flight crew descended below their cleared altitude when they set their altimeters to the pressure setting at their departure airport passing 18,000 MSL. ATC's initial inquiries as to their 'assigned' altitude failed to alert them as to their error. The issue was resolved only after ATC stated she showed them 600 FT low and advised of the correct altimeter setting.
summary: During descent into ORD, the crew descended below their assigned 11,000 feet after setting altimeters to the departure airport's 30.23 instead of the local 29.62. The pilot corrected the error and climbed back to 11,000 feet after realizing they had used an outdated ATIS printout.

synopsis: During a night visual approach to a runway with nearby high terrain an EMB175 crew responded to a 'caution Terrain' followed by an EGPWS 'pull up' warning. The warnings ceased immediately once the escape maneuver was initiated, and the visual approach was reestablished and continued to a successful landing.
summary: During a night visual approach, the flight crew received EGPWS "caution terrain" and "pull up" warnings while on a left base leg. The pilot executed a go-around with full thrust, cleared the terrain, and subsequently landed normally after reestablishing the approach.

synopsis: A First Officer questions the contradiction of text in MEL 33-50-03 for the number of emergency lights that must be illuminated at the forward and aft aisle emergency light strips compared with the light diagram in MEL 33-20-01. Maintenance Control says the diagram is correct and the text is wrong. Concern that numerous CE-560XLs may be out of compliance were also raised.
summary: During preflight, a crew member discovered forward and aft emergency light strips were swapped, contradicting MEL text but matching the diagram. Maintenance Control confirmed the text was incorrect, leaving uncertainty about fleet compliance due to conflicting MEL data.

synopsis: During climb in icing conditions, a B737-400 First Officer had a SPD flag alert along with an airspeed loss, a FMC buffet alert and other indications that his pitot static system was icing even though no pilot system alerts were present.
summary: The First Officer encountered unreliable airspeed indications during climbout due to a slowly failing pitot probe heater that did not illuminate the warning light. After completing the airspeed unreliable checklist, the crew attributed the issue to icing and continued the flight to the destination.

synopsis: Despite having received a signed security form advising the exterior compartments had been inspected as required prior to departure, the Captain of a CRJ-700 was advised after landing that the forward cargo compartment contained 'at least 600 LBS' of ballast weight, weight the reporter believes was added on a repositioning flight. The aircraft had flown at least three legs since that flight without notification to the crews that the ballast was aboard.
summary: The PIC reported that 600 lbs of unrecorded ballast was found in the forward cargo compartment after the first flight of the day, despite a signed security sweep form. The reporter attributed this to ground personnel failing to inspect the compartment and the First Officer failing to communicate the ballast's presence from a prior reposition flight.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An Air Carrier pilot was dispatched to IAD without an alternate or fuel, as were other company flights, when the actual arrival weather was 500 FT overcast 1 mile. The flight landed safely but during descend the Captain had a very high workload contacting Dispatch and making contingency plans.
summary: The pilot of an aircraft arriving at IAD in deteriorating weather considered diverting to ORF but continued the approach due to communication failures with Dispatch and concerns over operational control. The flight landed safely with 2,700 LBS fuel, though the pilot criticized the lack of an assigned alternate and Dispatch's failure to monitor weather for multiple inbound flights.

synopsis: The pilot of a Cessna 402 experienced a rough running engine in cruise flight. After cycling the magneto switch, he observed that the right engine had a malfunctioning right magneto, so he elected to return to the departure airport where a successful landing was performed.
summary: The pilot reported rough running, knocking, and rocking at 9,000 feet with low right CHT and a near-engine quit on the right engine left mag. The pilot returned to the departure airport without declaring an emergency, receiving radar vectors to final approach.

synopsis: An MD-80 diverted to a nearby airport when the flight crew determined they were unable to access fuel in the center fuel tank due to low fuel pump pressure.
summary: During cruise, the flight crew diverted to a hub airport after center tank pumps failed to generate sufficient pressure to feed fuel. Maintenance later reported the pumps were operational but could not deliver fuel at a normal rate, though the cause remained undetermined.

aircraft: Boeing Company Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An air carrier flight crew in VMC flying the Runway 08 RNAV [GNSS] approach to MDPP received a single EGPWS Terrain warning which they determined to be inappropriate. Their airport briefing page noted a history of such warnings.
summary: The First Officer and Captain experienced a single 'Terrain-Terrain, Pull up' alert during the RNAV (GNSS) RWY 08 approach at MDPP while descending in VNAV at 180 KTS with flaps 15. The crew identified it as a known nuisance warning, briefly leveled the aircraft, and continued the approach after the alert ceased.

synopsis: Because an MD-82 center fuel tank would not feed the engines, the flight diverted to a nearby airport while sufficient wing tank fuel remained.
summary: The crew diverted to an enroute airport after the center tank fuel failed to feed, landing safely under Max Landing Weight with adequate reserves. Maintenance could not determine the cause, and the crew declined to extend their duty day to wait for a replacement aircraft.

aircraft: Airbus Industrie Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Air Carrier Dispatcher voiced a complaint regarding the 'Braking Action' reports at JAC, noting the uncooperative nature of ATC personnel regarding information clarification.
summary: A dispatcher and Airbus crew encountered conflicting runway braking reports for Jackson Hole, with MU readings above 40 but a GA report indicating poor conditions. When the dispatcher contacted JAC Tower for clarification, the controller hung up, citing being too busy, leaving the crew concerned about the discrepancy.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A Medium Transport flight crew departing MMH got a momentary GLD UNSAFE warning as they approached 80 KTS. The Captain initially began to reduce thrust to reject the takeoff, but reconsidered, re-established takeoff thrust and continued the takeoff successfully.
summary: During takeoff from Runway 9 at MMH, a runway bump triggered a false 'GLD UNSAFE' caution, causing the Captain to briefly retard thrust before continuing. The reporter attributed the message to radar altimeter fluctuation but noted that aborting after thrust reduction would have been warranted.

synopsis: An A319 Flight Attendant reported he and other crew members exited the aircraft because of a strong toxic odor which Maintenance was unable to clear. The flight was canceled and he had physical symptoms the following day.
summary: Cabin crew detected a toxic odor in the aircraft cabin during preflight, prompting evacuation and a failed maintenance attempt to clear the air. The reporter attributed the incident to hydraulic fuel leaks in cabin air sources and noted subsequent crew health symptoms.

synopsis: A Lead Mechanic describes the breakdown in their A-Check Paper Package review process for verifying job card completions and sign-offs of work accomplished on a B737-800 aircraft. An Airworthiness Directive for lubing and checking aileron tab 'free play' was missed, aircraft was grounded. Lead Mechanic also notes that open access to their Sceptre maintenance computer allows anyone to enter another employee's name and file number without any identification of who entered the information.
summary: During a B737-800 A-Check, a lead mechanic failed to complete an aileron lubrication Airworthiness Directive because the job card was stapled to rescheduled tasks and mistakenly audited as deferred. The aircraft departed with the task incomplete, resulting in non-compliant operation due to failed safety nets and lack of secure electronic task tracking.

synopsis: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports a Ramp employee did not want to unload/load the baggage compartment of a B737-800 aircraft due to the Forward Cargo Door Balance Mechanism had failed. Adding to safety concern was a proviso in their MEL that allowed for an unguarded 2' X 4' inch board to be inserted between the 60-pound cargo door skin and the compartment sheet metal floor to hold the door up.
summary: Ramp agents and mechanics reported an unsafe condition where a B737NG forward cargo door balance mechanism failed, requiring a temporary wooden board per MEL. The crew feared the board could dislodge and drop the 60-pound door, prompting a request for engineering to install ceiling cables and update procedures.

synopsis: Three Aircraft Maintenance Technicians (AMTs) report about their involvement installing thermocouple harnesses on Number 1 Engine after being informed that three harness supports were found not secured on an EMB-145 aircraft.
summary: During an EMB-145 thermocouple harness installation, three mechanics failed to secure three harness supports before closing engine panels due to workflow interruptions and incomplete task handovers. The omission was discovered later by the lead technician, who attributed the error to rushing multiple tasks and relying on an inspector's earlier partial verification.

synopsis: A CL30 Captain railed against the intrusive nature of RAAS warnings when taxiing on busy airports. Believes flight crew control of warning volume is an acceptable alternative.
summary: Pilots at ORD reported missing ATC landing and taxi instructions due to intrusive RAAS warnings for an aircraft on short final and a runway not in use. The crew attributed these potentially dangerous situations to nuisance alerts and recommended adding a mute or override function to the system.

synopsis: When they took off from TEB with the pitch trim switch in the secondary vice primary position the pilot flying was unable to maintain the required 1,500 MSL level off on the RUUDY SID. After repositioning the switch operation returned to normal.
summary: The pilot reported that during departure from TEB Runway 24, the aircraft climbed to 1,800 feet because the pitch trim switch was left in the secondary position, overriding nose-down trim commands. The crew corrected the switch and descended to the assigned 1,500 feet, attributing the error to an overlooked Pre-Taxi Checklist item.

synopsis: At FL390 a Lear 60's Left and Right Bleed Air Warnings alerted indicating a tailcone overheat or fire so the checklist was completed successfully extinguishing the alerts. The crew then declared an emergency to divert when the aircraft lost cabin pressurization mandating a rapid descent to 10,000 FT.
summary: The crew experienced bleed air warnings and rapid depressurization near FL380 while en route, prompting an emergency descent to 10,000 feet. They declared an emergency and were vectored by ATC to a safe precautionary landing at ZZZ.

synopsis: Enroute Controller described an aircraft security event resulting from an air carrier squawking the hijack code followed by the no radio code, all leading to several 'no notice' hold instructions.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller managing a trainee during a hijack and fighter scramble scenario issued conflicting instructions to a B757 at 150 and a B737 at 130 due to sudden hold changes. The controller resolved the conflict by altering headings and altitudes, attributing the complexity to poor communication between Approach and Center regarding arrival acceptance.

synopsis: SBN Controller described an unsafe situation when inbound 'primary only' traffic was not on the prescribed LOA route and the RADAR equipment failed to display any type of target.
summary: An SBN Approach controller lost primary radar contact with a P28R aircraft lacking a transponder due to a known blocked area in the sector. The controller reestablished contact via identifying turns but reported that the radar's poor performance and FWA's non-compliant routing compromise separation safety.

synopsis: Tower Controller described a loss of separation event when an arrival and departure aircraft were not afforded the required separation.
summary: A newly certified Local Controller cleared an EMB135 for takeoff on Runway 31 while a Citation remained on the runway after missing its exit, creating a separation violation. The controller failed to cancel the clearance or act on CIC prompting, resulting in an unsafe situation attributed to poor judgment, inexperience, and lack of accountability.

synopsis: An air carrier Captain described his reasoning for suggesting that night visual approaches to BUR Runway 26 be prohibited.
summary: A pilot reported that crews might attempt a high-risk night circling approach to Runway 26 at Burbank if primary runways close, potentially causing a CFIT accident due to rising terrain, lack of visual glide path aids, and insufficient crew training for such maneuvers.

synopsis: An Air Carrier departed SBGR with a revised flight plan, the first plan rejected by ATC, and after passing BOMAL were notified by Amazonica Control that they had deviated from the flight plan. There may been NOTAMs not complied with.
summary: The crew reported that Amazonica Control flagged a routing deviation because ATC held an outdated flight plan from a rejected Release 1, despite the crew flying the compliant Release 2. The reporter attributed the error to a flight planning system failure to process NOTAMs and a dispatcher computer outage.

synopsis: Captain reports that during landing rollout when the autobrakes engaged, the braking was stronger than normal on their B737 Nex Gen aircraft. Brakes seemed to stick then release, when in Manual braking. Right Main Landing Gear (MLG) outboard main tire was found canted outboard with Wheel Spin Canon plug hanging out and brake disintegrated.
summary: During landing, the pilot experienced excessive autobrake force and sticking manual brakes on the right outboard main landing gear. Post-flight inspection revealed the brake assembly had disintegrated, prompting the crew to keep both engines running to the gate.

synopsis: An AFT CARGO DOOR OPEN ECAM alerted during takeoff, so the takeoff was rejected. At the gate the door handle was found out of place, closed properly, fuel topped off and the flight departed uneventfully.
summary: The crew aborted takeoff at 80 knots due to an ECAM indication of an open aft cargo door. Maintenance found the door handle unstowed, required no action, and the aircraft departed uneventfully after refueling.

synopsis: A Dangerous Goods (DG) Specialist reports he was informed about a damaged freight that had been improperly shipped from their Station, leaking hazardous fluid on an A320 flight.
summary: A DG Specialist reported that a warehouse manager at ZZZ authorized shipping leaking dangerous goods to ZZZZ1 after wrapping them in a plastic bag. The specialist stated that proper damaged DG procedures were not followed, which would have required the shipper to retrieve the freight instead of loading it.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An air carrier crew flying a DEN Runway 35L visual was about sixteen miles from the runway when they descended to 7,000 FT and out of Class B airspace where ATC notified them about the error which they corrected by climbing to 7,500 FT.
summary: The pilot monitoring and First Officer descended below the 7,500 FT Minimum Vectoring Altitude during a visual approach to Denver Runway 35L. A 30-knot headwind combined with Flaps 1 in FLCH mode caused an unexpectedly steep descent, triggering a low altitude alert before the crew climbed back to the correct altitude.

synopsis: An ERJ-175 engine failed in flight after an apparent fan failure so the QRH was completed, an emergency was declared, and the flight returned to the departure airport for an uneventful landing.
summary: During climb to 22,000 feet, the crew experienced an Engine 1 failure with loud bangs, yaw, and vibration, likely caused by prior FOD or bird strike damage. They manually secured the engine, declared an emergency, and landed safely, later finding a seized N1 fan and internal shrapnel.

synopsis: A CRJ-200 Master Warning CONFIG RUDDER EICAS alerted as takeoff power was set even with the rudder trim centered and in the green, so the takeoff was rejected and during communications with Maintenance they were instructed cycle and re-center the trim. The following takeoff was uneventful, but the crew realized a maintenance log entry and sign-off had not been completed.
summary: The pilot reported a 'CONFIG RUDDER' Master Warning during takeoff power application despite the rudder trim being centered. Maintenance released the aircraft after cycling the trim without verifying the warning under thrust, which the pilot later identified as an error in not questioning the release procedure.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A Corporate flight crew decided to declare a fuel emergency and divert to the filed alternate ZZZZ because the weather at their filed destination went below approach minimums.
summary: The crew diverted to alternate ZZZZ after destination weather degraded below minimums with poor braking action. They declared a low fuel emergency to land before ZZZZ closed for snow removal, a decision confirmed as safe by subsequent worsening conditions.

synopsis: An EC-135 triple tachometer failed on approach with the engine functioning normally. After several successful self tests the aircraft was flown to its home base where the tachometer failed during testing, so the aircraft was removed from service.
summary: The pilot experienced a triple tachometer failure on Engine 2 N1 during final approach to a hospital helipad, though the VEMD confirmed the engine was operational. The aircraft was grounded after maintenance confirmed the gauge failed self-tests, requiring a replacement part.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported wake vortex encounter in trail of a B747-400 on arrival to MIA that resulted in loss of pitch and roll control and 300 FT altitude excursion.
summary: Flight crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding 747-400 while at 10,000 feet on the FLIPR TWO arrival, causing a 400-foot altitude loss and 30-degree course deviation. The pilot attributed the incident to insufficient ATC spacing and calm winds, though no injuries occurred and control was recovered.

synopsis: A flight landed on CMH Runway 28L at dusk in rain and exited onto a closed taxiway after being cleared to exit on the next Taxiway C7. The barricades were not seen until they were on the closed taxiway well clear of the runway.
summary: The crew exited onto undeclared taxiway C6 instead of C7 after landing in rain at dusk, stopping upon encountering orange chalks. The incident resulted from C6 not being depicted on charts or NOTAMed, combined with poor visibility and ambiguous ATC instructions.

synopsis: DC-10 First Officer is informed 2.3 hours into flight that a large piece of the number one engine cowl departed the aircraft during takeoff. An emergency is declared for landing at destination where it is discovered that the number two engine is missing part of its cowl. Maintenance had been preformed on the engine two days prior.
summary: The flight crew discovered mid-flight that a #1 engine cowling piece fell off during takeoff, causing increased drag and fuel burn. Post-landing inspection revealed damage to the #2 engine, which had maintenance two days prior, though the crew could not determine the cause.

synopsis: When ground crew attempted to open the 1L door of the reporter's cargo configured MD11 the door bound up on a partially deployed flight crew rest module.
summary: A flight attendant reported that excessive bedding in the stowed Crew Rest Area caused the 1L door to bind and stop partially open during post-flight disarming. The reporter attributed the incident to bedding pressure on the locking mechanism, noting prior damage and recommending against storing extra materials in the bunks.

synopsis: A Flight Attendant was exposed to de-icing fluid that leaked through the cabin door seal during takeoff, prior to aircraft pressurization.
summary: A flight attendant reported de-icing fluid leaking through the main cabin door during takeoff, causing a loud noise, strong smell, and skin irritation. The crew member cleaned the spill, and the Captain was notified to ensure the aircraft is inspected before its next flight.

synopsis: An air carrier Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) contracted to perform maintenance on another air carrier's B757-200 aircraft, describes his efforts to install Lock-out pins on a Rolls Royce # 2 Engine Reverser assembly. The aircraft had lost hydraulic fluid on landing when hydraulic seals had failed in the reverser sync-lok module.
summary: During maintenance on the #2 engine thrust reversers, mechanics hydraulically cycled the system to align a deactivation pin after failing to install the outboard pin due to a hydraulic leak. Both reversers deployed despite the inboard pin being installed, causing internal damage to the inboard reverser and resulting in the aircraft being out of service.

synopsis: A Maintenance Controller describes how a lack of adequate communications between Maintenance Control and a Cessna 560 flight crew allowed the aircraft to depart while a chip on the # 1 Engine Exhaust Cone was still being evaluated. Aircraft had to divert for additional evaluation of the exhaust cone.
summary: A Cessna C560 crew reported a chip in the #1 engine exhaust cone, and Maintenance Control initially suggested it was non-issue before the manufacturer deferred judgment to Cessna. The aircraft departed without final approval, leading to a diversion for evaluation due to a communication disconnect between maintenance and the flight crew.

synopsis: A Composite Shop Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports why he refused to sign-off an Outboard Flap skin delamination of the aluminum honeycomb core as a Permanent Repair after the Bond Repair was accomplished in an uncontrolled Hangar environment.
summary: Mechanics discovered delamination on a left wing outboard flap and attempted an unauthorized on-wing repair without Quality Assurance involvement or proper equipment access. The reporter concluded the repair was improper due to bypassed verification steps and recommended removing the flap for shop repair.

synopsis: DA40 instructor pilot reports a NMAC with a PA28 pilot entering the pattern at LGU. The PA28 pilot had requested the TPA for BMC on the LGU CTAF, which had been provided without comment.
summary: A DA-40F instructor and student at LGU encountered a Cherokee 300 feet below TPA on downwind after the Cherokee pilot misidentified the airport and failed to monitor traffic. The reporter attributed the near-miss to the Cherokee pilot's poor planning, low altitude, and failure to see the DA-40F against the mountain background.

synopsis: CE501 Captain reports a rapid loss of cabin pressurization at FL430. An emergency is declared and descent initiated until the upper twenty flight levels, when cabin pressurization returns to normal. The Captain elects to return to the departure airport at FL190 uneventfully.
summary: The pilot experienced a cabin pressurization failure at FL430, causing a 7,000 FT/minute climb rate and requiring an emergency descent to FL190. After the system recovered, the crew returned to the departure airport due to poor weather at the destination, completing an uneventful flight.

synopsis: Tower Controller described a possible procedural violation when a Medevac Helicopter was cleared to the airport when IFR traffic was on approach.
summary: Air Traffic Controllers expedited a Medevac helicopter's SVFR arrival into IFR conditions by clearing it during a traffic gap. Although an IFR arrival penetrated the Class D airspace, the helicopter landed safely with separation maintained, avoiding a 20-minute delay.

synopsis: CRJ200 Captain reports rejecting the takeoff when the L WING ANTI ICE message doe not extinguish when takeoff thrust is set. Flight returns to the gate for maintenance.
summary: The flight crew rejected takeoff before 80 knots due to a persistent L WING ANTI ICE message during the roll in icing conditions. After maintenance inspection and clearance, the aircraft departed without further incident.

synopsis: A Maintenance Manager was informed he had installed four incorrect replacement bolts at the lower Eyelet Fitting for the cockpit windshield center-post to the forward fuselage on an EMB-145 aircraft. He had verified the Part Number (P/N) on a certification sheet had matched the Engineering Order (E/O), but was unaware that the bolts that were issued did not match the certification.
summary: A Line Maintenance Manager installed incorrect bolts during an Engineering Order task because issued hardware did not match its certification. This error triggered an FAA inquiry and caused a flight delay.

synopsis: EMB145 Captain reports rejecting a takeoff for an engine anti ice caution message. Maintenance is contacted and the fault is cleared, but the next takeoff attempt produces the same result.
summary: The flight crew aborted takeoff at 60 knots due to an E2 A/ICE FAIL caution, and a second attempt failed with the same fault. The crew returned to the gate, and after maintenance checks, they swapped to a spare aircraft to continue the flight.

synopsis: DHC8-100 First Officer reports flying the entire leg with the flaps left inadvertently at the 5 degree position. The published flap speed was exceeded by 32 knots.
summary: The flight crew operated the aircraft with flaps at 5 degrees, exceeding the 148-knot limit by cruising at 180 knots. This occurred due to failure to retract flaps to 0 at 1,000 feet AGL, missed checklist verification, and insufficient instrument scanning, prompting an immediate maintenance inspection.

synopsis: CE560 Captain experiences a thumping sensation from the elevator trim wheel when the flaps are selected to 7 on the downwind for landing with the autopilot engaged. The elevator trim indicator is noted at its full forward position and the autopilot is disengaged, anticipating a pitch up but none occurs. A normal approach and landing ensues.
summary: During approach on an extended vectored downwind, the pilot selected Flaps 7, causing the autopilot to drive the elevator trim to its full forward limit with audible thumps. The pilot disconnected the autopilot, continued the flight without declaring an emergency, and reported the issue, noting a prior trim indicator malfunction.

synopsis: Hawker 850 Captain experiences autopilot during descent and begins hand flying. This leads to the discovery that the rudder and aileron trim tabs are frozen. The crew is able to continue and land without difficulty and the trim tabs become unstuck during taxi in.
summary: During descent, the autopilot failed and aileron and rudder trim controls froze, though pitch trim remained functional. The pilot hand-flew the aircraft to a safe landing, noting the trim controls unstuck during taxi but required excessive force to move.

synopsis: A C-208 pilot being given a route check by a check airman received GPWS Terrain warning and an ATC issued Low Altitude Alert while conducting an RNAV (GPS) Runway 20L approach to FAI. A communications breakdown between the reporter and the Check Airman was cited as a contributing factor.
summary: During a route check on the GPS 20L approach into Fairbanks, the pilot and check airman received terrain and low altitude alerts due to a communications breakdown regarding minimum altitude. The pilot noted that better communication between the crew would have prevented the confusion and subsequent alerts.

synopsis: Tower Controller described an unsafe situation when IFR traffic on final was transferred to the Tower significantly off course in IFR conditions, the reporter listing a number of TRACON shortfalls in this event.
summary: A TRACON controller transferred a BE35 to Tower Control while the aircraft was half a mile left of the ILS course for Runway 32R due to the pilot selecting the incorrect localizer frequency. The report states the controller failed to recognize the deviation or assist the pilot in hazardous weather before handing off an unestablished aircraft.

synopsis: CRP Controller described an airspace incursion when information regarding the status of NQI TRACON's airspace was uncertain.
summary: A Valley North controller issued an IFR clearance to a King Air climbing to 6,000 feet, but the aircraft violated the airspace boundary because the controller was unaware that the intended handoff facility, NQI, had closed. The controller subsequently coordinated with ZHU, who accepted the aircraft, attributing the violation to the lack of notification regarding NQI's closure and the automation's failure to reject the handoff.

synopsis: Ground Controller taxiing multiple aircraft to the runway with a 'follow the preceding aircraft' type clearance observed one of the aircraft entering the runway after the preceding departure.
summary: An Air Coupe pilot deviated from taxi instructions and entered Runway 6 while following a Grumman during complex Runway 6 operations. The controller attributed the incident to the pilot's incorrect readback, which the controller failed to hear and correct, compounded by relying on the "follow" instruction.

synopsis: ZMP Controller expressed frustration regarding controllers at ZOB who reportedly assign the wrong frequency, especially when sectors are combined/split etc.
summary: Cleveland Center (ZOB) controllers repeatedly assigned a TVC lander at FL200 to the high sector frequency instead of the required low sector frequency. The reporter states this error creates an extreme safety hazard during critical icing conditions by causing loss of communication while vectoring for final approach.

synopsis: IAD Controller described a separation loss during an attempt to conduct visual approaches when reported weather indicated that conditions were such that no visual approaches should be attempted.
summary: A B737 on a visual approach to Runway 1R came within 1,000 feet of an E145 near IAD during deteriorating fog. The incident resulted from communication breakdowns and lack of leadership between Tower and TRACON teams, who incorrectly continued visual approaches despite official low visibility reports.

synopsis: PBI Controller described an MVA loss of separation event when a descent clearance was issued, but not realized by the reporter, additional video map highlights were suggested.
summary: An air traffic controller descended an aircraft to 1,500 feet near SUA, below the 2,000-foot MVA, causing a low altitude alert over a 1,000-foot obstruction. The controller attributed the error to forgetting the obstruction and requested better radar highlighting, while the pilot cancelled IFR after climbing to 2,000 feet.

synopsis: A flight deck observer reports that he and the crew are distracted during approach to HOU by a bright light on the Runway 12R center line, which turns out to be the first light of the new in ground high speed taxiway lead off lights at both Taxiways M1 and M3.
summary: Flight deck observers on approach to Runway 12R at HOU reported an illusion of an aircraft or vehicle caused by new LED taxiway turn-off lights. The reporter attributes this to the terminating lights being visible from the air and recommends shielding or crew awareness until fixed.

synopsis: B757 flight crew experiences a loss of cabin pressurization at FL380 and initiates an emergency descent and return to departure airport.
summary: The flight crew experienced a cabin altitude warning at FL380, prompting an emergency descent and return to the departure airport due to low visibility and an MELed thrust reverser. The aircraft landed safely after the cabin altitude peaked at approximately 12,000 feet without passenger oxygen masks deploying.

synopsis: At the end of an all night turnaround the flight crew of a B757-200 executed a go-around when they received a flap configuration warning at approximately 400 AGL on final. The reporters disagreed as to whether the conduct of the approach was optimum from a CRM/SOP perspective.
summary: During a manual night approach in choppy air, the crew failed to fully select flaps 25, triggering a GPWS configuration warning at 400 feet AGL. The Captain executed a go-around, and the aircraft landed safely on the subsequent approach with the correct flap setting.

synopsis: PA31 First Officer reports being passed on a five mile final to PFYU by another PA31. With the need to back taxi after landing the other pilot is encouraged to enter the pattern and land when the runway is clear. This is accomplished but with little room to spare.
summary: The reporting crew and Aircraft Y were on final approach to Runway 4 at FYU when Aircraft Y passed within 200 feet on the left, entered right traffic, and cut ahead. The reporter attributed the near-miss to Aircraft Y's poor piloting and multiple regulatory violations, including improper passing and traffic pattern deviations.

synopsis: A320 Captain reports being dispatched in an aircraft downgraded to CAT I with weather forecast to be above approach minimums. Enroute the weather goes below minimums and a diversion is requested from Dispatch but denied. After holding with no improvement, Dispatch suggests that the Captain attempt an approach with the weather below applicable minimums. The Captain diverts to his alternate.
summary: The pilot diverted to an alternate after Dispatch pressured them to attempt an RNAV approach despite the aircraft being downgraded to Cat 1 and weather below minimums. The crew later landed safely at the original destination using a Cat 3 autoland, suspecting maintenance parts availability drove the pressure to land.

synopsis: B737 First Officer reported a wake vortex encounter in trail of an A330 on approach to CYVR that resulted in a roll and speed deviation.
summary: The crew encountered severe wake turbulence from an A330 on final approach at CYVR, causing an uncommanded roll and subsequent airspeed deviation that required aggressive throttle correction. Later, heightened stress from the event contributed to a near-wingtip collision with another Airbus while taxiing on a bypass line, which was avoided after a jumpseat observer intervened.

synopsis: B777 Captain reports being awakened during his break on a flight to South America and informed of electrical fumes in the cockpit. No source is discovered and the Captain elects to divert to the nearest suitable airport.
summary: The Pilot in Command, alerted by the Number 1 Flight Attendant, encountered a heavy electrical odor in the cockpit during cruise. The crew donned oxygen masks, completed smoke checklists, declared an emergency to Center, and diverted 320 NM north to a suitable airport for a safe landing.

synopsis: CRJ-200 Captain reports abnormal rudder indications during a flight control check after pushback. Crew returns to the gate at Maintenance Control's direction and an aircraft swap is initiated.
summary: During the After Start checklist following pushback, the flight crew discovered the rudder was off-center and failed to deflect fully right. Mechanics confirmed an actual rudder malfunction rather than a sensor issue, resulting in the aircraft returning to the gate, deplaning, and swapping to a different aircraft.

synopsis: B737 flight crew reports getting low during a visual approach and leveling off at 1,000 AGL to finish configuring. ATC issues a low altitude warning.
summary: The pilot flying selected 1,500 feet in the MCP altitude window during a visual approach to runway 12L at MSP, causing a descent below 1,000 feet AGL. Tower issued a low altitude warning, but the crew leveled off, completed configuration, and executed a normal landing.

synopsis: An MD-11 on an overland international flight suffered the inability to change VHF comm. frequencies on any of their three comm. radios and was on the verge of going NORDO when they left their current FIR. A fingers crossed full VHF power reset was determined to be the only, albeit untested inflight, possible cure for the problem. As they approached the FIR the reset was initiated and proved successful. The flight continued to destination.
summary: During cruise at FL370, the crew experienced a Communications Control Panel failure preventing VHF radio frequency changes. After unsuccessful troubleshooting, the Captain performed an airborne reset of all VHF circuit breakers, restoring normal radio function before entering the next FIR.

synopsis: MD11 Captain experiences loss of communication radio frequency control while at FL370. ATC is advised of the inability to change frequencies and Maintenance Control is contacted. At Maintenance Control's suggestion all VHF circuit breakers are pulled and reset after one minute and all communication radios return to normal operation.
summary: During cruise at FL370, the crew experienced a failure of all VHF radios to tune frequencies, leaving them unable to change channels. After Maintenance Control advised an airborne reset, the Captain cycled the circuit breakers, restoring normal radio function before entering ZZZZ1 airspace.

synopsis: Air carrier flight crew, cleared for a visual approach to Runway 31 at BNA, confused MQY for BNA until advised by ATC.
summary: The Captain and First Officer flew a visual approach to BNA Runway 31 but mistakenly aligned with nearby Smyrna Airport due to a missed approach plate warning. After Tower queried their position, they corrected the error, climbed back to 4,000 feet, and completed a safe ILS approach.

synopsis: A B737-700 crew discovered a fuel imbalance during climbout caused by a fuel crossfeed fault with a circuit breaker tripped so, while completing the QRH, the crew diverted to landed with a 2,600 LBS imbalance as the left main tank was depleting.
summary: During climbout, the flight crew discovered a fuel imbalance caused by a tripped crossfeed valve circuit breaker. Unable to complete the original flight due to insufficient fuel, they diverted to a closer station and landed with a 2,600 LBS imbalance.

synopsis: EMB-170 Captain laments not being informed of potential severe turbulence by his Dispatcher prior to departure as required by the Operations Manual and FAR 121.
summary: The pilot reported that the Aircraft Dispatcher failed to provide available PIREPs regarding severe turbulence between FL220 and FL340, violating 14 CFR 121.601 and company manuals. Although the crew did not encounter the turbulence, the dispatcher's dismissal of the hazard raised safety concerns regarding crew notification procedures.

synopsis: A B737 coffee maker produced a hissing sound while dripping coffee, so the Flight Attendant opened the coffee tray and received second degree burns from exploding coffee grounds. An emergency was declared and the flight diverted for medical attention.
summary: A cabin crew member suffered second-degree burns to her face and chest when hot coffee grounds exploded from a malfunctioning coffee pot during cruise. The aircraft diverted for medical attention after the crew member lifted the handle of the hissing pot, an incident the reporter attributes to a lack of company warnings despite prior FAA advisories.

synopsis: PA18 instructor pilot reports damage to the propeller when his student attempts to correct a swerve, using brakes, after a wheel landing.
summary: A student pilot swerved right during rollout after a wheel landing and inadvertently applied brakes while correcting with rudder, causing the aircraft to nose over and the propeller to contact the ground. The instructor could not stop the student in time, resulting in minor cowl damage but no injuries.

synopsis: SR22 pilot experiences windshear during an ILS approach resulting in a loss of airspeed, descent below the glideslope and possible descent below minimums. ATC issues a low altitude alert and a missed approach is initiated after first leveling off at low altitude with the runway not clearly visible.
summary: The pilot encountered windshear on short final during an ILS approach, causing airspeed loss, altitude deviation, and a low altitude alert. After leveling off and initiating a missed approach, the pilot acknowledged descending below decision altitude and attributed the event to delayed airspeed monitoring.

synopsis: An IFR M20 instructor at 3,000 FT in VMC, experiences a NMAC with opposite direction traffic which had been reported by ATC at 2,900 FT. ATC offers no altitude or heading change to avoid and with the traffic at 12 O'clock and one mile and not in sight, a climb is initiated.
summary: The pilot reported a near-midair collision enroute at 3,000 feet when ATC failed to provide vectors despite repeated traffic alerts. The crew climbed to avoid an opposite-direction aircraft passing 100 feet below, later descending to 2,000 feet after Dover Approach questioned their altitude.

aircraft: Citationjet (C525/C526) - CJ I / II / III / IV
synopsis: CE525 Captain experiences a locked brake after landing and loss of directional control, resulting in a runway excursion at low speed. The right brake pads had been replaced six days prior, but not the left, although post flight revealed extreme wear on the left brake (the locked wheel).
summary: The pilot reported a left main gear tire blowout and rim lock upon landing, causing a loss of directional control and an exit from Runway 08L. Cessna mechanics attributed the incident to aggressive wear on the left brake pads, which caused the wheel to freeze despite recent tire replacements.

synopsis: C170 instructor pilot reports a loss of directional control by his student after landing. Directional control is regained by the instructor, but the student had applied brakes sufficient to cause the propeller to strike the runway.
summary: A student pilot lost directional control after landing, and subsequent braking caused the tail to rise and strike the propeller. The flight instructor regained control, and no injuries or property damage occurred.

synopsis: C172 instructor pilot experiences a rough engine during training and elects to divert to the nearest airport. Arriving overhead at 2,800 FT for a planned engine off landing the engine continues to run throughout and the instructor is able to taxi clear of the runway.
summary: A pilot and student experienced severe engine stumbling and power loss during a training flight, prompting a Pan-Pan call and an urgent landing at ZZZ. Although the aircraft landed safely and the engine ran normally on the ground, a mechanic found no abnormalities, leaving the cause of the in-flight roughness unknown.

synopsis: BE58 pilot experiences autopilot disengagement at low altitude on an ILS approach in IMC. An object falls from the ceiling causing further distraction and a missed approach is initiated with fully deflected needles and 14 degrees off runway heading.
summary: A single pilot practicing an ILS approach in IMC lost autopilot capture and was distracted by a loose vent nozzle falling from the cockpit ceiling. This caused a 14-degree heading deviation at 200 feet AGL, leading to disorientation and a precautionary climb to VFR conditions before a safe second landing.

synopsis: An A321 Flight Attendant reported nasal and throat irritation, headaches, fatigue, restless sleep, anxiety and panic attacks after exposure to toxic fumes of several types in aircraft cabins.
summary: Cabin crew on a through flight experienced toxic fume exposure from freshly treated trash bins, causing respiratory irritation, headaches, and panic attacks. The reporter attributes the incident to insufficient time for pesticide fumes to neutralize before the aircraft was enclosed with occupants.
