summary: A pilot reported that all cabin door slides were found pinned after flight attendants could not read slide bottle pressures. The reporter attributed this to missing maintenance documentation following ferry work at ZZZ1, where safety pins were installed but not properly logged for removal.

aircraft: Bell Helicopter Textron Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) with limited experience on Bell helicopters describes his efforts to re-install a Main Rotor Hub Assembly onto the mast of a BHT-407 rotorcraft.
summary: Three mechanics installing a Main Rotor Head on a Bell-407 during an AAIP inspection encountered binding despite verifying spline alignment. They successfully seated the rotor using ratchet straps and rubber mallets, causing minor tooling damage within limits, though the reporter cited limited experience and pressure as contributing factors.

synopsis: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) recommends his air carrier change their Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMT) to provide relief for technicians to use standard tooling instead of required Spanner Wrench SPL-8240, to remove and install Crew Oxygen (O2) bottles on their B757 aircraft. Spanner wrench was not stocked at their Station.
summary: A mechanic reviewing the B757 AMM after departure noted that the required SPL-8240 wrench for oxygen bottle removal is not stocked at ZZZ. The report recommends updating the manual to allow standard tooling or stocking the specific wrench to resolve this gap.

synopsis: C206 pilot describes a holiday weekend at NYL when the Tower is closed and a diverse mix of aircraft are using all eight runways for takeoffs and landings, in calm winds, using The CTAF to coordinate.
summary: A mapping pilot reported chaotic traffic at uncontrolled Yuma (NYL) during a holiday weekend, involving AV-8Bs, C-130s, a CRJ, and a foreign student pilot. Confusion arose from diverse operations, cross-traffic patterns, and poor radio communication, leading the reporter to recommend keeping the tower open during daytime hours.

aircraft: Medium Transport; High Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: Air Carrier Captain believes that the trees just south of Runway 01 at FLO have grown too tall and are interfering with a normal glide path to the runway.
summary: A pilot reported that during the final quarter-mile of an approach to RWY 01 at FLO Airport, tree tops were very close to the aircraft despite being on PAPI vertical guidance. The pilot attributes this to trees growing into the approach path, reducing vertical clearance and questioning if Part 139 criteria are still met.

synopsis: King Air pilot at 16,000 feet on autopilot experiences a pitch over losing 250 FT before manually recovering. ATC takes notice.
summary: The pilot reported an uncommanded 10-degree pitch down at 16,000 feet, resulting in a 250-foot altitude loss before manual correction. Suspecting a pitch servo failure, the crew continued the flight without the autopilot and will have the aircraft inspected by maintenance.

synopsis: C177 pilot describes a NMAC with a large formation flight flying straight into landing on the active runway without communicating their intentions on the CTAF.
summary: A pilot on an IFR flight transitioning to VFR at a non-towered airport encountered a formation flight that failed to make positional reports while landing. The pilot aborted the initial approach to avoid conflict, extended the downwind to wait for the formation to clear the runway, and landed safely after the formation exited without announcing they were clear.

synopsis: G-IV First Officer reports landing at the wrong airport after a night repositioning flight. After determining that a mistake has been made the aircraft is repositioned to the correct airport. There was no Tower at the first airport and the destination airport Tower was closed.
summary: A Part 135 crew repositioning under Part 91 at night landed at the wrong airport due to fatigue, optical illusions, and similar runway alignment. After realizing the error post-landing, they departed VFR to the correct destination without further incident.

synopsis: The pilot of a BE200 complied with a TCAS RA while conducting an ILS approach to a non-towered airport in IMC.
summary: A pilot conducting an ILS approach in IMC received a TCAS climb resolution advisory with no prior traffic warning, despite Center reporting no traffic. The pilot climbed 500 feet to avoid a VMC aircraft practicing an approach, which only reported its position after the conflict was resolved.

synopsis: An unruly passenger entered a lavatory on approach, apparently lit a cigarette and eventually set off the smoke alarm. The reporter/Flight Attendant's attempts to extricate the passenger were unsuccessful until the Captain made an announcement demanding she return to her seat. She then left the lav, which reeked with what she claimed was a feminine hygiene product, and excoriated the reporter in vulgar terms. The passenger was detained by airport police.
summary: During landing preparation on an Airbus, a flight attendant reported a passenger refused to leave a lavatory triggering a smoke alarm, allegedly due to smoking. The passenger eventually complied after crew intervention, but the reporter believes she violated FAA regulations by smoking and interfering with crew duties.

aircraft: Cessna Aircraft Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Cessna 162 Skycatcher pilot describes the circumstances leading up to a door coming open in flight, causing significant damage to the door.
summary: The pilot of a Cessna Skycatcher reported that the pilot-side gull-wing door opened in flight at 1,800 feet MSL after takeoff bumps likely jarred the latch. The pilot returned safely to the departure airport, attributing the incident to the door's design and difficult-to-see latches.

synopsis: An arriving IFR Air Carrier just exiting IMC suffered a close encounter with a VFR Cessna flying immediately below the cloud cover.
summary: A Boeing crew descending IMC for landing encountered a Cessna VFR aircraft at 3,000 feet while exiting clouds. The near mid-air occurred because the Cessna, which had no transponder or TCAS, was operating just below the cloud base without a TCAS alert.

synopsis: B737 First Officer describes an incident at the gate after landing and taxiing in during blizzard conditions with high winds. After gate arrival with passengers deplaning, and parking brakes set and all wheels chocked, the nose of the aircraft suddenly moves away from the jet bridge as the aircraft weather vanes in a strong gust of wind.
summary: During deplaning in a blizzard, a parked B737 weather-vaned 5-8 feet on an icy ramp, creating a large gap between the aircraft and jet bridge. Flight attendants stopped passengers from falling, and ground crew used de-icing fluid and a tow tractor to reposition the aircraft with no damage reported.

synopsis: Widebody flight crew reports sliding on a slippery taxiway during taxi to parking after landing at CYMX. A taxi light is damaged and the the aircraft is towed to parking.
summary: Pilots taxiing a jet at CYMX in freezing rain lost braking control on untreated Taxiway F, causing the aircraft to slide sideways and strike a taxiway light. The crew stopped the aircraft using reverse thrust, requested a tow, and noted that prior knowledge of available gravel truck treatment might have prevented the incident.

synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew experiences runaway rudder trim shortly after takeoff. Initially the full right rudder trim cannot be removed and an emergency is declared for immediate return. On downwind the trim becomes operable and is centered for landing.
summary: The First Officer flying experienced an abrupt right yaw at 500 feet due to the yaw trim jamming full right. After declaring an emergency and returning, the crew successfully centered the trim and landed normally.

synopsis: The saga of a medical diversion as related by the Dispatcher and First Officer involved. FAR 117 issues are involved.
summary: A dispatcher reported that a flight crew disregarded repeated instructions not to divert to a closed airport due to a medical emergency, causing operational delays and passenger deplaning issues. The dispatcher attributed the incident to the crew's failure to maintain joint authority and a premeditated agenda to bypass operational control.

synopsis: A Dispatcher advised that the commercial service providing flight planning services and/or flight crew tablet generated flight info frequently conflict with one another as to current FDC NOTAMs.
summary: A dispatcher found discrepancies between the Dispatch Monitor and WSI regarding FDC NOTAMs for Columbus and Kansas City, requiring manual updates. The reporter attributed this to failing automation and recommended system repairs or new procedures to ensure complete weather packets.

synopsis: A Captain and First Officer (F/O) report finding significant F.O.D. damage to the Left Engine inlet fan blades during post flight walk-around of an EMB-145 aircraft. One fan blade was bent outward at the tip and several blades had dime size pieces missing and cracks further into the fan blades. Flight was canceled.
summary: The First Officer discovered significant Foreign Object Damage to the left engine fan during a post-flight inspection at ZZZ1, suspecting the cause occurred after landing or during prior maintenance. The flight was cancelled to prevent potential catastrophic engine failure on the next departure, highlighting the critical value of thorough walk-around inspections.

synopsis: A B737-400 Captain flying a practice autoland in IMC saw his airspeed decrease toward stall and added max thrust to recover while the First Officer alerted him to an overspeed condition. The Captain transferred flying to the First Officer when recognized his instrument error.
summary: During an IFR approach in icing conditions, the Captain's airspeed indicator erroneously indicated a stall while the First Officer's showed overspeed, likely due to a frozen pitot tube. The crew disengaged automation, transferred control to the First Officer, and executed a go-around before landing uneventfully.

synopsis: CRJ-700 Captain reports skidding on an icy taxiway after landing, requiring engine shutdown, and a tow to the gate.
summary: The flight crew landed and taxied to Taxiway C, where they encountered nil braking action despite prior reports of fair conditions. Unable to stop with brakes or idle thrust, they shut down engines, applied sand, and were towed to the gate after the airport closed for de-icing.

synopsis: B777 First Officer reports discovering an improperly packed dangerous goods pallet during preflight. Three reinsertions are required before the pallet is acceptable for flight.
summary: A ground hazmat inspector found a dangerous goods pallet loaded with unsecured liquids and corrosives during a pre-flight inspection. The reporter attributed the issue to poor loading practices and a lack of proper securing tools, requiring four total inspections before the pallet was deemed suitable.

synopsis: A CRJ First Officer doing a post flight inspection noted cargo labeled to contain dry ice being removed from the cargo pit. No hazmat notification had been provided to the flight crew prior to their just concluded leg.
summary: The First Officer discovered three boxes containing 2.3 kilograms of dry ice during offloading, despite the cargo load report and Captain having no record of the hazardous material. The crew subsequently verified the 27-pound package in the cargo area, confirming the dry ice was loaded without proper documentation or notification.

synopsis: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports a circuit breaker (C/B) for the left #1 fuel tank, inner fuel boost pump continued to pop, even with the cannon plug to the fuel pump disconnected on an A300 aircraft. Burned wires in a wire harness to the boost pump C/B were found at a tie-wrap installation in the avionics compartment.
summary: Aircraft Line Mechanics investigated a popped Circuit Breaker for the Left Inner Tank #1 fuel pump on a grounded aircraft, suspecting wire fatigue or tight bundling caused the fault. The aircraft was not dispatched, and freight was moved using a layover aircraft while the team reviewed maintenance manuals to prevent recurrence.

synopsis: CL-600 Captain reports flying two legs with a main gear tire perceived as slightly low on pressure, which was also pointed out by ground crewmen. The pressure is checked after the last leg and is found to be 30 PSI instead of the 166 PSI required.
summary: Pilots operated two flights with a tire suspected of low pressure, delaying maintenance to meet Part 117 schedule requirements. Post-flight inspection revealed the tire at 30 PSI, well below the 166 PSI standard, rendering the aircraft unairworthy due to a slow leak missed during preflight checks.

synopsis: GGG Departure Controller reports a Radar outage caused by maintenance. A request is received from an airborne BE36 to pick up an IFR clearance, which cannot be issued due to the outage. A few minutes later the BE36 pilot states that he must have the clearance because he is now in IMC. A few more minutes and the Radar becomes operational and the clearance is issued.
summary: An air traffic controller lost primary and secondary radar when maintenance transferred panel control to the radar site, disabling the sole functioning channel. The controller could not issue an IFR clearance or vector a BE36 that entered clouds, providing only general obstruction avoidance until radar was restored.

synopsis: A B737-700 Wi-Fi system created a continuous static in COMM 1 so it was turned OFF which stopped the interference. In flight an automated ACARS advised the crew to turn the Wi-Fi ON which the crew refused to do because inflight troubleshooting was not acceptable.
summary: The flight crew experienced COMM 1 static during taxi caused by the Wi-Fi system, which was MEL'd inoperative under 25-10-1. Although an ACARS message later requested in-flight troubleshooting, the crew refused to work the open MEL and completed the trip with the Wi-Fi off.

synopsis: B737 Captain experiences a breakaway during pushback, but the ground crew does not convey that information in a succinct or timely manor. Time is not a factor however and the aircraft is stopped without damage.
summary: During pushback, the tow bar disconnected from the tug while the aircraft made an unexpected 90-degree turn. The pilot stopped the aircraft immediately; maintenance inspected the nose gear, found no damage, and the flight continued after reattachment.

aircraft: McDonnell Douglas Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: DC-6 flight crew reports discovering a fuel leak on the number 2 nacelle after landing at a remote airport. The aircraft is grounded until Maintenance can be summoned for repairs.
summary: The Captain discovered a fuel leak in the number two engine nacelle during a post-flight walk-around after landing. Mechanics determined the aircraft was not airworthy, requiring the crew to return to base on a passenger aircraft.

synopsis: A320 Captain experiences airframe buffet during approach in severe icing conditions. Believing tail icing is the cause airspeed is increased and a normal landing ensues.
summary: The Captain hand-flew an Airbus approach into Denver in unforecast severe icing, experiencing a tail-stall buffet on short final at 800 feet AGL. The pilot recovered by increasing speed and pitching the nose up, attributing the event to unprotected tail ice accretion despite manufacturer claims.

synopsis: Two Line Aircraft Maintenance Technicians (AMTs) report about an air turn back of a company B737-700 aircraft due to the Landing Gear Handle would not move to the 'Up' position after takeoff. A previously missing mount bolt for the forward glareshield was found in the handle mechanism preventing movement of the lever.
summary: Two Aircraft Maintenance Technicians performed a Right-1 windshield replacement and noted a missing glareshield mount bolt, which they replaced without locating the original. The aircraft later returned because the landing gear would not retract, as the missing bolt had fallen into the gear handle mechanism.

synopsis: A Progressive Aerodyne Searey pilot forgot to raise the landing gear before doing a river skip and go so that when he touched down the aircraft pitched over and filled with water.
summary: The pilot conducted a water landing in a Rotax 912 ULS aircraft after engine checks but failed to retract the gear due to distraction by river obstacles. The aircraft submarined upon touchdown, causing damage that the pilot attributed to not using the checklist or having gear position lights.

synopsis: G-IV Captain describes autopilot, auto thrust, and FMS malfunctions resulting in airspeed and altitude deviations while attempting to enter holding at 8,000 feet.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced a flight guidance failure while holding at JIIMS at 8,000 feet after a last-minute clearance change. The aircraft pitched up to 30 degrees and banked left due to unresponsive autopilot and trim controls, requiring manual pitch trim to recover from an altitude deviation to 8,800 feet.

synopsis: B737 First Officer describes the events leading up to a cabin altitude warning horn on climbout and the subsequent return to the departure airport.
summary: The First Officer, acting as Pilot Flying, failed to complete the after-takeoff checklist and inadvertently left bleed switches off, causing a pressurization failure and cabin smoke. The crew declared an emergency, descended to 10,000 feet, and landed safely, attributing the event to task saturation and poor checklist discipline.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: Two aircraft near FFU had a near miss at 7,500 FT after Salt Lake Approach Control pointed out their mutual traffic and issued suggest headings but still neither aircraft saw the other until the last second.
summary: During an instrument training flight at 7,500 feet, the pilot received conflicting ATC traffic advisories while holding near FFU VOR. A Traffic Alert System warning and visual contact revealed a near-collision with an opposing aircraft at the same altitude, which the pilot attributed to the other pilot's last-second evasive turn.

synopsis: C172 pilot experiences a NMAC with a PA44 during the turn to final in the traffic pattern. The PA44 was straight in on the ILS and did not make position reports that were heard. A very busy pattern along with garbled transmissions due to the CTAF being shared with a nearby airport were factors.
summary: A Cessna 172 pilot on final approach at a busy uncontrolled airport encountered a Piper Seminole conducting an ILS practice approach less than 200 feet above and to the right. The near-miss resulted from the Seminole's lack of radio calls, failure to yield right-of-way under FAR 91.113(g), and heavy radio congestion on the shared CTAF frequency.

synopsis: FAT Departure Controller describes a missed communication with a departing Air Carrier which the controller believes may be caused by a local policy that does not issue the frequency with the clearance to switch to Departure.
summary: A Departure Controller in the Fresno TRACON instructed a Small Aircraft to turn left, but an Air Carrier pilot mistakenly followed the instruction while on the wrong frequency. The Air Carrier failed to climb as directed and struck terrain at 2,900 feet, an outcome the controller attributed to the local airport's failure to issue the departure frequency.

synopsis: An A319 on the DFW BYP6 Arrival at 11,000 FT in Class B took evasive action following a TCAS RA DESCEND from a single engine aircraft at 11,500 FT outside of Class B and during the descent came with 700 FT of an another Air Carrier below him also in Class B.
summary: An A319 pilot reported a TCAS RA during arrival at 11,000 feet caused by a C182 operating 500 feet above the arrival path outside Class Bravo airspace. The pilot descended to 10,700 feet to comply with the RA, acknowledged traffic from an MD-80 below, and climbed back to 11,000 feet before landing safely.

synopsis: A ZNY Controller and one of the plots involved describe a three way TCAS event that may have resulted in collisions without TCAS intervention.
summary: Two separate incidents involved conflicting arrivals and departures on shared airways near ISP and JFK, where controllers failed to resolve altitude conflicts, forcing three aircraft to execute TCAS resolutions to avoid collision. A second event saw a crew receive an ambiguous descent clearance, leading to confusion and a TCAS climb resolution before proceeding safely.

synopsis: B737-300 flight crew experiences an aft cargo door warning at 80 KTS during takeoff with the First Officer flying. When the Captain says nothing, the First Officer announces the warning and the Captain rejects. Maintenance found a strap hanging out of the door.
summary: The First Officer called out an aft cargo door Master Caution near 80 knots, prompting the Captain to reject the takeoff at 100 knots. A loose strap was later found on the door, and the crew concluded the rejection was unnecessary but emphasized the need for clear verbalized intentions during takeoff.

synopsis: B737 Captain reports having to stop abruptly approaching the gate to avoid a tug pulling carts that suddenly cuts in front of the aircraft.
summary: The flight crew aborted taxiing into the gate Safety Zone when a tug towing baggage carts crossed rapidly five to ten feet in front of the aircraft nose. The pilot reported the safety violation and near accident to a supervisor, who agreed to investigate the incident.

synopsis: An air carrier Captain addressed the dilatory effects of flight schedules which require an extreme early AM departure, a minimum midday layover and a second duty period of back side of the clock flying, thus combining the two most mentally and physically debilitating types of flying into a single 24 hour period which contains no rest possibility during a normal sleep cycle.
summary: A pilot reported unsafe narrow-body scheduling practices involving early morning reports, short layovers, and late-night returns that disrupt circadian rhythms. The reporter stated these FAR 117-compliant pairings cause extreme fatigue and increase the risk of major accidents due to pilot exhaustion.

synopsis: Ramp employee reports witnessing a fuel truck back into the number two engine of the EMB170 he is sitting in.
summary: A ground employee on an Embraer 170 witnessed a fuel truck impact the belt loader and right engine cowling while the employee was in the front pit. The truck operator appeared to struggle with controls before moving the vehicle away, prompting police investigation and leaving the witness with physical symptoms and distress.

synopsis: ATR42 flight crew describes a LOC BC approach in icing conditions and turbulence, using an approach speed close to flap limit speed. The flying First Officer becomes confused, identifying stepdown fixes with GPS DME instead of LOC DME. At the MAP a missed approach is initiated but the go around button is not pushed and the aircraft remains in level flight until the trim switch is used, disconnecting the autopilot. The gear remains down and flap overspeeds occur. The flight diverts to an alternate airport.
summary: During a non-precision localizer approach in icing conditions, the crew missed step-down fixes and failed to disengage the autopilot during a missed approach, causing a delayed climb. This resulted in a flaps overspeed warning when the First Officer retracted the gear, prompting an immediate flap retraction and diversion.

synopsis: MD80 Captain experiences a Fuel Low Level light at FL290 with the fuel gauges indicating about 8,000 pounds. An emergency is declared and, being close to top of descent, the flight continues to destination.
summary: The flight crew experienced a FUEL LEVEL LOW light at FL290 and trim difficulties, likely due to fuel imbalance, prompting an emergency declaration and landing at the original destination. The crew noted the QRH circuit breaker location was unclear, though the landing was incident-free and both issues were logged.

synopsis: During descent from FL370 to FL350 at 1,300 FPM and a 15 degree AOB, the Captain notes the speed trend vector move into the overspeed area and assumes control of the aircraft to reduce airspeed.
summary: During a descent from FL370 to FL360, the First Officer selected 1300 FPM vertical speed, causing the speed trend to approach maximum operating speed during an ATC-mandated turn. The Captain disengaged the autopilot to level the aircraft, resulting in brief high-speed buffet and a Stick Shaker symbol, though no airspeed exceedance or maintenance action was required.

synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reports being issued a 160 degree heading as they are intercepting the Runway 24R localizer at LAX and complies. This is not what ATC intended and the crew is excoriated for crossing the south complex before being vectored back for another approach.
summary: Pilots flying a SADDIE6 arrival in IMC received a conflicting left turn to heading 160 degrees from one controller while intercepting the 24R localizer, causing a conflict with traffic on 25L. A second controller reacted aggressively, suspecting a read-back error, and issued climb and vector clearances to resolve the situation without incident.

synopsis: B757 flight attendants experience jumpseat failure at door 4L during takeoff. The failure was alleged to be caused by missing bolts. The 4R jumpseats exhibited the same anomaly.
summary: Flight attendants reported that the 4L jumpseat broke during takeoff due to a stress fracture caused by the seat not being bolted to the bulkhead. Consequently, the crew occupied passenger seats for landing after discovering the 4R jumpseat was also unsecured.

synopsis: PA31 Captain reports being unable to comply with an ATC heading instruction due to a thunderstorm and is instructed to declare an emergency, which is accomplished.
summary: The pilot, enroute in IMC through frontal storms, declared an emergency after MIA Center issued a left turn instruction into a thunderstorm cell. Unable to comply due to severe weather, the pilot selected transponder code 7700 once speed stabilized, then cancelled the emergency after clearing the storms.

synopsis: DAL Controller reports difficulties with traffic watch aircraft conflicting with arrivals.
summary: An air traffic controller managing a Cessna 172 on the LUNA transition encountered separation issues with descending Falcon and B737 arrivals, inadvertently violating DFW Tower airspace while directing the Cessna. The controller attributed the incident to outdated LOA protections and removed altitude restrictions, recommending revised procedures to eliminate reliance on visual separation.

synopsis: ZAB Controller describes a conflict between a VFR BE20 departing El Paso eastbound and a CRJ arriving from the east. The BE20 was receiving flight following from El Paso Departure but was canceled before being switched to ZAB, wasting precious seconds.
summary: An air traffic controller in Sector 19 reported a loss of separation between a descending CRJ and a climbing VFR BE20 after El Paso Approach terminated the BE20's flight following without transferring data. The aircraft passed within 0.25 miles at the same altitude, which the controller attributed to poor coordination and delayed information transfer.

synopsis: B737 flight crew experiences asymmetric flaps during approach. QRH procedures are complied with resulting in full leading flaps and trailing edge flaps up approach at 183 KTS. A go-around is issued by ATC due to an aircraft on the runway but the second approach is successful.
summary: During approach, the crew encountered an asymmetrical trailing edge flap failure and executed a flaps-up landing with alternate leading edge deployment. After a go-around due to poor braking ahead, the aircraft bounced on touchdown from dramatic nose-up pitch upon spoiler deployment but landed safely and taxied to the gate.

synopsis: Three ramp personnel describe a wingtip collision with a bag cart during marshalling.
summary: A marshall and wing walker guided an aircraft to the gate when the wingtip struck a baggage cart at the operational safety zone edge. The marshall attributed the collision to rushing the arrival, failing to perform a pre-arrival FOD walk, and limited visibility due to a hood worn in cold, windy conditions.

synopsis: When the two Captains of a Falcon failed to note the 720 MSL crossing restriction at WEBAC while conducting the RNAV (GPS) Runway 8 approach to 3R7 they descended too quickly and triggered an EGPWS warning. The performed a MAP and diverted to their alternate airport.
summary: Pilots flying an RNAV (GPS) Runway 8 approach at 3R7 received a GPWS obstacle warning at 600 FT after descending below the 720 FT WEBAC crossing restriction using a "dive and drive" technique. They executed a missed approach and diverted to an alternate due to weather and the altitude deviation.

synopsis: B757 First Officer reports engine anti-ice valve failure to open during climb. With a long flight ahead and icing conditions in the forecast, the crew elects to return to the departure airport for an overweight landing.
summary: During climbout, the flight crew encountered a left engine anti-ice valve failure requiring an emergency return and overweight landing. The aircraft landed smoothly with flaps 25 using reverse thrust only, and post-landing inspections confirmed the brakes were cold before normal taxi to the gate.

synopsis: When a B777-200 flight crew, arriving SBGR via the ANSUG 1A STAR, Runway 09R ILS, turned inside the charted track between westbound at MARPU (an IAF) on the STAR and eastbound at UTKET (a straight in IF on the approach) ATC directed a go-around. A mysterious fix CI09R inside of UTKET and prior to the LOM played a role. The aircraft's database also failed to utilize the published 8,000 MSL transition altitude.
summary: The B777 crew encountered FMS navigation and altitude conflicts during an ILS approach to SBGR while receiving ATC vectors. The FMS displayed non-charted fixes and incorrectly requested FL070 instead of 7,000 feet due to database discrepancies with approach plates.

synopsis: MD11 Captain reports a taxiway incursion at LFPG due to a First Officer that claimed to know the route and using the north side taxi chart which does not show Taxiway B turning south to connect to E.
summary: The Captain, First Officer, and Relief First Officer deviated from taxi clearance at LFPG due to truncated charts and the First Officer's incorrect assumption to turn onto taxiway F. The Captain stopped the aircraft to verify with Ground Control, attributing the error to the First Officer's arrogance and his own failure to assert authority.

synopsis: An Aeronca pilot in the pattern at a non-towered airport suffered an NMAC with a Cessna apparently crossing over the airport at cruise. The reporter heard no associated CTAF reports.
summary: A pilot on downwind at 1,300 feet for Runway 16 reported a Cessna crossing 50–100 feet above and 300 feet ahead at approximately 150 knots. The intruder, which did not transmit on UNICOM, appeared unaware of the proximity and took no evasive action.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: SCT TRACON Controller reported a Developmental Controller issued descent to an aircraft too early, which caused aircraft to violate the MVA rule.
summary: An IFR arrival to UDD clipped the 6,500 ft MVA at 6,200 ft after the controller issued a descent to 6,000 ft while the pilot was experiencing turbulence. The reporter attributed the incident to the controller issuing the clearance too early and advised delaying descents in adverse conditions to ensure MVA compliance.

aircraft: Cessna Citation Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: ZMA Center Controller descended aircraft in too close proximity of another aircraft due to the fact that he thought he would have lateral separation. Sector was busy and Controller did not have time to re-check the separation.
summary: An air traffic controller issued a descent clearance to an air carrier from FL370 through a business jet at FL360 during a congested, combined sector operation. The controller missed the conflict due to excessive workload, manual coordination demands, and failure to use separation tools like the polygon/Halo.

aircraft: Challenger Jet Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Challenger aircraft had a TCAS RA in IMC, after Tower Controller allowed a VFR helicopter into the Class D airspace.
summary: The Local Controller misheard a helicopter's VFR request as SVFR and issued an incorrect clearance while missing the ATIS code. This led to a near-midair conflict with a Challenger, triggering a Resolution Advisory, though both aircraft maintained visual contact and the Challenger landed safely.

synopsis: SBN Approach Controller reports many pilots becoming confused during the FISSK 2 RNAV arrival into MDW and descending before being cleared to do so. A descend via clearance is never issued for this arrival due to the LOA with Chicago Approach and the reporter believes the altitude restrictions at HILLS and SAILZ should be changed to expect altitudes.
summary: South Bend Approach controllers reported that single-air carrier pilots on the FISSK 2 arrival into MDW descended early or questioned clearance due to confusion over transition altitude restrictions. The controller attributed this to conflicting chart notes and recommended removing crossing restrictions and improving pilot training.

synopsis: B757 flight crew experienced TE and LE Flap Disagree caution lights on final approach and elected to continue to land without further incident.
summary: During a visual approach, the crew selected Flaps 30 below 168 knots, but speed increased, causing the First Officer to retract to Flaps 25, which triggered TE/LE disagree lights and locked flaps at position 20. The crew elected to land with Flaps 20, confirming airspeed, and executed a stabilized landing on the centerline.

synopsis: B757 experienced Flap Disagree EICAS message on approach and elected to go-around to accomplish QRH procedures. Extra speed on second approach led to another go-around in gusty wind conditions and Minimum Fuel was declared. Third approach and landing was successful.
summary: The Relief Pilot and Captain encountered a Flap Disagree EICAS message during an ILS approach, prompting a go-around to complete QRH procedures. Subsequent approaches were complicated by windshear and gusty winds, requiring two additional go-arounds before a safe landing with flaps 20 was achieved.

synopsis: B737 flight crew reports a loud banging noise and electrical fumes as ground power is connected to the aircraft at the gate. Ground power is quickly disconnected and the aircraft is taken out of service for maintenance.
summary: Pilots and ramp personnel experienced a loud bang and burnt smell when external power was connected at the gate. Smoke entered the flight deck, prompting a maintenance inspection that found no fire, resulting in the aircraft being removed from service.

synopsis: When the right engine oil quantity continually decreased to only 25% the flight crew of a B737 elected to declare and emergency and divert to a nearby airport.
summary: The flight crew enroute at FL360 diverted after Engine 2 oil quantity dropped from 72% to 25%, prompting an emergency declaration. They landed safely without shutting down the engine, noting no specific checklist existed for low oil quantity, only low pressure.

synopsis: B757/767 Captain laments the complexity of the QRH due to the variety of aircraft covered after the merger and the opportunity for error in an emergency situation.
summary: A pilot reported that the current Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) for B757 and B767 fleets is dangerous because it combines procedures for different subtypes into one document. The reporter argues this causes confusion and undesired aircraft states during emergencies, recommending separate QRHs for each specific aircraft subtype to improve safety.

synopsis: Not withstanding the Marshaller's still crossed wands directing no movement the flight crew of an E-135 initiated taxi away from the ramp.
summary: A Wing Walker reported that after disconnecting the tow bar, the aircraft applied power and turned while his wands were still crossed. The movement occurred despite the crew waiting for the push tractor and other Wing Walker to clear the area.

synopsis: A reporter advised the commercially provided IAP chart for the LOC 27 at SAN does not include the restriction against use of the Straight-in and Circling minima at night when the VGSI (PAPI) is out of service which is published on the government produced chart.
summary: A pilot reported a safety discrepancy between company and FAA instrument approach procedures for SAN LOC27, noting the commercial version omits a restriction prohibiting night approaches when VGSI is inoperative. This omission risks pilots attempting the approach without visual glide slope aids, exposing them to unlit obstacles in the visual segment.

synopsis: An Air Carrier pilot reported aircraft in Height Group IV (B757 and larger) with a cockpit to nose wheel height 22' or greater are prohibited from landing on PDX Runway 21 because the VGSI angle and runway end location are not compliant with FAA Flight Standards guidelines for aircraft in Group IV.
summary: A pilot reported that FAA/NGA guidance restricts Height Group IV aircraft from using PDX Runway 21 due to non-compliant VGSI settings, yet this safety restriction is absent from commercial charts and GPS databases. This omission risks crews attempting an illegal approach, prompting recommendations to annotate the Instrument Approach Procedure and remove the procedure from applicable aircraft databases.

synopsis: Air taxi pilot experiences low engine power which results in landing on a frozen lake. After landing the wheels break through the surface ice and come to rest on a second layer of ice. With the engine still running the reporter is able to taxi to the shore and call for assistance.
summary: A pilot flying an empty aircraft en route experienced engine roughness below 3,000 feet, forcing an emergency landing on a frozen lake. Post-landing, the engine repeatedly bogged out under full power while taxiing through snow to shore, though the pilot eventually secured the aircraft and initiated search and rescue.

synopsis: A First Officer and a Captain describe their efforts and frustration with Maintenance Control, Local Station Maintenance and Operations to resolve an illuminated REVERSER light that appeared during an ETOPS PDC (Pre-Departure Check) on a B737-800 aircraft. First Officer noted it would be helpful if the MEL stated what non-normal lights are acceptable or not acceptable on the P5 Aft Overhead ENG panel, for an MEL 78-1B Reverser deferral.
summary: Flight crew and maintenance personnel experienced a four-hour departure delay on a B737-800 ETOPS flight due to confusion over an illuminated REVERSER light on the P5 panel. The delay resulted from unclear MEL guidance regarding acceptable engine panel lights and miscommunication between maintenance control, local mechanics, and the flight crew regarding the discrepancy.

synopsis: CRJ200 flight crew track deviation due to interpreting 'on course' to a VOR differently than Controller who believed it to mean the same thing as 'direct' to the VOR.
summary: The pilot and First Officer intercepted the "on course" route to CTF after Departure Control cleared them to 10,000 feet. A misunderstanding occurred when the controller questioned their heading, turned them 90 degrees, and issued a conflicting "direct" clearance, failing to recognize the distinction between the two terms.

synopsis: A CRJ-200 received delaying vectors enroute to allow faster aircraft into the destination airport and so the crew declared an emergency with Approach Control because at 1,500 LBS any further delay could be disastrous.
summary: The flight crew declared an emergency due to low fuel after ATC vectors and slow speeds caused fuel to drop to 1,500 LBS on final approach. They landed safely with 1,400 LBS remaining, citing concerns that company fuel policies and potential flap failures left insufficient time to complete emergency checklists.

synopsis: The flight crew of an MD-83 rejected their takeoff at 90 knots due to a CAWS stabilizer warning.
summary: The crew rejected takeoff at 90 knots due to a stabilizer CAWS warning and exited to Taxiway Bravo. Maintenance determined a high-speed abort required a gate return, noting the same warning occurred three days prior at 120 knots when the takeoff was continued.

synopsis: B747 Captain experiences a TCAS RA at FL280 with the flying First Officer taking evasive action. A nearly head on B727 is seen to pass 500 feet below and 200 feet to the left.
summary: The crew experienced a Resolution Advisory at FL280 while en route on V717 between DAXUP and ENRON due to an oncoming B727. They climbed to 28,500 feet, allowing the B727 to pass within 500 feet vertically and 200 feet horizontally before returning to FL280 and notifying both Kabul and Turkmenabad control.

synopsis: An MD-11 Captain addressed concerns about a casual attitude on the part of Dangerous Goods handlers with respect to damaged packaging who were instructed to board possibly compromised packaging and remove it only if the flight crew refused it.
summary: Flight crew discovered damaged dangerous goods boxes and conflicting paperwork during pre-flight inspection. The reporter attributed these issues to a lack of standardized training and clear expectations for ramp agents regarding damage assessment and documentation accuracy.

synopsis: EMB145 Captain reports a thumping noise coming from the nose gear during climb. The Captain elects to return to the departure airport for an uneventful landing. The aircraft had been written up the day prior for the same problem and a repair was accomplished.
summary: During climb at 5,000 feet, the Captain and First Officer heard loud bangs and vibrations, prompting an emergency return and low approach. Maintenance attributed the noise to faulty nose gear proximity switches, which had been replaced the previous day but reportedly failed again.

synopsis: Confusion reigned when ATC cleared an E-170 flight crew direct to ALDAN, a fix on both their filed South Boston STAR into RDU and the 'ALDAN' STAR--which includes several common fixes. At no time were they cleared 'via' either STAR. The flight was eventually vectored for an approach and the confusion never satisfactorily resolved.
summary: Pilots flying the South Boston Four Arrival into RDU received a vector from Approach Control intended for the ALDAN ONE Arrival due to a misunderstanding about which procedure was active. The crew maintained their filed South Boston Four flight plan and landed safely, noting a need for clearer ATC-pilot communication regarding arrival selection.

synopsis: A B737-800 flight crew performed an in-flight shutdown of the left engine following receipt of a low quantity warning, rising oil temperature and lowering oil pressure. They consulted with Dispatch and opted to divert to the nearest suitable airport where they landed without incident.
summary: The crew detected low left engine oil quantity, rising temperature, and falling pressure during flight. They executed a precautionary engine shutdown procedure and landed safely at the nearest suitable airport.

synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported a flap overspeed as a result of a wake vortex encounter.
summary: The pilot selected flaps to 10 at 195 KTS but encountered wake turbulence, causing speed to increase to 212 KTS and deploy speedbrakes. Maintenance inspected the aircraft after the incident was logged, and the flight departed.

synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew experiences lost communications while on vectors to the ILS 12 at BZN in night VMC. The Captain elects to turn inbound to the airport to avoid terrain and contact Tower. Tower advises to try a different frequency which is successful.
summary: The crew lost radio contact with Big Sky Approach on 119.55 while being vectored for an ILS 12 approach at BZN in visual conditions. The Captain used emergency authority to turn base to avoid high terrain, contacted Tower, and switched to frequency 118.97 to complete the approach safely.

synopsis: When the B737 boarding door was repeatedly driven from the jetway during passenger deplaning by weathervaning winds on a slippery ramp the flight crew improvised an anchoring method including leaving a tug attached to the nose gear and spraying the nose gear and surrounding ramp with deicing fluid to enhance the coefficient of friction. Following these efforts the passengers were successfully deplaned.
summary: After parking with triple chocks and set brakes, a gust of wind weather-vaned the aircraft, moving the deplaning door away from the jetway. Attaching a tug to the nose gear and spraying it with de-icing fluid anchored the aircraft, allowing passengers to disembark safely.

synopsis: A321 flight crew reports an EGPWS terrain warning approaching WASON on a visual ILS to TUS and takes evasive action. The FCU altitude had been correctly set to 5,500 FT but the EGPWS software was not aware of the planned level off and triggered the warning.
summary: The Captain and First Officer received a GPWS terrain warning while descending toward 5,500 feet on a visual approach to Tucson Runway 11L, triggered by a predictive projection over a 4,565-foot obstacle near WASON. The crew executed a TOGA climb but continued the approach, attributing the event to tight terrain clearances and noting the Captain's fatigue from a potentially non-compliant 14-hour duty day.

synopsis: CE560 flight crew detects jammed elevator trim during climbout. After checklist procedures are unsuccessful an emergency is declared and the flight returns to the departure airport. The Captain states that 'This has been an ongoing issue with this model aircraft'.
summary: During climbout to FL210, the pilot flying encountered a jammed electric elevator trim that prevented nose-down trimming on a new aircraft model. The crew declared an emergency, returned to the departure airport, and completed an uneventful landing after control forces decreased with lower speed and configuration.

synopsis: DC10 First Officer discovers the number two thrust lever is stuck at 92% N1 when starting descent. The descent is continued to 10,000 FT where the engine is shut down and the Captain takes the controls for landing. A windshear alert at 800 FT results in a go-around with a second approach to a different runway being successful.
summary: During descent, the crew encountered a stuck throttle on Engine 2 at 92% power and descended with Engines 1 and 3 at idle. They executed a missed approach at 700-800 feet due to windshear and landed uneventfully on a different runway after completing the Engine Shutdown Checklist.

synopsis: A hearback\readback breakdown in communication between a B777 flight crew and ATC resulted in a temporary track deviation in the Middle East.
summary: The crew received a clearance direct to GADSI, but the controller later corrected it to TASMI due to a misunderstanding and language issues. The controller vectored the aircraft to intercept the correct course, resulting in no further action or unusual events.

synopsis: EMB145 Flight Attendant reports that a passenger had in his posession at least 14 mini (50 ML) bottles of alcoholic beverages and consumed most of them. The Flight Attendant questions whether these were brought through security.
summary: A flight attendant reported a passenger consuming alcohol during boarding and the flight, hiding bottles under his seat and lying about their location. The passenger became belligerent and unable to walk safely, prompting the crew to request security assistance upon arrival, where the manager took custody of him.

synopsis: An Aircraft Avionics Technician reports finding six relay bases installed incorrectly, contacting structure and adjacent relays inside the Left P-110 Power Panel located in the lower Main Equipment Center (MEC) on a B777-200 aircraft.
summary: A mechanic discovered six incorrectly installed relay bases in the P-110 Power Panel while installing new wiring. This improper installation caused four relays to contact the panel structure or adjacent relays.

synopsis: DA20 instrument flight instructor reports an altitude deviation by his student on vectors for an ILS, which is detected by ATC. After a stop and go, the Tower clears the training flight back to home base as filed (direct). This upsets the original Approach Controller who had been expecting the published missed approach initially.
summary: An instructor and student descended below the assigned 3,000 feet while setting up an ILS approach at night. After a stop-and-go, the pilot was criticized by Center for not flying the published missed approach, despite Tower clearing them direct to their home airport.

synopsis: A BE200 flight crew on a ferry flight landed in heavy snow at their destination and encountered a C182 slow taxiing down the runway in search of an exit. Emergency braking by the First Officer prevented a collision. The C182 had landed ahead of the reporter's aircraft at the uncontrolled airport and, although the pilot claimed he had been making CTAF reports, noone aboard the reporter's aircraft nor the airport CTAF operator heard the claimed transmissions.
summary: An IFR flight crew executing an ILS approach in heavy snow spotted a Cessna 182 taxiing on the active runway without clearance. The Cessna pilot, operating VFR on the wrong frequency despite deteriorating weather, was unaware of the approaching aircraft, forcing the crew to apply maximum braking to avoid a collision.

synopsis: A321 Captain describes a trip paring assignment that does not meet the new FAR 117 rules and the lack of any guidance from the Chief Pilot's Office.
summary: Scheduling assigned a pilot and crew an illegal trip pairing that exceeded FAR 117 duty limits, resulting in 13 hours 44 minutes of duty. Fatigue from this unsafe assignment caused a GPWS warning and escape maneuver during the final approach, which the reporter attributes to crew exhaustion and management pressure.

synopsis: GA pilot reports becoming confused approaching his destination with intentions to land on Runway 16 but instead entering the downwind and landing on Runway 34. The error is not discovered until after the ensuing takeoff.
summary: A pilot on a pleasure flight landed on Runway 34 instead of the intended Runway 16 at ZZZ due to holding an airport diagram upside down and misinterpreting the heading. The pilot departed the wrong runway without collision, realizing the error only after leveling off.

synopsis: A36 pilot experiences engine failure approaching the destination airport and elects to land in a farm field. The left wing fuel bladder was wadded up and off the bottom of the wing and in use at the time. The right tank contained sufficient fuel and was selected but the engine did not restart.
summary: The pilot experienced a complete engine failure during the approach phase after canceling an IFR flight plan, likely caused by fuel starvation from a faulty left fuel gauge and a bad fuel cap O-ring. The pilot successfully executed an off-airport landing in a farm field with no injuries or aircraft damage, though mechanics later found the left fuel cell bladder displaced.

synopsis: PA32 pilot reports planning three night takeoffs and landing for currency. On the second landing the landing gear is forgotten and a gear up landing ensues.
summary: The pilot of a Piper Saratoga performed night touch-and-go maneuvers and attempted a second full stop landing. The pilot forgot to lower the landing gear before touchdown, resulting in a gear-up landing.

synopsis: A taxiing C177 pilot misjudged his aircraft's wing tip clearance from a parked PA20 and allowed his upper wing tip to override a PA20's lower wing tip before coming to a stop and separating the aircraft with only superficial damage.
summary: The pilot reported a ground collision while taxiing at 5 MPH, where the aircraft's left wingtip struck and lifted the wing of a parked aircraft. The incident caused minor fabric damage to the parked aircraft but no structural damage to the reporting aircraft, attributed to the pilot misjudging clearance based on preceding traffic.

synopsis: Controller questioned pilot about destination after he saw the aircraft tracking north of anticipated track and discovered two flight plans on file.
summary: An air traffic controller discovered an aircraft was 40 miles off route due to a flight plan destination error showing ZZZ2 instead of the cleared ZZZ1. The controller corrected the route and destination after the aircraft traveled 850 miles, noting the error created a potential terrain conflict due to a 1,000-foot MEA difference.

synopsis: A B737 flight crew and a pass riding pilot report canceling a takeoff clearance and returning for deicing when the pass riding pilot informs a Flight Attendant of frost on the wings.
summary: A deadheading pilot passenger discovered frost on the wings during taxi and alerted the flight attendant, who informed the flight deck. The crew aborted the takeoff, returned to the ramp for deicing, and departed safely with a clean wing.

synopsis: B737 Captain experienced loss of directional control as the TOGA buttons are pushed during a rolling takeoff. The takeoff is quickly rejected when control cannot be regained with the tiller or rudder input.
summary: The pilot rejected a takeoff after the aircraft instantly veered right upon pressing TO/GA buttons at 40% N1, resulting in a loss of directional control despite full left tiller input. The aircraft stopped near the runway edge with no damage, and the crew returned to the gate, attributing the event to premature TO/GA selection.

synopsis: B737 First Officer laments the extremely bright LED lights being installed in airports across the country and suggests changes.
summary: Pilots reported that extremely bright LED taxiway and runway lighting at U.S. airports causes blinding, reducing the ability to detect hazards like FOD or animals. The reporter noted that ATC cannot dim the lights further and attributed the issue to non-user decisions on lighting system installation.

synopsis: B737 flight crew laments ATC handling of an approach to Runway 19R at SFO and a NMAC with an Airbus on the Runway 19L approach.
summary: A fatigued crew with an FAA inspector on board experienced a near mid-air collision while executing a visual approach to Runway 19R at SFO. The pilot attributed the incident to a chain of circumstances including fatigue, distraction, and non-standard ATC traffic calls that led to inadequate separation from another Airbus.

synopsis: With both pilots involved in post pushback activities they failed to note their B757 was rolling forward during engine start. When they both applied brakes to stop the movement several flight attendants lost their balance, one of whom during the flight suffered knee pain forcing her to remain seated for the duration of the flight.
summary: The flight crew inadvertently rolled forward during engine start while reviewing unusual takeoff data, requiring both pilots to apply brakes to stop the aircraft. This firm stop caused a flight attendant to injure her knee, leaving her unable to walk for the remainder of the flight.

synopsis: B757 First Officer reports being informed by the Purser that a deadheading pilot has noticed ice on the wing after de-icing has been completed. The flight returns to the de-ice pad where the crew does not believe that more de-icing is necessary.
summary: The flight crew discovered snow adhering to the left wing and flap during a pre-departure check and requested a return for deicing. The de-ice coordinator refused, claiming the snow would shear off, leading the crew to conclude the required clean surface check was omitted and de-ice personnel disregarded FOM requirements.

synopsis: CRJ-700 flight crew advised by ATC of a track deviation which was caused by Captain accidentally selecting HDG mode rather than NAV mode on RNAV departure.
summary: During an RNAV departure, the Captain accidentally selected HDG mode instead of NAV mode at 400 feet AGL, causing the aircraft to deviate from the route. The First Officer corrected the heading after ATC requested immediate track compliance, and the crew resumed normal navigation.

synopsis: A commercial air carrier flight crew had to brake abruptly when a fueling truck, apparently oblivious to their presence passed 10 to 15 yards in front of them.
summary: During taxi-out, a single-engine aircraft stopped abruptly to avoid a fuel truck crossing its path on the ramp. The truck driver appeared distracted, possibly by cell phone use, but no injuries occurred and the flight continued.

synopsis: An air carrier Dispatcher expressed concern that an interruption in providing valid takeoff data from load planning to one of his flights had not been directed through him.
summary: A pilot received an automated load planning message instructing the crew not to take off due to deleted weight and balance data. The pilot reported that the Dispatcher was unaware of the message and could not receive the requested acknowledgement, creating a communication gap.

synopsis: An ERJ taxiing to the gate after landing at ORD had to stop abruptly when a B777-300 exiting the International Ramp turned immediately in front of them. ATC later advised the aircraft were under the direction of separate Ground controllers who had not coordinated the conflict.
summary: The pilot of a landing aircraft stopped on Taxiway B at ORD to avoid a collision when a foreign B-777-300 turned left in front of them. The reporter attributed the incident to a lack of communication between two Ground Controllers who issued conflicting instructions on different frequencies.

synopsis: An A319 flight crew who had programmed the LYNDI RNAV STAR and the RNAV (GPS) Runway 27 approach to SAN were surprised when Approach Control advised they had failed to comply with STAR altitude restrictions at BARET and LUCKI waypoints and that LUCKI had, in fact, turned itself into the nearly co-located ZUSUB, a fix on the RNAV (GPS) approach. Review after landing determined that the waypoints and their restrictions on the STAR had autosequenced to 'similar' ones on the IAP but which included crossing altitudes of as much as 2,700 FT lower than their equivalent STAR crossings. Although they had not selected a 'VIA' mode, the changes were unilaterally (and repeatedly) altered by the FMGC.
summary: The flight crew experienced an altitude deviation during the LYNDI THREE arrival into San Diego while flying the RNAV 27 approach. Inserting the RNAV 27 procedure into the MCDU without a transition inadvertently deleted the LUCKI waypoint and its 6,100-foot crossing constraint, causing the aircraft to descend below the required altitude.

synopsis: Captain addresses multiple issues with Maintenance Control surrounding incorrect MELs being applied to an A319 aircraft's Aft Cargo Door that continued to drop down on Ramp personnel and belt loader equipment during loading operations. Concerns also raised that original MEL required maintenance items for the Aft Cargo door had not been accomplished.
summary: The Captain reported a cargo door actuator leak during preflight, causing the door to droop near belt loader rails. After Maintenance Control initially applied incorrect MELs and failed to complete required tasks, a second mechanic resolved the issue by bleeding air from the hydraulic lines, avoiding a three-hour delay.

synopsis: A CRJ-900 flight crew declared an emergency and landed safely following recognition of smoke and fumes on the flight deck.
summary: The flight crew detected smoke and fumes in the flight deck, declared an emergency, and complied with procedures. Despite communication difficulties caused by oxygen masks, flight attendants understood the situation, performed their duties, and the aircraft landed safely.

synopsis: A C-402 pilot declared an emergency immediately after takeoff due to a rough running and, per the Tower, smoking right engine and returned safely to the departure airport. The immediate symptoms abated after throttling back from takeoff power and the pilot opted not to shut it down.
summary: During takeoff, the pilot reported the right engine overboosted to 42 inches and ran rough with smoke at 600 feet. Reducing power to climb settings stopped the roughness and smoke, allowing a safe landing with emergency vehicles standing by.

synopsis: A B737NG Captain was effectively blocked from taxiing into his assigned gate when multiple vehicles refused to grant right of way as he approached on the lead-in line. Additional training and monitoring of ground crew compliance was cited as a viable fix.
summary: The pilot reported that ground vehicles repeatedly crossed the gate lead-in line during taxi and parking, causing multiple stops and a five-minute delay. The pilot attributed the incident to drivers lacking knowledge of safety procedures and noted Ramp Control's dismissive response to the reported violations.

synopsis: When a DC10 flight crew extended spoilers to assist compliance with their planned descent profile the aircraft abruptly banked 45 degrees and deviated from their cleared track. The pilot flying was unable to retract the spoilers while resisting the bank and directed the First Officer to do so. Normal flight was recovered and the landing was made without deploying spoilers as a precaution.
summary: During descent through 14,000 feet, extending speedbrakes caused an uncommanded 45-degree right turn due to binding in the spoiler handle. The crew manually retracted the speedbrakes, regained control, and completed an ILS approach to Runway 24 using flaps 50 with no spoilers.

synopsis: A300 First Officer reports descending below the glide path during an ILS approach in VMC, due to lack of attention to the automation. Both the crew and the Tower detect the low flight path at about 1,400 FT AGL and the aircraft is returned to glide path.
summary: During an ILS approach to LAX Runway 25L, the pilot flying engaged vertical speed mode, disarming the landing mode and causing a glide path deviation to 1,300 feet. The crew attributed the incident to lack of automation attention and delayed speed reduction, though they re-intercepted the glide path and stabilized before 500 feet.

synopsis: An instructor pilot aboard a PA-28 suffered an NMAC with an inbound PA-44 while departing CHD to the south.
summary: A pilot climbing from CHD to CGZ with an inoperative traffic alerting system observed a PA-44 descending inbound to CHD less than 500 feet overhead. The PA-44 passed without communication or collision, and the pilot noted the traffic alerting system was not working.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports he inadvertently serviced the Number 1 Hydraulic System on an EMB-145 aircraft with MIL-H-5606 red hydraulic fluid instead of blue Skydrol hydraulic fluid. Technician recommends that hydraulic fluid fittings be standardized to prevent Skydrol systems being serviced with MIL-H-5606 hydraulic fluid.
summary: A mechanic servicing an EMB-145 during a hangar A-Check mistakenly filled the Number 1 Hydraulic System with MIL-H-5606 fluid instead of Skydrol due to identical cart colors and a time crunch. The error was discovered immediately after connection, prompting a system shutdown and report to the Lead Mechanic.

synopsis: When the student pilot appeared unable to control their LSA on the landing roll the instructor took the controls after which the nose wheel snapped off and the aircraft slid to a stop. No one was injured.
summary: During a student training landing, the instructor took control after the aircraft drifted right with sluggish steering. After turning off the runway, the nose wheel collapsed upon braking, causing a 100-foot skid with no injuries.

synopsis: Confusion reigned between ATC and the flight crew of a B737NG with respect to both track and altitude as the flight approached its destination. An FMC stored company route which ended at a fix prior to the destination airport was cited as a contributing factor.
summary: The flight crew descended through QUBEE at 11,000 feet before receiving a clearance for 7,000 feet and a direct routing to FNT. Although ATC initially questioned the altitude compliance, subsequent investigation confirmed no violation occurred as the crew followed the intended route and clearances.

synopsis: B737 First Officer reports the air hose, from a ground air start cart, separating from the aircraft during engine start and striking the number two engine. The engine cowl is dented and the aircraft is taken out of service.
summary: During a ground air start of a -300 aircraft, the airstart hose disconnected and struck the #2 engine cowling, causing damage. The crew aborted the start, swapped to another aircraft, and reported the incident to highlight ground safety risks associated with loose hoses.

synopsis: B777 Captain reports refusing a shipment of lithium ion batteries due to their potential for fires that cannot be contained by the aircraft fire suppression system.
summary: The flight crew refused to depart with 2,800 pounds of lithium-ion batteries after receiving an ACARS notification indicating the cargo fire suppression system might fail. The cargo was offloaded, causing a 30-minute delay, as the Captain determined the risk of an uncontrollable fire on the overwater flight compromised safety.

synopsis: A B767 First Officer reported frequent failures of their iPad EFBs to delete the previous flight data and display data appropriate for the current operation.
summary: Pilots reported that the iPad WSI function frequently freezes on the last loaded route before flight. The issue requires deleting and reinstalling the app with an internet connection, which consumes time and risks losing saved charts.

synopsis: CRJ-200 flight crew discovers an unresponsive thrust lever upon level off at FL310. After some discussion it is decided to follow the jammed thrust lever QRH procedure and shut down the engine. A single engine approach and landing ensues.
summary: The flight crew encountered an unresponsive number one thrust lever at FL310, which they addressed using the 'Thrust Lever Jammed' checklist after Maintenance offered no assistance. They declared an emergency, shut down the engine, and successfully completed a single-engine landing in gusty IMC conditions.

synopsis: B757-200 Captain reported that the aircraft slowed 'well below' the selected value of 170 knots after descending in FLCH mode and commencing glideslope descent in APP with autothrottles armed. Reporter stated that the autothrottle did not 'wake up' to control speed as anticipated and that there was no AOM reference or caution regarding this specific scenario.
summary: During an ILS approach, the pilot descended in FL CH mode and leveled at 3,000 feet, but the auto-throttles failed to re-engage, causing airspeed to drop below the commanded 170 knots. The First Officer called out the deviation, the pilot manually applied power, and the aircraft landed safely, though the pilot noted the AOM inadequately addresses this specific auto-throttle behavior.

synopsis: B767-300 Captain reports ground personnel attempting to open the forward cargo door during gate arrival, with both engines still running.
summary: During a laser-guided gate arrival with engines running, ground crew triggered a cockpit siren by attempting to open the forward cargo door and subsequently entered the aircraft to manipulate power sources. The pilot reported that ground personnel routinely stand in the protected movement area, creating a safety hazard and risking laser guidance errors.

synopsis: B737 Captain exiting Runway 19R on Echo reports a near collision with a helicopter air taxiing southbound on Alpha at SNA.
summary: A jet exiting Runway 19R at SNA stopped short of Taxiway A to avoid a collision with a helicopter flying southbound at high speed. The helicopter passed 30 feet from the nose after Ground Control cleared it to takeoff opposite taxi flow, a practice the pilot deemed dangerous.

synopsis: Deadheading Captain reports being asked to examine the right wing for ice while airborne. Clear ice is detected on the inboard portion and the flight crew is informed. Flight continues to destination where the air temperature is 50 degrees F. Rain on a cold soaked wing was thought to be the source of the ice.
summary: A deadheading check airman discovered ice on the right wing during cruise and informed the flight crew. The Captain attributed the accumulation to cold-soaked wing conditions from rain and fuel, elected to increase approach speed, and the flight concluded safely as the ice sublimated.

synopsis: First Officer reports a Level One 'Cargo Fire Test Fail' alert appeared during a pre-flight check after one of the two fire bottles in the lower forward cargo compartment of their DC-10 had been deferred under MEL 26-22-01. The MEL did not address whether or not that was a proper indication. First Officer recommends the MEL be revised to indicate the 'Fail Alert' is a normal occurrence. Aircraft departed without additional information.
summary: The crew encountered a Level One 'Cargo Fire Test Fail' alert during pre-flight while operating with MEL 26-22-01 for an inoperative cargo fire bottle. Maintenance agreed the alert was logical, and the flight to ZZZ1 proceeded uneventfully, though the crew recommended updating the MEL to clarify if this indication is normal.

synopsis: Turboprop pilot reports being issued a low altitude warning by the BHM Tower while at minimums on the RNAV (GPS) Runway 36. Within a few seconds the aircraft TAWS system issued 'OBSTACLE' alert and the MFD indicated a yellow shaded circle directly in front of the aircraft. A go-around is initiated, followed by an approach to a different runway. It was reported that the following CE680 was issued the same warning by the Tower.
summary: The pilot flying a BHM RNAV (GPS) Runway 36 approach received a Low Altitude Alert and an "OBSTACLE" warning from the TAWS while slightly above the 1,480 FT MDA in IMC. The crew executed a missed approach and was vectored for an ILS 24 landing, noting a following Cessna Sovereign received a similar alert.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: MD80 maintenance crew reports a taxiway excursion due to ice while attempting to taxi from the gate area to a maintenance hangar.
summary: Two mechanics taxiing an MD-80 from the ramp to a hangar slid off a taxiway into grass while turning left on a solid sheet of ice. The aircraft could not be recovered despite deploying thrust reversers, leading the crew to shut down engines and request tower assistance.

synopsis: Pilot cleared for take-off questioned the Tower Controller about traffic on short final cleared to land.
summary: The pilot of a personal Dakota reported a potentially unsafe takeoff clearance from Tower while a commercial carrier was less than two miles from landing. The pilot questioned the safety of the instruction, received an abrasive response from the controller, and departed without incident despite concerns about a potential conflict.

synopsis: Tower Controller is advised of a NMAC by a helicopter pilot transitioning northbound through the Class D, with a C172 in the VFR traffic pattern.
summary: An air traffic controller handling five aircraft in the pattern forgot to issue a traffic advisory to a helicopter near a C172 on final for Runway 9L. This resulted in a reported 100-foot separation between the two aircraft, prompting the controller to acknowledge the need for better situational awareness.

synopsis: When the B737-700 flight crew started engines during pushback on a slippery ramp the thrust of the engines overcame the coefficient of friction of the push back tug's tires and the jet rolled forward striking the tug and breaking the tow bar. Damage to the aircraft was cosmetic only and the flight departed after separation from the tug and an inspection.
summary: During pushback at BWI on icy taxiways, the tug lost traction and jack-knifed, breaking the tow bar and scraping the aircraft's radome. The crew stopped the aircraft, repaired the damage, and completed the flight after delaying engine start until the push was finished.

synopsis: After experiencing multiple autoflight and FMC related failures while conducting an approach in challenging IMC weather the Captain of an A319 expressed measured but pointed concern at the failure of maintenance to conscientiously address multiple previous write-ups of similar failures, including one near identical episode. The reporter further cited the necessity of having to request a detailed maintenance history to learn of the chronic nature of the problem and the apparent fact that no substantive troubleshooting of the cause had been performed. That, in lieu of such substantive investigation, write-ups had been routinely resolved by merely cycling circuit breakers.
summary: The flight crew experienced partial FMGC 2 degradation and subsequent AP1 disengagement with unreliable guidance during an ILS approach in deteriorating weather. They completed a manual raw data landing, later discovering maintenance logs showed chronic, unresolved Auto Flight System failures that posed significant safety risks.

synopsis: Dispatcher reports that Boeing Direct messages to flight crews are causing confusion because the crews believe they are coming from Dispatch.
summary: Crews mistakenly replied to Boeing Direct ACARS re-route suggestions, believing they originated from Dispatch. The reporter attributes this confusion to the lack of guidance and testing when Boeing Direct was implemented, blurring the distinction between automated messages and verified Dispatch instructions.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: MD-80 Captain reports the nose landing gear failing to retract properly after takeoff producing numerous secondary warnings and anomalies. QRH procedures for the landing gear and spoiler are complied with, fuel was burned down to max landing weight before landing. The aircraft was deiced just prior to takeoff.
summary: The crew departed late in icing and experienced nose gear issues, multiple annunciator lights, and pressurization failure after takeoff. They executed emergency checklists, declared an emergency, and landed safely with no confirmed gear damage.

synopsis: When cleared to taxi to a specific runway at ORD behind two approaching air carrier jets the flight crew of a B737NG interpreted that to mean follow them to their cleared runway. During their taxi they became aware the two they were taxiing behind were cleared to a different runway. ATC switched their runway rather than try to reroute them to their original runway.
summary: The pilot taxied past the assigned holding point at ORD at night while following other aircraft due to confusing "follow" instructions and snow-covered signs. Ground control cleared the pilot to use an alternate route, and the pilot attributed the error to non-standard clearance phrasing and radio congestion.

synopsis: Flight instructor reports departing the runway and nosing over after taking over from his student who was over controlling after a wheel landing.
summary: During a student's second tailwheel lesson, the aircraft lost directional control on landing due to variable winds and student over-correction. The instructor took control to prevent a ground loop, but the nose pitched down, causing a prop strike and nose gear damage on the runway berm.

synopsis: A Citation pilot departing on a flight from FAT to SMF understood his clearance to depart Runway 29L at FAT, proceed direct LINDN, direct SAC, direct. After takeoff when, to Departure's surprise, he started the sharp left turn direct to LINDN intersection, 200NM south of FAT, Departure and the reporter realized the intended fix pronounced 'linden' was the LIN VOR 100NM north of FAT well on the way to his destination, not the airways fix LINDN just north of Los Angeles.
summary: A pilot flying from FAT to SMF confused two similarly named waypoints, LINDN and LIN, causing an initial turn away from the intended route. The controller corrected the heading and clarified the waypoint identifier, allowing the flight to proceed safely to the correct destination.

synopsis: Similar sounding call signs caused the wrong aircraft to begin a descent in another Centers airspace.
summary: An air traffic controller in Sector XX issued a descent clearance to Air Carrier X, but Air Carrier Y mistakenly accepted it and descended from FL310 due to similar call signs. The controller intercepted the error at FL298, instructed Air Carrier Y to maintain FL290, and reissued the clearance to Air Carrier X.

synopsis: When an A320 had their takeoff clearance cancelled at moderate speeds the ensuing inaccurate clearances from Tower to exit the runway resulted in delays and a go-around for an aircraft on approach.
summary: The crew aborted takeoff on Runway 22L at 50 knots after Tower canceled clearance due to inadequate separation with a landing aircraft. Tower later issued an incorrect exit instruction to taxiway S3, which was corrected to Y3 after the crew queried the non-existent designation.

synopsis: An EMB-145 flight crew declared an emergency, diverted to the nearest suitable airport, and evacuated all SOBs after experiencing smoke and electrical odors in the cockpit and cabin.
summary: The crew encountered electrical smoke while climbing through FL190, declared an emergency, and diverted to the nearest airport. After landing and evacuating the aircraft with no injuries, maintenance attributed the incident to a recirculation fan overload.

synopsis: Similar sounding four digit flight numbers both inbound to the same VOR were both cleared to maintain the same altitude. The first flight so cleared recognized the issue and returned to their originally cleared altitude while the error was corrected and all involved informed.
summary: Pilots of ACR ABBA at FL230 halted a descent to FL220 after hearing Center issue the same clearance to ACR AABA due to similar call signs. The crew climbed back to FL230, received a new clearance to FL210, and the controller advised both flights of the confusion.

synopsis: A CRJ200 First Officer reports encountering wake vortices on final approach into ATL.
summary: The crew encountered wake turbulence while vectored by ATC below a preceding aircraft on a visual approach to runway 9R at ATL. This resulted in a 25-degree bank angle and autopilot disconnect, creating a risk of aircraft upset and potential loss of control.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer describes the events leading up to a runway incursion at CYYZ, requiring an aircraft to go-around.
