synopsis: Regional jet Captain experiences a flaps fail caution message during approach when flaps are selected to 30. A go-around is initiated and the following approach and landing is conducted with flaps less than 30.
summary: During approach, the crew received a Flaps Fail caution while selecting flaps 30, prompting an emergency declaration and QRH execution. The aircraft landed safely with fire rescue standing by, and the rollout was uneventful.

synopsis: CRJ-700 Captain questions the advisability of using FL180 for crossing restrictions on RNAV STARS due to the impending change to QNH. An early change over may cause the restriction to be missed and a late change over may cause problems with the next restriction.
summary: Pilots on an ENDEE arrival into MDW crossed NOGEE below FL180 using standard pressure, but their altimeter briefly indicated above 18,000 feet after setting the local 30.50 inches. The crew believes the procedure is flawed because crossing restrictions at transition altitude create potential for deviations when changing altimeter settings.

synopsis: After suffering the loss of both MAUs (Modular Avionics Units) aboard their C-680 while in an IMC descent the flight crew declared an emergency to descent to VMC conditions and out of possible icing conditions. Once clear they were vectored by ATC for a visual approach and landing at their planned destination.
summary: During descent on a STAR, the crew experienced autopilot disengagement and total primary instrument failure due to MAU 1 and 2 faults, likely linked to a recent starter generator replacement. They declared an emergency, received vectors to 4,000 feet, and landed safely via visual approach in VMC.

synopsis: BE400 Captain reports being asked by the Tower during takeoff, 'Are you able to abort?' With the speed being low, the flying SIC begins the reject and stops easily. The Tower explains that a heavy jet has gone around on an intersecting runway.
summary: The crew aborted takeoff on Runway 26R below 60 KTS after MIA Tower queried their ability to abort due to a heavy aircraft going around on intersecting Runway 30. The pilot flying initiated the stop, and the crew later departed normally after the controller directed them to taxi clear and return.

synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer experiences a possible GPS jamming event during approach to SLC. Radio navaids are used for a successful VMC approach.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced a GPS map shift and terrain display error during a night visual approach to Runway 16R in a GPS-only aircraft. The crew attributed the issue to GPS jamming, switched to manual data, and completed an uneventful landing.

synopsis: A check airman conducting initial operating experience for a new First Officer was embarrassed when, after advising he was turning on engine anti-ice, instead turned off both B System hydraulic pumps, the switches for which are adjacent to the anti-ice switches. The err was quickly rectified when a Master Caution warning illuminated the error of his ways.
summary: The Pilot Monitoring mistakenly turned off the B System hydraulic pumps instead of engine anti-ice while climbing in IMC during an OE approach. The Master Caution light alerted the crew, allowing immediate correction within 10 seconds with no adverse outcome.

aircraft: Airbus Industrie Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An Airbus pilot reported the potential exists for flight crews to descend to unsafe altitudes with respect to mountainous terrain between the GS intercept altitude for a precision ILS approach to Runway 16R and the FAF for the non-precision GS out approach to the same runway at RNO.
summary: A pilot reported a safety concern during a night visual approach to Reno Silver ILS 16R, noting that using the FAF crossing altitude of 6,401 feet for descent could result in insufficient clearance over a 6,219-foot mountain. The pilot recommended moving the FAF to 7,100 feet to ensure safer glide slope intercept altitudes.

synopsis: A flight attendant crew did not have time to complete their originating flight TSA Security Check before the A Flight Attendant began an unannounced boarding. He had already signed the TSA Security sign-off sheet for the other three flight attendants.
summary: A lead flight attendant began boarding two minutes early without an announcement and signed for a crew member who had not finished her TSA security check. On a subsequent leg, the same attendant started boarding early again but stopped immediately when another crew member requested a halt to complete her security check.

synopsis: A C172 hooded student instrument pilot reported his instructor took evasive action from an aircraft inbound to the same runway after the other pilot failed to turn away as directed by the Tower.
summary: An instrument student and flight instructor in a C-172P executing an ILS 25 approach under the hood performed evasive maneuvers to avoid a mid-air collision. The conflict occurred when another aircraft, despite Tower warnings, turned toward the flight path of the approaching rental aircraft.

aircraft: Bombardier Learjet Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Lear jet Captain reports that on at least ten separate occasions his Number 1 Garmin 530 GPS completely powered off and restarted at roughly the same geographic location 30 NM north of HOM.
summary: The pilot reported that the aircraft's Number 1 Garmin 530 GPS powered off and restarted within one minute while approximately 30 DME north of the Homer VOR en route from ANC. The pilot noted this is the tenth occurrence at this specific location, though no cause was identified.

synopsis: The pilot of a PA28 was unable to reduce engine power while on final approach and resorted to shutting down the engine with the mixture lever. He performed a successful 'dead stick' landing with no damage or injuries. He learned later that the throttle cable had failed within the sleeve, with one end still attached to the throttle lever and the other to the carburetor.
summary: A pilot experienced a throttle cable failure inside the sleeve during the final approach of a practice landing in an older aircraft. The pilot executed a successful dead-stick landing with no injuries or damage after the throttle became inoperative.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) describes how he failed to retain control of the scope and nature of repairs that he had agreed to perform on a Cessna 337B aircraft and IO-360D engine. Reporter felt intimidated by the aircraft's owner who kept expanding the repair list but not extending the time required to properly accomplish the work.
summary: A mechanic, pressured by an abusive customer to meet impossible deadlines, rushed engine work and installed unapproved fasteners and experimental cables. This resulted in missed inspections, incorrect logbook entries, and the aircraft being towed to another facility with incomplete documentation.

synopsis: The pilot of a C182 experienced a loss of power and rough engine operation during cruise flight. An emergency was declared, followed by a successful landing. A loose mixture control fastener was determined to be causing a lack of fuel to the engine.
summary: The pilot experienced intermittent engine roughness and altitude loss at 6,500 feet due to a loose mixture cable bolt causing fuel starvation. After declaring an emergency and landing safely, the engine died upon taxiing off the runway, and the aircraft was towed for repairs.

synopsis: P31 Controller is informed by the pilot of a helicopter under his control that he is leveling to avoid a C172 passing overhead. The C172 had entered the Class C without clearance.
summary: An air traffic controller working Z-AR reported a C172 passing less than 100 feet above a helicopter climbing to 1,700 feet in Class C airspace. The controller attributed the near miss to a weak primary radar return and instructed the helicopter pilot to confirm visual clearance.

synopsis: Reporter states while attempting to do a point out the receiving facility doesn't answer the call, vectors aircraft but ends up having an airspace violation. Reporter also states conflict about a shelf of airspace that they would like changed.
summary: A Developmental controller and instructor could not contact IND ATC to transfer an RNAV RWY 17 arrival, forcing the aircraft to fly an extra 45 miles at low altitude. The reporter attributed this delay and increased fuel burn to the inability to coordinate the point-out due to the BMG shelf airspace boundary design.

synopsis: When the First Officer's O2 mask harness failed to inflate for donning B737-700 flight crew diverted to a nearby airport to have it replaced.
summary: The First Officer discovered a malfunctioning oxygen mask harness at cruise that failed to inflate or retract, rendering it ineffective for hands-free use. The crew diverted to replace the mask, arriving 45 minutes late, and recommended preflight checks to ensure mask functionality.

synopsis: B737 Captain reports a ramp person scurrying into the safety zone to retrieve some unseen chocks while the Marshall continued to wave the reporter forward on the lead in line. The Captain counseled the Marshall that he should have stopped the taxi in until the safety zone was clear.
summary: During night marshalling, a ramp worker entered the pilot's safety zone to retrieve chocks while the aircraft was being signaled in. The pilot stopped the aircraft, noting the marshaller failed to issue a stop signal despite the incursion, and later expressed concern over the lack of communication regarding the safety breach.

synopsis: A B767-300 EICAS alerted TE FLAP DISAGREE when flaps 20 were selected on final. Unable to complete the QRH, a go-around was executed, flaps 20 mistakenly selected and the QRH then completed for a normal landing. The Alert ceased with flaps 20 selection.
summary: During final approach, a trailing edge flap disagreement triggered an EICAS message, prompting the crew to execute a go-around. The crew followed the QRH to land safely with flaps at 20, noting that normal go-around procedures conflicted with the checklist regarding flap handle movement.

synopsis: A B737 First Officer expressed incredulity at a company directive advising that aircraft 'can and will' be de-iced at the gate with the jetway in place and the passenger door open. He stressed the risk of personal injury, the toxicity of the fluids involved and his belief that the procedure was implemented solely as a cost saving measure with safety relagated to a subordinate concern.
summary: A crewmember reported that the airline's cost-saving procedure at ORD requires de-icing aircraft at the gate with the jetbridge attached and main cabin door open. The reporter described this as unsafe due to the risk of toxic de-icing fluid spraying passengers or employees, citing a known incident where a crewmember was sprayed.

synopsis: A Dispatcher completing a training exercise was told he was assigned a dispatch shift eight hours after this training completion, but he complained because he needed an hour each way to and from home. The following day he had another shift after an eight hour break leading to continuous and unsafe fatigue.
summary: A dispatcher reported being junior assigned to a shift while scheduled for another the next day, creating a double quick turn. The dispatcher stated that fatigue from the desk check and lack of sleep would prevent safe operational control for the upcoming shifts.

synopsis: An A320 Captain's window began arcing, and then the outer pane shattered as the crew was completing the QRH. An emergency was declared and the flight landed at a nearby airport.
summary: The crew experienced arcing and subsequent shattering of the Captain's windshield at FL320. They declared an emergency, descended, and landed uneventfully after confirming the inner glass panel remained intact per QRH procedures.

synopsis: MD-83 flight crew reported experiencing compressor stalls in right engine on takeoff roll at approximately 100 KTS. Captain made the decision to reject the takeoff, and after maintenance inspection aircraft was taken out of service.
summary: The Captain rejected the takeoff at 100 KTS after the right engine experienced compressor stalls, two bangs, and thrust loss. Maintenance found damaged compressor blades, resulting in the aircraft being taken out of service.

synopsis: C172 instructor pilot reported his student descended to within 300 FT AGL near homes on a practice approach.
summary: During practice approaches with a student pilot controlling the aircraft, the student descended to 300 feet AGL near homes despite an instructor's instruction to maintain 600 feet AGL. The student subsequently climbed, and the remaining three approaches and landings were completed normally.

synopsis: A flight instructor and student pilot encountered a right main landing gear downlock problem in a C172RG while practicing maneuvers. They worked the appropriate checklist, but could not resolve the problem. The Instructor was able to visually confirm that the gear was not in the full down position. They were able to set down on the right gear during landing which fully extended and locked the gear leg.
summary: During a power-off stall training flight, the right main landing gear failed to fully extend and lock despite emergency checklists. The crew declared an emergency, performed a low approach for visual confirmation, and executed a controlled landing with no damage, attributing the cause to an undetected mechanical issue.

synopsis: C172 pilot reported an NMAC with an experimental aircraft at a non-towered airport and during evasive action he entered Class B airspace.
summary: A C172 pilot climbing to avoid a TIS-reported conflict inadvertently entered Class B airspace at 2,500 feet. The pilot immediately descended below the 2,000-foot shelf to re-enter the traffic pattern, citing safety deviation authority.

synopsis: A pilot and an Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) report a Cessna 182T aircraft was inadvertently returned to service prior to accomplishment of Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2004-10-14. The AD required an engine teardown and inspection due to significant damage to the propeller that was replaced.
summary: A pilot and mechanic inadvertently flew an aircraft twice after replacing a damaged propeller without complying with Airworthiness Directive 2004-10-14, which required an engine breakdown. The oversight, caused by heavy workload and misinterpretation, led to the aircraft being grounded for non-airworthiness.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: SMO Tower Controller reported an aircraft experienced an Class Delta airspace violation after leaving it west bound and then entering it again without clearance eastbound.
summary: A pilot departing SMO on VFR flight following turned back toward the airport at 1,800 feet after receiving confusing instructions to remain clear of Class D airspace while still inside it. The pilot attributed the incident to ambiguous tower phrasing and a unique local procedure requiring a squawk code for a specific westward departure.

synopsis: N90 TRACON Controller states it is facility policy to descend below the Class Bravo which causes conflict with busy VFR airport airspace on base leg to major airport.
summary: A pilot reported a near mid-air collision with a climbing VFR jet while operating a staggered 22L/R final approach below Class B airspace. The pilot attributed the risk to the current airspace design and approach procedures in VFR conditions.

synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported a high speed rejected takeoff (127 KTS, just under V1) because of smoke in the cockpit.
summary: During takeoff roll, the crew aborted at 127 KTS after observing smoke and smelling fumes near the Captain's EFIS panel. Fire personnel confirmed high temperatures on the main wheels and the Captain's side glareshield, leading to a safe return to the gate and passenger deplaning.

synopsis: After landing in MIA, a fatigued flight crew realized that they were on Approach Control frequency and had not received landing clearance.
summary: Two fatigued pilots landed on Runway 8R in Miami without landing clearance after forgetting to switch from Approach to Tower frequency during a night turn. They realized the error only after exiting the runway, attributing the incident to exhaustion and a missed frequency change.

synopsis: EMB190 flight crew experiences a break away during pushback requiring the use of the parking brake to stop the aircraft. The sudden stop causes both flight attendants to fall and be seriously injured.
summary: During pushback with engines off, a defective tow bar disconnected, forcing the Captain to stop the aircraft using the parking brake. The sudden stop injured two flight attendants who required hospitalization, while the crew coordinated medical aid and a replacement tow bar to return the aircraft to the gate.

synopsis: A SF-340 flight crew and Flight Attendant detected a strong odor during cruise just prior to descent. So they declared an emergency, completed the QRH and landed at the nearest divert airport where the aircraft was evacuated.
summary: During cruise, the flight crew and cabin crew detected smoke from a floor vent, prompting an emergency diversion. The Captain followed the QRH to isolate systems and dump the cabin, resulting in a safe landing and immediate evacuation by Fire Rescue.

synopsis: During climb after takeoff, a CRJ-900 EICAS alerted GEN 1 CAUTION and R BLEED DUCT so the flight returned to the departure airport for a precautionary landing.
summary: The crew experienced a GEN 1 Caution and R Bleed Duct Warning during flight, prompting a precautionary return to the field. The reporter attributed the event to an unavoidable maintenance irregularity, with no further incident occurring.

synopsis: During takeoff after a maintenance delay, an MD-83's right main landing gear indicated unsafe with the gear doors closed and the AUTOSPOILER DO NOT ARM light annunciated, so the QRH was completed, an emergency declared and the flight returned to the departure airport for an uneventful landing.
summary: The pilot departed after a two-hour maintenance delay for nose gear tires, then encountered unsafe right main gear and auto-spoiler warnings upon retraction. Following QRH procedures and an emergency return, the aircraft landed normally but was taken out of service.

synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reports an underspeed condition at FL370 resulting in autopilot disconnect and loss of 1,200 FT before the flying First Officer can add thrust and recover. The Captain was occupied with weather and planning a possible reroute.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced an autopilot disconnect and high-altitude stall warning at FL370 due to the Captain's distraction while planning a weather reroute. The First Officer recovered the aircraft using TOGA power and pitch control, allowing a descent to FL350, which the Captain attributed to complacency and training.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: After departing on the DCA NATIONAL 3, the Corporate First Officer turned before the 328 Radial and when correcting back to the radial, the FMS guidance overshot possibly causing a P40 violation.
summary: The flight crew executing the National 3 departure from DCA overshot the 328-degree radial due to an early turn and FMS guidance errors, placing the aircraft near a prohibited area. The controller issued a corrective heading, and the crew attributed the incident to poor situational awareness from low ceilings and inadequate FMS waypoint design.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: An instructor took the aircraft from his student after they saw two aircraft lights descend into them while in an instrument approach to DAB. ATC reported no nearby traffic.
summary: An instructor and student pilot flying an RNAV 7L approach reported seeing two white lights from an unseen aircraft descending above them. The instructor executed an evasive descent of 600 feet to 1,000 MSL, but ATC confirmed no conflicting traffic existed in the area.

synopsis: BE55 pilot experiences a loss of GPS signal during a RNAV GPS 36 approach to LIT. As the missed approach is being contemplated the reporter breaks out of the overcast and the signal returns. Reporter indicates that other pilots may have had similar problems with this approach.
summary: The pilot experienced a false GPS signal loss indication while crossing the final approach fix for the RNAV GPS 36 approach at LIT. After verifying course alignment on multiple systems, the pilot broke out of clouds with visual contact and landed safely, requesting an investigation into the approach procedure.

synopsis: A Corporate jet crew and light twin pilot both asked JST Approach about mutual traffic and were told to maintain visual but neither was advised of their converging tracks which resulted in the jet crew taking evasive action.
summary: A jet pilot descending into LBE accepted visual separation from a King Air, resulting in a TCAS advisory due to converging courses not disclosed by Johnstown Approach. The pilot increased descent rate to maintain safety, noting the controller failed to convey the threat level before issuing the separation instruction.

synopsis: A Quality Assurance Inspector reports a current Airworthiness Certificate for one of their AS355-F2 series helicopter was invalid due to the aircraft not being maintained in accordance with (IAW) the Manufacturer's instructions. He had reported to his Director of Maintenance (DOM) that an unauthorized Tail Rotor Gearbox had previously been installed on the AS355-F2, but the DOM chose to release the helicopter into service.
summary: A maintenance technician discovered an unauthorized tail rotor gearbox installed on an AS355-F2 helicopter during an Airworthiness Directive review. Despite the manufacturer confirming the part was invalid, management ignored the finding and allowed the aircraft to fly, rendering its airworthiness certificate invalid.

synopsis: C172 instructor reports an NMAC with another C172 in the traffic pattern at SGS. The reporter and his student never saw the other aircraft and the NMAC report is second hand, from the other pilot.
summary: A CFII and student flying a LOC approach at SGS passed within 100 feet of a Skyhawk on downwind for Runway 16. The near mid-air collision occurred due to the instructor's failure to monitor excessive student airspeed and delay breaking off the approach, compounded by both crews failing to visually acquire the Skyhawk.

synopsis: Air Traffic Controller reports repeated problem of duplicate oceanic flight plans identified while the aircraft was enroute. Possible incompatibility between HOST and ERAM computer systems.
summary: Moncton Center controllers discovered an air carrier aircraft flying a route different from its filed departure plan due to multiple conflicting flight plans in the system. This recurring issue, affecting ten aircraft from the New York Metro area, caused route divergence requiring immediate controller action to maintain separation.

synopsis: E10 TRACON Controller stated two aircraft operating in a Restricted Area busted their altitude assignment causing a third aircraft to climb due to RA.
summary: An air traffic controller observed Aircraft X and Y climb unauthorized to FL304 while Aircraft Z at FL320 received a TCAS climb resolution advisory. The controller instructed X and Y to descend immediately, and Z returned to FL320 after being advised of the descending traffic.

synopsis: A Ground Controller in Class C airspace observes a near-miss between a C172 and 2/F16's and provides Local Control input to help resolve the situation.
summary: A Ground Controller intervened when a Local Controller allowed an IFR Cessna on a published missed approach to climb across Runway 33, creating a conflict with descending F-16s on an overhead approach. The Cessna was ordered to turn immediately, resulting in zero vertical and minimal lateral separation, which the reporter attributed to conflicting instructions and controller inaction.

synopsis: A B737NG, southbound at 6,000 FT received a brief TCAS RA from an opposite direction Pilatus at 5,000 FT. Before action could be taken the warning ceased.
summary: A southbound pilot at 6,000 feet received a brief TCAS RA commanding a descent into a northbound Pilatus at 5,000 feet in IMC. The crew hesitated to comply because the command would have caused a collision, and the RA resolved before action was taken.

synopsis: At cruise, a B737-700 FMC center fuel tank indicated 29,440, the speed tapes, MCP speed indications all had maxed out readings and the autothrottles did not seem to have control of thrust. All indications except Center Fuel Tank quantity returned to normal during descent. A loose cannon plug was implicated.
summary: The crew experienced erroneous center fuel and speed indications enroute at FL410, causing autothrottle issues. They manually estimated fuel, updated the landing weight, and completed a normal approach and landing with no further anomalies.

synopsis: A B737 was parked at a location the crew was not accustomed to and after parking rolled back because of an uneven ramp. When the brakes were finally set to stop the aircraft an after flight attendant suffered a knee injury.
summary: The pilot stopped the aircraft on an uneven ramp after it rolled backward, causing a flight attendant to injure his knee during the sudden stop. The incident resulted in an outbound delay due to subsequent customer service issues.

synopsis: An A319 developed an uncommanded rudder movement during descent through FL240 at 320 knots significant enough to be heard in the cockpit and cause an aft galley flight attendant imbalance. No ECAM alerts coincident with the event.
summary: During descent through FL240 at 320 KTS, the flight crew experienced uncommanded rudder wagging that caused a flight attendant to fall. The pilot hand-flew the aircraft to 270 KTS, landed normally, and reported no ECAM indications or maintenance findings to explain the cause.

synopsis: A B737-800 pilot was notified of a flap overspeed and commented that this aircraft type is sensitive to environmental changes and additionally the autopilot does not aggressively respond to airspeed fluctuations.
summary: The pilot reported a brief 215 KTS airspeed indication at 6,300 FT during a 737 descent in turbulence while using autopilot level change. The pilot attributed the unobserved infraction to the airspeed indicator's excessive sensitivity to temperature fluctuations, which the autopilot could not aggressively correct.

synopsis: Air carrier flight crew on approach selected the incorrect altitude for the existing autoflight mode and the aircraft descended too low in an area of mountainous terrain just south of the airport. The flying crew initiated an escape maneuver following receipt of a GPWS Terrain warning. Of particular note was the reported reminder that the sterile cockpit environment is more appropriately described as 10,000 AGL vice MSL.
summary: During an ILS approach to OAIX Runway 03, the crew received a GPWS terrain warning after the altitude selector was inadvertently set to 7,000 feet instead of the cleared 12,500 feet. The pilot observer failed to monitor the altitude deviation, prompting a go-around and climb to recover above the minimum vectoring altitude before a successful landing.

synopsis: An EA50 pilot had difficulty entering the KRMSN waypoint in the FMS because it was on the FINGR 4 Arrival IRW transition, which was not on his route of flight and the FMS design did not allow an arrival without a transition.
summary: The pilot reported confusion during the arrival phase when ATC vectored to the KRMSN fix, which was difficult to locate on a cluttered approach plate. The pilot attributed the situation to EA50 FMS limitations regarding transition entry and unclear initial clearance instructions from ATC.

synopsis: A pilot departed a CTAF airport near ZZZ during a Presidential TFR after receiving an IFR clearance, but no transponder code. After takeoff while requesting a code, he was questioned by ATC about his behavior and later received a letter of investigation.
summary: A pilot departing a CTAF airport within a Presidential TFR received conflicting instructions from Flight Service and a TRACON controller regarding transponder codes and flight plan visibility. Although the pilot eventually received a code and completed the flight, they were later investigated for a TFR violation due to the initial procedural confusion.

synopsis: An SA-227 pilot mistook the 'W' in a NACO airport chart longitude marking (81.52W) as a taxiway designator at CLE and taxied southwest bound toward 6R after being cleared to runway 24L via Lima 2, Lima and Whiskey. The actual W taxiway is at the departure end of 24L.
summary: A pilot taxiing from an FBO to Runway 24L misread a longitude marking on the NACO chart as Taxiway W, causing an incorrect left turn on Taxiway L. Ground control directed the pilot to turn around on Pad 5, resulting in no collision threat but highlighting a chart design issue.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: A student instrument pilot flying a practice instrument approach to SGS Runway 16 had an airborne conflict with a departing aircraft, then a near miss with another aircraft already in the traffic pattern which they did not hear reporting positions.
summary: A student pilot and instructor flying a single-engine aircraft on a LOC approach to Runway 34 at SGS encountered two near-misses while transitioning to the Runway 16 pattern. The reporter attributes the incidents to inadequate briefing, flying an approach opposite the active runway, and failing to visually acquire traffic due to distraction and high airspeed.

synopsis: A Contract Repair Station Technician and an Inspector were informed that the flight crew of a customer airline's A320 aircraft had reported a flutter/tail vibration during a high-speed descent. Bushings for the Elevator Power Control Unit (PCU) rod ends were missing at the PCU attachments to the Elevator.
summary: A technician reported that missing elevator servo-control bushings, likely omitted during re-assembly due to a single-line sign-off task card lacking Required Inspection Items, caused tail vibration during high-speed descent. The incident highlighted the need for broken-down job steps and mandated inspections for primary flight controls.

synopsis: Reporter stated he observed Aircraft Y deviate from assigned altitude because of RA from Aircraft Z, causing separation loss with Aircraft X.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that Aircraft Z's altitude deviation triggered a Resolution Advisory for Aircraft Y, causing a descent that resulted in lost separation with Aircraft X. The controller attributed the incident to Aircraft Z being 100 feet below FL360, though the specific cause remained undetermined.

aircraft: Heavy Transport; Low Wing; 4 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: ZNY ARTCC Controllers state a flight had multiple flight plans and was using the one that the controllers were not using. This may have caused a loss of separation.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that Aircraft X flew an incorrect route due to multiple active flight plans, triggering system alerts that were initially ignored or deleted. The aircraft became off course and potentially lost lateral separation, prompting a recommendation to cancel invalid plans and improve verification procedures.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Enroute Controller stated workload and traffic volume was extremely high. Reporter did not notice close proximity of two aircraft until they were side by side losing required separation. Reporter stated conflict alarm never activated.
summary: An air traffic controller managing high traffic volume failed to separate Aircraft X and Aircraft Y due to workload and distraction. The aircraft passed with minimal vertical separation because the controller stopped Aircraft X's climb at FL250 instead of FL290, though no conflict alert sounded.

synopsis: Reporter states an Air Carrier on a visual approach responded to an RA due to a small aircraft in close proximity. Reporter also states LOA needs to be changed to encompass who owns what airspace in close proximity of airport and final approach course.
summary: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft X for a visual approach but failed to transfer communications, resulting in an RA when a traffic watch aircraft flew 200 feet below at 0.86 NM separation. The controller attributes this recurring conflict to an unsigned Letter of Agreement regarding airspace ownership between facilities.

synopsis: B737-800 was climbing in Vertical Speed mode, unnoticed by the flight crew. A near-stall and altitude excursion resulted.
summary: During climb, the First Officer failed to monitor the MCP after selecting FL410, allowing the autopilot to revert to Vertical Speed mode and disengage near minimum maneuvering speed. The Captain manually recovered the aircraft, resulting in a 500-foot descent before resuming the climb.

synopsis: A320 flight crew experiences a GPWS terrain warning at 5,200 FT 20 NM east of PDX and take evasive action. ATC indicated that 5,200 FT was the correct altitude and above the MVA for the area. A visual approach and landing ensues.
summary: The flight crew on an HHOOD arrival into PDX executed a GPWS escape maneuver after receiving a terrain warning while cleared to 5,200 feet. The Captain climbed to 5,450 feet into VMC, and the controller stated the aircraft was above the minimum vector altitude before a visual approach was cleared.

synopsis: Tug driver reports sliding on an ice covered ramp toward the running engine during pushback. No damage or injuries were reported.
summary: A pilot pushing back an aircraft on an icy ramp at 4 MPH lost control while turning, causing the plane to slide toward a running engine. The incident caused significant shock and elevated blood pressure for the pilot.

synopsis: A321 Captain experienced a low energy approach with the autothrust system (and the pilot flying) allowing the airspeed to drop to Vref minus 8 approaching the flare, with a hard landing to follow.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced a low-energy, hard landing in an A321 during the approach phase. The event occurred because airspeed drifted below Vapp without Autothrust intervention, likely due to prior FMGC1 malfunctions, leaving the crew with insufficient energy for a safe go-around.

synopsis: A First Officer and Maintenance Controller report how a left engine thrust reverser MEL deferral was inadvertently applied to a CRJ-200 aircraft that already had the left engine cowl anti-ice pressure relief valve deferred. Contributing factor was the lack of any cross-reference information in the thrust reverser MEL section that deferral of both items on the same side of aircraft, was not allowed.
summary: Maintenance deferred the left thrust reverser and anti-ice valve on a CRJ-200 at the gate, but the crew missed an MEL restriction prohibiting both deferrals on the same side. This oversight was discovered the next day, prompting a recommendation to add a note linking the two items in the MEL.

synopsis: A Captain and First Officer report about the loss of their crew O2 bottle pressure that read 'Zero' in cruise at FL300. Maintenance had replaced the crew O2 bottle and First Officer's oxygen mask regulator on their MD-83 aircraft prior to departure.
summary: An ATP reported that during cruise at FL300, the crew oxygen supply depleted due to a slow leak undetected after recent maintenance. The crew declared an emergency, executed QRH procedures, and landed safely at ZZZ, resulting in the aircraft being placed out of service.

synopsis: B757 flight crew reports flying a one plus hour flight with a dry ice waiver and the crew wearing CO2 monitors. During engine start both monitors alert and the Captain opens his window and the packs are turned on when available. The CO2 concentration quickly drops to zero from .7% and the flight departs.
summary: During pushback and engine start in a B-757 carrying dry ice, cockpit CO2 monitors alerted at 0.6% and 0.7% while packs were off. Crew activated packs and opened a window, clearing the alert, and continued the flight after consulting Dispatch, though the exact cause of the rapid CO2 buildup remains unknown.

synopsis: Air Carrier Dispatcher questions how to work up and send an update report to the crew for a CI500 [Cost Index] and where to get help after hours.
summary: Dispatchers assisting with a CI500 update to NRT faced a safety issue due to the unavailability of their Senior Manager. They resolved the query by contacting a Subject Matter Expert from a different facility, highlighting the risk of lacking 24/7 expert support for the four Sabre desks.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Fractional Jet Captain reported being cleared via the TBIRD1 RNAV departure from PBI expect Runway 10L. Runway 14 is requested due to wind and the clearance is revised to maintain 1,500 FT on departure. After takeoff, on the initial turn on the RNAV, it is discovered that ATC intended the crew to fly runway heading.
summary: The flight crew requested and received a Runway 14 departure with a 1,500-foot altitude assignment but flew the published TBIRD RNAV departure instead of a runway heading. The Departure Controller vectored them right, and the Tower Supervisor later explained that Runway 14 departures typically require a runway heading to avoid conflicts with other traffic.

synopsis: B737-700 Captain is informed of a runaway oven in the aft galley by flight attendants requesting permission to pull circuit breakers, which is granted. The oven does not appear to be cooling down and a halon fire extinguisher is discharged into the oven and the crew elects to run the QRH for smoke or fire that cannot be extinguished quickly and divert to a suitable airport.
summary: Flight attendants reported an aft galley oven overheat with intense heat and electrical odor, prompting the crew to discharge a Halon extinguisher and divert to ZZZ. Mechanics later identified a suspected runaway oven controller as the cause, with no injuries or structural damage reported.

synopsis: A cancelled international ferry flight was re-instated after the original flight plan had been cancelled. Believing a new plan had been filed and having been cleared by ATC the flight was completed after which the reporter was advised that there had been no ICAO flight plan filed for the re-instated flight.
summary: The pilot reported a ferry flight from MMMX to the U.S. where a lack of a primary handler caused a cancellation and subsequent re-filing of the ICAO flight plan. Although the crew received ATC clearance and departed, an attorney later claimed the flight operated without an authorized plan, despite the pilot's belief that the representative had properly filed it.

synopsis: B777 First Officer reported problems trying to access stored iPad contents in-flight.
summary: A relief pilot and the reporter experienced iPad database access failures in the van and during cruise due to a lack of Wi-Fi at the airport. The reporter's device displayed an offline account error, forcing reliance on the Captain's iPad while paper manuals were unavailable as backups.

synopsis: A First Officer reports about the difficulty flight crews will have pulling (opening) three Circuit Breakers (C/B) for the L/Main, Battery and R/Main that are referenced in their QRH procedures for a Gulfstream-200 aircraft. The three C/Bs were almost flush with the Overhead Panel and were not the same amperage capacity noted in their Flight Training Material.
summary: Pilots on a Part 91K Gulfstream-200 identified that three flush-mounted 75-amp circuit breakers required for the 'Emer Bus Fail' QRH procedure are difficult to pull bare-handed. They also noted a discrepancy where training materials incorrectly list these breakers as 60 amps and recommended replacing them for better grip.

synopsis: G-IV Captain reports flying ten passengers under FAR 135 without a flight attendant on board. After landing the reporter discovers that the passengers helped themselves to some of the amenities on board and had access to knives in the galley.
summary: On a FAR 135 passenger flight without a flight attendant, the pilot disabled the microwave and found a passenger illegally serving alcohol. The pilot refused future legs without a flight attendant due to unsecured hazardous items and legal risks.

synopsis: When cleared for a visual approach to Runway 18L at MCO, a B737NG experienced traffic conflicts and a TCAS RA with respect to traffic ahead of them. The reporter cited a company policy requiring crews to slow within 10K of minimum KIAS for the existing flap setting before extending greater deflection. He believes this policy results in the company's aircraft following significantly different vertical descent tracks from those of most carriers which do not utilize the same vertical planning regimen.
summary: During a visual approach to MCO 18L, the flight crew executed a TCAS climb after ATC pointed out traffic while the crew slowed for configuration. The pilot attributed the conflict to poor communication and ATC's failure to anticipate the reduced descent rate caused by the airline's specific flap extension speed requirements.

synopsis: When a Clearance Delivery revision to their filed clearance included the fix BAAMA or BAHMA the flight crew of a Citation X found the former in a logical position to suit their overall route and were on course toward it when they were questioned by ATC and given a vector. Only after searching diligently did the crew discovered BAHMA, the fix intended by ATC.
summary: The pilot received a ground clearance at OPF containing the waypoint BAAMA, which was pronounced as a word rather than spelled out. This led to a potential deviation because the crew navigated to the wrong fix due to confusion with a similarly named waypoint, BAHMA, despite the route appearing logical.

synopsis: C402 Captain reports discovering during a post maintenance test flight that the right landing gear will not extend. All attempts to get the right gear to extend are unsuccessful and a partial gear up landing ensues.
summary: During a training flight, the pilot encountered a right main gear failure indicated by a red unlocked light and hydraulic pressure warning. After emergency extension attempts failed, the pilot declared an emergency, shut down both engines, and landed on the left main gear, resulting in a runway excursion to the right side.

synopsis: Captain reports that during their preflight check on a B737-800 aircraft, the crew oxygen (O2) bottle pressure dropped to zero, then rebounded to 1200 PSI after crew O2 mask check Test button was released. Maintenance found O2 bottle 'Open/Close' handle safety-wired in the partially opened position.
summary: During preflight, crew oxygen pressure dropped to zero then rebounded to 1200 PSI due to an improperly connected and partially open oxygen bottle. Maintenance corrected the connection, causing an 18-minute departure delay attributed to a false indication from the bottle handle.

synopsis: When ATC advised the flight crew of Widebodied cargo jet of a low altitude alert while flying the ILS to visual conditions at IND the jet descended below the overcast and the crew noted four red PAPI lights although their glideslope indicator showed them within acceptable limits. When they corrected their path per the PAPI the glideslope indicator failed to reflect their altered vertical path. Although the reporters' noted an MD11 parked in the vicinity of the glideslope transmitter they opted to write up the anomalous glideslope indication.
summary: Two flight crews reported ILS glideslope deviations during final approach to Runway 5R, where cockpit indicators showed on-path while PAPI lights indicated low altitude. Both crews suspect interference from an MD-11 holding short of the runway, though no onboard warnings occurred and they executed safe manual landings.

synopsis: While descending on the LYNDI RNAV STAR to SAN at an assigned tactical speed of 280 KTS the First Officer inadvertently set the altitude alert at 5,000 FT for the crossing at LYNDI when cleared for the RNAV Runway 27 approach, forgetting to reset the airspeed to comply with the 250 KTS restriction below 10,000 FT.
summary: The First Officer and Captain descended below 10,000 feet at 280 KTS while cleared to cross JACKK at 10,000 feet. The pilot selected 5,000 feet in the altitude preselect before leveling, causing an inadvertent descent exceeding the 250 KTS limit due to distraction from frequency changes and approach clearance.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: A Light Transport flight crew experiences a TCAS RA with a CRJ during simultaneous instrument approaches to Runways 34L and 35L at DEN. TCAS issued a descend, then a climb, then another descend instruction to avoid the CRJ which was apparently at the wrong altitude.
summary: A crew vectored for ILS 34L in IMC encountered conflicting TCAS RAs due to a parallel aircraft on runway 35L deviating 2,000 feet below altitude and transgressing laterally. The pilot executed evasive maneuvers to avoid collision, attributing the loss of separation to ATC vectoring errors or the other aircraft's failure to follow instructions.

synopsis: After landing and a lengthy taxi the aircraft is stopped and the seat belt sign is turned off. The Lead Flight Attendant makes the arrival announcement and disarms door 1R before turning to door 1L and discovering the aircraft is not at the gate and the passengers are all standing with their luggage in the aisle. The Captain had inadvertently turned off the seatbelt sign while attempting to turn off the taxi light.
summary: A cabin crew member on an Airbus inadvertently prepared to disarm doors during taxi after the Captain accidentally turned off the seat belt sign and triggered arrival bells. The crew re-armed the doors and resumed taxiing, noting that passengers could not stow bags before reaching the gate.

synopsis: B737 Flight Attendant reports that the portable stairs used to board her aircraft are unsafe due to a large gap between the railing and the aircraft.
summary: A crew member reported that during deplaning, a dangerous gap existed between the aircraft door and the stair truck rail because ramp procedures prevent the rail from touching the aircraft. This gap was wide enough for a large person to fall through.

synopsis: C182 pilot reports flying the aircraft after the propeller has been replaced due to a large chip in the original propeller. Days later it is determined that the engine should have been torn down to check for internal damage in compliance with an AD.
summary: The pilot-in-command flew an aircraft after a propeller chip from ingested FOD was replaced, but later determined the damage required an engine breakdown per airworthiness directives. The pilot concluded they departed in a technically un-airworthy aircraft because they failed to verify the full maintenance requirements before flight.

synopsis: B737 Captain reports a TCAS RA inside DUANE during the ILS 31L approach to BFI. Evasive action is taken and the intruder passes 300 FT below the B737.
summary: Pilots on an ILS approach to 31L received a climb Resolution Advisory just after handoff from Approach to Tower. They manually climbed to avoid traffic passing 200–300 feet below, then resumed the glide-slope after the RA cleared.

synopsis: G-IV flight crew is issued a last minute hold at MUGSY, as depicted, on the LVZ4 arrival to TEB. The arrival chart shows left turns and the FMC shows a right turns which is accepted and executed. The FMC is not correct.
summary: The flight crew descended to 6,000 feet in IMC and accepted an incorrect right-turn hold from the FMS database for a left-turn procedure at MUGZY. The error stemmed from an outdated database and insufficient time to verify the clearance, though ATC successfully directed a re-entry with no separation loss.

synopsis: C172 instructor describes a hard landing with his student at the controls.
summary: During a student landing, excessive pitch corrections caused ballooning and a high sink rate, leading the instructor to execute a hard three-point landing. The aircraft returned to the ramp without further incident, though the reporter noted a go-around or earlier control transfer would have been preferable.

synopsis: LR45 Captain reports a flight plan with equipment suffix G for non RVSM but the strip received by ATC at the various ATC Centers' shows suffix L for RVSM certified and a comment stating non RVSM. One ARTCC takes exception to this situation.
summary: The Captain and First Officer of a Part 91 aircraft operating without RVSM approval experienced a flight plan equipment suffix error where 'G' was filed but displayed as 'L' to ATC. Although the crew verbally notified some sectors, Memphis Center reported they were not verbally advised of the Non-RVSM status, leading to a controller filing a report.

synopsis: PA46 pilot at FL260 reports detecting convective activity using on board Radar when none was forecast nor was it being displayed by weather datalink [Nexrad]. The decision is made to climb to FL280, out of IMC to visually avoid the cells, which is above the designed service ceiling for the PA46.
summary: The pilot flew a maximum altitude-limited aircraft at FL280, exceeding the FL270 limit, to avoid significant convective activity detected on onboard radar but not on weather datalink. The crew climbed above the weather tops for safety and descended once clear, noting the aircraft could operate at this level without damage.

synopsis: When, while descending via the EAGUL RNAV STAR to PHX, their FMS system failed to compute the need to cross HOMRR well below the maximum 16,000 FT in order to cross VNNOM 4.1 NM later between 11,000 FT and 10,000 FT, the flight crew initiated an expedited descent and exceeded the 250 KTS charted max IAS. Multiple runway changes by ATC, including a switch from a downwind arrival to land east to straight in to land west were cited by the reporter as likely contributing factors.
summary: Pilots descending on the EAGUL5 STAR into PHX crossed VNNOM high and fast after the FMS failed to account for the steep descent required from HOMRR. The crew attributed the error to high workload from multiple approach changes and a poorly designed STAR that did not warn of the conflict.

synopsis: Radio controlled model helicopter pilot flies his craft at LAL believing at the time he was in compliance with AC 91-57.
summary: A pilot operated a Radio Controlled quad-rotor helicopter at LAL to film a porch, reaching 15 feet AGL and 5 MPH. The reporter stated the aircraft remained near the operator, away from runways or other traffic, and believed the recreational flight was legal under FAA AC 91-57.

synopsis: Commercial Captain reported a discrepancy between charted procedural altitude constraints on the MAP from the ILS Runway 31C at MDW and the constraints published in the aircraft's FMS database.
summary: Pilots briefing an ILS 31C approach to Chicago-Midway noted a discrepancy between the approach plate's 2,100-foot missed approach altitude and the aircraft database's 2,600-foot setting. The reporter warns that relying on the database instead of the plate could lead to an incorrect altitude selection during a missed approach.

synopsis: An air carrier crew noted that their FMS showed crossing the MKE ILS Runway 01L final approach fix CUTMO at 2,700 feet while the commercial chart and ATC indicated crossing it at 2,600 feet.
summary: The flight crew identified a 100-foot altitude discrepancy between Jeppesen charts and the aircraft database for the CUTMO FAF during arrival at MKE Runway 01L. After confirming the correct 2,600-foot altitude with Air Traffic Control, the crew concluded the company database contained an error.

synopsis: A B737-300 flight crew descended from altitude and diverted to a nearby airport when the pressurization system malfunctioned and, during their descent and diversion they received a forward lavatory fire indication that, although evidence of a fire couldn't be verified, caused them to declare an emergency and request CFR to standby.
summary: The crew experienced cabin altitude warnings and a forward lavatory fire horn while climbing to FL350, likely caused by a wet battery in the baggage compartment. They diverted and landed overweight with fire trucks standing by, though no fire or smoke was found, and the horn was silenced by pulling the circuit breaker at the gate.

synopsis: After reaching cruise altitude, the flight attendants reported a burning electrical odor which the pilots then detected, so an emergency was declared, oxygen masks donned, and the flight returned to the departure airport while the QRH was being accomplished.
summary: The Captain and First Officer detected a burning electrical odor during climb and cruise, prompting an emergency return to the departure airport. The aircraft landed safely with no passenger injuries, though the cause remained unknown despite a recent right engine change.

synopsis: B737 experiences fluid loss and low hydraulic system A pressure during gear retraction. After gear retraction pressure is normal but quantity is very low and the decision is made to return to the departure airport for an overweight landing.
summary: After takeoff, both engine and electrical A system hydraulic low pressure lights illuminated during gear retraction. The crew returned for an approved overweight landing after declaring an emergency, with hydraulic quantity remaining between 31-35%.

synopsis: An A319 crew and the tug driver involved describe a breakaway with the aircraft hitting the tug with the number one engine running.
summary: During pushback of an A319 with one engine running, the tow bar disconnected unexpectedly, causing the aircraft to roll forward and strike the tug. The incident resulted in a flight attendant being thrown against the bulkhead, requiring passenger deplaning and a maintenance inspection.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain states runway changes added to workload upon arrival to destination.
summary: During descent below 10,000 feet into ZZZ, the flight crew faced excessive workload due to multiple runway changes from 16 to 34 and back to 16, combined with traffic advisories and vectoring. The controller's frequent last-minute decisions caused task saturation, requiring the crew to repeatedly reset avionics and request vectors to visually acquire the airport before landing safely.

synopsis: DHC-300 flight crew experiences fluctuating torque on the number one engine at rotation that quickly increases in amplitude until auto feather is triggered. An emergency is declared and flight returns to the departure airport. This engine had a history of similar incidents.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced a #1 engine torque surge and autofeather activation shortly after takeoff, triggering an emergency return and single-engine landing. The pilot reported this was the third recurrence on this aircraft and urged a complete engine overhaul or replacement to prevent future failures.

synopsis: B737-700 First Officer reports selecting a lower altitude on the MCP prior to the FAF and glideslope intercept resulting in descent below the glidepath. The Captain takes note and the reporter takes corrective action. Fatigue was cited as the main factor involved.
summary: The First Officer reset the Alt Select before glideslope capture on an ILS to 26L, causing a descent below the FAF. Fatigue led to the error, but the Captain intervened, the autopilot was disconnected, and the aircraft landed safely after re-intercepting the glide path.

synopsis: Captain notices the crew oxygen (O2) bottle handle was in the 'Close' position during their detailed pre-flight safety check of an EMB-145 aircraft. Logbook indicated the aircraft had just been released from a Heavy Maintenance Visit.
summary: The First Officer discovered an inoperative flashlight and a closed cockpit oxygen bottle valve on an aircraft returning from a C-Check in ZZZ. The mechanic repaired the flashlight while the crew opened the valve, highlighting a maintenance oversight that could have caused a dangerous emergency situation.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Air Carrier Captain experiences localizer oscillations during approach in VMC that he suspects may have been caused by an electronic device.
summary: The flight crew experienced intermittent localizer fluctuations and map shifts during an ILS approach to RDU Runway 5L starting at 4,000 feet MSL. The pilot attributed the signal interruptions to passenger portable electronic devices not in airplane mode, noting no maintenance faults were found.

synopsis: Two pilots in a PA28 Arrow experienced a complete electrical failure after takeoff. They performed the appropriate checklist and circled the field anticipating tower light gun signals. One pilot used his mobile phone to relay information on their issues and requested landing gear position confirmation. They then received a light gun signal and landed normally. They reported to suspect that the new alternator had seized.
summary: Two pilots experienced a total electrical failure immediately after gear retraction during takeoff. They executed emergency checklists, confirmed gear extension via low pass and light gun signals, and completed an uneventful landing.

synopsis: EA-500 pilot departing VPZ is given an expected departure clearance time with his clearance, but is not familiar with the phrase. After takeoff ATC assigns a 45 minute hold due to Florida airspace not accepting any aircraft. Reporter elects to return to VPZ to wait out the EDCT.
summary: The pilot departed VPZ Runway 27 under IFR but misunderstood an EDCT as a void time, failing to hold for release. SBN controllers later directed a 45-minute hold due to Florida airspace restrictions, causing the pilot to request a return before eventually completing the flight after clarification.

synopsis: Columbia 400 pilot experiences a runway excursion after landing behind a C130 doing a touch and go. The reporter believes that wake turbulence caused his loss of control.
summary: The pilot reported that after landing behind a C-130 performing a touch-and-go, the aircraft forcefully veered right off the runway due to suspected wake turbulence. No damage was found to the aircraft or runway, and the pilot attributed the incident to less than two minutes of separation without a wake turbulence warning.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reports that MLY has new Runway 18/36 and the old Runway 02/20 is closed, but the Alaska Supplement and AFD have yet to be updated by the FAA.
summary: Pilots reported that the FAA failed to update the Alaska Supplement for eight months after a new runway opened at Manley Hot Springs (MLY). The handbook still listed the closed runway, creating a discrepancy between available preflight information and actual airport status.

synopsis: General aviation pilot received modified clearance, questioned next facility about a restricted area on the modified route and received new clearance.
summary: The pilot, flying at 16,000 feet, accepted a direct clearance from Las Vegas Approach that would have entered restricted airspace R-4810 or R-4812. Upon realizing the conflict, the pilot contacted Nellis Control, reverted to the original V105 route, and avoided the restricted area.

synopsis: C182 pilot flying skydivers reports departing Runway 12 into a crop duster landing Runway 30 but intercepting the normal glideslope at very low altitude. Each pilot deviates to the left to avoid the other.
summary: A skydiving pilot taking off from Runway 12 nearly collided with a crop duster on short final for Runway 30 due to misjudging the duster's proximity. The pilot attributed the near miss to the duster flying low and not following standard traffic patterns, prompting a request for unified runway usage.

synopsis: IAI1125 flight crew experiences an altitude and track deviation while attempting to comply with the DELTA 3 RNAV arrival to SLC. Software issues and pilot error may have been factors in the deviations.
summary: During descent into SLC on the DELTA 3 arrival, the crew experienced an FMS VNAV failure to capture the 13,000 FT restriction at SPIEK, causing an altitude deviation below 13,000 FT. The pilot manually climbed back to 13,000 FT after ATC alert, suspecting the issue stemmed from recent avionics maintenance configuration.

synopsis: PA32 pilot reports pilot submitting the required international flight plan and eApis form in a timely manner prior to flight. The pilot believed that because it was VFR conditions at the time of flight, the flight could take place under VFR rules and that there was no requirement to talk to ATC and obtain a unique squawk code.
summary: The pilot departed the US under VFR conditions with a filed flight plan but assumed no ATC communication or unique squawk code was required. Consequently, the aircraft crossed the international ADIZ without two-way communication or a squawk code.

synopsis: A Contract Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports about the constant problem of having to request Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) and General Manual (GM) hard copies prior to performing maintenance actions on an Air Carrier's aircraft.
summary: A contract technician reinstalled a forward cargo bulkhead panel at ZZZ using a verbal maintenance reference from Air Carrier X, as company policy denied direct manual access. An FAA inspector questioned this practice, highlighting ongoing compliance issues caused by the lack of immediate access to Airbus manuals for contract maintenance personnel.

synopsis: ZDV ARTCC Controller stated sector was busy with traffic and receiving ride reports. While doing other duties D-Side Controller does not hear Radar Controller descend arrival into enroute traffic and loses separation.
summary: A Radar Controller managing high traffic missed a conflict between an overflight at FL310 and an arrival descending to FL270 due to tunnel vision while resolving a separate three-aircraft tie-up. The aircraft passed within 5 miles without a prior alert, and the subsequent sector could not prevent the loss of separation.

synopsis: A Captain became ill after deicing when the engine bleed air switches were turned ON with the engines off. Apparently deice fluid in the APU bleed air entered the left pack.
summary: The flight crew experienced deicing fluid fumes in the cockpit during the Post Deicing Checklist after turning on bleed switches, causing nausea and removal from the flight sequence. The crew attributed the incident to the Before Deicing Checklist failing to direct packs to be turned off, allowing fluid in the APU ducting to enter the left pack.

synopsis: A B737-300 flight crew diverted to a nearby airport after suffering the loss of the A hydraulic system.
summary: The crew experienced a #1 Engine A system pump low pressure light and rapid hydraulic fluid loss during climb after leaving ZZZ. They declared an emergency, diverted to a nearby airport, and made a normal landing.

synopsis: B737 Captain laments that his company will not allow use of an autobrake setting that produces a negative stopping margin when landing performance is calculated, requiring either 0 (manual braking) or max, even though the the calculations are wildly pessimistic. When landing on an unrestricted runway, medium autobrakes will easily stop the aircraft at maximum landing weight in 4,000 FT while the calculations show that much more than 5,000 FT would be required.
summary: A pilot landing a fully loaded B737-800 on a short runway reported that inaccurate calculated landing data forced the selection of autobrake 0 instead of the safer setting 3. The pilot manually braked the aircraft to a safe stop, concluding that the company's policy requiring the deactivation of autobrakes due to flawed data is unsafe.

synopsis: A320 First Officer experiences an ECAM for 'AIR ENG1 BLEED ABNORM PR' shortly after takeoff. QRH procedures are complied with, which included turning off the associated bleed valve. Questions arise concerning continuing the flight over the Rockies and climbing to higher altitude with one bleed system powering two packs. The crew elects to divert for maintenance, land overweight and continue to their original destination with another plane.
summary: The crew encountered an Engine 1 bleed abnormal pressure warning shortly after takeoff, triggering a QRH procedure that secured the bleed. Due to communication failures with Dispatch and Maintenance regarding altitude restrictions and fuel, the Captain diverted to ZZZ for an overweight landing, where a mechanic later suspected an incorrectly installed, leaking bleed valve.

synopsis: Air Carrier Captain laments the lack of high speed internet connections at many company flight planning facilities and the additional time required to print flight documents and do flight planning. Flight planning at the aircraft is especially maligned.
summary: Flight crews reported that slow internet and continuous time-outs at Hong Kong (VHHH) prevented proper preflight planning and access to critical weather data. The lack of reliable wireless connectivity in flight operations and at the aircraft may impact flight safety.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: After parking and releasing the brakes, an Air Carrier aircraft rolled backward about a foot because of ramp slope. The Captain was concerned about ramp personnel safety but was told they know to stay clear.
summary: The pilot released brakes upon the Ramp Agent's signal, causing the aircraft to roll back 6-12 inches at a sloped gate. No injuries or damage occurred, as the ramp crew follows standard practice to wait for this expected rollback before approaching.

synopsis: When the parking brake light illuminated in flight the flight crew of an EMB-145 declared an emergency and returned to their departure airport for maintenance attention. The landing and braking were normal on arrival.
summary: During initial climbout, the crew observed a flickering parking brake light after dialing a frequency on the number 2 RMU. They returned to the departure airport with fire trucks standing by, suspecting a link to an earlier 'TO CONFIG' error, but landed normally with functional brakes.

synopsis: An MD-82 Captain reported that when flying the RNAV Runway 27 approach to SAN the charted glidepath (3.5 degrees) inside the FAF failed to place the aircraft vertically at a point from which a stabilized approach and touchdown could be accomplished. Per a later conversation with the First Officer of that flight the reporter learned the problem appears to have been resolved via discussions and subsequent actions between government, airline and pilot union representatives.
summary: The pilot reported that the approach procedure places the aircraft too high at the Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA) for a normal landing, indicated by all-white PAPI lights. A safe landing was achieved only by breaking out 500–600 feet above MDA, whereas a previous attempt with a ceiling near MDA required a go-around.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A First Officer just returned from furlough and never having flown the DCA Runway 19 River Visual was nearly a 1,000 FT low to start with and only after the Captain commanded leveling twice did he return to profile.
summary: During a River Visual approach to Runway 19 at DCA, a relatively new First Officer descended below the recommended 3,000 feet due to difficulty identifying the river and confusing ADI guidance. The Captain intervened to stop the descent, and the aircraft landed uneventfully after ATC queried the low altitude.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air carrier Captain states ATC issued traffic but did nothing to prevent a potential conflict which resulted in a RA.
summary: Pilots on a visual approach to Runway 10L received a TCAS climb RA after ATC issued an early base turn clearance despite known traffic. The crew followed the RA, landed safely, and attributed the conflict to ATC clearing the visual approach with unresolved traffic.

synopsis: An acrimonious exchange resulted when supervisors from passenger boarding and Inflight Service Departments demanded that a Flight Attendant (the reporter) open the A330's 2R cabin level passenger service door from inside the aircraft in direct violation of the company's Flight Attendant's Operations Manual forbidding doing so, the intended reason being to remove a passenger's electric wheel chair from the aircraft to a catering truck and thence to be boarded in cargo. After compelling the Attendant to do so they discovered the lift vehicle intended to remove the chair was unable to access the door opening.
summary: A Flight Attendant was forced by an Agent Supervisor and an Inflight Supervisor to open an aircraft door from the inside to load an electric wheelchair, violating safety manuals. This resulted in a thirty-minute delay and exposed the crew to a four-story fall hazard, as the lift failed to reach the door and the issue could have been resolved via the jetway.

synopsis: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) cites a lack of communication between himself and a Maintenance Controller as the primary cause of their releasing an A320 aircraft with an incomplete MEL deferral of Air Conditioning Pack-1 for a Pack Regulator fault.
summary: The pilot and Maintenance Controller applied only MEL 21-51-01C for a Pack Regulator fault, missing the required MEL 21-52-01D. The aircraft flew one flight before the second MEL was applied due to poor communication and potential fatigue.

synopsis: While operating in the traffic pattern with a flight instructor, a student pilot did not comprehend the landing pattern flow and turned in front of an aircraft on a straight in approach. Following prompting by the Tower Controller, the instructor recognized the conflict, took over the controls, and extended the base leg. The Tower provided a clearance for a circle back to final approach for landing.
summary: An instructor and student in a training aircraft inadvertently flew in front of another aircraft on final approach after the student misidentified traffic during an extended downwind. The instructor took control, executed a go-around, and rejoined the pattern for a safe landing following a 270-degree right turn.

synopsis: PA-28 pilot reports encountering IMC on a night VFR flight at 11,500 feet and requesting an IFR clearance. The clearance is granted with a climb to 16,000 feet due to MEA considerations, which was not expected by the reporter. At 14,000 feet the airspeed indicator stops working and a descent is initiated and a request is made to divert to a suitable airport, which is accomplished.
summary: A pilot flying VFR at night encountered clouds and requested an IFR clearance, but Air Traffic Control assigned an unsafe altitude of 16,000 feet exceeding the aircraft's capability. The pilot experienced hypoxia and an airspeed indicator failure, likely due to ice, before asserting authority to descend and land safely at Shively.

synopsis: Reporter states traffic was issued by ATC and reporter had NMAC with traffic while in close proximity to destination airport.
summary: The pilot of a single-engine turboprop on a visual approach to Provo, UT, reported a near-midair collision with VFR traffic. Despite ATC advisories, the other aircraft emerged close to the left wingtip at the same altitude while the pilot was turning right and descending.

synopsis: EC135 pilot experiences loss of GPS signal during departure from MYF. Normal operation returns a few minutes later.
summary: The pilot experienced a temporary loss of satellite reception on a Garmin 530 GPS unit during initial climbout from MYF. The unit reacquired satellites a few minutes later.

synopsis: HS125 flight crew new to the aircraft, report getting well to the left of the localizer before realizing a mistake in mode selection on the MCP.
summary: The flight crew misselected the navigation mode while intercepting the ILS 13R approach at Seattle Boeing Field, causing a significant left deviation. Despite a crosswind delaying correction, the crew stabilized the approach for an uneventful landing, though the error highlighted risks from low type experience and potential traffic conflicts.

aircraft: Cessna Aircraft Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Reporters describe incident with one aircraft trying multiple approaches and buzzing the Tower. Aircraft turns into departing traffic path, pilot later reports to ATC that aircraft had a yaw problem leading to the left turn.
summary: A medevac pilot flying Aircraft X on a missed approach from ILS 19C at IAD ignored ATC instructions and turned left, causing a potential loss of separation with departing Aircraft Y. The pilot attributed the maneuver to a yaw damper issue, while the report cites unstable approaches, poor judgment, and equipment problems as causes.

synopsis: B737-700 Captain reported inadvertent flap retraction when arming the alternate flap position switch in response to a trailing edge flap abnormality. The reporter went on to recommend changes to the procedure to minimize the possibility of reoccurence.
summary: During final approach, the crew initiated a go-around when flaps stopped extending, then discovered the Alternate Flaps Position switch was inadvertently left in the UP position, causing flap retraction. The Captain corrected the switch to OFF, allowing a safe landing, and attributed the error to the switch's poor visibility and lack of a verification step in the checklist.

synopsis: During descent in icing conditions the crew of an EMB-145 received multiple anti-ice fail messages, declared an emergency, and requested an immediate descent to lower altitude. The Captain then realized the anti-ice bleed sources were incorrectly selected to the APU and were then properly selected to the engines, restoring normal operation.
summary: During a reposition flight descent to 11,000 feet, the crew encountered anti-ice failure warnings caused by the First Officer failing to switch bleeds from the APU to engines during the 10,000-foot flow. The Captain corrected the bleed configuration, extinguishing the warnings and allowing the crew to cancel the declared emergency.

synopsis: CRJ-700 Captain reported receiving erroneous GPWS warnings on an approach in IMC, resulting in deviation from assigned altitude. Reporter was critical of company Maintenance response to this ongoing equipment malfunction.
summary: During an ILS approach in IMC, the Captain's radio altimeter malfunctioned, triggering false GPWS terrain warnings and forcing an escape maneuver that deviated from ATC clearance. The pilot attributed the event to a repeat, unresolved maintenance issue with the radio altimeter system.

synopsis: B757-200 pilot reported a 'L AFT ENTRY DOOR' EICAS message on climb out through 9,000 feet. An emergency was declared and the flight returned to departure airport.
summary: During climb out at 9,000 feet, the crew received a left aft entry door EICAS message and observed cabin pressure anomalies after the door handle moved and light appeared. The crew declared an emergency, descended, and made an overweight landing; the cause was unknown, though the pilot suggested foreign objects may have fouled the door.

synopsis: B777 Captain reported his aircraft 'just made' the BGC2A SID restrictions even with full takeoff power, which was not required by the procedure.
summary: The pilot reported that full takeoff power was required to meet SID restrictions and avoid terrain before turning away from the SE procedure. They concluded that the BGC2A SID should be prohibited if reduced power is used, as no derates are needed to reach a safe altitude.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Inspector was informed that a slip bushing for the Left-Hand (LH) Main Landing Gear (MLG) Auxiliary (Aux) Retract actuator was found missing on a CRJ-900 aircraft, approximately three weeks after he inspected the actuator installation. The Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) Figures (drawings) were incorrect.
summary: Maintenance personnel on a CRJ-900 found a missing slip bushing on the left main landing gear auxiliary retract actuator during routine overnight maintenance. The error resulted from an incorrect Aircraft Maintenance Manual illustration and note, which was later corrected by a temporary revision, with fatigue cited as a contributing factor.

synopsis: SR-22 pilot reported he became hypoxic when his oxygen bottle emptied at 16,000 feet.
summary: The pilot and passenger, cruising at 16,000 feet in holding, ran out of portable oxygen, causing the pilot to become hypoxic and fly erratically. After the controller vectored the aircraft for an ILS approach, the pilot landed safely, noting that hypoxic pilots often fail to recognize their condition.

synopsis: C320 pilot reported his landing gear failed to fully retract after takeoff, and would not extend fully even after manual crank procedures were followed. Aircraft landed with partial gear and no injuries were reported.
summary: The pilot experienced a nose gear retraction failure after takeoff, hearing a loud bang and unable to lock the gear despite cycling attempts and manual cranking. The aircraft was diverted and landed gear-up with the nose held off as long as possible, resulting in no injuries to occupants.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Recip Eng
synopsis: Pilot declared emergency and ATC had issues with what pilot needed to do to get aircraft on the ground as soon as possible.
summary: A pilot declared an emergency due to a loud thumping noise at 5,000 feet and descended without clearance to 1,800 feet to become visual for a safe landing. Although ATC restricted descent to 2,800 feet and claimed the pilot violated rules, the pilot landed safely and disputes the controller's authority to override emergency actions.

synopsis: CE750 First Officer reported descending below charted altitude in IMC on approach to BIKF because the altimeter was mis-set by 1 inch of mercury. ATC called the flight when they received a low altitude alert.
summary: Pilots of a CE750 descending for an ILS 20 approach into BIKF set their altimeters to 29.82 inches instead of the correct 28.82 inches. ATC alerted them to a 1,100-foot altitude deviation, prompting a climb to the assigned 2,000 feet before a successful landing.

synopsis: The pilot of a C182 felt unable to go-around following an unstable approach and departed the end of the runway during rollout.
summary: A C182 pilot practicing landings turned base too early, resulting in a high-speed approach and a bounced landing. The aircraft slid off the runway end into grass after braking, but post-incident inspections confirmed no damage and the airplane was safe to fly.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
