summary: A flight crew departing IAH on the MMUGS ONE SID deviated 500 feet above 4,000 feet due to ambiguous chart text and PDC phrasing regarding climb constraints. The crew reported that six similar deviations occurred that day, prompting a recommendation to rewrite the procedure and improve training.

synopsis: While researching a question from another Dispatcher the reporter discovered that--a few days earlier--a transpacific flight had been dispatched under aegis of FAA 'Operations Specification (OpSpec) B043' which allows the use of a hybrid mix of domestic and International fuel reserve requirements but is predicated on being able to precisely fix their position at least once each hour. In the instant case that degree of precision had not been possible for the entire flight and, thus, those portions of the flight during which such precision was not possible the appropriate international reserves had to have been aboard. The calculated reserve fuel on board had been just 45 minutes, consistent with precise navigation 100% of the flight.
summary: A dispatcher discovered a flight in North Pacific Airspace along A590 may have been released inappropriately under OpSpec B043 due to a misinterpretation of rules regarding position fixing and reserve fuel. The error likely stemmed from discussions between dispatch and operations management, prompting a recommendation for updated training and manual procedures.

synopsis: CRJ-200 First Officer experiences confusion attempting to 'climb via the RITAA 1 maintaain 11,000 FT' departing IAH. The first two crossing restrictions are overshoot which is noted by ATC.
summary: The flight crew departed on the RITAA1 RNAV SID at IAH and violated two altitude crossing restrictions due to confusion over the "except maintain 11,000 FT" clearance phraseology. After ATC notified them of the deviation, the crew descended to comply with the SID restrictions.

synopsis: Hawker 900XP Captain reports getting low on the DELTA 3 arrival to SLC after the landing runway is changed in the FMC and the arrival is reloaded.
summary: Pilots flying the DELTA 3 arrival into SLC failed to notice their autopilot remained in VVS mode instead of capturing the glidepath after a runway change. This resulted in a low altitude alert at 12,500 FT MSL, requiring an immediate climb to 13,000 FT MSL.

synopsis: A quick rejected landing and go-around by the flight crew of a Beech Baron averted a likely collision with the reporter's maintenance vehicle when he pulled onto the runway without a thorough scan of the pattern and without a functioning radio to monitor CTAF transmissions at the uncontrolled airport.
summary: A maintenance vehicle operator entered Runway 31 without a functioning radio or proper hold-line stop, nearly colliding with a landing Beechcraft Baron 55. The pilot avoided a serious accident by retracting gear and accelerating to pass over the vehicle, which the operator attributed to distraction and complacency.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: A pilot suggested a Hot Spot on ILG airport charts at the intersection of Runway 32 and 1, at Taxiway F1 and F2 after he failed to turn onto Runway 32 at Taxiway F2 even having two electronic charts available.
summary: The pilot taxied past Taxiway F2 toward Runway 1 instead of Runway 32 while using two electronic charts. Ground Control challenged the deviation, issued an amended clearance for Runway 1, and the aircraft stopped immediately with no other traffic nearby.

synopsis: PA25 pilot experiences a runway excursion after landing with the aircraft pulling to the right and departing the right edge of the runway despite full left rudder and brake. Damage occurs to the propeller and tailwheel and the right brake is found to be leaking fluid.
summary: The pilot of a PA-25 Pawnee veered right off the paved runway onto dirt during landing, striking an embankment and damaging the propeller and tail wheel. The deviation was attributed to differential surface friction or a leaking right main brake.

synopsis: Communication between FLM and CPC did was not complete causing confusion over if an UAV aircraft had permission to leave one warning area for another. Major problem with the aircraft was that it was a known NORDO on departure and while flying.
summary: A UAV pilot and an FLM issued conflicting clearances for Aircraft X to transit from A3 to A4, causing a potential Whiskey Alert. The controller attributed the incident to the FLM issuing a clearance without sector approval and the UAV failing to squawk 7600 despite alleged communication loss.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: P31 Controller reports of traffic almost exceeding the abilities of the two controllers working everything combined in the TRACON due to staffing.
summary: Air traffic controllers managed 59 operations, including unscheduled military practice approaches, on a single radar scope due to staffing shortages from retirements. Although no errors occurred, the reporter attributes the unsafe and inefficient conditions to facility management's refusal to use overtime and a lack of coordination with military squadrons.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: D10 Controller reports of another controller not utilizing the PACP correctly by not displaying the full data block while in the airspace.
summary: An instructor and trainee observed Aircraft X climbing into prearranged airspace without a full data block. The reporter attributed this to D10 controllers failing to follow procedures, expressing concern that this attitude compromises traffic monitoring safety.

synopsis: A B737-700 crew flying the JAGGR 2 RNAV expected a Runway 16L visual but ATC assigned Runway 17L RNP and while the Captain was programming the FMC, all speeds and crossing restrictions dropped. The aircraft transitioned to CWS, out of VNAV and accelerated above the Arrival speed constraints.
summary: During descent into DEN on the JAGGR2 arrival, the crew exceeded airspeed and possibly altitude between DANDD and HARUM due to a communication breakdown regarding runway selection. The Captain's FMC changes while the First Officer searched for plates caused VNAV disengagement and loss of speed restrictions, attributed to poor CRM and the Captain's heavy accent.

synopsis: A321 Captain reports receiving a company message during takeoff which is ignored until safely airborne. The message reads W/B do not takeoff. Takeoff weight had increased by 2,000 LBS with flap setting and V-speed changes.
summary: The First Officer continued the takeoff after noticing a company message on the ECAM, later discovering the aircraft was 2,000 lbs overweight and required a flaps 2 configuration. The pilot attributed the error to delayed Weight and Balance updates and poor message visibility, recommending audible alerts and additional staff.

synopsis: An A320 Dispatcher received a call from an upset Captain who received a Load Planning message during the takeoff roll which stated 'Do Not Takeoff Without Corrected Weight and Balance.' He did not reject.
summary: The Captain received a Load Planning weight and balance warning during takeoff roll but elected not to abort. The reporter states this should not recur and requires final weight and balance data to be sent sooner.

synopsis: EMB145 Captain believes that his company's aircraft are involved in chronic smoke and fume events and the flight crews are not being given notice of occurrences or follow up of mechanical history of the aircraft.
summary: Flight crews reported recurring smoke and fume events on an Embraer aircraft, citing a lack of maintenance follow-up and crew notification despite an accelerating trend of 40 incidents since March 2014. The reporter requested enhanced reporting procedures, improved training on fume recognition and physiological effects, and better coordination with aeromedical and rescue teams.

synopsis: The flight crew of an A320 mistakenly responded to a line up and wait clearance intended for another aircraft and was asked to vacate the runway for the intended recipient. The Captain reporter cited excessively complicated ground movement procedures at IAH, a short taxi to Runway 15L and an inexperienced and overtaxed First Officer as contributing factors.
summary: The Captain and First Officer entered departure-only Runway 15L at IAH after the First Officer misheard a clearance due to task saturation and complex ground procedures. Tower subsequently instructed them to exit the runway, though no collision occurred and the flight departed shortly after.

synopsis: An A320 flight crew, cleared to depart IAH on the BNDTO RNAV SID, CRGER transition, inexplicably departed BNDTO on the JCT transition. ATC noted the deviation and asked the crew to call after arriving at their destination. Noteworthy was the fact that JCT VOR was also an enroute fix on their flight plan not withstanding their assignment of the CRGER transition.
summary: The flight crew departed Runway 15L on the BNDTO RNAV SID but flew the wrong transition to JCT instead of CRGER due to FMC programming errors. ATC vectored them direct to CUZZZ to resume the correct path, noting this error had occurred over 100 times recently.

synopsis: A B737 First Officer expressed concern about the altitude dichotomies on the BNDTO RNAV SID from IAH, believing that a 'climb via' clearance is incompatible with a procedure that depicts both 'at or below 500' and 'at or above 13,000 feet' restrictions during the climb to cruise but also contains a 'ROUTING' note advising all departures to maintain 4,000 feet. Reporter believes their airways' clearance should have stated cleared via the procedure, maintain 4,000 feet and the 'climb via' the SID clearance given only by departure control as appropriate.
summary: The flight crew received a PDC clearance to "CLIMB VIA SID" which included a "MAINTAIN 4,000 feet" restriction, causing confusion as they expected the instruction to negate the altitude limit. The reporter attributes this ambiguity to the differing interpretation of "CLIMB VIA" on the ground versus in flight, recommending specific altitude instructions be issued separately.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An air carrier crew on vectors about 50 NM from EWR had a near miss with a relatively large turboprop aircraft at about 7,000 FT and executed a descending escape maneuver.
summary: Pilots on a flight to EWR received a climb clearance from ATC that conflicted with a TCAS descent resolution advisory due to a rapidly climbing, uncommunicating turboprop. The crew aggressively followed the TCAS command to descend, avoiding a collision while passengers became ill from the maneuver.

synopsis: B737 Captain reports missing the 4,000 FT restriction in the routing section of the BNDTO 1 RNAV SID description. ATC detects the error.
summary: The flight crew misinterpreted the PDC clearance for the BNDTO1 SID, believing they could climb to FL220 while missing the 4,000-foot restriction at SHAAK. The Departure Controller corrected them to maintain 4,000 feet, noting this was a common error with no separation issues.

synopsis: An A320 flight crew departing IAH on the BNDTO RNAV SID departed BNDTO on the JCT transition in stead of the CRGER as shown in the revised portion of their PDC.
summary: The crew climbing from IAH on the BNDTO One departure was vectored by ATC after passing BNDTO due to a suspected routing error. The discrepancy was caused by a confusing PDC display showing an unselected transition that differed from the flight plan and MCDU.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: ZHU issued an air carrier a late DESCEND VIA GUSHR ONE RNAV Arrival clearance descent to IAH and then began issuing vectors when the crew advised unable to meet waypoint altitude constraints.
summary: Flight crew flying an IAH RNAV arrival received delayed ATC clearances, resulting in excessive altitude at FL240 and FMS VNAV errors. The crew rejected multiple "descend via" instructions as impossible, forcing ATC to vector the aircraft off the arrival due to late clearance issuance.

synopsis: Regional jet Captain lands on Runway 14 at DIK planning on using Taxiway A for taxi. Taxiway A is closed and a U turn is not advisable. A NOTAM closing Taxiway A had expired but a new one was issued, which the crew did not have access to.
summary: The flight crew of a Regional Jet at Dickinson (DIK) blocked Runway 14 after attempting to exit onto a closed Taxiway A due to a missing NOTAM. The aircraft was repositioned by a tug after the airport supervisor confirmed the closure was active under a reissued NOTAM not yet in the system.

synopsis: An air ambulance helicopter was parked idling as a patient was transferred from an ambulance on a stretcher. The empty stretcher then rolled into the tail rotor forcing the pilot to promptly shut it down and assess damage.
summary: During a hot load at ground idle, a stretcher rolled into the helicopter's tail rotor while the pilot remained at the controls. The incident occurred because no tail rotor guide was designated, and the crew approached the aircraft out of the pilot's view.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: After takeoff both MD-80 Main Electric Horizontal Stabilizer trim switches were inoperative, so maintaining a slow airspeed to control the aircraft, the crew worked through the QRH and declared an emergency for a return. The Alternative Trim did function for the landing.
summary: The Captain hand-flew a DC-9 departure after discovering the primary trim switches failed to trim nose-down, requiring manual thrust reduction to control pitch. The crew stabilized the aircraft, completed checklists, and returned for a normal landing after burning fuel to stay under maximum weight, attributing the issue to a primary trim malfunction.

synopsis: Two pilots report about a Captain's right rudder pedal attach bolt that sheared (broke), while setting the parking brake on a B757-200 aircraft when they stopped to hold short for another aircraft to land. Aircraft towed back to gate.
summary: While taxiing to hold short at ZZZ, the Captain's right rudder pedal assembly separated due to a sheared pushrod bolt when setting the parking brake. The crew used the First Officer's brakes to stop, shut down engines, and requested a tow back to the ramp for repairs.

synopsis: When cleared to descend via the KIDDZ RNAV STAR the pilot flying began a descent from FL240 prior to MMAXX which must be crossed at or above FL240. The pilot not flying of the ERJ promptly advised the descent was premature and they corrected. Both reporters addressed their concerns about the complexity of the arrival and the high workload it incurs during a phase of flight that includes conflicting demands on the flight crew's attention.
summary: The flight crew descended prematurely on the KIDDZ1 RNAV arrival to HOU before crossing MMAXX. The non-flying pilot corrected the altitude to FL240, attributing the error to the complex STAR requiring undivided attention during a phase with other required duties.

synopsis: A B757-200 Flight Attendant noticed Overhead Cabin EXIT signs at Row 11 A-C and 32 A-C where no exits exists and speculated Maintenance had used an incorrect seat plan while the aircraft was undergoing maintenance. Concerns also raised that passengers may pile up during a darkened environment at seat rows with incorrectly located EXIT signs.
summary: A cabin crew member reported finding unexplained overhead exit signs at Rows 11 and 36 during a pre-flight safety demonstration. The reporter noted these signs were located where no exits exist and expressed concern they could cause passenger confusion in an emergency.

synopsis: A Lead Flight Attendant reported that all the flight attendants on a leg were extremely fatigued, dizzy, nauseous and light headed. After landing the flight attendant crew were met by paramedics and sent to a medical facility where the physician said the issue was political not medical. One Flight Attendant reported a dirty socks odor.
summary: During cruise, all flight attendants experienced symptoms like dizziness and nausea, possibly from a "dirty socks" odor noted before takeoff. Paramedics and doctors evaluated the crew post-landing, but the cause remains undetermined as the Captain did not file a report and the flight deck crew validated no issues.

synopsis: A Line, Lead Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) and a Maintenance Controller describe their involvement with an MEL deferral of an Additional Center Tank (ACT) Fuel Transfer Valve that was incorrectly moved to the 'open' position instead of the 'closed' position, on an A321 aircraft. Lead Technician also notes the reference pictures in the Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) for the Transfer Valve Motor actuator position indicators are confusing.
summary: A mechanic incorrectly set an A321's Additional Center Tank transfer valve to 'open' instead of 'closed' during MEL application due to poor lighting and viewing angles. The pilot reported unintended fuel transfer, prompting maintenance to correct the valve position upon the aircraft's arrival.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A Corporate Jet flight crew, departing Runway 15R at IAH failed to level at 4,000 while flying the BNDTO RNAV SID from IAH. After reading the INITIAL CLIMB text clearing them to fly the charted route and having been cleared to 'climb via' the SID they climbed so as to cross SCAMM at or below 5,000 as charted. Departure Control took exception to climb beyond 4,000 FT as was shown in the ROUTING text.
summary: The flight crew and Houston Departure Controller experienced a clearance discrepancy where the Pre-Departure Clearance lacked an initial altitude for the BNDTO ONE RNAV departure. The controller assigned 16,000 feet after the crew clarified the missing restriction, and the PIC was instructed to contact the TRACON regarding the new SID issue.

synopsis: A narrow body Airbus First Officer reported that after verifying the IVANE RNAV crossing restrictions the flight received spacing vectors then returned to the arrival where he discovered subsequent crossing restrictions were as much as 3,000 FT below the charted constraints. ATC Descend Via phraseology standardization was also questioned.
summary: During descent, the Captain initiated a steep descent based on an unclear ATC clearance and a derisive attitude, causing the FMS to project fixes 1,000 to 3,000 feet below charted floors. The First Officer failed to monitor the flight path due to the Captain's behavior, requiring manual intervention to arrest the descent and prevent further deviations.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: After departing on the IAH BNDT1 RNAV, a corporate Captain climbed to 5,000 FT because the chart design listed 5,000 FT in bold distracting from the ROUTING verbiage, 'MAINTAIN 4,000;' with its minimized font and distance location.
summary: The pilot departed IAH on the BNDT1 departure and was questioned by ATC for reaching 5,000 feet at SCAMM instead of the required 4,000 feet. The error occurred because the pilot relied on the bolded 5,000-foot restriction on the SID chart and FMS, overlooking the smaller 4,000-foot text in the routing box.

synopsis: A PA-24 at 1,400 FT in the ZZZ SFRA made an emergency landing at a major Class B airport because of a rough running engine. The engine appeared normal, so he continued to his filed destination where a Mechanic cleared the aircraft. On the next departure, the problem appeared again forcing a return to land.
summary: The pilot experienced severe engine roughness and airspeed loss while flying below 1,500 feet MSL in the SFRA, prompting an emergency diversion and landing. The issue recurred shortly after a subsequent takeoff, forcing another return and grounding the aircraft for a thorough mechanical review.

synopsis: EA-500 pilot reports encountering severe turbulence at FL310 while attempting to avoid thunderstorms using XM Radar and altitude deviations occur. The next XM update showed the gap chosen as closing up.
summary: The pilot deviated northeast of GCK at FL340 based on XM radar, but severe turbulence in a closing weather gap caused autopilot disconnect and altitude deviations of 600–800 feet. This resulted in a conflict with traffic at FL320, attributed to XM data lag and pilot complacency regarding the weather opening.

synopsis: SZD-50 Puchacz glider canopy opened in flight and shattered, so the pilot closed what remained of the canopy and landed without a problem. This aircraft's canopy has been the subject of past failures.
summary: The pilot of an SZD-50 Puchacz glider experienced a canopy failure during a left-wing low slip, causing the canopy to open and shatter. The pilot attributed the event to possible latch dislodgement, improper closure, or mechanical failure, noting the aircraft landed safely despite the damage.

synopsis: An A330 crew reported that after a North Atlantic Track change they had difficulty entering the coordinates in the FMGC because limited FMGC memory required the waypoints be entered with the full nine digit latitudes and longitudes. They then had a track deviation when the Controller unaccustomed to hearing the full nine North, West and East waypoint digits incorrectly confirmed an erroneous waypoint which the crew read exactly from the FMGC display.
summary: The flight crew experienced multiple delays and MEL issues before deviating from their oceanic route due to incorrect latitude/longitude coordinates entered into the FMGEC after a Gander ATC clearance change. The crew corrected the navigation error by re-entering the full coordinates, resulting in a filed navigation report by ATC.

synopsis: A General Aviation pilot reports being cleared for the visual approach to Runway 24 at BHM but becomes confused and lines up for Runway 6. A loud squeal from the radio caused by TV antennas 7 NM southwest of the field causes the radio volume to be turned way down and calls from the Tower go unheard.
summary: The pilot, en route to BHM during a visual approach, mistook Runway 6 for Runway 24 and landed on the wrong runway. The error occurred because the pilot turned the radio volume down to zero to avoid interference from nearby TV towers, preventing the Tower from issuing a correction.

synopsis: BE35 pilot experiences a catastrophic engine failure at 8,000 FT within easy gliding range of a suitable airport and lands safely. A large hole is found over the number five cylinder.
summary: The pilot experienced a catastrophic engine failure at 8,000 feet, likely caused by undetected metal flaking, resulting in a hole in the #5 cylinder casing. Despite the sudden loss of power, the pilot executed a safe emergency landing at ZZZ with no injuries or fire.

synopsis: King Air flight crew experiences two consecutive TAWS alerts during two ILS 32 approaches into BBG resulting in go arounds. Other aircraft are successfully landing off the ILS 32 approach, so the TAWS is disabled and the third approach is successful.
summary: The Captain and Co-Captain executed two missed approaches on ILS 32 into BBG due to TAWS warnings while stabilized. They subsequently inhibited the TAWS terrain feature and landed safely, though they later acknowledged disabling the system was imprudent without confirming the database or equipment status.

synopsis: C182 pilot experiences a rough running engine at 6,000 FT and accepts vectors to the nearest suitable airport. Arriving overhead at 4,900 FT with the engine still producing power, a gliding circling approach is planned and executed successfully. Maintenance discovers that bent pushrods were the cause of the rough running engine.
summary: The pilot reported an in-flight engine failure and violent shaking in a Cessna 182, caused by two bent pushrods discovered post-landing. The pilot declared a Mayday, vectored to an alternate airport, and executed an emergency landing after the engine failed again during the approach.

synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reports that the runways at FMH do not have REIL's and the beginning of the runway is difficult to judge.
summary: A pilot reported that during night VMC operations, the facility lacked runway approach end identifier lights because green threshold lights were installed with black lenses. This absence of threshold indication on Runways 5 and 14 created a risk of landing short due to the lack of approach lights.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) Inspector was informed he had installed two O-Rings on each Fuel Injector on a Teledyne-Continental IO-550-N, Non-Turbocharged Engine where only one was required. The Cessna-350 aircraft engine had run rough on three flight legs. Two Injector O-rings had come with a Gasket Kit for each of the six cylinders he replaced.
summary: A mechanic mistakenly installed two O-rings on fuel injectors of a Teledyne-Continental IO-550 engine during cylinder replacement, causing rough running and a spark plug failure. The pilot flew the aircraft between three locations despite the power loss before a technician identified the error at the final destination.

synopsis: P80 Controller describes a large jump of an aircraft on final, possibly caused by fusion radar.
summary: An air traffic controller reported a potential radar display error on the new FUSION system while managing Aircraft X on an ILS RWY 28R approach and a faster air carrier on a visual approach to RWY 28L. The controller observed Aircraft X's target jump over half a mile between localizers, suspecting a system malfunction rather than actual flight path deviation, and plans to investigate with QA.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: ZME controller reports of problems associated with similar sounding and written intersections. Confusion of aircraft that may or may not be coming into their airspace.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that erroneous flight plans for Aircraft X and Y, caused by confusing intersections JAWSS and JAWWS, passed through ZJX and ZTL uncorrected. ZTL later instructed the controller to remove strips for both aircraft via phone, bypassing automated coordination despite the known route error.

synopsis: B737 First Officer reports noticing the Captain rubbing his jaw and right ear then turning red and convulsing in his seat. The Captain regained his composure and stated he had just blown out his ear drum. Flight continues to destination.
summary: During cruise at FL340, the Captain suffered a ruptured eardrum and convulsed, causing a 600-pound fuel imbalance while the First Officer protected flight controls. The Captain declined medical attention or descent, deemed the imbalance within limits, and the flight landed uneventfully.

synopsis: B737 Captain reports confusion during vectors off the KIDDZ 1 arrival due to similar sounding fix names and expectation bias. The Captain suggests that in order for these complex RNAV arrivals to be flown successfully they need to be entered into the FMC at altitude and not altered by ATC during descent.
summary: Pilots flying a Boeing 737 on the KIDDZ 1 NNEAL arrival misinterpreted a clearance for JAAES as CAASE due to poor radio quality, similar waypoint names, and cockpit noise. The crew later clarified runway transition expectations with Approach, highlighting the need for earlier specific clearances to reduce FMC workload and confusion.

synopsis: A320 Captain experiences a tire fuse plug failure at the gate after landing at LAS with OAT of 95, increasing to 105 before departure. The hottest brake was 425 C upon gate arrival, with a two hour lay over, and the brake fans were not turned on.
summary: During a two-hour layover in LAS, rising ground temperatures caused a brake thermal plug to melt and deflate a tire, which ground crew discovered before loading. The pilot attributed the incident to high ambient heat and noted a procedural conflict between flight and maintenance departments regarding brake fan usage.

synopsis: Q400 flight crew experiences a Flight Director failure on departure and cannot find any direction in the FOM or Abnormal Checklist. After accepting and flying an RNAV arrival it is determined that perhaps they should not have.
summary: The crew lost both flight directors after the Captain used the TCS button during initial climbout. They inadvertently violated procedures by accepting an RNAV-1 arrival without flight directors due to an inability to locate the relevant limitations in the Abnormal Checklist or FOM during the flight.

synopsis: An A320 flight crew lost contact with Center for an extended period when ATC failed to hand them off to the next sector. Another flight crew forwarded an appropriate frequency to them. A malfunctioning ACARS was a contributing factor.
summary: The non-flying pilot on a westbound transcontinental flight reported that Fort Worth Center failed to hand off the aircraft to Albuquerque Center due to heavy weather and training. The crew discovered this only after landing, as their ACARS was inoperative without an ECAM advisory, preventing them from realizing the communication gap during flight.

synopsis: EMB-145 First Officer reports being switched from 26R to Runway 26L during the DRLLR RNAV arrival. When the runway is changed the transition drops out and is not re-entered by the crew, resulting in a track deviation at DOMNO.
summary: Pilots reported that after receiving a runway change from 26R to 26L during the DRLLR one arrival, their FMS failed to execute the turn at the DOMNO fix. The crew attributed this deviation and subsequent altitude confusion to FMS software defects and conflicting runway assignments, identifying both as major safety threats.

synopsis: A pilot questions the application of a 10-day 'Emergency' Non-Essential Function (NEF) deferral for structural missing/loose rivets in the Aft Accessory Bay of a Cessna 560XLS for the Air Cycle Machine (ACM) mounting hardware. Pilot also addresses the inconsistent application of an 'Emergency' NEF when other Maintenance Control personnel will ground the aircraft (AOG) for the same condition.
summary: An Airline Transport Pilot questioned the legality of an "Emergency Non-Essential Function" deferral for missing and loose structural rivets on a Cessna 560XLS Air Cycle Machine. The pilot cited concerns regarding the lack of documented procedures, inconsistent maintenance application, and the extended eight-day duration of the deferral.

synopsis: B747-400 Captain experiences a dual FMC failure shortly after takeoff although no EICAS annunciation of FMC failure was present. The first attempt to reload the FMC's is not successful and ATC is advised and vectors requested. The second attempt to restore the FMC's is successful and the flight continues to destination.
summary: During climb from ZSPD, both FMCs timed out, causing loss of autopilot, flight directors, and left radio, resulting in a 5-7 mile deviation. Radar vectors were provided until systems were restored; the crew selected the right FMC as master for the remainder of the flight, which landed ahead of schedule.

synopsis: MD80 First Officer detects low airspeed at FL300. Autothrust is disconnected and the thrust levers pushed up with no apparent effect. When the Captain turns on the engine anti ice an immediate thrust increase is noted and the aircraft accelerates back up to normal cruise speed.
summary: The Pilot Flying experienced unexplained thrust loss at FL300 while flying through light cirrus clouds with engine anti-ice off. Activating engine anti-ice immediately restored thrust and airspeed, leading the crew to conclude that closer airspeed monitoring and using anti-ice in any cloud would have prevented the event.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: MD80 pilot experiences a Tail Compt Temp Hi Light passing 10,000 feet during climbout. QRH procedures are complied with and the flight returns to the departure airport.
summary: The crew experienced a Tail Compartment Temperature High light at 10,000 feet during climbout. They declared an emergency, returned to the departure airport, and landed below minimum landing weight after the light extinguished and ARFF cleared the aircraft.

aircraft: De Havilland Canada Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: After a normal landing and during the deceleration/roll out phase, a De Havilland Canada aircraft flight crew reports the aircraft veering hard to the left. Braking and reverse were utilized and the aircraft was stopped on the left side of runway. A nose wheel steering fault caused by lack of lubrication was thought to be the cause.
summary: During the landing roll-out, the aircraft veered hard left due to drag in the nose wheel steering collar. The crew stopped the aircraft safely, maneuvered around a runway light, and maintenance resolved the issue by lubricating the steering collar.

synopsis: C172 instructor reports a NMAC when his student overshoots the turn to final for the right runway, coming very close to a Lear on approach to the left runway. The student had been informed of the traffic by the Tower and had reported the traffic in sight.
summary: A student pilot flying a high-wing aircraft overshot final for Runway 31R during a 30-degree bank, inadvertently aligning with Runway 31L where a Learjet was 100 feet below. The instructor estimated a 75-foot vertical separation, attributing the near miss to obscured visibility and the student's wide turn.

synopsis: DA-20 instructor pilot reports departing a runway with an airport vehicle on the edge spraying weeds. The runway was apparently closed at the time, but this information was not conveyed to the reporter.
summary: A flight instructor and student attempted a takeoff on Runway 5 while an airport sprayer truck occupied the pavement, unaware of a runway closure due to missing NOTAMs and UNICOM broadcasts. The pilot departed from the left side of the runway to avoid the vehicle but acknowledged the incident resulted from poor communication by the airport authority.

aircraft: Beechcraft Twin Piston Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Twin Beechcraft instructor pilot, above Gillespie Fields class D airspace, is informed by ATC that he may have had a NMAC. The reporter laments the very constricted airspace.
summary: A flight instructor in a light twin reported a near mid-air collision with another twin while approaching Montgomery Field for a single-engine ILS approach. The other pilot stated they were 50 feet above and 100 yards right of the instructor's aircraft, attributing the incident to high tower workload and congested airspace funneling traffic.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: DAB Approach/Departure Controller reports of a near miss with a VFR aircraft that he was not talking to or was under his control.
summary: An air traffic controller failed to issue a traffic alert to Aircraft X due to low radar alarm and display settings, resulting in a reported near miss with Aircraft Y near DAB. The controller identified the equipment configuration as the cause and plans to adjust settings to prevent recurrence.

synopsis: N90 controller reports of working a combined sectors and having an operational error due to distractions of VFR aircraft calling him.
summary: An air traffic controller managing three combined radar positions failed to turn Aircraft X off the BUONO4 arrival due to distraction by VFR traffic, causing a loss of separation with Aircraft Y. The aircraft passed within 1.43 NM and 400 FT vertically, an outcome attributed to excessive workload and the normalization of combined positions overriding standard procedures.

synopsis: B737 First Officer reports receiving an aircraft from Maintenance after an 'A' check. At FL350 Hydraulic System A quantity is noted to be solely decreasing and crew elects to return the departure airport.
summary: Following an overnight A-check, the crew observed a progressive drop in Hydraulic System A quantity during cruise at FL350. The Captain declared an emergency and returned to the departure airport for a safe landing with no external mechanical indications found.

synopsis: A B737NG flight crew misinterpreted Center's clearance to '...leave a holding pattern direct to JLI and continue via the VISTA STAR, cross CYNDE at 12,000 FT to mean 'descend via' the STAR. Shortly after passing CYNDE and continuing their descent ATC advised that all altitudes on the STAR were 'expect to cross' and they had not been cleared below 12,000.
summary: The flight crew descended below the cleared 12,000 feet while holding at JLI and flying the VISTA 2 Arrival due to misinterpreting expected altitudes as published clearance. Air Traffic Control corrected the error at 11,600 feet, confirming no loss of separation occurred.

synopsis: MD-82 Captain rejected takeoff at 120 KTS due to 10% less N1 and 25 degrees lower EGT on right engine than left engine. EPR's were matched at 2.04. Successful reject with no issues other than required brake cooling.
summary: The pilot flying rejected takeoff at 120 KTS after observing a significant right engine N1 drop while EPRs remained matched at 2.04. The crew taxied clear and briefed passengers following the power split detected during the acceleration phase.

synopsis: B757 flight crew reports getting low during the FMS Bridge Visual to Runway 28R at SFO, after getting high due to ATC speed restrictions. In order to get back on profile the aircraft was configured early and descends below the normal approach path resulting in a low altitude alert from the Tower. The approach is continued to a normal landing.
summary: The crew descended behind a B777 on the MOD 5 Arrival, ending up high and then below the glideslope due to ATC speed control and an altimeter setting discrepancy. Although they intercepted the glideslope and landed, the pilots later agreed a go-around was the correct response to the rushed approach.

synopsis: An ERJ Captain reported his belief that IAH ATC's phraseology when clearing flights to specific altitudes using 'climb via' on the new RNAV SIDs is imprecise and may lead to flights failing to comply with intervening crossing restrictions.
summary: A pilot reported that IAH Departure's phraseology "Climb via the XYZ SID, except maintain one six thousand feet" is non-standard and potentially unsafe. The pilot argues the word "except" creates ambiguity regarding altitude restrictions, suggesting crews unfamiliar with local usage might misinterpret the clearance.

synopsis: A Repairman at an FAA-145 Contract Maintenance Repair Station reports he found a Bonded Metal Repair to a B717 Aft Flap Upper Vane to be defective during a Tap Test in the leading edge area of the vane repair. Repairman also raised concerns the Back Shop Manager pressured the repairing Mechanic and Inspector, who all knew of the disbond, to approve the repair. Safety concerns about an inflight failure of repair also noted by Reporter.
summary: A non-certificated mechanic discovered a disbonded aft flap upper vane repair on a Boeing B717 during refurbishment at a 145 repair station. The defect was knowingly passed by a technician and manager to meet time constraints, bypassing required rework per the Structural Repair Manual.

synopsis: Pilot of C185 on floats reports the aircraft nosing over when power is added to begin a step taxi. The reporter believes that the floats may be undersized for the C185.
summary: A pilot operating a C185 with EDO 2790 amphib floats nosed over immediately after applying power for a step taxi run on a lake. The pilot attributed the incident to the propeller striking the water and suggested the floats may be marginal for this aircraft.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: NCT controllers describe situation where SFO Tower launches aircraft into NCT airspace not correctly separated causing the Controller to have to react and separate traffic.
summary: SFO Tower controllers vectored departing aircraft off published SIDs without coordinating with the CI-1, causing conflicts with transitioning traffic and placing aircraft below Minimum Vectoring Altitudes. The reporter states these uncoordinated actions created immediate terrain and mid-air collision risks that required emergency heading changes to resolve.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: PHF controllers describes situation where a tug is reporting its position on the runway, while an aircraft attempts to depart. Tower Controller uses radio and tells departing aircraft to stop. Tower is not open when this happens.
summary: A tug and Aircraft X entered Runway 20 simultaneously on CTAF 118.7 before tower opening, causing a near collision. The controller ordered Aircraft X to stop after the tug exited, attributing the incident to the pilot failing to hear the tug's announcements.

synopsis: An aircraft departed ZZZ and hit several birds a 400 feet causing damage to 13 right engine fan blades and the right leading edge slat. At reduced power engine vibrations decreased so the engine remained running until after landing.
summary: The pilot reported striking birds at 400 AGL during departure, causing right engine fan vibration to reach 5.0 and damaging 13 fan blades and a slat. An emergency was declared, resulting in a safe visual landing after the preceding aircraft reported windshear at 400 feet.

synopsis: During taxi out, both EMB-145 pilots and the Flight Attendant detected a strong cabin odor, so the aircraft returned to the gate and was evacuated. During troubleshooting, a failed APU was found.
summary: The flight crew and cabin crew detected strong electrical smoke during taxi, prompting an immediate return to the gate and passenger evacuation. Subsequent inspection revealed APU failure caused scorching and fire damage to the aircraft's right side after a failed start attempt.

synopsis: An apparent breakdown in Mode Control Panel SOP, fatigue, and poorly coordinated efforts by the flight crew of a B777 resulted in an unstabilized approach and subsequent go-around. Contributing factors were conflicting comfort levels with LNAV/VNAV conducted descent to ILS intercept and the failure of the Captain (pilot flying) to assume control of the MCP panel when conflicts arose between his autoflight configuration preferences and the First Officer's reluctance to abide by his planned utilization of LNAV/VNAV to join the approach.
summary: The Captain and fatigued First Officer on a Boeing 777 experienced a high approach at SBGL due to incorrect MCP altitude settings that disrupted the vertical PATH. The Captain intervened with degraded autopilot modes and executed a go-around, attributing the event to crew confusion over LNAV/VNAV usage and the need for the pilot flying to manage MCP settings.

synopsis: MD-83 Captain reported encountering wake turbulence on approach to LAS that resulted in 30 degree roll both sides. Wake was generated by preceding B737 that crossed his arrival path.
summary: The pilot encountered wake vortices from a preceding B737 on 7-mile final for Runway 1L while both aircraft were cleared for visual. The vortices caused smooth roll moments exceeding 30 degrees, but the landing remained uneventful.

synopsis: A C414 instructor administering an Instrument Proficiency Check and BFI became distracted during an approach with the student under the hood so he missed the student's descent below the 1,220 feet MDA.
summary: During an IFR training flight, a student pilot descended below the 1,220-foot MDA while under the hood, confusing height above ground with the minimum descent altitude. The instructor, momentarily distracted by scanning for traffic, noticed the error at 1,050 feet, prompting an immediate climb and missed approach.

synopsis: A B737 takeoff was BLEEDS OFF with a 102 degree ambient temperature. After lift off the LEFT WING BODY OVERHEAT light illuminated, so the QRH was completed, an emergency declared, and the flight returned to land. The reporter points out that the WING BODY OVERHEAT procedure begins with the Bleeds ON, not OFF and APU air OFF, the reverse of their configuration.
summary: Pilots of a heavy B737 experienced a left Wing Body Overheat warning during departure on a hot day after a bleeds-off takeoff. They returned for an overweight landing, declaring an emergency due to bleed system concerns, and noted the QRH was confusing for this specific takeoff configuration.

synopsis: B757 First Officer reported encountering possible wake turbulence at FL380. ATC reported an A380 in the vicinity.
summary: The crew encountered moderate turbulence at FL380 while investigating potential causes like weather or wake turbulence. After reporting to ATC and informing passengers, the Captain learned an A380 had recently flown nearby, though specific distance, altitude, or time details were unknown.

synopsis: A B757 EICAS alerted RT SYS QTY so the QRH was completed and the flight continued with both RT system pumps OFF. After the destination airport close, the flight diverted and turned the pumps on prior to landing.
summary: The pilot reported a cruise altitude RT SYS QTY EICAS message, followed by checklist compliance to turn off electric and engine pumps. After diverting due to weather, both pumps were reactivated before landing, resulting in an uneventful remainder of the flight.

synopsis: During takeoff at about 100 knots an A321 crew heard two loud bangs accompanied by a red Engine 1 EGT, so the Captain rejected the takeoff and returned to the gate where the flight was canceled.
summary: The Captain rejected takeoff at 100 knots after hearing loud bangs and observing Engine #1 EGT in the red. Compressor stalls caused the over-temperature and noise, leading to Engine #1 shutdown, a flight cancellation, and deplaning after a maintenance inspection found no tire damage.

synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported he executed a rejected landing at LAX when he encountered wake turbulence at 50 FT AGL in trail of an A380.
summary: A Boeing 737-800 crew encountered severe wake turbulence from an Airbus A380 during the final approach to LAX Runway 6R. The pilot executed a go-around below 50 feet AGL due to wing rock and airspeed fluctuations, suspecting the A380 had landed long.

synopsis: A helicopter pilot reported a near miss with a drone flying on the shoreline near a Class B airport which would have resulted in a disaster had they hit.
summary: A pilot flying a helicopter near a Class B airport experienced a near mid-air collision with a drone at the same altitude. The pilot attributed the incident to commercial drone operators violating FAA regulations, creating a significant risk to low-level aviation.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A fractional flight crew reported that a recent FMS software revision allowed VOR autotuning after takeoff which caused this flight to lose the departure airport DME for a required turn. The solution is to manually tune the VOR.
summary: Pilots on a departure following the Loupe 2 SID lost DME signals when the FMS autotuned to the LIN VOR instead of the SJC VOR due to new software. NORCAL provided the required turn after the crew reported the loss, and no altitude or airspeed deviations occurred.

aircraft: Piper Single Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An instructor on short final to O61 Runway 13 made the appropriate CTAF position calls but after touchdown were overflown by an opposite direction antique military trainer whose pilot stated he had not heard the previous calls before his takeoff.
summary: A flight instructor and student on a Cessna training flight at O61 experienced a near-midair collision with a military trainer departing Runway 13. The trainer flew over the landing aircraft at 50 feet due to not hearing radio calls, though no damage occurred.

synopsis: During landing a BE-9L pilot selected BETA to help slow the aircraft but the left engine oversped causing the aircraft to exit the runway and strike a runway sign which damaged the left propeller, engine, leading edge and flap. No injuries resulted. Additionally, an unauthorized oil access cap repair had been made which did not contribute to the overspeed.
summary: The pilot reported that during landing, left engine overspeed in beta caused a hard left yaw, making the aircraft uncontrollable and running off the runway, damaging the propeller, wing, and flap. An unauthorized oil cap repair on the right engine was noted but deemed not a contributing factor to the accident.

synopsis: A B777 Captain advised he considers the elevated runway modifications to the east end of Runway 10R/28L at FLL currently under construction to be too confining should an evacuation from the included EMAS runway extension be necessary.
summary: A B777-200 pilot reported that FLL Runway 10R/28L's design, featuring 60-foot walls and an EMAS bed, prevents safe evacuation during a fire due to prevailing winds. Consequently, the pilot refused to operate on this runway to avoid jeopardizing the safety of 289 passengers and crew.

synopsis: The pilot of a Cessna 172M had an engine failure after approximately 3 hours of flight and made an off-field emergency landing.
summary: The pilot reported an in-flight power loss at 3,500 feet due to fuel exhaustion after a lineman failed to top off the tanks despite a visual check. The pilot executed a forced landing in a wheat field with no injuries or aircraft damage, attributing the cause to inaccurate visual fuel estimation.

synopsis: The pilot of a King Air 350 experienced a heading deviation while attempting to program the unfamiliar FMS during an RNAV approach, resulting in a traffic alert.
summary: A single-pilot crew descending from 8,000 to 4,000 feet missed a descent rate decrease while troubleshooting an FMS discontinuity and auto-sequencing inhibition. The distraction caused a traffic alert and blocked ATC's traffic avoidance instructions, requiring a heading change to 090 before the approach could be completed.

synopsis: MRI Controller reports of an aircraft that is supposed to follow a route into the airport and does not, while a departure reports having a NMAC with the arriving aircraft. Routes would have been separated if the arrival was following the prescribed route.
summary: A Light Sport aircraft and a Piper Aztec experienced a reported NMAC near Campbell airstrip. The conflict occurred because the Light Sport deviated from the Campbell Arrival procedure, placing it in the Aztec's departure path despite the controller's expectation of lateral separation.

synopsis: TRACON Controller reports of operational error due to aircraft slowing more than he thought on final, causing the Controller to re-sequence the following aircraft. Controller also attributes the loss of separation due to the use of Fusion Radar, which was his first time actually using it.
summary: An air traffic controller lost separation between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y during final approach on the first day of using fusion radar. The controller attributed the incident to skewed speed perception and inaccurate target positioning caused by the new radar system.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: ZHU Controller describes scenario where a departure is taken off its route to allow its climb, while it comes into conflict with two arrivals. The Controller describes the routes are not able to climb or descend traffic laterally but controllers do this everyday.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that a CXO departure climbing to FL160 was delayed and vectored to avoid two WAPPL arrivals due to a lack of procedural separation. The controller described this daily occurrence as an unsafe condition caused by insufficient separation standards for north satellite departures.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: A11 Controller describes situation where two facilities are using the same SOP, which recently was changed, but is causing confusion in both facilities.
summary: North Radar and Local Controllers at ANC Tower issued conflicting signals regarding automatic departures during Aircraft Y's GPS approach to MRI. A Local Controller mistakenly believed a green light resumed Runway 7L releases, causing Aircraft X to depart into conflict with Aircraft Y due to confusion over a new joint SOP.

synopsis: B737-800 Firrst Officer reported encountering wake turbulence on approach to ATL in trail of B757 that resulted in a go-around. Reporter cited new minimal ATC separation techniques as causal.
summary: The crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding B757 at 100 feet during a visual approach to Atlanta Runway 27L, prompting a go-around. The pilot attributed the event to tight separation under new rules, though the aircraft landed uneventfully after a second approach.

synopsis: A Captain reports the First Officer (F/O) noticed during his walkaround that the Left and Right Fuel Vent scoops had been installed backwards on their B757 aircraft. Rather than venting the tanks, the Fuel Vent ducts were pressurizing the tanks.
summary: The First Officer discovered during a walkaround that both fuel vents were installed backwards, pressurizing the tanks instead of venting them. This error occurred because the left and right vents were switched during reinstallation in May 2014, allowing the aircraft to fly incorrectly for over two weeks.

synopsis: EMB145 First Officer reports his aircraft failing to turn for VLDEZ over DOMNO on the DRLLR 1 RNAV to IAH. Manual intervention is required to turn the aircraft toward VLDEZ.
summary: During the DRLLR ONE arrival into IAH, the FMS failed to initiate a turn to VLDEZ at the DOMNO fix, causing the autopilot to enter ROLL mode. The Captain immediately took control to correct the course, and the undesired state was quickly resolved without ATC involvement.

synopsis: EMB145 First Officer experiences the autopilot switching from LNAV to roll mode as the aircraft passes DOMNO turning toward VLDEZ on the DRLLR 1 RNAV to IAH. ATC detects the track deviation and advises that previous company aircraft have had similar issues.
summary: The flight crew experienced an autopilot LNAV deactivation and roll mode engagement at the DOMNO waypoint during the DRLLR ONE arrival into IAH. The reporter attributes this RNAV failure to outdated avionics, noting three other company aircraft had identical issues that day.

synopsis: During cruise flight the crew of an MD-83 experienced autopilot and autothrottle disconnects as well as numerous annunciator warnings along with erratic flight instrument failures. The nature of the fault indications initially led the Captain to believe that an engine failure had occurred. An emergency was declared and a diversion initiated. The true nature of the problem was eventually determined to be a CSD failure, appropriate procedures were followed, and the flight continued uneventfully to the original destination airport.
summary: Two reserve captains on an S80 experienced an uncommanded autopilot disconnect and erratic instruments in cruise due to a Left CSD failure causing unstable electrical power. The crew diverted, stabilized the aircraft by disconnecting the CSD, and landed safely, though the Captain attributed the initial confusion to fatigue and inexperience.

synopsis: B757 flight crew is informed of burn marks on the right emergency exit door by the Purser. The First Officer on break investigates and determines there is a burn mark plus several other hot spots on the door. The crew elects to return to the departure airport.
summary: The flight crew and IRO discovered an overheating over-wing hatch heater at row 20F causing a hot burn spot and plastic damage. Unable to isolate the heat source, the crew returned to the departure airport rather than crossing water.

synopsis: A320 Captain experiences the loss of the Yellow Hydraulic System pressure during cruise flight. ECAM procedures are complied with and after consulting with Maintenance Control, the flight returns to the departure airport.
summary: During cruise, the crew received an ECAM alert for low Yellow Hydraulic System pressure. Following procedures and consulting maintenance, they declared an emergency, returned to the departure airport, and landed uneventfully due to a mechanical failure.

synopsis: CRJ-200 flight crew reported encountering wake turbulence in trail of a B757 after takeoff at ATL that resulted in 30 degree roll and a stick shaker at low altitude. Crew cited new ATL ATC separation procedures as causal.
summary: The flight crew encountered severe wake turbulence from a preceding B757 immediately after takeoff on Runway 26L, causing a 30-degree roll and stick shaker activation. The pilot recovered control, but the incident highlighted insufficient separation under new rules, prompting the crew to reject future immediate departures behind B757s.

synopsis: When an electrical odor dissipated after running the Smoke/Fire/Fumes Checklist the flight crew of an MD-82 opted to continue to destination. When the odor returned during descent they declared an emergency and got priority handling to the airport where they landed without incident. The odor again dissipated during the descent.
summary: During cruise at FL320, pilots and cabin crew detected a burning electrical odor that temporarily ceased after turning off the galley switch. The odor returned during descent, prompting an emergency declaration and expedited vectoring to the airport for an uneventful landing.

synopsis: An MD-11 flight crew shut down the right engine diverted following the loss of oil quantity and pressure.
summary: The crew experienced a loss of oil quantity and pressure on Engine 2, prompting a shutdown per the QRH. They declared an emergency and diverted to a nearby airport.

synopsis: EMB505 Captain questions the advisability of a gear down ferry from a high altitude airport due to performance considerations.
summary: The pilot reported a ferry flight with landing gear extended due to a maintenance discrepancy, noting that performance data indicated insufficient obstacle clearance if an engine failed in mountainous terrain. Management provided no data for missed approaches and pressured the crew despite the lack of training and contradictory emergency instructions.

synopsis: C177 pilot experiences a NMAC at 8,500 feet near SAX (VOR) with an airliner overtaking from behind. Garmin traffic provided enough warning to narrowly avoid a collision. The Air Carrier crew apparently did not detect the C177.
summary: A pilot cruising at 8,500 feet en route to PHL received a Garmin TCAS warning of a passenger jet on a collision course from the right rear. The pilot executed a 90-degree left turn and climb to avoid a strike, noting the airliner did not see them.

synopsis: A B757 flight crew diverted from ZZZZ to ZZZZ3 due to weather and fuel remaining. While enroute they learned their diversion airport was not an approved alternate although it was for company B767's. Due to fuel remaining they continued and landed under the Captain's command authority.
summary: The crew diverted to ZZZZ3 due to low weather at the destination, but later learned it was not a valid 757 alternate. They landed safely with 4.5 tons of fuel, causing extra work for ground staff due to the crew's failure to verify aircraft-specific alternate requirements.

synopsis: CL-300 flight crew reported encountering wake turbulence on approach to JFK in trail of a B747 that caused a deviation from initial approach altitude.
summary: During approach to JFK Runway 4R, the aircraft encountered wake turbulence from a B747 and descended below the assigned 2,000 FT altitude while on autopilot with ILS coupled. The crew recovered to the assigned altitude without incident, incursion, or impact to other aircraft.

synopsis: During climb through about 9,000 FT a PC-12 warning horn similar to the gear warning sounded, but with horizontal trim activation it ceased. At about 15,000 FT the aircraft began an uncommanded pitch over indicating a runaway stabilizer trim, so the QRH was completed, the warning silenced and the flight continued to the filed destination with alternate trim. A failed relay was found.
summary: The pilot flying and captain experienced a primary stabilizer trim runaway caused by a bad relay during climb in a Pilatus PC-12. After pulling the circuit breaker and using alternate trim, they continued to their destination and landed safely despite initially misidentifying the warning horn.

synopsis: PA46 pilot experiences autopilot disengagement along with loss of backup gyro horizon a FL270 resulting in at least one 360 degree turn and the loss of 1,000-2,000 feet before it is detected and recovery commenced.
summary: A passenger in the copilot seat inadvertently disengaged the autopilot at FL270 in IMC, causing a spiral and 1,000–2,000 feet altitude loss, compounded by a dual vacuum pump failure. The pilot regained control, diverted for a pump replacement, and later attributed the disconnect to the passenger bumping trim switches while reaching for the gyro compass.

synopsis: A C210-T landed gear up when the gear failed to extend. No injuries resulted.
summary: The pilot executed a gear-up landing at 90 knots with 20 degrees of flaps after the landing gear system actuated but remained inoperative. The aircraft skidded 300 feet to a stop on the runway edge with no injuries or damage, and airport staff subsequently removed it using jacks and dollies.

synopsis: After about one hour of silence, a LR-45 crew attempted ATC communications and discovered a VHF system malfunction which caused both radios to autotune random frequencies without the crew's input. Careful monitoring was then required.
summary: Pilots experienced intermittent radio contact loss during cruise due to a malfunctioning clearance delivery radio head that caused tuning units to cycle frequencies. The crew initially suspected pilot deviation, which delayed recognizing the equipment failure and increased workload for approximately one hour.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: Pilot describes clearance issued by MIC Tower Controller as something he has never received before. Pilot questioned himself if it was alright to taxi as instructed across four runways.
summary: The pilot landed at MIC and, after refueling, received a taxi clearance to Wiley North from Ground Control. Relying on an outdated interpretation of FAR 91.129, the pilot crossed four active runways without explicit clearance, assuming the instruction implied permission to cross all intersecting runways.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: A pilot reported entering into a parachute jump zone while trying to increase the distance between their aircraft and a gyrocopter at BXK.
summary: The pilot approaching Buckeye Airport for Runway 17 inadvertently overflew a parachute jump zone while attempting to avoid a gyrocopter. The reporter attributed this unnecessary conflict to poor situational awareness and a lack of pre-planned evasive action.

synopsis: A B737NG flight crew cleared via the ENDEE RNAV STAR, expect the RNAV Y approach to Runway 22L at MDW via fix STERE was unable to successfully program the procedure and, instead, requested, received and conducted a circling visual approach to 22L.
summary: Pilots flying an RNAV arrival into MDW could not program the FMC for a last-minute RNAV Y approach via MIING, causing a deviation from the prescribed track and speed. They subsequently accepted a visual approach and landed safely, noting the FMC limitation requires analysis for IMC conditions.

synopsis: A B737-300 pilot described the difficulty communicating using that aging flight station intercom/communication system which actually hampers pilot to pilot and ATC interaction.
summary: A pilot reported that poor intercom functionality on a -300 aircraft exacerbated a climb phase incident caused by an unexecuted FMS route. The noise level led to miscommunication between crew members regarding VNAV and LNAV failures, highlighting the safety risk of unclear flight deck communication.

synopsis: An air carrier crew did not hold short of Taxiway R taxiing eastbound on Taxiway B at night because the Taxiway R signage is either poorly lit or poorly placed.
summary: The flight crew overshot Taxiway R while taxiing after landing on Runway 24R, likely due to a missing or unlit sign and distractions from single-engine taxi configuration and an ECAM fault. Another crew confirmed the sign was not visible from the eastbound direction, suggesting a potential signage issue.

synopsis: An A300 ECAM alerted MID 1 MAIN DECK LOOP A OFF during approach so the loop was turned OFF and tested. No smoke was detected but the mid cargo temperature was rising with numerous fault lights: PACK 2, ISOLATION VALVE, OVERHEAT, HOT AIR. An emergency was declared before landing.
summary: The crew encountered multiple cargo system faults and excessive duct temperatures en route to downwind, prompting an emergency declaration. They landed uneventfully after fire trucks detected heat, and post-flight checks confirmed no smoke despite the loop failure.

synopsis: A Captain describes his efforts to regain control of an EMB190 aircraft during initial climb when the aircraft suddenly pitched 'Full Down' after he had attempted to retrim Pitch 'Up', using the Manual Pitch Trim switch on his Control column. Aircraft had accelerated to 265 knots. Emergency declared. Two mechanics also report their involvement with replacement of the Captain's Pitch Trim switch that was later found installed backwards.
summary: During an RNAV departure at 1,000 feet MSL, the autopilot failed to engage and pitch trim ran full down due to a Captain's switch wired backwards. The crew declared an emergency, followed the QRH, and landed safely after mechanics replaced the faulty switch and HS-ACE computer.

synopsis: CRJ-200 Captain reported encountering wake turbulence in trail of an A319 on takeoff from ATL that resulted in multiple violent rolls at low altitude.
summary: The crew departed behind an A319 on Runway 26L and encountered wake turbulence at 500 FT AGL, causing violent left rolls and a missed turn to SNUFY. They recovered at 1,200 FT AGL, attributed the upset to proximity to preceding traffic, and reported the incident to the Tower supervisor.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A fatigued flight crew landed at CMH during late night operations without clearance. Fatigue and distractions including bright LED approach lights and a lull due to the lack of frequency activity.
summary: The flight crew landed on CMH Runway 28L without landing clearance after Approach Control failed to hand them off to the Tower. The crew attributed the error to fatigue, distracting LED lights, and infrequent radio transmissions, while ATC noted the incident was low risk due to VMC conditions and no traffic.

synopsis: A BE-400XP left MAG alerted while holding short of LGA Runway 13 so the crew taxied clear and recycled the left radio master which cleared the alert. When they taxied back to the runway both left and right MAG's alert so they were able to taxi down the runway to clear both before takeoff.
summary: Pilots at LGA experienced magnetic compass warnings on PFDs and MFDs while lining up on Runway 13 due to interference from the runway bridge. After exiting and repositioning clear of the bridge, displays returned to normal, allowing a successful full-length departure.

synopsis: A B737-800 flight encountered severe turbulence and mountain wave at FL360 and suffered a loss of separation with an aircraft above unable to maintain altitude. One flight attendant was injured in the two to three minute exposure to the turbulence.
summary: The flight crew encountered severe mountain wave turbulence at FL360 while responding to a TCAS RA, causing an uncommanded climb and injuring a flight attendant thrown from their seat. The injured crew member was treated by EMS on arrival and transported to a hospital for further evaluation.

synopsis: As they approached 200 AGL on final approach the Captain (pilot not flying) of a B777-200 noticed airspeed was at reference, decreasing, and the autothrottles had somehow been disengaged. An abrupt power increase resulted in excessive acceleration and the landing was aborted prior to touchdown and a probably flap overspeed was noticed by a Relief Pilot. A subsequent approach was uneventful. No explanation for the inactive autothrottles was provided.
summary: The pilot monitoring noticed autothrottle disconnection on final, leading to a low-speed call and a missed approach at 50–100 feet AGL. Distraction by a traffic call during the climbout resulted in a suspected flap overspeed, though the aircraft landed safely on a second approach.

synopsis: A widebody Captain flying his first approach utilizing HUD failed to achieve stabilized approach criteria until right at 1,000 AGL at which time the First Officer advised a go-around was appropriate per SOP. The Captain opted to continue the approach and landed safely. A complete debrief of the event ensued after parking.
summary: The Captain continued an unstable approach to Pudong 17R while distracted by HUD setup and Tower communications, resulting in late configuration at 1,000 feet. The First Officer called for a go-around due to the incomplete checklist, which the Captain accepted as a failure in leadership and CRM.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: CRJ-200 Dispatcher describes a flight he is controlling that is vectored away from the planned destination (OKC), and winds up on the west side of a line of thunderstorms in a low fuel situation. Despite his best efforts to get the Captain to divert for fuel the flight continues to destination, landing with just 21 minutes of fuel on board.
summary: The flight crew departed with insufficient fuel, allowed ATC to vector them 80 NM northwest into thunderstorms, and ignored dispatcher directives to divert to COS. They arrived at OKC with minimum fuel after the crew failed to assert priorities or accept operational control, resulting in a loss of safety margins.

synopsis: A Flight Attendant reports that Stowage hooks on the Escape slide Girt Bars at Forward Cabin Doors L-1 and R-1 on a 737-400 aircraft were not very tight and allowed the Girt Bars to be easily dislodged from their hooks. Door L-1 Girt Bar had re-attached itself to the floor brackets during door opening procedures.
summary: A cabin crew member struggled to open the L1 door at ZZZ1, causing the Girt Bar to dislodge from loose stowage hooks and partially deploy the slide. Mechanics retracted and removed the slide, allowing deplaning, while the reporter attributed the incident to excessive door opening force and inadequate hook tension.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Inspector (AMI) reports finding Emergency Pressurization Check Valve flappers on a Cessna CE-560XL aircraft would not open freely, during a Detailed Inspection of the Cabin Air Distribution Check Valves. Previous application of RTV sealant had penetrated the flapper opening and secured the flapper to the opening, preventing movement.
summary: A maintenance inspector found that RTV sealant seeped into emergency pressurization check valve flappers on a Cessna CE-560XL during a routine inspection, preventing them from opening freely. The blockage occurred because a previous installer used excessive sealant as a fay seal without verifying flapper movement, despite following the maintenance manual.

synopsis: A pilot decides to ferry his Schweizer SGS 2-33 glider back to Base with spoilers that were difficult to operate and especially difficult to 'Close' if fully deployed. On final, after release from aero tow, he fully opens spoilers by mistake, realizes he cannot close them and lands with spoilers fully deployed.
summary: The pilot flew a Schweizer SGS-2-33 glider from ZZZ1 to ZZZ despite known difficult spoiler closure, admitting fatigue and dehydration contributed to accidentally fully deploying spoilers on final. Unable to close them in gusty wind, the pilot landed with fully open spoilers, clearing the threshold with insufficient margin.

synopsis: WW24 (IAI1124) First Officer describes a loss of cabin pressurization at FL360 resulting in an emergency descent and diversion for maintenance.
summary: The flight crew experienced a cabin pressure fluctuation at FL360, likely caused by a faulty weight-on-wheels switch. They declared an emergency, descended, and landed uneventfully at a local airport before the aircraft was sent to maintenance.

synopsis: SCT Departure Controller and SMO departing pilot describe situation where the departure didn't turn when expected and became a conflict for a departure off of LAX.
summary: A Beechcraft 400XP departing Santa Monica and an aircraft departing LAX converged during initial climb due to a communication gap and noise abatement procedures. The controller separated the traffic by turning the LAX departure and immediately vectoring the Santa Monica aircraft to heading 265, issuing a pilot deviation advisory.

synopsis: A B737-700 flight crew report discovering a significant gap where the forward vertical stabilizer attaches to the dorsal fin during the preflight inspection. The aircraft is refused, but another crew is assigned to fly it and eventually agrees to do so. A report from the First Officer of the crew that accepted the aircraft is also included.
summary: Pilots and cabin crew refused to fly a Boeing 700 due to a significant gap at the forward vertical stabilizer attachment, which Maintenance Control claimed was normal per a Service Bulletin. The crew's refusal caused a delay until a returning Captain accepted the aircraft after inspecting the gap, though the reporter noted the discrepancy should have been logged for formal verification.

synopsis: An air carrier crew with a MEL'ed ADS system was not filed with correct ICAO equipment codes and later in flight notified that ADS B, C and CPDLC were inoperative. After lengthy inflight discussions with Dispatch and Maintenance it was determined a rushed departure and improper troubleshooting were involved.
summary: The flight crew departed with an improperly filed ICAO flight plan showing ADS capability after Maintenance incorrectly deferred a total ADS failure as ADS-B only. This error caused CPDLC failures, ATC confusion, and potential separation risks during oceanic operations due to the aircraft being invisible to ADS-B In-Trail Climb procedures.

synopsis: An A320 pilot noted the HHOOD 2 RNAV BLRUN waypoint has no crossing restriction but a 7,200 feet MEA. The FMGC will attempt to descend below the MEA in order to cross the SHAFR constraint at 6,700 feet so as to make subsequent descent constraints.
summary: Pilots reported a potential terrain conflict on an Airbus executing the HHOOD2 RNAV arrival to PDX, where the FMGC descended below the 7,200-foot MEA between HHOOD and BLRUN. The crew prevented the conflict by manually inserting a 7,200-foot restriction at BLRUN, as the automated VNAV path ignored the MEA to meet speed and altitude constraints at SHAFR.

synopsis: After delaying their approach while thunderstorms passed over the airport the flight crew of a B757-200 still encountered windshear requiring a go-around during their initial approach. A subsequent approach from the opposite direction was successful.
summary: The crew encountered windshear at 900 feet during an ILS 27R approach to PHL in marginal VFR with thunderstorms, triggering a go-around and escape procedure that resulted in a lowest altitude of 620 feet. They attributed the event to an act of God, noting that simulator-trained procedures ensured safety despite outdated ATIS wind reports and the decision to proceed due to fuel constraints.

synopsis: A CRJ900 Captain rotated the aircraft at a low airspeed after he understood the First Officer to state V1, when in fact he said 'Power Set.' The aircraft would not rotate so the Captain rejected the takeoff.
summary: The Captain and First Officer aborted a takeoff after the Captain rotated prematurely due to mishearing a V1 callout, resulting in no control response. The aircraft stopped safely on the runway, returned to the gate, and the crew attributed the error to poor situational awareness and communication.

synopsis: CRJ200 First Officer experiences a flap Fail Caution Message during approach and goes around. An approach and landing at the current flap setting is planned and executed by the Captain. The aircraft had a long history of flaps Fail Caution Messages.
summary: The First Officer initiated a go-around during approach after a flaps fail caution appeared, with flaps asymmetric at 6 and 8 degrees. The Captain landed safely on a different runway after declaring an emergency, noting the aircraft had recurrent flap failures over the previous 30 days.

synopsis: A C208B pilot reported adverse reactions while operating an aircraft with the TKS anti-ice system installed, during both summer and winter operations.
summary: During a hot training flight in a TKS-equipped Caravan, both pilots experienced throat irritation, nausea, and burning sensations due to TKS fluid vaporization and cabin air contamination. The reporter attributes these symptoms to extreme heat increasing fluid vaporization and dripping fluid contaminating the cockpit air system.

synopsis: As they began their approach the MD-82 flight crew received a DR (dead reckoning) warning they switched from GFMS guidance to raw data. After established inbound with the ILS and VASI centered and the runway in sight they received an EGPWS TERRAIN warning which they silenced and proceeded to a safe landing. At the time of the warning the NAV display showed them well to the right of the runway.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced false EGPWS terrain warnings and GFMS dead reckoning alerts during a mountainous ILS approach due to a map shift and RAIM limit exceedance. They switched to raw data navigation, overrode the EGPWS, and landed safely after confirming their position visually.

synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reports entering the ramp at MMGL on the wrong taxiway due to tall grass obscuring a sign and night time conditions.
summary: A fatigued crew unfamiliar with MMGL mistakenly entered taxiway F instead of D at night due to obscured signage and delayed checklist completion. Ramp denied a direct turn, forcing a backtrack to the correct route without incident, prompting recommendations for better sign visibility and enhanced taxi cross-checks.

synopsis: A B737 Flight Attendant reported a Gate Agent threatened a delay to their flight was possible if he did not take an unaccompanied minor on the aircraft after he refused because it was the first flight of the day and time was needed for security checks and crew briefing.
summary: A flight attendant reported that an Operations Agent pressured them to skip mandatory preflight checks and security sweeps to meet an on-time departure target. The crew member completed the safety procedures but noted the lack of briefing time and unrealistic pace created an unsafe atmosphere and friction between ground and inflight personnel.
