summary: An air traffic controller handling arrivals to Dallas reported that an SR22 on the YEAGR1 arrival entered too close to DR1 airspace due to a published "Heading 310" instruction. The controller attributed the proximity issue to the procedure's lack of VOR guidance and recommended changing the arrival to ensure proper separation from adjacent airspace.

aircraft: Beechcraft / Beech Aircraft Corp Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An SCT TRACON Controller reported a small Beechcraft airplane departing RAL via a standardized 'Tower Enroute Control (TEC)' route, ONTN10 to SNA failed to follow a segment consisting of a radial out of PDZ to intercept V363, instead proceeding via V21-8 to SLI, this event only the last of a number of similar occurrences.
summary: A pilot flying a Beech Bonanza on an IFR flight from RAL to SNA reported that the FMS/GPS omitted the PDZ 270 radial and V363 airway when entering the clearance. The pilot attributed this routing error to a known system limitation and recommended avoiding clearances containing radial-to-airway transitions.

synopsis: ZMP Controller reports of an aircraft that turns off course and then is put back on course by ATC. Reporter then states aircraft has difficulty holding correct altitude and headings later in the session.
summary: An air traffic controller observed a UAV deviating from its cleared route to RDR twice while in route. The controller attributed the deviations to the UAV's difficulty holding altitude and heading, citing inefficient radio lag as a safety hazard in the NAS.

synopsis: A B737 flight crew returned to their departure airport after receiving a report of fumes and odor from flight attendants. When CFR reported a hot spot on the lower left aft fuselage an uneventful evacuation was executed from the right side exits.
summary: During climbout, a Flight Attendant reported strong chemical odors in the aft cabin, prompting a return to the departure airport. Fire crews detected a fuselage hot spot, leading to an evacuation where Flight Attendants were hospitalized for throat irritation while pilots and passengers remained uninjured.

synopsis: B737-700 Fligt Crew reports being cleared to 'Climb via SID, except maintain 17,000 feet'. The First Officer read back, 'climb unrestricted to 17,000' and was not corrected. The crossing restriction at ARILE was not clomplied with.
summary: During the climb on the RAMBL 1 Departure, the Pilot Monitoring incorrectly read back a clearance to climb unrestricted to 17,000 feet, which ATC failed to correct. The crew proceeded to 17,000 feet, and the reporter noted that both the controller and pilot shared responsibility for the communication error.

synopsis: When the B737 flight crew was cleared to 'descend via' the BELLR RNAV STAR to HOU, ATC was unable to provide the planned landing runway. When the flight crew then asked to what altitude they were, therefore, cleared to descend the Controller's response was delayed, and ultimately equivocal, when the response began with, 'I think between 11,000 and 13,000 at BELLR' although the STAR continued to HNTRR which is to be crossed between 10,000 and 8,000 and at 210K.
summary: Pilots en route to HOU experienced confusion regarding the BELLR1 RNAV arrival and runway transition clearance from HOU ATC. After clarifying the Runway 4 transition with Approach, the crew correctly set the MCP to 6,000 feet for the GEEEO restriction.

synopsis: A B737 NG Captain manually activated the elevator trim and broke the First Officer's hand as the trim wheel turned while he stowed the QRH checklist away under the wheel following its use for a shattered windshield.
summary: During a night descent at 12,000 feet following a windshield shatter, the First Officer fractured his left hand when the Captain instinctively activated the trim wheel while the First Officer's hand was near it. The reporter attributes the injury to the Captain not seeing the hand and a lack of caution during a busy approach phase.

synopsis: After receiving a 'descend via' clearance from ATC and setting the altitude alert at 4,000 FT per the procedure the flight crew of a B737NG received a cabin altitude warning and began an emergency descent, cleared to 10,000 FT. They failed to reset the new cleared altitude and a modest overshoot occurred before ATC recleared them to 9,000 FT.
summary: The flight crew initiated an emergency descent at FL330 after the cabin altitude warning horn sounded, declaring an emergency and descending to 9,000 feet for a visual approach to Runway 26. The reporter attributed the event to a failure to cross-check the FMC and CDU after setting 4,000 feet in the altitude window prior to the descent.

synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew discovers a fuel leak from the left wing tank while airborne. The flight diverts to a suitable airport for an overweight landing.
summary: During climbout, the crew discovered a left wing fuel leak caused by a failed flapper valve and diverted for an overweight landing. After CFR inspection confirmed safety, passengers deplaned without evacuation.

synopsis: An EMB-145 Captain encountered a fuel leak in the left wing of the same aircraft on flights a day apart. Inadequate maintainence was cited by the reporter.
summary: The crew encountered a slow, intermittent fuel leak in the left wing tank during two enroute legs. Following Aircraft Operation Manual procedures and continuous monitoring, they safely landed at ZZZ with 3,500 lbs of fuel, prompting a deeper maintenance investigation.

aircraft: Dash 8 Series Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: A DHC-8-100 First Officer called for a reject after he saw the Master Warning and OIL PRESSURE lights illuminated during the takeoff roll. After clearing the runway all indications were again normal but at the gate oil was added and a cannon plug cleaned.
summary: The flight crew rejected takeoff on runway 34 at 85–90 knots due to a master warning and #1 engine low oil pressure light. They returned to the gate after maintenance reportedly found low oil and cleaned cannon plugs, though the reporter suspects a false indication as systems later appeared normal.

synopsis: A First Officer expressed concern regarding SAN traffic pattern when flying a Visual Approach to Runway 27. The Downwind leg descends below the floor of the SAN Class B (4,800 feet MSL), where it abuts the MYF and SEE Class D associated quadrants, north of the MZB 084 Radial.
summary: The pilot reported a potential inadvertent descent below the 4,800 MSL Class B floor during a right-hand visual approach to Runway 27 at KSAN. The reporter attributes this to the unusually high altitude required for the downwind leg and suggests issuing a bulletin until airspace redesign is complete.

synopsis: Two flight attendants report operating a B737-800 flight with three flight attendants and discovering the next day that the aircraft had been reconfigured with more than 150 seats, requiring a fourth Flight Attendant.
summary: A cabin crew of three flight attendants operated a reconfigured 737-800 with over 150 seats, unaware it required four attendants. The crew realized the staffing error the next day when a fourth member joined, prompting union contact and a call to confirm aircraft staffing requirements.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports a Gulfstream G-200 aircraft required excessive rudder trim to keep aircraft in coordinated flight. Found rudder right-hand lower close-out Panel 323AR hardware making contact with stop on vertical stabilizer.
summary: A mechanic reported excessive left rudder trim was required during flight due to the RH lower rudder closeout panel 323AR hardware contacting the vertical stabilizer stop prematurely. This interference prevented full rudder travel to the nose right stop, prompting a recommendation for rudder travel checks after panel reinstallation.

synopsis: Cleared for a Visual Approach to TPF airport, the pilot of a TBM700 mistakenly landed at MCF, a military airport that has a nearly identically oriented runway.
summary: The PIC and three passengers landed a multi-engine aircraft at MacDill instead of TPF during a visual approach due to the pilot's fixation on the TCAS screen. The crew was detained by security, completed paperwork, and subsequently flew VFR to the correct destination.

synopsis: G550 flight crew describes a night circling approach that is allowed to get very low before realizing that the intended runway is not in sight. Towers are noted by the First Officer off the nose of the aircraft as he calls for a, 'Pull up, pull up hard.'
summary: The pilot flying accepted a night circling approach to runway 15R but misidentified the runway, triggering a go-around at 400 feet after the first officer intervened. The crew subsequently landed uneventfully on runway 33L, with the pilot attributing the incident to accepting a circling approach instead of a straight-in ILS.

synopsis: B737-800 Captain reports being offered a night visual approach to Runway 7R at LAS from over KEPEC, and accepting. During the maneuver a terrain warning is annunciated and the reporter pulls up to silence the warning before continuing.
summary: The pilot flying a KEPEC arrival to runway 7R received a visual clearance at 20 miles out and descended to 6,000 feet before triggering a terrain warning. The pilot attributed the incident to the controller's setup, noting that KEPEC is a poor position for night visual approaches without RNAV guidance or terrain clearance.

synopsis: A small aircraft at 01A struck a 'shrub' on final rollout.
summary: During landing rollout, the aircraft contacted a shrub with the right wing outboard leading edge. No substantial damage occurred.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: LAF Tower Controller while instructing observes something that isn't going to work. He sends an aircraft around but uses the wrong (similar) call sign. Correct aircraft goes around but turns into another aircraft on the pattern and takes evasive actions to avoid it.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller and trainee on Local control issued conflicting go-around instructions during Aircraft X's departure and Aircraft Y's final approach, causing Aircraft Y to take evasive action to avoid a collision. The incident resulted from the controller's misidentification of the next aircraft on final and allowing the trainee to clear a departure without adequate separation.

synopsis: A B737 flight crew and the Tower Controller involved, describe a rejected takeoff commanded by the Tower Controller due to the previous landing aircraft not completely clearing the runway. An aircraft on final is also sent around.
summary: The flight crew aborted takeoff at 105 knots after ATC ordered a go-around for an arriving aircraft, citing insufficient runway spacing. Maintenance measured brake temperatures at 525 degrees, requiring a 75-minute cooling delay before the aircraft could depart.

synopsis: A319 Flight Crew experiences an EGPWS terrain warning at 6,500 feet while on a night visual approach to LAS Runway 25L from southeast of the airport. An immediate climb is initiated and the approach is continued to a normal landing.
summary: The flight crew received a GPWS "terrain, terrain" warning while descending on a visual approach to runway 25L at LAS after ATC vectored them early. The pilot flying initiated an aggressive climb to clear terrain, attributing the event to a lack of situational awareness regarding the ND display while visually scanning for the runway.

synopsis: CRJ-200 First Officer reported slowing aircraft to 180 KTS to configure for landing despite ATC instruction to maintain 250 KTS. ATC advised that pilots should have informed ATC of speed reduction.
summary: A CRJ200 crew slowed to 180 kts on the base leg of an ILS 36R approach in IMC to configure for landing. The approach controller stated the crew violated the assigned 250 kts restriction by slowing without clearance, though the pilot noted maintaining that speed would have prevented a stabilized approach.

synopsis: C208 Captain reports TKS equipped aircraft have a constant overwhelming chemical odor in heat, even when not in use. In flight, the pilot noticed throat irritation and difficulty breathing. The TKS 406B Material Safety Data Sheet warns of extreme dangers of repeated exposure.
summary: A pilot flying a TKS-equipped C208 Caravan experienced throat irritation and breathing difficulties due to toxic fumes from the belly pod TKS fluid in extreme heat. The pilot recovered after exiting the aircraft, noting that the system was not operated but the chemical odor and fluid exposure caused symptoms consistent with MSDS warnings.

synopsis: An A300-600 was cleared for an ILS 30L approach at OAK for which their company provided approach plate was not yet valid and for which their nav data base had no data. Cooperative assistance from ATC ultimately provided the tools to fly the approach.
summary: Pilots flying an RNAV30 approach to Oakland were cleared by NORCAL approach for an ILS30 using a non-existent waypoint, causing confusion due to outdated NOTAMs and plates. The crew executed a go-around after being too high, eventually landing on vectors, and reported that communication regarding the approach change had not reached end users.

synopsis: Flight Attendant encounters two passengers vomiting on her flights and has the flight crew call paramedics to meet the aircraft. The passengers are examined and released.
summary: Cabin crew managed two passengers from an international group who vomited repeatedly during boarding, cruise, and landing. After initial assessment, the crew broke sterile cockpit to alert pilots, and paramedics were called upon arrival to evaluate the ill travelers.

synopsis: When the flight attendants aboard an A319 discovered they were unable to communicate either with each other or the flight deck during taxi for takeoff they attempted to advise the flight crew by sliding a note under the door and knocking. A subsequent takeoff attempt was rejected when the cockpit received an ultimately unrelated lavatory smoke/fire warning. The flight returned to the gate for maintenance.
summary: Flight attendants reported inoperative interphones and erratic cabin lighting during taxi, prompting a takeoff abort after the captain received a false aft lavatory smoke alert. Maintenance incorrectly attributed the communication loss to a smoke detector, but the aircraft was reset and departed uneventfully after the issue was resolved.

synopsis: PA32 pilot reports a rough running engine and power loss at 3,500 feet. An emergency is declared and the flight diverts to the nearest suitable airport, 11 miles away where upon taxiing to ramp he forgets to change to Ground frequency.
summary: The pilot declared an emergency after an engine lost 50% power, landing safely and shutting down the vibrating engine on a taxiway. While exiting the aircraft, the pilot accidentally transmitted on the tower frequency instead of ground, prompting a recommendation to verify frequency selection before transmitting.

synopsis: PA32 instructor pilot experiences a power loss in IMC, rendering communication, navigation and heading reference systems inoperative. A cell phone is used to communicate with ATC and an iPad with approach plates and geo referencing is used to successfully complete an approach to landing.
summary: During an IFR training ILS approach, the pilot lost all communication, navigation, and heading systems without prior power failure indications. The crew squawked 7600, used a cell phone to coordinate with the tower, and successfully self-vectored to landing using battery-backed GPS units and light gun clearance.

synopsis: C172 instructor experienced a power loss and a rough running engine at 600 feet AGL on departure with the student flying. A downwind entry to a visual approach is planned, but when hot oil smells begin entering the cockpit a short approach is accomplished successfully.
summary: A pilot and student experienced sudden power loss and severe engine roughness at 600 feet during initial climb, likely due to oil loss. They executed a turnback and landed safely on runway 35R with no injuries or damage beyond the engine.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: ROA TRACON Controller reports of an airborne conflict caused by the Developmental becoming confused and issuing an incorrect heading.
summary: An air traffic controller and a developmental controller managed Aircraft X and Aircraft Y near Lynchburg, where a routing error caused separation to decrease to 1.5 miles. The controller attributed the incident to the developmental confusing the DAN destination with the SBV VOR, highlighting that increasing flight training traffic has created unsafe workload conditions.

synopsis: DAB Controller reports of window washing equipment being out of service and foggy windows.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that the Tower's exterior window sprinkler system failed, causing fog on the northeastern window overlooking Taxiways W, E, and Runway 16. This obscured visibility of the complex intersection with Runway 7L, a critical area for Ground and Local Control, requiring immediate repairs.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: JAX Controller approved a short turn on to final for an aircraft, received numerous low altitude alerts and then had to resequence the aircraft for another approach.
summary: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X for an RNAV approach to runway 11 at GNV but issued an early clearance before the pilot was established. This resulted in low altitude alerts, requiring the pilot to climb and the controller to re-vector the aircraft to final.

synopsis: ZAB Controller describes a session where aircraft were deviating due to weather. This made the workload more complex, while involving SUA, and bad routes.
summary: An air traffic controller in sector 80 at ZAB managed complex PHX arrivals and departures during weather and active military airspace. The controller attributed the unsafe, unmanageable situation to inherent flaws in the new KATMN and SUNSS procedures, which create head-on conflicts and separation risks.

synopsis: When a B737-700 First Officer updated his (personal tablet based) EFB navdata while not first properly updating the operating software to a newer version he had good data displayed for the first day of the trip but when the company force updated all un-updated tablets the day after the data revision was active he no longer had access because the new data had to be loaded after the revised software was installed.
summary: The First Officer and Captain discovered the Jepp FD-Pro app on the First Officer's EFB was out-of-date at the gate due to a forced app update without data. Consequently, the First Officer used paper charts for the legs while the Captain used his iPad, as the new app version was non-functional without a large data download.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: A Captain reported the PAPI at PTSA/KSA has been unserviceable for several months, a situation he believes uancceptable due to the short 5,700 FT length of the runway with both approaches over open water.
summary: A pilot reported that the PAPI system for PTSA is unserviceable, turning off after 10 seconds of pilot-controlled lighting activation during approaches to runways 5 and 23. The reporter noted this issue has persisted for months on a 5,700-foot runway surrounded by water, where operable PAPIs are essential for approaches to minimums.

synopsis: Flight crew, initially cleared to 5,000 feet and 160 knots, slowed to Vref after being cleared for an ILS Approach. When switched to Tower frequency, Tower advised that the flight was supposed to maintain 160 knots. Aircraft was vectored around for another ILS Approach.
summary: The pilot and First Officer slowed to landing configuration below the assigned 160 kts during arrival. Tower rejected the approach due to the speed violation, vectored the aircraft for a retry, and no further issues occurred.

synopsis: When inbound to ATL, the CRJ700 flight crew was given a new PRM runway assignment and direct to GAASS fix, which weren't associated with their previously briefed approach. As they descended through 14,000 FT, a further clearance to descend to 11,000 FT was either never given or was lost over the runway and arrival changes. ATC quickly asked why they hadn't started down and the issue was resolved.
summary: The flight crew, arriving at Atlanta, received a direct GAASS clearance for ILS PRM RWY 8R without an altitude restriction while reprogramming the FMS. ATC queried the lack of descent, prompting the crew to clarify they had not been given a descent clearance, which was subsequently issued to 11,000 feet.

synopsis: EMB-145 crew failed to change the departure runway in their FMS when cleared to Runway 15R at IAH (vice their planned Runway 9). They took off with the wrong waypoints displayed for their clearance via the GUMBY RNAV SID. Assistance from ATC got them back on course. Fatigue and an inexperienced First Officer were cited as contributing factors.
summary: The Captain entered the wrong departure runway in the FMS due to fatigue and complacency while the First Officer flew. The error was detected at 75 KIAS during takeoff roll, leading to a request for vectors to correct the flight path after initial confusion.

synopsis: First Officer reports about the cause of a Master Warning sounding due to a Rudder Configuration issue on a CRJ-700 aircraft. Second takeoff attempt aborted when similar Master Warning sounded and 'Rudder Config' appeared. Pilot resets the Rudder Trim a third time and departs. Why the Rudder Trim moved out of center position uncommanded on the takeoff roll, is unknown.
summary: The crew aborted a takeoff on runway 34R at 20 knots due to a Master Warning for Rudder Configuration caused by an unknown trim displacement. After the captain re-centered the trim and confirmed operation, the aircraft departed successfully without maintenance assistance.

synopsis: When the right generator control failed on a long range B777 overwater flight, the fuel burn and drag penalties associated with utilizing the APU generator precluded continuing the flight. Crew dumped fuel and returned to their departure airport.
summary: The crew experienced a right generator fault shortly after departure, leading to an unsuccessful reset and APU start. Due to fuel concerns for the long flight, they dumped fuel and returned to the departure airport, landing 3,000 pounds below maximum landing weight.

synopsis: Air carrier flight crew describes being cleared for takeoff as soon as a previous departure was cleared for takeoff. Pilot waited until aircraft was safely airborne then started the takeoff roll.
summary: The First Officer selected the wrong tower frequency, causing a delay that resulted in the tower clearing the crew for takeoff while another aircraft was still on the runway. The crew held short until the preceding aircraft was safely airborne, despite the controller insisting separation was adequate.

synopsis: Pilot reported of not being able to communicate with ATC on a consistent basis and has questions about the routing that ATC has issued.
summary: The flight crew experienced two lost communication periods with LA Center during climb out due to the controller managing multiple frequencies. This prevented timely clearances for weather deviations and route changes, forcing the aircraft to penetrate thunderstorms and creating uncertainty over a revised direct routing.

synopsis: CRJ200 flight crew reports a NMAC with a warbird at 4000 feet east of SBN. Evasive action is taken by both aircraft and a collision is narrowly avoided.
summary: During a descent to 4,000 ft, the crew executed an abrupt pitch-up and left turn to avoid a non-transponder-equipped warbird that passed dangerously close. The TCAS did not alert due to the warbird's inactive transponder, but the aircraft avoided contact and completed a normal landing at SBN.

synopsis: During climb, an ERJ-190 flight crew detected a wet mold or musky smell that resembled dirty socks or severe body odor. After leveling at FL240 and being unable to find the source of the odor, the crew elects to return to the departure airport.
summary: The flight crew experienced an unidentified musky odor and physical symptoms during climb, forcing an overweight return to ZZZ. No smoke or source was found, but the crew landed safely and were medically evaluated after the incident.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Regional Jet Captain approaching SAF learns that only the VOR DME A is available for approach in night VMC. The ILS is out of service and the RNAV 15 is not authorized at night. A visual approach to Runway 15 is accepted and the RNAV is used as backup.
summary: The flight crew and approach controller faced a safety issue during night arrival at SAF in mountainous terrain when RNAV approaches were unavailable and ILS/VASI systems were out of service. The crew rejected a straight-in visual clearance due to lack of vertical guidance and performed a 360-degree turn to descend safely.

synopsis: Citation flight crew reported NMAC at UNV due at least in part to an inoperative TCAS.
summary: Pilots operating an aircraft with an MELed TCAS flew 300 feet vertically above another aircraft during a visual approach to runway 24 at UNV. The near-miss occurred because New York Center vectored the flight without resolving traffic conflicts, a situation the crew attributes to the inoperative TCAS.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported they were parked near Taxiway B after pushback and were almost hit by a B747 taxiing past them. Darkness was a factor, and the crew suggested push procedure should not position them that close to the taxiway.
summary: The flight crew reported a near-collision with a high-speed B747 while starting engines on the MMMX ramp in pre-dawn darkness. The B747's winglet passed 10–15 feet from the cockpit, prompting a recommendation to release aircraft 20 feet before the painted roadway near Taxiway Bravo.

synopsis: CRJ-200 flight crew reported an unstable approach with speed and altitude deviations to MSO. Weather, ATC procedures, and First Officer inexperience were factors in this report.
summary: The First Officer and Pilot Monitoring attempted a VOR DME B approach to Runway 29 in MSO, executing two missed approaches due to ATC vectoring, crosswinds, and an airspeed decay triggering a stall shaker. The Pilot Monitoring took control, switched to an ILS Z Runway 11 approach, and landed safely.

synopsis: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) taxiing a company B757 aircraft reports coming up on a dark, unpowered ERJ-145 aircraft with no external lighting on. Light on the towbarless Supertug tractor only minimally visible, with completely dark aircraft between their B757 and Tow tractor. Technician notes long established standards requiring Anti-Collision and Nav lights not enforced during aircraft tow.
summary: A B757 crew taxiing to a hangar encountered a dark, unpowered ERJ-145 being towed by a minimally lit supertug on active taxiways. The reporter cited noncompliance with lighting regulations and FARs, noting the confusing lack of external lights on the towed aircraft created a safety hazard.

synopsis: A M20J pilot suffered a right main gear collapse while exiting the runway after landing.
summary: The pilot reported a possible flat tire on the right main gear after landing on RWY XX. The right main gear collapsed while the aircraft was turning left to exit the runway.

synopsis: Single engine aircraft pilot reports striking a deer at touchdown at DYL airport that resulted in damage to the landing gear and prop.
summary: The PIC of an IFR flight struck a deer while rounding out on RWY 23 at DYL. The deer wrapped around the nose gear, snapping the strut and causing the propeller to strike the runway before the aircraft stopped.

synopsis: PA-28-180 pilot reported loss of control during landing in gusty wind conditions that resulted in excursion from the runway surface into grass and brush. No damage noted.
summary: During a practice landing on runway 26L, a pilot lost directional control after a left crosswind gust caused the aircraft to balloon and veer off into tall grass. The pilot attributed the incident to delayed flap retraction and excessive speed, resulting in no aircraft damage after being pushed back onto the runway.

synopsis: C177 pilot described a NMAC after takeoff from CNO.
summary: The pilot reported a near-miss with an unknown aircraft while climbing to 2,500 ft after departing CNO. The pilot executed evasive maneuvers after the unknown plane approached within 600–700 ft, causing the pilot to deviate from the F70 course before both aircraft separated.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: Pilot attempting to make a visual approach receives instructions from Approach Control and also receives landing clearance from the Tower. He is only on one frequency, Approach, and wonders how he is hearing the Tower. Pilot queries Tower after being switched over and the confirm that earlier they did clear him to land.
summary: A pilot descending for a visual approach to RWY 29L received conflicting instructions from Fresno Approach and Tower due to suspected cross-frequency transmissions. The pilot landed safely without incident, attributing the confusion to Tower inadvertently transmitting on the Approach frequency before handoff.

synopsis: RV6 pilot reports a NMAC with a Cessna at 7,000 feet. The Cessna was flying in roughly the same direction, had been reported by ATC and was showing on the RV6 pilot's PCAS. The RV6 pilot was descending and overtaking the Cessna and had been intending to stop at 7,000 feet until clear, but became distracted.
summary: The pilot, flying IFR at 9,000 feet, diverted to ZEF and canceled IFR after receiving traffic advisories for a Cessna at 7,000 feet. While distracted by an iPad, the pilot descended through 7,300 feet and passed 150 feet above the Cessna before adjusting course to increase separation and landing safely.

synopsis: While flying a standard pattern entry and circuit, the pilot of an aircraft not equipped with communication radios, suffered a close encounter on final with a straight-in another small aircraft.
summary: A glider tow pilot and student experienced a near mid-air collision at LRY while entering standard left traffic for Runway 18. The incident occurred because another aircraft ignored standard procedures by executing a non-standard six-mile straight-in approach, forcing both pilots to take evasive action.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: An instructor pilot on approach to LAF Runway 10 noted the PAPI indication for slightly low was RED, WHITE, RED, RED but according to the FAA AIM should be WHITE, RED, RED, RED.
summary: A pilot and student observed a non-standard PAPI light sequence (Red, White, Red, Red) instead of the correct "Slightly Low" indication while inbound to LAF Runway 10. The pilot reported this equipment malfunction to the ATCT ten days prior, but no corrective action had been taken.

synopsis: Flight instructor reports being unable to locate Taxiway C5 while southbound on Taxiway C due to no sign at the intersection. Airport construction is underway.
summary: The pilot reported missing the C5 taxiway sign while turning off Runway 34R and proceeding from C3 to C5. The crew overshot the intended exit because no sign for C5 was visible on taxiway C, causing them to pass C4 and reach C7 instead.

synopsis: C152 pilot reports a NMAC shortly after takeoff with an opposite direction Cessna. The takeoff had been announced on CTAF with no response then the radio switched to AWOS and the takeoff initiated.
summary: A pilot practicing spot landings took off from runway XY on the wrong frequency while distracted by passenger conversation. The pilot executed an evasive right turn to avoid a collision with an unidentified aircraft on short final, attributing the incident to poor radio monitoring and frequency selection.

synopsis: C172 Instructor believes that signage, markings and lighting at OJC are not up to current standards.
summary: A pilot reported that poor night markings and signage at Johnson County Executive Airport (OJC) make it difficult to identify taxiway exits and distinguish grass areas from taxiways. The reporter attributed this safety risk to a lack of reflectant striping, modern hold bars, and adequate lighting, urging the county to upgrade facilities.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: An instructor reported the LAF pilot controlled lighting requires the each mike key be held at least one second to turn the runway lights ON and then the lights extinguish prior to the specified 15 minutes. At one second per mike key, 7 seconds would select High intensity, verse the 5 seconds specified.
summary: A flight instructor and student reported unusual pilot-controlled lighting behavior at LAF during night VFR operations. The system required deliberate one-second clicks to activate, exhibited intermittent runway flashers, and turned off in less than 15 minutes, suggesting a high squelch setting and incorrect auto-off timing.

synopsis: B757 Captain experiences a track deviation when ATC issues a runway change during the SKEES 3 arrival. When the runway is changed in the FMC, the arrival disappears.
summary: The pilot flying reported that changing the FMS runway from 16R to 16L at SKEES fix caused the arrival to drop and an uncommanded right turn. The crew manually corrected the heading, received a direct clearance to IRRON from ATC, and landed safely with no loss of separation.

synopsis: B737-300 flight crew reports rejecting a takeoff due to the Captain's airspeed indicator being inoperative. The inoperative indicator is detected at 80 knots, but the takeoff is rejected at 120 knots.
summary: The Captain aborted takeoff at 80 knots due to an inoperative airspeed indicator on the Captain's side. The aircraft taxied to the gate, where a #1 tire went flat approximately 10 minutes after parking.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain believes that his company should assign international flying only to crews who are specifically trained to fly these routes.
summary: The Pilot-in-Command reported that uneventful flights to CUN highlighted the need for frequent international experience to handle complex local procedures. The Captain recommends restricting international duties to a subset of pilots with monthly recency to ensure safety and avoid operational risks.

synopsis: B737 First Officer experiences a compressor stall at FL410 while flying in IMC and light turbulence at -61 degrees C. The engine anti-ice was off but continuous ignition was selected. The engine recovered by itself and the flight continued to its destination.
summary: The flying pilot and Captain experienced a temporary N1 drop and vibration on the number two engine while in IMC at 41,000 feet during night flight. The Captain attributed the event to a compressor stall, after which the engine recovered to normal thrust and the flight landed uneventfully.

synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reports being pushed back too far with the left main wheels off the hard surface. The ground crew does not accurately describe the situation but an attempt to taxi out proves fruitless. The engines are shut down and the tug reattached, but the aircraft cannot be moved.
summary: During pushback in darkness, the left main wheels departed the pavement onto the grass, likely due to inadequate wing walker coverage. A subsequent tug attempt to recover the aircraft snapped the towbar, resulting in passenger deplaning and an aircraft swap.

synopsis: When the B737 flight crew was cleared to 'descend via' the KIDDZ1 RNAV STAR to HOU, the crew was unable to complete programming the STAR until ATC provided the expected landing runway. STAR tracks and altitude restrictions beyond GLUVR are dependent on programming the associated runway. When asked, the Center Controller advised they had no idea which runway was in use.
summary: During a cruise at FL 340, the crew received a "descend via" clearance from Houston Center without a runway transition, as the controller claimed to be unaware of the active runway. The crew descended to 9000 feet at GLUVR until Houston Approach provided the Runway 4 transition, highlighting a need for better Center-TRACON coordination.

synopsis: A B757-200 pilot questions whether maintenance incompetence or intentional misrepresentation by Maintenance was responsible for three separate logbook sign-offs involving a Captain's crotch seatbelt that was installed backwards and not secured under the seat. Captain notes the event illustrates a lack of attention to basic aircraft maintenance procedures, inspection and repair.
summary: A B757 pilot discovered the captain's crotch seatbelt was installed backwards at ZZZ, rendering it insecure despite three prior maintenance sign-offs. The error, originating from improper installation at ZZZ1 and missed by subsequent inspections, caused a departure delay and required swapping the seat.

synopsis: When both left and right packs over temped and shut down, the flight crew of a B757 began an emergency descent and declared an emergency. Communication on the flight deck was compromised by improper use of the oxygen mask microphones. The packs were reset during the descent, the cabin stabilized at 10,000 feet, and the descent stopped at FL240. A normal descent for landing was made as they approached their destination.
summary: The crew of a flight at FL380 experienced dual air conditioning pack failures, prompting an emergency declaration and descent to FL240. Communication difficulties arose due to unswitched oxygen masks and limited jumpseater radio access, but the crew reset the packs to regain cabin altitude control.

synopsis: A319 flight crew describes a preconditioned air hose being sucked into the number one engine when the jet bridge is pulled back, after starting at the gate due to an inoperative APU.
summary: During a ground start with an inoperative APU, ramp personnel failed to remove the preconditioned air hose before clearing engine #1, causing the hose to be ingested. The crew immediately shut down the engine, deplaned passengers safely, and reported no injuries.

synopsis: Ramp Marshall reports an A320 Captain taxiing too fast and not following directions during taxi into a gate requiring two Marshalls and a dog leg turn for alignment.
summary: A primary marshaller reported that an A320 captain turned the aircraft too early and fast at a dog-leg gate, forcing the marshaller to retreat to avoid the #1 engine. The final marshaller stopped the aircraft just in time, but the flight crew did not perform a walk-around or address the incident.

synopsis: Initially, the Captain of an EMB-145 felt no impairment after being struck in the eyes by a ground based green laser. However, he soon suffered increasing amounts of pain. Therefore, he directed the First Officer to take the controls, declare an emergency and return to their departure airport. EMTs met the aircraft and took the Captain to a hospital.
summary: The Captain reported a green laser strike while climbing through 8,000 ft on an RNAV departure, causing worsening eye pain that necessitated an emergency return. The First Officer landed the aircraft safely, and the Captain was transported to a hospital, delaying the flight until a replacement Captain arrived.

synopsis: MD80 flight crew experiences an altitude deviation leveling at 11,000 feet on the KLNDR 1 Arrival into DFW. The First Officer was new and the Captain believes that the vertical speed wheel may have been bumped during the level off. He also believes that the MD80, an aircraft without a true VNAV capability, is a 'deviation waiting to happen.'
summary: The Captain and new First Officer flying an MD80 on the KLNDR 1 arrival into DFW descended 250 feet below 11,000 feet because the aircraft failed to capture altitude. The Captain attributed the deviation to the First Officer likely moving the vertical speed wheel and noted high workload with new arrivals on an aircraft lacking true VNAV.

synopsis: A CRJ-900 flight crew just five miles from KOLTT on the KOLTT RNAV STAR--having planned for, programmed and briefed for a landing on Runway 8R--was instead changed to land on Runway 9R. The First Officer was unable to program the substantial changes of routing and approach, causing multiple track deviations and the ultimate disengagement of all auto flight tools to execute a manual approach and landing.
summary: During a KOLTT RNAV STAR arrival, the crew received a last-minute runway change to ILS PRM 9R, leading to FMS programming errors and a missed turn. High workload and incorrect FMS transitions caused a one-mile course deviation at 21 DME, which the pilot corrected by disengaging the autopilot before completing a normal landing.

synopsis: B737 Flight Attendant reports passengers boarding before she was ready and without any communication from the gate agent or operations.
summary: Cabin crew reported that passengers began boarding while they were stowing luggage, without prior notification or an operational readiness check. The reporter stated that operations should verify crew readiness before initiating boarding.

synopsis: Two B737 flight attendants describe a takeoff while they are standing in the isle, having not completed their final walk-through and takeoff PA.
summary: Cabin crew reported that the aircraft began takeoff immediately after the "cleared for departure" chime, preventing a final walk-through and PA announcement. The crew member was thrown against the galley while securing a door and struggled to buckle in before the aircraft was airborne.

synopsis: B737 Flight Attendant reports passenger boarding commencing before her safety and security checks have been completed. When asked to sign the preflight checklist, it is signed as half complete. This results in a delay as the Flight Attendant involved is asked to do the security checks that were not completed with passengers on board.
summary: A cabin crew member could not finish the preflight security check under seats because boarding had started. Management pressured the crew to complete the check with passengers onboard rather than deplaning, resulting in a compromised inspection.

synopsis: An International Flight Attendant reports being rushed to complete an aircraft swap, then having the aircraft door closed prior to the completion of all preflight duties.
summary: Management rushed a crew swap to LHR to prevent flight attendants from going illegal, forcing the aircraft door closed despite objections. This prevented the crew from completing required SOPs, including jumpseat assignments, safety checks, and door arming procedures.

synopsis: A321 Flight Attendant reports donning an oxygen mask, after 30 minutes of waiting for takeoff, due to foul smelling air in the cabin. The Captain is informed and the flight returns to the gate.
summary: A flight attendant on an A321 parked on the tarmac reported incapacitation due to strong toxic fumes, likely from a bleed air mechanical issue. The Captain returned to the gate to deplane passengers and crew after the crew member required portable oxygen.

synopsis: C208 Captain departing Runway 5 at OGG experiences a runway incursion by a B757 that had been instructed to hold short of Runway 5 after landing on Runway 2. The reporter is able to takeoff before the intersection and climb above the B757.
summary: The pilot reported that while taking off from Runway 5, a B757 holding short crossed the hold short line and entered the runway during rotation. The tower ordered the B757 to stop, allowing the departing aircraft to cross approximately 100 feet above it, which the pilot described as a potential close call had rotation occurred later.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 2 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: A pilot filed and was issued the SDL JCOBS2 arrival but was notified by ABQ that the arrival was NOTAMed canceled but still available in databases. Many other SDL and PHX SIDs and STARs have been NOTAMed unavailable.
summary: A Part 135 pilot filed the JCOBS2 arrival to SDL but was informed by ABQ Center that the procedure was deleted despite remaining published in navigation databases. The pilot corrected the flight plan to the DSERT1 arrival and completed the flight uneventfully.

synopsis: Lancair pilot reports a NMAC with a Bonanza while flying the sound Visual to RWY 34 at HPN at 3000 feet. ATC issued instructions to the two aircraft to avoid a collision but they came too late to have much effect. The Lancair pilot, on an IFR flight plan had accepted the Sound Visual and the Bonanza pilot was VFR. See and avoid.
summary: An IFR pilot on approach to HPN experienced a near-midair conflict with a VFR Bonanza after the controller failed to issue traffic warnings. The pilot attributes the incident to controller overload and improper integration of the VFR aircraft into Class B airspace, resulting in a 100-200 foot separation.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: D01 Controller describes a situation where two aircraft are deviating due to rain and lightning. One aircraft is NORDO and in a higher MVA than the aircraft is.
summary: The FR3 controller managed arrivals to 34R in severe weather and lightning, facing high workload due to Traffic Management pressure and uncoordinated departures. After one aircraft reported lightning strikes and another went NORDO in turbulence, all aircraft landed safely, but the controller refused further duty due to fatigue and excessive arrival volume.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: ZTL Controller describes being told to get out another Controller for a break, while another Controller goes and opens a position. The Controller is then told to go to the new sector and that Controller was opening and that Controller was to give the FLM a break. While the Controller is moving to open the new position, aircraft are heard on the sectors frequency. The FLM had already split up the sector and taken the frequencies from the original Controller.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that a Flight Line Manager closed sectors and transferred frequencies without verifying readiness, leaving five aircraft unable to communicate. The controller immediately restored operations after the supervisor's lack of communication caused a temporary loss of contact with departing traffic.

synopsis: ZMA reports of an aircraft spill out that area had no information about.
summary: An air traffic controller observed aircraft spilling out of Warning Area W168 due to a vague briefing package lacking UAV mission details. The reporter attributed the issue to insufficient information and recommended comprehensive briefings including times, altitudes, and lost link procedures.

synopsis: B737 sencond generation flight crew describes two go arounds at ATL. The first due to not tuning a new localizer frequency after ATC assigns a runway change. The second is due to the failure of the First Officer's localizer receiver. The Captain takes over on the third attempt when the First Officer's localizer indicator flags, and lands safely.
summary: Pilots flying a B737 into Atlanta experienced three go-arounds due to incorrect ILS frequency tuning, misheard tower clearances, and an intermittent First Officer localizer failure. The crew eventually landed safely on Runway 8R after the Captain took control, attributing the issues to incomplete briefings and a recurring equipment defect.

synopsis: B737-700 Captain reports diverting to the nearest suitable airport when the flight attendants report smoke in the cabin. QRH procedures are complied with.
summary: Flight crew diverted to ZZZ from FL380 after cabin crew reported worsening smoke odor. Fire rescue inspected the aircraft post-landing but could not identify the source of the fumes.

synopsis: The reporter expressed concern that during winter months with icy taxiways an aircraft transitioning from DEN Taxiway D5 to Taxiway WB may be in danger of a taxiway excursion on the south side of that intersection and risk serious damage or injury because of a forty foot drop off.
summary: A pilot reported a safety hazard at Denver International Airport where a steep drop-off at the D5 and WB junction could cause significant aircraft damage and injury if an aircraft departs the taxiway while turning eastbound on contaminated surfaces. The reporter recommends prohibiting D5 use when snow, slush, or braking action less than good is present.

synopsis: B757 Captain experienced a pack overheat at FL380 and the pack shuts down. Two minutes into the QRH procedure the other pack does the same thing. An emergency descent is initiated while the First Officer continues to work the problem using the QRH. At some point the Captain elects to push the pack reset buttons, without specific QRH direction and the packs reset. The Captain discovers later that the aircraft had a history of pack failures that was not available to the flight crew.
summary: The flight crew experienced dual air conditioning pack failures at FL380, triggering an emergency descent to FL240 due to confusing QRH procedures. The pilot reset the packs manually, resolving the issue, but later learned the aircraft had a similar unreported failure two weeks prior.

synopsis: A B777 First Officer addressed unanticipated and untrained for interaction between programming of NADP (Noise Abatement Departure Procedure) thrust settings and modifications to the ACARS software that caused a default to a reduced thrust takeoff setting when the intent was to utilize max thrust for a MTOGW takeoff.
summary: During a Sydney takeoff in a Boeing 777, the crew inadvertently loaded reduced thrust via the new ACARS 2 system while monitoring fuel burn. The Captain manually corrected the thrust to maximum N1 after noticing the error, highlighting a lack of training on the system's default settings.

synopsis: A319 First Officer believes that rampers are not being properly trained at some stations to chock all gear and how to complete a baggage count form.
summary: Flight crew and ground crew at a contract station experienced delays due to unchocked main gear and conflicting baggage counts. The reporter attributed these issues to inadequate ground crew training, which led to safety shortcuts and confusion over load sheet reconciliation procedures.

synopsis: When the Flight Attendant aboard an EMB-145 fell ill and incommunicado two passengers rose to the occasion managing to alert and contact the flight crew who diverted to a nearby airport where the flight attendant was met by EMT personnel and taken to the hospital for treatment.
summary: During cruise, the crew diverted after a passenger reported a flight attendant was sick with a severe headache and weakness. Paramedics met the aircraft upon landing, and the flight attendant eventually agreed to a hospital evaluation for her serious medical condition.

synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew reports receiving reroutes and vectors along their route for weather, leading to a declaration of minimum fuel with ATC. With no perceived change in the way they are being handled by ATC. They advised ATC of a low fuel urgency situation. This achieves the desired results and the flight lands safely.
summary: The flight crew declared a fuel emergency during en-route operations to ZZZ after ATC re-routes and thunderstorm deviations threatened to leave insufficient fuel for the alternate. Declaring the emergency secured a direct clearance to ZZZ, allowing a safe landing with adequate fuel despite heavy weather and dispatcher communication delays.

synopsis: A BE-400 R Thrust Reverser ARM and Master Warning flashed momentarily during descent accompanied by a violent 45 degree right roll and loud rumbling noise. The whole event lasted approximately 2 seconds and conditions returned to normal. The approach was continued to a normal landing.
summary: During a descent to 2500 feet with idle power and autopilot engaged, the aircraft briefly rolled 45 degrees right while flashing a 'R TR ARM' light and Master Warning. The event lasted two seconds, cleared automatically, and the crew completed a normal landing without incident.

synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew reports a track deviation departing OKC Runway 17R, when the Captain confuses the initial climb instructions for Wiley Post with those for OKC. An iPad was in use and had been zoomed in to Runways 17L/R for Wiley Post.
summary: During an OKC departure on the TRUPR1, the captain misread the departure text for a different airport and incorrectly turned to heading 200 instead of runway heading. The error was corrected after ATC issued new instructions, though the crew noted confusion caused by shared departure texts and unilateral pilot action.

synopsis: CRJ-700 Captain reported ground personnel failed to follow SOP and hooked up to fuel when an engine was still running.
summary: The pilot reported that while the aircraft was at the gate with one engine running, untrained ground personnel attempted to fuel the aircraft. The pilot immediately shut down the aircraft and emergency power, citing a total breakdown in the safety chain due to inadequate ramp training.

synopsis: MD-82 flight crew reports they were alerted to a tire failure on takeoff by several loud bangs and a burning rubber smell. They declared an emergency and returned to the departure airport.
summary: During gear retraction, a tire explosion caused burning rubber and debris ingestion on the left engine. The crew performed an unpressurized landing and safely evacuated passengers via aft stairs due to concerns over further tire failure.

synopsis: The flight crew of a commercial fixed wing aircraft flying the RNAV (GPS) Runway 13 approach at BIS utilized an LNAV MDA of 2,100 MSL as depicted in the Jeppesen Minima box vice what they believed to be a 'number 2' ball noted MDA of 2,380 MSL depicted on the profile view in three locations. During the approach they received an EGPWS terrain warning and, when visual noted a building in front of them. They climbed to extinguish the warning and continued the approach.
summary: Flight crew on an RNAV (GPS) runway 13 approach used an incorrect 2100' MDA instead of the 2380' LNAV-only minimum due to confusing chart depiction. This resulted in an enhanced ground proximity warning and a pull-up maneuver before a visual landing.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Inspector reports about a company A319 aircraft that had both 'in-arm' and 'seat-back' tray tables installed at the left and right Emergency Exit rows. If both tables are extended at the same time, they will block egress of passengers. If they are all extended at the same time there will be six tray-tables overlapping each other and blocking the exit path on both sides of the plane.
summary: A Maintenance Inspector on the ramp reported that an A319 had both in-arm and seat-back tray tables installed in row 14 exit seats. This configuration could block emergency egress if all six tables are extended simultaneously, prompting a recommendation to verify installation with engineering.

synopsis: A Flight Instructor describes the efforts of a student pilot and himself to manually extend the landing gears on a Cessna C210 aircraft after takeoff when all three gears failed to fully retract. Landing gears were hanging in the 'Wasp Leg' position. Low Hydraulic fluid quantity was a contributor.
summary: The pilot and student departed for instrument training after a mechanic dismissed low hydraulic fluid concerns following gear service. The landing gear failed to retract due to low fluid, requiring emergency extension and an uneventful return landing after ground checks confirmed the leak.

synopsis: After completing the charted JAIKE RNAV STAR, given a vector and cleared to descend to 4,000 MSL, a Falcon 10 flight crew noted they would be passing below the New York Class B floor of 7,000 MSL and reduced their airspeed to 200 KIAS as required. Approach Control remonstrated them for doing so, advising they were not to reduce below 250 knots without approval--appearing to reference the SPEED note on the STAR chart--and vectored them out of sequence, advising they had been moved from number one for the airport to number six.Fatigue, the STAR chart format and the inadequacy of their EFB tablets to display the entire chart were cited as contributing factors.
summary: A fatigued flight crew flying a commercial aircraft into TEB reduced speed below 250 knots without ATC approval during the Jaike3 arrival. The error resulted from overlooking a chart note and a misunderstanding of arrival requirements after receiving a vector, causing the crew to be repositioned in the arrival sequence.

synopsis: C182 pilot reports being coerced into flying on a windy day by his Chief Pilot. Upon returning to the grass strip, the reporter loses control during landing in a crosswind and hits the windsock pole.
summary: A pilot and Chief Pilot flew a C182 on a grass runway in gusty 20-knot winds despite the pilot's expressed discomfort. The pilot lost directional control during landing, veered off the sloped runway, and struck a windsock pipe, attributing the accident to poor decision-making and ignoring high wind hazards.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A Technician reports that ORD Airport has been allowing large Regional aircraft, including CRJ and ERJ airplanes, to be towed with towbarless high speed Douglas and Goldhofer Super tugs (tractors). No one is in the cockpit, no hydraulic power, no electrical power, no aircraft beacon and no aircraft navigation lighting is required even at night. He notes that darkened aircraft are a safety hazard.
summary: Pilots report that unoccupied CRJ and regional aircraft are towed across active and inactive runways day and night without beacons or navigation lights. Large transport aircraft following behind cannot see the tow vehicle due to the towed aircraft's fuselage, creating a risk of serious accident.

synopsis: A Captain taxiing into the CRP air carrier terminal ramp on Taxiway L was blinded and disoriented by extremely high luminosity white lights. The Captain was unable to distinguish ramp markings and had difficulty following his Marshaller.
summary: Pilots reported that extreme glare from low-mounted, high-lumen halogen ramp lights at CRP obscured taxiway markings and the marshaller during post-landing taxi to the gate. The reporter attributed this hazard to the lights' height, spacing, and angles, which blinded the crew and made navigation nearly impossible.

synopsis: A320 flight crew reported they encountered an engine stall and returned to departure airport.
summary: The pilot reported that while passing 5,000 feet, turning off engine anti-ice caused an engine stall and yaw. The crew declared an emergency, performed the checklist, and diverted back to the departure airport uneventfully.

synopsis: During a pneumatic air start, a Ramp employee alerts his Ramp Lead that the air hose was lying under Number 1 Engine. Air hose was ingested by Number 1 Engine after Lead attempted to disconnect the pneumatic hose after the air start was completed.
summary: A mechanic assisting with a pneumatic air start noticed the aircraft hose under engine one, but the Lead waved off the concern. The Lead then disconnected the hose, which was immediately ingested by engine one.

synopsis: A Captain and First Officer report about uncommanded left yaw motions similar to choppy, jerk like movements while climbing from 11,000 feet to 29,000 feet on a CRJ-200 aircraft. Yaw Damper-1 had disconnected twice while uncommanded yaw oscillations and roll motions (Dutch Roll) continued with Autopilot 'On' or 'Off'. Aircraft control became increasingly difficult, flight diverted.
summary: The flight crew of a CRJ-200 experienced uncommanded left yaw and Dutch Roll during climb and cruise due to repeated Yaw Damper 1 disconnections. Following QRH procedures, they diverted to ZZZ2 for a safe landing, noting the aircraft had a history of similar unresolved maintenance issues.

synopsis: A Flight Attendant reports the steps on the Main Cabin Door of a CRJ-700 aircraft were incorrectly configured during a Maintenance C-Check. With cabin door open, the position of raised steps two and three from the bottom of the door had been swapped, affecting the location of the door open/close handgrip and instruction placards for door operations, emergency lights and emergency exiting of aircraft.
summary: A flight attendant on a CRJ-700 discovered the main cabin door stairs were installed incorrectly, placing emergency instructions and lights in the wrong location. This misconfiguration could delay evacuation if the attendant were incapacitated, prompting the crew to contact Maintenance before flight completion.

synopsis: Pilot of an ERJ-170 aircraft explains the importance for maintenance to have a clear, precise checklist when deferring any MEL item, in order to ensure a faulty component is properly secured and the aircraft is in fact airworthy. He added that employees must have a sense of integrity and that lying to flight crews not be tolerated. Mechanic told Captain that he had verified a Water Compressor C/B had been pulled and collared, but was later found not pulled.
summary: The pilot discovered a deferred electric compressor MEL was not properly secured by a pulled circuit breaker, despite a mechanic falsely claiming it was. A subsequent inspection confirmed the breaker was not pulled, revealing the mechanic's dishonesty and a failure to follow MEL procedures before the aircraft was eventually dispatched.

synopsis: Air carrier flight crew intending to land on Runway 13L at BFI and cleared to descend via the CHINS STAR misinterpreted the chart crossing restrictions. They crossed RADDY at 11,000 instead of 16,000 as directed by the generic 'TURBOJETS LANDING SOUTH' that pertains to arrivals at 'all' airports served by the arrival.
summary: Pilots flying a turbojet on the CHINS9 arrival to Boeing Field (BFI) descended to 11,000 feet at RADDY instead of the required 16,000 feet due to a misleading chart note specific to runway 31L. Air Traffic Control corrected the error, noting the chart's ambiguity for multiple airports caused the misinterpretation, though no traffic conflict occurred.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew extends their duty day at the company's request to fly a leg to LGA. Expecting the VOR RWY 4 and briefing same, ATC issues a clearance for the ILS RWY 22 circle to land Runway 13. The approach is accomplished successfully although the approach may have been unstabilized and the minimums used were not to company standards.
summary: A fatigued crew on a duty extension flew an ILS 22 circle-to-13 approach into LGA after Runway 4 closed. Rushed by ATC and Port Authority demands, they set the wrong MDA, experienced an unstable approach with bank and sink rate warnings, but landed safely in the touchdown zone.

aircraft: Boeing Company Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: After experiencing an NMAC with a light aircraft arriving the same uncontrolled airport, MIV, the pilot of a BV-234 helicopter expressed the opinion the airport is busy enough to warrant at least a daytime ATC presence.
summary: A pilot conducting an instrument approach in VFR conditions at MIV observed a private aircraft passing within 100 feet below without traffic advisories from the facility. The reporter attributes the near-midair incident to uncontrolled airspace, high traffic volume, and other pilots failing to make accurate radio calls.

synopsis: Helicopter instructor experiences an NMAC with a Twin Turboprop on final approach. The helicopter was on a steep approach and making position reports, while the King Air was on the straight in ILS and apparently not making position reports. The Twin Turboprop pilot detected the helicopter and went around to the right side.
summary: During a helicopter training flight on a steep approach to Runway XY, a Twin Turboprop executed a go-around nearby. The instructor and student did not hear the turboprop's transmissions because the helicopter's Com 1 was inoperative, prompting a safety meeting and a NOTAM to change traffic flow.

synopsis: A80 Controller describes a conflict in which he gives a sector a point out. The other Sector Controller says traffic observed. A conflict happens later between the aircraft he was trying to point out and an opposite direction aircraft displayed in yellow on his scope.
summary: The TAR D controller lost separation with a small prop aircraft while holding Aircraft X at 7,000 feet in SAT F airspace due to misunderstood phraseology regarding a traffic point-out. The reporter attributes the incident to poor communication and high traffic density caused by thunderstorms at ATL.

synopsis: ZSE Controller describes a situation where aircraft are turning at different places in reference to a fly-by fix which lead to an operational error.
summary: An ATC specialist reported that Aircraft X and Y at FL390 converged to 4.57 miles near fix TOU due to inconsistent FMS turn lead distances on a fly-by fix. The controller restored separation, but the event highlighted a safety risk caused by unpredictable FMS turn initiation requiring potential regulatory changes.

synopsis: B777 First Officer is informed during a bathroom break that a Flight Attendant injured her elbow when she hit it on a galley door. The injured Flight Attendant deadheads home after seeking medical attention for the elbow which turns out to be fractured and caused by turbulence.
summary: A flight attendant fractured her elbow after striking it on a galley door during a flight with moderate turbulence. The pilot reported the injury was not turbulence-related, and the crew member was hospitalized before dead-heading back the next day.

synopsis: An A319 flight crew, descending via the HAWKZ RNAV STAR to SEA and maintaining assigned .73M, was criticized by Center for not being at 280 KTS when checking in with the next Controller. The chart, however, specifies flights are to descend via Mach number until 'intercepting' the required 280 KIAS until slowed by ATC.
summary: Pilots descending via the Hawker 3 arrival into SEA were assigned .73 Mach by SEA Center but reported 310 kts to a new controller who expected 280 kts. The discrepancy arose from conflicting speed restriction notes, though the flight continued without incident.

synopsis: A320 Captain discovers his iPad database containing charts and other necessary in flight information to be deleted. The flight continues to destination using the remaining iPad, where the faulty iPad is replaced.
summary: During cruise, a pilot's company iPad failed to load the menu and subsequently deleted all content after a restart. The crew reverted to single iPad procedures per the FOM and received Dispatcher authorization via ACARS to continue the flight with one device.

synopsis: B757 Flight Crew reports crossing KIKKR high during the GIBBZ arrival to IAD. The local altimeter setting of 30.30 was set passing FL190 and the FMC path shown on profile while crossing KIKKR 1,000 feet high.
summary: During the GIBBZ TWO RNAV arrival to Washington DC, the crew deviated up to 1,000 feet high at KIKKR despite VNAV PATH indicating on-path status. The pilots attributed the error to a high altimeter setting and FMC lag, manually correcting with speed brakes and autopilot disconnect before landing uneventfully.

synopsis: B767 First Officer reports being delayed for an engine change and once enroute the left hydraulic system is found to be losing fluid and not suitable for an ETOPS flight. A diversion is planned for the hydraulic issues and due to one Flight Attendant being injured by meal cart and another with blood clots.
summary: The crew diverted an ETOPS flight to ZZZ after the left hydraulic system quantity dropped below verification limits during climb. They also landed overweight after dumping fuel and coordinating medical support for two injured or ill flight attendants.

synopsis: B737 flight crew experiences an engine overheat shortly after takeoff. QRH procedures are complied with and the flight returns to the departure airport with the offending engine at idle until short final. The flaps will not extend beyond 25 degrees but the approach and landing is continued with thrust equalized.
summary: The crew experienced a right engine overheat light shortly after takeoff, which extinguished after reducing thrust to idle. They returned for an overweight landing with flaps limited to 25 degrees due to a flap extension failure.

synopsis: B757 flight crew reports departing with an inoperative interphone/selcal chime. Enroute an MEL page is found that indicates the chime cannot be deferred. Also deferred was a first class seat that should have had its circuit breakers pulled but did not.
summary: The Captain and First Officer discovered inoperative cockpit chimes and SELCAL during preflight, initially deferring them under an incorrect MEL before correcting the logbook to comply with regulations. Additionally, a mechanic failed to pull the required circuit breaker for a deferred seat, violating MEL procedures before eventually clearing the item.

synopsis: B737 Captain reports being disconnected from the tow bar by the ground crew without instructions to do so or instructions to set the parking brake. The aircraft rolls forward nearly hitting the tug before realizing the tow bar is not connected. The towbar is reconnected to push deeper into the alley per ramp instructions.
summary: During pushback, the line crew disconnected the towbar before the flight crew set parking brakes, causing the aircraft to roll forward toward the tow truck. The pilot attributed this near-collision to the ground crew's lack of situational awareness and poor communication, noting the towbar was reattached to complete the maneuver.

synopsis: B767 flight crew experiences an uncommanded LE slat extension climbing through FL230. As quickly as the slat extended it retracted, but the crew elected to dump fuel and return to the departure airport for an overweight landing.
summary: During climb, the crew experienced a sudden pitch change and LE slat asymmetry with flaps moving from UP to 1 and back while the autopilot was engaged. The crew executed checklists, dumped fuel, and performed a safe landing with flaps 30, followed by a 75-minute brake cooling delay on the runway.

synopsis: B767 flight crew experiences a hot start during pushback and terminates the start. Maintenance Control is contacted and another start is attempted using both igniters successfully. Maintenance Control requests another start using the original ignitor, again successfully. The crew is cleared to go with instructions to make an informational log entry, which is never accomplished. Later, Maintenance discovers that the engine has been damaged.
summary: During pushback, the left engine experienced a hot start exceeding EGT limits, prompting an aborted start and subsequent successful restarts per Maintenance Control advice. The crew departed with an intended enroute maintenance message that was forgotten, later revealing engine damage despite normal flight indications.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain laments the fact that London Heathrow Airport does not have its own on-site medical/EMT/paramedic staff on the field. This results in a long delay after returning to the gate with a sick passenger.
summary: The flight crew returned to the gate at Heathrow after a refugee child from Ethiopia vomited and sweated profusely in the lavatory. While airport staff arrived quickly, it took over 1 hour and 20 minutes for off-site London Ambulance EMTs to reach the aircraft for treatment.

synopsis: EMB-175 flight crew reports being issued a holding clearance at VALRE at 11,000 FT. A database hold that matches the clearance is selected in the FMC. As the aircraft crosses the holding fix at 11,000 FT and starts to turn, autothrust advances to climb power and the nose pitches up. The Captain quickly takes control and returns the aircraft to the proper altitude and flight path. Autothrust is normal for the remainder of the flight.
summary: During the HAARP3 arrival into LGA, the aircraft aggressively climbed from 11,000 ft while entering a VALRE hold due to a suspected FMS software error. The Pilot Monitoring manually overrode the autopilot to restore the assigned altitude and speed, preventing a potential conflict with other traffic in the holding pattern.

synopsis: A319 flight crew reports a late ATC assigned turn to final resulting in an overshoot into the approach path for the adjacent runway and a TCAS RA to avoid the traffic directly below. The Captain is able to comply with the RA, get back on course and land safely. A 50 knot direct crosswind at altitude was a large factor in the incident.
summary: Pilots on a Boeing aircraft approaching ORD 10L overflew the final approach course for 9R due to a late ATC vector and strong tailwinds, placing them 400–500 feet above another aircraft. The crew manually corrected the course and followed a resolution advisory, noting the incident resulted from the late vector, wind conditions, and delayed traffic alert.

synopsis: A First Officer (F/O) describes his efforts and frustration with an unresolved cabin safety issue involving emergency light battery packs that are found dead on their Cessna CE-560XL aircraft during preflight. Misunderstandings between flight crew and Maintenance Control about how the emergency lights function when operated from the aircraft's main battery or from the emergency light battery packs, continue to plague the discussion.
summary: During preflight, the crew found a dead rear emergency light battery pack, but Maintenance Control and the Assistant Chief Pilot insisted the aircraft was airworthy despite the inoperative system. The reporter attributes this to flawed company procedures and incorrect wiring information that mask the failure, creating a safety risk for night evacuations.

synopsis: Despite the HS-125 having just successfully undergone a maintenance inspection for possible engine damage (for reasons not provided) and returned to service the next assigned flight crew experienced vibrations and buzzing sounds they deemed serious enough to divert for further maintenance. More acute inspection after landing illuminated one stator potentially damaged on the right engine and unquestionable blood and damage to the left.
summary: The First Officer and Captain diverted shortly after departure due to control wheel vibration and slow airspeed caused by damaged engine stators missed during prior maintenance. Post-landing inspection confirmed the damage and blood stains, leading the crew to conclude that better maintenance inspections are required.

synopsis: When an IT technician remotely accessed the computer of an air carrier dDspatcher it disrupted his tasks and could have led to a flight following anomaly.
summary: An IT worker remotely accessed a dispatcher's computer without warning or permission, moving windows and opening programs during flight release and forecast work. This unauthorized access removed control from the dispatcher, creating a risk of operational loss or erroneous flight amendments.

synopsis: A C-208 Captain reported multiple physiological impairments following performing a required inflight check of the aircraft's TKS surface anti-icing system.
summary: A pilot experienced nausea, headache, and lightheadedness while enroute after activating the TKS anti-ice system for a weekly check. The reporter attributed these symptoms to fluid exposure, noting a sticky film on the yoke and hands, and recommended wearing an oxygen mask during the procedure.

synopsis: Center's failure to provide the planned landing runway when clearing the MD-82 for the DEBBB RNAV STAR to DFW contributed to a track deviation at NCONA where they should have tracked toward PHAUP but, instead, attempted to redirect the jet to THASA.
summary: The crew flying the DEBBB1 arrival incorrectly turned away from PHAUP due to relying on a zoomed pictorial while missing text instructions. ATC broke them off the approach and assigned a heading after the crew corrected the path, though no disciplinary action was taken.

synopsis: During approach, B737-800 flight crew experiences autopilot and flight director anomalies and the autopilot cannot be reconnected. The Captain elected to go-around. On the second approach autopilots and approach mode can still not be selected but the First Officer had a functioning flight director and flies the approach to landing.
summary: During final approach, both autopilots failed to engage despite no cockpit warnings, prompting a go-around and emergency declaration due to fuel and instrument issues. The First Officer landed the aircraft using raw data after the Captain handed over control, with post-flight maintenance revealing 18 PSEU faults.

synopsis: A commercial fixed wing flight into SUN conducted a GPS X Runway 31 approach to decision height with no contact and went around, climbing to 12,500 FT per the MAP. When in contact with ATC they were advised the actual MAP altitude was only 8,700 FT with a requirement to obtain ATC authorization to continue the climb to 12,500. The reporters cited an excess of options at decision height and the decision to place the 12,500 altitude in the MAP description as contributing factors.
summary: The flight crew executing a missed approach at Sun Valley (SUN) mistakenly climbed to 12,500 ft instead of the required 8,700 ft due to misinterpreting the approach plate. The reporter attributes this altitude deviation to the confusing inclusion of an ATC-authorized hold altitude within the missed approach procedure and insufficient briefing time.

synopsis: International Flight Attendant expressed her concern over an insufficient number of rubber gloves available for cabin staff in light of Ebola epidemic.
summary: Cabin crew reported a shortage of rubber gloves on international flights exceeding five hours, specifically noting a 13-hour Asia flight requiring 40 gloves but receiving only 10–12. The reporter attributed this to insufficient supply after switching from film-type gloves, creating a health hazard for crew and passengers during meal and lavatory services.

synopsis: Flight Attendant reports experiencing extreme fatigue resulting from her flight assignment.
summary: A flight attendant reported severe fatigue and impaired task management during a four-day trip assigned by scheduling, which included overnight deadheading and insufficient rest. The crew member experienced memory lapses regarding door arming, service errors, and physical instability, ultimately declining a subsequent trip due to safety concerns.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: MD-80 First Officer reported that when they ran the QRH for Lavatory Smoke Alarm, one of the steps called for pulling circuit breakers that disabled communication with the cabin.
summary: The First Officer reported a dual aft lavatory smoke alarm after departure, prompting a return to the field where the crew landed uneventfully.
