synopsis: Pilot reports of an approach into LAX where SCT Approach wanted them to do a visual approach. The weather wasn't good enough for them to do so due to a cloud layer and inability to see traffic to follow. Crew was sent around and then sequenced again for a visual approach which they told the Controller that they couldn't accept a visual because of the weather.
summary: During an ILS 24R approach in fog, ATC incorrectly cleared the crew for a visual approach and issued conflicting go-around altitude instructions. The crew executed a descending go-around, rejected a second visual clearance due to weather, and completed an uneventful ILS approach.

synopsis: A B737 air crew discovered that they were unable to bring up the required STAR and approaches in FMC. They were later notified that incorrect Airbus data had been loaded in the aircraft by mistake.
summary: The copilot reported that an aircraft flew from the mainland to Kona with an incorrect Airbus navigation database, preventing FMC loading of Hawaii arrivals and approaches. The crew flew raw data for an uneventful ILS landing after maintenance confirmed the wrong database was installed.

synopsis: An air carrier gate agent reported the leveling system of the jetway he was utilizing to deplane a B737 malfunctioned, resulting in it sinking below the passenger entry/exit threshold and potentially impacting the fully open cabin door. After calling for maintenance the reporter implored the cabin attendants to expedite the passenger deplaning.
summary: A CSR reported that a Boeing 737's auto leveler malfunctioned during passenger deplaning, causing the aircraft to rise rapidly and threatening the door. Maintenance attributed the incident to old, unrepaired equipment, while the CSR noted the company was aware of recurring issues with 737s at this gate.

synopsis: An EMB-145 air crew were given instructions to taxi to the gate with no restrictions. While taxiing, another aircraft being taxied by maintenance personnel cut them off at a high rate of speed. Ground control would not answer calls. The Captain called the Tower on the telephone and was informed that they were training a controller that evening.
summary: Pilots reported a near-collision at Airport ZZZ while taxiing on Bravo after exiting Runway XX. A maintenance aircraft on Taxiway E cut them off at high speed because ground control was unavailable and no hold-short instructions were issued during a training session.

synopsis: A CRJ-700 flight crew, taxiing for takeoff, were distracted by unusual nose gear sounds they determined to be associated with the cold conditions. When they were then cleared for takeoff in advance of arriving at the departure runway they mentally entered the 'takeoff mental mode' and departed without completing the before takeoff checklist and, thus, had failed to advise the flight attendants of their imminent departure. Upon climbing through 10,000 feet the flight attendants called to notify of their incomplete SOP.
summary: The flight crew forgot to complete the Before Takeoff checklist during departure from Airport ZZZ, failing to notify cabin crew before takeoff. This oversight caused a flight attendant to rush to her seat after the aircraft climbed above 10,000 feet, creating a potential injury risk.

synopsis: EMB-145LR flight crew reported while they were getting de-iced they noticed smoke coming from the de-ice truck and became concerned about fire danger to their aircraft. They also reported seemingly substandard de-ice procedures by the same de-ice crew.
summary: The Captain observed a de-icing truck emitting smoke and flames due to spilled hydraulic fluid on the heat exchanger, yet the crew proceeded to de-ice the aircraft despite warnings. The crew later attempted an incomplete re-application with a replacement truck, forcing the Captain to reject the service and delay departure until proper de-icing was performed.

synopsis: CRJ-200 Captain reported ATC communication difficulties on arrival to MMHO.
summary: Pilots reported that Hermosillo Approach issued an invalid clearance and failed to respond to their distress calls while they were high at FL200. The crew eventually contacted Tower for a visual approach after losing communication with Approach, attributing the incident to the controller's poor clearance and lack of response.

synopsis: CRJ-200 FO reported the left engine flamed out on landing roll.
summary: The Pilot Monitoring reported that the left engine flamed out after landing an aircraft with a deferred right thrust reverser, though the exact timing was uncertain due to SOPs limiting engine gauge monitoring during rollout. Ground control observed smoke, but post-flight inspections found no fire or abnormalities, and the crew taxied to the gate on one engine.

synopsis: B757 Captain reported two flight attendants were slightly injured when he had to unexpectedly stop taxiing to avoid another aircraft.
summary: During taxi to runway 1R, the crew stopped to confirm clearance after another aircraft entered taxiway A. Later, two flight attendants reported injuries from a cart and a knee wrench during the taxi, declined medical aid, and continued working.

synopsis: B757 First Officer reports being cleared direct to UROWT on the QUABN3 arrival to BOS which causes confusion in the cockpit due to the way UROWT is pronounced by the ZBW Controller (your route) and believes it should be changed.
summary: Pilots flying the QUABN3 STAR to Boston held at ONDEC due to a stuck snowplow, then received a clearance direct to UROWT. The pilot reported that UROWT sounds like "your route," causing initial crew confusion, though the flight continued uneventfully after the misunderstanding was resolved.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported the onboard pubs were out of date and had gone unnoticed for several days, with the flight crew using their EFB for normal operations.
summary: The Captain and First Officer departed with expired Jeppesen publications after assuming digital charts were sufficient. Upon reaching cruise, the Captain contacted the Flight Operations Documentation Manager via ACARS to obtain a required meter authorizing the flight.

synopsis: EMB-145 FO reported a track deviation when the FMS failed to navigate direct to the cleared fix.
summary: During cruise to CLT, the aircraft turned 60 degrees past the MEI waypoint despite FMS entry and crew verification. The crew corrected the 15-second deviation after ATC confirmed the aircraft was back on course, attributing the error to unverified course interception.

synopsis: EMB-145 FO reported a track deviation on approach when the FMS reverted to roll mode, apparently related to a known duplicate waypoint anomaly.
summary: The flight crew descended via the DRLLR 4 arrival to runway 26L but encountered a Flight Management System error duplicating the DOMNO fix. This caused the autopilot to revert to roll mode after passing the fix, creating an undesired aircraft state and potential traffic conflict due to a known, uncorrected company software issue.

synopsis: B737 pilot reported multiple seemingly unrelated aircraft equipment anomalies, complicated by a bathroom smoke detector blaring that continued to the gate.
summary: During descent and approach, the flight crew encountered a loud bathroom smoke detector alarm and sluggish #2 engine response, leading to asymmetric flaps, control issues, and autopilot disengagement. The crew declared an emergency, followed the QRH, and landed safely on runway 27L with flaps 5 due to multiple simultaneous equipment failures.

synopsis: A320 Captain reported they departed the gate with undetected ice on the wings that was brought to their attention by a deadheading crew member.
summary: The flight crew and a deadheading pilot identified ice on the wings during taxi, contradicting the First Officer's initial walk-around assessment from the jetway stairs. The aircraft was diverted to deicing bays for Type 1 fluid application before departing without incident.

synopsis: A320 Captain reported returning to destination airport when they received a nacelle high temperature ECAM warning that was apparently related to a High Pressure bleed valve stuck open.
summary: The crew returned to Airport ZZZ during climb-out after Engine 1 NAC temperature warnings and a stuck open High Pressure bleed valve caused suspected leaks. They performed an overweight landing with no damage, though the pilot admitted failing to document the overweight landing as required by checklist procedures.

synopsis: A319 Captain reported frequently experiencing difficulty updating his company issued iPad.
summary: A pilot reported that the company iPad's electronic library frequently fails to download updated documents like the QRH and MEL, displaying blank pages instead. This known IT issue prevents crew from verifying which procedures were successfully updated, creating a safety risk regarding access to current information.

synopsis: EMB145 flight crew reported receiving a Rudder System 2 EICAS message after takeoff, their response was to declare an emergency and return to departure airport.
summary: The First Officer and Captain received a RUDDER SYSTEM 2 INOP EICAS message during initial climb, prompting an emergency return to base. After landing and a negative fire inspection, maintenance met the crew to address the issue, which the reporter noted was a previous write-up.

synopsis: A First Officer reports he was returning from a lavatory break when the cockpit door on an ERJ175 aircraft fell off its hinges and almost dropped straight out into the galley area as the door was opened. The housing (catch) that holds the door upper hinge post had broken vertically, allowing the door post to easily separate from the upper housing. Pressure on Contract Maintenance personnel to sign-off non-airworthy aircraft also noted by First Officer.
summary: The flight crew reported a cockpit door hinge failure at cruise altitude, which they temporarily secured before landing. Despite maintenance repairs, the door failed again in flight on a subsequent leg, causing a diversion due to improper repair and pressure to sign off non-airworthy aircraft.

synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported they experienced a failure of the Air Data Computer Number 2.
summary: During climb through FL300, the First Officer managed an ADC 2 failure with no EICAS warnings but red flags, complying with QRH procedures. ATC cleared the crew to descend to FL280 to exit RVSM airspace, and the flight landed safely after notifying dispatch and passengers.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported the Captain experienced vertigo during an instrument approach so a go-around was executed, and the FO flew the subsequent approach.
summary: The Captain, acting as Pilot Flying on a CAT III ILS approach in snow, experienced vertigo, deviated from course, and initiated a poorly executed go-around that resulted in an overspeed with flaps extended. The First Officer took control to stabilize the aircraft and completed a safe landing, attributing the incident to the Captain's disorientation and degraded cockpit communications caused by high noise levels.

synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported declaring an emergency and returning to departure airport after receiving a Steering Inop caution message.
summary: The flight crew experienced 'Steering Inop' and 'gear disagree' warnings shortly after liftoff, prompting a return to Airport ZZZ. After burning fuel to land below maximum weight, the aircraft landed safely, stopped on the runway, and was towed to the gate for repairs.

synopsis: EC145 helicopter pilot reported abandoning his approach below 200 feet AGL when a snowplow drove onto the runway.
summary: A helicopter pilot on short final to runway 17 encountered a snowplow entering the runway below 200 feet AGL. The pilot side-stepped to a parallel taxiway to land, noting the snowplow likely lacked a radio and was unaware of the approach.

synopsis: CRJ900 Captain stated the difference in intensity and brightness between incandescent runway edge lighting and LED centerline lighting at BOI RWY 10R is hazardous.
summary: A pilot reported a hazard during a night landing on Runway 10R at BOI. The new LED centerline lights were excessively bright and inconsistent with the traditional incandescent edge lights, creating a safety risk.

synopsis: Despite having an IFR clearance and ready to depart FXE, the pilot of a Cessna 350 was held for over 45 minutes as ground control advised no taxi clearances for takeoff would be provided until all inbounds were handled. In the reporter's experience this is not uncommon and needs to be addressed.
summary: A pilot waited over 45 minutes on the tarmac after receiving an IFR clearance because Ground Control held all taxi requests to manage incoming traffic. The reporter attributed the delay to a lack of ground area separation or additional runways at the airport.

synopsis: A Cessna 172 pilot inadvertently entered the New York Class B when a change was made in the planned itinerary. Upon discovery of the aircraft's location via digital navaids the pilot expedited a descent to exit the airspace.
summary: A pilot inadvertently entered New York Bravo airspace at 4,500 feet while flying from POU to a nearby airport after a last-minute route change and over-reliance on new GPS software. The pilot discovered the incursion via an iPad app, descended below the shelf, and landed uneventfully after ATC assistance.

synopsis: CE560 pilot reported he became disoriented while referring to his iPad after takeoff, and was unsure how to fly the departure.
summary: The pilot became disoriented after takeoff when an iPad ForeFlight geo-position symbol appeared on the NOTWN3 SID, causing a deviation from the assigned left turn. The pilot subsequently accepted ATC vectors to avoid high terrain and completed the flight safely, attributing the incident to over-reliance on the tablet display.

synopsis: Small aircraft pilot believes that the recent change at VGT from using runways 7 and 12L/R as the calm wind runways to using runways 30L/R is dangerous due to opposite direction instrument approaches and Controller training. A recent NMAC is cited as an example.
summary: A pilot practicing touch-and-goes at VGT encountered a Cessna at 3000 feet and a helicopter during base descent, forcing evasive maneuvers due to conflicting traffic on Runway 30L. The reporter attributes these near-misses to inappropriate runway usage, trainee controller errors, and delayed supervisor intervention.

synopsis: A G280 First Officer, preparing for a pre-dawn departure from a frigid EWR airport, encountered numerous interruptions and freezing temperature related system difficulties while conducting his pre-flight. The Captain was otherwise engaged with passenger greeting and boarding and was, thus, unavailable for consultation or assistance. After takeoff the Captain's ASI and altimeter were inoperative, which reminded the First Officer that the last interruption of his pre-flight prevented him from completing the left side exterior inspection and he had forgotten to return to complete the task. The static port cover, as a result, was still in place preventing associated instrumentation from operating. They returned safely to the VFR airport.
summary: The pilot reported that a pitot/static cover was left on the left side during takeoff from Newark due to preflight interruptions, fatigue, and cold weather. The crew returned and landed safely after receiving false airspeed and altitude indications, attributing the error to a broken preflight flow and divided crew duties.

synopsis: C310 pilot reported the left engine failed due to fuel exhaustion and would not restart when a new tank was selected. Engine was feathered, an emergency declared, and a safe single engine landing ensued.
summary: The pilot of a Cessna 310 experienced a left engine failure en route at 8,000 ft after running auxiliary tanks to exhaustion and switching back to mains. The engine failed to restart in flight, requiring a feathered landing, but started normally on the ground with no determined cause.

synopsis: A DA-50 Captain descending into LAX on the RIIVR STAR misinterpreted ATC clearances for higher than charted airspeeds and maintained an IAS well above 250K below 10,000 feet. The First Officer, expressing timidity, failed to share his concerns and it fell to ATC to intervene. The Captain cited his misunderstanding of permitted ATC discretion with respect to maximum airspeeds below 10,000 feet.
summary: During an approach to LAX, the crew maintained 325 KIAS below 10,000 feet after misinterpreting an ATC clearance to fly 250 KIAS or greater. The controller subsequently restricted speed to 200 KIAS, explaining that only the FAA Administrator can authorize speeds exceeding 250 KIAS below 10,000 feet.

synopsis: SB-20 Captain reported receiving a GPWS obstacle warning while deviating from cleared track and altitude. Troubleshooting an autopilot issue was a factor in this incident.
summary: During a descent to 3,000 feet, the autopilot turned the aircraft west past the GLISS fix, causing the crew to disengage it and inadvertently descend to 2,700 feet. This triggered an 'Obstacle Ahead' GPWS warning and ATC altitude advisories, which the pilot attributed to the autopilot's incorrect turn and a missed level-off.

synopsis: C152 pilot reported an NMAC in the pattern at 1Q4.
summary: The pilot of aircraft number 1 in a short-field landing pattern at uncontrolled New Jerusalem airport took evasive action and climbed to 1,500 feet to avoid a head-on conflict with an unidentified Cessna 172. The intruder subsequently made a bad landing off-center and departed northwest, which the reporter attributed to the other pilot disregarding traffic.

aircraft: Piper Single Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Single-engine Piper pilot reported encountering wake turbulence in trail of a business jet departing VNY that resulted in a course deviation.
summary: A pilot departing VNY behind three business jets encountered significant wake turbulence during initial climb due to an incorrect offset vector. The pilot struggled to maintain control and missed a turn to heading 210, attributing the incident to insufficient separation time and a failure to request a delay.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: After a night landing at a seaplane base, the pilot realized that his landing on an unlighted waterway violated FAR 135.229
summary: A pilot flying a 135 charter flight with two passengers departed ZZZ and returned after sunset, executing a glassy water landing. The pilot attributed the incident to "get-home-itis," which created a false sense of security regarding twilight visibility and obscured potential underwater obstructions.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: ZBW Controller has two aircraft in conflict and then is distracted by another aircraft asking a question. The Controller responds to the questioning aircraft and another Controller yells at that they have two at 17,000 feet. The Controller then resolves the situation by turning and descending the conflicting aircraft and does not have a loss of separation.
summary: An air traffic controller failed to maintain separation between Aircraft X and Y at 17,000 feet due to distraction by a clearance query from Aircraft Z and route changes. The controller issued an expedited descent to X and a turn to Y, but Y executed a TCAS climb instead, resulting in a loss of separation that the controller admitted was inexcusable.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: ZJX Controller reports of a situation where one was maintaining visual separation from the other. The one not maintaining visual, responds to an RA and later calls the facility and declares an NMAC.
summary: An air traffic controller reported a near mid-air incident involving Aircraft X and Y during descent when Aircraft Y responded to a Resolution Advisory despite being cleared for visual separation. The controller stated Aircraft X maintained visual separation, but the event was classified as a near mid-air based on Aircraft Y's account and proximity criteria.

synopsis: A B737-800 flight crew described a low altitude encounter with severe windshear including rapid acceleration, deceleration and loss of altitude.
summary: The flight crew of a heavy -800 departing BNA Runway 20L encountered rapid airspeed decay and a stick shaker activation shortly after takeoff in turbulence and rain. The reporter attributed the event to autothrottles retarding thrust during flap retraction and resolved the situation by manually adding full thrust and reducing angle of attack.

synopsis: The Captain of a B737-700 had been unable to arm the auto-throttle during taxi-out, but attributed the fault to the very cold ambient air and elected to depart using manually set max thrust. The decision to do so was predicated on the incorrect assumption that a previously noted broadly fluctuating TAT reading was merely the result of the cold OAT and the fact the probe was heated thus producing unreliable readings. They rejected their takeoff at ~70 Knots when their max takeoff thrust setting failed to produce calculated N1 levels.
summary: Pilots rejected a takeoff at 70 knots due to insufficient thrust and acceleration after the autothrottle failed to arm because of a TAT probe fault. The aircraft returned to the gate for maintenance investigation of the erratic probe readings.

synopsis: A malfunctioning Flight Director, for which maintenance had no immediate resolution, ultimately resulted in multiple MEL deferrals that were intended to be resolved at a subsequent stop. After two uneventful legs maintenance was unable to resolve the problem at the planned repair station. Instead, they found another item they believed was required to be deferred. A subsequent in depth investigation, including emailed pictures of the original write-up, uncovered the source of the confusion, it was the incorrect interpretation of the letter 'A' instead of 'D', thus changing 'AC' to 'DC'.
summary: The crew departed an hour late with seven MELs after maintenance found a popped AFCS EXC AC circuit breaker. Repairs failed at ZZZ1, a non-existent breaker was identified, and the aircraft was terminated, though the captain felt the plane should have been grounded initially.

synopsis: B747 First Officer reported they lost Number 1 Hydraulic System at the same time they were dealing with moderate to severe turbulence.
summary: The pilot encountered severe turbulence at FL370, causing airspeed fluctuations and a subsequent loss of hydraulic system #1 pressure. After climbing to FL390 worsened conditions, the crew descended to FL350, managed the hydraulic failure, and landed uneventfully at the nearest airport.

synopsis: Dispatch of a B767 flight from the US to South America was compromised by a dispatch program error requiring it to be conducted under ETOPS requirements, which was abnormal. A breakdown in normal ETOPS protocol resulted when an inspection required for such a departure wasn't completed and went undetected. Fortunately, by the time the error was noted the computer problem had been resolved and the flight was re-dispatched as non ETOPS.
summary: The pilot departed a non-ETOPS flight as ETOPS due to a dispatch system error and distractions that prevented completion of the required Pre Departure Service Check. The crew amended the release to non-ETOPS in cruise after discovering the missing check, highlighting a disconnect between dispatch and maintenance that failed to block the departure.

synopsis: A B-737 air crew, taxiing to the gate had a miscommunication between the pilots. The Captain commanded shutdown of Engine Number 2 but the copilot began to shutdown Engine Number 1. Realizing his mistake he returned the Number 1 start lever to the detent and shutdown Engine Number 2. As a result both engines were shutdown and the aircraft coasted to a stop five feet from the gate. They restarted Engine Number 1 to finish the taxi to the gate.
summary: During post-landing taxi, the First Officer inadvertently moved the number 1 engine start lever out of idle, causing an unintended shutdown while shutting down engine number 2. The crew stopped the powerless aircraft, coordinated with ground personnel, and restarted engine number 1 to complete the taxi to the gate.

synopsis: B737 First Officer reported his concerns with what he sees as an inadequate recurrent training program at his airline.
summary: A B737 pilot reported that recurrent training in a fixed base trainer was inadequate due to an overloaded syllabus, skewed visual displays, and outdated ACARS software. These equipment and scheduling issues prevented realistic line-oriented training and hindered the completion of required maneuvers within the allotted time.

synopsis: C208B Captain reported icing in flight that made it impossible to maintain minimum vectoring altitude in an area of high terrain. They descended to warmer air and landed safely at departure airport.
summary: Pilots encountered icing at 6,900 feet MSL while climbing enroute, preventing a climb to 120 knots or maintaining the 7,000-foot minimum vectoring altitude. They descended below the minimum altitude to 3,000 feet MSL to shed ice and land safely after verifying terrain clearance with GPS.

synopsis: An EMB-145 flight crew returned to their departure airport shortly after takeoff when they received a fuel imbalance message and observed a fuel stream exiting the right wingtip. Maintenance was unable to duplicate the problem and returned the aircraft to service.
summary: The crew experienced a rapid right fuel tank leak and FUEL IMBALANCE message during departure climb, prompting a return to the departure airport. They landed safely but overweight after maintenance failed to duplicate the issue and returned the aircraft to service.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A Captain reported an uncomfortable visual approach to SLC that included a low altitude RA and no go-around option because of an aircraft in near proximity above them.
summary: A flight crew operating a visual approach to SLC Runway 34R received a TCAS Resolution Advisory to descend due to a converging aircraft on Runway 35. The crew followed the RA, descended below the glideslope, and landed safely after the conflict cleared, attributing the event to poor traffic separation by the tower controller.

synopsis: Fractional First Officer (FO) reported he and his Captain, as well as two other flight crews, refused to fly an aircraft into a marginal weather situation with several autoflight systems inoperative and deferred. Reporter stated he was concerned with his employer's attitude and pressure.
summary: The PIC and co-pilot refused a ferry and passenger leg due to excessive MELs, including deferred autopilot, yaw damper, and right flight director. They reported that the company attempted to assign three crews to the aircraft, which they deemed unsafe due to increased workload and compromised automation.

synopsis: A B767-300 First Officer makes a cogent and convincing argument for the inadequacy of the crew rest facility provided by his company to allow for meaningful rest, let alone actual sleep. The facility, three seats across the back of the cockpit which must be creatively modified with meal trays and spare blankets to provide a flat surface on which to lie, results in an intrusive domain for both the crew member at rest and the operating crew inasmuch as they are not separated and some compromise must be reached for adequate lighting and activity for the flying pilots to remain alert but dark enough and quiet enough for the resting pilot to...well...rest.
summary: The flight crew reported that the lack of a dedicated crew rest area on this aircraft threatened safety during a long-haul flight. Attempting to rest on makeshift jumpseat beds resulted in sleep deprivation, blocked lavatory access, and compromised alertness for operating pilots due to noise and lighting conflicts.

synopsis: Wide-Body Transport FO reported they encountered extremely slippery conditions on taxi out that necessitated the use of reverse thrust to come to a stop.
summary: The Captain lost steering and braking control while taxiing a snow-covered aircraft on a ramp with hidden ice, causing it to slide. The pilot stopped the aircraft using thrust reversers, resulting in no damage, though the report cited inadequate snow removal as the cause.

synopsis: Unable to complete a necessary communication with Approach control regarding a descent clearance into busy PSP traffic below them, an EMB-120 flight crew delayed their descent, but then received a TCAS 'descend' RA to which they complied.
summary: The flight crew, while being vectored for landing at Palm Springs, refused an ATC descent instruction due to conflicting traffic below and an overtaking aircraft. After receiving a Resolution Advisory, the crew complied with the RA and landed safely, attributing the incident to congested airspace and an overwhelmed controller who ignored their safety concerns.

aircraft: B787 Dreamliner Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports finding three Crew Oxygen bottles with damaged (bent) pressure gauges during a Receiving Inspection procedure prior to putting the bottles in service. Concerns also raised as to where the damage had been occurring and whether other aircraft may be flying around with damaged bottles.
summary: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician in ZZZ inspected three B787 oxygen bottles and found one low, one empty, and one at 2000 psi, all with damaged gauges. The technician reported this alarming pattern and requested an investigation to identify the damage source and check other B787s for similar issues.

synopsis: A Caravan 208B flight crew departed Runway XY and turned to 165 degrees direct to their destination as cleared. When a Baron reported inbound from the southwest to the downwind for Runway XY the Caravan crew believed there would be no conflict, since Runway XY utilizes a right hand pattern. A 200 foot vertical and horizontal NMAC resulted when the Baron pilot, admittedly, was unaware of the non-standard right hand pattern and had instead proceed to the east to enter left traffic.
summary: A departing pilot and an inbound Baron pilot experienced a near-miss during climb-out from Runway XY. The conflict occurred because the Baron pilot entered a left downwind instead of the published right-hand pattern, placing him in the departure corridor with only 300 feet of vertical separation.

synopsis: PAO Controller observes people not authorized near a runway on a taxiway. Controller stops operation until a airport vehicle removes the people.
summary: Local Control observed two photographers enter the movement area near Runway 31 and Taxiway Zulu, prompting the controller to hold Aircraft Z and send Aircraft X and Y around. The incident was caused by Aircraft A requesting photos without proper escort, leading to a temporary suspension of operations until Airport 1 issued deviations.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: SCT Departure Controller describes coordination problems with LAX Tower and the tower not following SOP.
summary: A Malibu Radar controller reported that LAX Tower repeatedly interrupted communications and violated LOA procedures during a busy session. This caused the controller to talk over the tower, resulting in a conflict where Aircraft Y was stopped 2,000 feet below Aircraft X.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: ASE TRACON Controller reports of ASE Tower sending three aircraft off the runway into his airspace that needed to be separated more. He tries to separate the aircraft and hand off to ZDV but has difficulties. He violates airspace and eventually hands off all three aircraft.
summary: An air traffic controller reported a potential separation loss between departing Aircraft Y and Z at Aspen due to distraction by a handoff issue with Aircraft X. The controller manually separated the aircraft before they reached minimums, attributing the incident to system errors, staffing levels, and delayed handoff acceptance.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: ZNY Controller reports of an NMAC due to poor coordination of altitudes between two aircraft and possibly a slow climbing aircraft.
summary: Air Traffic Controller approved Aircraft X's climb from FL340 to FL390 via FL370, coordinating with SJU Center regarding Aircraft Y at FL370. Shortly after, Aircraft X reported a TCAS alert with a 150-foot separation, though the controller was unsure of the vertical direction or appropriate recommendation.

synopsis: Dispatched in an aircraft that had just had the right engine driven pump replaced due to two previous system failures, the flight crew of a B737-700 nonetheless suffered yet another failure followed closely by a failure of the right electric pump. They diverted to the nearest suitable airport. The reporter expressed concern that, even after three write-ups and a replaced engine driven pump, Maintenance had apparently failed to properly diagnose and repair the system.
summary: The flight crew experienced repeated failures of the engine-driven B-system hydraulic pump and a subsequent electric pump failure, causing total system loss and yaw damper failure. The crew diverted and landed safely, attributing the incident to improper diagnosis and repair by maintenance following earlier write-ups.

synopsis: B737 flight crew reported receiving a low altitude alert from the Tower on a Localizer/Back Course approach to HRL.
summary: The First Officer flying an older aircraft on a LOC/DME back course approach in HRL deviated laterally and vertically due to unfamiliarity and distraction, triggering a low altitude warning. The crew executed a go-around and landed successfully after a second approach, citing poor weather reporting and lack of modern navigation equipment as contributing factors.

synopsis: Upon descending to exit moderate to severe turbulence, the flight crew of a B747 was met by a hydraulic system one failure. They continued to descend to an efficient altitude and landed uneventfully.
summary: The crew encountered severe turbulence at FL370/390, descending to FL350 with no injuries. Subsequently, the #1 hydraulic system failed, resulting in a safe landing without nose gear or body steering, requiring a tow to the gate.

aircraft: Regional Jet CL65; Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: As they climbed through icing conditions in a heavy CRJ shortly after takeoff, the Departure Controller several times repeated a request that they accelerate more quickly to 250 knots due to faster traffic behind them. In part because of the resulting disruption of normal SOP they discovered some time later that the power had never been reduced following takeoff and had been operating at or near takeoff thrust since the start of the takeoff roll. Rules at the air carrier reportedly allow pilots to cross qualify on CRJ models with and without autothrottle/VNAV capability, and was cited as a contributing factor as the SOPs for accomplishing routine tasks vary between the various types.
summary: The CRJ200 crew left thrust levers in the takeoff detent during climb after ATC interruptions disrupted their after-takeoff checklist. Maintenance confirmed no engine exceedances occurred due to FADEC monitoring, though the pilot attributed the error to mixed fleet scheduling.

synopsis: When asked to help relocate their inbound aircraft to make the gate available for a later inbound flight, the flight crew of an A319 inadvertently deployed the main cabin door slide. The First Officer went aft to confer with the station manager about technical problems with respect to towing the aircraft with only battery power available and was unaware that door had been armed by the Captain after they boarded.
summary: During a late-night gate move with a deferred APU, the First Officer opened an armed cabin door while the Captain was on the phone, causing the emergency slide to partially deploy. A mechanic stopped the slide by pinning the bottle, and the incident was attributed to human error and a lack of specific checklists for the situation.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: The flight crew of an Aircraft X inbound to the gate at ATL had to stop abruptly for a crossing Aircraft Y that failed to acknowledge or slow before passing the reporter's aircraft.
summary: The pilot reported a near-collision while taxiing from runway 27L to ramp X at ATL after an Aircraft Y approached at high speed with nose lights on. The pilot stopped abruptly to avoid impact, and Aircraft Y passed just off the nose before ground control was notified.

synopsis: Pilot reports pitch forces on a Cessna CE-750 aircraft higher than normal when airborne. Although concerned about being called into office for making a repeat write-up, pilot notes that during landing roll when thrust reversers were deployed and with normal heavy nose down push on the yoke, the nose wheels rose off the ground. Maintenance believes left elevator is malfunctioning and not sending any type of EICAS message due to a possible electrical ground.
summary: A pilot reported abnormally high pitch forces and nose wheel lift during landing roll on a CE-750, suspecting a left elevator malfunction or ground fault following a Service Bulletin. The pilot recommends fleet-wide reporting and maintenance checks due to concerns that the issue may affect other aircraft without triggering EICAS messages.

synopsis: The pilot of a Small Transport aircraft, taxiing to the ramp at BWI, had to stop aggressively to avoid colliding with a catering truck whose driver apparently failed to note the illumination from the aircraft's fully illuminated landing, taxi, courtesy and strobe lights on a clear dark night. The reporter advised conflicts with inattentive drivers are common at the location where the event took place.
summary: The pilot reported that while taxiing to the ramp on Taxiway Juliet at night, a catering truck failed to stop at a service road crossing, forcing an emergency stop with full reverse. The maneuver caused the nose strut to compress and the tail to strike the ground, though the aircraft missed the truck by two to three feet.

synopsis: An air crew on a departure were cleared to 6,000 feet. The Captain was confused about the transition level procedure and set the standard altimeter setting initially until he was corrected. ATC then cleared them to Flight Level 080, which they overshot because of not having the correct standard altimeter setting.
summary: The flight crew experienced confusion regarding altimeter settings during a climb from 6,000 feet to FL080 after departing LHR on the WOBUN 3G SID. A late switch to standard pressure combined with an aggressive climb rate caused a near-overshoot and a TCAS traffic advisory, though no loss of separation occurred.

synopsis: MD-11 flight crew deviated to nearest suitable airport due to a Fire Suppression System fault. The First Officer was injured when the escape slide did not properly inflate, allowing him to hit the ground hard.
summary: Deadheading pilots observed a cargo noise and FSS activation during cruise, prompting a diversion and evacuation. The First Officer was injured after jumping onto a slide that failed to fully inflate due to uninflated support tubing.

synopsis: Flight Attendant reported considerable difficulty disarming door L1 after gate arrival. Several other crewmembers tried without success also, and after about five minutes they were able to disarm the door.
summary: A flight attendant and captain struggled to disarm the L1 boarding door due to excessive resistance on the arming lever, despite the cabin pressure light remaining off. After ten attempts over five minutes, the lever finally moved, allowing the gate agent to open the door and the crew to disarm the remaining doors normally.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reports frequency congestion when trying to obtain flight following with SCT while departing enroute to Burbank. Pilot offers concern as to why one Controller is responsible for two different frequencies.
summary: A departing SMO pilot reported that an irritated Burbank controller switched them to an overloaded 124.6 frequency, where the controller admitted being unable to speak to them due to high workload. The pilot eventually exited Class C airspace and contacted 125.5 for flight following without establishing two-way communication on the assigned frequency.

synopsis: BE35 pilot reports arriving at LHW on a weekend day to find the Tower open. He is cleared to land Runway 15L, but elects to depart the pattern when his iPad/charts wind up on the floor due to turbulence. The charts are quickly retrieved and the reporter returns for landing, after communicating with the Tower. When ready to depart, several attempts to contact the Tower are made without success before it is assumed that the Tower is now closed as indicated by the AFD. Once airborne the Tower can be heard asking who just departed without clearance.
summary: The pilot of a Bonanza departed Runway 24R at LHW without tower clearance due to an intermittent radio and a mistaken belief the tower was closed on a weekend. The pilot also diverted inbound due to turbulence knocking charts onto the floor, later returning to land safely on Runway 15L.

synopsis: A B757 flight crew encountered a UAV on final approach to LAX as they descended through 3,000 feet MSL.
summary: During an ILS 25L approach to LAX, the Pilot Monitoring observed a red drone passing approximately 100 to 200 feet right of the aircraft near 3,000 feet. The crew reported the close encounter to Tower, noting the drone was too close for comfort but did not strike the airplane.

synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reports chronic fatigue problem flying the schedules his airline builds, with no help from FAR 117.
summary: A pilot reported severe fatigue and illness during a multi-leg turn following a redeye to IAH, citing insufficient sleep, lack of meals, and adverse weather. The pilot attributed these conditions to airline scheduling practices that violate contracts and FAR 117, creating unsafe flying conditions due to fear of retaliation.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: GSP TRACON Flight Line Manager (FLM) reports of a loss of separation by a training team on West radar. The controllers did not separate two aircraft one VFR climbing and one IFR descending.
summary: A radar trainee and supervisor at West Radar allowed a VFR departure to climb to 10,000 feet, creating a high-closure conflict with a descending arrival. The trainee's misjudgment of position and closure rate, combined with improper "altitude your discretion" clearance, resulted in a TCAS RA and a 2.55-mile lateral proximity.

synopsis: An air crew descended below assigned altitude after passing the transition altitude. They confused the altimeter setting of 998 millibars with 29.98 inches.
summary: A fatigued crew descending into Frankfurt descended 400 feet below 6,000 feet after misinterpreting the controller's 998 millibar altimeter setting as 29.98 inches. The deviation resulted from communication errors involving a congested frequency, accented English, and the controller failing to correct the crew's repeated incorrect readbacks.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An air crew, after having applied takeoff thrust, heard a radio call that stated that an aircraft had snow contamination on its left inboard flap. Thinking that the call may have been meant for them, they rejected the takeoff. The call was not for them.
summary: The First Officer rejected takeoff at 50–60 knots on runway 27 after an ambiguous radio call regarding snow contamination on another aircraft. Following confirmation from Tower that the report did not concern their flight, the crew returned to the gate to refuel before departing safely.

synopsis: Widebody international flight crew reported a track deviation when they got an unexpected clearance on arrival into LAX and had some difficulty programming the FMC correctly. Reporter cited fatigue as a factor.
summary: A fatigued flight crew missed an ATIS update regarding an ILS outage during descent to LAX, leading to incorrect FMC programming and a deviation from the STAR. The Pilot Flying manually corrected the course after the aircraft bypassed a waypoint, resulting in a direct clearance from ATC and a breakdown in crew communication.

synopsis: B757-200 Captain reported receiving a Wheel Well Fire EICAS warning, as well as a Duct Leak LP message, in cruise flight on an overwater leg. The flight diverted to the nearest suitable airport.
summary: The crew diverted a cruise flight at FL360 after a wheel well fire warning and duct leak message illuminated. Maintenance later confirmed an actual duct leak in the right wheel well, which extinguished after 15 minutes, allowing for a safe landing with ARFF standby.

synopsis: EMB-145 Captain reported an anomaly with his Honeywell FMS. When changing runway assignment on arrival to RIC the FMS loaded the waypoint SPIDR twice.
summary: The pilot reported that changing the runway in the Honeywell FMS during the SPIDR1 arrival caused the SPIDR waypoint to duplicate, resulting in a loss of lateral guidance before DEEER. The crew manually re-engaged LNAV to remain on course and identified the software error as the cause.

synopsis: EMB-145XR flight crew reported abnormal nose wheel steering and a STEERING INOP EICAS message on takeoff roll. A rejected takeoff was performed, and the Captain found the nose wheel tiller was being affected by iPhone ear buds that had been placed there.
summary: The Captain reported a steering issue on takeoff caused by cell phone earbud cords obstructing the tiller, triggering a 'Steering INOP' message. The crew rejected takeoff, cleared the obstruction, and completed the flight without further incident.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: Light Transport pilot reported his unoccupied and parked aircraft was turned 90 degrees and displaced from its chocks by a taxiing air carrier aircraft's jet blast.
summary: A parked aircraft was rotated 90 degrees by jet blast from a taxiing air carrier, causing it to hop its chocks. The reporter suggests restricting power during taxi or using a pushback position that avoids exposing other aircraft to jet blast.

synopsis: B777 international Captain reported extreme fatigue was a factor in overshooting a cleared altitude on leg two following a 10:31 first leg.
summary: A fatigued crew on the second leg of a 12-hour flight overshot a 5,000-foot level-off by 700 feet during climb-out. The reporter attributed the deviation and subsequent unsafe conditions to severe fatigue caused by the schedule and time zone changes.

synopsis: A flight crew elected to divert to the closest suitable airport after the Fire Suppression System deployed into the Accessible Dangerous Goods container. The diversion was flown effectively but the First Officer was injured during the subsequent evacuation when the Evacuation Slide did not deploy properly.
summary: During cruise at FL360, the Fire Suppression System discharged into an ADG container at position 1R, prompting a diversion and evacuation at ZZZ. The First Officer was injured when the L1 evacuation slide failed to fully inflate, while the Fire Department initially prioritized clearing the taxiway over inspecting the cargo.

synopsis: An Air Carrier Flight Attendant had to deal with a non-compliant passenger who suffered from dementia. He refused to obey commands to fasten his seatbelt and on final approach, stood up in the cabin and alarmed other passengers with his odd behavior. The flight attendants kept the unruly passenger from the armed exit doors until blocked in at the gate.
summary: A flight attendant managed a passenger with dementia who repeatedly unbuckled his seatbelt and stood in the aisle during landing. The passenger attempted to grab an infant, became combative with another passenger, and required crew members to physically restrain him until the aircraft stopped at the gate.

synopsis: Flight Attendant reported concern that she could be injured by unsecured tablets or other electronic devices used by passengers sitting across from her jumpseat if those passengers lost control of the device during a rejected takeoff or other unusual event.
summary: A flight attendant reported that passengers used unsecured tablets during taxi, takeoff, and landing, creating a safety hazard for crew and distracting exit row occupants. The attendant attributed this risk to airline policies allowing devices to be held rather than stowed, contradicting training on securing carry-on items during critical flight phases.

synopsis: Pilot reports of excessive chatter on CMA Tower frequencies.
summary: A pilot reported that excessive and repeated read-backs by Camarillo Airport controllers congested the radio frequency during takeoff and pattern operations. This unnecessary chatter prevented effective communication, forcing the pilot to depart the Class D airspace without making a position report due to safety concerns.

synopsis: BE58 pilot reported an NMAC with a Cessna at BRL.
summary: A pilot inbound to BRL on VFR experienced a near mid-air collision with a departing Cessna while holding for visual contact. The Cessna passed less than 200 feet below and in front of the pilot after the departing pilot incorrectly stated that Runway 18 was right-hand traffic.

synopsis: B777 flight attendant expressed concern about the possibility of injury to flight attendants when placing bags in the overhead bins that require a long reach.
summary: A flight attendant reported that Boeing 777 overhead bins, located over 6 feet high, cause back and shoulder injuries when lifting 75–150 lbs to close them before door closure. The reporter states these bins often open during takeoff and landing due to closure difficulties, creating a safety hazard for shorter crew members.

synopsis: Two Tower controllers and a Helicopter pilot describe a near miss at a busy airport where communications and radar were hampered by outages.
summary: Local controllers lost sight of Helicopter X due to tower obstructions and a radar outage, causing the pilot to fly fast and disoriented toward a Cessna on final. The helicopter reported a near mid-air collision after failing to extend downwind as instructed, requiring the Cessna to go around and the helicopter to rejoin the pattern.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: A ZDV Controller and pilot report confusion after the aircraft departs IFR at one airport while the Controller was waiting for the aircraft to depart off of a different airport. The identifiers for the airports are close and caused the confusion.
summary: A pilot departing Worland (WRL) received an IFR clearance from Oakland Flight Service that incorrectly listed Rawlins (RWL) as the departure airport due to a communication error. The aircraft subsequently contacted Salt Lake Center instead of Denver, resulting in a mismatched transponder code and a situation where the responsible controller was unaware of the operation.

synopsis: E10 Front Line Manager, Controller, and pilot report of not seeing the correct airport and lining up for another airport incorrectly. Tower Controller gets the aircraft heading towards the correct airport.
summary: The pilot flying Aircraft X mistakenly identified Apple Valley (APV) as Victorville (VCV) during a visual approach due to similar runway layouts and hazy conditions. The error was caught when the localizer failed to capture, prompting a go-around and subsequent safe landing at the correct airport.

synopsis: LAX Tower Controller reports of false target on a runway and no targets associated with the aircraft on a taxiway for thirteen minutes. Controller also reports of other false targets in various places on the airport.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that Aircraft X generated false targets on Runway 25L and Taxiway H, while also disappearing from ASDE-X for 13 minutes. The controller attributed these issues to continuous ASDE-X malfunctions and warned of safety risks during fog.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported the ship set bag restricts the cockpit seat to less than full aft travel, possibly inhibiting rapid egress.
summary: A pilot reported that a Ship Set Bag restricted cockpit seat travel, hindering movement over the center pedestal and potentially delaying emergency egress. The reporter questioned the legality of using non-permanent equipment to limit flight deck seat movement.

synopsis: A B767 flight crew climbing out of EWR reported two instances of the altitude alert window setting advancing 1000 feet above that previously set per their clearance as they approached their cleared altitude. Operation returned to normal after the two events. They wrote up the anomaly.
summary: The pilot flying reported that during departure from EWR, the altitude window spontaneously changed from 6000 to 7000 and later to 8000 despite correct manual entry. The crew leveled at 6200, received clearance for 7000, and wrote up the aircraft for the malfunctioning altitude window.

synopsis: A320 First Officer reported being cleared below class B airspace without notice from ATC.
summary: The flight crew reported that Washington Approach cleared them to descend to 2000 feet below the Class B floor without specific authorization. The crew delayed the descent to remain above the floor, citing regulatory requirements, and were subsequently transferred to Tower without incident.

synopsis: During a pre-departure walk-around, a First Officer (FO) notices two different light bulbs would illuminate on opposite wing tips when the A320 Navigation light switch was moved to either the # 1 or # 2 position. When in position #2, the right wing tip outboard aft Nav light was illuminated correctly, but on the left wing the inboard forward bulb was illuminated.
summary: A pilot reported a navigation light discrepancy during a pre-flight walk-around where switch positions appeared to illuminate opposite wing tip bulbs compared to training. Maintenance confirmed the operation was normal per wiring diagrams, leaving the pilot uncertain if training or documentation was incorrect.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported possible interference from cell phones in the cabin that could account for the electronic anomalies they were experiencing during the flight.
summary: The flight crew experienced frequent ACARS interruptions and autopilot speed deviations during the PHLBO3 STAR into EWR. After the captain requested a passenger announcement to turn off cell phones, the interference ceased and no further issues occurred.

synopsis: Dash 8-400 flight crew reported receiving warnings for LDG INOP, WT ON WHEELs, and FUSELAGE DOOR. Flight diverted to a suitable airport, and landed safely.
summary: The flight crew experienced multiple landing gear and door warnings after takeoff, leading to a diversion due to weather and maintenance limitations. They landed safely using alternate gear extension procedures, though the APU remained inoperative because the system falsely indicated the aircraft was airborne.

synopsis: A fractional carrier flight crew expressed concerns that too much administrative detail is allowed to be passed on to flight crews. In the instant case a flight was conducted without proper resolution of an MEL item due to distractions with foreign documentation requirements.
summary: The pilot departed an Embraer with a deferred rudder gust lock because a required maintenance procedure was not completed before flight. This oversight occurred after the pilot became distracted resolving an expired Mexican authorization form and failed to verify the Minimum Equipment List requirements.

synopsis: A First Officer reported flying a challenging circling approach in marginal weather to MHRO that was complicated by what he felt was inadequate training and substandard ATC procedures.
summary: The Captain and First Officer executed an untrained circling approach to runway 23 at MHRO in deteriorating weather due to a lack of operational guidance. Shifting winds and wind shear caused a pod clearance issue on touchdown, while high terrain made a go-around inadvisable.

synopsis: MD-11 flight crew reported wake vortex encounter in cruise flight that resulted in an altitude deviation.
summary: Pilots flying at FL290 encountered wake turbulence from an aircraft 15 NM ahead and 1,000 feet above after removing a 2 NM SLOP offset. The turbulence caused an uncommanded climb of approximately 400–500 feet, which was arrested within 10 seconds using altitude hold and vertical speed inputs while the autopilot remained engaged.

synopsis: C172 unknowingly departed from closed Runway 26 at CDC causing some concern to a helicopter training crew.
summary: The pilot departed runway 26 without checking NOTAMs, unaware it was closed, while an R44 helicopter sat at the opposite end. The pilot climbed away safely but later learned the R44 pilot knew of the closure, which was not indicated by AWOS or ground markings.

synopsis: C172 instructor pilot reported an NMAC with a helicopter at PRC during a time the Tower's radar was out of service.
summary: A student pilot and instructor in a fixed-wing aircraft experienced a near mid-air collision with a Bell Jet Ranger helicopter on final approach to Runway 30 at Prescott. The incident occurred due to the helicopter crossing the final approach course while tower radar was out of service, forcing the pilot to take evasive action to avoid impact.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: Pilot reports of poor service with Travis TRACON on multiple times and especially on the trip reported.
summary: A pilot returning VFR to an IFR approach at a marine-layer-covered airport experienced multiple vectoring errors and conflicting instructions from a trainee controller at the Travis TRACON. The controller's poor traffic management caused a TCAS alert, a cancelled approach clearance, and a missed approach due to being high and behind the glideslope.

synopsis: SMF Front Line Manager and Local Controller report of an Opposite Direction Operation (ODO) that resulted in a loss of required ODO separation.
summary: Ground and Local controllers reported that during a runway change, NCT failed to meet Opposite Direction Operation separation requirements for Aircraft Y, X, Z, and A. This resulted in multiple aircraft landing with less than the required 15-mile spacing and reduced lateral separation due to unclear coordination responsibilities.

synopsis: I90 controller reports of issuing a climb via clearance, the pilot reads it back correctly, but the aircraft misses a crossing restriction which leads to a loss of separation.
summary: An air traffic controller training a CPC-IT issued a climb via clearance to Aircraft X departing IAH, but the aircraft climbed rapidly through 6,800 feet, conflicting with an arrival at 6,000 feet. The controller attributed the deviation to unclear phraseology regarding altitude restrictions and noted the aircraft climbed 4,000 feet in 3 nautical miles.

synopsis: ZDC Controller reports of problems with the IVANE 5 Arrival into CLT and a specific type of aircraft having problems continually making crossing restrictions. This report also removed the IVANE 5 but the aircraft in question was given a crossing restriction which they didn't meet as well.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that Aircraft X violated a MAYOS FL220 restriction on the IVANE 5 arrival to CLT by crossing at FL265. The controller attributed the altitude deviation to potential pilot training issues and had to urgently coordinate a handoff to CLT33 and request a descent from LEEON.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: S46 Controller describes a training session where he and the Developmental do everything correct, in their mind. Two weeks later the instructor (reporter) is asked by a Front Line Manager if he thought the positions should have been spilt that day. The Controller then finds out he is being charged with a loss of separation that he thinks management is wrong in placing the blame. Controller cites from 7100.65 and LOA between facility and tower, reporting who has the responsibility for separation.
summary: An S46 trainee conducting OJT experienced a loss of separation between Aircraft X and Y during RNAV 34L missed approaches at PAE. Management attributed the 1.76-mile, 100-foot conflict to the trainee's failure to provide diverging instructions, despite the reporter citing LOA responsibilities assigned to PAE Tower.

synopsis: IAH Local Controller (LC) describes a situation where the other LC and other final monitor had a loss of separation, due to the final monitor not slowing the aircraft and/or the other local not sending the aircraft around. The other local asked the Front Line Manager what to do, but got no response.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller reported a loss of IFR separation between two aircraft on approach to runway 08R in low visibility due to conflicting roles between Local and Final Monitor controllers. The Final Monitor failed to act despite having separation responsibility, and the Front Line Manager provided no guidance, resulting in the aircraft landing without resolution.

synopsis: Pilot reports a B737-700 aircraft in service at a gate had failed a Standby Rudder Check due to the Standby Rudder Shutoff Valve would not open. He noted that an hour and a half later it was obvious that nobody had an understanding of how the system worked or how it was supposed to test. He was told by a Chief Pilot that he was overzealous and should not have tested the system since the Standby Check had already been removed from the pilot's checklist.
summary: The pilot performed a Standby Rudder check after a passenger alert, causing the system to fail and delaying the flight over 1.5 hours. Management deemed the test overzealous, removed the check from procedures, and attributed the delay to the pilot's disregard for company policy.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported using his EFB for taxi orientation on a snowy day in DEN, even though it was against company procedure to do so.
summary: The flight crew at Denver International Airport faced poor visibility and obscured taxiway markings after a runway change during deicing. The pilot used the prohibited EFB Own Ship feature to verify their position, concluding it was necessary for safety despite violating standard operating procedures.

synopsis: During preflight a B777 flight crew shut down the APU, pneumatic system and the packs when the cabin filled with smoke shortly after the APU was started. After Maintenance investigated and deferred the APU due to its oil entering the pneumatic system the flight was boarded and began taxi. Shortly thereafter, the smoke returned to the cabin, the shutdown procedures were repeated and the aircraft returned to the gate where the flight was canceled.
summary: The flight crew experienced APU oil entering the pneumatic system, causing smoke and activating the flight crew rest alarm during ground operations. After shutting down packs and engine bleeds, the crew returned to the gate and cancelled the flight.

synopsis: A B737 Captain discussed, with pertinent details, his concerns with respect to the fatigue inducing manner in which flight crew pairing sequences including all night flying are scheduled by his air carrier. He follows up the discussion of those issues with suggested solutions.
summary: Pilots on a multi-leg pairing involving an all-night flight and a short layover called themselves fatigued before the final leg. They attributed the fatigue to company scheduling that violated circadian rhythms and provided insufficient rest after the night flight.

synopsis: A ramp worker reports that at his location, because of ramp contamination that even after aircraft are chocked, aircraft roll backwards when the parking brake is released. The chocks merely slide along with the aft moving aircraft.
summary: The flight crew stopped the aircraft on a contaminated ramp after it rolled back three feet while chocks were being applied and the PLB approached. The reporter attributes the movement to the release of aircraft brakes, noting this issue occurs repeatedly regardless of ramp conditions.

synopsis: A320 flight crew reported they overshot a charted restriction on an RNAV arrival into CLT when the FMS dropped an altitude constraint and the crew did not catch it.
summary: Pilots flying an Airbus on an RNAV arrival from FL240 experienced a low crossing at MAYOS when the FMS unexpectedly deleted the FL240 altitude constraint. The reporter attributes the error to the FMS logic and suggests that historical constraint changes contributed to the oversight.

synopsis: A Gulfstream IV flight crew inbound to ADS were cleared direct to JERIT and given a late runway change to land Runway 15 vice 33 as planned, maintain 2,000 feet. As the Pilot Monitoring (PM) programmed the changes the reporter Pilot Flying (PF) disconnected the autoflight to prevent undesired autoflight directed course and/or vertical navigation directed changes during the reprogramming. While proceeding direct the PM asked if he should set the altitude alert to field elevation? Notwithstanding they had not been cleared to a lower altitude or for an approach, the PF acceded to the request. Shortly thereafter ATC issued a low altitude alert warning.
summary: During a night visual approach to ADS Runway 15, the crew descended below the assigned 2,000 feet due to task saturation after a late runway change, triggering an EGPWS alert at 1,000 feet AGL. The pilot corrected the altitude to 1,500 feet, acquired the airport, and completed an uneventful landing.

synopsis: A Citation air crew noticed after about an hour's flight at FL400 that the rudder trim knob would not move and that inputs to the rudder pedals resulted in only very slight yaw. They continued to their destination and found that rudder trim and rudder inputs were restored to normal operation after they descended through lower, warmer altitudes.
summary: The crew experienced frozen rudder trim and pedals while cruising at FL400, likely due to moisture freezing in the rear access compartment. Control was restored during descent at FL230 as temperatures rose, allowing a safe landing despite higher-than-normal rudder forces on the ground.

synopsis: A flight crew tried to help a Flight Attendant solve a dilemma posed by a passenger wishing to bring aboard a number of lithium batteries. The flight attendant Manual had a chart which provided guidance but unfortunately, they misinterpreted the chart.
summary: The captain and crew encountered a passenger with excess lithium batteries near departure, leading to conflicting interpretations of regulations between flight attendants, ground agents, and the pilot. The passenger boarded with some batteries while others were held, but the captain later admitted misreading the manual and noted a critical need for standardized hazardous material training across all personnel.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: When the right engine started making continuous loud banging sounds similar to compressor stalls shortly after takeoff, a flight crew advised ATC, performed an inflight shut down of the engine and returned to their departure airport.
summary: During climb through 2,000 feet, the right engine banged and oscillated, prompting a shutdown and return to the departure airport. The crew landed safely in icing conditions after ARFF found the right engine's bullet cone detached from the cowling.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: B757-200 flight crew reported confusion departing MIA because of what they called a 'confusing and non-standard' PDC format.
summary: Flight crew at MIA 26L received a confusing PDC departure clearance with buried routing changes, causing initial misunderstanding. The controller pressured the crew to taxi or take off due to traffic, later admitting this is an ongoing issue with the airline's crews.

synopsis: Airline flight crew reported their forward visibility was obscured on takeoff roll and initial climb when Type IV fluid flowed over the windscreen as their speed increased.
summary: The flight crew experienced zero visibility during takeoff at ASE when Type IV deicing fluid pooled and flowed over the windshield just before V1. The fluid obscured the view for the initial climb, forcing the pilots to rely on rudder feel to maintain centerline due to the high terrain and narrow runway.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A flight crew on arrival at the gate noted that a caterer opened up an armed door with the red tape still across the viewport and the slide pack flopped out onto the deck of a catering truck. The slide did not inflate. Mechanics were called. The slide was long overdue for inspection.
summary: After parking in DEN, a caterer opened the armed 1R door without authorization, causing the slide pack to flop onto a truck without inflating. The reporter attributed the incident to the door failing to disarm and a slide pack with a 1994 date, noting the failures were likely due to excessive age.

synopsis: After wing walking the aircraft into the gate and chocking the right main gear, a ramp person was alarmed when the aircraft moved backward approximately three feet. Cold and icy conditions were likely contributing factors to the aircraft's unsolicited movement.
summary: A ramp agent opening the cargo door on a parked aircraft was struck by the door when the aircraft slid back three feet due to released brakes in icy conditions. The incident occurred after the agent had chocked the main gear, but no injuries or damage resulted as the passenger bridge was not fully raised.

synopsis: B767-300 Captain reported receiving an alert for low quantity in the center hydraulic system. Crew declared an emergency and landed safely.
summary: The flight crew experienced a center hydraulic low quantity alert at cruise, with fluid dropping to 0.09–0.14 and intermittent low pressure messages. They declared an emergency, landed with flaps 20, and were towed to parking with emergency equipment standing by.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Light Transport Captain reported being confused by PKB ATC procedures and a single hold line in the vicinity of Runways 10/28 and 3/21 at Taxiway G.
summary: A pilot taxiing at PKB stopped at a hold short line with signs for runways 10/28 and 3/21 while a Cherokee landed on runway 3. The pilot queried ATC, who cleared crossing only runway 10/28, prompting the pilot to report that clearance for both runways is required to safely cross that specific line.

synopsis: An HS-125-800 Captain found and reported multiple corroded screws on his aircraft upper wing surface. His Chief pilot was unhappy with the Captain because his action affected the aircraft's availability.
summary: A pilot discovered severe corrosion on hundreds of wing screws during preflight for a passenger reposition and grounded the aircraft for evaluation. The Chief Pilot agreed the condition was horrendous but requested a written report, which the pilot interpreted as intimidation to discourage reporting discrepancies.

synopsis: CL30 pilot reported an NMAC with a light aircraft climbing out of APC, commenting that an earlier heads-up from ATC would have been appreciated.
summary: The pilot reported a TCAS RA during initial climb after Oakland Center cleared the aircraft direct to a distant fix while VFR traffic was nearby. The crew leveled off to avoid a Cirrus passing overhead, noting the controller failed to prioritize traffic advisories over long-range routing.

synopsis: A B737-800's flaps failed to extend on approach, therefore, the Alternate Flap extension method employed, and the flight diverted to a nearby airport.
summary: The pilot reported that flaps failed to deploy during approach. Flaps were extended using the alternate method, ATC was advised, and the aircraft diverted for an uneventful landing.

synopsis: A B-737-800 flight crew noted dark grey smoke in the cockpit after takeoff at about 2,000 feet. They requested level off at 3,000 feet, and requested return to departure airport. They turned off the left recirculation fan and the smoke stopped. They landed uneventfully at 1,000 pounds over max landing weight.
summary: The flight crew experienced dark gray smoke in the cockpit at 2,000 feet after takeoff from Airport ZZZ. Turning off the left recirculation fan cleared the smoke, allowing an uneventful overweight landing at 145,000 pounds.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An MD-80 series aircraft flight crew shut down the right engine, and returned to their departure airport after recognizing there was low oil quantity and an associated high oil temperature.
summary: During cruise, the First Officer reported a right engine oil quantity drop to 3 quarts with rising temperature, prompting an emergency declaration and inflight shutdown. The crew returned to the departure airport for a single-engine, overweight landing after coordinating with ATC and requesting ARFF support.

synopsis: A GLF5 flight crew experienced seriously compromised pitch trim capability during climb through FL220, ultimately generating FGC 1 and then 2 FAIL CAS messages which alternately went away when they switched between them. They diverted to a nearby airport utilizing manual pitch trim, the use of which also required excessive effort. The reporter speculated that a cable off its pulley or ice on a cable restricting passage may have been the culprit.
summary: During enroute climb at FL220, the crew experienced dual Flight Guidance Computer failures and severe manual trim binding, likely caused by frozen water or a disengaged cable from overnight rain. They diverted and landed safely hand-flying with manual trim after rejecting QRH recovery steps that would have disabled critical systems.

synopsis: A B777-200 flight crew described anomalous behavior of the autoflight system when programming the FMS in order to comply with ATC alterations to the crossing window at BHAWK on the FYTTE RNAV STAR to ORD. In addition, ATC assigned an airspeed well in excess of those charted. The FMS Inexplicably altered the active waypoint from BHAWK to STNLE, which was the first fix beyond BHAWK. The aircraft began an abrupt right turn when to track to STNLE would have only required a modest left turn. The flight crew abandoned VNAV operations in order to regain the assigned lateral track and while engaged in doing so descended below their cleared altitude at BHAWK. The First Officer's report was appended with detailed (and commonly reported) complaints with respect to the effects on flight crew workload and situational awareness imposed by ATC modifications to complex RNAV terminal area procedures.
summary: The crew descended below the FL220 constraint at BHAWK while executing a speed change on the FYTTE RNAV STAR. Modifying FMC speed constraints caused the aircraft to deviate laterally and descend prematurely, requiring manual intervention to rejoin the path.

synopsis: A B767-300ER flight crew experienced receipt of a L/E SLAT DISAGREE message upon selecting a landing flap setting of 25 degrees and the PF called for a go-around during which the landing gear was retracted, autoflight modes and autothrottles were deselected or misemployed...due in part to the blaring landing gear warning horn which was a substantial distraction until silenced. A subsequent flap over speed occurred when the thrust levers were not retarded in a timely manner. They advised ATC, completed the associated QRH and checklists, requested a longer runway and landed safely.
summary: The crew executed a go-around at 1,400 feet due to a leading edge slat disagree light, experiencing a momentary flap overspeed and a distracting gear warning during the climb. Contributing factors included icing, IFR conditions, and a rapid tailwind loss, but the aircraft landed safely on a parallel runway with no injuries.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A Flight Crew were cleared for a visual approach by Center. After landing they were asked by the Ground Controller if, 'they are allowed to do visuals since he had never seen a crew accept that clearance'. They looked over their 'notes' and found 'Visual Procedures N/A'.
summary: The flight crew accepted a visual approach clearance for Runway 31 after reporting field in sight, but ground control later questioned the validity of such clearances. The crew realized the airport notes state "Visual Procedures N/A," causing confusion over whether visual approaches are permitted and highlighting a need for clearer airport information.

synopsis: A student pilot aboard a PA-28 receiving dual instruction on cross-wind soft field landings drifted downwind during the flare and floated while letting let the airspeed decrease. When the instructor pilot/reporter attempted to assume control the student responded verbally but retained his grip on the flight controls resisting the instructor's inputs. A second assumption of control expression was successful and the instructor regained aircraft control but the left main landing gear had already contacted gravel alongside the runway, some of which was thrown aft and struck the aircraft. After completing the go around and returning for a safe landing they discovered moderate dent and puncture type damage to the stabilator.
summary: During a student pilot's second landing attempt in crosswinds, a go-around resulted in a stall warning and left wheel contact with gravel after the instructor struggled to take control. The incident caused a hole in the left stabilator from gravel impact, leading to the aircraft being grounded for maintenance inspection.

synopsis: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) was asked to take over the duties of another AMT who was leaving in the middle of an ongoing MEL Special Procedures task for deferral of a Low-Pressure Light hydraulics indication problem. The Relieving Technician finished the maintenance. A flight crew later reported that the light was still on. The Relieving Technician had disconnected a Canon Plug at the # 2 engine hydraulic pump instead of the # 2 electric pump in the wheel well.
summary: A mechanic relieved a colleague to service Aircraft X at the gate and incorrectly disconnected the engine hydraulic pump cannon plug instead of the wheel well plug per MEL procedures. This error caused the low-pressure light to remain on after takeoff, requiring a fix by contract maintenance upon arrival in ZZZ.

synopsis: Two Maintenance Controllers are directed under threat of discipline to issue two deferrals under their General Maintenance Manual (GMM) for a water scavenge system in an A300's aircraft fuel tank and a Scavenge Fuel Pump Control Circuit Breaker (CB) K63 that would not reset.
