Both Controllers believed an Engineering Order (EO) was required due to the scavenge pump control CB's association with Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 and Critical Design Configuration Control Limitation (CDCCL). The Line Mechanic also requests clarification of the two contradicting statements in their GMM as to the necessity of an EO when deviating from an MEL.
summary: Maintenance Controllers refused to approve deferrals for a tripped Scavenge Fuel Pump circuit breaker on an A300, citing CDCCL safety concerns and lack of root cause analysis. Management pressured them to issue the deferrals using General Maintenance Manual 03.05.01 instead of an Engineering Order, causing an aircraft delay.

synopsis: A CE680 main landing gear failed to retract after takeoff with the gear handle up. Due to a CRM issue the QRH actions were delayed, during which time the main gear retracted on its own.
summary: During takeoff, the crew experienced a landing gear retraction malfunction where the main gear failed to retract initially. A breakdown in Crew Resource Management occurred when the Second in Command attempted to return to the airport against the pre-flight plan, but the gear eventually retracted on its own, allowing a normal landing at the alternate home base.

aircraft: Cessna Twin Piston Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: The pilot of a turbocharged Cessna twin was climbing to his cleared altitude of 4,000 MSL when he noted the latest example of a recurring nuisance heading failure alert on his GARMIN PFD. As before, the alert went away shortly and the climb was continued. After leveling, ATC advised he was reporting 4,400 MSL vice 4,000 as cleared and provided the altimeter setting of 30.34, the same as was set in the PFD prior to departure. When the reporter checked he was surprised to note that the setting had changed to 29.92, apparently during the previous PDF heading anomaly. Of particular interest is his last paragraph addressing the little discussed but widely realized fact that few converts to glass cockpit retrofits in their aircraft are totally familiar with all that is included in the several hundred page users' manuals.
summary: The pilot reported that during a climb from CLT, a Garmin G500 heading failure caused the altimeter setting to reset from 30.34 to 29.92, resulting in an unintended level-off at 4,400 feet instead of the assigned 4,000 feet. The pilot attributed the error to the equipment anomaly and noted a failure to cross-check the backup steam gauge altimeter.

synopsis: Despite efforts to reduce landing gear exposure to the winter elements during preflight and taxi out, following takeoff the flight crew of a LJ-31 was unable to raise the landing gear. Despite a variety of creative efforts to overcome/eliminate the suspected accumulation of frozen material preventing retraction, the landing gear refused to respond. After a period of delay vectors to reduce the landing gross weight they landed the aircraft and, upon inspection, determined that their suspicions were accurate.
summary: The flight crew encountered landing gear retraction failure after takeoff due to ice accumulation on the main gear squat switches. They returned to Airport ZZZ, burned fuel to reduce weight, and landed safely after observing significant ice on the gear.

synopsis: Pilot reports of being under flight following then told to contact the Tower. Tower controllers advise pilot of Class D Violation. Pilot thought since he was under flight following the Tower would have known his position.
summary: A VFR pilot descending from 2800 feet MSL into San Carlos (SQL) Class D airspace believed a handoff from NorCal TRACON satisfied entry requirements. The pilot was cited for a deviation because TRACON did not coordinate the transfer, requiring the pilot to establish direct contact with SQL Tower before entering the airspace.

synopsis: The flight crew of an HS125 attempted to fly the RUUDY SID from TEB using a rapid reprogramming of heading and navigation modes in order to comply with the charted heading and fix to fix routing involved. Unfortunately, due to the aged minimalism of their FMS capability, the programming after TASCA was incorrect and the jet turned direct to GAYEL via a heading of 280 degrees after RUUDY as charted. Departure control caught the error and corrected their track.
summary: The captain and PNF departed TEB on the RUUDY5 procedure but deviated when the PNF engaged NAV mode early, causing an unintended turn to GAYEL. The crew corrected the heading after ATC intervention and subsequently rejected this departure due to excessive mode switching and FMS limitations.

synopsis: When given a climb from 4000 to 6000 feet and, quickly thereafter, issued an 'expect' lateral routing, the pilot of a CE-510S failed to monitor the aircraft's vertical track while pre-programming the expected new routing. ATC enquired as to why the aircraft was descending vice climbing as cleared. The reporter included a wise commentary on the need, especially for single pilot operations, to always pay greater attention to 'aircraft 'state' monitoring' even while engaged in required FMS programming.
summary: The pilot, flying at 4,000 feet, inadvertently descended after ATC issued climb clearances to 6,000 and 7,000 feet while the autopilot disengaged from vertical speed mode. The pilot attributed the error to distraction while pre-loading an expected route, noting that ATC's query prompted the manual correction.

synopsis: A PA-31 pilot on a short hop lost power in both engines as he climbed through 1500MSL. He landed safely alongside a canal with no reported damage or injuries. As he set up for the approach and landing he attempted to restart the engine/s but was unsuccessful.
summary: The pilot reported engine failure in IMC at 1500 feet while being vectored by ATC. After unsuccessful troubleshooting, the pilot executed a safe forced landing in a canal away from people and property.

synopsis: BE36 pilot reported wake vortex encounter on approach to FRG from a B757 inbound to JFK that resulted in a hard hit and a 45 degree bank.
summary: A pilot flying a general aviation aircraft on a visual descent to FRG encountered severe wake turbulence from a descending Boeing 757 heavy near JFK. The encounter caused a 45-degree roll and pilot injury, though the aircraft was recovered for an uneventful landing.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reports bleed through to MWA ASOS from PNT ASOS even though it is far away and on a different frequency. Also reported was the omission of the mandatory procedure turn at JONNY on the ILS 20 at MWA.
summary: The crew of an aircraft arriving at MWA misinterpreted ATC clearances and failed to perform a required procedure turn for the ILS 20 approach due to compressed workload and assumptions about radar vectoring. This resulted in an unstable approach with an abrupt autopilot pitch-down command, though the landing was completed safely after the error was identified post-landing.

synopsis: ZAB Controller describes a loss of separation he attributes to one of the aircraft taking five transmissions to receive information.
summary: An air traffic controller lost separation between climbing Aircraft X and descending Aircraft Y near FL300 due to Aircraft Y's delayed response to five descent clearance transmissions and ZLA's failure to update the data block. The controller attributed the 3.75 NM conflict to the pilot's lack of immediate compliance and the system's data lag.

synopsis: Two ASE Controllers and an air carrier flight crew report of an Opposite Direction Operation [ODO] where an aircraft is late to depart and does not take new heading to avoid inbound traffic.
summary: The Controller in Charge and local controller managed a conflict between departing Aircraft X and arriving Aircraft Y on opposite runways. Aircraft X initially failed to comply with a runway heading instruction, turning right instead of left, but eventually corrected to pass 1,000 feet above Aircraft Y after repeated instructions.

synopsis: A B737 Captain reported that while descending with very high altimeter settings of 30.30 plus, the FMC VNAV PATH reverts to VNAV SPD at the transition altitude requiring pilot intervention to comply with altitude constraints.
summary: Pilots reported fleet-wide VNAV PATH disengagement during arrival transitions at high altimeter settings (30.30+), causing failure to meet 17,000-foot crossing restrictions. The reporter attributes this to a VNAV software limitation requiring manual intervention to comply with charted restrictions.

synopsis: A B737-700 flight crew inbound to ATL on the KOLTT RNAV STAR, Precision Runway Monitor (PRM) runway 08L received a last second runway change to 09R which requires an entirely different routing from KOLTT and branches off the common portion of the STAR 3.3NM sooner than required for 08L. Unable to complete the altered programming and immediately cleared for the PRM Runway 09R approach the FMS was unable to direct the ~80 degree course change required at ANDIY. The flight crew struggled to manually make the adjustment and ATC simultaneously provided a vector in a commingled attempt to save the arrival and maintain separation with other aircraft. Both pilots cited the difficulty associated with complying with very late runway change assignments on complex RNAV STARs.
summary: During an RNAV arrival into Atlanta, the flight crew failed to close the FMS discontinuity before the ANDIY fix after a runway change, causing the aircraft to miss the turn to DFINS. The crew manually initiated the turn and accepted an ATC vector, landing safely despite the navigation error.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A pilot attempted to update his iPad because of an FOM change and discovered that all Company material and manuals had been deleted from the APP folder. Others reported the loss also.
summary: A pilot discovered the Company APP folder, containing flight manuals and FOMs, was missing from their iPad during pre-flight preparation. The flight office confirmed hundreds of pilots experienced this unauthorized removal without prior notification.

synopsis: ATC turned a B767 in close to the final approach fix and high on a CAT III. The Captain executed a go-around at about 1,200 feet since the aircraft could not descend and slow down safely.
summary: The flight crew executed a go-around during a CAT III ILS approach to RWY 8L after intercepting the localizer high and fast due to an unexpected early turn. The pilot forgot missed approach callouts, but the copilot retracted flaps and gear, allowing a safe second approach.

synopsis: An air carrier Captain flying as a passenger on a B737 witnessed an incomplete Type IV de-icing application prior to gate departure, a failure he had previously experienced himself. As there was no current precipitation he opted not to attempt to contact the flight crew until the end of the flight, but they had deplaned prior to his being able to do so.
summary: A passenger on a Boeing 737 observed inadequate Type IV deicing fluid application at the gate, evidenced by orange and green stripes on the wing. The reporter noted no immediate danger as precipitation had ceased, but warned that the incomplete application could compromise anti-ice protection if weather conditions worsened.

synopsis: An air carrier crew departed a CTAF airport VFR while another air carrier jet was on approach but in hindsight felt they should have delayed to prevent the perception of conflict given CTAF communications limitations.
summary: The pilot departed runway 28 after Center released them with a 737 on approach 10 miles away, despite the jet failing to announce its specific approach. The pilot concluded the release was unwise due to high closure rates and poor communication, though no collision occurred and the aircraft separated safely.

synopsis: A DHC-8-200 right engine auto-feathered after takeoff. The Below Acceleration Height Checklist was completed and the flight returned to the departure airport.
summary: The Captain reported an unscheduled #2 engine feather on a jet at 500 feet during departure from runway 4L, caused by an engine abnormality. The crew executed engine failure procedures, returned for an ILS approach, and landed safely without further incident.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An air carrier crew departed BUR on the VNY 1 but were given a vector by SCT which they misunderstood, were given a second misunderstood vector, and finally got the correct heading.
summary: The flight crew departed BUR on the VNY 1 departure but deviated from ATC instructions by turning to heading 310 instead of the assigned 210 due to miscommunication. This error resulted in a pilot deviation notification, prompting a recommendation for improved crew coordination and assertive clarification of ATC vectors.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An air carrier crew departed CMH and thought were cleared to 15,000 feet by departure, but when they called Center they were notified 10,000 feet was their climb limit. So, they started descending down to 10,000 feet only to be cleared to FL230.
summary: The pilot reported a conflicting altitude clearance during the initial climb from CMH after being told to maintain 15,000 feet, then 10,000 feet, and finally FL230. The crew stopped the climb to 15,000 feet upon ATC's denial of the previous instruction before receiving the final clearance.

synopsis: Air carrier pilot reports of two instances where they were instructed to maintain a speed higher than 250 knots while below 10,000 feet.
summary: The flight crew complied with ATC instructions from SOCAL Departure and Chicago Center to maintain 280 and 300 knots respectively below 10,000 feet during climb and descent. The crew assumed these non-standard speeds were issued for aircraft separation.

synopsis: While descending on the ORD FYTTE2, ATC issued a 300 knot speed restriction. When the B777 Captain modified the waypoint speed constraints it caused LNAV and VNAV to disconnect. The aircraft descended below profile and deviated from the desired heading until manually corrected.
summary: During the FYTTE 2 arrival descent, the pilot's extensive FMC edits caused the aircraft to lose the BHAWK fix and vertical crossing restrictions. This confusion led to an uncommanded turn and a subsequent crossing of BHAWK below the required 220 feet altitude before the autopilot was re-engaged.

synopsis: During climbout, a B767 developed a loud banging sound which the crew could not positively identify, but suspected an engine because a power reduction stopped the noise.
summary: During night VFR climb on a Boeing 767, loud banging occurred after the Air Driven Pump was turned off. The crew reduced power, returned the pump to on, and landed safely; a fluid leak under the left engine was found, requiring a single-engine taxi to the gate.

synopsis: An A321 Captain reported that during ground de-ice procedures a ground employee came so close to a running engine his headset was sucked into the nacelle.
summary: The flight crew, operating an Airbus with an inoperative APU, was instructed to shut down the left engine for de-icing. A ground crew member approached too soon, causing their headset to be sucked into the left engine inlet, though the employee was unharmed.

synopsis: B767-300ER First Officer reported losing the center hydraulic system. An emergency was declared and the aircraft was towed to the gate after a safe landing.
summary: The flight crew experienced a center hydraulic fluid leak at FL 350, which they managed by cycling pumps and using flaps 25 for an uneventful landing in freezing rain. They stopped on the contaminated runway to await a tow due to low fluid levels, noting the checklist lacked guidance on preserving fluid by turning pumps off.

synopsis: Pilot reported an Approach Controller demanded he accept a visual approach to follow other traffic. When the pilot refused the clearance, the Controller became irate, causing distraction during a critical phase of flight.
summary: The pilot rejected an approach controller's demand to accept a visual approach following other traffic at night. The controller became irate and distracted the pilot during a critical phase of flight by insisting the pilot assume horizontal separation responsibilities.

synopsis: PA-28 instructor pilot reported his student descended steeply to 150 feet AGL during a practice non-precision instrument approach in IMC conditions.
summary: During a student pilot's first IMC encounter on a LOC 10R approach, the student lost situational awareness and descended to 150 ft instead of leveling at 380 ft MDA due to broken clouds at 300 ft. The instructor took control to recover the flight path and prevent a crash on short final.

synopsis: C172 pilot reported an NMAC with another light aircraft in the pattern at DED. Reporter stated lack of adherence to radio procedures was a major factor in the incident.
summary: The pilot reported a near collision with a Cessna training flight on short final at Deland (DED) while 100 feet above the fence. The Cessna, which had departed Ormond Beach without radio calls or lights, appeared 10 feet below, forcing an immediate go-around.

synopsis: F2TH Captain reported exceeding charted speed on the MNNDO1 RNAV arrival into DAL when he misunderstood the controller's clearance.
summary: Pilots flying into Dallas reported inconsistent controller instructions regarding the MNNDO1 arrival, including conflicting speed and altitude clearances that deviated from the published STAR. The crew attributed the resulting vectoring and speed conflicts to a lack of consistency in applying "descend via" procedures during the transition to new RNAV arrivals.

synopsis: PA-18 flight instructor reported his student lost directional control during landing roll that resulted in a 180 degree turn and scraping a wing tip.
summary: During pre-solo instruction in a tail dragger, a student pilot failed to release controls after the instructor intervened, causing a hard right turn that scraped the left wing on the ground. The aircraft stopped after a 180-degree turn with no injuries and non-substantial damage.

synopsis: G100 flight crew reported feeling a vibration and noting a rise in interstage turbine temperature in #2 engine during descent. Reducing thrust brought temperature back to normal, and flight landed safely. After parking, flight crew noted that there was significant damage to the engine.
summary: During descent from FL400, the crew experienced aft vibration and high #2 engine temperatures, reducing thrust to restore normal readings. Post-landing inspection revealed an N2 Low Pressure Turbine blade had departed through the exhaust, though no power was lost and the aircraft landed safely.

synopsis: A80 Controller reports of an aircraft slowing on final prior to the FAF, reporting it to the Front Line Manager (FLM), and the FLM not doing anything about it. Reporter then goes on to tell this is happening all the time with this one company and nothing is being done about it. Weather is a factor on final.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that Aircraft X deviated from an assigned speed clearance by slowing early on final approach to runway 10 in low visibility, forcing the controller to slow a trailing aircraft. The controller attributed the incident to the pilot disregarding the clearance and criticized facility management for ignoring the deviation due to an unwritten agreement with the airline.

synopsis: A B737-700 flight crew discovered frost on the leading edges and surfaces of the wing and stabilizer during preflight. After making the required request for de-icing, they were alarmed and irate when local operations--and eventually their Dispatcher--instead suggested they needed to review a recent company bulletin which they believed superseded the Captain's request. The Captain succinctly suggested the airplane was unacceptable to all parties and the de-icing was completed.
summary: The Captain and First Officer identified significant frost on the aircraft surfaces prior to sunrise and requested deicing, despite Operations and Dispatch questioning the need due to above-freezing temperatures. The crew faced delays and procedural conflicts as ground personnel refused to deice at the gate, contradicting published station procedures for overnight frost.

synopsis: B737-700 Captain reported receiving a windshear warning and a loss in airspeed at 800 feet AGL after takeoff from AUS.
summary: The flight crew experienced a windshear warning at 800–900 feet AGL during takeoff from Runway 35L at AUS, noting a sudden wind shift from 020/6 to 190/32. After lowering the nose and advancing thrust, the warning cleared, allowing for a normal climbout and subsequent notification to Tower and Dispatch.

synopsis: A B737 inbound on the ILS 08 to BUR responded twice on separate approaches to TCAS RAs with conflicting VNY VFR traffic operating below an intervening under/overcast. One reporter suggested modified restrictions on VNY traffic during such conditions to lessen the exposure to conflicts.
summary: The flight crew executing an ILS 08 approach at Burbank encountered two Resolution Advisories from Van Nuys traffic below an overcast deck, forcing missed approaches. After ATC issued climbout instructions, the crew successfully landed on a third attempt once weather cleared and conflicting traffic departed.

synopsis: Air carrier dispatchers reported an illegal flight plan was generated that would have taken the aircraft into Class II airspace had the error not been caught in time.
summary: A training dispatcher inadvertently filed a flight into Oceanic Class II airspace after using the 'Reset/Plan' button, which replaced the planned route with a computer-generated User Defined route. The crew discovered the error post-departure and altered the route to comply with regulations before entering the restricted airspace.

synopsis: Following a delayed taxi out due to weather and field conditions the B737 was deiced and configured for takeoff with the engine bleeds off and the APU utilized for aircraft pressurization per SOP. As they approached V1, vapor (clearly identified as from deicing fluid) began to exit the air vents. The takeoff was continued and after configuring to normal bleeds/APU off the vapor/fumes dissipated and the flight continued. The First Officer, the pilot flying, considered but did not suggest a rejected takeoff. Runway heading was maintained until the bleed reconfiguration was completed at which time they complied with their cleared departure.
summary: The crew experienced smoke from improper deicing fluid entering the APU intake during takeoff on runway 4L. The First Officer turned off the APU bleed to clear the smoke, while the Captain corrected a 2-3 mile deviation from the assigned SID after realizing the aircraft remained on runway heading.

synopsis: A long serving B757/67 Captain stressed two factors which compromised flight crew communications. First, there is ambient noise from the air conditioning system/recirculation fans. Second, the use by some crew members of noise canceling headsets in order to lower the ambient noise, which restricts the precise communication of vital command and response exchanges between the Pilot Flying and Pilot Monitoring. The reporter believes the second factor is the result of the attempt to mitigate the impact of the first. He further believes that previous programs in place to monitor and mitigate the source of excess ambient noise have been abandoned, thus providing the impetus for the use of the personal noise canceling headsets. Finally, he believes the use of some of the personal headsets precludes utilization of some features of the OEM equipment intended for use during emergency conditions.
summary: A 757-300 pilot reported excessive pneumatic duct noise and inconsistent noise-canceling headsets hindering cockpit communication and ATC contact. The pilot attributed the hazard to a lack of active maintenance inspections and proposed reinstating service bulletins and standardizing headsets.

synopsis: An A321 flight crew flying the IVANE RNAV STAR to CLT was cleared to cross MAYOS at FL220 and, then, to reduce IAS to 250 knots. After doing so it became obvious they couldn't cross MAYOS at FL220 even with speedbrakes extended. ATC then removed the airspeed and the rate of descent was increased until the FMGC indicated the crossing would be met. Upon selecting managed descent, the FMGC made no attempt to manage the FL220 crossing at MAYOS and it was crossed at FL237. ATC made no comment about the failure to comply.
summary: The pilot reported that a Washington Center speed restriction to 250 knots prevented crossing MAYOS at FL220, resulting in a crossing at 23,700 feet. The pilot attributed the deviation to the controller's lack of understanding regarding speed effects on descent and the pilot's failure to assertively decline the conflicting clearance.

synopsis: While descending to their destination the flight crew of an EMB-190 experienced a massive loss of electrical systems to the extent that the RAT automatically deployed. They conducted QRH checklists and opted to divert to a nearby airport with longer runways than were available at their destination. They landed safely after having regained some systems via the APU generator. Previous reports of anti-icing system failure to provide and EICAS icing alerts and inappropriate operation of wing anti-ice suggested a path of investigation for Maintenance.
summary: During a STAR descent, the flight crew experienced an electrical emergency with RAT deployment and EICAS alerts, prompting a diversion to ZZZ1. The cause remained unclear, though the crew noted unexplained wing temperature fluctuations and persistent lighting control failures after landing.

synopsis: A de-ice crew reported a CRJ-700 clean of ice and snow but when the First Officer completed a walk around after returning to the gate to reduce takeoff weight, ice and snow were discovered on the wings and flaps.
summary: Flight crew and deice personnel at Airport ZZZ experienced a departure delay due to tailwinds and a subsequent return to the gate after discovering snow and ice remained on the wings. The deice crew failed to clean the aircraft because flaps were set to 45 degrees, preventing access, yet falsely reported the aircraft was clean.

synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported he accidentally hit the TOGA button on an ILS approach and chose to go-around. Other errors were made during the next approach before he and the First Officer regained full situational awareness.
summary: The pilot accidentally activated Go-Around mode during an ILS approach to DCA Runway 1, triggering a missed approach. A subsequent failed intercept occurred because the Course Selector remained set to the missed approach radial instead of the inbound course, though the crew eventually landed safely after correcting the setup.

synopsis: A B767-300ER flight crew opted to divert to an enroute airport when both automatic pressurization controllers failed.
summary: The flight crew diverted a cruise-phase flight from South America to MIA after an EICAS Cabin Auto Inoperative message indicated a pressurization failure. Maintenance later identified a large water leak causing ice formation, forcing an overnight stay before the crew continued home the next evening.

synopsis: Widebody Transport flight crew reported Number 2 Engine displayed high exhaust gas temperature even after thrust reduction, therefore, the engine was shut down, and executed an uneventful landing.
summary: The crew experienced an Engine 2 EGT exceedance of 997 degrees at FL240, initially reducing thrust to idle. After temperatures rose again at 14,000 feet, they shut down Engine 2 per the QRH and completed a Cat II autoland in low visibility.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports that the current fueling and defueling procedures in their maintenance hangars result in employees being exposed to high amounts of fuel vapors, environmental non-compliance, and an unsafe workplace. A previous system of fuel tank venting did not allow vent ducts on the hangar floors.
summary: Mechanics at the ZZZ Maintenance Base reported that current fuel sumping and venting procedures using air-driven equipment release hazardous vapors into hangars, causing employee health issues and potential environmental non-compliance. The reporter attributes this to the deactivation of the original built-in venting system and the use of damaged, ungrounded portable tubing.

synopsis: While in a descent, cleared to FL330, the flight crew of a CL30 responded as directed to a TCAS TA followed shortly by an RA. Upon completion of the avoidance maneuver they continued their descent while monitoring the traffic visually. While doing so they inadvertently descended approximately 500 feet below their cleared altitude.
summary: Pilots received a TCAS RA during a descent to FL340, causing an unintended descent to FL335 while visually acquiring traffic. Post-flight, ATC confirmed an 800-foot separation loss, and the crew attributed the altitude deviation to distraction from scanning for traffic during the RA resolution.

synopsis: BE33 pilot reported an NMAC with a light aircraft on approach to VPZ.
summary: A VFR pilot flying a practice ILS approach to Runway 27 executed a missed approach after observing a climbing aircraft on Runway 09 at less than one mile final. The pilot attributed the near-miss to not hearing the other aircraft's CTAF calls prior to the second position report.

synopsis: A King Air B100 pilot reported getting low on the ILS to APA airport while flying in icing conditions and experienced erratic localizer and glideslope signals, possibly related to ice accumulation.
summary: The pilot encountered moderate mixed ice and intermittent ILS localizer and glide slope errors while approaching APA RWY 35. The reporter attributed the signal interference to ice accumulation on the aircraft antennas, which was confirmed by another pilot and observed as over 1.5 inches upon landing.

synopsis: A Southern California TRACON Controller reports of a loss of separation with an aircraft he was vectoring to an airport while another faster aircraft departed a different airport. The departing aircraft speed was too fast and the aircraft was wide in turning leading to the loss of separation.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller reported that Aircraft X, an HHR arrival at 3000 feet, and Aircraft Y, a fast LGB departure, likely lost 1.5 miles lateral separation due to pilot heading deviations and non-compliance with the SID. The controller attributed the event to a narrow airspace margin and recommended raising the handoff altitude to 4000 feet.

synopsis: A B777 flight crew, while in cruise, detected that the autothrottles were not maintaining .82 Mach and were retarding further even as airspeed was decreasing. The Captain disengaged the autothrottle system and manually set the throttles to maintain Mach .82. He then reengaged the autothrottle system and it operated normally for the remainder of the flight.
summary: A 777 captain reported that during cruise in Russian airspace, the auto throttle system unexpectedly retarded thrust levers, causing airspeed to drop 20 knots below target without warnings. The pilot manually overrode the system to prevent a potential stall, logged the failure, and noted maintenance found no prior issues but would inspect the aircraft on the ground.

synopsis: An A320 Captain reported receiving a GPWS terrain alert on arrival into PDX in IMC. The pilot flying executed an escape maneuver. The reporter feels it was likely a closure rate alert.
summary: The First Officer flying HHOOD2 received a GPWS "terrain terrain" warning at 5300 feet during a descent to 5000 feet in clouds. The pilot applied power and pitched up to stop the alert, assuming the warning was caused by a high closure rate.

synopsis: A CRJ200 Flight Crew experiences an autopilot malfunction at 500 feet AGL during a low visibility approach to Runway 8L at ATL. A missed approach is initiated but not before the aircraft has turned 15 degrees toward 8R. When the Take Off Go Around (TOGA) button is pushed the autopilot disconnects causing a late turn away from Runway 8R and late gear retraction. The second approach is a Category (CAT) III and successful.
summary: During a low-visibility ILS PRM approach to Runway 8L, the autopilot unexpectedly turned the aircraft right due to a trim fault, causing a course deviation at 500 feet AGL. The crew executed an immediate go-around, initially climbing toward Runway 8R before turning north as directed by tower to avoid conflict.

synopsis: An A319 Captain reported he was concerned when ramp personnel began working around the aircraft after taxi in while an engine was still running.
summary: At PBI, ground personnel approached the aircraft while Engine 1 was running, triggering ECAM warnings for open cargo doors. The pilot reported this as a serious safety hazard due to fan and exhaust dangers, recommending a policy prohibiting ground access while engines operate.

synopsis: An A319 Flight Crew was running behind schedule and was given a break release time in compliance with FAR Part 117. The Captain then noticed frost on the wings. He called crew scheduling to advise them. The Scheduler wanted to know why he needed to be de-iced when other departures were not being de-iced.
summary: The captain of a delayed MSP flight reported that Crew Scheduling and Operations pressured him to skip deicing despite visible frost on the aircraft. The reporter described a hostile culture where unqualified staff challenged the captain's safety decision, creating a mob mentality to avoid delays and maintain on-time performance.

synopsis: A B767 flight crew while enroute experienced a cabin automatic pressurization failure of systems 1 and 2. The standby pressurization system was difficult to control and they elected to divert and landed. Post flight revealed that a water leak had frozen both auto cabin pressurization controllers.
summary: The Relief Pilot diverted a Boeing 767 due to inoperative automatic cabin controllers caused by ice from a leaking aft galley coffee maker. The leak froze both controllers, forcing difficult manual pressurization that caused crew and passenger ear discomfort before maintenance isolated the water system.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported 'dangerous and unsatisfactory' de-ice procedures on his aircraft at DTW.
summary: Pilots at DTW reported dangerous, unsupervised de-icing by inexperienced contractors using central radio communications, resulting in multiple false "clear of ice" reports and a four-hour delay. The incident was caused by inadequate supervision and communication disconnects, requiring a return to the gate for proper service by a new crew before safe departure.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 2 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: A twin engine aircraft crew experienced left engine surging after takeoff. As a precaution they shut the engine down. They then restarted the engine while returning to land and it ran normally. However, when they lowered the landing gear the left main gear indicator did not light. Since the gear unsafe light did not illuminate, they continued to a normal landing.
summary: The pilot experienced a left engine surge after departure, shut it down, and restarted it on crossfeed. Although the left main gear indicator light failed to illuminate, the pilot landed safely after the controller confirmed the gear appeared down and the unsafe light remained off.

synopsis: A Lear 35 flight crew diverted to EWR from their intended destination due to weather, icing conditions, and short runway. Enroute flight conditions worsened and ice formed on the surfaces. In addition, the attitude indicator of the pilot flying (PF) gave evidence of anomalous behavior by showing a different bank attitude from both the standby and the reporter's indicators. The Captain, and PF, elected to continue as PF and flew a modestly flawed but successful approach and landing. Upon landing they made a pilot report of their observations. Post flight, the flight crew realized the reporter's Navigation (NAV) systems were in the GPS vice NAV mode.
summary: A crew diverting to EWR due to severe icing and weather encountered task overload, a failed pilot-flying attitude indicator, and a navigation mode discrepancy. These factors caused significant ILS deviations until the crew corrected the navigation source and landed visually after exiting clouds at 1500 feet.

synopsis: CE560 Captain departing Runway 30 at SUA experiences lost comm with PBI Departure on 132.8, with the crew able to hear Departure but Departure could not hear the crew. No problems were experienced on Tower frequency prior to or ZMA after the event. The exact same scenario repeated three days later.
summary: Pilots departing SUA Runway 29 experienced two-way radio failure with Palm Beach Departure on frequency 132.8, requiring multiple attempts and an ident to establish contact. The controller eventually cleared the aircraft to 5,000 feet and transferred them to Miami Center, which acknowledged immediately.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: CAE Ground Controller taxis aircraft to Runway 29. Previously the airport was departing Runway 29, and ten minutes ago changed to using Runways 11 and 5. Ground Control later hears Local Control issuing traffic alerts to the aircraft he taxied to Runway 29 and another aircraft on final for Runway 11.
summary: Ground Control taxied Aircraft Y to the inactive Runway 29 after a runway change, and the Local Controller cleared it for takeoff on Runway 11, creating a head-on conflict with Aircraft X on final. The controller attributed the error to fatigue, using a handset instead of a headset, and a lack of visual runway-in-use indicators.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A Denver Center Controller describes a situation where an aircraft is reporting that it will be high at a crossing restriction and wants relief. The Controller attempts coordination to be high with Denver TRACON (D01) and the D01 controller replies they are unable and to spin the aircraft. The aircraft is told to turn but is slow in doing so and violates D01 airspace. The Controller then goes on to complain about the performance of the D01 controllers and how they think there service is diminishing over the last couple of years.
summary: A Center controller issued a spin clearance to Aircraft X on the wrong frequency while coordinating a handoff to North Departure, causing the pilot to enter Approach airspace without turning. The reporter attributes the incident to a transmission error and claims Approach controllers unnecessarily forced the maneuver due to negligence or spite.

synopsis: An ARR Tower Controller reports of staffing issues at the Tower. Reporter sites a specific day where he thought they did a good job with the short staffing, but management thinks they did not.
summary: Aurora ATCT controllers reported that severe understaffing forced them to prioritize safety over training during complex morning traffic, resulting in shortened breaks. Management later issued a false performance record claiming poor resource management and safety compromises, despite controllers maintaining safety margins with appropriate break times.

synopsis: A B737-700 Captain reported he was not sure he was legal to continue on his approach to DEN when severe rime ice might have been in the area.
summary: A crew inbound to Denver encountered conflicting severe rime icing reports from ATIS, Center, and preceding aircraft before landing. Despite heavy icing obscuring wing visibility, they continued the approach based on moderate reports from two aircraft ahead, later questioning if the anticipated severe conditions should have grounded the operation.

synopsis: A B737-700 flight crew reported they noticed an abnormal 'shimmy' on the takeoff roll that might have been nosewheel steering related. They diverted to an alternate for maintenance.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced two abrupt left nose wheel shimmies at 100 and 130 knots during takeoff roll, which the crew attributed to a potential nose wheel steering issue. Consequently, they diverted the aircraft for a maintenance inspection after consulting Dispatch.

synopsis: A B737-700 First Officer reported airspeed indicator anomalies, including a stall indicator (rudder shakers) activation, on an ILS approach.
summary: The First Officer experienced two false speed tape indications and rudder shaker activations during an ILS approach in low overcast, despite the aircraft remaining stable. The crew added power for recovery, increased approach speed, and landed safely before maintenance logged the flight display malfunction.

synopsis: A B737 Captain reported that when he refused to fly an aircraft to SNA because of heavy light aircraft traffic and an inoperative TCAS his company 'shopped' the aircraft to other flight crews hoping someone would take it.
summary: The Captain refused an aircraft for a flight to SNA because the TCAS was inoperative per the MEL, deeming it unsafe. Dispatch subsequently assigned the same aircraft to two other crews, both of whom also refused to operate the flight.

synopsis: A B747 Air Crew, after receiving a dispatch release from their Dispatcher, asked the Dispatcher if a more northerly route would save time and fuel. It would have but the Dispatcher stated that the process of changing the routing would have taken more time than he had available.
summary: The flight crew identified an inefficient flight plan filed by the dispatcher that resulted in burning 12,000 extra pounds of fuel due to a suboptimal southerly route. The dispatcher rejected a more efficient northerly alternative, citing insufficient time to validate the complex routing with European ATC.

synopsis: A CE-560XL Captain found an APU fuel leak inside the APU compartment. While investigating Maintenance found a loose 'B' nut spraying fuel inside the compartment and on the APU containment box.
summary: Flight crew discovered a jet fuel leak from a loose 'B' nut on an APU fuel line coupling during post-flight inspection after taxiing to the hangar. Maintenance confirmed the leak sprayed fuel onto the exciter box and burner can, creating a significant fire hazard that was repaired overnight.

synopsis: A Captain explains why he twice refused, even under company pressure, to accept the same SAAB SF-340B aircraft that had a trailing edge crack on one of the prop blades for # 1 engine. Although the Propeller Representative said the crack was OK for service, the Captain noted the crack had exceeded the 2.5 inches allowed for continued limited flight. Maintenance later confirmed Captain's observation.
summary: The Captain refused to fly a SAAB SF340B due to a propeller crack exceeding the 2.5-inch deferral limit and an improper repair. Despite company pressure, the crew persisted, leading mechanics to discover a deeper crack, resulting in a cancelled flight.

synopsis: A B757 Captain reported receiving a GPWS terrain alert on a night visual approach to LAS even though he felt he was clear of terrain.
summary: During a night descent into LAS on the Tyssn2 arrival, the crew received a GPWS "Caution Terrain and Pull Up" alert after being cleared direct to SHAND for a visual approach. The pilot climbed to clear the terrain, attributing the warning to a predictive vector message, and completed an uneventful landing.

synopsis: A B737-800 Captain reported going around at SNA after the tower cleared an aircraft for takeoff in front of them, with what the reporter felt was insufficient spacing.
summary: The pilot executed a go-around at 700 AGL on final approach because a departing aircraft, cleared to line up and wait, had not begun its takeoff roll. The pilot attributed the event to the tower's practice of clearing departures ahead of short-final traffic, citing a history of similar unsafe occurrences at this airport.

synopsis: A B757-200 filled with smoke while at the gate with the APU running. The smoke dissipated with the packs off and bleeds closed. Apparently the de-ice crew allowed fluid to enter the APU intake.
summary: Flight crew at the gate experienced heavy smoke from flight deck vents while the APU and packs were running. The reporter suspects unnotified de-icing caused moisture to enter systems, though fire and maintenance found no heat evidence.

synopsis: An EMB-145 flight crew reported both right main gear tires failed near V1 on takeoff. A rejected takeoff was executed safely.
summary: During takeoff roll near V1, both right main tires blew out, causing the Captain to abort. The crew safely stopped the aircraft, verified no fire, and evacuated passengers to buses with no injuries reported.

synopsis: Regional jet flight attendants discover that the prerecorded passenger safety briefing incorrectly refers to life vests under the seats. The flight crew is notified of the discrepancy and they turn it into a prank stating they will have to make an emergency diversion. A few minutes later they call back to reveal the prank and that they are continuing to destination.
summary: A flight attendant reported that pilots jokingly declared a Code Yellow emergency diversion due to a miscommunication about inaccurate safety video instructions regarding life vests. This prank caused a breakdown in Crew Resource Management, resulting in the flight deck failing to make required descent announcements and the captain making demeaning remarks to the crew.

synopsis: A pilot in a flight of two C-337's at 13,000 feet reported detecting the other pilot's conversational hypoxia symptoms so they descended and diverted. The Mountain High O2D2 regulator was a decade old and not serviced regularly.
summary: During cruise at 13,000 feet in an unpressurized aircraft, a trailing pilot suffered hypoxia due to a likely malfunctioning 10-year-old Mountain High O2D2 regulator. The lead pilot recognized the symptoms, descended, and coordinated with ATC for a safe landing with no injuries.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A corporate jet landed at 7M5 and had difficulty stopping. They discovered the runway was resurfaced with a Bituminous Pavement Rejuvenator, which FAA Advisory Circular 150/5370-10G recommends only be used on surfaces where aircraft weighing less than 12,500 pounds operate.
summary: A corporate flight crew landed a small jet on runway 4 at 7M5, noting reduced braking effectiveness likely caused by a Bituminous Pavement Rejuvenator treatment applied to the dry surface. The crew safely stopped within the 3,302-foot runway but recommended terminating operations until a risk assessment confirms the surface friction meets aircraft weight requirements.

synopsis: A non IFR rated helicopter pilot describes his experience after inadvertently entering IMC, then requesting ATC assistance for an IMC diversion to a nearby airport.
summary: The pilot and crew inadvertently entered IMC while avoiding smoke from brush fires during a transport mission. After declaring an emergency and receiving vectors from ATC, the pilot completed an RNAV approach guided by Operational Control and landed safely at a nearby airport.

synopsis: An Aeronca Champ Instructor reported a wind gust pushed the aircraft toward the Runway's left side causing the aircraft to ground loop.
summary: During the seventh landing of the day, a gust of wind pushed the aircraft to the left side of the runway. The pilot was unable to regain control, resulting in a ground loop.

synopsis: An ATP rated pilot purchased a small UAV and inadvertently flew it within five miles of an airport but never at an altitude above 76 feet and, thus, did not consider the operation to have been a hazard to manned aircraft.
summary: A pilot flew a DJI Inspire 1 UAV near FTY airport, reaching a maximum altitude of 76 feet for less than one minute. The reporter stated the flight did not interfere with air traffic or enter Class B airspace, but acknowledged the need for future airport reconnaissance.

synopsis: A GFK Controller reports of a runway incursion during a moderately busy session involving a student pilot.
summary: A student solo pilot (Aircraft C) deviated from taxi instructions and entered active Runway 35L while Aircraft Z was taking off, resulting in a 300-foot vertical separation. The incident was caused by the student's failure to hold short and a lack of active scanning by Ground Control, though no collision occurred.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A ZJX Controller reports of an airborne conflict and an aircraft altitude deviation, in which he questions another ZJX Controller about the altitude the aircraft is descending to. The other Controller states he doesn't know. The reporter is also reporting the complacency and laziness of another group of ZJX controllers.
summary: An R78 controller reported that an R33 controller refused to coordinate spacing for Aircraft X, Y, and Z on LEESE and PIGLT arrivals, ignoring SOPs and failing to provide altitude information. This lack of coordination caused a conflict alert and forced the R78 controller to wait over 10 nautical miles to establish communication with Aircraft X.

synopsis: An IAH Controller departs an aircraft and then less than 2 minutes later departs another aircraft. The Controller didn't have the required separation between the two aircraft due to the lack of knowledge of the re-classification of wake turbulence rules.
summary: An air traffic controller reported insufficient radar separation and potential time interval violations between two departures from runway 15L under new RECAT rules. The controller attributed the error to inadequate training, specifically a lack of simulator time and rushed instruction on the updated procedures.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An MCO Controller reports of a loss of separation between two aircraft on final. The Controller tried to break out the second aircraft but it was not on frequency until the loss had happened. The second aircraft landed.
summary: Final controller and Aircraft Y experienced deteriorating wake turbulence separation on final for runway 36L due to failed radio contact. After Aircraft X landed, the controller issued a cautionary clearance to Aircraft Y, which landed safely, prompting a recommendation to ensure communication or cancel approaches before separation is lost.

synopsis: ZJX Controller reports vaguely of a loss of separation, but his major complaint is about the lack of work and planning that he thinks the TMU (Traffic Management Unit) does.
summary: A radar controller in Sector 34 became overwhelmed by unsafe traffic volumes caused by ATCSCC initiatives and unnecessary sector de-combining. This stress led the controller to take unnecessary risks while meeting a ZTL LOA crossing restriction, resulting in a loss event.

synopsis: ZMA Controller reports of airborne conflict between commercial traffic and unknown traffic at the time. Pilot of unknown aircraft reports that he was in the confines of a MOA when he saw a commercial aircraft off his right side in a 10 degree bank.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller managed two unidentified military jets rapidly maneuvering between 8,000 and 10,000 feet in the Tampa area, issuing traffic advisories and altitude changes to Aircraft X. The jets later climbed to 15,200 feet near Aircraft X, causing a close pass, which the controller attributed to the military formation operating without direct ATC contact.

synopsis: A B737-700 was cleared for a visual approach with LNAV engaged to the FAF but after overshooting, zero was set in the MCP Altitude Alert. ATC called low altitude while the EGPWS alerted Caution Too Low Obstacle.
summary: The pilot flying set the MCP altitude to zero during a visual approach, causing an uncommanded descent and GPWS obstacle warnings after an overshoot. ATC cleared the crew to land on Runway 31L, where they leveled off, re-intercepted the glideslope, and completed a normal landing.

synopsis: An air carrier Captain reported his HOU INDIE ONE RNAV SID printed chart contained a waypoint named WWELL which was not in the aircraft's FMS database. That chart edition may be in error.
summary: The flight crew departed HOU on the INDIE ONE departure and found the 'WWELL' fix missing from their updated database despite appearing on the chart. ATC confirmed the database was correct and the chart contained an error, noting the fix was not depicted on government charts.

synopsis: A fatigued B777 crew failed to execute a missed approach when they discovered flaps 25 were not set at 600 feet AGL. Flaps 25 were set for landing.
summary: Two fatigued pilots on an all-night ILS approach in snow failed to set final flaps until below 500 feet due to distraction and exhaustion. Although the crew recognized the unstabilized approach, they elected to land with Flaps 25 rather than execute a go-around.

synopsis: A B737 crew reported calling in fatigued before a third coast to coast all-night flight on the same trip with inadequate hotel sleep due to interruptions.
summary: Pilots reported fatigue after flying three consecutive all-night coast-to-coast segments with inadequate rest due to hotel noise and irregular weather operations. The crew notified Dispatch they were too fatigued to continue the final scheduled leg, citing unsafe pairing construction that violates their recommended rest requirements.

synopsis: A B737 on a transcontinental flight diverted for fuel due to unplanned fuel usage and extended their duty day two hours to comply with FAR 117 limitations.
summary: The flight crew of a transcontinental flight diverted for an unplanned fuel stop due to high burn rates and flow control. They completed the mission using a FAR 117 two-hour extension, though the reporter later discovered the total duty time exceeded legal limits.

synopsis: An A321 air crew lost V-speeds, FDs, and autothrust on takeoff. They were able to reengage FDs, autothrust, and autopilot. The delay in reestablishing automation caused them to exceed speed limitations and to deviate from the RNAV Departure.
summary: During takeoff on runway 07L at Airport ZZZ, the crew lost V speeds, flight directors, and autothrust without ECAM messages. The delay in reengaging automation caused a speed exceedance of approximately 20 kts above 250 kts and a late turn onto the RNAV departure.

synopsis: A CRJ-200 pilot reports that an overabundance of deicing fluid applied to his model aircraft results in the fluid being ingested by the APU and passed into the aircraft interior as 'smoke' and fumes like vapor on takeoff. He suggests alternate methods of deicing as well as alternate methods of configuring the aircraft for takeoff to alleviate the problem.
summary: Pilots reported that excessive Type IV deicing fluid applied by Company X to a CRJ200 fuselage at Airport ZZZ was ingested by the APU during rotation, causing fumes and smoke-like vapor in the cabin. The crew continued the flight after the event resolved, attributing the hazard to systemic deicing procedures that force an unsafe situation with no reasonable alternative.

synopsis: CRJ-200 Captain reported encountering wake turbulence on takeoff from ATL in trail of a B757.
summary: The crew delayed takeoff behind a 757 on 26L in gusty windshear conditions. Shortly after rotation, a windshear warning triggered an escape procedure, causing slight airspeed loss and minimal roll, but the flight continued safely without exceeding limitations.

synopsis: Widebody Transport flight crew reports being fueled at MPTO without the required fuel contamination check. The truck is called back and the test is performed but it is not clear if fuel had been added to the truck in the meantime. Enroute it is discovered that an MEL for the Auto Speed Brake System is not correct and should be for the Auto Brake System. Dispatch is notified.
summary: The flight crew encountered a missing required fuel test and a mismatched MEL number for the auto brake system during pre-flight at MPTO. The fuel test was eventually performed on the truck, and the crew corrected the MEL data to ensure proper landing distance penalties were applied.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air carrier Captain experiences a terrain warning during a night visual approach to Runway 11L at TUS. The First Officer was flying and descending at 800 FPM just northwest of LIPTE and descending through 5,800 feet when the warning was annunciated.
summary: The Captain and First Officer received a GPWS warning at 5,800 feet during a visual approach to runway 11L at TUS. The alert was caused by a high descent rate of 800 fpm, prompting the First Officer to disconnect the autopilot and level the aircraft.

synopsis: B777 flight crew is informed by ATC of a volcanic ash plume ahead that will require deviation to miss and the crew accepts a revised route. This particular volcanic ash plume had not been part of the Dispatch Release and the crew only became aware when informed by Magadan Control.
summary: The First Officer and relief pilot rerouted the aircraft north of a volcanic ash plume at FL350 after Magadan ATC issued a PIREP, as the Captain was resting. The crew avoided the hazard without engine issues, though the reporter criticized Dispatch for failing to proactively monitor the flight path or share satellite imagery of the ash.

synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported descending below charted altitude and receiving a GPWS terrain warning on approach to SKBO, following a late runway change. Crew had some difficulty with FMS programming that was cited as a contributing factor.
summary: The crew diverted from a planned ILS 13L approach to an RNAV 13R approach due to thunderstorms, but FMC waypoint resequencing inadvertently removed the 12,000-foot altitude constraint at NEPOP. This caused an unintended descent triggering terrain warnings, though the crew visually identified terrain and completed a normal landing.

synopsis: B737 First Officer reports a rushed takeoff caused by a short taxi with a delayed engine start. During the event the Captain had sent for new takeoff data which showed a flap setting change from 1 to 5. As the First Officer begins the takeoff roll, the Captain moves the flap lever from 1 to 5.
summary: The First Officer and Captain were involved in a runway 9 departure where the Captain changed the flap setting from 1 to 5 during the takeoff roll. The Captain attributed the change to a new performance uplink received while the First Officer was starting the second engine, resulting in a higher gross weight calculation.

synopsis: B737 Captain reports a missed approach after attempting and ILS with the wrong altimeter setting. This results in the missed approach being initiated 400 feet above DH. The error is detected and corrected with the second approach being successful
summary: During an ILS arrival, a pilot transposed the altimeter setting (29.57 instead of 29.87), causing the aircraft to be 400 feet above decision height and 400 feet above the published missed approach altitude. After correcting the setting, the crew executed a second approach and landed without incident.

synopsis: After configuring the aircraft and checking in with the de-ice supervisor, a CRJ200 Captain notes that no steam is rising from the Type I fluid as it is being applied. The process is stopped and another truck is summoned with heated fluid. It is also noted that a tactile check is not accomplished when the Supervisor reports the process complete.
summary: The Captain and First Officer reported that de-icing crews applied cold fluid without steam during an "engines on, APU off" procedure, likely due to ill-prepared crews or faulty equipment. The crew halted the operation, corrected the issue with a second truck, and warned another aircraft of the same problem.

synopsis: B747 flight crew experiences a fuel imbalance several minutes after turning on the stab fuel pumps in cruise. Whether a leak or a gauge anomaly is involved cannot be determined and the crew elects to return to the departure airport.
summary: The flight crew diverted during cruise after a suspected fuel leak caused a 3000 lb imbalance and required jettisoning fuel. Mechanics confirmed accurate gauges post-landing, revealing an unexplained loss of 7000–8000 lbs, resulting in a smooth but 2000–3000 lb overweight landing.

synopsis: B737 flight crew experiences a track deviation on the FOOXX4 arrival to TPA, when a runway change is entered in the FMC approaching DADPE. A route discontinuity appears and the aircraft does not make the turn to BAYZZ until manually selected by the crew.
summary: During descent on the FOOXX4 arrival, the crew changed the FMS runway from 01L to 01R near DADPE, creating a discontinuity that caused the autopilot to revert to CWS Roll and deviate 2 nm east. The pilots manually rejoined the course to BAYZZ, confirmed routing with Tampa Approach, and landed uneventfully on 01R.

synopsis: After the leading edge flaps had been MELd, a B737 Flight Crew rejected a takeoff below 100 knots due to a Takeoff Configuration Warning.
summary: The pilot rejected a takeoff below 100 knots after a Takeoff Configuration Warning Horn sounded due to an MEL on the leading edge flaps. The aircraft returned to the gate without requiring emergency equipment.

synopsis: A319 Captain experiences FMGC anomalies during descent on the SKNRD3 arrival to IAH. Although the FMGC shows the correct altitude window at each waypoint, the PFD shows only the upper limit and the autopilot choses to level off there at each fix.
summary: Pilots descending via SKNRD3 into IAH reported the FMGC displayed correct altitude windows, but the autoflight treated them as hard constraints, causing unwanted level-offs. This discrepancy increased workload, forced manual flight, and required switching to OPEN DES to manage restrictions.

synopsis: A320 flight crew reported triggering a terrain warning from the GPWS when they descended below MVA on a night visual approach to RWY 22L at EWR.
summary: The flight crew descended below the 2,000-foot minimum vectoring altitude during a night visual approach to Newark Runway 22L, triggering a GPWS terrain warning. The crew immediately climbed to 2,000 feet after ATC advised of the terrain ridge, and the aircraft landed normally.

synopsis: Pilot is issued clearance and advised to hold for release. Crew gets aircraft airborne and realize they didn't call for release. Center advises they listened to tapes and the controller didn't catch that they didn't say hold for release.
summary: The flight crew experienced a GEN 1 failure during engine start and later received a TA ONLY alert after departing without a readback of the "hold for release" clearance. Denver Center confirmed their controller failed to correct the missing readback, resulting in a potential operational error report.

synopsis: An EMB-190 Captain experiences two EICAS status messages 'RT BRAKE FAULT' and 'LT BRAKE FAULT' that disappear after three seconds during initial climb out. The faults appear and disappear again later in the flight. Upon landing at the destination airport the brakes appeared to function normally.
summary: The flight crew experienced intermittent brake fault EICAS messages during initial climb and later in flight, prompting a QRH procedure and coordination with Fire/Rescue for a runway stop. After a normal landing with no visible leaks, the aircraft was towed to the gate, the flight was canceled, and the fault did not recur during the subsequent reposition flight.

synopsis: DHC8-400 flight crew experiences vibration during landing roll. Upon arrival at the gate it is discovered that one of the left main tires has shed half of its tread. A passenger volunteers that he saw something fly off the tire during takeoff.
summary: The flight crew reported significant vibration during landing caused by a shredded left main inboard retread tire, which a passenger noted wobbling during takeoff. The tire failure damaged the rear wheel well door and gear fairing, with the crew attributing the incident to a trend with retreaded tires.

synopsis: Pilot reports of discussion with his First Officer about getting more spacing between them and the previous departure before they take the runway. When they take the runaway they ask for an additional 30 seconds for separation. The controller advises the distance they already have and they depart.
summary: The pilot reported a potential wake turbulence hazard while taxiing for departure behind a B767 on runway 25R, admitting they delayed requesting spacing verification due to distraction. Although the controller confirmed 8 miles separation, the pilot acknowledged that late communication added stress to the tower during runway closure adjustments.

synopsis: An MD82 Captain describes the circumstances surrounding a weather diversion to MMMX and the problems this causes with the Mexican aviation authorities.
summary: The flight crew diverted from MMMY to MMMX after Dispatch advised that their alternate, MMQT, was unsuitable. Although Mexican authorities initially questioned the diversion, the issue was resolved after the crew provided identification and an explanation.

synopsis: An ERJ-175 Flight Attendant reported they landed before the cabin was safe and ready because the flight crew rushed due to weather concerns.
summary: A flight attendant reported that the flight deck initiated landing without securing the cabin or notifying crew, causing passengers to be unbelted and standing. The crew requested a go-around, but the aircraft landed safely after the flight attendants quickly secured the galley and seated themselves.

synopsis: Flight Attendant reported becoming ill from noxious fumes (that smelled of rotten eggs or dirty socks) in the cabin.
summary: A flight attendant suffered severe respiratory distress and disorientation during the preflight demonstration due to noxious fumes from the aircraft's bleed air system. Despite an emergency gate return and maintenance running engines without replacing wet seals, the crew member was pressured to continue the flight while ill.

aircraft: Bombardier Learjet Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Three Line Aircraft Maintenance Technicians (AMT) report observing Regional Jets being towed on active taxiways without navigation or anti-collision lights illuminated and no personnel in cockpit of aircraft. Technicians note that movement of aircraft at airport per City DOA Rules, require proper lighting and activation of aircraft systems while under tow.
summary: An aircraft was observed being towed on an active taxiway with no navigation or anti-collision lights and no person in the cockpit. The reporter recommends following City DOA rules by placing mechanics in the cockpit and powering the aircraft to ensure proper lighting, braking, and transponder activation.

synopsis: C182 instructor with another instructor aboard, experiences a NMAC with a SR20 while practicing instrument procedures in VMC over LFD. The NMAC was detected by the SR20 pilot and reported to the C182 instructor.
summary: Two VFR instructors flying near Litchfield VOR climbed from 3,000 to 3,500 feet after hearing a training aircraft on a company frequency, avoiding a 300-foot separation. The onboard Skywatch failed to warn them, leading the crew to conclude that monitoring local approach frequencies is essential for safety in this area.

synopsis: A Pilot reports Cessna is being 'tight lipped' about incidences involving failures of the Anti-Skid Systems on Cessna-680 Citation Sovereign aircraft. During a recent landing using slight application of the brakes, he noticed a Master Caution illuminated with the 'AMBER ANTISKID FAIL CAS' message and a loud squeal/skid noise, the left main landing gear inboard tire was found flat. Bad valves and bad Anti-Skid Controllers were noted as recurring contributors.
summary: The pilot reported an antiskid failure and flat left inboard main tire on a Citation Sovereign during landing at ZZZ1, despite good braking action. The reporter attributes the recurring issue to defective valves and controllers, criticizing the manufacturer's lack of transparency regarding fleet-wide problems.

synopsis: PA-31 pilot experiences brake failure during landing and requires the assistance of his passenger to stop the aircraft before the end of the runway. Water in the brake fluid and very cold temperatures are suspected as the cause.
summary: A single-pilot Part 91 flight experienced reduced braking effectiveness and a left veer during landing due to frozen water in the brake fluid. The pilot and passenger applied maximum braking to stop the aircraft less than 20 feet from the runway end.

synopsis: C172 student pilot reported losing directional control during landing when he failed to properly correct for a crosswind.
summary: The pilot executed a go-around due to wind changes, then veered off the runway on the second landing attempt while failing to correct for crosswind. Excessive braking caused the left wing to lift, and continued braking on the right wheel exacerbated the situation, turning the aircraft sharply right.

synopsis: Light aircraft pilot reported an NMAC on approach to ABE.
summary: A Cherokee pilot reported that while inbound for Runway 31 at ABE behind a CRJ, an Arrow aircraft ignored instructions to follow and flew directly over them for a minute. The pilot attributed the close proximity to delayed ATC intervention, noting the Arrow was faster and descended right over the Cherokee before being ordered to turn away.

synopsis: PA-31 pilot reported making a forced landing when he began having engine trouble related to fuel starvation.
summary: The pilot experienced dual engine power loss shortly after takeoff due to illuminated boost pump lights, likely caused by fuel starvation from using only inner tanks. Despite ATC instructions, the pilot executed a forced landing on soft grass at a nearby airport, resulting in collapsed gear but no injuries.

synopsis: Panther light sport pilot reported light damage after a forced landing caused by fuel starvation, even though there apparently was fuel in the tank.
summary: The pilot experienced a loud thumping sound and low fuel pressure warning at 50 ft AGL during initial climb, likely due to fuel starvation. The pilot executed an emergency landing on the runway overrun, resulting in light damage to the cowling and landing gear with no injuries.

synopsis: A M20J landing gear collapsed after landing. The aircraft had been in a maintenance status for a gear failing to retract fault discovered on the annual.
summary: The pilot reported that during a landing following a known right main gear retraction issue, the gear handle was lowered and the green indicator confirmed down, yet the gear failed to lock. This caused the aircraft to scrape the runway and the propeller to stop, resulting in an emergency response arrival.

synopsis: Controller reports of observing a poor performance by the Local Controller resulting in a NMAC.
summary: A Local Controller issued a confusing runway change request to Aircraft Y on final for Runway 32L, causing it to deviate and fly close to Aircraft X on Runway 32R. The controller's poor judgment and lack of corrective instructions forced both pilots to execute extreme low-altitude maneuvers to maintain separation.

synopsis: An SLC Controller reports of an operation that resulted in a go-around due to traffic on the runway and an arrival being higher than normal.
summary: The controller canceled Aircraft A's takeoff clearance after Aircraft B initiated a missed approach due to being too high, preventing a potential conflict. The reporter attributed the tight situation to TRACON pressure causing unstabilized approaches and their own sequencing decisions during a runway use plan transition.

synopsis: A B737-700 Captain reported landing with a 22 knot tailwind component in rapidly changing weather conditions.
summary: The pilot reported landing an aircraft at ONT with a 22-knot tailwind, exceeding the limitation by over twice, due to a sudden wind shift from 300 to 020 degrees at 30 knots. Despite Tower reporting a wind decrease at 200 feet, the crew felt a strong tailwind during the flare and confirmed the excessive tailwind component post-landing.

synopsis: B737-700 flight crew dispatched with fuel system MEL reported related anomalies in flight that led to a precautionary divert to a nearby airport.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced a crossfeed valve failure during cruise after the circuit breaker tripped, preventing fuel transfer from the center tank. This caused an increasing fuel imbalance, forcing a diversion and an overweight landing without declaring an emergency.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: CLT TRACON alerted a flight crew that red airport lights to the left of Runway 5 appeared as false PAPI lights which at the time was inoperative.
summary: Pilots flying a night visual approach to CLT Runway 5 encountered construction lights that appeared as four red PAPI lights, creating a dangerous optical illusion. Although the crew relied on the ILS and ignored the lights per controller advice, they recommended shielding the lights to prevent future confusion.

synopsis: B737 First Officer reported ineffective brakes in the gate area when they encountered black ice on the ramp. The aircraft was stopped with reverse thrust.
summary: The crew encountered a large patch of black ice while approaching the J-line, rendering brakes ineffective and requiring thrust reversers to stop the aircraft. The reporter attributed the incident to a lack of ramp inspection and failure by airport personnel or operations to alert the crew of the hazard.

synopsis: B737 FO on an ILS approach to RWY 35R at CYYC reported ignoring a GPWS terrain alert because the runway was in sight and an Ops bulletin warned of possible false GPWS warnings on that approach.
summary: The crew flying a stabilized approach to runway 35R at CYYC received a 'TOO LOW TERRAIN' EGPWS alert at 75 feet AGL. They continued to a safe landing after verifying their position, localizer alignment, and lack of terrain hazards despite the warning.

synopsis: A B-747 Air Crew experienced an EICAS message warning of a fuel imbalance between tanks 1 and 4. They consulted with maintenance, dumped fuel, and diverted.
summary: The crew experienced a #4 fuel spar valve fault and subsequent fuel imbalance during cruise, causing a 7,000-pound discrepancy. They diverted for maintenance after dumping fuel, though the #4 tank quantity was later confirmed correct by ground checks.

synopsis: B737 Captain reading a company bulletin concerning false EGPWS warnings under certain circumstances, then experiencing an EGPWS terrain warning at 50 feet on final to Runway 35R at CYYC. In VMC with the First Officer flying, the Captain allows the approach to continue to landing without silencing the warning.
summary: The First Officer hand-flew the aircraft during a short final approach to RWY 35R at CYYC in VMC when an unreliable EGPWS issued a "Too Low Terrain" warning at 50-75 ft AGL. The Captain chose not to inhibit the warning to avoid potential abnormal situations, allowing the First Officer to complete a safe landing.

synopsis: A B747 crew diverted after horizontal stabilizer fuel transfer initiation resulted in a rapid fuel tank 4 quantity decrease. Tank to engine fuel feed was near normal.
summary: The crew diverted during cruise after observing rapid fuel quantity loss in tank #4 during stabilizer transfer, suspecting a leak or gauge error. They landed slightly overweight at a divert airport where maintenance confirmed actual fuel matched gauge indications, though the cause of the initial discrepancy remained unexplained.

synopsis: B757 flight crew describes a FMS Bridge Visual Approach, which in their perspective becomes unstable and is allowed to get too low. The Tower issues a low altitude alert on final and the flying Captain regains the glideslope and completes configuration for landing. CRM issues were described by the First Officer.
summary: The crew descended below the glideslope on a visual approach to SFO after the autopilot mode inadvertently switched to FLCH, triggering a tower low altitude alert. The captain's hostile demeanor hindered crew communication, though the aircraft was safely reconfigured and landed uneventfully.

synopsis: An Airbus Captain executed a go-around on short final to PHL because the preceding aircraft was not clear of the runway, and failed to acknowledge ATC's request for an expedited runway exit.
summary: The pilot executed a go-around on a visual approach to RW 27R at KPHL due to a preceding company aircraft failing to clear the runway and not responding to tower instructions. The pilot attributed the event to insufficient spacing and the preceding crew's lack of radio communication, though a safe landing was achieved shortly after.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: EYW Departure turned an aircraft toward R-2916 at 9,000 FT so the crew took evasive action as the EGPWS alerted Obstacle, Obstacle, Pull UP.
summary: After departing Key West, the crew received a direct routing to CARNU that led toward a weather balloon in restricted airspace, triggering an EGPWS "Obstacle, Obstacle, Pull Up" warning. The pilots executed an immediate climb and turn to avoid the balloon before contacting Miami Center, which issued further right turns to resolve the conflict.

synopsis: An air carrier Captain called in fatigued on the his sixth day of duty after scheduling added an additional round trip. As a result, the pilot was concerned about disciplinary action.
summary: A pilot working an extended schedule was forced to call in fatigued at an outstation due to fear of punitive action under the airline's current policy. The reporter states that the threat of accumulating occurrences and losing their job influenced their safety decision-making, highlighting a need for a non-punitive fatigue reporting system.

synopsis: An A319 departed after a confused fueler clarified manual fueling procedures. In flight the ECAM alerted FUEL R WING TK LO LVL and the crew had difficulty maintaining fuel balance. After landing maintenance found all fuel valve switches in the unlocked position.
summary: A fueler left refuel panel switches unlocked, causing right wing fuel to transfer to the center tank and creating a 10,000 lb imbalance shortly after takeoff. The crew managed the trim issue by cross-feeding and burning fuel, landing safely after maintenance confirmed the switch positions caused the event.

synopsis: While flying the IAH TEJAS3 RNAV, an EMB-175 FMS inserted an arrival duplicate after GLAMM when the runway was assigned. The original points had altitude constraints but the duplicate did not so the aircraft crossed GLAMM high.
