synopsis: First Officer reported that during pushback ground personnel used nonstandard commands and phraseology. The reporter felt this issue was due primarily to the use of outsourced ground staff.
summary: The flight crew experienced a hazardous pushback at an outsourced station where one instructor supervised too many trainees. The tug driver issued non-SOP engine start commands and gave an all-clear signal while still connected, creating a near-incident due to lost supervision and poor oversight.

synopsis: A B757 flight crew, distracted by a report of a coyote on the runway, failed to set flaps to 30 until receiving a 'Too Low Flaps' warning. The crew set flaps to 30 and proceeded with an uneventful landing.
summary: During a VFR approach to ORD Runway 27R, the flight crew was distracted by a coyote report and tower cautions, delaying flap extension to 30 until a GPWS "Too Low Flaps" warning. They landed safely but acknowledged they should have executed a go-around per SOP.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: An air carrier crew landed on LRD Runway 17R and were cleared to exit at Taxiway D, cross Runways 14 and 17L to the ramp. When the Taxiway D centerline turned right the crew followed it because at night it appeared D ended at 17L and turned. They actually turned on Runway 14.
summary: The Captain and First Officer inadvertently entered Runway 14 while taxiing at night at LRD after landing on Runway 17R. The error resulted from a confusing intersection, obscured taxiway markings, and the crew's failure to verify their position before proceeding.

synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew received pitch trim warnings and experienced related elevator control anomalies. Crew diverted to a nearby airport without incident.
summary: During climb at 16,000 feet, the crew experienced autopilot and pitch trim failures, prompting a diversion to a nearby airport. Despite increasing nose-down tendencies during descent, the captain manually flew a smooth landing after the crew followed QRH procedures and coordinated with ATC.

synopsis: Upon post flight inspection a gash was noticed on the underside of the aircraft near the single point refueling station. The reporter attributed the damage to FOD encountered during the takeoff or landing phase.
summary: The crew discovered a 16-inch gash near the single point refueling door during post-flight inspection at ZZZ. They attributed the damage to FOD kicked up by the nose gear during takeoff or landing, noting it was not visible during preflight checks.

synopsis: A Captain was informed by Maintenance Control that the B767-300 aircraft he had just landed in a foreign country required an immediate Service Check because the aircraft was not compliant prior to his departure. The First Officer showed Captain the FOM Chapter that stated the Airworthiness Release block sign-off was a Maintenance function responsibility for servicing, checks, and inspection intervals.
summary: The Captain of a B767-300 was grounded in ZZZZ for an expired Service Check after the aircraft sat in ZZZ1. A local mechanic performed the inspection, causing a delay, while the Captain noted conflicting maintenance responsibilities between the crew and headquarters.

synopsis: B757-200 First Officer reported multiple false alerts, including false engine fire warnings, from a probable EICAS malfunction.
summary: The crew received false engine fire and flap EICAS messages shortly after takeoff from Airport ZZZZ at 8,000 feet. They returned to the field where fire trucks found no fire, suggesting an electrical or EICAS computer malfunction.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A flight crew on a gear down ferry flight at FL200 encounters icing conditions and begins to lose airspeed with max power set. Flight level 200 is the maximum allowable altitude with the gear extended and the MEA for the airway. A vector off the airway allows a descent to FL180 where the ice melts and airspeed is regained.
summary: Pilots on a maintenance ferry flight with landing gear locked down encountered unforecast icing at FL200, causing airspeed to degrade. ATC vectored them off the airway to FL180, allowing them to exit the ice and recover airspeed for a safe landing.

synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported getting an RA on approach from another air carrier who he felt was operating somewhat recklessly.
summary: The pilot reported receiving a climb Resolution Advisory on approach due to an air carrier aircraft on a parallel runway being too close. The crew climbed to avoid the conflict, attributing the incident to the other flight disregarding safety while racing to the runway.

synopsis: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports he was directed by a Maintenance Supervisor to replace both nose tires on a B747 aircraft instead of replacing the Nose Wheel Steering Control Valve (Metering Valve) per the Fault Isolation Manual (FIM) troubleshooting tree. Pilots had made a repeat write-up of a nose wheel wobbling vibration after rotation when weight was removed from nose wheels.
summary: A B747 experienced nose wheel vibration at rotation, prompting mechanics to replace tires and check brakes per management direction rather than the recommended valve replacement. The reporter believes the issue remains uncorrected and the aircraft is unsafe, despite another mechanic signing off the discrepancy.

synopsis: Bell 206L4 pilot reported an NMAC with a flight of two F18s in the pattern at NFW.
summary: A helicopter pilot transitioning through Class D airspace encountered two F-18 jets crossing their path without prior tower notification. The pilot descended to avoid a collision, noting the lack of TCAS and radar made visual separation critical, while the tower offered an unexplained apology.

synopsis: A GA Pilot's engine was not producing normal power during initial climb even at full power input. All engine indications were normal during takeoff roll but were out of normal range for the remainder of the flight. The Pilot returned to land without incident.
summary: The pilot reported an engine power loss during initial climb through 2,000 feet with abnormal oil indications, prompting an immediate return request. The aircraft landed without incident after the tower controller instructed other traffic to go around to provide priority.

synopsis: Hot air balloon pilot reports encountering stronger than forecast winds and elects to land in a suitable field. A tree is used to scrub off speed and once clear the balloon is vented. The landing is firm and the balloon drags about 30 to 40 feet before deflating. A passenger is slightly injured.
summary: A hot air balloon pilot with three passengers experienced unexpected winds exceeding 10 mph mid-flight, prompting an emergency landing in a field. Although the pilot executed a safe landing, one passenger later confirmed a broken tibia sustained during the 30 to 40-foot drag upon touchdown.

synopsis: Two Controllers and a flight Crew were involved describe a runway incursion by rescue vehicles on a training mission. The lead vehicle had been instructed to cross Runway 4L and hold short of 31C, but read back cross 4R and hold short of 31L and was not corrected by the Ground Controller. The crew is at rotate speed when the vehicles are detected and the takeoff is continued.
summary: An air traffic controller working ground control experienced a runway incursion when rescue vehicles crossed active runway 31C during a departure roll due to a missed incorrect readback and expectation bias. The controller advised the departing aircraft to use caution, and the plane lifted off safely before the vehicles, though the incident highlighted the need for improved vehicle training on radio communications and airport layout.

synopsis: GFK Tower Controllers receive a call that a deer is close to the runway. Airport operations reports the deer in sight and the vehicle is permitted to get on the runway. Airport vehicle wants another airport vehicle to come to its position to remove the deer. Controller wants to use runway for departures and airport vehicle won't clear runway.
summary: Local Control 2 reported that an airport vehicle refused three ATC instructions to exit Runway 35R while pursuing a deer, forcing the controller to cross a second vehicle into the Runway Safety Area. Management later dismissed the incident as a vehicle deviation to avoid conflict with the Airport Authority, despite the potential for a runway closure.

synopsis: A GSP TRACON Controller reports of a deviation to the Opposite Direction Operation because the second aircraft was not within the standards for the operation to occur.
summary: The controller cleared Aircraft Y for a visual approach to Runway 19 while Aircraft X was on short final for an opposite direction ILS Runway 1 approach. Although Aircraft Y was only 5 miles out instead of the required 10 miles, no separation issue occurred, leading the controller to discontinue authorizing opposite direction approaches.

synopsis: A B737 flight crew reported encountering severe turbulence that resulted in a 1,400 foot excursion from their cleared altitude.
summary: The crew encountered severe turbulence over Pensacola at FL350, causing LNAV/VNAV disconnection and a 1,300–1,400-foot altitude deviation. The pilot manually recovered the aircraft, advised ATC, and landed safely with no injuries.

synopsis: An EMB-145 Captain reported a precautionary shutdown of the number one engine when low pressure and quantity became an issue.
summary: During enroute descent, the Captain (PM) and First Officer (PF) managed an E1 engine oil pressure drop caused by a leak at Generator 3, executing a precautionary shutdown just outside the FAF. The crew maintained the FO as Pilot Flying to avoid control errors, resulting in a normal landing and safe taxi to the terminal.

synopsis: CRJ-200 Captain reported encountering 'severe' wake turbulence 6 miles in trail of a B747 on the DIRTY arrival into ATL.
summary: During a dirty arrival descent through 13,000 feet, the crew encountered severe wake turbulence from a heavy B747 ahead and above. The pilot attributed the event to the B747's weight and atmospheric conditions, leveled at 12,500 feet, and landed safely.

synopsis: An EMB-175 Flight Crew had decided to divert because of a line of thunderstorms over their destination airport. The Company Dispatcher talked them into continuing to their scheduled destination. They encountered severe turbulence and then they diverted as they had originally decided.
summary: The crew diverted from OMA to MCI after encountering severe turbulence despite dispatch pressure to proceed based on conflicting radar data. The aircraft was written up for the turbulence, preventing further attempts to land at OMA.

synopsis: A Medium Large Transport Flight Crew on a twelve minute flight entered a SID and then an arrival at their destination which omitted a waypoint which would have aided them in detecting the MEA on their arrival. They briefly descended below the MEA. ATC advised them of their error and they continued on to their destination.
summary: The flight crew descended below the 4500-foot MEA near ZZZZ1 Intersection during an approach due to a missing FMC waypoint and ambiguous ATC clearance. This occurred after route changes and communication delays, though the crew maintained terrain awareness and no collision occurred.

synopsis: EC135 Captain reported becoming aware of a possible hazardous material violation related to aircraft occupants wearing compressed gas bottles as part of their life vest equipment.
summary: A pilot reported that a specialty medical team carried HEEDS devices, which are 3000 psi compressed gas cylinders classified as Class 2.2 hazardous materials, on a Part 135 flight. The pilot determined these unapproved vessels violated company policy and FAA regulations prohibiting the transport of such hazardous materials without specific authorization.

synopsis: B-767 Captain received NOTAMs for destination airport in Spanish. Another crewmember was able to translate.
summary: The pilot reported receiving destination NOTAMs in Spanish on both legs of a flight, requiring a crewmember to translate them. The pilot attributed the issue to excessive information volume, non-English NOTAMs, and dispatchers being too busy to review the data adequately.

synopsis: EMB-175 Captain reported communication difficulties with ATC that were complicated by what he felt was an antagonistic attitude on the part of the Controller.
summary: During approach to Atlanta, pilots and an air traffic controller experienced a speed assignment misunderstanding regarding 200 knots. The controller's unhelpful response prevented immediate resolution, and the crew never received results from the promised tape review to determine the source of the error.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Regional Jet First Officer reported receiving a GPWS terrain warning, while performing a 360 to lose altitude, on a night visual approach to EUG.
summary: The pilot flying incorrectly configured the FMS descent, causing the aircraft to be too high on a visual approach to EUG at night. A descending 360-degree turn initiated by the Captain triggered a GPWS caution, requiring a go-around maneuver before an uneventful landing.

synopsis: Q400 Flight Attendant reported a passenger boarded with a large service dog that became a hazard to anyone walking down the aisle.
summary: A flight attendant reported that a large service dog obstructed the aisle during boarding and flight, causing two crew members to trip. The owner failed to keep the dog under the seat despite reminders, prompting the crew to request stricter size guidelines for cabin animals due to emergency safety concerns.

aircraft: Bell Helicopter Textron Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports about the efforts made to locate a 1/4' inch drive, 7/16' inch shallow socket that was unaccounted for after a Forward (FWD) Fuel Cell replacement on a Bell BHT-407 helicopter. Inspections of critical areas that would effect safety of flight were accomplished, socket not found. Fuel tanks were not drained. Training Flight crew accepted aircraft for service.
summary: Mechanics lost a 7/16' shallow socket during fuel cell replacement and pump torque work. After a facility search and critical area inspection, the aircraft was released for service, with the reporter citing a lack of assertiveness as the cause.

synopsis: Baron 55 pilot reported an airborne conflict after taking off from DVT on Runway 25R and spotting an unannounced aircraft taking off from 7R.
summary: The pilot departed Runway 25R while a training aircraft simultaneously took off from opposite parallel Runway 7R, creating a reduced safety margin. The incident was attributed to ineffective CTAF monitoring, sun glare, and the lack of a designated calm wind runway in the Airport Facility Directory.

synopsis: M20F pilot reported a rough running engine for a few moments after takeoff. Reporter stated the aircraft was refueled in a heavy rain.
summary: The pilot reported that heavy rain during fueling at an FBO likely introduced water into the tanks, causing engine roughness shortly after takeoff. The pilot maintained altitude below the cloud deck while troubleshooting, allowing the engine to clear and the flight to continue safely.

synopsis: Lear 45 Captain reported a track deviation related to a misunderstanding of the spelling of an enroute fix.
summary: The pilot misspelled the SARAA intersection as SARRA in the FMS after PTW, causing the aircraft to fly 30 degrees off course for 10 miles until ATC detected the deviation. The reporter attributes the error to the similar spelling of the two points and suggests renaming one or updating the SID to prevent recurrence.

synopsis: GGG TRACON Controller reports of a loss of separation due to a flight of aircraft that deviated due to weather. The flight had previously cancelled IFR, but could not maintain VFR due to the weather.
summary: A trainee controller managing a military flight of four and a climbing aircraft failed to re-clear the military flight IFR after they cancelled, issuing conflicting headings that caused a loss of 4NM separation. The reporter attributed the incident to the trainee's error and the OJT instructor's failure to intervene sooner.

synopsis: LAS Tower Controller reports on the use of visual separation during a training session, with the second aircraft performing better than the trainee expected. TRACON Controller turned aircraft further to avoid more separation issues.
summary: A turboprop (Aircraft Y) cleared for visual separation behind a jet (Aircraft X) on a STAAV6 departure turned onto a heading that conflicted with Aircraft X's path. The departure controller issued a corrective turn to avert a collision, while the OJTI noted the training scenario highlighted the need for greater separation margins for turboprops.

synopsis: A80 Controller and pilots of aircraft report of a speed reduction on final that could have led to a loss of separation. Final monitor caught the aircraft slowing and issued speed again for it to maintain. Pilots slowed aircraft before final approach fix as per their flight manual.
summary: Aircraft X slowed below the assigned 180 knots prior to the FAF on the ATL 26R ILS approach to configure for landing. The controller intercepted the speed reduction, restored separation, and threatened the crew with a deviation report for violating the clearance.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: N90 TRACON Controller and both pilots report of a RA and a loss of separation due to the aircraft climbing above its assigned altitude. Pilots report of a problem with the aircraft that took their attention away from the altitude deviation.
summary: An air traffic controller and a flight crew were involved in a near-midair conflict during departure from HPN and arrival at LGA. The incident was caused by a departing aircraft deviating from its SID and subsequent flight deck system failures that led to erroneous guidance, requiring evasive maneuvers to maintain separation.

synopsis: ZDC Center Controller reports of a close call because an aircraft was on a different route than what ATC had. This has been a problem in the past but was reported to be fixed. Problem of incorrect routing is surfacing again.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that a pilot deviated from the filed FKN ISO route to fly J193 to CVI, causing a potential conflict with FL340 traffic. The controller attributed the recurring issue to a discrepancy between the flight plan and tower clearances rather than pilot error.

synopsis: ORD Tower Controller reports of having a loss of separation due to an extended time period passing before the aircraft was airborne. Controller approved a departure that would enter his airspace, but the aircraft was not ready. Time period passed and Controller let one of his departures go around the same time the other approved departure went airborne. Separation was lost due to both aircraft being on the same heading and close proximity.
summary: The 28R controller and the west departure controller failed to coordinate a one-time MYKIE departure for Aircraft X due to workload and delays, resulting in Aircraft X and Aircraft Y departing on the same heading with less than standard separation two miles from the airport.

synopsis: TRACON Controller reports of a hang glider operation that was affecting his traffic. Controller reported the operations to Center who then issued a pointer NOTAM to advise aircraft of the hang gliders in the area.
summary: A pilot reported that over 100 hang gliders operating near ZZZ airport overlapped active approach courses and a federal airway without ATC communication or radar visibility. The reporter attributed the lack of pilot awareness to a poorly issued NOTAM and questioned the authorization of gliders in Class D and E airspace.

synopsis: Controller reports of a VFR pilot who didn't initially turn as instructed away from another aircraft that was IFR. Pilot took turn and then questioned Controller as to why they had to turn. Controller advised it was for traffic. Pilot questioned if something had changed to the LOA. Controller advised no, they were turned for traffic. Company owner called TRACON and wanted the Controller 'tuned up.'
summary: A controller in Sector X issued a turn to Aircraft X, a skydiving operation, to avoid conflict with descending Aircraft Y near ZZZ. The skydiving pilot questioned the instruction multiple times, and the aircraft owner later called the facility to complain about the controller's actions.

synopsis: M98 controller reports of receiving a briefing that the relieving Controller said there was only one aircraft on the frequency. Controller observed another aircraft in the airspace, and Controller assumed it had been handed off and communications transferred. The aircraft was on a different tag so this also led the Controller to think it had been handed off. The aircraft was found to be on the reporters frequency and ended up violating the Center's airspace without a handoff. Possible related issue was someone possibly had changed the data tag, and this showed the Controller that it was someone else's aircraft.
summary: The relieving controller and the reporter misinterpreted a briefing, believing Aircraft X had been handed off when it remained on frequency. Consequently, the reporter terminated the track prematurely, forcing a late verbal handoff to Sector 5 after the aircraft entered their airspace.

synopsis: ZAU Controller describes a shift where aircraft area deviating and the sectors that he is working have been combined. Aircraft are not flying as instructed because of weather and one aircraft is not accepted by the facility he would normally hand it off to. Controller reported that this was a staffing issue.
summary: An air traffic controller in the North Area reported unsafe conditions while managing combined low-altitude sectors with insufficient staffing during heavy ORD traffic and severe weather. The lack of a communicated plan and staffing shortages led to coordination failures, resulting in a Code 7700 aircraft being vectored into another sector after MKE Approach rejected the assigned route due to weather.

synopsis: ZME Controller and two pilots report of a loss of separation. Controller descends aircraft to get away from conflicting traffic but the aircraft receives a RA and it tells pilots to climb. Controller couldn't see data tag and assumed descending was the best option. Pilot questioned Controller as to why they said descend and RA said to climb.
summary: An Air Traffic Controller and the Captain of Aircraft X experienced a near-midair conflict at FL310 near ZZZ2 due to sector congestion and data block overlap. The controller issued conflicting descent instructions while the pilot executed a TCAS climb Resolution Advisory, resulting in a separation of 200 feet before lateral separation was achieved.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: ZLC Controller has an aircraft that is encountering icing conditions and requests lower altitude. The Controller issues the lowest altitude he can due to the MIA and the pilot is still getting icing on the aircraft. The Controller aids the aircraft and issues an even lower altitude and vectors it towards lower terrain. The aircraft eventually gets into VMC conditions and no longer is getting iced up. The Controller then gets a briefing that he shouldn't have done what he did and asks for clarification on how to help the pilot when in this type of condition.
summary: An air traffic controller assisted a pilot in Aircraft X who encountered severe icing while deviating for weather. The pilot descended below the Minimum IFR Altitude to escape the icing, highlighting a conflict between safety needs and a strict facility memo prohibiting instructions below that altitude.

synopsis: B737 flight crew experienced a landing gear indication problem. After following all QRH procedures, the crew was confident that the landing gear was down. The crew elected to allow a local F-16 to fly close by and reconfirm the landing gear position. The aircraft landed normally.
summary: The flight crew discovered a missing right main gear down indication during the before landing checklist, prompting a go-around and a USAF F-16 visual inspection. After the F-16 pilot and a flight attendant confirmed the gear was extended and locked, the crew completed checklists and executed a normal landing.

synopsis: B767 Captain reports accepting an aircraft with previous write ups for shaking/vibration under the aft galley floor. The problem reappears as the aircraft is pushed back and Maintenance is called. The problem is traced to an equipment cooling fan, which Maintenance Control wants the crew to take as is and the crew declines.
summary: The captain and cabin crew detected shaking in the aft galley during pushback, caused by a faulty equipment cooling fan. After Maintenance Control incorrectly advised deferring the issue, the captain refused the aircraft, leading to a full repair and a one-day flight delay.

synopsis: B767 Captain reported they received a message during cruise changing their final takeoff weights and CG.
summary: The flight crew departed using final weights provided by dispatch, which were later identified as being in kilograms instead of pounds. One hour into the flight, a printer update and dispatch message revealed the unit error, though the crew had utilized the originally sent figures.

synopsis: Ramp worker reported a 'significant weight shift' during passenger disembarkation in a B737-900ER even though they had already unloaded considerable weight from rear pits.
summary: Ground crew offloaded 20 rear bags from a B737-900ER due to a tail tip risk warning from operations. The reporter attributed the unsafe load plan to Load Planning's failure to account for the aircraft's tail-heavy nature, causing significant weight shifts during deplaning.

synopsis: A320 flight crew reported discovering several anomalies in the weight and balance data after takeoff. Apparently station personnel used numbers from a flight on a different date.
summary: The pilot and flight attendant discovered a manifest error post-departure showing an armed individual and 12 extra passengers due to an incorrect date from gate agents. The crew recalculated weights, finding the aircraft 2,300 lbs heavier than expected, which reduced V speeds by 2-3 knots without exceeding performance limits.

synopsis: EMB-175 First Officer reported the Captain flew the airplane into a stall warning while they were troubleshooting a mechanical issue.
summary: The First Officer reported that the Captain, flying in unauthorized FPA mode, induced a stick shaker activation at 2,000 feet MSL after departure from IAH due to excessive pitch and bank. The First Officer intervened to recover airspeed, attributing the stall to the Captain's improper mode selection and inadequate response.

synopsis: Dispatcher reported the flight crew discovered a fuel leak on their B777 that would have gone unnoticed by the Dispatcher because enroute fuel reports transmitted to Dispatch are calculated rather than actual fuel on board numbers.
summary: Flight crew and dispatch identified a growing fuel discrepancy between the totalizer and calculated fuel on a B777, leading to a diversion and emergency landing. The dispatcher attributed the delayed detection to automated position reports relying solely on calculated fuel rather than totalizer readings.

synopsis: CRJ-200 Captain reported receiving a GPWS terrain warning on a night visual approach to EUG.
summary: During a night approach to EUG, the Captain and First Officer became too high due to poor descent planning, triggering a GPWS caution while executing a 360-degree turn. The Captain ordered a go-around, which the First Officer executed, resulting in a safe landing after the Captain acknowledged his commands lacked sufficient assertiveness.

synopsis: First Officer files another report about the same A320 aircraft with the left wing-tip navigation lights operating opposite the right wing-tip NAV lights. Pilot requests some definitive information on whether this aircraft is wired correctly and every other aircraft is wrong or if it matter which bulb illuminates with the NAV switch in Position-1 or Position-2.
summary: A pilot reported that the aircraft's left wing-tip navigation light operates opposite to standard configuration during routine walk-around inspections. Maintenance in ZZZ1 suspected incorrect behavior relative to cockpit switch positions, prompting the pilot to request definitive clarification on the aircraft's wiring or switch logic.

synopsis: A Captain and First Officer describe the pitch oscillations their B767-300 aircraft experienced in smooth air about two hours after departure. The right elevator indicator on the EICAS status page was oscillating at the same rate that was consistent with what was felt in the back of the aircraft. The oscillations were more noticeable as the aircraft slowed and continued all the way to a diverted landing. Aircraft was ferried to a maintenance base.
summary: The flight crew experienced uncommanded pitch oscillations caused by a failed right elevator and a popped ALT FLAP CONT circuit breaker during cruise. They diverted to ZZZZ, manually flew the approach due to persistent oscillations, and landed safely with the right elevator found drooped vertically.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported receiving an IAS Disagree warning. Crew followed procedures and flew a safe approach and landing.
summary: During cruise at FL360, the crew experienced simultaneous IAS and altimeter disagreements on the Captain's side, followed by EEC, Speed Trim, and VNAV failures. After managing multiple checklists and receiving priority handling, the instruments suddenly normalized, allowing the First Officer to complete a safe landing with ARFF standby.

synopsis: B767 First Officer reported noticing an elevator anomaly on an international flight that led the crew to divert to the nearest suitable airport.
summary: The crew discovered a tripped ALT FLAP CONT circuit breaker and right elevator instability during pre-coast preparations, causing noticeable pitching. They diverted to the nearest airport and executed an uneventful Flap 25 landing, later finding the right elevator fully deflected down.

synopsis: CRJ-200 First Officer reported responding inappropriately to a hot start and then failing to write up the anomaly.
summary: During a bottle start with low pressure, the First Officer inadvertently pressed the starter cutout instead of the fuel shut-off lever when the Captain called for an engine shutdown due to high ITT. The engine parameters normalized without a HOT icon, allowing the flight to continue, though the crew acknowledged potential damage risk and the need for better start pressure guidelines.

synopsis: A Captain reports about the continuing practice by his Company Maintenance Control to have pilots accept an Aircraft Manufacturer's Guidance Letter as approval to operate their EMB-505 (Phenom 300) with moisture in the sealed NAV lights of both wings. Pilot notes that Guidance Letters have to be incorporated into their FAA approved Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM) prior to being used for aircraft release. Aircraft refused.
summary: The pilot discovered moisture in both wing NAV lights and refused Maintenance Control's request to mark the write-ups as "entered in error" because the manufacturer's guidance lacked AFM approval. The pilot cited FAA regulations stating that OEM guidance is invalid without AFM incorporation, deeming the dispatch of water near electrical systems unsafe.

synopsis: B767-300ER FO noted a track deviation and a low airspeed condition on approach to a South American destination. Autothrottles were out of service.
summary: During an RNAV RNP approach with inoperable autothrottles and EEC, the crew experienced near-stall airspeed at 800 feet AGL due to distraction from logbook entries and failure to recognize a mandatory holding fix. The captain corrected the speed, stabilizing the approach before 500 feet AGL.

synopsis: An MD-11 Flight Crew, fatigued from an all night flight and flying into an unfamiliar airport, deviated from assigned altitudes and then flew an unstable approach. They did not go around when procedure dictated that they should have.
summary: The flight crew received vectors instead of a STAR while approaching ZZZZ, resulting in missed altitude restrictions and an autopilot turn error that caused a 400-foot deviation below the glideslope. The crew manually corrected the flight path and landed normally, though they acknowledged the situation pushed limits and a go-around should have been executed.

synopsis: CRJ-200 flight crew reported overshooting an altitude restriction on a descend via clearance into DEN. Fatigue was cited as a factor.
summary: The pilot descended below the FL300 restriction at SUSHE while flying the ANCHR3 arrival due to fatigue, distraction from a disorganized chart binder, and excessive focus on a downstream fix. Denver Center notified the crew of the deviation, but no traffic conflicts occurred.

synopsis: Airline International Captain reported he feels he is getting non-compliant flight planning information from his company's resources, specifically Sabre.
summary: The pilot reported that dispatch failed to provide critical NOTAMs and weather data for CYQD via the Sabre flight plan, rendering the destination unusable due to thunderstorms and approach restrictions. This deficiency violated FAR 121.601 and 121.603, exposing the pilot to regulatory action while preventing safe diversion planning.

synopsis: EMB-145LR First Officer reported responding to what was probably a false TCAS RA.
summary: During a climb on the EWR1 departure, the crew received a TCAS resolution advisory to descend aggressively at 2,500 FPM due to a traffic return at 2,500 feet MSL. No traffic was visually observed or detected by ATC, leading the pilot to conclude the event was an automation error.

synopsis: DA-2000 flight crew reported being struck by lightning in their destination terminal area. They noted some popped circuit breakers, burn marks, and a burnt smell.
summary: During a descent to 11,000 feet while deviating around thunderstorms, the crew was struck by lightning at 13,000 feet, causing sparks, two circuit breakers to pop, and burn marks on the overhead panel. The flight continued uneventfully with immediate vectors for an ILS approach after the crew briefed passengers and noted the wing anti-ice system was active.

synopsis: Dispatcher discovers that a B767 flight he is to dispatch has departed without a current dispatch release. The aircraft had been on an unscheduled overnight due to maintenance and the outbound crew had been handed the prior days release which was not detected. A new release is issued via ACARS.
summary: A relief pilot reported that a crew departed with yesterday's flight plan due to station personnel using outdated paperwork and a communication failure. The flight continued safely after the pilot verified fuel sufficiency and filed the correct flight plan once airborne.

synopsis: A300 flight crew reported the cockpit filled with smoke and fumes shortly after takeoff during a maintenance test flight.
summary: During a Part 91 post-maintenance test flight at Airport ZZZZ, heavy oil-smelling fumes and Level 3 ECAM cargo smoke warnings occurred shortly after takeoff at 1,000 feet. The crew landed safely 14 minutes later; no fire was found, and the cause remains unknown pending maintenance review.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: After being cleared direct to 'PUMKN' crew incorrectly typed 'PMPKN' resulting in aircraft track error.
summary: The pilot inadvertently entered the fix "PMPKN" instead of "PUMKN" in the FMS prior to departure, causing the aircraft to turn toward the wrong location. ATC detected the deviation and vectored the aircraft to the correct fix after the pilot corrected the identifier.

synopsis: Falcon 900EX flight crew reported receiving an RA on approach to APC when ATC gave them a turn clearance, which they felt could have resulted in a collision had it been followed.
summary: While being vectored for the VOR RWY 6 approach at 4,000 feet, the crew received conflicting TCAS Resolution Advisories to descend then climb, avoiding a small Cessna that passed below. The pilot attributed the conflict to insufficient separation between VFR and IFR traffic, noting that the initial turn would have directed the aircraft into the Cessna's path.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported inadvertently taxiing over several temporary chevron 'bricks' at SAW.
summary: Pilots at SAW back-taxied onto temporary mesh chevrons on Runway 01 due to poor visibility of the markings, crushing holding blocks while repositioning. The tower later confirmed the damage, prompting the crew to acknowledge the need for better cross-checking and situational awareness.

synopsis: Following a flight with many children on board, the flight attendants realized that they did not have the required number of spare life vests on board.
summary: Three flight attendants discovered a shortage of spare life vests after boarding 12 lap children on a flight with only 10 vests available. The crew focused on oxygen mask spacing during seating, and the discrepancy was identified by the destination operations agent upon arrival.

synopsis: The flight attendants were legal to operate the late assignment but felt that they were severely fatigued, which could have impacted their effectiveness if an emergency situation arose.
summary: Flight attendants reported operating a flight while exhausted after receiving last-minute assignment with less than 10 hours of rest, resulting in 27+ hours awake. Despite notifying scheduling they felt unsafe, they were kept working, raising concerns about their ability to handle emergencies.

synopsis: EMB-175 Flight Attendant notices a young lady crying during the safety demonstration and inquires as to the cause. She is informed that the lady is a fearful flyer and the A Flight Attendant is informed. The A Flight Attendant, after learning that the young lady is 20 years old, offers an alcoholic beverage in violation of company rules.
summary: A cabin crew member reported that a senior flight attendant offered an alcoholic beverage to a 20-year-old passenger with flight anxiety, despite knowing her age. The passenger's clinical counselor found the offer inappropriate, prompting the reporter to apologize and inform the captain of the incident.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports placing a 2' x 4' board against the outer lip of the Left Main Landing Gear (MLG) door after completing a Center Axle alignment on a B777 aircraft. MLG door was closed later, but the 2X4 fell out of the wheel well after takeoff also told from the perspective of the Captain of the flight. Distractions, workload and limited staffing were contributors.
summary: A mechanic left a wooden 2x4 tool on a B777's main landing gear door during maintenance, causing it to fall out as Foreign Object Debris after takeoff the next day. The aircraft sustained no damage or flight control issues, and the crew continued to the destination after confirming the runway obstruction.

synopsis: Two Maintenance Controllers, an Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) and a Captain describe their involvement with a reported # 2 Engine Fuel Spar Valve Overhead Blue light fault that was miscommunicated and deferred as an Engine Valve Blue fault light on a B737-800 aircraft. A downline Maintenance Station noted that the original discrepancy and the resolution did not match. Spar valve was replaced and Engine Valve MEL cleared.
summary: A Maintenance Controller misidentified a reported Spar Valve light as an Engine Valve light due to communication errors and workplace interruptions. This caused an incorrect Minimum Equipment List application and circuit breaker collar, which were later corrected by maintenance at the destination.

synopsis: PA-28 student pilot experiences an airborne conflict with an Army helicopter over XS09 at 1500 feet. The reporter takes evasive action to avoid a collision and believes the helicopter pilot did not see the PA-28, as it did not alter its course.
summary: A PA-28 pilot reported a near mid-air collision with an Army Apache helicopter at 1,500 feet MSL near XS09. The pilot executed an emergency descent and left turn to avoid the helicopter, which did not alter its course despite the closing proximity.

synopsis: F/A-18 pilot reports misunderstanding a taxi instruction to cross Runways 24R&L at NKX which was not the case. Many similar call signs were in use at the time.
summary: The pilot experienced a runway incursion on unusable RWY 24R while taxiing after landing, mistakenly believing they were cleared to cross both runways. The reporter attributed the error to unfamiliarity with the airfield and confusion caused by multiple similar call signs receiving similar taxi instructions.

aircraft: Citationjet (C525/C526) - CJ I / II / III / IV
synopsis: CE525 Pilot is advised during the GPS A approach to SMO, that if the field is not in sight at CULVE (1,120 feet) a missed approach is required due to the Tower being closed. With a 700 foot ceiling the field is not seen and the flight diverts. The reporter believes that this restriction should be published as part of the approach and not announced at the last minute, especially to a single pilot aircraft.
summary: A single-pilot aircraft en route to SMO executed a missed approach on the GPS A procedure due to unexpected low ceilings and a late ATC restriction requiring visual contact at CULVE. The pilot attributed the event to unpublished tower closure restrictions issued too late to safely comply, resulting in a diversion to VNY.

synopsis: C172 pilot on an instrument training flight at 7,000 feet experiences surging power and RPM. Carb ice is suspected but carb heat has no positive effect. A diversion is planned and executed with the engine continuing to run throughout the descent and landing. A thorough visual inspection of the engine and another run up reveals no anomalies. The aircraft is flown back to base for an inspection by an A&P mechanic and no anomalies are noted. Carb ice is the primary suspect.
summary: A student pilot and CFII experienced sudden engine surging and power loss in a Continental O-300 aircraft during cruise at 7,000 feet, prompting a precautionary VFR landing. Post-flight inspections found no mechanical faults, leading the crew and an A&P to conclude the transient issue was likely induction system icing.

synopsis: General Aviation Pilot experienced a hard landing and blown tire after floating results from excessive speed on approach to a down-sloping runway.
summary: The pilot of a Bonanza F33 executed a hard landing at an unfamiliar airport with a 1.3% slope and out-of-service glide slope, causing a blown left main tire. The pilot attributed the incident to insufficient recent experience, mental fatigue, and the decision to land with excessive energy instead of performing a go-around.

synopsis: A PA-44 crew reported a NMAC with a drone beneath PHX Class B airspace after departing FFZ.
summary: During climb-out 4 miles south of FFZ at 3,300 feet, a student passenger reported a 3-foot red drone passing 50 feet below on the right. The pilot did not see the object but reported the sighting to FFZ Tower with location and description.

synopsis: C182 pilot reports being unable to contact the Tower and assumes the Tower is closed. During taxi, movement in the Tower indicates that it may be open. A second check of the radio reveals that the volume and squelch are not properly adjusted.
summary: The pilot attempted to contact ground control at an unfamiliar airport but received no response due to mis-set radio squelch and volume. After mistakenly assuming the tower was closed, the pilot corrected the radio settings, obtained clearance, and completed an uneventful flight.

synopsis: An Extra Pilot departed after unsuccessfully attempting to contact Tower and assumed the Tower was not in operation. He later discovered his single point headset jack had not been fully seated and that his departure airport Tower was in operation.
summary: The pilot attempted a VFR departure but failed to contact ground or tower due to a defective helmet/headset single-point connection. After taking off on CTAF, the pilot discovered the tower was operational and reported the radio malfunction that caused the communication loss.

synopsis: G-IV Captain experiences a 'L REV Unlock' CAS message during climb and the reverser was stowed via the emergency stow switch. Shortly afterwards, 'COM HYD FAIL' and 'SNGL RUDDER LIMIT' CAS messages are observed and the flight diverts to a suitable airport.
summary: The flight crew experienced a left reverser unlock followed by a complete loss of the Combine Hydraulic System during flight. After completing checklists and landing successfully on a visual approach, the aircraft was pinned and towed to the FBO instead of taxiing.

synopsis: C340 pilot, on a visual approach to Runway 32 at PLN, reports a NMAC with a BE58 on a straight in approach to the same runway. The reporter had made position reports on the CTAF and entered on the left base while the other pilot made no position reports.
summary: A pilot on a visual approach to runway 32 at PLN experienced a near mid-air collision when a Beechcraft Baron passed 50 feet above. The reporter attributed the incident to the Baron's failure to broadcast position reports on CTAF, fly a standard pattern, or contact Center, combined with the pilot's inability to see the aircraft.

synopsis: A PA-24-260 pilot reported his landing gear would not fully extend and an electrical odor developed. After troubleshooting and preparing for a diversionary landing, the gear became safe so he returned to his home airport for a normal landing.
summary: The pilot experienced a landing gear malfunction and intermittent electrical failures during a local flight, prompting a diversion to a towered airport. After ATC confirmed the gear was down but not locked, the pilot returned to the home base where systems stabilized, allowing for a safe landing.

synopsis: An airfield maintenance crew was authorized by Ground to proceed onto a runway but hold short of the intersecting runway. Several minutes later an aircraft performed a touch and go on the runway they were on then passed close overhead.
summary: Maintenance vehicles entered Runway 15/33 for minor work while holding short of Runway XX/XY. A small aircraft executed a touch-and-go on Runway 33, passing over the vehicles due to failures by Ground and Tower controllers and the ASDEX system.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: Pilot reports of flying to an airport which he knows has a Control Tower operating during football games. Pilot calls CTAF and reports position. Tower Controller answers and pilot responds asking if the Tower is open today. Controller says yes its been open for 21 years. Reporter lands at airport with out any other issues. Pilot would like the Towers hours listed on the sectional, approach plates, and on the ATIS.
summary: A VFR pilot mistakenly assumed Athens airport's tower was closed, confusing it with past special event operations, and contacted the controller on CTAF. The pilot realized the tower had been open for 21 years after the controller responded, noting that missing AWOS operating hours caused the confusion.

synopsis: A Bonanza V35B pilot failed to place his fuel tank selector completely in the right main tank detent which starved the engine of fuel. He diverted to a nearby airport but the engine had restarted before landing with the tank selector fully in the detent.
summary: The pilot of a Beech Bonanza V35B experienced an engine failure during cruise after inadvertently moving the fuel selector handle out of the detent while switching from the Right Main to Left Main tank. The engine restarted after returning the selector to the original tank, allowing a normal landing, attributed to deviating from standard switching procedures and difficulty visually verifying the handle position.

synopsis: A student pilot lost control of the aircraft during landing but the instructor recovered. Both pilots failed to notice wing tip and horizontal stabilizer damage during postflight. His next student also did not see the damage during preflight, but discovered it during that postflight.
summary: During a student touch-and-go on Runway 35L, the student's nose drop caused a runway excursion where the left wing and elevator tips struck gravel. The instructor missed the damage during post-flight checks, and a subsequent student also failed to report it before completing nine landings.

synopsis: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports about an unrecognized critical safety issue that exists for pilots to lose control of B757/B767 aircraft on approach, if the pilot seat shifts unexpectedly due to broken Seat Track Lock Control assemblies. Technician suspects the routine seat inspection task card is not sufficient to maintain adequate serviceability of crew seats.
summary: A mechanic reported a faulty captain seat track lock assembly on a Company B757-200, which could cause unexpected seat shifts and loss of control during approach. The mechanic replaced the assembly in June 2015 and requested increased scrutiny of this mechanism across B757/B767 fleets.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Recip Eng
synopsis: Pilot reports of requesting a deviation for weather. Controller did not want to give the deviation but did. Controller let aircraft deviate for a while then told pilot they had to return to the previously assigned heading. Pilot stated this would put aircraft back into the storm and did not want to. Controller demanded the aircraft return to the heading. Pilot was in VFR conditions and cancelled IFR.
summary: A pilot flying IFR to AGC requested a weather deviation from Columbus Approach, but the controller demanded a return to heading 090 despite onboard radar showing a thunderhead. The pilot canceled the IFR flight plan to proceed VFR, concluding the controller's refusal to deviate compromised flight safety.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: ZLA Controller reports of weather deviations that were affecting the flow into SCT Feeder sectors airspace. Feeder Controller requested one flow instead of two due to weather. Previous center sectors were not giving the last Center sector the flow needed and was told by the reporter to spin aircraft to allow deviations and increased flow.
summary: The CIC reported that a supervisor gaining currency in Sector XX allowed aircraft to run into KONZL at 250 knots, causing unsafe situations in Sector 20 due to feeder restrictions and poor coordination. The incident resulted in the CIC reassigning traffic to Sector XY and highlighted staffing shortages and currency issues during complex weather.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: ZID Controller reports that everything is normal reference a specific tracked aircraft on his display. The aircraft is shipped to Approach Control and then the data block disappears. The advised the Front Line Manager (FLM) to investigate and called the Approach Control to ask them what happened. Approach said they still had a data tag, they did not do anything strange but they did get a remove strip message.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that while monitoring Aircraft X descending to 11,000 feet at CMH, the data block vanished and the target changed to an intruder without controller input. The controller verified with CMH Approach that they retained the data block but received a "Remove Strip" message.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: Front Line Manager (FLM) reports of having to supervise other areas that he has little or no knowledge of. Facility is mandating this to the FLM and the FLM reports that he feels this is an unsafe practice.
summary: An Air Traffic Control Front Line Manager reported being scheduled to supervise unfamiliar operational areas and perform Traffic Management Unit duties despite lacking currency, certification, and knowledge of personnel. The reporter stated this management practice violates JO 7210.3 and creates unsafe conditions by forcing supervisors to manage operations without proper training or experience.

synopsis: A LCH Controller reports of releasing an aircraft off one airport and issuing traffic at the same time to the Tower. The Tower knows about the traffic and releases the aircraft. Both aircraft end up with less than standard separation.
summary: Air Traffic Control issued an IFR release to Aircraft X departing Runway 15 while low-level VFR Aircraft Y patrolled nearby. Aircraft X executed an atypical climb-out, resulting in less than minimum altitude separation from the VFR traffic, prompting a recommendation to install a delayed D-BRITE system to improve situational awareness.

synopsis: ZMA Controllers report of aircraft deviations due to weather. Controllers ask for a plan of action from the Traffic Management Unit (TMU) and are instructed to point out aircraft. The Controllers do so until the other facility no longer accepts point outs which results in airspace deviations due to aircraft deviating for weather.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that a departure aircraft clipped the west side of active Warning Area W465A after TARPON denied point-out requests due to lost communication with another aircraft. The controller attributed the unsafe event to a lack of proactive traffic management plans and insufficient separation between warning areas during weather deviations.

synopsis: A Ramp Agent loading bags in a B737 noticed smoke from a bag on a belt loader before it entered the Cargo Compartment, threw the bag on the ramp, and notified the Captain. The smoke's source was stick matches next to a striker pad ignited within a baggie.
summary: A Ramp Agent discovered a smoking duffle bag containing matches on the belt loader and removed it before it entered the cargo compartment. Police removed the passenger for investigation, maintenance confirmed no damage, and the aircraft departed safely after a delay.

synopsis: Captain reported observing a fuel burn/imbalance anomaly during climbout. After completing the appropriate fuel system troubleshooting checklists he elected to return to the departure airport and landed uneventfully.
summary: The flight crew experienced a significant fuel quantity indicator discrepancy shortly after departure, causing the right tank gauge to fluctuate wildly. Suspecting inaccurate readings due to the aircraft's history, they returned to the departure airport and landed safely after maintenance confirmed the actual fuel matched the gauges on the ground.

synopsis: B737 Captain as the pilot not flying, reports being queried by ATC for switching to Tower at the FAF without being instructed to do so.
summary: The Pilot Flying an RNAV Y 22L approach into MDW switched to Tower at KEEEL without explicit clearance, causing a conflict with ATC. The pilot attributed the error to assuming standard procedure rather than verifying instructions, while noting ATC should have issued timely handoff clearances.

synopsis: B737 Flight Crew laments the speed restrictions (160 to REEBO) applied by SCT during LOC 27 approaches to SAN, believing that the speed restrictions leads to unstabilized approaches.
summary: The flight crew flying a LOC 27 approach into SAN was threatened with removal by ATC for refusing a 160-knot speed restriction to REEBO, which conflicted with stabilized approach requirements. Despite the pressure, the crew accepted the restriction and completed a stabilized landing, though the report highlights the risk of ATC intimidation and requests procedural changes to mitigate future unsafe speed assignments.

synopsis: Captain reported several rows of cabin lighting would not turn off. The reset procedure caused the crew rest area lighting to cycle on/off, impinging FAR 117 rest requirements. This was reported as a chronic occurrence.
summary: Cabin crew reported that reading lights in rows 9, 10, and the first three coach rows would not turn off. Maintenance resets failed and caused pilot bunk lights to cycle, disturbing crew rest and violating FAR 117 requirements for a Class 1 facility.

synopsis: A loss of left hydraulic system quantity was reported. The flight crew completed appropriate checklists and returned to the departure airport.
summary: During initial climb, the crew lost left hydraulic system quantity. They executed applicable checklists and performed an air return to the departure airport.

synopsis: A320 Captain experiences a 'Y HYD Res OVHT' ECAM message just before reaching a cruise altitude of FL340. The pump is turned off and the overheat subsides. The pump is turned on and the overheat returns. The crew elects to divert to the nearest suitable airport. The pump is turned on during the approach and full hydraulics are available throughout the approach and landing.
summary: The flight crew diverted to ZZZ after a Y HYD Res OVHT caused repeated overheating of the right engine pump, resulting in degraded flight controls. They reengaged the pump for the approach, landed safely in thunderstorms, and taxied to the gate after ARFF inspection found no anomalies.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew received a revised routing from ATC before takeoff. They inserted the coded revised routing into the FMS and cross checked their entries. After takeoff, they received a vector to on course. After crossing the first fix they received another vector and a phone number to contact ATC. The FMS coded reroute omitted a fix that ATC was expecting them to fly to. ATC remarked that it may be a problem with some aircraft's FMS.
summary: The flight crew departed Denver on a DENZZZ1 CD-R but flew direct from YOKES to DEHLI, violating arrival corridors. The error resulted from ambiguous charting, an FMC failure to load the required CHICI waypoint, and a late clearance change.

synopsis: The flight crew experienced an airspeed variance during takeoff roll and climbout. They performed checklists which validated the correct airspeed input and continued. However, they expressed concern of a possible flap over speed and a noise abatement deviation.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced a growing airspeed discrepancy and EICAS messages during takeoff and climb, delaying rotation, flap retraction, and autopilot engagement. After cross-checking with the backup indicator and switching to alternate air data, all indications normalized at 13,000 feet, allowing the flight to continue without further issues.

synopsis: An A320 Captain noted a blue arcing in the low left of his forward window prior to a loud bang and the entire window fracturing. After completing the QRH and determining an outer pane anomaly, the flight descended and diverted to a nearby airport.
summary: During climb through 25,000 feet, the captain observed arcing and a loud bang as the forward left cockpit window fractured, likely caused by a windshield heat short. The crew leveled at 26,000 feet, diverted to Airport ZZZ, and landed normally with the inner layer intact.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: While conducting an approach the flight crew encountered unknown VFR traffic in close proximity which was not displaying on TCAS, possibly due to no or inoperative transponder. ATC was queried and requested help in identifying the aircraft type. No RA was generated by this event.
summary: During approach to Runway 11 at STL, the crew encountered a non-transponder VFR aircraft crossing 300–500 feet above at 2,500 feet. No TCAS RA occurred, and ATC was unaware of the traffic in time to issue a warning, though the flight continued without incident.

synopsis: A CRJ-900 Captain reports about a continuing Right Engine oil leak that led him to refuse the aircraft as a non-airworthy aircraft. After a previous short flight, nine quarts of oil had been added to the GE34-8C5 Right Engine with no other corrective action. That flight was followed by the Right Engine Oil quantity dropping 5% every 6 minutes, causing total oil loss prior to destination. Aircraft diverted to the nearest suitable airport.
summary: The Captain diverted a reposition flight due to a severe right engine oil leak caused by poor maintenance diagnosis and a previous starter replacement. Despite adding oil, the leak persisted, leading the Captain to refuse further flight after maintenance and the Chief Pilot insisted the aircraft was airworthy.

synopsis: An off duty pilot reports about an EMB-505 (Phenom 300) aircraft that was grounded for a jerk to the left when stopping. Tires were changed and a Brake Assembly was repaired. As soon as it landed at the next airport, the Right Brake Assembly caught fire.
summary: An off-duty Airline Transport Pilot reported that a Phenom, grounded at Airport ZZZ for a left jerk during stopping, caught fire in the right brake assembly immediately after maintenance and a flight to Airport ZZZ1. The pilot attributed the fire to the recent tire and brake repairs.

synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported encountering wake turbulence from preceding aircraft on takeoff from SEA.
summary: The crew received takeoff clearance while sighting a preceding same-type aircraft but encountered wake turbulence on climbout, causing full aileron deflection and excessive speed below 10,000 feet. The pilot attributed the incident to not delaying takeoff or requesting a runway heading to extend the ground track beyond the preceding aircraft's turn point.

synopsis: A B737-800 primary and secondary stab trim failed after takeoff, manual trim was operational. The crew completed the QRH and returned to the departure airport for an uneventful landing.
summary: The First Officer reported primary and secondary stabilizer trim failures after takeoff. The crew followed QRH procedures, used manual trim, and returned to land the aircraft overweight without further incident.

synopsis: Pilots departing RJAA report requesting a high speed climb below 10,000 feet. The request was approved by Departure Control. The next Controller asks about the aircrafts speed and the crew tells them that they were approved for a no speed restriction climb. The Controller responds that they had not been approved for the high speed climb.
summary: A crew climbing from RJAA on Cupid 2 misunderstood a Departure Control response as a high-speed climb clearance, which Tokyo Control later denied. The pilot attributed the resulting confusion to English language difficulties between the flight crew and controllers.

synopsis: Two Aircraft Maintenance Inspectors report using unapproved LED Ultraviolet (UV) lamps for Fluorescent Penetrant Inspection (FPI) of Engine components for approximately two years, believing an Engineering Variance had been issued to allow use of the LED UV lamps.
summary: A Maintenance Inspector admitted to using unapproved LED UV lamps for Fluorescent Penetrant Inspection on engine components over two years. The inspector believed an Engineering Variance covered the use, but realized the equipment lacked proper approval.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Inspector reports using LED Ultraviolet type lights for Fluorescent Penetrant Inspection (FPI) of Rolls Royce Engine parts for more than two years, believing an Engineering Variance had been issued to allow the use of the LED lights.
summary: A mechanic reported using a company-issued LED black light to inspect Rolls Royce engine components for several years. The mechanic was recently informed that no Engineering Variance was issued to authorize the use of these lights.

synopsis: Upon commencing descent the number 2 throttle would not respond to pilot inputs. The crew advised ATC of the situation and requested a lower altitude. However, during the descent, the throttle became responsive again and a normal approach and landing was accomplished.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced a stuck #2 engine throttle during descent from FL390 to FL370 while approaching Airport ZZZ. Although the throttle later became responsive allowing a normal landing, ATC activated emergency services due to the reported issue, prompting a maintenance inspection.

synopsis: A320 crew received an RA while on a parallel approach. Uneventful landing completed after 'Clear of Conflict.'
summary: During a visual approach to Denver Runway 36R, the crew received a TCAS Resolution Advisory to descend due to a nearby Boeing 737 on parallel Runway 16L. The pilot manually disconnected the autopilot and descended approximately 400 feet at 1,800 feet AGL to resolve the conflict while maintaining visual contact with the traffic.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: The flight crew reported that they were unable to control the cabin pressurization. Several lower altitudes were requested from ATC until the aircraft leveled at 10,000 feet. The cabin altitude never exceeded 9,200 feet and a normal approach and landing was accomplished.
summary: Pilots experienced a cabin pressurization failure at FL320, indicated by a rising cabin altitude and steady flow light despite both auto controllers and manual outflow valve overrides. They executed an emergency descent to 10,000 feet to manage the cabin climb rate, reaching a maximum cabin altitude of 9,200 feet before landing safely.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Pilot reports of flying into LAX on the SADDE6 arrival and at the SAPPI intersection the aircraft turns to join the Runway 24R final. Pilot does not recall being issued a heading to fly after SMO. Pilot called SCT after landing and had discussion with Operations manager who stated this had been happening a lot lately and were wondering why it was happening and how they could fix it.
summary: Pilots deviated from ATC's 068 heading instruction during the SADDE SIX STAR to ILS 24R transition at LAX due to conflicting FMGC flight plan data and approach plates showing a turn at SAPPI. High workload and task saturation prevented verification of the discrepancy, though ATC is working to update plates and clarify instructions.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A fuel odor, later identified as an APU fuel issue, was detected as passengers began to deplane at the gate. A partial, uncommanded, evacuation was initiated by several passengers via the over wing exits. No injuries were reported.
summary: The flight crew and cabin crew detected a fuel smell at the gate caused by an APU leak, leading passengers to uncommandedly exit via overwing exits due to a communication misunderstanding. The crew shut down the APU, secured the aircraft, and confirmed no injuries after ground personnel inspected the 15-foot fuel spill.

synopsis: C-172 pilot experienced loss of electrical system. Pilot made radio transmissions in the blind and squawked 7600. After receiving a green landing clearance light from the Tower, pilot landed safely.
summary: The pilot experienced a total electrical failure during the night arrival at SFB, losing transmit capability after contacting Orlando Approach. Squawking 7600, the pilot received a light gun clearance to land on runway 9L and taxied to the ramp without conflict.

synopsis: While on a VFR flight plan, C-172 pilot encountered IMC while attempting to descend below clouds in aircraft's path. Pilot climbed out of clouds and continued in VMC.
summary: A VFR pilot flying south over Marin County at 3,500 feet entered clouds at 1,200 feet while descending to comply with an ATC clearance to 2,000 feet for SFO Class B entry. The pilot stopped descent at 800 feet, climbed back to clear air, and attributed the incident to rushing the descent due to the cloud deck and altitude restriction.

synopsis: A BE36 pilot experiences a terrain warning climbing through 1,500 feet for terrain on the right after departing Runway 19 at RUT. They elect to remain on runway heading and not turn right to DYO NDB.
summary: A pilot departing RUT on an instrument flight plan received a terrain warning while climbing past 1,500 feet, causing reluctance to execute the required right turn. After ATC advised complying with the procedure or proceeding direct ALB after 6,400 feet, the pilot maintained runway heading until that altitude before turning direct, completing the flight without incident.

synopsis: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports about his Maintenance Manager who continually attempts to cover up discrepancies with the aircraft they have at their Flight Facility. Technician also includes examples of the same Manager applying pressure to perform maintenance or modifications to their aircraft, not in compliance with their Practices and Procedures Manuals.
summary: A mechanic reported that Manager X repeatedly pressured staff to bypass proper maintenance procedures on turboprop aircraft, including ignoring out-of-rig landing gear doors, approving unanalyzed drawing changes, and attempting to reuse defective ignitor leads. The mechanic refused these unsafe requests, corrected the discrepancies, and warned that the manager's corner-cutting endangered flight safety.

synopsis: MWH Tower Controller reports of another Controller who the reporter thinks is complacent in their duties. Reporting Controller reports of a Call for Release(CFR) for traffic that is in the pattern and eventually going back to the airport that has the CFR. Aircraft leaves the traffic pattern and goes to departure who then issues a beacon code and clearance. Controller did not call for release on the aircraft. Reporter states the other controller is not held accountable for his actions.
summary: A pilot reported that a controller failed to issue traffic advisories for gliders during Aircraft X's approach, forcing the pilot to use TCAS to avoid conflict. Later, the controller cleared Aircraft X to a departure airport with a Call for Release without advising the pilot of the delay, resulting in a late release coordination.

synopsis: SFO describes a crossing situation where the communications between Ground and Local became confusing. Local held up a strip and said after this one you can cross a tug. Ground thought it was the aircraft departing and crossed the tug. Local had another aircraft in the lineup they were talking about which had been cleared for takeoff, but luckily did not depart until the tug had crossed the runway.
summary: A Ground Controller reported that a Local Controller casually released a tug onto the active runway area while a second departure was rotating in low clouds and haze. The reporter attributed the safety risk to the Local Controller's failure to follow standard operating procedures and coordination protocols.

synopsis: ZAN Controller reports of issuing an altitude he thought would be safe for an aircraft. Moments later the MSAW alarm went off and the Front Line Manager (FLM) came over to investigate. The Controller then checked the approach plate and discovered that he was wrong and attempted to contact the pilot to have him climb. Contact was not made. The pilot later called and asked if he was supposed to be higher and the Controller then climbed the aircraft and cleared it for the approach.
summary: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft X direct to HUBUK at 3,000 feet for the RNAV 30 approach into AQH, unaware the Terminal Arrival Area required 6,700 feet. An MSAW alarm prompted the controller to verify the Minimum IFR Altitude, resulting in a climb clearance to 5,200 feet after the pilot confirmed the altitude discrepancy.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A Phoenix TRACON (P50) Controller reports of a pilot issue with communications. The Controller climbed the aircraft to a higher altitude, but it wasn't climbing well. The Controller asked the pilot if he had the terrain insight and issued two vectors away from the higher terrain. The pilot reported he was looking for traffic. The Controller continued to vector the aircraft, and the pilot took the second heading.
summary: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X departing SDL after the pilot failed to climb to FL210 and ignored the first terrain avoidance heading. The pilot claimed to be looking for traffic despite the controller's concerns about terrain proximity and repeated vector instructions.

synopsis: While giving instruction to a Developmental, ZJX Controller did not list in on a phone call and relied on the Developmental to tell him what the conversation was about. The activation of restricted airspace was what the conversation was about. The airspace was considered hot by the military but the Developmental thought they would call back to activate the airspace. Aircraft were in the now hot area and the controllers had not coordinated with other sectors in the Center.
summary: A ZJX military trainer and trainee failed to activate Tail Hook 'A' airspace because the trainee, using a non-speaker handset, missed the Navy coordinator's confirmation. This communication error caused a delay in activation while fighters were already operating in the airspace.

synopsis: While taxiing to the gate with guidance from ground personnel the flight crew reported that the aircraft wingtip struck a ground vehicle
summary: During taxi to the gate, the flight crew's winglet contacted a fuel truck positioned just outside the safety zone. The collision occurred while the aircraft was following the lead-in line and approaching the stop bar under marshaler guidance.

synopsis: After receiving takeoff clearance, A320 crew advanced thrust levers and commenced takeoff roll. Tower then cancelled their takeoff clearance. Crew stopped aircraft and 1-2 minutes later received a second takeoff clearance.
summary: The pilot was holding on runway 25R when Tower cancelled the takeoff clearance due to inbound traffic on an intersecting runway. The crew stopped the aircraft, waited 1-2 minutes, and subsequently completed an uneventful takeoff.

synopsis: C680 flight crew entered KINGG intersection instead of KINNG in the FMS route section. The names of both intersections sound the same and both are located in the New England area, approximately 200 NM apart. ATC advised the crew of the correct intersection spelling, which was then correctly entered into the FMS.
summary: The flight crew, climbing to FL350, mistakenly turned left toward a misspelled KINNG intersection instead of the cleared KINGG due to FMS input errors and fatigue. New York Center corrected the deviation by issuing an immediate right turn after the crew identified the spelling error.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew had briefed an ILS approach prior to their descent. During their descent they were assigned a different runway and approach. Unfortunately, they briefed the wrong approach. They discovered their error and briefed and flew the correct approach. Reporter suggests a change be made to the 10-7 chart so others don't mistake the different ILS's to the same Runway.
summary: The flight crew descended into DTW and initially loaded the ILS Y 22R approach instead of the cleared ILS Z 22R due to Jeppesen selection and missed ATC instructions. They corrected the FMC and radios before intercepting the correct approach, noting the significant differences between the two procedures.

synopsis: While bags were being offloaded at the destination airport ramp personnel noticed smoke emanating from a bag. The bag, which contained 5 Lithium batteries and other electronic devices, subsequently caught fire on the ramp and was successfully extinguished after several attempts. The Captain expressed his concern over not discovering batteries during TSA screening and also what he felt were slow reaction times by both fire and police responders.
summary: A passenger's bag containing five lithium batteries and film equipment, which was gate-checked at ZZZ1, began smoking and ignited on the ground at ZZZ2 after arrival. The crew evacuated and shut down the aircraft while rampers attempted to extinguish the fire, which burned three times before fire departments arrived 30 minutes later to find the bag destroyed.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: While on final approach, the flight crew was advised of an active microburst near their approach path. The flight crew reported that the Tower did not respond in a timely fashion to their request for a vector away from the fast moving cell.
summary: The crew, arriving at IAD on an ILS approach to Runway 01R, rejected landing due to a microburst and requested a turn to avoid weather. ATC initially vectored them toward Runway 1C into the hazard before turning them away, leading the crew to criticize the exposure to the fast-moving storm.

synopsis: An A319 crew departed a foreign airport after a two hour delay and a flight plan change which resulted in the FMC dropping the departure airport and flight plan. Because the performance pages were not rebuilt the V-speed and flex power did not set with the TOGA selection, but the crew continued the takeoff.
summary: Two pilots experienced a takeoff delay after a maintenance hold when a revised clearance caused the flight plan to lose performance data. The crew corrected the missing FLEX temperature and speeds mid-roll, realizing that deleting the runway from the MCDU erases critical takeoff parameters.

synopsis: Three B737 Flight Attendants reported their air conditioning was unable to sufficiently cool on the ground or in flight because of extreme heat. The Lead Flight Attendant received emergency medical attention because of the prolonged triple digit heat exposure.
summary: Flight attendants and a captain on flight XXX experienced severe heat exposure when departing with an aircraft having five prior A/C write-ups and a hangar alert. The captain admitted to leaving the gate overwhelmed, causing crew illness, dehydration, and an ER admission due to the non-functional air conditioning.

synopsis: Pilot reports of being told directions by ATC and pilot attempts to do as instructed. Pilot reports to ATC traffic that he would overfly if following ATC instruction. Pilot deviated from what ATC told him to do to avoid over flight of taxiing aircraft. Aircraft then departed and pilot observed other traffic, was told to turn one direction and turned the opposite to avoid the traffic and possible collision.
summary: The pilot reported that after receiving conflicting taxi instructions, an F-16 departing aggressively turned right into their path. The pilot was forced to descend to 500 feet to avoid a collision while turning east.

aircraft: Small Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A corporate jet flight crew on approach to EMT were confused by a SCT Controller's disapproval of their descent for the airport after they cancelled IFR and began a visual approach at night.
