summary: An air traffic controller issued a departure clearance to an air carrier while a NORDO helicopter was nearby, resulting in the departing aircraft responding to a Resolution Advisory. The controller attributed the incident to human error for not waiting for the NORDO helicopter to exit the airspace before clearing the departure.

synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported lining up for the wrong airport in a ground white-out condition. Poor internal cockpit communications was a factor.
summary: A fatigued Captain and First Officer attempted to land at MAF in fog and snow but initially aligned with the wrong airfield due to poor visibility and missed CRM calls caused by a missing hot MIC. After Tower correction at 1,300 feet AGL, the crew executed a go-around and landed safely at the correct runway.

synopsis: After takeoff, B737 crew raised the flaps from flaps 1 to up prior to reaching the minimum cleanup altitude or attaining minimum maneuvering speed for flaps up. Crew received an 'Airspeed Low, Airspeed Low' aural alert and reacted by lowering the nose and quickly gaining sufficient airspeed.
summary: During climb out, the Pilot Monitoring (Captain) inadvertently retracted flaps instead of landing gear, triggering an 'Airspeed Low' alert. The reporter attributes this error to inattention and fatigue, noting the Pilot Flying recovered the airspeed and the flight continued uneventfully.

synopsis: Captain reports that ground crews at ORD are not properly trained in aircraft deicing procedures.
summary: The pilot reported that improperly trained de-icing crews at ORD failed to follow SOPs, requiring prompts for Type 1 fluid dilution and leaving the aircraft partially de-iced before driving away. A supervisor eventually dispatched a new crew to properly de-ice the aircraft, but the pilot described this as a recurring systemic issue where crews falsely claim aircraft are clean.

synopsis: Junior First Officer reports a lack of compliance with company procedures and ATC clearances by the Captain.
summary: A Junior First Officer reported that an experienced Captain ignored required checklists, briefings, and speed restrictions during a two-day trip. The Captain also turned off anti-ice systems despite icing conditions and failed to acknowledge ATC clearances until prompted, creating safety risks due to non-compliance with procedures.

synopsis: EMB-175 Captain reported rejecting the takeoff when Tower cancelled their clearance because of a conflict on a crossing runway.
summary: Tower initiated a rejected takeoff at 10 knots due to an aircraft landing on a crossing runway. The pilot executed a low-speed abort at 10 knots.

synopsis: Dash 8 Captain reported his aircraft lost contact with the tow bar during push back when the ground crew failed to use the safety pin.
summary: During pushback, the tow bar disconnected because ground crew failed to install a safety pin, causing the aircraft to roll backward after the tug stopped. The pilot applied brakes and used an upslope to stop the plane safely, resulting in no damage to the nose gear.

synopsis: C560XLS First Officer reported that the left brake pedal felt spongy. The cable snapped while pumping the brakes and checking the pins on the brake pads.
summary: Mechanics investigating a recurring spongy brake discrepancy on the left pedal snapped a brake cable while pumping the brakes to observe pad pins. The reporter attributes the failure to cable corrosion and recommends more frequent inspections or an Airworthiness Directive.

aircraft: Dash 8 Series Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Aircraft experienced multiple failures preventing IMC flight. After takeoff returned to field.
summary: During climb out, the crew experienced ADI and HSI roll mismatches, lost both yaw dampers and flight directors, and received an AHRS data invalid message. Consequently, the crew decided to return to the airport.

synopsis: Flight crew reported an NMAC while on a visual approach after they received a traffic call from ATC as well as an Resolution Advisory, related to an aircraft that took off from Bermuda Dunes.
summary: The crew descending into PSP on the SBONO 1 Arrival received a Resolution Advisory near CEKMA, requiring a climb to avoid traffic 400 feet below. The pilot attributed the conflict to a late approach call and suggested the RNAV visual procedure's waypoint placement near an uncontrolled airport was a contributing factor.

synopsis: A B767-300 developed an asymmetric leading edge slat accompanied by a binding flap handle and roll motion when flaps 25 was selected on short final. The approach was abandoned, the checklist completed and the flight returned for an uneventful landing.
summary: The pilot monitoring experienced flap asymmetry and binding while configuring for landing on runway 7R, causing an amber ICAS message and leading edge light. The crew abandoned the approach, landed on runway 7L with flaps at 20 degrees, and discovered inboard slats remained in the takeoff position while outboard slats were in the landing position.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Flight crew was cleared to taxi on SLC Taxiways H, Y to de-ice pad 6Y but did not identify the H to Y Taxiway transition. After missing Taxiway Y, the crew was cleared H3 to Y but they could not identify the Taxiway H3 transition to Y off Runway 34R. The large physical island in the deice pad south of H3 and north of 6Y is not depicted on any airport or taxi diagram.
summary: The flight crew missed Taxiway Y while taxiing to the 34R de-ice pad at night due to outdated charts omitting Taxiway H3 and a physical island. This discrepancy, combined with distraction from an ATC speed instruction, caused the crew to misinterpret the clearance, highlighting a safety issue requiring chart updates.

synopsis: Immediately after takeoff, CRJ-200 crew experienced smoke in the cockpit which they determined to be Type 4 anti-ice fluid being burned by the APU caused by runoff from the fuselage. The smoke quickly dissipated and none entered the cabin. Crew recommends that until the recently imposed requirement by Canada Transport, that the fuselage of any CRJ-200 be anti-iced if the wings and tail require anti-icing, is rescinded that company policy be modified to permit unpressurized takeoffs following deicing/anti-icing.
summary: Pilots of a CRJ-200 departing YUL reported cockpit smoke after takeoff caused by Type 4 anti-ice fluid dripping into the APU inlet. The reporter attributes this to a Transport Canada mandate requiring fuselage anti-icing, which forced the aircraft to take off pressurized with packs on.

synopsis: C172 experienced a rough-running engine on base leg. Aircraft landed without incident.
summary: The pilot reported that during the extended base leg of an arrival, the aircraft engine power decreased and vibrated three times before returning to normal. After informing ATC of a potential road landing, the crew received clearance and landed safely with no further issues.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: Captain reported rejecting the takeoff when one propeller failed to come out of start lock position.
summary: The pilot aborted takeoff on runway 18R after the left engine showed no torque due to a stuck feathering valve preventing the propeller from releasing start locks. Maintenance confirmed the valve failure, requiring the aircraft to return to the ramp.

synopsis: Due to weather conditions and wrong parts sent, Maintenance was unable to make necessary repairs to the damaged wire harness.
summary: Mechanics A and B attempted to repair a flap failure on an aircraft during a road trip, facing extreme weather, fatigue, and conflicting instructions from Maintenance Control. The event resulted in a 24-hour delay and improper work procedures due to poor communication, lack of system knowledge, and unsafe environmental conditions.

synopsis: Aircraft in the traffic pattern at GFK, reported misunderstanding the Tower Controller's instruction to land number 2 behind another aircraft on a straight in approach. The Tower had told the straight in pilot to land number 2 behind another aircraft on final and then the traffic pattern Cessna to land number 2 a few seconds later. The number 1 aircraft had landed in the meantime causing the confusion and resulting in a NMAC. The report from the Instructor of the straight in aircraft is also included.
summary: Two Cessna 172s conducting training at Grand Forks International Airport experienced a near mid-air collision on final approach to Runway 35L. The incident resulted from conflicting "Number 2" landing clearances and pilot misidentification of the lead aircraft, requiring an immediate go-around.

synopsis: An Epic pilot reported refiling prior to departure to avoid severe weather over Mississippi. XM radar is used to navigate around the southern end of a line of thunderstorms, through weather that appeared as green and light green on the XM image. ZHU agreed that the intended route was good showing no severe weather. The weather turned out to be anything but benign with two separate periods of severe turbulence with lightning. The autopilot remained engaged throughout the incident and the reporter continued to his destination.
summary: The pilot encountered severe turbulence and lightning in cruise at 28,000 feet despite weather radar showing only light precipitation. This resulted in non-functional pitch and rudder trim, a loose rudder cable, and carbon fiber blowouts on the control surfaces, requiring the aircraft to be towed for inspection.

synopsis: B737-800 First Officer reported the Captain's airspeed indicator malfunctioned shortly after takeoff. Flight returned to departure airport.
summary: During climb out from Santo Domingo, the Captain's Primary Flight Display showed unreliable airspeed and intermittent stickshaker activation while the First Officer's instruments remained normal. The crew executed the Airspeed Unreliable checklist, returned to the airport, and performed a safe heavy-weight landing with no further incident.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: MD-80 Captain reported diverting to an alternate after heat and odor were noticed in the cabin.
summary: During cruise at FL330, the crew detected a strong odor and extreme heat in the aft left lavatory, suspecting a ballast issue. The Captain declared an emergency, diverted, and landed safely after fire services identified glowing bags in the aft cargo compartment via infrared.

synopsis: TBM 700 pilot reported encountering severe wake turbulence while on final approach to LGB airport in trail of an A320.
summary: A pilot on a visual approach to LGB Rwy 30 encountered severe wake turbulence from a preceding Airbus A320 between 1,000 and 1,500 feet, causing an uncommanded 80-degree right roll. The pilot recovered using full left aileron and power, then diverted to Rwy 25L after a denied request for a 360-degree turn.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: ZID ARTCC Controller reported a loss of separation event between southbound and westbound traffic. Reportedly, one of the flight crews leveled off at FL314 rather than continue climbing to FL350 as instructed.
summary: An OJT instructor and student controller managed Aircraft X climbing to 35,000 feet and Aircraft Y at 34,000 feet. Separation was lost after the pilot falsely reported being level at 35,000 feet while actually at 34,100 feet, despite the instructor descending Aircraft Y to avoid a collision.

synopsis: P50 TRACON Controller reported being very busy with aircraft conducting instrument approaches to the main airport as well as the satellite airports. Reporter suggested an additional sector in their unit be opened instead of having to perform both functions by himself. The Supervisor was not able to open the combined sector due to lack of staffing at the time.
summary: The Traffic Management Coordinator reported an unsafe situation at PHX and SDL during high-volume IFR arrivals caused by combining the ARC position with TMC duties. Due to staffing shortages, the request to staff a standalone ARC was denied, leaving the controller overloaded and unable to manage traffic flow effectively.

synopsis: MEM Tower controllers reported a Tower tour distracted the Ground Controller allowing an aircraft to taxi to the wrong runway and Local departed traffic off that runway. Departure was in conflict with arrival traffic, so the Local Controller vectored the departure and sent the arrival around.
summary: A ground controller, distracted by a tower tour, taxied Aircraft X to the wrong runway (18C) and cleared it for departure into incorrect airspace. The controller corrected the situation by maneuvering Aircraft X and an intersecting Aircraft Y to maintain separation.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: ZNY ARTCC Controller reported an ATC Computer assigned a beacon code to an aircraft 200 miles from the Controller's airspace. The inconsistency was only realized after the Controller issued control instructions to the aircraft and none were complied with. Eventually the error was caught shortly before the aircraft transitioned out of the sector.
summary: An air traffic controller in a busy sector misidentified Aircraft Y as Aircraft X due to an ERAM beacon code error, issuing a descent clearance to the wrong flight. This caused Aircraft X to descend prematurely in non-radar airspace, resulting in multiple loss of separation incidents with other traffic.

synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported that during pushback the tug became disconnected from the tow bar, and the tug collided with the aircraft.
summary: During pushback, the tow bar disconnected from the tug, causing the tug to collide with the aircraft. The crew reported the tug driver stated the tug malfunctioned, prompting the pilot to reset the parking brake and notify operations.

synopsis: B737-800 First Officer reported they deviated from cleared track because they failed to see a change to their route in the PDC.
summary: Two pilots flying a Boeing 787 enroute at FL370 deviated from their clearance due to an incorrect FMC route entry caused by a confusing partial PDC amendment. The Denver ARTCC controller queried the deviation and cleared the aircraft direct to JALAP.

synopsis: B737 flight crew reported encountering nil braking action on taxi out that resulted in a taxiway excursion.
summary: The crew lost control while taxiing on an icy, sloping taxiway after receiving a Mu report, resulting in the aircraft exiting the prepared surface. With Engine 1 MEL'd and braking action nil, the aircraft stopped in snow, causing the airport to close and requiring the following aircraft to be towed.

synopsis: Regional Jet crew reported being rushed to pushback by the ramp supervisor. Crew also reported that the supervisor had not connected the tug before requesting that the aircraft brakes be released.
summary: A ramp supervisor rushed a flight crew at the gate to release the parking brake with engines running, despite the tug being 15–30 feet away and chocks still in place. The crew refused the unsafe request, preventing a potential collision with the jet bridge, and attributed the incident to the supervisor's lack of training and focus on on-time departure over safety.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported landing and departing LIH without weather information.
summary: The crew landed and later departed from uncontrolled LIH despite ASOS reporting missing visibility and temperature, concluding the Operations Manual requirements were unclear. The reporter believes both actions were errors because the manual mandates an approved weather source with specific elements, which the ASOS failed to provide.

synopsis: An AS-350 pilot described a helicopter dolly rotating on an icy ramp during engine start while preparing to fly off the dolly.
summary: A helicopter pilot reported that while starting on an icy ramp with the tow truck attached per standard procedure, the dolly rotated 60 degrees toward a hangar. The pilot aborted the start with no damage, noting a conflict between company SOPs and a towing policy requiring truck separation that was not in the operations manual.

synopsis: A first officer reported unsafe practices for flying night-time approaches into MKK airport using the published MKK VOR Approach. The practice of using radar altimeter for terrain clearance at night reduced adequate altitude clearance above terrain of varying heights.
summary: During a night enroute phase at MKK, the First Officer reported the Captain descended below minimum IFR altitudes on a VOR approach, relying on the radar altimeter despite terrain risks. The Captain ignored the First Officer's concerns and continued descending toward terrain, highlighting unsafe practices regarding night visual approaches and minimum altitude adherence.

synopsis: An A321 right engine compressor stalled during takeoff so the flight returned to the departure airport. A Mechanic reported the aircraft's previous crew reported a compressor stall ECAM during descent, but did not state visual or auditory confirmation. This resulted in the aircraft being released on the minimal inspection condition.
summary: The crew experienced repeated right engine compressor stalls and thrust loss immediately after takeoff, prompting an immediate return for an overweight landing. The aircraft was taken out of service after fire crews inspected the smoking engine, and the crew opted out of extending duty time due to fatigue concerns.

synopsis: A B777 Flight Attendant was injured after very short notice about its impending severe turbulence event.
summary: Flight attendants were injured during severe turbulence while attempting to resume service after takeoff. The reporter suffered back and neck injuries when thrown to the floor, while a colleague twisted a foot, forcing both to cease duties and seek medical attention.

synopsis: Maintenance Technician reported a broken emergency button on the Captain's O2 mask which was not properly reported.
summary: A mechanic reported a 737 with a broken Captain's O2 mask emergency button, suspecting the pilot found it during preflight but delayed reporting to reach a hub station. The mechanic believes this violates the carrier's FOM, which requires immediate documentation of no-go items upon discovery.

synopsis: Flight of two helicopters with two GPS sources flew a course 2 miles outside the Washington DC SFRA, yet PCT TRACON claimed the aircraft was inside the SFRA by two miles.
summary: The pilot reported an inadvertent 1-2 mile penetration of the DC SFRA boundary while enroute from EVY at low altitude to avoid turbulence. Although both GPS units indicated the aircraft was outside the restricted area, the pilot acknowledged responsibility for the deviation and intends to maintain a 5-mile buffer in the future.

synopsis: LR-40XR Captain reported loss of cabin pressure at FL395.
summary: The crew experienced a cabin pressure loss at FL395, triggering the emergency pressurization system. They reported the event to air traffic control and followed manufacturer checklists, with no other abnormalities occurring.

aircraft: M-20 Series Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Mooney pilot reported a ground conflict after landing at ABE. Reporter stated this could have developed into a dangerous situation.
summary: A pilot conducting an ILS 6 approach at ABE in gusty winds received a late hold short instruction for Runway 31 while a King Air was landing. The controller's delayed clearance created a potential conflict, but strong winds enabled the Mooney to stop safely before the intersection.

synopsis: A DA40 pilot reported landing at HND without seeing a light gun signal after total loss of electrical power.
summary: A pilot flying a Diamond DA40 experienced a total electrical failure at 7,500 feet and entered Class D airspace without communication to land on Runway 35L. The aircraft floated due to unavailable flaps and landed on the second half of the runway, with the pilot noting no light gun signals were received.

synopsis: The Local Controller cleared an aircraft for takeoff. The crew of the aircraft told the Controller they would wait because it appeared a taxiing aircraft had not cleared the runway. The Controller's ASDE-X (Ground Radar) indicated the taxiing aircraft was clear of the runway.
summary: Local Control cleared Aircraft X for takeoff based on ASDE indications that a crossing aircraft was clear, though the pilot initially doubted runway clearance. The pilot held position until confirming the crossing aircraft was clear, after which Local Control re-issued the takeoff clearance and the departure proceeded safely.

synopsis: An aircraft entered ARTCC airspace on a different route than what the ARTCC flight plan showed.
summary: Air traffic controllers identified a routing discrepancy between Miami Center and ATOP for an inbound foreign aircraft. The pilot confirmed holding the original routing, prompting a new clearance, which the controller attributed to unreliable equipment in the foreign country.

aircraft: Any Unknown or Unlisted Aircraft Manufacturer
synopsis: Restricted Airspace was in use. The military agency responsible for the use of airspace failed to notify the ATC facility. Aircraft were routed through Restricted Airspace while it was in use by the military.
summary: Air traffic controllers reported flying two aircraft at 7,000 and 8,000 feet through an active restricted area because Range Control failed to notify them of the activation. The incident resulted from a procedural change and lack of timely communication, prompting a call for retraining and reverting to previous notification methods.

synopsis: The Tower Controller asked the TRACON to break an aircraft out because there was insufficient spacing with the preceding aircraft. The TRACON Controller refused and told the Tower Controller to break the first aircraft out. After the second aircraft contacted the Tower, the Tower issued a go-around instruction and put the aircraft back on the TRACON frequency.
summary: A local controller managed a conflict between Aircraft X circling and Aircraft Y descending during marginal VFR conditions after the approach controller ordered a missed approach. The reporter attributed the unsafe situation to poor spacing planning by the approach controller and systemic issues caused by TRACON consolidation.

synopsis: Pilot flying selected a heading mode vice speed. ATC intervened to put aircraft back on course.
summary: During approach, the Captain incorrectly set the Mode Control Panel heading knob to 160 instead of the airspeed knob, causing the aircraft to deviate from the assigned 180 heading. The Pilot Monitoring corrected the setting after ATC queried the deviation, which the Captain attributed to using non-standard callouts from a previous airline.

synopsis: B777 flight crew reported that while enroute on a transoceanic flight they diverted to an alternate after noticing an acrid burning odor.
summary: The flight crew diverted an aircraft at FL350 due to an unexplained electrical odor and smoke in the cockpit, later linked to a reported cargo bulk ventilation fan failure. After a bird strike on final approach, the aircraft landed safely, but maintenance could not isolate the odor source, resulting in the aircraft being removed from service.

synopsis: Air carrier crew responded to insufficient thrust warning during takeoff roll and rejected the takeoff.
summary: The crew rejected takeoff on a short runway due to insufficient thrust and an ENG TLA NOT IN TOGA caution. The Captain stopped the aircraft at 4,000 feet after failing to achieve required ATTCS parameters, then returned to the gate.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A crew pushed back from the EWR C Concourse with clearance to disconnect at a gate near Taxiway RG, then taxi via B, D, Hold Short of V. Because of signage confusion the crew taxied out the throat to A then S, D to hold at V.
summary: The Captain exited the ramp via an "Entry only" taxiway instead of the instructed Taxiway RG, causing a deviation from the ground clearance. The pilot attributed the error to the sign's placement and lack of "DO NOT EXIT" markings, requiring a re-route to Runway 4L.

synopsis: CRJ-700 pilot reported they were advised they failed to meet crossing restrictions on the HABBS3 STAR arrival into CYUL.
summary: The pilot reported being above profile altitudes on the HABBS3 STAR after Montreal Center assigned a descent to 8,000 feet without a "descend via" clearance, which is not required in Canada. The crew descended to 6,000 feet and completed the approach safely, noting the regulatory difference was only discovered after landing.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC with a helicopter shortly after takeoff from MAF airport.
summary: The flight crew of a departing aircraft at Midland Airport encountered a brown helicopter that violated airspace during climb-out after takeoff from Runway 34L. The crew maintained visual contact and continued climbing, passing approximately 300 feet above and 100 yards in front of the helicopter, which took no evasive action.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported EWR Terminal A taxi lines between Taxiways RA and RC are faded, hard to follow, and may allow aircraft to taxi closer to the terminal and into unsafe proximity to parked aircraft.
summary: A pilot departing Terminal A at EWR reported that poorly painted taxi lines between Taxiway RA and RC are difficult to see, especially at night or in rain. The pilot stated this condition could cause an aircraft to taxi too close to the terminal or parked aircraft, potentially striking an obstruction.

synopsis: All three B777 pilots failed to notice Flap 20 set for landing even though the First Officer, flying pilot, call Flaps 25. The Captain missed the earlier Flaps 25 call but a 1,000 feet stabilized approach call is no longer required.
summary: The First Officer hand-flew a visual approach to Runway 26R, landing with flaps 20 instead of the required 25 due to an incomplete before-landing checklist. Although the approach was high and fast, the crew continued to a safe landing rather than executing a go-around after noticing the configuration error.

synopsis: A321 flight crew reported executing a go-around after experiencing uncommanded thrust on approach to LAX.
summary: The flight crew executed a go-around during approach to LAX after an uncommanded power surge occurred following a late runway change from 24R to 25L. The subsequent gear overspeed resulted from rapid configuration changes while the aircraft was unstable, though the crew completed a normal landing.

synopsis: MD-83 Captain reported he was not properly notified of a shipment of Li-metal batteries on his flight.
summary: The pilot reported that off-load station personnel identified lithium-metal batteries in the cargo during the off-load phase. The pilot stated they had no Notice to Captain (NOTOC) for this flight.

synopsis: CRJ200 flight crew reported a rejected takeoff after deicing due to the flaps not being set for takeoff. ATC miscues helped precipitate the chain of events that led up to this RTO, but the current requirement to keep the flaps up after deicing until takeoff clearance is received was the final straw.
summary: The flight crew received an incorrect departure clearance and a CONFIG FLAPS warning during takeoff at SLC after initiating flaps late due to deicing procedures. The pilot attributed the event to flawed Standard Operating Procedures that disrupt normal operational rhythm and increase the risk of configuration errors.

synopsis: A CRJ-700 EICAS alerted R BLEED DUCT at cruise altitude. The crew completed the immediate action checklist which closed both bleed valves and depressurized the cabin. The cabin oxygen masks deployed during descent to 10,000 feet and diversion to a nearby airport.
summary: The flight crew received a right bleed duct warning at cruise, causing rapid cabin depressurization and oxygen mask deployment. They executed emergency checklists, declared an emergency, and diverted to the departure airport, suspecting a faulty indicator or faster-than-expected valve closure.

aircraft: MD-80 Series (DC-9-80) Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Aircrew experienced an in-flight engine failure and successfully diverted to an interim airport.
summary: The flight crew experienced an in-flight engine failure on an MD-80 at FL330, characterized by shuddering, a bang, and high EGT on the #2 engine. They diverted safely, attributing the failure to the airline's maintenance program allowing engines to operate at excessive temperatures.

synopsis: Student pilot under instruction flared too high resulting in a stall. Aircraft struck the runway with enough force to cause damage, but no crew injuries resulted.
summary: A flight instructor and student pilot experienced a stall and ground impact during a landing lesson in a student-owned aircraft. The student prematurely flared at two feet, believing he was on the ground, causing a stall that resulted in a propeller strike and bent landing gear, though no injuries occurred.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; Low Wing; 1 Eng; Retractable Gear
synopsis: While flying a VOR approach in VMC conditions, GA pilot misinterpreted the GPS approach presentation and descended early. This resulted in flight below minimum altitude for that location and subsequent ATC altitude alert call. By the time the radio call for the altitude alert was completed, the aircraft was inside the FAF and at a safe altitude.
summary: The pilot flying a VOR Rwy 04 approach to PIE mistakenly descended early by confusing a GPS pseudo fix (FF04) with the step-down fix JULSO. Tower issued an altitude alert when the aircraft was 500 feet above minimums, but the pilot corrected the descent upon reaching JULSO and landed safely under VFR conditions.

synopsis: G-IV Captain was informed by ATC that he had leveled off at 2100 feet on the RUUDY5 while all three aircraft altimeters show 1500 feet. A few minutes later the aircraft altimeters agree with the Mode C read out. Thirty minutes into the flight the number two air data computer failed. The aircraft had been deiced just prior to departure.
summary: During the RUUDY 5 departure, pilots were told by ATC to descend despite altimeters showing 1500 feet, while radar indicated 2100 feet. The discrepancy was attributed to a deicing issue, followed by a #2 digital air data computer failure that caused First Officer instrument failures, resolved by switching to DADC #1.

synopsis: The TRACON Controller observed an unidentified VFR aircraft depart an airport on a converging course with an air carrier on a visual approach to an adjacent airport already in communication with the Tower. The TRACON Controller pointed the traffic out to the Tower Local Controller. The air carrier responded to a TCAS RA.
summary: Aircraft X on a visual approach to Runway 6 merged with an unknown VFR aircraft at the same altitude over the 5-mile final, triggering a TCAS RA. The pilot attributed the 0.22-mile lateral separation to the Class C airspace not extending to the ground, recommending an airspace change to protect the final approach course.

synopsis: An aircraft was making an emergency descent. ATC issued a heading to opposite direction climbing traffic to avoid the descending traffic. The climbing traffic turned to the wrong heading causing a conflict with the emergency descending traffic.
summary: A Radar Controller managed Aircraft X's emergency descent from 24,000 feet due to cabin pressure loss while Aircraft Y climbed. Aircraft Y misheard a heading clearance, turning 140 degrees instead of 240, resulting in less than standard separation before both pilots visually acquired each other.

synopsis: An aircraft in a refueling track departed the refueling track and began its flight back to its base without a clearance.
summary: An air traffic controller issued a Brasher warning to military tanker Aircraft X after it left a refueling block and requested a higher altitude without ATC clearance while Aircraft Y was nearby. The controller attributed the deviation to the pilot's misunderstanding of MARSA requirements and the need for clearance to alter routing.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported tugs that are outfitted with LED headlights blind the flight crew resulting in difficulty seeing the safety zone and/or the Marshaller.
summary: Ramp personnel reported that new LED headlights on tugs are so bright they obscure the safety zone and marshaller, causing confusion when the crew flashes lights to signal. The tugs remain running without a light switch due to fears of cold-weather restart failure, preventing the lights from being turned off.

synopsis: B737-700 Captain experienced an over speed during descent in VNAV with the speed programed to .78/284 for no apparent reason. Speed increased from .78 to .82 Mach, without turning on the engine anti ice or a wind shift.
summary: During descent from FL300 in VNAV, the aircraft accelerated from Mach .780 to the overspeed warning without wind shift or engine de-ice use. The First Officer disconnected the autopilot and abruptly deployed speedbrakes, attributing the event to software incorrectly calculating altitude and speed.

synopsis: On approach in a B737, ATC issued an improper vector which sent the flight crew through the localizer. While attempting to recapture the localizer and glideslope the flight crew began to fall behind the aircraft resulting in breaking out of the clouds to the right of the runway.
summary: A tired Pilot Monitoring and a senior Captain flew an IFR ILS approach in IFR conditions where the Captain chased the glideslope and deviated from the localizer after a bad vector. The crew landed safely without incident, though the PM regretted not calling a go-around despite aural warnings and being low and off-course.

synopsis: B767 flight crew experienced an unusual vibration and excessive noise coming from the nosewheel area after gear retraction. They returned to departure airport where Maintenance determined that the connecting rod from nose landing gear to the nose gear door was disconnected.
summary: The crew experienced vibration and noise from a failed nose gear door rod during climb out from ZZZZ. They returned for an overweight landing after confirming no damage, with maintenance identifying the broken rod as the cause.

synopsis: Baggage handler reports nearly being injured when a bag strap gets caught in the drive wheels of a belt loader and the laser beam that is commonly used to stop the belt loader is not installed on this fixed rail loader.
summary: A ramp agent loading the rear pit of a flight suffered a near-miss when a bag snagged in a fixed-rail belt loader, pulling their hand toward the wheels. The agent discovered the loader lacked a laser safety sensor due to removed bumpers, but the bag broke free before injury occurred.

synopsis: An A320 pilot reported that when the destination airport ILS was selected, the frequency defaulted to a previously 'Hard' tuned frequency. Once the Flight Crew cleared the 'Hard' frequency they got the proper signal for the ILS. Later it was uncovered that Maintenance had manually entered a unused frequency in the ILS for an Autoland test and had not cleared it. This frequency turned out to be the ILS for an airport nearby the destination airport.
summary: Line maintenance hard-tuned an unused ILS frequency during an A320 autoland check, causing a 'RW LS MISMATCH' and erroneous left turn during the approach. The crew identified the error, cleared the hard tune, and completed a visual landing in VFR conditions after descending below the glide slope.

synopsis: Shut down #1 engine due to loss of oil pressure.
summary: The crew shut down Engine #1 due to rapidly decreasing oil pressure. The loss of oil pressure directly caused the engine shutdown.

synopsis: Flight crew lost control of the aircraft when they encountered black ice on the taxiway. They regained control and continued with extreme caution.
summary: The pilot reported that while taxiing at RNO, the aircraft hit black ice at the B and A taxiway junction, causing an involuntary 360-degree spin. Ground control dispatched a sand truck, but the crew proceeded to the runway with good braking action and departed without delay.

synopsis: B737-900 Captain reported encountering wake turbulence departing JFK in trail of a B757.
summary: A B737 pilot encountered wake turbulence shortly after takeoff behind a departing B757, causing a 15-degree left roll that required aileron input to correct. The pilot attributes the event to reduced separation standards for B737s following B757s and plans to request a two-minute delay in the future.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Flight crew neglected to connect the generators due to not completing the checklist properly. Transitioning from old procedures to new procedures caused the flight crew to get out of sequence while accomplishing the checklist.
summary: The First Officer and Captain missed the after-start checklist during climbout due to fatigue and distraction from new procedures, leaving generators disconnected until 14,000 feet. The Captain restored electrical power, and the flight continued to a safe landing without further incident.

aircraft: Medium Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported the iPad's navigational software did an update automatically causing it to go to a black screen then to the home screen. This causes the iPad as a navigation aid to be undependable.
summary: Pilots reported that the X app on company iPads initiated an unstoppable automatic map update while parked at the gate prior to pushback, rendering the devices unusable for 10–15 minutes. The reporter noted the app also displayed outdated Class B airspace charts and warned that such interruptions during critical flight phases could compromise safety.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported being cleared for a visual approach to Runway 4 at ELP and commencing descent only to discover that terrain was between the aircraft and the runway. The terrain was cleared and the approach was continued.
summary: The pilot initiated a visual descent for Runway 4 but encountered terrain between the aircraft and the runway. The crew climbed to a safe altitude, cleared the obstacle, and landed safely, attributing the incident to failing to follow instrument procedures despite visual conditions.

synopsis: The Captain thought that the weather was improving and that it would be at or above minimums at the ETA and therefore it was legal to depart, while the Dispatcher did not. The Dispatcher held the flight until the weather improved to minimums.
summary: A dispatcher and captain debated departing for KRNO during freezing fog with visibility below minimums. The dispatcher initially refused authorization until a positive weather trend was confirmed, after which the flight departed and landed safely.

synopsis: After troubleshooting and replacing the #1 Stabilizer Control Unit on a CRJ-701 Maintenance was told to replace the Linear Actuator for the Pitch/Trim system. Before installing the replacement actuator it had to be sequenced and rigged using a variable power supply. Since they didn't have one available, Maintenance Control told the maintenance crew to use the battery on the aircraft as a power supply. Maintenance refused until the proper power supply was available.
summary: Two avionics technicians replaced a Stabilizer Control Unit to resolve pitch/feel faults, but Maintenance Control later ordered an unnecessary linear actuator replacement. When technicians refused unsafe power supply instructions, a charter flight delivered the required equipment, highlighting risks from poor judgment and unnecessary maintenance.

synopsis: On a field trip to investigate a 'Flap Half Speed Message' on a CRJ-700, aircraft maintenance technicians found broken wires and poorly soldered connections in the Brake Position Sensing Unit (BPSU). Unable to repair the component due to the wrong parts being sent, the aircraft was ferried to the company maintenance center for repairs.
summary: Two mechanics at an outstation attempted to repair a CRJ-700 flap harness after discovering broken wires and a poor splice. The event was caused by Maintenance Control's lack of planning, failure to obtain a ferry permit, and poor communication, which forced inexperienced staff to perform complex avionics work in freezing conditions without proper parts or support.

synopsis: During a postflight walkaround, Aircraft Maintenance Technician discovered the #1 engine pylon access panel was missing.
summary: During a postflight walkaround, the crew discovered that the number one engine pylon access panel had departed the aircraft. The narrative does not specify the cause or the phase of flight during which the panel detached.

synopsis: A320 First Officer reports discovering Enroute that NRS waypoint KD45U has been inadvertently entered into the FMC as KD54U. This is detected and corrected before a significant deviation results.
summary: Both pilots entered KD54U instead of the cleared KD45U waypoint in the FMS despite a pre-departure review and readback. The error was discovered enroute during vectors, corrected after a thorough flight plan review, and the flight continued uneventfully.

synopsis: Cruising in a PA28-235 at 9,000 feet the ATC instruction was to climb to 11,000 feet where the aircraft began to accumulate ice. Requested a lower altitude but ATC denied the request due to altitude restrictions in that area. Temporarily lost communication with ATC and landed at the nearest airport. After landing, the leading edges of the wings and stabilator were still significantly iced over.
summary: Pilots encountered severe icing while climbing to 11,000 feet, causing the aircraft to lose altitude despite full power. After the controller briefly left the frequency, the crew descended to 7,000 feet, broke out of clouds, and landed visually with significant ice accumulation on the wings and stabilator.

aircraft: Piper Single Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: During takeoff in a Piper PA-12 the engine failed and the pilot notified the tower, returned, and landed without incident.
summary: The pilot experienced an engine power failure on takeoff, notified the tower, and returned to land safely on runway 4. The aircraft subsequently taxied to the hangar without incident.

synopsis: After a quick decent from 11,500 ft. in a Navion Rangemaster, the engine failed to power up. The engine restarted successfully after performing a Fuel, Mixture, Switches check.
summary: During a VFR arrival descent from 11,500 feet, the pilot experienced an engine power failure, likely due to a 2–3 second delay in throttle recognition. The engine was successfully restarted after an F-M-S check, allowing for an uneventful landing and subsequent mechanical adjustment of idle RPM.

synopsis: A PA-28 pilot reported encountering ice during an IFR flight cannot avoid icing at 3,600 feet required by ATC. He is prompted to declare an emergency or cancel IFR and chooses the later. The approach was successful.
summary: The pilot encountered icing at 3,600 feet during an IFR approach to ZZZ and requested a descent to 3,000 feet. After communication difficulties and a brief diversion consideration, the pilot elected to continue the approach on their own and subsequently canceled the IFR flight plan.

synopsis: PA28 pilot on short final to Runway 30 at WHP experienced a NMAC with a drone flying in the opposite direction.
summary: A pilot on short final for Runway 30 encountered a black drone flying a reciprocal track just below and to the left. The near-miss was avoided because the aircraft was slightly high and right of the glide path, though the pilot noted no evasive action was possible due to the drone's low visibility and high closing speed.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turboprop Eng
synopsis: Twin engine aircraft with an engine out emergency attempted to land conducting an ILS approach. The aircraft was unable to intercept the localizer twice. ATC vectored the aircraft on to an ASR approach and the aircraft landed.
summary: A pilot experiencing an engine failure and suspected autopilot issues struggled to join the ILS localizer while icing was reported. Air Traffic Control vectored the aircraft for a non-flight-checked ASR approach, allowing a safe landing on one engine despite the lapse in ASR certification and controller proficiency.

aircraft: Light Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A90 TRACON Controller had difficulty coordinating a point out with a Tower. After approving the point out, the Tower departed an aircraft into a confliction with the pointed out aircraft.
summary: An air traffic controller reported difficulties coordinating a pointout for Aircraft X during IFR vectoring for an ILS approach due to poor communication with Tower. Tower subsequently launched Aircraft Y on a conflicting heading, which the controller attributed to a lack of accountability and inadequate airspace monitoring.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A flight plan for an active enroute flight was removed from the ATC system. The aircraft's 'full' data block dropped off the Controller's scope and only a partial data block remained on the radar display. The controllers did not notice for approximately 50 miles and did not realize an aircraft was flying through their airspace.
summary: Flight Data staff inadvertently removed strips and flight plans for Aircraft X while deleting a duplicate general aviation plan, causing the aircraft to fly 50 miles without radar services. This error occurred during parallel arrivals, leaving controllers unaware of the aircraft's presence until the pilot contacted them while already in the next sector.

synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported encountering an over stressed Ground Controller during an attempted push back during a very busy time of the night. The flight crew had to ask for clarification on the taxi instructions which seemed to infuriate the Controller.
summary: Pilots reported an unprofessional Ground Controller who became abusive and refused to provide operating initials during a busy taxi phase complicated by construction and poor signage. The crew stopped to verify their position when instructions conflicted with charts, leading to the controller's frustration before they eventually departed safely.

synopsis: Aircraft had a ground near miss with another aircraft while taking the runway for departure.
summary: The pilot reported a near-miss during a non-standard taxi turn onto E8 while lining up for runway 24L. Another aircraft following closely obstructed the Captain's view, resulting in an 18-inch separation as the pilot initiated an emergency stop.

synopsis: Aircraft on a non-precision approach executed a go around due to heavy rain at the missed approach point. The flight crew then decided to divert to a more suitable airport.
summary: The crew of a straight-wing aircraft with an MEL'd fuel gauge and no intercom executed a missed approach at SAN due to heavy precipitation and poor visibility. Extreme cockpit noise from rain and wipers caused critical pilot-to-pilot miscommunications, resulting in a flap overspeed, FMC lock, and diversion.

synopsis: B737-700 flight crew configured flaps to briefed position late in the approach just before touchdown.
summary: The Pilot Flying called for flaps 30 instead of the briefed flaps 40 during a CAT II approach in low visibility. Recognizing the error at 400 feet AGL, the crew extended flaps to 40 and landed safely, with the Pilot Flying determining this was the safest option despite violating stabilized approach criteria.

synopsis: First Officer comments that on his new fleet all Captains use the overhead speaker for all ATC communications.
summary: A newly trained pilot reported that captains on this aircraft type consistently use the cockpit speaker during all phases, including ground operations. The pilot stated this practice violates the company operations manual and creates an unsafe, distracting environment.

synopsis: During test flight left engine EICAS indicated overheats. Engine secured and flight landed single engine.
summary: Following engine removal and re-installation, the crew received left engine overheat and strut overheat messages at FL300 during a test flight. They secured the engine, declared an emergency, and performed a single-engine landing with no external damage found post-flight.

aircraft: Medium Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A flight crew reported encountering windshear conditions on final approach and performed a go-around. The missed approach maneuver was successfully accomplished, however dynamic flight conditions resulted in a deviation from their assigned altitude.
summary: The pilot flying and copilot encountered windshear on final approach to IAH Runway 8R, triggering a go-around at 1,400 feet AGL. The crew managed the event despite ATC initially assigning a 2,000-foot level-off altitude while windshear warnings persisted, ultimately stabilizing at 3,000 feet.

synopsis: A ramp agent's hand was caught beneath a belt loader's moving belt which nearly pulled him out of a B757's rear cargo. Both belt emergency stop activation buttons had been removed.
summary: A ramp agent loading the rear cargo bin had their hand caught in a moving belt after safety sensors and the Emergency Stop button were removed. The agent narrowly avoided being pulled from the aircraft, dislodged their hand, and reported the incident to a supervisor.

synopsis: A321 flight crew reported observing a #2 engine N1 overspeed warning during the takeoff roll. The Captain aborted the takeoff and returned to the gate for maintenance. This event was originally thought to be a low speed abort, however the takeoff was actually rejected at 90 knots.
summary: The flight crew rejected takeoff shortly after applying TOGA thrust due to an Engine 2 N1 overspeed ECAM warning. Although the crew believed they were below 80 knots, FOQA data later confirmed the aircraft reached 90 knots before the Captain reduced power and exited the runway safely.

synopsis: DHC-8-200 Captain reported returning to the departure airport after shutting down a malfunctioning engine.
summary: The pilot flying reported a lagging and unresponsive #2 engine torque during climb after departure in freezing rain, causing a return to the field. The crew successfully shut down the engine, managed a rhythmic pulsing during feathering, and completed a safe landing with emergency services standing by.

synopsis: A C208 pilot described his physiological 'buzzed' feeling after exposure to TKS anti-ice fluid in flight during freezing IMC conditions.
summary: The pilot flew a Caravan IFR in IMC with TKS icing protection, experiencing symptoms like a "buzzed" feeling, coughing, and difficulty concentrating. The reporter attributes these effects to TKS fluid exposure, noting the system had 19 minutes of range remaining upon landing.

synopsis: While enroute, a CRJ-900 crew thought fuel was decreasing more rapidly than expected and assumed a fuel leak. After landing a fuel odor was detected, but no leak discovered so the aircraft was ferried to a maintenance station.
summary: The crew experienced rapid fuel loss and cabin fumes enroute, suspecting a leak despite normal fuel flow. They diverted to a direct route to preserve reserves, landed safely with trucks standing by, and ferried the aircraft to maintenance after ground checks failed to duplicate the leak.

aircraft: Airbus Industrie Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: Airbus Captain experienced a loss of V speeds during the takeoff roll resulting in the First Officer calling V1 well before the actual V1 and the Captain initiating rotation. The Captain notes the sluggish rotation and the aircraft is allowed to fly off the runway.
summary: The Captain and First Officer experienced a sluggish rotation during a snowy takeoff due to a FMS error displaying a default 100 KTS blue line instead of V2. The incident resulted from misinterpreting this erroneous speed reference and a non-standard "V1" call, leading to an early rotation.

synopsis: A320 flight crew reported encountering a bird strike at high speed during the takeoff roll. The takeoff was continued, however a significant vibration in one engine was noted. They reduced power on the affected engine and safely returned to the departure airport, where major damage to the engine was discovered.
summary: The crew encountered a seagull strike on the left engine during takeoff from ZZZZ, causing high vibration and noise above 120 kts. They continued the flight, returned to ZZZZ, and landed safely; maintenance later found major fan blade damage with no core damage.

synopsis: CRJ-900 flight crew reported a heading deviation occurred when the pilot not flying misunderstood the pilot flying's request.
summary: The pilot monitoring misinterpreted the pilot flying's speed call of 250 knots as a heading instruction during the departure phase. This confusion caused the aircraft to turn to 250 degrees instead of the assigned 330, requiring ATC to issue a corrective heading of 270.

synopsis: EMB170 First Officer reported being level at 17,000 feet then assigned FL180 by ATC. The altimeter is not reset to 29.92 until reaching 18000 feet resulting is a 200 foot overshoot.
summary: The flight crew climbing to FL180 experienced an altitude deviation to 18,200 feet after switching to standard pressure at the transition altitude due to a significant pressure difference. The crew corrected the deviation immediately and noted that switching to standard earlier might prevent such excursions.

synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew reported overshooting a crossing altitude when a late runway change caused confusion and distraction.
summary: During the ZEEKK arrival into IAH, the crew failed to update the FMS after ATC switched the runway from 26R to 26L, resulting in a 2,000-foot altitude deviation. The pilot attributed the error to rushing the runway change without a proper cross-check, though ATC issued the approach clearance based on the reported 6,000 feet.

synopsis: CRJ-200 flight crew reported they began takeoff roll with flaps incorrectly set, but caught it early in the roll and rejected the takeoff.
summary: A Boeing crew at PHL aborted a takeoff on runway 8 after the First Officer selected flaps 8 instead of the planned 20 degrees. The error was attributed to cross-chatter regarding runway 8 and perceived ATC pressure, resulting in a flight cancellation.

synopsis: A321 Captain reported his takeoff clearance was cancelled by ATC because of conflicting traffic.
summary: The crew expedited taxi to meet a flow time and received immediate takeoff clearance for Runway 1R, but Tower ordered a go-around when an MD-80 was seen aligned for the same runway. The reporter attributed the incident to pressure to meet flow times compressing safety margins, though the controller's timely intervention prevented a collision.

synopsis: A319 First Officer reported a flap overspeed on arrival, citing overreliance on automation as a contributing factor.
summary: During descent, the crew executed a 360 turn to lose altitude, triggering a speed warning bell when indicated speed increased. The Pilot Flying manually raised the nose to restore normal speed, and maintenance cleared the aircraft for the next leg after a post-landing check.

synopsis: B737 flight crew reported executing an autoland even though the Captain's Master light was not illuminated as required.
summary: The Captain and First Officer conducted an Autoland approach into ORD where the Captain's Flight Director Master light failed to illuminate despite both Autopilots engaging. Although the system passed self-tests and the aircraft landed smoothly, the crew logged a maintenance item and filed a report, attributing the decision to continue to fatigue and insufficient systems training.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported that new First Officers the he flies with are under the mistaken impression that they must brief the engine inoperative go-around procedure for every approach to an airport with a special engine out missed approach procedure.
summary: A captain reported that new first officers on Boeing 737s incorrectly brief engine-inoperative go-around procedures for normal approaches due to outdated training. The captain stated this violates Flight Operations Manual rules requiring only one approach and one go-around to be briefed, potentially compromising safety.

synopsis: CRJ-900 flight crew reported taking off with flaps set to 8 when they should have been set to 20, after several runway changes by ATC during taxi out. The Captain described the First Officer as being well behind the aircraft.
summary: The Captain and First Officer took off from Runway XYC with flaps set to 8 instead of the required 20 for an intersection departure. The error occurred after multiple runway changes and a hold for a MedEvac aircraft, causing the crew to skip a full checklist review, though the flight continued safely to the destination.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported being cleared for takeoff behind a B757 without wake turbulence separation. The Tower is queried and states that the separation standards have been changed. The Flight Manual for the company involved does not reflect those changes.
summary: Pilots departing LAS behind a B757 requested wake turbulence separation per their Flight Manual, but controllers denied it, citing revised visual separation rules or divergent paths. The crew self-imposed separation or exited the runway to comply with their safety standards, highlighting a conflict between FAA ATC procedures and company requirements.

synopsis: A PA31 flight crew reported a loss of control during landing with the First Officer flying. The landing had been normal up until the brakes were applied, then the aircraft began a slow turn to the left rapidly increasing to a full skidding rotation to the left with a runway excursion.
summary: The pilot flying landed a Chieftain on runway 03 in gusty winds but lost directional control during rollout, causing the aircraft to skid sideways off the left runway shoulder. No injuries or damage occurred, and the cause of the sudden left turn remains undetermined.

synopsis: Flight Attendant reported sitting between flights in an inhospitable company conference room in the middle of the night as part of a regular, fatiguing crew sequence with inadequate rest accommodations.
summary: Flight Attendants experienced a four-hour sit time between flights with no designated rest area, forcing them to use a conference room with hard chairs. The reporter states this lack of rest facilities increased fatigue and created an unsafe situation due to poor scheduling planning.

synopsis: CRJ-200 Flight Attendant reported that the seat backs in rows 12 and 13 were not secured in the upright position. There are no procedures, information, or education regarding these seat backs and how they are supposedly meant to allow access to emergency equipment.
summary: A flight attendant reported that CRJ200 seat backs in rows 12 and 13 were unsecured and folded forward during preflight, which Maintenance claimed was normal for emergency equipment access. The attendant found no manual support for this practice and raised concerns regarding passenger egress and regulatory compliance.

synopsis: A B737 Flight Attendant described a continuous duty over night during which only one hour of actual sleep is obtained.
summary: The flight crew experienced severe fatigue after a long sit with delayed hotel transport and only one hour of sleep. The pilot reported that the crew was not fully alert for the next flight due to inadequate rest and recommended pre-arranged logistics and longer layovers.

aircraft: Small Aircraft; High Wing; 1 Eng; Fixed Gear
synopsis: A pilot was cleared to cross the runway and hesitantly began crossing but detected an approaching aircraft and stopped just over the hold short line. The approaching aircraft executed a go-around.
summary: The pilot, while taxiing to active runways 15 and 19, crossed the hold short line for runway 19 after ground control instruction, despite seeing a Cessna on final. The Cessna executed a go-around, and the pilot stopped before entering the runway, later resolving to decline crossing instructions when traffic is visible.

synopsis: A student pilot reported making multiple left hand closed pattern approaches but was then told to make right traffic. After he failed to turn right downwind ATC notified the Pilot of a near miss.
summary: A student pilot conducting solo stop-and-go practice in the traffic pattern inadvertently flew left-hand traffic instead of the cleared right-hand traffic on the sixth pattern. This deviation, attributed to distraction and routine, resulted in a near miss that was discovered by ATC after the flight.

synopsis: A PA23 pilot receiving instruction reported a right gear collapse after a firm landing with a slight bounce. The aircraft became uncontrollable and went off the right side of the runway.
summary: A pilot conducting a short-field landing in VMC at dusk experienced a hard landing and bounce, causing the aircraft to veer off the runway into soft grass. The right main gear collapsed, likely due to the gear getting caught in the grass, resulting in a propeller strike on the right engine.

synopsis: A sight seeing Helicopter Pilot reported a near miss with another touring helicopter after converging over Black Point near Hoover Dam. One helicopter pilot was in the right seat while the other pilot flew left seat and neither pilot saw the other.
summary: Two helicopter pilots experienced a near-midair collision while converging at Black Point at approximately 4,500 feet. The incident occurred because opposing seat positions and convergence angles prevented visual detection, resulting in less than 100 feet of vertical separation.

synopsis: An ACA Scout pilot reported a runway excursion after landing due to a gust of wind. Power is applied and the aircraft is flown back to base. Post flight revealed damage to the right wingtip and the aircraft is subsequently flown to another airport for repairs.
summary: The pilot relocated an ACA Scout for maintenance after a wind gust blew it into grass, causing right wingtip damage from a taxiway sign impact during the subsequent takeoff. A bore scope inspection deemed the aircraft airworthy for relocation, and the factory will remove the wing for repairs.

synopsis: A PA-31T corporate pilot reported his aircraft made a 180 degree turn while IMC after a faulty alternator output affected the Captain's HSI, Flight Director and autopilot. GPS heading was flown to the VMC alternate airport.
summary: The pilot reported that during an IFR flight, electronic failures caused the HSI, flight director, and autopilot to fail while the copilot's heading indicator precessed. This led to an unnoticed 180-degree turn, forcing the crew to divert to an alternate airport using GPS and land in visual conditions.

aircraft: Cessna Single Piston Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: A Cessna pilot reported an apparent loss of engine power while climbing out of the traffic pattern. After advising ATC and performing a successful return to the field, the pilot discovered that the fuel shutoff valve had been closed rather than the cabin heat valve opened as intended.
summary: The pilot experienced a total engine failure during climb out from Runway XXR after accidentally pulling the fuel shutoff knob while adjusting the nearby cabin heat control. The aircraft landed safely with no damage, attributed to the pilot's low experience and the proximity of the two controls.

synopsis: ZSE Controller issued an IFR clearance altitude below the Minimum Enroute Altitude for the airway.
summary: An air traffic controller issued an IFR descent clearance below the Minimum Enroute Altitude to a pilot transitioning from VFR to IFR flight. The error was identified by the receiving TRACON during handoff, prompting a supervisor notification and a reminder to verify MEA data.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: HCF Controller reported of saving an operational error due to correcting the aircraft altitude. Controller released aircraft off on a 320 heading. Aircraft came off on a 020 heading and was a conflict for an arrival. Controller stopped the departing aircraft altitude and then corrected the heading.
summary: An air traffic controller resolved a near mid-air collision between departing Aircraft X and inbound Aircraft Y after X departed on a 020 heading instead of the assigned 320. The controller attributed the conflict to a possible pilot deviation or controller error, noting the situation was a close call that required immediate altitude and heading corrections.

synopsis: B737 Captain described over speeds during VNAV arrivals and departures caused by FMC software and believes that updating the software would be less expensive than over speed inspections and smoother for the passengers.
summary: A B-737 pilot reported that poor LNAV/VNAV and autothrottle software caused rough climbs, aggressive pitch changes, and Mach overspeeds at 39,000 feet. The pilot attributed these issues to inadequate automation, which risks costly flap inspections and suggests upgrading the software to prevent future overspeeds.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew experienced aircraft damage during gate arrival when the left scimitar winglet contacted a catering truck. The truck was parked outside the safety zone but very close to it and the aircraft, under a Marshalls direction, was on the lead in line.
summary: The Captain of an -800 series aircraft reported that the left lower scimitar winglet contacted a catering truck parked just outside the safety zone while taxiing to a gate in BOS. The pilot attributed the minor winglet damage and truck scrape to the truck's proximity to the safety zone, a slight tail drift, and the marshaller's guidance.

synopsis: At about 1,000 feet after departure, a B737-700 encountered a bird flock which caused left engine surging. The aircraft returned to the departure airport where severe left engine damage was discovered as well as bird remains in the functioning right engine.
summary: The First Officer flew a takeoff in dark VFR conditions when the aircraft struck a bird flock at 1,000–1,100 feet AGL, causing left engine surge and fan blade damage. The crew returned for a safe landing with reduced thrust, finding bird remains on both engines.

synopsis: B737 flight crew experienced a GPWS terrain warning during a night visual approach to Runway 33 at BUR and went around. The second visual approach was successful.
summary: The crew executed a go-around during a visual approach to Runway 33 at BUR after a GPWS terrain alert occurred due to a delayed turn and task saturation. The pilot attributed the incident to insufficient assertiveness in correcting the flight path and noted slow tower response during the go-around.

aircraft: Large Transport; Low Wing; 2 Turbojet Eng
synopsis: A Captain taxiing at night to LAX Runway 24L via Taxiway D-8, E-8 became confused because the signage and lighting were reportedly not clear.
summary: The pilot reported difficulty taxiing at night from D-8 to Runway 24L at E-8 due to poor line markings and confusing lights. The crew identified this as a serious hazard risking runway incursions and requested an enlarged Jepps diagram for the area.

synopsis: When the B737-800 engine and APU bleeds were opened after de-icing, the cockpit filled with a thick white mist so the aircraft was towed back to the gate and deplaned. The pilots became ill and were treated according to the MSDS guidelines then departed after recovering from de-ice fluid ingestion.
summary: During pushback, deicing fluid mist entered the cockpit via bleed air, causing respiratory symptoms for the flight crew. The aircraft was towed back, passengers deplaned, and after medical clearance and maintenance checks, the crew completed the flight, attributing the incident to potential deicer inexperience.

synopsis: B737 Captain was informed arriving LAS that ground power was available and leave the APU off. Ground power at LAS is not available until the jetway is mated with the aircraft, so the left engine is kept running. During this time the left wing walker grabs the chocks and walks directly in front of the running engine.
summary: During a no-APU taxi-in at LAS, the crew kept Engine 1 running because the ground power cord was not pre-positioned. A marshaller then walked in front of the running engine, creating a serious injury risk and revealing that safe no-APU taxi-ins are not possible at this airport.

synopsis: Brake system fault light illuminated at initial take-off roll. Aircrew rejected the take-off at low speed.
summary: The First Officer detected a Brake System Fault 1 ECAM during the initial takeoff roll, prompting a low-speed rejected takeoff. After maintenance restored normal operation and issued a new release, the crew completed checklists and resumed the flight.

synopsis: DHC 8-100 flight crew reported being cleared for takeoff right after a windshear event on the runway they are using. The executive jet elects to go around as the DHC 8 rotates causing a conflict which ATC must unravel. The crew becomes distracted during this time and the landing gear is forgotten until it is time to extend on approach.
summary: Pilots reported that multiple ATC heading changes and a go-around by an executive jet caused task saturation, leading them to forget retracting the landing gear after takeoff. The crew discovered the gear remained down during the approach callout, evaluated the situation, and executed a safe landing.

synopsis: EMB-170 Captain discovered after arrival that six boxes had been transported, five of which contained dry ice, without being included on the cargo manifest.
summary: The First Officer discovered six unmanifested boxes, five containing dry ice, being off-loaded after arrival from CLE. The reporter attributed the error to CLE ground operations failing to document the hazardous materials on the cargo manifest and bag sheet.

synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reports being dispatched with a L BLEED inop MEL and discovers during climb that cabin pressure cannot be maintained with wing and engine anti ice on. The Captain elects to divert to the nearest suitable airport.
summary: The crew experienced a cabin pressure loss and right bleed warnings while climbing through 26,000 feet after using anti-ice. They diverted and landed safely after deciding to avoid further risk due to the crew's inexperience and lack of dispatch support.

synopsis: A pilot reported that while taxiing to the gate he was notified by a Flight Attendant of a fire in the cabin. The aircraft was stopped on the taxiway and the source of the fire was identified as an E-cigarette device. The fire was quickly extinguished and the aircraft proceeded to the gate where the passengers disembarked in an orderly manner.
summary: During taxi to the gate, an E-cigarette battery in a passenger's carry-on bag overheated and ignited, causing a fire in the cabin. A Flight Attendant extinguished the flames with an onboard fire extinguisher, resulting in no injuries or schedule disruptions, though the cause of the battery failure remains unknown.

synopsis: An air carrier flight crew was advised by a Flight Attendant of smoke in the cabin associated with a passenger's personal computer. The computer was removed to a safe area and an uneventful landing was accomplished at the destination airport.
summary: The captain reported a passenger's computer smoking twice during cruise and approach, prompting a high-energy battery checklist and priority landing. Although crash fire rescue was requested, no personnel arrived, so the crew moved the device off the aircraft before deplaning passengers.

synopsis: A Dispatcher reported his Load Planner allowed an aircraft on an oceanic flight to leave the gate over gross even after discussions about removing payload because the Captain requested additional fuel because of winds.
summary: A dispatcher and load planner managed a weight-restricted flight to Hawaii where the load planner ignored dispatch warnings and loaded unauthorized payload, causing an inadequate fuel situation. The aircraft was stopped on the taxiway, returned to the gate to remove cargo and refuel, and subsequently departed safely after the load planner corrected the weight.

aircraft: Airbus Industrie Undifferentiated or Other Model
synopsis: An air freight carrier Dispatcher reported about exceeding structural limits when over fuelling an Airbus aircraft, some dispatchers continue the unsafe tankering practice.
summary: The reporter identified repeated overtankering violations on Airbus aircraft exceeding the 36,000 lbs max Fuel on Departure limit. These policy breaches occurred on the same flight route and involved the same personnel as a previous report.

synopsis: CRJ-200 First Officer reported the APU had an uncommanded shutdown and he didn't know whether he was required to write it up or have Maintenance make the write-up.
summary: The pilot reported an APU failure and fire during pre-flight deicing, resulting in fan blade fragments on the ramp and a cancelled flight. The incident highlighted a lack of clear guidance on whether the pilot or nearby mechanics should complete the Aircraft Maintenance Log discrepancy write-up.

synopsis: Flight attendants are now required by the Company to carry iPads to perform preflight and safety duties. The Flight Attendant reported that there is no place to store them near the jump seats or on their person.
summary: Cabin crew reported that the company's requirement to carry new iPads for safety duties is unrealistic due to a lack of storage space near jump seats and insufficient uniform pockets. The crew noted that while the technology is a positive step, current equipment and uniform designs do not support the mandated carriage during flight.

synopsis: B737 Flight Attendant reported being held up at security with two other Flight attendants, due to paper work which the company should have provided. While waiting for the reporter and the two others, the Captain elects to board the aircraft with one Flight Attendant. Upon arrival at the aircraft the reporter explained that the full crew is required for boarding and the aircraft needed to be deplaned and a security sweep accomplished. The Captain refuses to do so.
summary: Flight Attendants 1, 2, and 4 were stranded at security while the Captain boarded the aircraft with insufficient crew, ignoring their objections regarding FAR violations. The Captain overruled the crew's refusal to board without a full complement, resulting in a security and regulatory violation despite repeated warnings.

synopsis: While performing a retest, mechanics pulled three different circuit breakers which affected the nose wheel steering and the brakes which caused the loss of control and caused the aircraft to run off the taxiway into the mud.
summary: During CRJ200 thrust reverser testing on the run-up area, mechanics pulled circuit breakers while taxiing, causing loss of steering and brakes. The aircraft veered off the taxiway into a ditch, sinking the left main gear in mud, due to an ambiguous procedure allowing actual wheel speed simulation.

synopsis: B757 Captain reported experiencing an uncommanded 45 degree bank angle at FL370 that the reporter felt was related to jet stream activity.
summary: The crew encountered severe turbulence at FL370 east of DUSAC, causing a 45-degree bank that disengaged the autopilot. The pilot manually recovered the aircraft with no injuries or damage, attributing the event to a jet stream crossing rather than wake turbulence.

synopsis: An aircrew experienced a CSD (Constant Speed Drive) failure and mistakenly used the wrong checklist to remedy the situation.
summary: During cruise at FL240, the First Officer mistakenly selected the engine low oil pressure checklist instead of the CSD checklist, causing an unnecessary left engine shutdown. The crew identified the error, performed the correct CSD checklist, restarted the engine, and landed safely, attributing the incident to rushing and poor communication.

synopsis: LR45 Captain experienced a failure of the landing gear to retract after takeoff along with a nose wheel steering fail message and elects to divert to a more suitable airport. After landing it is discovered that the nose gear strut has collapsed.
summary: The flight crew encountered a nose gear retraction failure and NWS FAIL warning during departure, causing a diversion. Post-landing inspection revealed a collapsed nose gear strut likely due to a nitrogen leak, which prevented proper centering and retraction.

synopsis: A flight instructor reported that he became distracted by his student's question during taxi and crossed onto an active runway as an air carrier began a takeoff roll.
summary: During landing rollout, a flight instructor taxied across a parallel runway instead of holding short due to mishearing ATC clearance while distracted by a student's question. This caused a runway incursion with a commercial airliner beginning its takeoff roll, though the instructor crossed before the aircraft reached that position.

synopsis: A general aviation pilot reported a near-mid-air-collision with an aircraft at a non-towered airport that was not using a radio and was flying a non-standard pattern.
summary: The pilot conducting touch-and-go circuits at KGIF encountered an uncommunicating aircraft flying a non-standard right-hand pattern. This intruder appeared directly ahead and above during takeoff and later crossed below on base, forcing the pilot to execute a go-around to avoid conflict.

synopsis: SCT Controller reported that there was confusion whether an aircraft that went on a missed approach was on an IFR code. Controller did not know if the crew were IFR or VFR and asked. Pilot stated VFR on the missed. More confusion ensued when the pilot then said they wanted to cancel IFR and go VFR to another airport.
summary: An air traffic controller reported that Aircraft X went missed on a TACAN approach at SLI and requested to cancel IFR for VFR flight to NFG. The controller cited a lack of direct communication with SLI and inconsistent pilot reporting of missed approach status as the cause of potential conflicts with protected airspace.

synopsis: Flight crew delayed climb to higher altitude due to traffic.
summary: During climb out, the Captain refused an ATC climb clearance to 15,000 feet due to TCAS traffic at 1,000 feet above and five miles ahead. The Captain maintained 5,000 feet and turned heading 060 to avoid a potential TCAS Resolution Advisory, resulting in a conflict with the controller who questioned the safety decision.
